MEDINA

Pages 9-10

an eminent painter, was the son of Medina de l'Aiturias, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>; where the son was born, and instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by Du Chatel. He married young; and in 1686 came into England, where he drew portraits for several years. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Leven encouraged him to go to Scotland, and procured him a subscription of 500l. worth of business. He painted most of the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and at Wentworth-castle is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piece, containing the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle and his sons, the two late dukes John and Archibald, in Roman habits; the style Italian, and superior to most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> performers. The portraits of the professors in the Surgeons-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> were painted by him, and are commended; and in that hall are two small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-pieces by him. He was knighted by the duke of Queensberry, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>; and was the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> made in Scotland before the Union. He was not, however, rich; for he had 20 children. He died in Scotland; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>. yard of the Gray-friars at Edinburgh in 1711, aged 52. He was capable both of history and landscape. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> in the octavo edition of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were designed by him.

MEDIOLANUM

Pages 10-10

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Insubres, built by the Gauls on their settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. A municipium, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength. The seat of the liberal arts; whence it had the name of Novae Athenae. Now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, capital of the Milanese, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Olona and Lombro, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 30'. N. Lat. 45° 25'. MEDIOLANUM Aulercorum (anc. geogr.), a town of Gallia Celtica, which afterwards took the name of the Eburovium Civitas (Antonine); corrupted to Civitas Eburocorum, and this last to Eburocæ; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> appellation <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, a city of Normandy. E. Long. 1° 12'. N. Lat. 49° 21'. MEDIOLANUM Gaggernum (anc. geogr.), a town of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, now the village Meyland, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>. MEDIOLANUM Ordocicum (anc. geogr.), a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, now Llan Vethlin, a market-town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. MEDIOLANUM Santonum (anc. geogr.), which afterwards taking the name of the people, was called Santonica Urbs; also Santones and Santoni. A town of Aquitain. Now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAINTES">Saintes</a>, capital of Saintonge in Guienne, on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>. W. Long. 36° 0'. N. Lat. 45° 50'.

MEDITERRANEAN SEA

Pages 10-10

extends from the Straits of Gibraltar to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, being above 2000 miles in length, but of very unequal breadth; the west <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it separating <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> east part of it, dividing <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> from Africa, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe, and Anatolia, or the Lesser Asia, bounding it on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, Algiers, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARCA">Barca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, bounding it on the south. The Strait of Gibraltar being about 15 or 16 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, a strong current sets through it out of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a> into the Mediterranean constantly, which requires a good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to stem it.

MEDITULLIUM

Pages 10-10

is used by anatomists for that spongy substance between the two plates of the cranium, and in the interstices of all laminated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See Diploe.

MEDIUM

Pages 10-10

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, that space <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> region through which a body in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> passes to any point; thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is supposed to be the medium through which the heavenly bodies move; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the medium wherein bodies move near our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the medium wherein fishes live and move; and glass is also a medium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as it affords it a free passage. That density or consistency in the parts of the medium, whereby the motion of bodies in it is retarded, is called the resistance of the medium; which, together with the force of gravity, is the cause of the cessation of the motion of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. Subtile or Ethereal Medium. See Ether, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, Fire, &c. Medium, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, any substance through which light is transmitted.

MEDUSA

Pages 10-10

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. The body is gelatinous, roundish, and depressed; and the mouth is in the centre of the under <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. There are twelve <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all natives of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The most remarkable is the simplex, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> armlets, with a plain circumference; four apertures beneath; no tentacles. These animals inhabit all our seas; are gregarious; often seen floating with the tide in vast numbers; feed on insects, small fish, &c. which they catch with their clasps or arms. Many species, on being handled, affect with a nettle-like <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, and excite a redness. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and some of the moderns, add that they have an aphrodisiac <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and in several languages they are called by an obscene name. They were known to the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the names of ἐλαττονες, and pulmo marinus, or sea-lungs. They attributed medicinal virtues to them. Dioscorides informs us, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> rubbed fresh on the diseased part, they cured the gout in the feet, and kibed heels. Elian says, that they were depilatory; and, if macerated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, would take away the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. Their phosphoric <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is well known; nor was it overlooked by the ancients. Pliny observes, that if rubbed with a stick it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear to burn, and the wood to shine all over. The same naturalist observes, that when they sink to the bottom of the sea, they portend a continuance of bad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>.

MEETING

Pages 123-123

the falling off <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> change of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, feathers, skin, horns, or other parts of animals, which happens in some annually, in others only at certain stages of their lives: but the generality of beasts mew in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. An old <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">hart</a> casts his horns sooner than a young one, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in the months of February and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, after which they begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> in March or April: and as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> grows strong, and the season of the year puts forth the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, so their heads grow, and are trimmed full by the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. It is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a hart be gelt before he has a head, he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> never have any; and if he be gelt after he has a head, he will never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his horns; again, if he be gelt when he has a velvet-head, it will always be so, without fraying, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>.

MEGALE POLIS

Pages 10-11

(anc. geogr.), dividedly (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Paulusias); <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> conjunctly Megalopolis, (Strabo): A town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, built under the auspices of Epaminondas, after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEUCTRA">Leuctra</a>; many inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> being joined together in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, MEI [4883] MEL Megameter the better to withstand the Spartans. It was the greatest city of Arcadia, according to Strabo. MEGAMETER. See Micrometer.

MEGARA

Pages 11-11

a noble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Megaris, which for many years carried on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Corinthians and Athenians. It had for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> a school of philosophers, called the Megarici, successors of Euclid the Socratic, a native of Megara. Their dialect was the Doric; changed from the Attic, which it formerly had been, because of Peloponnesian colonists who settled there. MEGARA (anc. geog.) formerly called Hybla, a town towards the east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; extinct in Strabo's time, though the name Hybla remained on account of the excellence of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It was a colony of Megareans from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Risus Megarius denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-laugh.

MEGARIS

Pages 11-11

a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, joined to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. Now called Castello dell' ovo.

MEGIDDO

Pages 11-11

(Judges v. 19.) A town of Galilee, recited (Joshua xvii. 11.) among the cities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, in the tribe of Issachar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Asher, on the west side of Jordan. Famous for the fate of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> and Joash, who perished there: near it was an open plain, fit for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>. It was situated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, contrary to its position in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> maps. The Canaanites being tributary to the Israelites, dwelt in it, Joshua xvii. It was rebuilt by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, 1 Kings ix.

MEIBOMIUS

Pages 11-11

the name of several learned Germans.—John Henry Meibomius was professor of physic at Helmstadt, where he was born, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>; he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Maccabaei, published at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1653, with several other learned works.—Henry, his son, was born at Lubeck in 1658; became professor of physic at Helmstadt; and, besides works in his own profession, published Scriptores rerum Germanicarum, 3 vol. folio, 1688; a very useful collection, first begun by his father.—Marcus Meibomius, of the same family, published a collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Greek authors who had written upon <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, with a Latin version by himself; dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who invited him to her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But the engaging him one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> to sing an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ancient music, while somebody was ordered to dance to it, the immoderate mirth which this occasioned in the spectators so disgusted him, that he immediately left the court of Sweden. His edition of the Greek mythologists, and notes upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius in Menage's edition, shows him to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of learning; but he suffered no little raillery for his attempt to correct the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, by a kind of metre he fancied he had found out in those ancient writings.

MEISSEN

Pages 11-11

a considerable town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in the margravate of Misnia, with a castle. It formerly belonged to the bishop, but is now secularized, and the inhabitants are Lutherans. In this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 13, 33, N. Lat. 51° 15'.

MELA

Pages 11-11

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writer, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Baetica in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and flourished in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. His three books of Cosmography, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> De situ orbis, are written in a concise, perspicuous, and elegant manner; and have been thought worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and labours of the ablest critics. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius gave an edition of them in 1658, 4to. with very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and copious notes. To this edition is added Julli Noriori oratoris excerpta ex cosmographia, first published from the manuscript, and Ethelici cosmographia. Gronovius afterwards published another edition with illustrations by medals. In his last edition are added five books De geographia, written by some later author, by Jornandes, as Fabricius conjectures. MELÆNA, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>, in medicine. See Medicine, n° 495.

MELAMPYRUM

Pages 11-11

cow-wheat; a genus of the angiospermae order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them natives of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and growing spontaneously among cornfields. They are excellent food for cattle; and Linnaeus tells us, that where they abound the yellowest and best <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> is made. Their seeds, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, give it a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and, according to some authors, produce a vertigo, and other disorders of the head; but this is denied by Mr Withering, though he allows that they give it a bitter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.

MELANCHOLY

Pages 11-11

a kind of delirium attended with gloomy thoughts, heaviness and sorrow. See Medicine, n° 185, 428, 429.

MELANCTHON

Pages 11-12

born at Bretten in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> in 1495, was one of the wisest and most able men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> among the Reformers, though of a mild temper, disposed to accommodate rather than inflame disputes. In his youth he made an admirable progress in learning, and was made Greek professor at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a> in 1509. Here his lectures upon <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, and the Greek text of St Paul's epistle to Titus, drew to him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of auditors, and entirely effaced the contempt to which his low stature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance had exposed him. Melanchthon reduced the sciences to systems; and acquired such reputation, that he had sometimes 2500 auditors. He soon entered into an intimate friendship with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, who taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the same university; and in 1519 they went together to Leipzig, to dispute with Erasmus. The following years he was continually engaged in various employments; he composed several books; he taught divinity; took several journeys, in order to found colleges and visit churches; and in 1530 drew up a confession of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, which goes by the name of the Confession of Augsburg, because it was presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> at the diet held in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. All <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> was convinced, that he was not, like Luther, backward to accommodate the differences between the various sects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. He hated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> disputes, and was drawn into them only through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> he was called to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the world; and therefore would have sacrificed many things, to have produced an union among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. For this reason, Francis I., the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, wrote... wrote to desire him to come and confer with the doctors of the Sorbonne, in order to agree with them about putting an end to all controversies; but though Luther endeavoured to persuade the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> to consent to that journey, and though Melanchthon himself desired it, that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, whether he distrusted Melanchthon's moderation, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> was afraid of quarrelling with the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. would never <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> his permission. The king of England also in vain desired to see him. Melanchthon, in 1529, affilied at the conferences of Spire. In 1541, he was at the famous conferences at Ratishon. In 1543, he went to meet the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> to assist him in introducing the reformation into his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; but that project came to nothing; and in 1548, he affilied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> conferences on the subject of the interim of Charles V. and wrote a censure on that interim, and all the writings presented at these conferences. He was extremely affected at the dissensions raised by Flaccus Illyricus. His last conference with those of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> was at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, in 1557. He died at Wittemburg in 1560, and was interred near Luther. Some days before he died, he wrote upon a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> the reasons which made him look upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them was, that it "delivered him from theological persecutions." <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> had given Melanchthon a peaceable temper, which was but ill suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was to live in. His moderation served only to be his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. He was like a lamb in the midst of wolves. Nobody liked his mildness; it looked as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he was lukewarm; and even Luther himself was sometimes angry at it. Melanchthon was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in whom many good as well as great qualities were wonderfully united. He had great parts, great learning, great sweetness of temper, moderation, contentedness, and the like, which would have made him very happy in any other times but those in which he lived. He never affected dignities, or honours, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, but was rather negligent of all these things; too much so in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, considering he had a family; and his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> Sabius, who was of a more ambitious make, was actually at variance with him upon this very article. Learning was infinitely obliged to him on many accounts; on none more than this, that, as already observed, he reduced almost all the sciences which had been taught before in a vague <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> manner, into systems. Considering the distractions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the infinity of disputes and tumults in which he was engaged, it is astonishing how he could find leisure to write so many books. Their number is prodigious, insomuch that it was thought necessary to publish a chronological catalogue of them in the year 1582. His works indeed are not correct, and he himself owned it; but as he found them useful, he chose rather to print a great number, than to finish only a few; "which however," as Bayle says, "was postponing his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to the advantage of others." His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was very weak, and required great tenderness and management; which made Luther, as hot and zealous as he was, blame him for labouring too earnestly in the vineyard.

MELANTERIA

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a very beautiful foil, of a dense, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and regular texture, and of an extremely bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, resembling nothing so much as the purest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. It is remarkably heavy; and is sometimes found in little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> masses of the bigness of a pigeon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, which are broken with a slight blow; but it is usually met with in the form of a fine gold-coloured efflorescence on vitriolic and pyritical bodies; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in loose, shattery, and friable masses of a more dusky yellow; in which latter state it so much resembles a native sulphur, that it is frequently mistaken for one; however, it is not inflammable; but calcines in the fire to a greyish powder, which by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> longer changes to a deep and fine purple. The Greeks used it externally, as a gentle echarotic and a styptic: they made it an ingredient in their ointments for old ulcers, and used to sprinkle the powder of it on fresh wounds in order to stop the hemorrhage.

MELASTOMA

Pages 12-12

the American gooseberry-tree; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them natives of the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and very beautiful on account of the variegation of their leaves. Most of the leaves are of two different colours on their surfaces; the under side being either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rufset, and their upper parts of different shades of green; so that they make a fine appearance in the hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> all the year round. There are but few of these plants in the European gardens; which may perhaps have been occasioned by the difficulty of bringing over growing plants from the West Indies; and the seeds being small when taken out from the pulp of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, rarely succeed. The best way is to have the entire fruits put up in dry sand as soon as they are ripe, and forwarded by the quickest contrivance to England. They should be immediately taken out when they arrive, and the seeds sown in pots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and plunged into a moderate hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of tanner's bark. When the plants come up, and are fit to be removed, they must each be planted in a small pot, and plunged into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>-bed; and afterwards treated as other exotic plants.

MELCHISEDECH

Pages 12-13
or Melchisedek, (the order of); an order of priesthood, according to the scriptures of the Old and New Testament. The first mention of Melchisedech is in Genesis xiv. 16, 17, 18, where it is related, that, when Abraham had rescued his brother Lot and all his goods out of the hands of the five kings, he was met, upon his return, by Melchisedech, king of Salem, who "brought forth bread and wine; and he was the priest of the Most High God." It is added, that he blessed A- The next mention of Melchisedech is by the Royal Psalmist, who, speaking prophetically of the Messiah, says, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedech." Lastly, St Paul applies the story of Melchisedech to our Saviour, citing the very words of the Psalmist. And, in another place, he gives this account of Melchisedech: "This Melchisedech, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him; to whom Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation king of righteousness, and after that also king of Salem, which is, king of peace; without father, without mother, without descent; having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God, abideth a priest continually." From these passages it appears, that Melchisedech, whoever he was, was a type of Jesus Christ, and his priesthood an image of our Saviour's. Innumerable difficulties have been started upon the subject of Melchisedech. The first relates to his country, or the place where he reigned. Most authors take Salem to be the same as Jerusalem: but St Jerome places it near Scythopolis, where they still pretended to show the ruins of Melchisedech's palace. He thinks it was at this place that Jacob arrived, after his passage over Jordan, when he returned from Mesopotamia. The next difficulty relates to his person. It is generally agreed by learned men, that, when the apostle says he was without father and without mother, no more is meant than that he is introduced into the history of Abraham without acquainting us who he was or whence he came, when he lived or when he died. Nevertheless, some have taken St Paul's words literally, and contended, that he was not of human, but divine nature. Origen and Didymus took him to be an angel; and the author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament pretended he was the Holy Ghost, who appeared to Abraham in a human form. About the beginning of the third century, arose the heresy of the Melchisedechians, who affirmed, that Melchisedech was not a man, but a heavenly power, superior to Jesus Christ: For Melchisedech, they said, was the intercessor and mediator of the angels; but Jesus Christ was so only for men, and his priesthood only a copy of that of Melchisedech. This heresy was revived in Egypt by one Hierax, who pretended that Melchisedech was the Holy Ghost. The Arabic catena upon the ninth chapter of Genesis makes Melchisedech to be descended from Shem by his father, and from Japhet by his mother. Heracles, or Heracles, his father, was, they say, son or grandson of Phaleg, and son of Heber; and his mother, named Salatibiel, was daughter of Gomer, son of Japheth. Cedrenus, and others, derive Melchisedech from an Egyptian stock. They say his father was called Sidon or Sida, and was the founder of the city of Sidon the capital of Phoenicia. Suidas says, he was of the cursed race of Canaan; for which reason the scripture does not mention his genealogy. The Jews and Samaritans believed Melchisedech to be the same with the patriarch Shem; which opinion has been followed by a great number of modern writers. M. Jorieu has undertaken to prove, that he is the same as Cham or Ham. It would be endless to recount all the opinions upon this matter; we shall therefore only add, that Peter Cunzeus, and Peter du Moulin, have asserted, that Melchisedech, who appeared to Abraham, was the Son of God; and that the patriarch worshipped him, and acknowledged him for the Messiah.

MELCHITES

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name given to the Syriac, Egyptian, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The Melchites, excepting some few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> no importance, which relate only to ceremonies and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, are in every respect professed Greeks: but they are governed by a particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who resides at Damas, and assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of patriarch of Antioch. They celebrate mats in the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> among the Melchites follow the rule of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rule of all the Greek monks. They have four fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> distant about a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from Damas, and never go out of the cloister.

MELCOMB-REGIS

Pages 13-13

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 32. N. Lat. 50. 40. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and paved; and there is an excellent harbour, by which they carry on a pretty good foreign trade.

MELEAGER

Pages 13-13

a Greek poet, the son of Eucrates, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and flourished under the reign of Seleucus VI. the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Syria. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>; and died in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Coos, anciently called Meropoe. He there composed the Greek epigrams called by us the Anthologia. The disposition of the epigrams in this collection was often changed afterwards, and many additions have been made to them. The monk Planudes put them into the order they are in at present in the year 1380.

MELEAGRIS

Pages 13-14

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinace. The head is covered with spongy caruncles; and there is likewise a membranaceous longitudinal caruncle on the throat. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. 1. The gallopavo, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> American turkey of Ray, has a caruncle both on the head and throat; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> is bearded. He lives upon grain and insects: when the cock struts, he blows up his breast, spreads and erects his feathers, relaxes the caruncle on the forehead, and the naked parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> and neck become intensely <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>.—Barbott informs us, that very few turkeys are to be met with in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and those only in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the chiefs of the European forts; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> declining to breed any on account of their tenderness, which sufficiently proves them not to be natives of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. He also remarks, that neither the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> nor ducks are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to Guinea, any more than the turkey. Neither is that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>: the first that were seen in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> were brought from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> by some Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. They are bred in Ceylon, but not found wild. In fact, the turkey, properly so called, was unknown to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists, and even to the old world, before before the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It was a bird peculiar to the new continent, and is now the commonest wild-fowl in the northern parts of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It was first seen in France, in the reign of Francis I.; and in England, in that of Henry VIII. By the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the reign of these monarchs, the first turkeys must have been brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, the conquest of which was completed A.D. 1521. Ælian mentions a bird found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, which some writers have suspected to be the turkey; but Mr Pennant concludes, with Gesner, that it was either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, or some bird of that genus. On consulting some gentlemen who had resided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the Indies, Mr Pennant is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that though the turkey is bred there, it is only considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> bird, and not a native of the country. 2. The cristata, or Brazilian pheasant of Ray, has an erect crest of feathers on the head, and violet-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; it has a caruncle on the throat, but none on the head. 3. The satyra, or horned pheasant of Edwards, has two blue horns behind its eyes, and a red body spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>.

MELES

Pages 14-14

(anc. geog.), a fine river running by the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, with a cave at its head, where <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is said to have written his poems. And from it Homer takes his original name Melafigenea, given him by his mother Crithies, as being born on its banks. (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>).

MELIA

Pages 14-14

Azaderach, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the Bead-tree; a genus of the monogyne order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them exotic trees of the Indies, rising near 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pinnated or winged leaves, and clusters of pentapetalous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. They are all propagated by seeds sown on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>.

MELIANTHUS

Pages 14-14

Honeysuckle; a genus of the angiosperma order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> hath a thick, ligneous, spreading root; many upright, ligneous, durable stalks, rising six <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pinnated leaves, of four or five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> lobes terminated by an odd one; and, from the sides and tops of the stalks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> spikes of chocolate-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, hath a root like the former; upright, ligneous, soft, durable stalks, rising four or five feet high; garnished with smaller pinnated leaves; and from the sides and ends of the branches, long, loose, pendulous bunches of flowers tinged with green, saffron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. Both the species flower about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>; but rarely produce seeds in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They are very ornamental, both in foliage and flower, and merit admittance in every collection. They are easily propagated by suckers and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>. They thrive best in a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and in a sheltered warm exposure.

MELIBOEA

Pages 14-14

(anc. geog.), an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>; which, before it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, forms a spreading lake round it. This island was famous for its purple dye. Thought to be a colony of Thessalians; and hence Lucretius's epithet Thessalian.

MELICA

Pages 14-14

Roriflax; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the Melicera nutans. It is a native of several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and the inhabitants of some of the western islands make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of it for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>-nets, as it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> without rotting.

MELICERES

Pages 14-14

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a kind of encysted tumours, so called when their contents are of the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>.

MELILLA

Pages 14-14

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Garet. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1469, but returned back to the Moors. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 9. N. Lat. 35. 20. MELILOT. See Trifolium.

MELINDA

Pages 14-14

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated, according to some, between the third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of South Latitude; though there is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disagreement among geographers as to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is allowed by all, however, that the coasts are very dangerous; being full of rocks and shelves, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at some seasons very liable to tempests. The kingdom of Melinda is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> rich and fertile; producing almost all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> except wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, both which are brought thither from Cambaya and other parts; and those who cannot purchase them make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of potatoes in their stead, which are here fine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and in great plenty. They likewise abound with great variety of fruit-trees, roots, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and other eculents, and with melons of exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. They have also great plenty of venison, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, oxen, sheep, hens, geese, and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, &c. and one breed of sheep whose tails weigh between 30 and 40 pounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also called Melinda.

MELINUM

Pages 14-14

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, famous in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, being the only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of the greatest painters of antiquity; and, according to Pliny's account, one of the three colours with which alone they performed all their works. It is a fine, white, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> earth, of a very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, yet remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; a sort of texture which must render any earth fit for the painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, that is of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It is frequently found forming a stratum in the earth, lying immediately under the vegetable mould. It is of a very smooth but not glossy surface; is very soft to the touch; adheres firmly to the tongue; is easily broken between the fingers; and stains the skin in handling. It melts readily in the mouth, and is perfectly fine; leaving not the least grittiness between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; thrown into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it makes a loud bubbling and hissing noise, and moulders away into a fine powder. It does not ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; and suffers no change in the fire. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> by which the melinum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is distinguished from all other white earths. It is still found in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from which the painters of old had it, viz. the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Milo <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>, from whence it had its name; and is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in most of the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It has of late been tried here as a paint; but is found not to make such a bright paint as the other substances now employed. It is not, however, liable, like them, to turn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; hence it would seem to be worth the consideration of persons in the colour-trade; especially as it might be had, in any quantities, for the carriage.

MELISSA

Pages 14-15

Baum; a genus of the gymnosperma order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable are the following. 1. The officinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> baum, hath <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> perennial roots; many upright, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, branchy, annual stalks, rising two or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, indented, opposite leaves by pairs, two or three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and half as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and, from the upper axillas, verticillate clusters of small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, upon single footstalks. There is also a kind with variegated leaves. 2. The grandiflora, or Heterian calaminth, hath fibrous perennial roots, and annual stalks, rising about a foot high; garnished with oblong, oval, indented, hairy opposite leaves; and from the upper axillas verticillate clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> purple flowers, on forked footstalks. 3. The calamintha, or common calaminth of the shops, hath fibrous perennial roots; upright, square, branchy hairy stalks, rising a foot high; roundish, indented, opposite leaves; and verticillate clusters of small bluish flowers, on forked footstalks as long as the flowers. All these species are easily propagated by offsets. Medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a>. The first species, when in perfection, has a pleasant smell, somewhat of the lemon kind; and a weak, roughish, aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The young shoots have the strongest flavour; the flowers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> itself when old, or produced in very rich moist soils, or rainy seasons, is much weaker both in smell and taste. Baum is appropriated, by the writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, to the head, stomach, and uterus; and in all disorders of these parts, is said to do extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. So high an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> have some chemists entertained of this plant, that they have expected to find in it a medicine which should prolong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> beyond the usual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The present practice, however, holds it in no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem; and ranks it (where it certainly deserves to be) among the weaker corroborants. Infusions of the leaves in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> smell agreeably of the herb, but have not much taste, though on being infusitated they leave a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a bitterish astringent extract. Infusions of baum do not, like other aromatics, offend the head, as is complained off from sage, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">Cold</a> infusions in water, or spirit, are far better than the cohabited distilled water, and are the best preparations from the plant. On distilling the fresh herb with water, it impregnates the first running pretty strongly with its grateful flavour. When large quantities are subjected to the operation at once, there separates and rises to the surface of the aqueous fluid a small portion of essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which some call sp. Spirit, and others of Germania. It is of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and a very fragrant smell.

MELISSUS OF SAMOS

Pages 15-15

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of Rhagines and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Parmenides; and lived about 520 B.C. The Ephesians gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and invested him with extraordinary power. He pretended that the universe is infinite, immoveable, alone, and without a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>.

MELITE

Pages 15-15

(anc. geog.), an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> referred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; but nearer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and allotted to it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; commended for its commodious harbours; for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> well built, with artificers of every kind, especially weavers of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; all owing to the Phoenicians, the first colonists. Now <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>; remarkable for St Paul's shipwreck. Melita, Melita, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Melitina Insula; an island on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Illyricum in the Adriatic. The Catuli Me- litai, (Pliny), were famous. Now Melite, the name of the island <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>.

MELITENSIS TERRA

Pages 15-15

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>; an earth, of which there are two very different kinds; the one of the genus of boles, the other of the marle. The latter is that known by medicinal authors under this name, the former is the Malta earth now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but both being brought from the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are confusedly called by the same name. The Maltese marle, which is the terra Melitensis of medicinal authors, is a loose, crumbly, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> earth, of an unequal and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture; and, when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, soon falls into fine soft powder: but, when preserved and dried, it becomes a loose, light <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>: it is rough to the touch, adheres firmly to the tongue, is very easily crumbled to powder between the fingers, and stains the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it swells, and afterwards moulders away into a fine powder. It ferments very violently with acid menstruums. Both kinds are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, and the latter has been much esteemed as a remedy against the bites of venomous animals. The other has supplied its place in the German shops; and is used there as a cordial, sudorific, and astringent.

MELITIS

Pages 15-15

(anc. geog.), a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, struck out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on account of the arrogance of the people, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> admitted in lieu of it. The situation not said.

MELITO

Pages 15-15

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> in Lydia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century; is remarkable for the apology he presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelius, in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; on which Eusebius and the other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers bestow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> praises: but that apology and all Melito's other works, are lost.

MELITUS

Pages 15-15

Greek orator and poet, the accuser of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. The Athenians, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Socrates, discovering the iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> they had passed against that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, put Melitus to death 400 B.C.

MELLER

Pages 15-15

a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, 80 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; on which stands the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

MELLI

Pages 15-16

with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mundingoes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The country formerly called Melli, now chiefly inhabited by the Mundingoes, who still retain pretty much of the character ascribed to the people of Melli, lies to the south of the river <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>; on the west it borders on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kaboo; on the south it has Melli, properly so called, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> it from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; and on the east it extends to the kingdom of Gago. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of this country we are little acquainted with; as is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to most of the inland territories of Africa, but towards the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> this country is a little better known. The first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> we meet with is Kachao, a Portuguese colony, situated on the river of St Domingo, which falls into the sea about 26 leagues below this town.—About 26 leagues above Kachao, on the same side of the river, is another trading town called Farinii, where, in the months of October and November, one may trade for about half the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wax and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> which is traded for at Kachao. Here are also some slaves to be bought.—But is a village near the mouth of the river Gelves, where most of the traders buy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; which is in great plenty there, and very good. Gefves is a village on a river of the same name, on which the Portuguese have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. At Gefves one may trade yearly for 250 slaves, 80 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 quintals of wax, and as many of ivory. Near the mouth of the river of Gefves is a village called Karbali, where there is a considerable trade for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; here are also some slaves and ivory. Rio Grande, or the Great River, runs about 10 or 12 leagues to the south of the river of Gefves. About 80 leagues from the mouth of it is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, who are good traders in ivory, rice, millet, and some slaves. They are called Anadus. Over-against the mouth of Rio Grande, is a cluster of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Bifugo Isles; the most considerable of which is Caffagot, being about six leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very good, and produces millet, rice, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, besides <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and palm-trees, and many others. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, with those of Caracca, Canabac, and La Gallina, are the only ones where the Europeans may trade with some security. They trade, however, sometimes at the other islands, but they must be extremely cautious; and yet, after all their precautions, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be robbed and murdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they venture to go ashore. The river Nunho runs 16 leagues to the south of Rio Grande; it is very considerable, and comes from a vast distance in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. One may buy here 300 quintals of ivory and 100 slaves a-year. Rice grows here admirably well, and is very cheap. There are everywhere <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes which grow naturally; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, which might turn to good account. The trade is carried on here from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> till August. In the river of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, the late <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> African <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of England had, in the year 1728, two islands; the one, called Tafra, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat island, near three leagues in circumference, in which the company's slaves had a good plantation; the rest of the island is covered with wood, among which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cotton-trees of an unaccountable size. The other island is Benfe, wherein stood a regular fort. It was formerly the residence of one of the English chiefs.

MELOCHIA

Pages 16-16

Jews mallow; a genus of the pentandria order, belonging to the monodelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the only remarkable one is the olitorius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Jews-mallow, which is a native of the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is an annual plant, which rises about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, dividing into several branches, garnished with leaves of different sizes and forms: some are spear-shaped, others are oval, and some almost heart-shaped: they are of a deep green, and slightly indented on their edges, having near their base two bristly reflexed segments. They have very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender footstalks, especially those which grow on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> sit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> on the opposite side of the branches to the leaves, coming out singly; they are composed of five small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> petals, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stamens surrounding the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> germen, which is situated in the centre of the flower and afterwards turns to a rough swelling <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> two inches long, ending in a point, and having four cells filled with angular greenish seeds. This species is cultivated about the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and in the East Indies, as a pot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>; the Jews <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the leaves, and eating them with their meat. It is supposed by Rauwolf to be the clas daicum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, and the corchorum of Pliny.

MELODUNUM

Pages 16-16

(anc. geog.), Cesar; a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENONES">Senones</a> in Gallia Celtica above Lutetia; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>.

MELODY

Pages 16-17

in music, a succession of sounds ranged in such a manner, according to the laws of rhythm and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, that it may form a sentiment agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Vocal melody is called singing; and that which is performed upon instruments may be termed symphonic melody. The idea of rhythm necessarily enters into that of melody. An <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is not an air but in proportion as the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> are observed. The same succession of sounds is susceptible of as many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as many different kinds of melody, as the various ways by which its emphatic notes, and the quantities of those which intervene, may be diversified; and the change in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the notes alone, may <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> that very succession in such a manner that it cannot be known. Thus, melody in itself is nothing; it is the rhythmus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> measure which determines it, and there can be no air without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> measure from both, we cannot compare melody with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; for to the former it is essential, but not at all to the latter. Melody, according to the manner in which it is considered, has a relation to two different principles. When regarded only as agreeable to the proportions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and the rules of modulation, it has its principle in harmony; hence it is a harmonical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, which exhibits the different gradations of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, the chords peculiar to each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, and the laws of modulation, which are the sole elements that compose an air. According to this principle, the whole power of melody is limited to that of pleasing the ear by agreeable sounds, as the eye may be pleased with an agreeable assemblage of suitable colours. But when considered as an imitative art, by which we may affect the mind with various images, excite different emotions in the heart, inflame or soothe the passions; by which, in a word, we produce different effects upon our moral faculties, which are not to be effectuated by the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> alone, we must explore another principle for melody: for in our whole internal frame there appears to be no power upon which either harmony alone, or its necessary results, can <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, to affect us in such a manner. What then is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> principle? It is as much founded on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as the first; but, in order to discover its foundation in nature, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> require a more accurate though simpler observation, and a more exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> in the observer. This principle is the same which varies the tone of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, when we speak, according as we are interested in what we say, and according to the different emotions which we feel in expressing it. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> of languages which determines the melody of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; it is the accent which determines us to employ the emphasis of speaking while we sing, and to speak with more or less energy according as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is more or less accented. That language whose accents are the most sensible, ought to produce a more passionate and more lively melody; that which has little accentuation, or none at all, can only produce a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and languid melody, without character. Melody. rather and without <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. These are the true principles: in proportion as we depart from them, when we speak of the power of music upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, we shall become unintelligible to ourselves and others; our words will be without meaning. If music does not impress the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> with images but by melody, if from thence it obtains its whole power, it must follow, that all musical sounds which are not pleasing by themselves alone, however agreeable to harmony they may be, is not an imitative music; and, being incapable, even with its most beautiful chords, either to present the images of things, or to excite the finer feelings, very soon cloy the ear, and leaves always the heart in cold indifference. It follows likewise, that notwithstanding the parts which harmony has introduced, and which the present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of music so wantonly abuses, wherever two different melodies are heard at the same time, they counteract each other, and destroy the effects of both, however beautiful each may be when performed alone: from whence it may be judged with what degree of taste the French composers have introduced in their operas the miserable practice of accompanying one air with another, as well in singing, which is the native expression of passions and sentiments, as in instrumental performances; which is the same thing as if whimsical orators should take it in their heads to recite two orations at the same time, that the elegance of each might derive more force from the other. So much for Rousseau. The translator, however, has reason to fear, that the causes by which national melody is diversified and characterized, are more profound and permanent than the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accentuation of language. This indeed may have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence in determining the nature of the rhythmus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of emphatic notes; but very little in regulating the nature of the emphasis and expression themselves. If Rousseau's principle be true in its full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, he must of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> acknowledge, that an air which was never set or intended for words, however melodious, cannot be imitative; he must likewise confess, that what is imitative in one nation cannot be such in another: nor can it be denied upon his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, that the recitative, which is formed upon the mode of speaking, is the most forcible of all melodies; which is absurd. His other observations are at once judicious and profound. Though it is impossible to exhibit the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variety of harmony by playing the same melody at the same time upon different keys, admitting those keys to form among themselves a perfect chord, which will of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> preserve all the subsequent notes in the same intervals; yet this perfect harmony would by no means be uniformly pleasing to the ear. We must therefore of necessity introduce less perfect chords to vary and increase the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and these chords in any complex system of music must of necessity produce dissonances. It then becomes the business of the composer to be careful that these dissonances may arise as naturally from, and return as naturally to, perfect harmony as possible. All these causes must inevitably vary the melody of the different parts; but still amidst all these difficulties, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> ought to be zealous in preserving the melody of each as homogeneous with the others as possible, that the result of the whole may be in some measure uniform. Otherwise, by counteracting each other, the parts will reciprocally destroy the effects one of another.

MELOE

Pages 17-18

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera. The antennae are jointed, the last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> being oval; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> is roundish; the elytra are soft and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; and the head is inflected and gibbous. There are 16 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The most remarkable is the vesicatorius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cantharis of the shops; which, when bruised, is universally used as a blistering <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>.
