These insects are of a shining green colour, intermingled with more or less of a blue and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. They are found adhering to different kinds of trees and herbs, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and France; the largest and most esteemed come from Italy. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">Cantharides</a> are extremely acrimonious: applied to the skin, they first inflame, and afterwards excoriate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, raising a more perfect blister than any of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and occasioning a more plentiful discharge of serum. All the blistering compositions have cantharides for their basis. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> application of cantharides is often followed by a strangury, accompanied with thirst and feverish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: this inconvenience may be remedied by soft unctuous or mucilaginous liquors liberally drank. Cantharides taken internally often occasion a discharge of blood by urine, with exquisite pain: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the dose is considerable, they seem to inflame and exacerbate the whole intestinal canal; the stools become mucous and purulent; the breath fetid and cadaverous; intense pains are felt in the lower belly; the patient faints, grows giddy, raving mad, and dies. All these terrible consequences have sometimes happened from a few grains. Herman relates, that he has known a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a grain inflame the kidneys, and occasion bloody urine with violent pain. There are nevertheless <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which this stimulating fly, given in larger doses, proves not only safe, but of singular efficacy for the cure of diseases that yield little to medicines of a milder class. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> phlegmatic sluggish habits, where the viscera are overloaded, and the kidneys and ureters obstructed with thick viscid mucous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, cantharides have excellent effects: here the abounding mucus defends the solids from the acrimony of the fly, till it is itself expelled; when the medicine ought to be discontinued. Groenvelt employed cantharides with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success in dropsies, obstinate suppressions of urine, and ulcerations of the bladder; giving very considerable doses made into boluses with camphor; and interpolating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> draughts of emulsions, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or other emollient liquids: by this means, the excessive irritation, which they would otherwise have occasioned, was in great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> prevented. The camphor did not perhaps contribute so much to this effect as is generally imagined: since it has no sensible <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that promises any considerable abatement of the acrimony of cantharides: nitre would answer all that the camphor is supposed to perform; this, with milk, or emollient mucilaginous liquors, drank in large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, are the best correctors. Cantharides, in very small doses, may be given with safety also in other cases. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a> observes, that the obstinate gleetings which frequently remain after the cure of venereal maladies, and which rarely yield to balsamic medicines, cines, are effectually remedied by cantharides; and that no one remedy is more efficacious in leprous disorders; in which last, proper purgatives are to be occasionally taken during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the cantharides. The best and safest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of cantharides for these purposes, is a spirituous tincture; and indeed in all cases, the tincture is far preferable, for internal use, to the fly in substance. The virtues of cantharides are extracted by rectified spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirit, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but do not arise in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The watery and spirituous extracts blister as freely as the fly in substance; whilst the fly remaining after the several menstrua have performed their office, is to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> insipid, and does not in the least blister or inflame the skin.

MELOTHRIA

Pages 18-18

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the pendula, a native of Carolina, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and also many of the American <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. The plants strike out roots at every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, which fasten themselves into the ground, by which means their stalks extend to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance each way. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are very small, in shape like those of the melon, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The fruit in the West Indies grows to the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, is of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and changes to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> when ripe: there are by the inhabitants sometimes pickled when they are green. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> the fruit are much smaller, and are so hidden by the leaves that it is difficult to find them. The plants are too tender to be reared in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>.

MELPOMENE

Pages 18-18

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, and the inventress of tragedy. She is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> represented with a serious countenance, and in a theatrical dress, holding crowns and sceptres in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a dagger in the other.

MELREY

Pages 18-18
or MELROSE, a town of Scotland, in the county of Merse, and on the confines of Tweedale, seated on the south-side of the river Tweed; with an ancient abbey now in ruins. W. Long. 2. 32. N. Lat. 55. 32. This abbey was founded by king David I. in 1136. He peopled it with Cistercians, brought from Rivale abbey in Yorkshire, and dedicated it to the virgin Mary. At the reformation James Douglas was appointed commendator, who took down much of the building, in order to furnish materials for a large house to himself, which still remains, and is dated 1590. Nothing is left of the abbey, excepting a part of the cloister walls, elegantly carved; but the ruins of the church are of most uncommon beauty. Part is at present used for divine service, the rest uncovered; but every part does great honour to the architect.—Alexander II. was buried beneath the great altar, and it is also the place of interment of the Douglas and other potent families.—Its situation is extremely pleasant.

MELT

Pages 18-18
or FISHES. In the melt of a living cod there are such numbers of those animalcules said to be found in the semen of all-male animals, that in a drop of its juice, no larger than a grain of sand, there are contained more than 10,000 of them; and, considering how many such quantities there are in the whole melt of one such fish, it is not incredible, that there are more animals in one melt of it, than there are living men at one time upon the face of the earth. MEMNON. However strange and romantic such a conjecture must appear, a serious consideration and calculation will make it appear very plain. An hundred such grains of sand as those just mentioned will make about an inch in length; therefore in a cubic inch there will be a million of such sands; and if there be 10,000 animals in each of those quantities, there must be in the whole 150,000 millions; which is a number vastly exceeding that of mankind, even supposing the whole earth as populous as Holland.

MELTING COSS

Pages 18-18

in effaying, an hollow cone of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, into which melted metallic substances are thrown, in order to free them from their scoriae. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is melted, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to rub the inside of the cone with grease; but when the quantity is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it contains any thing sulphureous, this caution of following the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> is not sufficient. In this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the effayer has recourse to a late reduced to thin pap with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which effectually prevents any injury to the cone.

MELVIL

Pages 18-18

descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Scots family, being the third son of the laird of Kaeth, was born about the middle of the 16th century. He went to France, very young, in the capacity of page to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, then married to the dauphin; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of her husband, followed her to Scotland, where he was made <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of her chamber, and admitted a privy-counsellor. She employed him in her most important concerns, till her unhappy confinement in Lochleven, all which he discharged with the utmost fidelity; and, from his own accounts, there is reason to conclude, that had she taken his advice, she might have avoided many of her misfortunes. When she was prisoner in England, she recommended him strongly to her son James; with whom he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour and employment until the death of queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>: James would then have taken him to England; but Melvil, now grown old, was desirous of retiring from business, and in his retirement he drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his son. These memoirs were accidentally found in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> castle, in the year 1660, though nobody knew how they came to be deposited there; and were published in folio in 1683.

MEMBER

Pages 18-18

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, denotes any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; as a frieze, cornice, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. This word is also sometimes used for the moulding. MEMBER OF <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">PARLIAMENT</a>. See PARLIAMENT.

MEMBRANE

Pages 18-18

in anatomy, a pliable texture of fibres interwoven together in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>.

MEMMON OF RHODES

Pages 18-18

one of the generals of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, advised that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in order to deprive Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of support, and afterwards to attack Macedon; but

MEMNON

Pages 18-18

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was the son of Tithonus and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. Having led his troops to the assistance of Priam, in order to raise the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, he was killed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>; when his body being placed on a funeral pile, was, at Aurora's desire, transformed into a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>.

MEMOIRS

Pages 18-19

in matters of literature, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, written by persons who had some share in the transactions they relate; answering to what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called Commentaries.—The journals of the proceedings of a literary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a collection of matters transacted therein, are likewise called Memoirs.

MEMORY

Pages 19-20

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, whereby it retains and recalls the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> it has once perceived. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, p. 42. Memory depends very much upon the temper and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the body. In some, it is not so susceptible of impressions; in others, it is not sufficiently retentive; and as the seat of the memory is in the brain, whatever is hurtful to this latter, must <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the former. Too much <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> the brain, and too little over-heats it; therefore either of these extremes must of course hurt the memory. All intemperance likewise, and excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, have the same ill effect. When we would commit any thing to memory, our first concern should be to understand it thoroughly. For we can never retain those things <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, of which we have but an imperfect knowledge. Likewise order and method in the discourse itself is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> help to the memory. Where things have a mutual dependence upon each other, and go on in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, the thoughts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> more readily from one to another, than where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> confused and without any connection. The mind should also be free at such times, and have nothing else to take off its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Nothing is a greater hindrance to the memory than a crowd of ideas, and those of different kinds, flowing in upon the mind at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They jostle out one another, so that but few of them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they do, it is in such a confused and disorderly manner, that when they come to be surveyed by reflection, little can be made of them. To write <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any thing is likewise a great advantage towards remembering it. For the very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> helps very much to imprint it upon the mind, by engaging it to a closer attention, and causing it to dwell longer upon every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> than otherwise it would do only in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a>. And therefore the Jewish doctors tell us, it was for this reason that the kings of Israel were enjoined always to write out a copy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> with their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. And the fairer a thing is written, it is with greater ease committed to memory. This may possibly at first seem to have little in it; but if we consult <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, we shall generally find, that those things make the deepest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon the mind, which affect the senses in the most lively and agreeable manner. As we receive most of our ideas through them, the stronger impulse is made upon the organ, the greater attention it excites in the mind; and what we most attend to, we retain longest. A little experience and observation <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> help a person to discover the strength of his memory. And care should be taken not to overburden it. A long discourse therefore should be committed to memory by parts, so much at once as the memory can well receive and retain. These parts should not be too many, for fear of confusion. And as it is most likely we may be at a loss in passing from one part to another, it will not be amiss in a more particular manner to impress upon the mind the beginnings of them. One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> often helps us to recover a word; that word a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>; and the first sentence a whole argument. Some have therefore advised, for the assistance of weaker memories, to write each part of the discourse in a separate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a>, and the first word in larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which may strike the fancy like a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> when we come to those places. For everyone is sensible of the powerful effect of imagery to excite and recall our ideas; and therefore it has been thought a further advantage, if the first letter of each word, written in larger characters, could be joined together in one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> word; for then the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of that word would give us the first letter of each of those initial words, which letters would help us to recollect the whole words, which was the thing designed by writing them in different characters. We find this method of bringing several ideas together into one artificial word of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. So the figures of tylograms being distinguished by technical words, are better known, and more easily remembered; as every one perceives, who is conversant in logic. As the mind is not at all times equally disposed for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of this faculty, such seasons should be made choice of as are most proper for it. The mind is seldom fit for attention presently after meals; and to call off the spirits at such times from their proper employment in digestion, is apt to cloud the brain, and prejudice the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Both the mind and body should be easy and undisturbed when we engage in this exercise, and therefore retirement is most fit for it; and the evening, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before we go to rest, is generally recommended as a very convenient season, both for the stillness of the night, and because the impressions will then have a longer time to settle before they come to be disturbed by the accession of others proceeding from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects; and to call over in the morning what has been committed to the memory over-night, must, for the same reason, be very serviceable. For, to review those ideas while they continue fresh upon the mind, and unmixed with any others, must necessarily imprint them more deeply. Some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers speak of an artificial memory, and lay down rules for attaining it. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a> the poet is said first to have discovered this, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> at least to have given the occasion for it. The story they tell of him is this: Being once at a feast, he recited a poem which he had made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the person who gave the entertainment. But having (as is usual in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>) made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> digression in praise of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>; when he had repeated the whole poem, his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> would give him but half the sum he had promised, telling him he must get the other part from those Memory: those deities who had an equal share in the honour of his performance. Immediately after, Simonides was told that two young men were without, and must needs speak with him. He had scarce got out of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, when the room where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was fell down, killed all the persons in it, and so maimed their bodies, that, when the rubbish was thrown off, they could not be known one from another: upon which Simonides recollecting the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where every one had sat, by that means distinguished them. Hence it came to be observed, that to fix a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of places in the mind in a certain order, was a help to the memory: As we find by experience, that, upon returning to places once familiar to us, we not only remember them, but likewise many things we both said and did in them. This action therefore of Simonides was afterwards improved into an art, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of it is this: They bid you form in your mind the idea of some large place or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which you may divide into a great number of distinct parts, ranged and disposed in a certain order. These you are frequently to revolve in your thoughts, till you are able to run them over one after another without hesitation, beginning at any part. Then you are to impress upon your mind as many images of living creatures, or any other sensible objects which are most likely to affect you, and be soonest revived in your memory. These, like characters in short-hand, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, must stand to denote an equal number of other words, which cannot so easily be remembered. When therefore you have a number of things to commit to memory in a certain order, all that you have to do is, to place these images regularly in the several parts of your building. And thus they tell you, that, by going over several parts of the building, the images placed in them will be revived in the mind; which of course will give you the things or words themselves in the order you desire to remember them. The advantages of the images seems to be this; that, as they are more like to affect the imagination than the words for which they stand, they will for that reason be more easily remembered. Thus, for instance, if the image of a lion be made to signify strength, and this word strength be one of those I am to remember, and is placed in the porch; when in going over the several parts of the building I come to the porch, I shall sooner be reminded of that image than of the word strength. Some ancient as well as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers relate wonderful effects of this artifice. But they all agree it much more assists us to remember any number of separate and unconnected words, than a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> discourse; unless so far as the remembrance of one word may enable us to recollect more. And in this respect it does not much differ from some of those methods above-mentioned as helps to the memory. Quintilian therefore, though he does not wholly pass it over, yet seems to lay no great stress upon it. And, doubtless, the most effectual way to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a good memory is, its constant and moderate exercise. —In a word, the memory, like other habits, is strengthened and improved by daily use and practice. Wherefore those who have most occasion for it, as orators, should not suffer it to lie idle, but constantly employ it in treasuring up and frequently reviewing such things as may be of most importance to them.

MENASSEH

Pages 21-22

a celebrated rabbi, born in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> about the year 1604, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Ben Israel, and followed his father into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he was educated by rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Uziel, under whom, he in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> made such progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, that at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he succeeded him in the synagogue of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and married Rachel of the family of the Abarbanels, whom the Jews imagine to be descended from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. He afterwards went Mencke went to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ephraim, a rich merchant, who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; by whose advice he entered into trade. Some time after, the hopes of a more agreeable settlement induced him to come into England, under the protectorship of Cromwell; who gave him a very favourable reception, and one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> entertained him at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with several other learned divines. However, he soon after passed into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a> about the year 1657. The Jews at Amsterdam obtained his body, and interred it at their expense. He was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; had a lively <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgment, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and all the virtues that can adorn private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote many works in Hebrew, Latin, Spanish, and English. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of those published in Latin, are: 1. His Conciliator; a learned and curious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which he reconciles those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture which seem to contradict each other. 2. De resurrectione mortuorum. 3. De termino vitae. 4. Dissertatio de fragilitate humanæ ex lapsu Adamæ, deque Divino in hominem auxilio. 5. Spec Israel. Dr Thomas Pococke has written his life in English.

MENCKE

Pages 22-22

son to the preceding. After his studies he travelled into England and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and upon his return was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at Leipzig in 1699. He gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his lectures as well as his writings. He died in 1732, aged 58. He wrote many pieces. His De Charlataneria eruditorum declamationes dux, is an excellent satire, designed to expose the artifices used by false scholars to raise themselves a name. As he named and pointed at certain persons, it exasperated them, and they procured his book to be seized; but it spread, and editions of it were multiplied. He likewise published Méthode pour étudier l'Histoire, avec un catalogue des principaux historiens, &c. He made a great many additions to Mr Lenglet's book, especially with regard to the German historians.

MENDICANTS

Pages 22-22
or BEGGING FRIARS, several orders of religious in Popish countries, who having no settled revenues, are supported by the charitable contributions they receive from others. This sort of friars began in the 13th century. The Waldenses, who made profession of renouncing their estates, and leading a life of poverty, gave occasion to this institution. Two of that sect, Bernard and Durand of Osca, set up a congregation in the province of Tarragon, and called it The Poor Cathars. The same year, Dominick de Guzman, with nine more of his companions, founded the order of Preaching Friars, called from their founder Dominicans. The other three Mendicant orders are, the Franciscans, Augustins, and Carmelites. "A great many have embraced this severe order, (says Puffendorf), out of an opinion of a particular holiness and merit which they believed did belong to it, or rather an ecclesiastic ambition; the pride of mankind being so great and natural to some, that they did not think the commands of God sufficient, but would receive heaven rather as a desert than a gift, and were ambitious of having a preference before others even in another life." Buchanan tells us, the Mendicants in Scotland, under an appearance of beggary, lived a very luxurious life; whence one wittily called them, not Mendicants, but Manducant, friars.

MENDOZA

Pages 22-22

an Augustinian friar, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Castile, was made <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. In 1593, he was made bishop of Lipari in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. In 1607 he was made bishop of Chiapa in New Spain, and the next year was removed to the see of Papaian in the West Indies. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of China in Spanish, which has been translated into several languages.

MENECRATES

Pages 22-22

a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, who flourished about 360 B.C. is famous for his skill in his profession, but much more for his vanity. He would always be followed by some of the patients whom he had cured, one drest like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, another like Esculapius, a third like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, &c. As for himself, he would be called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the father of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, with this superscription, "Menecrates Jupiter to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Philip, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>." When that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> ridiculed him by replying, "Philip to Menecrates, Health and Good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>." Menecrates composed a book of Remedies, which is lost.

MENEDEMUS

Pages 22-22

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Erythreum, was the son of Calisthenes, and one of Phedo's followers. He was in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, and enjoyed several important posts in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He several times defended Erythreum with great bravery, and died of grief when Antigonus became <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. A person one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> saying to him, "It is a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to have what we desire," he replied, "It is a much greater to desire nothing but what we have." He flourished about 300 B.C.

MENELAUS

Pages 22-22

the son of Atreus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Agamemnon, reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> deprived him of his wife Helen. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> occasioned the famous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. See Helen. Menelaus, a mathematician in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, wrote three books on the Spheres, which have been published by father Merenne.

MENES

Pages 22-22

born at This, a town of Thebais in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the founder of the Egyptian empire. He had three sons, viz. Athois, who ruled after him at This and Thebes; Curudes, who, in Lower Egypt founded the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, which afterward was the kingdom of Diofpoli; and Nechrophes, who reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. It is thought this Menes reigned 117 years after the birth of Phaleg, son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, which was the very year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the people throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> Memphis, he stopped the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> near it, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a MENE-

MENESTRIER

Pages 22-23

a native of Dijon, and one of the most learned and curious French antiquaries of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, wrote, 1. A treatise on the medals, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments of the Roman emperors, in folio. 2. The most famous medals of the ancient Roman emperors and empresses, in quarto. He died in 1634, aged 70.

MENIALS

Pages 23-23
domestic or household servants, who live under their lord or master's roof.

MENINGES

Pages 23-23
or Meninges, in anatomy, a name given to the dura and pia mater of the brain. See Anatomy, n° 394.

MENISPERMUM

Pages 23-23

moonseed; a genus of the dicotyledon order, belonging to the dioecious class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them climbing plants, rising 14 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and natives of warm climates; but noway remarkable for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The seeds of a kind which grows in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, being formed into a paste, are regarded by the inhabitants as specific against <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> and cutaneous eruptions. The same paste is likewise used for the purpose of intoxicating fishes.

MENIXN

Pages 23-23

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean, to the west of the Syrtis <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. Supposed by Strabo and Polybius to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTOPHAGI">Lotophagi</a>; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> and Eratosthenes denominate the island Lotophagitis, with a cognominal town Meninx. The country of Vibius <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and of Volusianus. Now called Gerbi and Zarbi.

MENNITH

Pages 23-23
or Minnith, Judges xi. 33, a town near Heshbon, (Jerome), in Arabia Petraea; in a district named Ecopis, or twenty-towers, (Cellarius). There is also a Minnith mentioned Ezekiel xxvii., as being in a good wheat country; but whether the same with the foregoing is uncertain; though some think, that the first Minnith lay in the country of Ammon, (Wells). Mennonites, a sect of baptists in Holland, so called from Mennon Simonis of Friesland, who lived in the 16th century. This sect believe, that the New Testament is the only rule of faith; that the terms Person and Trinity are not to be used in speaking of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; that the first man was not created perfect; that it is unlawful to swear or to wage war upon any occasion; that infants are not the proper subjects of baptism; and that ministers of the gospel ought to receive no salary. They all unite in pleading for toleration in religion, and bar none from their assemblies who lead pious lives, and own the scriptures for the word of God. The Mennonites meet privately; and every one in the assembly has the liberty to speak, to expound the scriptures, to pray and sing. They assemble twice every year, from all parts of Holland, at Rynsburg, a village about two leagues from Leyden; at which time they receive the communion, sitting at a table, where the first distributes to the rest; and all feasts are admitted, even the Roman Catholics, if they please to come.

MENOCHIUS

Pages 23-23

vulgarly Menochia, (James), a famous lawyer, meanly born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, but who became so skilful in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that he was called the Balbus and Bartholomew of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; all the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> soliciting him to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. He read at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> 23 years together; and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> removed to Pavia, and succeeded Nicholas Gratiani. He hath got an immortal fame by his works, De recuperanda possessione; De adspicientia possessione; De praefuminatione; De arbitrariorum judicium questionibus & causis conciliariis, tom. 13. &c. He died in 1607, aged 75.

MENOLOGY

Pages 23-23

the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, in which the lives of the saints in short, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> barely their names, are cited; answering nearly to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">Martyrology</a> of the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

MENSA

Pages 23-23

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> that includes in it all patrimony, and necessaries for livelihood.

MENSALIS

Pages 23-23

mensalia, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, such livings as were formerly united to the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and hence called mensal benefices. See the article Benefice.

MENSES

Pages 23-23

fluors, Courses, Catamenia, in medicine, the monthly evacuations from the uterus of women not with child and not giving suck. With regard to the causes of this evacuation, the best physiologists are entirely at a loss. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> disputed whether the menstrual blood flowed from the uterus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>, but some observations of retroverted uteri have determined in favour of the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>.—For the disorders which follow a suppression, or too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a flow of the menses, see Medicine, n° 488, 259—264, and p. 4871.

MENSTRUUM

Pages 23-23

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, any body which in a fluid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> subtilized state is capable of interposing its small parts betwixt the small parts of other bodies, so as to divide them subtilly, and form a new uniform <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the two.

MENSURATION

Pages 23-23

in general, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> art of measuring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, superficies, or solids. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>.

MENTHA

Pages 23-24

mint; a genus of the gymnospermia order, belonging to the didynamia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but not more than three are cultivated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, namely, the viridis <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> spearmint, the piperita or peppermint, and the pulegium or pennyroyal. All these are so well known as to need no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; and all of them are very easily propagated by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, parting the roots, or by offsets. Uses. For culinary purposes, the spearmint is preferable to the other two; but for medicine, the peppermint and pennyroyal have in some places almost entirely superseded it. A conserve of the leaves is very grateful, and the distilled waters both simple and spirituous are universally thought pleasant. The leaves are used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> salads; and the juice of them boiled up with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> is formed into tablets. It has been imagined that cataplasms and fomentations of mint, would dissolve coagulations of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in the breasts; but Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> says, that the curd of milk, digested in a strong infusion of mint, could not be perceived to be any otherwise affected than by common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; however, milk in which mint-leaves were let to macerate, did not coagulate near so soon as an equal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the same milk kept by itself. Dr Lewis says, that dry mint digested in rectified spirits of wine, gives out a tincture, which appears by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a fine dark green, MEN green, but by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-light of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The fact is, that a small quantity of this tincture is green either by day-light or by candle-light, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of it seems impervious to common day-light; however, when held betwixt the eye and a candle, or betwixt the eye and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, it appears red. The virtues of mint are those of a warm stomach and carminative: in loss of appetite, nausea, and continual reaching to vomit, there are few simples of equal efficacy. In colicky pains, the gripes to which children are subject, lientecies, and other immoderate fluxes, this plant frequently does good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. It likewise proves beneficial in many hysterical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and affords an useful cordial in languors and other weaknesses consequent upon delivery. The best <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> in these cases is a strong infusion of the dried <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in water, (which is much superior to the green), or rather a tincture or extract prepared with rectified spirit. These possess the whole virtues of the mint; the essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and distilled water contain only the aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; the expressed juice only the astringency and bitterness, together with the mucilaginous substance common to all vegetables. The peppermint is much more pungent than the others. Pennyroyal has the same general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> with the mint, but is more acid and less agreeable when taken into the stomach. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, and not undeservedly, as an aperient and deobstruent, particularly in hysterical complaints and suppressions of the menses. For these purposes the distilled water is generally made use of, or, what is of equal efficacy, an infusion of the leaves. It is observable, that both water and rectified spirit extract the virtues of this herb by infusion, and likewise elevate the greatest part of them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The expressed juice with a little sugar, is not a bad medicine in the chincough.

MENTZ

Pages 24-24

an archbishopric and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> in Germany. It lies on the banks of the river Mayne, between the electorate of Triers on the west, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> on the south, Franconia on the east, and the Wetterau on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is about 60 miles in length from north-east to south-west, and about 50 in breadth. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>'s revenue arises from the toll on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the Mayne, and from the tax on the excellent wines produced in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of any trade are, 1. Mentz, on the Rhine, near its confluence with the Mayne. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> claims a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, (see <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Printing.) Here is a very beautiful quay along the river, defended by several works well fortified with cannon. That part of the city which extends towards the river is most populous. The best vineyards for Rhenish wine being in this neighbourhood, Mentz has a flourishing trade in that commodity more particularly; and its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is the brisker, by reason that all the merchandise which passes up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Rhine stops in its harbour to change bottoms. In this neighbourhood is Hockheim, so celebrated for good wines, that the best Rhenish is from thence called old hock. 2. Bingen is a pleasant small town, which stands in the district called Rhingau, which is so populous, that it looks like one entire town, intermixed with gardens and vineyards. The rising grounds about it produce wines that are esteemed preferable to those of Baccharac, so much in vogue heretofore. 3. Elfeld, five miles west from Mentz, is a strong fortified town, on the north side of the Rhine, and the chief of the Rhingau.—Here is Rodeheim, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> noted for the growth of the best wines in these parts. 4. Weilbaden lies between six and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues from Frankfort, and about five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six miles north of Mentz: it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of a country belonging to the branch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Saarbruck, and is famous for its mineral waters.

MENYANTHES

Pages 24-24

Marsh-trefoil, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Buckbean; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandrae class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. This plant grows wild in moist marshy places in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It has three oval leaves standing together upon one pedicle, which issues from the root; their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is very bitter, and somewhat nauseous. According to Mr Lightfoot, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of this plant are so extremely beautiful, that nothing but their native foil could exclude it from a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in every garden. They grow in an elegant spike; are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, dished with pink, and fringed internally with hairs. The highlanders esteem an infusion or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of the leaves as good to strengthen the stomach. According to Mr Withering, an infusion of the leaves is prescribed in rheumatism and dropsies; a dram of them in powder purges and vomits, and is sometimes given to destroy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. In a scarcity of hops, the plant is used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to bitter the ale. The powdered roots are sometimes used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, but they are unpalatable. Some people say, that sheep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> eat it, and that it cures them of the rot; but from the Upsal Experiments it appears, that though goats eat it, sheep sometimes will not. Cows, horses, and swine, refuse it.—As to its medical virtues, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> informs us, that it is an efficacious aperient and deobstruent; promotes the fluid secretions; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> liberally taken, gently loosens the belly. It has of late gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation in scrofulous and scrophulous disorders; and its good effects in these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> have been warranted by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Incurable cutaneous diseases have been removed by an infusion of the leaves, drank to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a pint a-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, at proper intervals, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some weeks. Boerhaave relates, that he was relieved of the gout by drinking the juice mixed with whey.

MENZINI

Pages 24-24

a celebrated Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, was professor of eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> Della Sapienza at Rome, where he died in 1704. He wrote, 1. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. 2. Satires, elegies, hymns, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. 3. Academia Tusculana, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, which passes for his masterpiece.

MEOTIS

Pages 24-24
or Palus Maeotis, a sea of Turkey, which divides Europe from Asia; extending from Crim Tartary to the mouth of the river Don or Tanais.

MEPHITIC

Pages 24-24

a name expressing any kind of noxious vapour; but generally applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vapour called fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. See Air, Fixed Air, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAS">Gas</a>, &c.

MERCATOR

Pages 24-26

one of the most celebrated geographers of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Ruremonde in 1512. He applied himself with such industry Mercator, dainty to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, that he is said to have frequently forgot to eat and drink. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. had a particular esteem for him, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Juliers made him his cosmographer. He composed a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, some geographical tables, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, &c. engraving and colouring the maps himself. He died in 1594. His method of laying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> is still used, and bears the name of Mercator's charts. Mercator (Nicholas), an eminent mathematician in the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; and came to England about the time of the restoration, where he lived many years. He was fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and endeavoured to reduce astrology to rational principles, as appeared from a MS. of his in the possession of William Jones, Esq.; He published several works, particularly Cosmographia. He gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a> by an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; which was the first appearance in the learned world of a series of this sort drawn from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curve, and that in a manner very new and abstracted. Mercator's Sailing, that performed by Mercator's chart. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>. Merchant, a person who buys and sells commodities in grofs, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> deals in exchanges; or that traffics in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, either by importation or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Formerly every one who was a buyer or seller in the retail way was called a merchant, as they still are both in France and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but here shopkeepers, or those who attend <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, have lost that appellation. Previous to a person's engaging in a general trade, and becoming an universal dealer, he ought to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> up such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of useful knowledge, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable him to carry it on with ease to himself, and without risking such losses as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ill-concerted undertakings would naturally expose him to. A merchant should therefore be acquainted with the following parts of commercial learning. 1. He should write properly and correctly. 2. Understand all the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> that have any relation to commerce. 3. Know how to keep books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and single entry, as journals, a leger, &c. 4. Be expert in the forms of invoices, accounts of sales, policies of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-parties, bills of lading, and bills of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. 5. Know the agreement between the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of all parts. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he deals in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, he ought to know the places where the different sorts of merchandizes are manufactured, in what manner they are made, what are the materials of which they are composed, and from whence they come, the preparations of these materials before working up, and the places to which they are sent after their fabrication. 7. He ought to know the lengths and breadths which silk, woollen, or hair-stuffs, linen, cottons, fulfians, &c. ought to have according to the several statutes and regulations of the places where they are manufactured, with their different prices, according to the times and seasons; and if he can add to his knowledge the different dyes and ingredients which form the various colours, it will not be useless. 8. If he confines his trade to that of oils, wines, &c. he ought to inform himself particularly of the appearances of the succeeding crops, in order to regulate his disposing of what he has on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to learn as exactly as he can, what they have produced when got in, for his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in making the necessary purchases and engagements. 9. He ought to be acquainted with the sorts of merchandize found more in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than another, those which are scarce, their different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> and qualities, and the properest method for bringing them to a good market either by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. 10. To know which are the merchandizes permitted or prohibited, as well on entering as going out of the kingdoms or states where they are made. 11. To be acquainted with the price of exchange, according to the course of different places, and what is the cause of its rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 12. To know the customs due on importation or exportation of merchandizes, according to the usage, the tarif, and regulations, of the places to which he trades. 13. To know the best manner of folding up, embaling, or tumbling, the merchandizes for their preservation. 14. To understand the price and condition of freighting and insuring ships and merchandize. 15. To be acquainted with the goodness and value of all necessaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and repairs of shipping, the different manner of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; what the wood, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, cordage, cannons, sails, and all requisites, may cost. 16. To know the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the captains, officers, and sailors, and the manner of engaging with them. 17. He ought to understand the foreign languages, or at least as many of them as he can attain to; these may be reduced to four, viz. the Spanish, which is used not only in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, but on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; the Italian, which is understood on all the coasts of the Mediterranean, and in many parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; the German, which is understood in almost all the northern countries; and the French, which is now become almost universally current. 18. He ought to be acquainted with the consular jurisdiction, with the laws, customs, and usages of the different countries he does or may trade to; and in general all the ordinances and regulations both at home and abroad that have any relation to commerce. 19. Though it is not necessary for a merchant to be very learned, it is proper that he should know something of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, particularly that of his own country; geography; hydrography, or the science of navigation; and that he be acquainted with the discoveries of the countries in which trade is established, in what manner it is settled, of the companies formed to support those establishments, and of the colonies they have sent out. All these branches of knowledge are of great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to a merchant who carries on an extensive commerce; but if his trade and his views are more limited, his learning and knowledge may be so too; but a material requisite for forming a merchant is, his having on all occasions a strict regard to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and his avoiding fraud and deceit as corroding cankers that must inevitably destroy his reputation and fortune. Trade is a thing of so universal a nature, that it is impossible for the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or of any other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, to determine all the affairs relating to it; therefore all nations, as well as Great Britain, shew a particular regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>-merchant, which is a law made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> among themselves; however, merchants and other strangers are subject to the laws of the country in which they reside. Foreign merchants are to sell their merchandize at the port where they land, in grots, and not by retail; and they are allowed to be paid in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>, in foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> or jewels, which may be exported. If a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arises between the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> and any foreign state, the merchants of that state are allowed six months time to sell their effects and leave the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; during which time they are to remain free and unmolested in their persons and goods. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Commerce, and Mercantile Law.

MERCHET

Pages 26-26

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> paid by inferior tenants to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to dispose of their daughters in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. No baron, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tenant, could marry his sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heir, without such leave purchased from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, pro maritanda filia. And many of our fertile tenants could neither send their sons to school, nor give their daughters in marriage, without express leave from the superior lord. See Kennet's Glossary in Maritagium. See also Marchet.

MERCIA

Pages 26-26

the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> kingdoms founded in England by the Saxons. Though the latest formed, it was the largest of them all, and grew by degrees to be by far the most powerful. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it was bounded by the Humber and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, which separated it from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the territories of the East-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> and Saxons; on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>. It comprehended well nigh 17 of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> counties, being equal in size to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France; very little, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all, less than the kingdom of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and superior in size to that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. Penda is regarded as its first monarch; and the kingdom is thought to derive its name from the Saxon word merce, which signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, bound, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> limit, because the other kingdoms bordered upon it on every side; and not from the river Mersey, as some would persuade us. Penda assumed the regal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> A.D. 626, and was of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 50 at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his accession; after which he reigned near 30 years. He was of a most furious and turbulent temper, breaking at different times with almost all his neighbours, calling in the Britons to his assistance, and shedding more Saxon blood than had been hitherto spilled in all their intestine quarrels. He killed two kings of Northumberland, three of the East-Angles, and compelled Kenwall, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the West-Saxons to quit his dominions. He was at length slain, with most of the princes of his family, and a multitude of his subjects, in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought not far from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, by Offa, king of Northumberland. This battle, which the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> tells us was fought at Winwidfield, A.D. 655, made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> change in the Saxon affairs, which the unbridled fury of Penda had thrown into great confusion. He had the year before killed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>, king of the East-Angles in battle, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> notwithstanding took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> with Penda. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Penda the eldest son of Penda, to whom his father had given the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdom of the Mid-Angles, had two years before married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of king Offa, and had been baptized at his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. At that time it should seem that Offa and Penda were upon good terms; but after the latter had conquered the East-Angles, he resolved to turn his arms against the kingdom of Northumberland. Offa by no means had provoked this rupture; on the contrary, Bede tells us that he offered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and jewels of great value, to purchase peace; these offers being rejected, he was reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of deciding the quarrel by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The river near which the battle was fought overflowing, there were more drowned than killed. Amongst these, as the Saxon chronicle says, there were 30 princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> line, some of whom bore the title of kings; and also Ethelred, king of the East-Angles, who fought on the side of Penda against his family and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His son Peada, who married the daughter of that conqueror, became a Christian, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after murdered as is said by the malice of his mother. His brother Wolfer becoming king of Mercia, embraced in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the Gospel, and proved a very victorious and potent monarch; and is, with no fewer than seven of his immediate successors, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> styled king of the Anglo-Saxons, though none of them are owned in that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> by the Saxon chronicle. But though possibly none of them might enjoy this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, they were undoubtedly very puissant princes, maintaining great wars, and obtaining many advantages over the sovereigns of other Saxon states, and especially the East-Angles, whom they reduced. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the Mercian territories was so ample as to admit, and so situated as to require, the constituting subordinate rulers in several provinces; to whom, especially if they were of the royal line, they gave the title of kings; which occasions some confusion in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Besides the establishing episcopal sees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the Saxon monarchs took other methods for improving and adorning their dominions; and as Mercia was the largest, so these methods were most conspicuous therein. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, as being situated in the centre, was usually, but not always, the royal residence. Penda, who was almost continually in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, lived as his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations directed, in some great town on the frontiers. Wolfer built a castle or fortified <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for his own residence, which bore his name.—Offa kept his court at Sutton Walls near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>. In each of the provinces there resided a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; and if he was of the royal blood, had usually the title of king. Peada, at the time he married Offa's daughter, had the title of king of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>.—Ethelred made his brother Merowald king of Hereford; who, dying without issue, bequeathed it to his younger brother Mercelm. The like honours were sometimes conferred upon the princesses; and hence, in Mercia especially, we occasionally read of vice-queens. By these means the laws were better executed, and the obedience of the subjects more effectually secured, and the splendor of these residences constantly kept up and augmented. At length, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> devolving sometimes on minors, and sometimes on weak princes, intestine factions also prevailing, the force of this hitherto mighty kingdom began sensibly to decline. This falling out in the days of Egbert, the most prudent as well as the most potent monarch of the West-Saxons, he took advantage of these circumstances; and having

MERCURIALIS

Pages 27-27
Mercury; a genus of the enanadria order, belonging to the dioecia clas of plants. There are three species. 1. The annus, or French mercury, with spiked flowers, male and female. This is an annual plant, with a branching stalk about a foot high, garnished with spear-shaped leaves of a pale or yellowish green colour. The male plants have spikes of herbaceous flowers, growing on the top of the stalks; these fall off soon; but the female plants, which have tecticated flowers proceeding from the side of the stalks, are succeeded by seeds, which, if permitted to scatter, will produce plenty of plants of both sexes. 2. The perennial, mountain or dog's mercury, with spiked and tecticated flowers, grows under hedges and in woods, in many parts of Britain. This hath a perennial root, which creeps in the ground; the stalks are single, and without branches, rising ten or twelve inches high, garnished with rough leaves, placed by pairs at each joint, of a dark green colour, indented on their edges: these have their male flowers growing in spikes, upon different plants from those which produce seeds. 3. The tomentosa, or shrubby hairy mercury, is a native of the south of France, Spain, and Italy. It hath a shrubby branching stalk, growing a foot and an half high, garnished with oval leaves placed by pairs, and covered with a white down on both sides. The male flowers grow in short spikes from the side of the stalks upon different plants from the first. All the species are easily propagated by seeds, and are apt to become troublesome weeds where they have once got a footing. Properties. The perennial, according to Mr Lightfoot, is of a soporific deleterious nature, noxious both to man and beast. There are instances of those who have eaten it by mistake instead of chenopodium, bonus Henricus, or English mercury, and have thereby lost their last. In the isle of Skye, it is called farglen-bracadoles; and an infusion of it is sometimes taken to bring on a salivation; but our author knows not how the experiment answers. Tournefort informs us, that the French make a syrup of the juice of the annus, two ounces of which is given as a purge; and that they use it in pellacies and chylities, mixing one quantity of honey, to one and a half of the juice. Mr Withering differs greatly from Lightfoot concerning the qualities of the perennial. "This plant," says he, "dressed like spinach, is very good eating early in the spring, and is frequently gathered for that purpose; but it is said to be hurtful to sheep." Mr Ray relates the case of a man, his wife, and three children, who experienced highly deleterious effects from eating it fried with bacon; but this was probably when the spring was more advanced, and the plant became acrimonious. Steeped in water, it affords a fine deep blue colour. Sheep and goats eat it; cows and horses refuse it.

MERCURY

Pages 27-29
