in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, n° 153, 205, 250, 214. See also <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, and Quicksilver. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of mercury in medicine seems to have been little known before the 15th century. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> looked upon it as a corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, though of itself perfectly void of acrimony, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and smell; there are examples of its having been lodged for years in cavities both of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and fleshy parts, without its having injured <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> affected them. Taken into the body in its crude state, and undivided, it passes through the intestines unchanged, and has not been found to produce any considerable effect. It has indeed been recommended in asthmas and disorders of the lungs; but the virtues attributed to it in these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> have not been warranted by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Notwithstanding the mildness and inactivity of crude quicksilver undivided; when resolved by fire into the form of fume, or otherwise divided into very minute particles, and prevented from re-uniting by the interposition of proper substances, or combined with mineral <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, it has very powerful effects; affording the most violent poisons, and the most excellent remedies, that we are acquainted with. The mercurial preparations, either given internally or introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> application, seem to liquify all the juices of the body, even those in the minutest and most remote vessels; and may be so managed as to promote excretion through all the emunctories. Hence their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use in invertebrate chronic disorders proceeding from a thickness and sluggishness of the humours, and obstinate obstructions of the excretory glands; in scrophulous and cutaneous diseases; and in the venereal lues. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> their power is not restrained by proper additions to certain emunctories, they tend chiefly to affect the mouth; and, after having fused the juices in the remoter parts, occasion a plentiful evacuation of them from the salival glands. The salutary effects of mercurials do not depend on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sensible evacuation. This medicine may be gradually introduced into the habit, so as, without occasioning any remarkable discharge, to be productive of very happy effects. To answer this purpose, it should be given in very small doses, in conjunction with such substances as determine its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to the kidneys or the pores of the skin. By this method invertebrate cutaneous and venereal distempers have been cured, without any other sensible excretion than a gentle increase of perspiration or urine. Where there are ulcers in any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, they discharge for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> a very febrile <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the quantity of which becomes gradually less. Mercury, lefs, and at length the ulcer kindly heals. If the mercury should at any time, from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or the like, affect the mouth, it may be restrained by omitting a dose, and, by warmth or suitable medicines, promoting the perspiration. Mercury, in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. See Hermes. Most of the actions and inventions of the Egyptian Mercury have likewise been ascribed to the Grecian, who was said to be the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. No one of all the heathen divinities had so many functions allotted to him as this god; he had constant employment both <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, having been the common minister and messenger of the whole Pantheon; particularly of his father Jupiter, whom he served with indefatigable labour, and sometimes indeed in a capacity of no very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> kind. Lucian is very pleasant upon the multitude of his avocations; and, according to the confession of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, Mercury was no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, but rather one who inspired mankind with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, learning, and the ornamental arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, than with courage. The pious emperor, however, omits some of his attributes; for this god was not only the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of trade, but also of theft and fraud. Amphion is said, by Pausanias, to have been the first that erected an altar to this god; who, in return, invested him with such extraordinary powers of music (and masonry), as to enable him to fortify the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of his lyre. Horace gives us the best part of his character. Thou god of wit, from Atlas sprung, Who by persuasive power of tongue, And graceful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, refin'd The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> kind, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a>! winged messenger of Jove, And all th' immortal pow'rs above. Sweet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> lyre, Thy praise shall all its sounds inspire. Artful and cunning to conceal What'er in sportive theft you steal, When from the god who gilds the pole, E'en yet a boy, his herds you stole; With angry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> the threat'ning pow'r Had thee thy fraudulent prey before; But of his quiver too beguiled, Pleas'd with the theft, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> smil'd. You were the worthy Prism's guide, When safe from Agamemnon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, Through hostile <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, which round him spread Their flaming fires, as they lay hid. Unscathed spirits you convey To blissful seas and joys divine; And, powerful, with thy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> wand, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, unshaded crowd command: Thus grateful does thy office prove To gods below, and gods above. Francis. This ode contains the substance of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Mercury, attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets relate the manner in which the Grecian Mercury discovered the lyre; and tell us that it was an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> strings; a circumstance which makes it essentially different from that said to have been invented by the Egyptian Mercury, which had but three. However, there have been many claimants besides Mercury to the seven-stringed lyre. See Lyre. His most magnificent temple was on mount Cyllene, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. He is described by the poets as a fair beardless youth, with flaxen <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, lively blue eyes, and a smiling countenance. He has wings fixed to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and sandals, and holds the caduceus (or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> with two wings on the top) in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and is frequently represented with a purse, to show that he was the god of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>. The animals sacred to him were the dog, the goat, and the cock. In all the sacrifices offered to him, the tongues of the victims were burnt; and those who escaped imminent danger, sacrificed to him a calf with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Mercury, § in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. See Astronomy, n° 4, 20, 44, 108, 112. Mercury, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, for the purple <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> used in the arms of sovereign princes. Mercy-seat, in Jewish antiquity. See Propitiatory. Merganser. See Mergus. Mergus, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus of birds of the order of anseres; distinguished by having the beak of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and hooked at the extremities, and its denticulations of a subulated form. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The cucullatus, or crested diver of Catesby, has a globular crest, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> on each side; and the body is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> above, and white below. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. See Plate CLXXVI. fig. 4. 2. The merganser, or goosander, is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. These birds frequent our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and other fresh waters, especially in hard winters; they are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, and live on fish. They are never seen in the southern parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; when they retire far <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to breed; for in that season they have been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>. They are uncommonly <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and scarce eatable. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> weighs four pounds: its length is two feet four inches; the breadth three feet two. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is three inches long, narrow, and finely toothed or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>; the colour of that and of the irises is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUN">dun</a> divers, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, is less than the male: the head and upper part of the neck is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a>; the throat white: the feathers on the hind part are long, and form a pendent crest: the back, the coverts of the wings, and the tail, are of a deep ash-colour: the greater quill-feathers are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, the lesser white; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and middle of the belly are white, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. 3. The serratior, or redbreasted merganser, weighs about two pounds: the length is one foot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches, the breadth two feet seven; the bill is three inches long; the lower mandible red; the upper dusky; the irises a purplish red: head and throat a fine changeable black and green: on the former a long pendent crest of the same colour; the tail short and brown; the legs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured. The head and upper part of the female are of a deep rust-colour, and the tail ash-coloured. These birds breed in the northern parts of Great Britain. 4. The cafter has a crested ash-coloured head, a white throat, and a black bill and legs. It inhabits the south of Europe. 5. The albellus, or smew, weighs about 34 ounces: the length 18 inches, the breadth 26; the bill is near two inches long, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> colour; the head is adorned with a long crest, white above, and black beneath: the head, neck, and whole under part of the body, are of a pure white; the tail is of a deep ash-colour, the legs a bluish grey. The female, or buff diver, 6. The minutus, or redheaded smew, weighs about 15 ounces; the length one foot four inches, the breadth one foot eleven; the bill is of a lead colour; the head slightly crested, and of a rust colour; the hind part of the neck is of a deep grey, the forepart clouded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> colour of the same kind; the back and tail are of a dusky ash-colour, the legs of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> ash-colour.—It is a native of Europe.

MERIDIAN

Pages 29-29

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle supposed to be drawn through any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; and to which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is always perpendicular at noon.—In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the circle is supposed to be in the heavens, and exactly perpendicular to the terrestrial one.

MERIONETHSIRE

Pages 29-29

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, on the south has the county of Cardigan, on the north those of Carnarvon and Denbigh, on the east those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a> and Denbigh, and on the west the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Its length is about 35 miles, its breadth 25, and its circumference 108; containing between 4 and 50,000 acres, 637 parishes, 3 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 26 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and about 17000 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this county, which is more encumbered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> than any other in Wales, is exceeding sharp and bleak; and would be very unwholesome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the vapours from the Irish sea were not in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> dispersed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> winds to which this county is subject. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very rocky and barren; except in the valleys, which yield good corn, and pasture for cattle and sheep. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is so mountainous, the inhabitants apply themselves chiefly to grazing, keeping vast flocks of sheep, deer, and goats, in the mountains, and living much upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, fowl, and fish, especially herrings. They have but little corn, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle are generally sold to the English. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> rivers of the county are the Dyfi <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Tory, the Avon, the Drwydy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, which last runs through the lake called Llyn Tegid or Pimble Meer, without mixing its waters with those of the lake, as is supposed: for the salmon, with which the river abounds, are never taken out of the main stream; and the givineads, a fish peculiar to the lake, are never found in it. This lake is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; and winds, it is pretended, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make it overflow, but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-floods never. The fish in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and the herbs on the rocks and mountains here, like those in Caerarvonshire and other hilly parts of Wales, are said to be much the same as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. This county lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>: it sends no member to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, except a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire; for it has no towns of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>.—Dr Campbell is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this county is capable of much improvement, if the inhabitants understood their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and were industrious.

MERIT

Pages 29-29

signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is more particularly applied to signify the moral goodness of the actions of men, and the rewards to which those actions entitle them.

MERLIN

Pages 29-29

a famous English poet, and reputed prophet, flourished at the end of the 5th century. Many surprising and ridiculous things are related of him. Several English authors have represented him as the son of an incubus, and as transported from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to England the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> plain. Extravagant prophecies and other works are also attributed to him, on which some authors have written commentaries.

MERLON

Pages 29-29

in fortification, is that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> which is terminated by two embrasures of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>.

MERMAID

Pages 29-30
or Merman, a sea-creature frequently talked of, supposed half human and half a fish. However naturalists may doubt of the reality of mermen or mermaids, we have testimony enough to establish it; though, how far these testimonies may be authentic, we cannot take upon us to say. In the year 1187, as Layar informs us, such a monster was fished up in the county of Suffolk, and kept by the governor for six months. It bore so near a conformity with man, that nothing seemed wanting to it but speech. One day it took the opportunity of making its escape; and, plunging into the sea, was never more heard of. Hist. de Angleterre, P. I. p. 493. In the year 1430, after a huge tempest, which broke down the dikes in Holland, and made way for the sea into the meadows, &c., some girls of the town of Edam in West-Frieseland, going in a boat to milk their cows, perceived a mermaid embarrassed in the mud, with a very little water. They took it into their boat, and brought it with them to Edam, dressed it in women's apparel, and taught it to spin. It fed like one of them, but could never be brought to offer at speech. Some time afterwards it was brought to Haarlem, where it lived for some years, though still showing an inclination to the water. Parival relates that they had given it some notion of a Deity, and that it made its reverences very devoutly whenever it passed by a crucifix. Delices de Hollande. In the year 1560, near the island of Manar, on the western coast of the island of Ceylon, some fishermen brought up, at one draught of a net, seven mer men and maids; of which, several Jesuits, and among the rest F. Hen. Henriques, and Dimas Bosquez physicians to the viceroy of Goa, were witnesses. The physician, who examined them with a great deal of care, and made dissection thereof, affirms, that all the parts both internal and external were found perfectly conformable to those of men. See the Hist. de la compagnie de Jésus, P. II. T. IV. n° 276, where the relation is given at length. We have another account of a merman, near the great rock called Diamond, on the coast of Martinico. The persons who saw it, gave in a precise description of it before a notary. They affirmed that they saw it wipe its hand over its face, and even heard it blow its nose. Another creature of the same species was caught in the Baltic in the year 1531, and sent as a present to Sigismund king of Poland, with whom it lived three days, and was seen by all the court. Another very young one was taken near Rocca de Sintra, as related by Damian Goes. The king of Portugal and the grand master of the order of St James, are said to have had a suit at law to determine which party these monsters belong to. In Pontopidan's href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of Norway, also, we have accounts of mermaids; but not more remarkable or any way better attested than the above. MERNs, or Kincardinshire, a county of Scotland, stretching 27 miles in length, and 20 in breadth, is bounded on the east by the German ocean, on the south by the river of North Esk, on the west by Angus, and on the north by the river Dee and Aberdeenshire. The country is pretty plain and level, fruitful in corn and pasturage, producing an infinite number of fir-trees, besides a great number of agreeable plantations; and along the sea-coasts there are many convenient creeks and harbours.—The people are Lowlanders, civil, hospitable, and industrious.—The name Merns is by some derived from that of a valiant nobleman, who, subduing the country, received it in reward from Kenneth II. Cambden supposes it to retain part of the ancient name of Vernicones. The other name is derived from Kincardin, its ancient capital, now an inconsiderable village. The stocking-trade employs the natives from the banks of the Dee to Stone-hive; from thence to the Northesk they are wholly employed in weaving.

MEROE

Pages 30-30

(anc. geogr.), an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; with a cognominal town, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Ethiopians. Here the shadow is said to decrease twice a-year, viz. when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is in the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Taurus and in the 14th of Leo. (Pliny.) Josephus says, that its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name was Saba; but changed to Meroe by Cambyses, either after his father <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> after his consort, who died there, (Strabo). All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> represent Meroe as an island, but in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times it is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; to which greater <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> is to be given, as more accurate than the ancient accounts.

MEROPS

Pages 30-30

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of picae. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is crooked, flat, and carinated; the tongue is jagged at the point; and the feet are of the walking kind. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. 1. The apiafter, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-eater, has an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-coloured back; the belly and tail are of a bluish green; and the throat is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. It inhabits the south of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. 2. The viridis, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bee-eater, is green, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> belt on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and the throat and tail are black. 3. The congener is yellowish, with a green rump. It inhabits the south of Europe. 4. The fulvicollis is green, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> line both above and below the eyes, and a yellow throat. It is found in Madagascar. 5. The cinereus is variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and yellow, with the two longest quill-feathers of the tail red. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. 6. The cafer is grey, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> tail. It is a native of Ethiopia.

MERSE

Pages 30-30

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, called also <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a>. This last name it derives from the town of Berwick, which was the head of the shire before it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, and obtained the appellation of Mers <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, because it was one of the borders towards England. It is washed on the south and east by the river Tweed and the German Ocean, bounded on the west by Tweedale, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>. It extends 24 miles from east to west, and the breadth amounts to 16. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rough and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, exhibiting hills, moors, and mosses, with intermediate valleys, which are pleasant and fruitful. It is watered by many streams; and particularly by the famous Tweed, which, rising from Mersenne, the same hills that gave birth to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNAN">Annan</a>, runs with a rapid course thro' Tweedale Forest and Teviotdale, and after a course of 50 miles disembogues itself into the German Ocean. Notwithstanding the length of its course, it is not navigable above Berwick, where there is a noble <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over it, consisting of 15 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>: there was another at Melros, where nothing but the piers now remain. A third, of five arches, is maintained at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEEBLES">Peebles</a>; and a fourth has some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago been built at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a>. The shire of Berwick is generally distinguished into the three divisions of Mers, Lammermuir, and Lauderdale. The Mers is low, pleasant, and tolerably fruitful in corn. Lammermuir is a hilly country, abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and yielding good pasture for sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. Lauderdale is a tract of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> lying on each side of the river Lauder, agreeably varied with hill, dale, and forest, producing good store of corn and pasturage, and giving the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Maitland; but the most fruitful and populous parts of Berwickshire, are those that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> along the Tweed, and on both sides of the lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">Water</a>, Black Water, and Eye. The seats of noblemen and gentlemen abound in this county. Berwick was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town until it fell into the hands of the English, and was annexed to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward IV. At present the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Duns.

MERSENNE

Pages 30-30

in Latin Mercennius, a learned French author, born at Oyé, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, anno 588. He studied at La Flèche at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> with Des Cartes; with whom he contracted a strict friendship, which lasted till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and studied at the Sorbonne, and in 1611 entered himself among the Minims. He became well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. He was of a tranquil, sincere, and engaging temper; and was universally esteemed by persons illustrious for their birth, their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and their learning. He taught philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and at length became superior of that convent; but being willing to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with more freedom, he resigned all the posts he enjoyed in his order, and travelled into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are: 1. Questiones celeberrimae in Genesim. 2. Harmonicarum libri. 3. De sonorum natura, causis, & effectibus. 4. Cogitata physico-mathematica. 5. La vérité des Sciences. 6. Les questions immortelles. He died at Paris in 1648. He had the reputation of being one of the best men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. No person was more curious in penetrating into the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and carrying all the arts and sciences to their utmost perfection. He was in a manner the centre of all the men of learning, by the mutual correspondence which he managed between them. He omitted no means to engage them to publish their works; and the world is obliged to him for several excellent discoveries, which, had it not been for him, would perhaps have been lost.

MERULA

Pages 31-31

born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, a famous lawyer, historian, and linguist, was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> after Lipsius. He wrote, 1. Commentaries on Ennius. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Erasmus and Junius. 3. A cosmography. 4. A treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and died in 1607.

MERUS

Pages 31-31

(anc. geogr.), a mountain of the Hither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hanging over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> Nyssa, built by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Cophen and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. The name, denoting the thigh, gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Bacchus being inserted into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s thigh, and being born twice; because in this mountain he and his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are said to have been preserved, when <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and pestilence raged in the plains below. MERA-DE-Astra, formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, seated on the river Guadalata, between Arcos and Xeres de la Frontera; but now only a large heap of ruins. Here the Arabs conquered Roderick the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, and by that victory became masters of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 713.

MESCHED

Pages 31-31

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Khorasan; fortified with several towers, and famous for the magnificent sepulchre of Iman Rifa, of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, to whom the Persians pay <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. It is seated on a mountain near this town, in which are fine turquoise-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 59° 25', N. Lat. 37° 0'.

MESPILUS

Pages 31-32

the Medlar; a genus of the pentagynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz: 1. The Germanica, German mespilus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> medlar, rises with a deformed tree-stem, branching irregularly 15 or 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; spear-shaped leaves, downy underneath; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, singly from the sides of the branches; succeeded by large roundish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> fruit, the size of middling apples, which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in October, but are not eatable till beginning to decay. The varieties are, common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> German medlar—smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a> medlar—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-shaped Italian medlar. This species and varieties are all cultivated in the English gardens for the fruit; but the German or Dutch medlar, and the Nottingham kind, are the most common; and the latter of which two, though a smaller fruit, is rather preferable for richness and poignancy of flavour. These kinds of fruit are never eatable until they begin to rot; for when firm and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, they are of a singularly austere disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; yet having lain some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after being gathered, till they begin to assume a state of decay and become soft, they acquire a delicious flavour, extremely agreeable to many, though to others altogether unpalatable. All the sorts ripen in the latter-end of October, or beginning of November; when being gathered, some should be laid in moist bran, in several layers, to forward their decay; others on straw in the fruiteries; those in the bran <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> begin to be ready for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in about a fortnight; and those laid on straw will come gradually forward in succession. 2. The arbutusfolia, arbutus-leaved mespilus, hath a shrubby stem, branching erectly five or six feet high; lanceolate, crenated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> leaves, downy underneath; and from the sides and ends of the branches, small white flowers in clusters; succeeded by small, roundish, purple fruit, like haws. 3. The amelanchier, or shrubby medlar, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fruit, rises with several shrubby, slender, hairy stems, branching... Mespilus branching moderately about four feet high, having purplish branches; oval, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> leaves, downy underneath; and small white flowers, in clusters at the ends of the branches; succeeded by small black fruit. 4. The chamomile-pilus, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> medlar, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called balsam quince, hath a shrubby, slender, smooth stem, branching weakly four or five feet high, having purplish branches; oval, serrated, smooth leaves, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> foot-stalks; and from the axillae, purple flowers, collected into round heads, with narrow, purplish, deciduous bracteas; succeeded by small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> fruit. 5. The cotoneaster, commonly called dwarf quince, rises with a shrubby, smooth stem, branching four or five feet high, the branches slender and reddish; oval entire leaves on short foot-stalks; and from the axillae, small close-fitting purple flowers, two or three together; succeeded by small, roundish, bright-red fruit. 6. The Canadensis, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> snowy mespilus, hath a shrubby, smooth stem, branching four or five feet high, with smooth, purplish branches; oval-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, serrated, smooth leaves, on long footstalks; and all the branches terminated by clusters of snowy-white flowers; succeeded by small, purplish fruit, like haws. 7. The pyracantha, or ever-green <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, rises with a shrubby, spinous stem, branching diffusely 12 or 14 feet high, the branches slender and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, with a dark-greenish bark, armed with long sharp spines; spear-shaped-oval, crenated, ever-green leaves; and all the shoots terminated by numerous clusters of whitish flowers; succeeded by large bunches of beautiful red berries, remaining all winter, and exhibiting a very ornamental appearance. All these seven species of mespilus are of the tree and shrub kind; the first six sorts are deciduous, the seventh an ever-green: the leaves are universally simple; those of the mespilus Germanica very large, the others mostly of moderate size, and which in most of the sorts grow upon short foot-stalks. They all flower abundantly every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the flowers universally hermaphrodite, and consisting each of five large roundish petals, 20 stamens, and five styles. They are all very hardy, and succeed in any common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation, and their propagation and culture is very easy. The first sort and varieties are cultivated as fruit-trees, principally as standards, sometimes also as espaliers for variety. The other species are very proper furniture for any ornamental plantation, where they will make an agreeable variety with their different foliage; and their flowers make a fine appearance, as also their fruit in autumn and winter, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not devoured by birds, remain long on the branches, and afford a fine variety in those seasons. The pyracantha, being rather of flexible growth, is most commonly trained against walls or the fronts of houses, both for the support of its flexible branches, and that it may exhibit its berries more ornamentally. When it is designed to have any of the common medlars as fruit-trees, they may be trained either as dwarfs, for dwarf standards, or for espaliers, or trained as half or full standards; and managed in either of those modes of training nearly as other fruit-trees, particularly the apple and pear; and are raised either by seed, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, or by budding, but either of the two latter methods are the most certain for continuing the sorts without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>: observing, after shortening their first shoots from the graft or bud, where it shall seem necessary to force out a proper supply of wood to form a head, to train the branches afterwards principally at full length, and let the standards branch out in their own way.

MESSANA

Pages 32-32

(anc. geog.), the first town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> on crossing over from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situate on the strait now called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, (Italics). Anciently called Zanclis, according to Diodorus Siculus, from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Zanclus; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> Zanclon, denoting a sickle, alluding to the curvity of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>: a name appropriated by the poets; and hence Zanclites, the people, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Pausanias). The other name Messana is from the Messenii of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, (Strabo). <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> ascribes its origin to Anaxilas the Messenian, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Rhegium, who received all comers, calling the town after the name of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Greeks always call it Messene; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Messana constantly, to distinguish it from Messene of Peloponnesus. Now Messina.

MESSENA

Pages 32-32
or Missene, an inland town, and the capital of Messenia, a country of Peloponnesus; erroneously placed by Ptolemy on the coast. It was built by Epaminondas, who recalled all the Messenian exiles, and gave the town the name of Messene. A place varying in point of strength and situation with Corinth, according to Strabo; and therefore Demetrius Pharius advised Philip, father of Perseus, that if he wanted to have Peloponnesus in his power, he should make himself master of these two towns, as thus he would have the ox by both horns.

MESSENGERS

Pages 35-35

are certain officers chiefly employed under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the secretaries of state, and always in readiness to be sent with all kinds of dispatches foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. They also, by virtue of the secretaries warrants, take up persons for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other offences against the state. The prisoners they apprehend are usually kept at their own houses, for each of which they are allowed 6s. 8d. per <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: and when they are sent abroad, they have a fixed allowance for their journey, viz. 30l. for going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; 25l. for going to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and to other places in the same proportion; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is advanced, for the expense of their journey. Their standing salary is 45l. per annum; and their posts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> purchased, are deemed worth 300l. The messengers wait 20

MESSENIA

Pages 32-35

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, mostly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a>, situate between <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol6.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a> to the west, and Laconica to the east. Anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a> under Menelaus, and called Messene by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; interpreted by the scholiast, Messenae Regia. Messenii, the people, reduced to a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> and subjection by the Spartans; Messenius, the epithet. This country is famous in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, on account of the resistance made by the Messenians against the Spartans, and the exploits of their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Aristomenes. The first hostilities commenced about the year 652 B.C. on what occasion is uncertain. Though the Messenians were inferior in the knowledge of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> to the Spartans; yet, by keeping for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the defensive, they improved so much, that in three years time they found themselves in a capacity of giving <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to their enemies in the open field; nor did they appear to be in any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> inferior either in courage <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> conduct: the war was therefore protracted, with various success, on both sides. At last, both consulted the oracle at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; and received for answer, "that whoever should first dedicate 100 tripods in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at Ithome, a strong-hold of the Messenians, should be masters of The inhabitants of Messenia, on hearing this, having no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to make the tripods of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, fell to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them out in wood; but before this could be accomplished, a Spartan having got into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> by stratagem, dedicated 100 little tripods of clay: which threw the Messenians into such despair, that they at last submitted to the Spartans. The new subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> were treated with the utmost barbarity by these cruel tyrants; so that in 685 B.C., a new war commenced under Arimomenes, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of unconquerable valour, and enthusiastically fond of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He perceived that the Argives and Arcadians, who were called the allies of the Lacedemonians, adhered to them only through fear of their power; but that in reality they hated them, and wished to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injuries they had done them. To these Arimomenes applied; and receiving an answer conformable to his wishes, he engaged his countrymen unanimously to take up arms. About a year after the revolt began, and before either party had received any auxiliaries, the Spartans and Messenians met at a village called Derce, where an obstinate engagement ensued. Arimomenes was conceived to have performed more than mortal achievements: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> therefore, respect being also had to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, his countrymen unanimously saluted him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he modestly waved, alleging, that he took up arms to set them free, and not to make himself <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>: he consented, however, to accept the title of general, with a power of doing whatsoever he thought requisite for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public. Knowing well the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, he resolved to intimidate the Spartans, by showing them what he was sure they would take for an ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. Disguising himself therefore, he went privately to the city, where, in the night, he hung up a shield on the wall of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, with this inscription: Arimomenes dedicates this, out of the spoils of the Spartans, to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. It was easily perceived that this war would be both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and bloody; the Lacedemonians therefore sent deputies to Delphi, to inquire of the oracle concerning its event: the answer they received was, That it behoved the Spartans to seek a leader from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The Athenians, naturally envious of the Spartans, granted their request indeed, but in such a manner as manifested their spite; for they sent them for a general Tyrtaeus, a schoolmaster and poet, lame of one foot, and who was suspected to be a little out of his wits. But here their skill failed them; for this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, notwithstanding his despicable appearance, proved of great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to Sparta, teaching them how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> good, and how to bear up under evil fortune. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Arimomenes had drawn together a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the Eleans, Argives, Sicyonians, and Arcadians, having sent troops to his assistance; the Spartans in this, as in the former war, having no ally but Corinth. The Spartan kings, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of their city, no sooner took the field, than, notwithstanding their inferiority in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they offered the enemy battle, which Arimomenes readily accepted.—It was long, obstinate, and bloody; but in the end the Messenians were victorious, and the Lacedemonians put to flight, with a great slaughter. It is scarce to be conceived how much the Spartans were struck with this defeat: they grew weary of the war, dissatisfied with their kings, disdained of their own power, and, in a word, sunk into a state of general uneasiness and want of spirit. It was now that the Athenian general convinced them, that he was capable of fulfilling all the promises of the oracle; he encouraged them by his poems, directed them by his counsels, and recruited their broken armies with chosen men from among the Helotes. Arimomenes, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, acted with no less <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and vigour. He thought it not enough to restore the reputation of the Messenians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not also restore their wealth and power: he therefore taught them to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively against their enemies; and, entering the territories of Sparta, he took and plundered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHAROS">Pharos</a>, a considerable borough in Laconia, putting all such as made any resistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, carrying off at the same time an immense booty. This, however, was an injury which the Spartans could not brook with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>; they therefore sent immediately a body of forces to overtake the Messenians, which accordingly they did: but Arimomenes routed these pursuers, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make a mighty slaughter of them, till such time as he was disabled by having a spear thrust in his side, which occasioned his being carried out of the battle. His cure, which took up some time, being finished, he resolved to carry the war even to the gates of Sparta; and to that purpose raised a very great army: but, whether he found his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> impracticable, or was really diverted by some dream, he gave out, that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, with their sister Helena, had appeared to him, and commanded him to desist. A short time after this retreat, going with a small party to make an incursion, and attempting to take prisoners some women who were celebrating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> near Egira, a village in Laconia, those zealous matrons fell upon him and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with such fury, that they put them to flight, and took him prisoner: however, he soon afterwards made his escape, and rejoined his forces. In the third year of the war, the Spartans, with a great force, entered Messenia, whither Arimocrates king of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> came, with a great body of troops, to the assistance of his allies: Arimomenes therefore made no difficulty of fighting when the Spartans approached; but they entering privately into a negociation with Arimocrates, engaged him with bribes and promises to betray his confederates. When the battle began, the deceitful Arcadian represented to the forces under his command, the mighty danger they were in, and the great difficulty there would be of retreating into their own country, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the battle should be lost: he then pretended, that the sacrifices were ominous; and, having terrified his Arcadians into the disposition of mind fittest to serve his purpose, he not only drew them off from both wings, but, in his flight, forced through the Messenian ranks, and put them too in confusion. Arimomenes and his troops, however, drew themselves into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> order, that they might defend themselves the best they could: and indeed they had need of all their valour and skill; for the Lacedemonians, who expected this event, immediately attacked and surrounded them on all sides. Fortune was, on this occasion, too powerful either for the courage or the conduct of the Messenians; so that, notwithstanding excepting that Aristomenes had leave to put on his armour. Three days he continued in this dismal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, lying upon, and covered over with, dead bodies. The third <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was almost famished through want of food, and almost poisoned with the stench of corrupted carcases, when he heard a fox gnawing a body near him. Upon this he uncovered his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and perceiving the fox <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> by him, he with one hand feized one of its hind-legs, and with the other defended his face, by catching hold of its jaw when it attempted to bite him. Following as well as he could his struggling guide, the fox at last thrust his head into a little hole; and Aristomenes then letting go his leg, he soon forced his way through, and opened a passage to the welcome rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, from which the noble Messenian had been so long debarred. Feeble as he was, Aristomenes wrought himself an outlet with his nails; and travelling by night with all the expedition he could, at length arrived safe at Era, to the great joy and amazement of his countrymen. When this news was first blazed abroad, the Spartans would have had it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a fiction; but Aristomenes soon put the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it out of doubt, by falling on the posts of the Corinthians, who, as allies of the Spartans, had a considerable body of troops before Era. Most of their officers, with a multitude of private men, he slew; pillaged their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and, in short, did so much mischief, that the Spartans, under the pretence of an approaching festival, agreed to a cessation of arms for 40 days, that they might have time to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead. On this occasion, Aristomenes for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time celebrated the hecatomphalia, or the sacrifice appointed for those who had killed 100 of the enemy with their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He had performed the same before and after his second battle; and he lived to do it a third time: which must appear wonderful to the reader, when he is informed, that, notwithstanding this truce, certain Cretan archers in the service of the Spartans, seized Aristomenes as he was walking without the walls, and carried him away a prisoner. There were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of them in all; two of them immediately flew with the news to Sparta, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> remained to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, whom they bound, and conducted to a lone cottage inhabited only by a widow and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. It so fell out, that the young woman dreamt the night before, that she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a lion without claws, bound, and dragged along by wolves; and that she having loosed his bonds, and given him claws, he immediately tore the wolves to pieces. As soon as Aristomenes came into the cottage, and her mother, who knew him, had told her who he was, she instantly concluded that her dream was fulfilled; and therefore plied the Cretans with drink, and, when they were asleep, took a poniard from one of them, cut the thongs with which Aristomenes was bound, and then put it into his hands. He presently verified her vision, by putting all his guards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and then carried her and her mother to Era, where, as a reward for her service, he married the young woman to his son Gorgus, then about 18 years of age. When Era had held out near eleven years, it fell into the hands of Sparta by an accident: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of one Empiramus, a Spartan commander, driving his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s cattle to drink at the river Neda, met frequently with the wife of a Messenian, whom he engaged... engaged in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>. This woman gave him notice, that her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was without the wall; so that he could come to it without danger, when the good man was abroad; and she likewise gave him intelligence when her husband was upon duty in the garrison. The Spartan failed not to come at the time appointed; but they had not been long in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> before the husband returned, which put the house into great confusion: the woman, however, secured her gallant; and then let in her husband, whom she received, in appearance, with great joy, inquiring again and again by what excess of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> she was blessed with his return. The innocent Messenian told her, that Aristomenes being detained in his bed by a wound, the soldiers, knowing that he could not walk the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, had a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to retire to their houses, to avoid the inclemency of the season. The Spartan no sooner heard this, than he crept softly out of doors, and hastened away to carry the news to his master. It so happened, that the kings were at this time absent from the camp, and Empiramus had the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> command of the army. As soon as he received this information, he ordered his army to begin its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, though it rained excessively, and there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-light. The fellow guided them to the ford, and managed matters so well that they seized all the Messenian posts: yet, after all, they were afraid to engage; darkness, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, heavy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, together with the dread of Aristomenes, keeping them quiet in the places they had seized. As soon as it was light, the attack began; and Era had been quickly taken, if only the men had defended it; but the women fought with such fury, and, by their mingling in the fray, brought such an accession of numbers, as made the event doubtful. Three days and two nights this desperate engagement lasted: at last, all hopes of preserving the city being lost, Aristomenes drew off his wearied troops. Early the fourth morning, he disposed the women and children in the centre, the Messenian youth in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and rear, the less able men in the main body: himself commanded the van; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a> was brought up by Gorgus and Manticles, the former the son of Aristomenes, the latter of Theocles, a Messenian of great merit, who fell with much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in this attack, fighting valiantly in the cause of his country. When all things were ready, Aristomenes caused the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to be thrown open; and, brandishing his spear, marched directly towards the Spartan troops, in order to force a passage. Empiramus, perceiving his intent, ordered his men to open to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, and fairly gave them a passage; so that Aristomenes marched off in triumph, as it were, to Arcadia. The Arcadians, when they heard that Era was taken, were very desirous of succouring their old confederates in this deep distress: they therefore intreated their king Aristocrates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them into Messenia. But he, corrupted by the Lacedemonians, persuaded them that it was too late; that the Messenians were all cut off; and that such a step would only expose them to the fury of the conquerors. When the thing appeared to be otherwise, and it was known that Aristomenes was on the frontiers of Arcadia, they went in crowds to carry him <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and to testify their readiness to afford him and those under his command all the assistance in their power. Aristomenes desired to be heard before a general <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; which being accordingly convoked, he there opened one of the boldest and best-laid schemes recorded in history: he said, that he had yet 500 undaunted soldiers, who, at his command, would undertake anything; that it was very probable most of the Spartans were employed in pillaging Era, and that therefore he determined to march and surprize Sparta; which appeared so sensible, that all the assembly loudly commended his great capacity and unshaken courage. Aristocrates, however, took care to betray him; having, by various pretences, retarded the execution of the project. The Arcadians, who began to suspect him, waited for and surprized the messengers as they came back. They took the letters from him, and read them openly in the assembly. The purport of them was, that they acknowledged his great kindness both now and in the battle; and promised, that the Lacedemonians would be grateful. As soon as the letters were read, the Arcadians fell to stoning their king, frequently calling upon the Messenians to assist them; which, however, they did not, waiting for Aristomenes's orders; who, far from triumphing in this spectacle, stood still, with his eyes fixed on the ground, which he wet with his tears, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> pierced with sorrow to see a crowned head so shamefully and so deservedly put to death. The Arcadians afterwards erected a monument over him, with an inscription to perpetuate his infamy. As for the Messenians under the command of Gorgus and Manticles, they passed over into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; where they founded the city of Messene, one of the most famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Aristomenes remained, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; where he married all his daughters, except the youngest, to persons of great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, inquiring of the oracle at Delphi whom he should espouse, that his subjects might be happy under his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, was directed to marry the daughter of the most worthy of the Greeks; which answer was immediately understood to point at the virgin daughter of Aristomenes. Her therefore he demanded, and received; Aristomenes accompanying him back to his dominions, where he formed a scheme of uniting the Lydians and Medes against the Spartans, resolving, with this view, to go into Media, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>: but while he meditated these great things, death surprized him, and thereby freed Lacedemon from the most formidable enemy she ever had.

MESSIAH

Pages 35-36

a word signifying one anointed, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> installed into an office by unction. It was usual among the Jews to anoint kings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priests, and sometimes prophets, at the designation or installment of them, to signify emblematically the mental qualifications necessary for discharging these offices. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, and Joash, kings of Judah, received the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> unction. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons received the sacerdotal, and Elisha the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Elijah received the prophetic, unction.—The name Messiah, Anointed, or Christ (Χριστός), was given to the kings and high-priests of the Jews. The patriarchs and prophets are also called by the name of Messiah or the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s anointed. See 1 Sam. xii. 3, 5; 1 Chron. xvi. 22; Psa. cv. 15. But this name Messiah was principally and by way of eminence given by the Jews to their expected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Deliverer, whose coming they'd fill vainly wait; and is a name the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> apply to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, in whom the prophecies relating to the Messiah were accomplished. The sum of these prophecies is, That there should be a glorious person, named Messiah, descended from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, who should be born at Bethlehem, of a virgin of the family of David, then in its decline, before the Jews ceased to be a people, while the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> temple was standing, and about 500 years after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; who, though appearing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumstances, should be introduced by a remarkable forerunner, whose business it should be to awaken the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the people. That this illustrious person called Messiah, should himself be eminent for the piety, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and benevolence of his character, and the miraculous works he should perform: yet that, notwithstanding all this, he should be rejected and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the Jews; but should afterwards be raised from the dead, and exalted to a glorious throne, on which he should through all generations continue to rule, at the same time making intercession for sinners. That great calamities should for the present be brought on the Jews for rejecting him: whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God should by his means be erected among the Gentiles, and disperse itself even unto the ends of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; wherever it came, destroying idolatry, and establishing true <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and righteousness. In a word, That this glorious Person should be regarded by all who believed in him, as a divine teacher, an atoning sacrifice, and a royal governor: by means of whom God would make a covenant with his people, very different from that made with Israel of old; in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they should be restored to, and established in, the divine favour, and fixed in a state of perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. See Jesus Christ, and Christianity.

MESSUAGE

Pages 36-36

Messuagium, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> adjoining assigned for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. By the name of messuage may a garden, shop, mill, cottage, chamber, cellar, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>.—In Scotland, messuage denotes what is called in England the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-house; viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> dwelling-house within any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>.

METACARPUS

Pages 36-36
