a father of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, bishop of Olympus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Patara in Lycia, and afterward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, suffered martyrdom at Chalcei in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> toward the end of Diocletian's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> in the year 302. He composed many works in a clear and elaborate style, which were extant in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Father Combesius collected several considerable fragments of this writer, cited by Epiphanius, Photius, and others; and printed them with notes of his own, together with the works of Amphilochius, and Andreas Cretenis, in folio, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1644.

METIUS

Pages 122-123

of Alkmaer, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the inventor of telephones with glasses, one of which he presented to the States-General in 1609. Tubes extended, by uniting them, to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length, were known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; but Metius was the first who added glasses, and he was indebted to chance for the discovery: he had frequently observed some schoolboys playing upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their co- py books rolled up in the shape of tubes, to look at each other, to which they sometimes added pieces of ice at each end, to view distant objects: this led him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of optic glasses.

METO

Pages 123-123

a famous mathematician of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, 432 B.C., published his Analecatoride, that is, his Cycle of Nineteen years, by which he endeavoured to adjust the course of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and to make the solar and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> years begin at the same point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See CYCLE OF THE MOON.

METONYMY

Pages 123-123

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, is a trope in which one name is put for another, on account of the near relation there is between them. See ORATORY, no. 51.

METOPE

Pages 123-123

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIGLYPHS">triglyphs</a> of the Doric freeze, which among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used to be painted or adorned with carved <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, representing the heads of oxen, or utensils used in sacrifices.

METOPOSCOPY

Pages 123-123

the pretended art of knowing a person's dispositions and manners, by viewing the traces and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Ciro Spontoni, who has wrote expressly on metoposcopy, says, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> lines are examined in the forehead, and that each line is considered as having its particular planet: the first is the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the third of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, &c. Metoposcopy is only a branch of physiognomy, which founds its conjectures on all the parts of the body.

METRE

Pages 123-123

μέτρον, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a system of feet of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> length. The different metres in poetry, are the different manners of ordering and combining the quantities, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables: thus hexameter, pentameter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IAMBIC">iambic</a>, sapphic verses, &c. consist of different metres, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. See HEXAMETER. In English verses, the metres are extremely various and arbitrary, every poet being at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to introduce any new form that he pleases. The most usual are the heroic, generally consisting of five long and five short syllables, and verses of four feet, and of three feet, and a caesura, or single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by variously combining and transposing their quantities, made a vast variety of different measures, by forming spondees, &c. of different feet. See POETRY, no. 124, &c.

METROPOLIS

Pages 123-123

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> metropolis is also applied to archiepiscopal churches, and sometimes to the principal or mother-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of a city. The Roman empire having been divided into 13 dioceses and 120 provinces, each <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> and each province had its metropolis, or capital city, where the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> had his residence. To this civil <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> was afterwards adapted, and the bishop of the capital city had the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of affairs, and the preeminence over all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the province. His residence in the metropolis gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of metropolitan. This erection of metropolitans is referred to the end of the third century, and was confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. A metropolitan has the privilege of ordaining his suffragans; and appeals from sentences passed by the suffragans are preferred to the metropolitan.

METRORODUS

Pages 123-123

a Greek physician, born at Chios, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> the physician and Anaxarchus the philosopher. He maintained, that the universe is infinite and eternal: but his works are lost. He lived about 444 B.C.

METZ

Pages 123-123

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and strong town of France, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Meffin, with a citadel, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and a bishop's see, whose bishop assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is one of the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">Coffin</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the governor, are worth seeing. The Jews live in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town by themselves, where they have a synagogue. The sweetmeats they make here are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Moselle and Seille. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 16. N. Lat. 49. 7.

MEURSIUS

Pages 123-123

a learned and laborious writer, born at Lofsdam, near the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, in 1579. He early discovered a fondness for polite literature and the sciences; and went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> with the son of Barneveldt, whom he accompanied in his travels. In 1610 he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and afterwards Greek professor. His reputation daily increasing, Christian IV. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> made him professor of history and politics, in the university of Sola. Meursius filled that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> with universal applause; and died in 1641, aged 62. He wrote many learned works, several of which relate to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>: 1. De populis Atticae. 2. Atticarum lectionum libri vi. 3. Archontes Atheniens. 4. Fortuna <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. 5. De Athenarum origine. 6. De fatis Graecorum, &c. John Meursius, his son, was also the author of several works. It seems almost needless to observe, that the scandalous obscene Latin <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, intitled Meursius, is not either of our author <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> his son; but, as is said, the notable production of one John Weiramus, a lawyer at the Hague.

MEXICO

Pages 123-142

otherwise called New-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by New-Mexico, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Mexico and the North <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, and on the south and west by South America and the South Sea; extending upwards of 2000 miles in length, and from 60 to 600 in breadth. This country was first discovered, though imperfectly, by a Spaniard named Nunez de Balboa; but, in 1518, the conquest of it was undertaken by a celebrated adventurer named Ferdinand Cortez. It was not... Mexico; however, without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty that he got his expedition set on foot; being persecuted by the Spanish governors in the West Indies, so that he was at last obliged to throw off his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to them, and proceed without any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. However, on the 10th of February 1519, he set sail from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>; and soon landed on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COZUMEL">Cozumel</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Yucatan, discovered the preceding year. Here he joined one of his officers named Pedro d'Alvarez, who had arrived some days before, and collected some booty and taken a few prisoners. But the general severely censured his conduct; and the prisoners were dismissed, after they had been informed by an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> interpreter named Melchior, that such injuries were entirely disagreeable to the intentions and wishes of Cortes. Here he mustered his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and found that it amounted to 508 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, 16 horsemen, and 109 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, pilots, and mariners. Having encouraged his men by a proper speech, and relieved, by means of some Indian ambassadors, a Spaniard named Jeron de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUILAR">Aguilar</a>, who had been detained a prisoner for eight years, he proceeded to the river Tabasco, where he hoped to be received in a friendly manner, as one Grijalva had been a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before; but, from some unknown cause, he was violently attacked by them; however, the superiority of the Spanish arms soon decided the victory, and the inhabitants were obliged to own the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Castile as their sovereign. The Spaniards then <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their course westward, to the harbour of St. Juan de Ulua; where they were met by two Mexican canoes, who carried two ambassadors from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of that country, and shewed the greatest signs of peace and amity. Their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was unknown to Aguilar; but one of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> slaves above-mentioned understood it, and translated it into the Yucatan tongue; after which Aguilar interpreted the meaning in Spanish. This slave was afterwards named Donna Marina, and proved very useful in their conferences with the natives. At this time the Mexican empire, according to Dr Robertson, was arrived at a pitch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> to which no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> had ever attained in so short a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Though it had subsisted only for 130 years, its dominion extended from the north to south seas; over territories stretching about 500 leagues from east to west, and more than 200 from north to south; comprehending provinces not inferior in fertility, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and opulence, to any in the torrid zone. The reigning emperor was called Montezuma, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Motecuzoma, whose authority was very despotic, and his temper haughty and cruel. Though by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> he possessed a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of courage and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; yet from the first moment that the Spaniards appeared on his coast, he discovered symptoms of timidity and embarrassment, and all his subjects were embarrassed as well as himself. The general dismay which took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on this occasion was partly owing to the strange <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> the Spaniards made, and the prodigious power of their arms; but partly also to the following circumstance. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> prevailed almost universally among the Americans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe the earliest and most authentic historians, that some dreadful calamity impended over their heads, from a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of formidable invaders who should come from regions towards the rising <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, to overrun and defoliate their country. Whether this disquieting <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> flowed from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> calamity which had afflicted that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mexico, the globe, and impressed the minds of the inhabitants with superstitious fears and forebodings; or whether it was an imagination accidentally suggested by the astonishment which the first sight of a race of new men occasioned, it is impossible to determine. But as the Mexicans were more prone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> than any people in the new world, they were more deeply affected with the appearance of the Spaniards, whom they instantly supposed to be the instruments destined to bring about that fatal revolution which they dreaded; and this produced the embassy above-mentioned. By means of his two interpreters, Donna Marina, and Aguilar, Cortes learned that the chiefs of the Mexican embassy were deputies from Pilpatoe and Teutle; the one governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> under the emperor, and the other the commander of all his forces in that province: the purport of their embassy was, to inquire what his intentions were in visiting their coasts, and to offer him what assistance he might need in order to continue his voyage. Cortes, in his turn, also professed the greatest friendship; and informed the ambassadors, that he came to propose matters of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the welfare of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; which he would more fully unfold in person to the governor and the general. Next morning, Cortes landed without waiting for any answer, he landed his troops, and fortified his horses, and his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>; began to erect huts for his men, and to fortify his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The natives, instead of opposing the entrance of these fatal guests into their country, assisted them in all their operations, with an alacrity which they had ere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reason to repent. The next <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> the ambassadors had a formal audience; at which Cortes acquainted them, that he came from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Carlos of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, king of Castile, the greatest monarch of the east, and was intrusted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> of such moment, that he would impart them to none but the emperor himself, and therefore required to be conducted immediately to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. This demand immediately produced the greatest uneasiness; and the ambassadors did all in their power to dissuade Cortes from his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, endeavouring to conciliate his good-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> by the presents sent him by going to Montezuma. These they introduced with great parade, and consisted of fine cotton-cloth, of plumes of various colours, and of ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver to a considerable value, the workmanship of which appeared to be as curious as the materials were rich. But these presents served only to excite the avidity of the Spaniards, and to increase their desire for becoming masters of a country which abounded with so many precious commodities. Cortes indeed could scarcely refrain himself so far as to hear the arguments made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the ambassadors to dissuade him from going to the capital; and, in a haughty, determined tone, insisted on his former demand of being admitted to a personal interview with their sovereign. During this conversation, some painters in the retinue of the Mexican chiefs had been diligently employed in delineating, upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cotton cloths, figures of the ships, horses, artillery, soldiers, and whatever else attracted their eyes as singular. When Cortes observed this, and was informed that these pictures were to be sent to Montezuma, he resolved to render the representation still more striking and interesting. The trumpets, by his orders, sounded an alarm; the troops... troops formed in order of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and showed their agility and strength in the best manner they could; while the artillery was pointed against the neighboring trees, among which it made dreadful havoc. The Indians for some time looked on with silent astonishment; but at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of the cannon, some fled, others fell to the ground, and all were so confounded, that Cortes found it difficult to quiet and compose their minds. When the painters had exerted their utmost efforts in representing all these wonderful things, messengers were immediately dispatched to Montezuma with the pictures, and a full account of every thing that had passed since the arrival of the Spaniards, together with some European curiosities to Montezuma; which, though of no great value, Cortes believed would be acceptable on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>. The Mexican monarchs, in order to obtain the earliest information of every occurrence in all parts of their empire, had couriers posted at proper stations along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; and as these were trained to agility by a regular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, they conveyed intelligence with surprising rapidity. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> in which Montezuma resided was above 180 miles from St Juan de Ullus, Cortes's messengers were carried thither, and an answer returned to his demands, in a few days. As the answer was unfavourable, Montezuma had endeavored to mollify the Spanish general by the richness of his presents. These consisted of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the country; cotton-stuffs so fine, and of such delicate texture, as to resemble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; pictures of animals, trees, and other natural objects, formed with feathers of different colours, disposed and mingled with such skill and elegance as to rival the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. But what chiefly attracted their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, were two large plates of a circular form; one of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> gold representing the sun, the other of silver representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. These were accompanied with bracelets, collars, rings, and other trinkets of gold; and that nothing might be wanting which could give the Spaniards a complete idea of what the country afforded, some boxes filled with pearls, precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and grains of gold unwrought, as they had been found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, were sent along with the rest. Cortes received all with an appearance of the most profound respect for Montezuma; but when the Mexicans, presuming upon this, informed him, that their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, though he desired him to accept of what he had sent as a token of his regard for the prince whom he represented, would not give his consent that foreign troops should approach nearer to his capital, or even allow them to continue longer in his dominions. Cortes declared, in a manner more resolute and peremptory than formerly, that he must insist on his first demand; as he could not, without dishonor, return to his own sovereign until he was admitted into the presence of the prince whom he was appointed to visit in his name. The Mexicans were astonished at the sight of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who dared to oppose the will of their emperor; but not being willing to come to an open rupture with such formidable enemies, with much ado they prevailed upon Cortes to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> that he would not move from his present camp until the return of a messenger whom they sent to Montezuma for further instructions. The pacificity of the Indian monarch afforded time to the Spaniards to take <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which would have been out of their power had they been vigorously attacked on their first refusal to obey his orders. Cortes used every method of securing the affections of the soldiers; which indeed was very necessary, as many of them began to complain against the rashness of his attempt in leading them against the whole force of the Mexican empire. In a short time Tezontepec arrived with another present from Montezuma, and together with it delivered the ultimate orders of that remonstrant monarch to depart instantly out of his dominions; and when Cortes, instead of complying with his demands, his dominions renewed his request of audience, the Mexican immediately left the camp with strong marks of surprise and resentment. Next morning, none of the natives appeared; all friendly correspondence seemed to be at an end, and hostilities were expected to commence every moment. A sudden conflagration ensued among the Spaniards, and a party was formed against him by the adherents of Velazquez; who took advantage of the occasion, and depopulated one of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, a principal officer, to remonstrate, as if in name of the whole army, against his rashness, and to urge the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of his returning to Cuba. Cortes received the message without any appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>; and as he well knew the temper and wishes of his soldiery, and foresaw how they would receive a proposition to fatal to all the splendid hopes and schemes which they had been forming with such complacency, he pretended to comply with the request now made him, and issued orders that the army should be in readiness next day to embark for Cuba. Upon hearing this, the troops, as Cortes had expected, were quite outrageous; they positively refused to comply with these orders, and threatened immediately to choose another general if Cortes continued to insist on their departure. Our adventurer was highly pleased with the disposition which now appeared among his troops; nevertheless, dissembling his sentiments, he declared, that his orders for embarking had proceeded from a persuasion that it was agreeable to his fellow-soldiers, to whose opinion he had sacrificed his own; but now he acknowledged his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and was ready to resume his original <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of operation. This speech was highly applauded; and Cortes, without allowing his men time to cool, set about carrying his designs into execution. In order to give a beginning to a colony, he Villa Rica assembled the principal persons in his army, and by founded, their suffrages elected a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and magistrates, in whom the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was to be vested. The persons chosen were most firmly attached to Cortes; and the new settlement had the name of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz; that is, the rich town of the true <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. Before this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of his own making, Cortes did not hesitate at relinquishing all his authority, and was immediately re-elected <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the colony, the governor and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general of its army, with an ample commission, in the king's name, to continue in force till the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> should be farther known. The soldiers eagerly ratified their choice by loud acclamations; and Cortes, now considering himself no longer accountable to any subject, began to assume a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> more extensive powers, than he had done before. Some of the soldiers began to complain against the proceedings of the council as illegal; but the ringleaders were instantly Mexico: instantly sent on board the fleet loaded with irons. By this timely severity the rest were overawed; and Cortes, knowing of how great importance unanimity was to his future success, soon found means to reconcile those who were most disaffected; to which purpose a liberal distribution of the Mexican gold, both among friends and foes, contributed not a little. Cortes, having thus strengthened himself as well as he could, resolved to advance into the country; and to this he was encouraged by the behaviour of the cacique or petty prince of Zempoalla, a considerable town at no great distance. This prince, though subject to Montezuma, was exceedingly impatient of the yoke; and so filled with dread and hatred of the emperor, that nothing could be more acceptable to him than an appearance of being delivered from that subjection; and a deliverance of this kind he now hoped from the Spaniards. For this reason he sent ambassadors to Cortes, with offers of friendship, which were gladly accepted by him; and in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, he very soon visited Zempoalla. Here he was received in the most friendly manner imaginable, and had a respect paid towards him almost <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>. The cacique informed him of many particulars relating to the character of Montezuma.—He told him, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, haughty, cruel, and suspicious; who treated his own subjects with arrogance, ruined the conquered provinces by his extortions, and often tore their sons and daughters from them by violence; the former to be offered as victims to his gods, the latter to be referred as concubines for himself and favourites. Cortes, in reply, artfully insinuated, that one great object of the Spaniards in visiting a country so remote from their own was, to redress grievances, and to relieve the oppressed; and having encouraged him to hope for this interposition in due time, continued his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to Quiahislan, the territory of another cacique, and where, by the friendly aid of the Indians, a Spanish colony was soon formed. During the residence of Cortes in these parts, he so far wrought on the minds of the caciques of Zempoalla and Quiahislan, that they ventured to insult the Mexican power, at the very name of which they had been formerly accustomed to tremble. Some of Montezuma's officers having appeared to levy the usual tribute, and to demand a certain number of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> victims, as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> of their guilt in presuming to hold intercourse with those strangers whom the emperor had commanded to leave his dominions; instead of obeying his orders, they made them prisoners, treated them with great indignity, and, as their superstition was no less barbarous than Montezuma's, they threatened to sacrifice them to their gods. From this last danger, however, they were delivered by the interposition of Cortes, who manifested the utmost horror at the mention of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of rebellion firmly attached the two caciques to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Cortes; and without hesitation they acknowledged themselves vassals of the king of Spain. Their example was followed by the Totonaques, a fierce people who inhabited the mountainous parts of the country. They willingly subjected themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Castile; and offered to accompany Cortes with all their forces in his march towards Mexico. Though Cortes had now taken such measures as in a manner ensured his success; yet, as he had thrown off all dependence on the governor of Cuba, who was his lawful superior, and apprehended his interest at court, he thought proper, before he set out on his intended expedition, to take the most effectual measures against the impending danger. With this view, he persuaded the magistrates of his colony to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the king, containing a pompous account of Villa Rica and its own services, of the country they had discovered, &c., and of the motives which had induced them to throw off their allegiance to the governor of Cuba, and to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> a colony dependent on the crown alone, in which the supreme power civil as well as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> Cortes had been vested in Cortes; humbly requesting their sovereign to ratify what had been done by his royal authority. Cortes himself wrote in a similar strain; but as he knew that the Spanish court, accustomed to the repeated exaggerations of American adventurers, would give little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the splendid accounts of New-Spain, if they were not accompanied with such a specimen of what it contained as would excite an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> idea of its opulence, he solicited his soldiers to relinquish what they might claim as their part of the treasures which had hitherto been collected, in order that the whole might be sent to the king. Portocarrero and Montejo, the chief magistrates of the colony, were appointed to carry this present to Castile, with express orders not to touch at Cuba in their passage thither. But while a vessel was preparing for their departure, an unexpected event produced a general alarm. Some soldiers and sailors, secretly disaffected to Cortes, formed a design of seizing one of the brigantines, and making their escape to Cuba, in order to give such intelligence to the governor, as might enable him to intercept the vessel which was to carry the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> and dispatches to Spain. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was conducted with profound secrecy; but at the moment when every thing was ready for execution, the secret was discovered by one of the associates. The latent spirit of disaffection which Cortes Cortes was now too well convinced had not been extinguished amongst his troops, gave him very great uneasiness. The only method which he could think of to prevent such conspiracies for the future was, to destroy his fleet; and thus deprive his soldiers of every resource except that of conquest; and with this proposal he persuaded his men to comply. With universal consent therefore the ships were drawn ashore, and, after being stripped of their sails, rigging, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and whatever else might be of use, they were broke in pieces. Cortes having thus rendered it necessary for his troops to follow wherever he chose to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, began his march from Zempoalla with 500 infantry, 15 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and six field-pieces. The rest of his troops, consisting chiefly of such as from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or infirmity were unfit for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he left as a garrison in Villa Rica, under the command of Escalante, an officer of merit, and warmly attached to his interest. The cacique of Zempoalla supplied him with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and with 200 of those Indians called Tamanes, whose office, in a country where tame animals were unknown, was to carry carry burdens, and perform all manner of servile labour. He offered likewise a considerable body of troops; but Cortes was satisfied with 400; taking care, however, to choose persons of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, that they might serve as hostages for the fidelity of their master. Nothing memorable happened till the Spaniards arrived on the confines of the republic of Tlascalans. The inhabitants of that province were warlike, fierce, and revengeful, and had made considerable progress in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and some other arts. They were implacable enemies to Montezuma; and therefore Cortes hoped that it would be an easy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for him to procure their friendship. With this view, four Zempoalans of high <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> were sent ambassadors to Tlascalans, dressed with all the badges of that office usual among the Indians. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> were divided in their opinions with regard to the proposals of Cortes: but at last, Magicatzin, one of the oldest senators, and a person of great authority, mentioned the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and the revelations of their priests; that a race of invincible men, of divine origin, who had power over the elements, should come from the east to subdue their country. He compared the resemblance which the strangers bore to the persons figured in the tradition of Mexico, their dominion over the elements of fire, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; he reminded the senate of their prodigies, omens, and signals, which had lately terrified the Mexicans, and indicated some very important event; and then declared his opinion, that it would be rashness to oppose a force apparently assisted by heaven, and men who had already proved, to the full <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of those who opposed them, that they were invincible. This orator was opposed by Xicotencatl, who endeavoured to prove that the Spaniards were at best but powerful magicians; that they had rendered themselves obnoxious to the gods by pulling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their images and altars, (which indeed Cortes had very imprudently done at Zempoalans); and of consequence, that they might easily be overcome, as the gods would not fail to resent such an outrage. He therefore voted for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and advised the crushing of these invaders at one blow. The advice of Xicotencatl prevailed; and in consequence of it, the ambassadors were detained; which giving Cortes the alarm, he drew nearer the city of Tlascalans. In this transaction we may easily see how little the Tlascalans, notwithstanding all their ferocity, were skilled in military affairs. They suffered Cortes, with his army drawn up in good order, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a strong wall between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which might have been very advantageously defended against him. He had not advanced far beyond this pass, however, before a party of Tlascalans with plumes were discovered, which denoted that an army was in the field. These he drove before him by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of six horse, obliged them to join another party, and then reinforcing the advanced detachment, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the enemy with such vigour that they began to retire. Five thousand Tlascalans, whom Xicotencatl had placed in ambush, then rushed out of their hiding places, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the infantry came up to assail their slender body of cavalry. The enemy attacked with the utmost fury; but were so much disconcerted by the first discharge of the fire-arms, that they retreated in confusion, furnishing the Spaniards with an opportunity of pursuing them with great slaughter. Cortes, however, supposing that this could not be their whole force, advanced with the utmost caution, in order of battle, to an eminence, from whence he had a view of the main body of the Tlascalan army commanded by Xicotencatl, consisting of no fewer than 40,000 men. By these the small army of Cortes was entirely surrounded; which Xicotencatl no sooner perceived, than he contracted the circle with incredible diligence, while the Spaniards were almost overwhelmed with showers of arrows, darts, and stones. It is impossible but in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> many of the Spaniards must have perished, had it not been for the insufficiency of the Indian weapons. Their arrows and spears were headed only with flint, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of fishes; their stakes hardened in the fire, and wooden swords, though destructive weapons among naked Indians, were easily turned aside by the Spanish bucklers, and could hardly penetrate the quilted jackets which the soldiers wore. These circumstances gave the Spaniards a prodigious advantage over them; and therefore, the Tlascalans notwithstanding their valour and superiority in number, could accomplish no more in the present instance, than to kill one horse, and slightly wound <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> soldiers. The Tlascalans being taught by this, and some subsequent encounters, how much they were inferior to the Spaniards, began to conceive them to be really what Magicatzin had said; a superior order of beings, against whom human power could not prevail. In this extremity they had recourse to their priests, requiring them to reveal the causes of such extraordinary events, and to declare what means they should take to repel such formidable invaders. The priests, after many sacrifices and incantations, delivered their response, That these strangers were the offspring of the sun, proceeded by his animating energy in the regions of the east; that, by day, while cherished with the influence of his paternal beams, they were invincible; but by night, when his reviving <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> was withdrawn, their vigour declined and faded like herbs in the field, and they dwindled down into mortal men. In consequence of this, the Tlascalans acted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to one of their most established maxims in war, and ventured to attack the enemy in the night-time, hoping to destroy them when enfeebled and surprised. But the Spanish sentinels having observed some extraordinary movements among the Tlascalans, gave the alarm. Immediately the troops were under arms, and falling out, defeated their antagonists with great slaughter, without allowing them to approach the camp. By this defeated and after the Tlascalans were heartily disposed to peace; for but they were at a loss to form an adequate idea of the enemies they had to deal with. They could not ascertain the nature of these surprising beings, or whether they were really of a benevolent or malignant disposition. There were circumstances in their behaviour which seemed to favour each opinion. On the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as the Spaniards constantly dismissed the prisoners whom they took, not only without injury, but often with presents of European toys, and renewed their offers of peace after every victory; this lenity amazed people accustomed to the exterminating system of war known in America, and who sacrificed and devoured without mercy all the captives taken in battle; Mexico, and disposed them to entertain sentiments favourable to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. But, on the other hand, as Cortes had seized 50 of their countrymen who brought provisions to their camp, and cut off their heads; this bloody spectacle, added to the terror occasioned by the fire-arms and horses, filled them with dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of their ferocity. Accordingly they addressed them in the following manner: "If, (said they), you are divinities of a cruel and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nature, we present to you five slaves, that you may drink their blood and eat their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. If you are mild deities, accept an offering of incense and variegated plumes. If you are men, here is meat, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and fruit, to nourish you." After this address, the peace was soon concluded, to the great satisfaction of both parties. The Tlascalans yielded themselves as vassals to the crown of Castile, and engaged to assist Cortes in all his operations; while he took the republic under his protection, and promised to defend their persons and possessions from injury and violence. This reconciliation took place at a very seasonable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> for the Spaniards. They were not only worn out with incessant toil, but to destitute of necessaries, that they had no other salve to dress their wounds but what was composed of the fat of Indians whom they had slain. Their distresses, in short, were arisen to such an height that they had begun to murmur, and even to despair, insomuch that Cortes had much difficulty in restraining them within any kind of bounds; but the submission of the Tlascalans, and their own triumphant entry into the city, where they were received with the reverence due to a superior order of beings, banished at once all memory of past sufferings, dispelled every anxious thought, and fully convinced them that they could not be baffled by any power in America. Cortes left no method untried to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the favour and confidence of the Tlascalans; which, however, he had almost entirely lost, by his untimely zeal in destroying their idols as he had done those of Zempoalla. But he was deterred from this rash <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by his chaplain, father Bartholomew de Olmedo; and left the Tlascalans in the undisturbed exercise of their superstition, requiring only that they should desist from their horrid practice of offering human victims. As soon as his troops were fit for service, he resolved to continue his march towards Mexico, notwithstanding the remonstrances of the Tlascalans, who looked upon his destruction as unavoidable if he put himself into the power of such a faithless prince as Montezuma. But the emperor, probably intimidated with the same of his exploits, had resolved to admit his visit; and informed Cortes that he had given orders for his friendly reception at Cholula, the next place of any consequence on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Mexico. In this, however, he was by no means sincere. Cholula was looked upon by all the inhabitants of the empire as a very holy place; the sanctuary and chief seat of their gods, to which pilgrims resorted from every province, and a greater number of human victims were offered in its principal temple than even in that of Mexico. Montezuma therefore invited the Spaniards thither, either from some superstitious hope that the gods would not suffer this sacred mansion to be desecrated; or from a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, that he himself might there find an opportunity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them off with more certainty of success, when under the immediate protection of his gods. Cortes, however, was received with much seeming cordiality; but 6000 Tlascalan troops who accompanied him were obliged to remain without the town, as the Cholulans refused to admit their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> enemies within their precincts. Yet two of these, by disguising themselves, got into the city, and acquainted Cortes that they observed the women and children belonging to the principal citizens retiring every night in a great hurry, and that six children had been sacrificed in the great temple; a sign that some warlike enterprise was at hand. At the same time Donna Marina, the interpreter, received information from an Indian woman of distinction, whose confidence she had gained, that the destruction of the Spaniards was concerted; that a body of Mexican troops lay concealed near the town; that some of the streets were barricaded, in others deep pits or trenches were dug, and slightly covered over, as traps into which the horse might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; that stones and missile weapons were collected on the tops of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, with which to overwhelm the infantry; that the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was already at hand, and their ruin unavoidable. Cortes, alarmed at this news, secretly arrested three of the chief priests, from whom he extorted a confession that confirmed the intelligence he had already received. As not a moment was to be lost, he instantly resolved to prevent his enemies, and to inflict on them such dreadful vengeance as might strike Montezuma and his subjects with terror. For this purpose the Spaniards and Zempoalans were drawn up in a large court, which had been allotted for their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, near the centre of the town; the Tlascalans had orders to advance; the magistrates and chief citizens were sent for under various pretexts, and seized. On a signal given, the troops rushed out, and fell upon the multitude, destitute of leaders, and so much astonished, that the weapons dropped from their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and they fled motionless, and incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. While the Spaniards attacked them in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, the Tlascalans did the same in the rear; the streets were filled with slaughter; the temples, which afforded a retreat to the priests and some leading men, were set on fire, and they perished in the flames. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror continued two days; during which the wretched inhabitants suffered all that the destructive rage of the Spaniards, or the implacable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of their Indian allies, could inflict. At length the carnage ceased, after the slaughter of 6000 Cholulans, without the loss of a single Spaniard. Cortes then released the magistrates; and reproaching them bitterly for their intended treachery, declared, that as justice was now appeased, he forgave the offence; but required them to recall the inhabitants who had fled, and re-establish order in the town. Such was the ascendant that the Spaniards had now obtained over this superstitious race, that this order was instantly complied with; and the city was in a few days again filled with people, who paid the most respectful service to those men whose hands were stained with the blood of their relations and fellow-citizens. From Cholula, Cortes advanced directly towards Mexico; and throughout the whole of his journey was entertained with accounts of the oppressions and cruelties of Montezuma. This gave him the greatest hope of accomplishing his designs; as he now perceived that the the empire was entirely divided, and no sort of unanimity prevailed among them. No enemy appeared to check his progress. Montezuma was quite irrefutable; and Cortes was almost at the gates of the capital, before the emperor had determined whether to receive him as a friend, or oppose him as an enemy. But as no sign of open hostility appeared, the Spaniards, without regarding the fluctuations of Montezuma's sentiments, continued their march to Mexico, with great circumvention and the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, though without seeming to suspect the prince whom they were about to visit. When they drew near the city, about 1000 persons, who appeared to be of distinction, came forth to meet them, adorned with plumes, and clad in mantles of fine cotton. Each of these, in his order, passed by Cortes, and saluted him according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> deemed most respectful and submissive in their country. They announced the approach of Montezuma himself, and soon after his harbingers came in sight. There appeared first 200 persons in an uniform dress, with large plumes of feathers, alike in fashion, marching two and two, in deep silence, barefooted, with their eyes fixed on the ground. These were followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of higher rank, in their most showy apparel; in the midst of whom was Montezuma, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> or litter richly ornamented with gold, and feathers of various colours. Four of his principal favourites carried him on their shoulders, others supported a canopy of curious workmanship over his head. Before him marched three officers with rods of gold in their hands, which they lifted up on high at certain intervals; and at that signal all the people bowed their heads, and hid their faces, as unworthy to look on so great a monarch. When he drew near, Cortes dismounted, advancing towards him with officious haste, and in a respectful posture. At the same time Montezuma alighted from his chair, and leaning on the arms of two of his near relations, approached with a slow and stately pace, his attendants covering the street with cotton cloths, that he might not touch the ground. Cortes accosted him with profound reverence, after the European fashion. He returned the salutation, according to the mode of his country, by touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his hand, and then kissing it. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, the customary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of reverence from inferiors towards those who are above them in rank, appeared such amazing condescension in a proud monarch, who scarcely deigned to consider the rest of mankind as of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> with himself, that all his subjects firmly believed those persons, before whom he humbled himself in this manner, to be something more than human. Accordingly, as they marched through the crowd, the Spaniards frequently, and with much satisfaction, heard themselves denominated "tendes," or divinities. Nothing material passed in this first interview. Montezuma conducted Cortes to the quarters which he had prepared for his reception; and immediately took leave of him, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> not unworthy of a court more refined. "You are now, (says he), with your brothers, in your own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; refresh yourselves after your fatigue, and be happy until I return." The place allotted to the Spaniards for their lodging was a house built by the father of Montezuma. It was surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-wall, with towers at proper distances, which served for defence as well as for ornament; and its apartments and courts were so large as to accommodate both the Spaniards and their Indian allies. The first care of Cortes was to take precautions for his security, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the artillery so as to command the different avenues which led to it, by appointing a large <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of his troops to be always on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and by posting sentinels at proper stations, with injunctions to observe the same vigilant discipline as if they were within sight of an enemy's camp. In the evening Montezuma returned to visit his guests with the same pomp as in their first interview; and brought presents of such value, not only to Cortes and to his officers, but even to the private men, as proved the liberality of the monarch to be suitable to the opulence of his kingdom. A long conference ensued, in which Cortes learned what was the opinion of Montezuma with respect to the Spaniards. It was an established tradition, he told him, among the Mexicans, that their ancestors came originally from a remote region, and conquered the provinces now subject to his dominion; that after they were settled there, the great captain who conducted this colony returned to his own country, promising, that at some future period his descendants should visit them, assume the government, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> their constitutions and laws; that, from what he had heard and seen of Cortes and his followers, he was convinced that they were the very persons whose appearance and prophecies taught them to expect; that accordingly he had received them, not as strangers, but as relations of the same blood and parentage, and desired that they might consider themselves as masters in his dominions; for both himself and his subjects should be ready to comply with their will, and even to prevent their wishes. Cortes made a reply in his usual style with respect to the dignity and power of his sovereign, and his intention in sending him into that country; artfully endeavouring so to frame his discourse, that it might coincide as much as possible with the idea which Montezuma had formed concerning the origin of the Spaniards. Next morning, Cortes and some of his principal attendants were admitted to a public audience of the emperor. The three subsequent days were employed in viewing the city; the appearance of which, so far superior in the order of its buildings and the number of its inhabitants to any place the Spaniards had beheld in America, and yet so little resembling the structure of an European city, filled them with surprise and admiration. Mexico, Tenochtitlan, as it was anciently called by the natives, is situated in a large plain, environed of the city by mountains of such height, that though within the torrid zone, the temperature of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is mild and healthful. All the moisture which descends from the high grounds is collected in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, the two largest of which, of about 90 miles in circuit, communicate with each other. The waters of the one are fresh, those of the others brackish. On the banks of the latter, and on some small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> adjoining to them, the capital of Montezuma's empire was built. The access to the city was by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> causeways or streets, formed of stones and earth, about 30 feet in breadth. As the waters of the lake, during the rainy season, overflowed the flat country, these causeways were... considerable length. That of Tacuba on the west a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half; that of Tezcuco on the north-west three miles; that of Cuoyacan towards the south six miles. On the east there was no causeway, and the city could be approached only by canoes. In each of these causeways were openings, at proper intervals, through which the waters flowed; and over these beams of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> were laid, which being covered with earth, the causeway or street had everywhere an uniform appearance. As the approaches to the city were singular, its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> was remarkable. Not only the temple of their gods, but the houses belonging to the monarch and to persons of distinction, were of such dimensions, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with any other buildings which had been discovered in America, they might be termed magnificent. The habitations of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, resembling the huts of other Indians. But they were all placed in a regular manner, on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which passed through the city, in some of its districts, or on the sides of the streets which intersected it in other quarters. In several places were large open spaces or squares, one of which, allotted for the great market, is said to have been so spacious, that 40,000 or 50,000 persons carried on traffic there. In this city, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the New World, and the noblest monument of the industry and art of man, while unacquainted with the use of iron, and destitute of aid from any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal, the Spaniards, who are most moderate in their computations, reckon that there were at least 60,000 inhabitants. But how much forever the novelty of those objects might amuse or astonish the Spaniards, they felt the utmost solicitude with respect to their own situation. From a concurrence of circumstances, no less unexpected than favourable to their progress, they had been allowed to penetrate into the heart of a powerful kingdom, and were now lodged in its capital, without having once met with open opposition from its monarch. The Tlascalans, however, had earnestly dissuaded them from placing such confidence in Montezuma as to enter a city of such a peculiar situation as Mexico, where that prince would have them at mercy, shut up as it were in a snare, from which it was impossible to escape. They assured him that the Mexican priests had, in the name of the gods, counselled their sovereign to admit the strangers into the capital, that he might cut them off there at one blow with perfect security. The Spaniards now perceived, too plainly, that the apprehensions of their allies were not destitute of foundation; that, by breaking the bridges placed at certain intervals on the causeways, or by destroying part of the causeways themselves, their retreat would be rendered impracticable; and they must remain cooped up in the centre of a hostile city, surrounded by multitudes sufficient to overwhelm them, and without a possibility of receiving aid from their allies. Montezuma had, indeed, received them with distinguished respect. But ought they to reckon upon this as real, or to consider it as feigned? Even if it were sincere, could they promise on its continuance? Their safety depended upon the will of a monarch in whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> they had no reason to confide; and an order flowing from his caprice, or a word uttered by him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, might decide irrevocably concerning their fate. These reflections, so obvious as to occur to the Mexico, meaneft soldier, did not escape the vigilant sagacity of their general. Before he set out from Cholula, Cortes had received advice from Villa Rica, that Quilpites, one of the Mexican generals on the frontiers, Spaniards having assembled an army in order to attack some of the people whom the Spaniards had encouraged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off the Mexican yoke, Escalante had marched out with part of the garrison to support his allies; that an engagement had ensued, in which, though the Spaniards were victorious, Escalante, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of his men, had been mortally wounded, his horse killed, and one Spaniard had been surrounded by the enemy and taken alive; that the head of this unfortunate captive, after being carried in triumph to different cities, in order to convince the people that their invaders were not immortal, had been sent to Mexico. Cortes, though alarmed with this intelligence, as an indication of Montezuma's hostile intentions, had continued his march. But as soon as he entered Mexico, he became sensible, that, from an excess of confidence in the superior valour and discipline of his troops, as well as from the disadvantage of having nothing to guide him in an unknown country but the defective intelligence which he received from people with whom his mode of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> was very imperfect, he had pushed forward into a situation, where it was difficult to continue, and from which it was dangerous to retire. Disgrace, and perhaps ruin, was the certain consequence of attempting the latter. The success of his enterprise depended upon supporting the high opinion which the people of New Spain had formed with respect to the irresistible power of his arms. Upon the first symptom of timidity on his part, their veneration would cease, and Montezuma, whom fear alone restrained at present, would let loose upon him the whole force of his empire. At the same time, he knew that the countenance of his own sovereign was to be obtained only by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of victories; and that nothing but the merit of extraordinary success could screen his conduct from the censure of irregularity. From all these considerations, it was necessary to maintain his station, and to extricate himself out of the difficulties in which one bold step had involved him, by venturing upon another still bolder. The situation was trying, but his mind was equal to it; and after revolving the matter with deep attention, he fixed upon a plan no less extraordinary than daring. He determined to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> Montezuma in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and carry him a prisoner to the Spanish quarters. From the superstitious veneration of the Mexicans for the person of their monarch, as well as their implicit submission to his will, he hoped, by having Montezuma in his power, to acquire the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their affairs; or at least, with such a sacred pledge in his hands, he made no doubt of being secure from any effort of their violence. This he immediately proposed to his officers. The timid started at a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> so audacious, and raised objections. The more intelligent and resolute, conscious that it was the only resource in which there appeared any prospect of safety, warmly approved of it, and brought over their companions to cordially join the same opinion, that it was agreed instantly to make the attempt. At his usual hour of visiting Montezuma, Cortes went to the palace, accompanied by Alvarado, Saucedo, Mexico. Sandoval, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUGO">Lugo</a>, Velasquez de Leon, and Davila, five of his principal officers, and as many trusty soldiers. Thirty chosen men followed, not in regular order, but sauntering at some distance, as if they had no object but curiosity; small parties were posted at proper intervals, in all the streets leading from the Spanish quarters to the court; and the remainder of his troops, with the Tlascalan allies, were under arms, ready to fall out on the first alarm. Cortes and his attendants were admitted without suspicion; the Mexicans retiring, as usual, out of respect. He addressed the monarch in a tone very different from that which he had employed in former conferences; reproaching him bitterly as the author of the violent assault made upon the Spaniards by one of his officers, and demanded public reparation for the loss which he had sustained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of some of his companions, as well as for the insult offered to the great prince whose servants they were. Montezuma, confounded at this unexpected <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>, and changing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> either from the consciousness of guilt, or from feeling the indignity with which he was treated, affected his own innocence with great earnestness; and, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it, gave orders instantly to bring Quipopoca and his accomplices prisoners to Mexico. Cortes replied, with seeming complaisance, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> so respectable left no doubt remaining in his own mind; but that something more was requisite to satisfy his followers, who would never be convinced that Montezuma did not harbour hostile intentions against them, unless, as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of his confidence and attachment, he removed from his own palace and took up his residence in the Spanish quarters, where he should be served and honoured as became a great monarch. The first mention of so strange a proposal bereaved Montezuma of speech, and almost of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. At length he haughtily answered, "That persons of his rank were not accustomed voluntarily to give up themselves as prisoners; and were he mean enough to do so, his subjects would not permit such an affront to be offered to their sovereign." Cortes, unwilling to employ force, endeavoured alternately to soothe and intimidate him. The altercation became warm; and having continued above three hours, Velasquez de Leon, an impetuous and gallant young man, exclaimed with impatience, "Why waste more time in vain? Let us either seize him instantly, or stab him to the heart." The threatening <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and fierce gestures with which these words were uttered, struck Montezuma. The Spaniards, he was sensible, had now proceeded so far, as left him no hope that they would recede. His own danger was imminent, the necessity unavoidable. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> both; and abandoning himself to his fate, complied with their request. His officers were called. He communicated to them his resolution. Though astonished and afflicted, they presumed not to question the will of their master, but carried him in silent pomp, all bathed in tears, to the Spanish quarters. When it was known that the strangers were conveying away the emperor, the people broke out into the wildest transports of grief and rage, threatening the Spaniards with immediate destruction, as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> justly due to their impious audacity. But as soon as Montezuma appeared with a seeming gaiety of countenance, and waved his hand, the tumult was hushed; and upon his declaring it to be of his own choice that he went to reside for some time among his new friends, the multitude, taught to revere every intimation of their sovereign's pleasure, quietly dispersed. The Spaniards at first pretended to treat Montezuma with great respect; but soon took care to let him know that he was entirely in their power. Cortes wished that the shedding the blood of a Spaniard should appear the most heinous crime that could be committed; and therefore not only took a most exemplary vengeance on those who had been concerned in the affair of Villa Rica, but even put the emperor himself in chains till the execution of the Mexican general was over. By these, and other insults, he at last gained entirely the ascendant over this unhappy monarch; and he took care to improve his opportunity to the utmost. He sent his emissaries into different parts of the kingdom, accompanied with Mexicans of distinction, who might serve both to guide and to protect them. They visited most of the provinces, viewed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and productions, surveyed with particular care the districts which yielded gold or silver, pitched upon several places as proper for future colonies, and endeavoured to prepare the minds of the people for submitting to the Spanish yoke: and while they were thus employed, Cortes, in the name and by the authority of Montezuma, degraded some of the principal officers in the empire, whose abilities or independent spirit excited his jealousy; and substituted in their place persons who he imagined would be more obsequious. One thing, however, was still wanting to complete his security. He wished to have such a command of the lake as might ensure a retreat, if, either from levity or disgust, the Mexicans should take arms against him, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> down the bridges or causeways, in order to inclose him in the city. In order to obtain this without giving disgust to the emperor or his court, Cortes artfully inflamed the curiosity of the Indians with accounts of the Spanish shipping, and those floating palaces that moved with such velocity on the water, without the affluence of oars; and when he found that the monarch himself was extremely desirous of seeing such a novelty, he gave him to understand, that nothing was wanting to his gratification besides a few necessaries from Vera Cruz, for that he had workmen in his army capable of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> such vessels. The bait took with Montezuma; and he gave immediate orders that all his people should assist Cortes in whatever he should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> concerning the shipping. By this means, in a few days, two brigantines were got ready, full-rigged and equipped; and Montezuma was invited on board, to make the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of their sailing, of which he could form no idea. Accordingly he embarked for this purpose, and gave orders for a great hunting upon the water, in order that all his people might be diverted with the novelty presented by the Spaniards. On the day appointed, the royal equipage was ready early in the morning; and the lake was covered with a multitude of boats and canoes loaded with people. The Mexicans had augmented the number of their rowers on board the royal barges, with an intention to disgrace the Spanish vessels, which they regarded as clumsy, unwieldy, and heavy. But they were soon undeceived; a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a> started up; the brigantines hoisted sail, to the utter astonishment of all the spectators, and soon left all the canoes behind; while the monarch monarch exulted in the victory of the Spaniards, without once considering that now he had effectually riveted his own chains. Cortes having obtained this important point, resolved to put the condescension of the emperor to a trial still more severe. He urged Montezuma to acknowledge himself a vassal to the crown of Castile; to hold his crown of him as superior; and to subject his dominions to the payment of an annual tribute. With this requisition, humiliating as it was, Montezuma complied. He called together the chief men of his empire, and, in a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a>, reminded them of the traditions and prophecies which led them to expect the arrival of a people sprung from the same stock with themselves, in order to take possession of the supreme power; he declared his belief that the Spaniards were this promised race; and that therefore he recognized the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of their monarch to govern the Mexican empire, would lay his crown at his feet, and obey him as a tributary. While uttering these words, Montezuma discovered how deeply he was affected in making such a sacrifice. Tears and groans frequently interrupted his discourse. The first mention of such a resolution struck the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> dumb with astonishment. This was followed by a sullen murmur of sorrow mingled with indignation; which indicated some violent eruption of rage to be near at hand. This Cortes foresaw, and feebly interposed to prevent it, by declaring that his master had no intention to deprive Montezuma of the royal dignity, or to make any innovation upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and laws of the Mexican empire.
