The milk of women, mares, and asses, agree very much in their qualities, being very <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a>, having little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> contents, and, when evaporated to dryness, having these very soluble, containing much caseinaceous matter, of a very ready aceticity, and, when coagulated, their coagulum being tender and easily broken <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. From this view they have less oil, and seem to have less coagulable matter, than the rest. The milk of cows, sheep, and goats, agree, in opposite qualities to the three <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned; but here there is somewhat more of gradation. Cow's milk comes nearest to the former milk; goat's milk is less fluid, less sweet, less glutinous, has the largest proportion of insoluble part after coagulation, and indeed the largest proportion of coagulable part; its oily and coagulable parts are not spontaneously separable, never throwing out a cream, or allowing butter to be readily extracted from it. Hence the virtues of these milks are obvious, being more nourishing, though, at the same time, less easily soluble in weak stomachs, than the three first, less acetic than these, and so more rarely laxative, and peculiarly fitted for the diet of convalescents without fever. The three first, again, are less nourishing, more soluble, more laxative, as more acetic, and adapted to the convalescents with fever. These qualities, in particular milks, are considerably diversified by different circumstances. First, Different animals, living on the same diet, give a considerably different milk; for there seems to be something in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, abstracting from the aliment, which constitutes a considerable diversity of milk, not only in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals, but also in the same animal, at different ages, and at different distances after delivery: this applies to the choice of nurses. Secondly, Milk follows the nature of the aliment more than any other juice in the human body, being more or less fluid and dilute, more or less solid and nourishing, in proportion as these qualities are more or less in the aliment. The nature of the aliment differs according to its time of growth, e.g., old grass being always found more nourishing than young. Aliment, too, is always varied according to the season, as that is warm or dry, moist or cloudy. The milk of each particular kind of animal is fitter for particular purposes, when fed on proper food. Thus the cow delights in the succulent herbage of the vale; if the sheep be fed there he certainly rots, but on the higher and more dry side of the mountain he feeds pleasantly and healthily; while the goat never stops near the bottom, but ascends to the craggy summit: and certainly the milks of these animals are always best on their proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and that of goats is best on a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. From a dissertation of Linnæus, we have many observations concerning the diversity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> on which each animal chooses to feed. All the Swedish plants which could be collected together, were presented alternately to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, and then it appeared that the goat lived on the greatest variety, and even on many which were poisonous to the rest; that the cow chose the first succulent shoots of the plant, and neglected the fructification; which last was preferred by the goat. Hence may be deduced rules concerning the pasturage of different animals; e.g., Farmers find, that, in a pasture which was only fit to feed a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sheep, an equal number of goats may be introduced, while the sheep are no less nourished than before. It is not easy to assign the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between milk fresh-drawn and that detained in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> for some time; but certainly there is some material one, otherwise nature universally would not have directed infants to sucking; and indeed it seems, better than the other, fitted for digestion and nourishment. Physicians have supposed that this depended on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of some spirit, but our author cannot conceive any such, except common water here; and besides, these volatile parts can hardly be nutritious. A more plausible account seems deducible from mixture: milk, new drawn, has been but lately mixed, and is exposed to spontaneous separation, a circumstance hurtful to digestion; none of the parts being, by themselves, so easily assimilated as when they are all taken together. Hence, then, milk new-drawn is more intimately blended, and therefore then is most proper to the weakly and infants. Another difference in the use of milk exposed for some time to the air, is taking it boiled or unboiled. Physicians have generally recommended the former; but the reason is not easily assigned. Perhaps it is this: Milk kept for some time, exposed to the air, has gone so far as to a spontaneous separation; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> thoroughly blends the whole, and hence its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> is not so easy in the stomach; and thus boiled milk is more coltive than raw, and gives more feces. Again, when milk is boiled, a considerable quantity of air is detached, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> on the surface; and air is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of fermentation in bodies; so that, after this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, it is not liable to aceticity: for these reasons it is proper for the robust and vigorous. Another difference of milk is, according as it is fluid or coagulated. The coagulated is of two kinds, as induced by rennet, or the natural aceticity of the milk. The former <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> makes the firmer and less easily soluble coagulum; though, when taken with the whey unseparated, it is less difficult of solution, tho' more so than any other coagulum in the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Many nations use the latter form, which is easier soluble, but very much acetic, and therefore, in point of solution, should be confined to the vigorous, in point of aceticity, to those who live on alkaline food; and in the last case the Laplanders use it as their chief acetic condiment. From the same considerations it is more cooling, and in its other effects like all other acetic vegetables. Milk by evaporation yields a sweet saline matter, of which Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> gives the following proportions: | Twelve ounces of | Left of dry matter | From which water extracted a sweet saline substance amounting to | |------------------|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------| | Cows milk | 13 drams | 1½ drams | | Goats milk | 12½ | 1½ | | Human milk | 8 | 6 | | Asses milk | 8 | 6 | The saline substance extracted from asses milk was white, and sweet as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; those of the others <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and considerably less sweet; that from cows milk had the least sweetness of any. On distilling 12 quarts of milk in balne mariae, at least <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> quarts of pure phlegm were obtained: the liquor which afterwards arose was acidulous, and by degrees grew sensibly more and more acid as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. After this came over a little spirit, and at last an empyreumatic oil. The remaining solid matter adhered to the bottom of the retort; in the form of elegant shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which being calcined and eluated yielded a portion of fixed alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. Milk, set in a warm place, throws up to the surface an unctuous cream, from which, by agitation, the butter is easily separated. The addition of alkaline salts prevents this separation, not (as some have supposed) by absorbing an acid from the milk, but by virtue of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of intimately uniting oily bodies with watery liquors. Sugar, another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> intermediate between oils and waters, has this effect in a greater degree, though that concrete is by no means alkaline, or an absorbent of acids. The sweet saccharine part of the milk remains dissolved in the whey after the separation of the curd or cheesy matter, and may be collected from it in a white crystalline form, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the whey till all remains of the curdled substance have fallen to the bottom; then filtering, evaporating it to a due consistence, setting it to float, and purifying the crystals by solution in water and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>. Much has been said of the medicinal virtues of this sugar of milk, but it does not seem to have any considerable ones: It is from cows milk that it has been generally prepared; and the crystals obtained from this kind of milk have but little sweetness. When milk is suffered to coagulate spontaneously, the whey proves acid, and on standing grows more and more so till the putrefactive state commences. Sour whey is used as an acid, preferably to the directly vegetable or the mineral acids, in some of the chemical arts; as for dissolving <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in order to the staining of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. This acid was commonly made use of in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a> of linen, for dissolving and extracting the earthy particles left in the cloth by the alkaline salts and lime employed for cleansing and whitening it. Butter-milk is preferred to plain four-milk or four-whey: This last is supposed to give the cloth a yellow colour. Dr Home, in his ingenious treatise on this subject, recommends water acidulated with spirit of vitriol, (in the proportion of about half an ounce, or at most three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an ounce, to a gallon), as preferable in many respects to the acid of milk, or of the more directly vegetable substances. He observes, that the latter are often difficultly procurable, abound with oleaginous particles, and hsten to corruption; whilst the vitriolic acid is cheap, and pure, and disposed to putrefy: That milk takes five days to perform its office, whilst the vitriolic acid does it in as many hours, perhaps in as many minutes: That this acid contributes also to whiten the cloth, and does not make it weaker though the cloth be kept in it for months. He finds, that acids as well as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol4.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, extract an oily matter from the cloth, and lose their acidity and alkalinity. Since this treatise appeared, the use of four-milk is very generally superseded by oil of vitriol. It is observable, that asses milk is greatly disposed, on standing for a little time, to become thick and ropy. In the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> collection for the year 1720, there is a remarkable account of milk (which probably was that of the ass) grown so thick and tenacious as to be drawn out into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> strings, which, when dried, were quite brittle. New cow's milk, suffered to stand for some days on the leaves of butterwort or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, becomes uniformly thick, slippery, and coherent, and of an agreeable sweet taste, without any separation of its parts. Fresh milk, added to this, is thickened in the same manner, and this successively. In some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, as we are informed in the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, milk is thus prepared for food. New milk has a degree of glutinous quality, so as to be used for joining broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. There is a far greater tenacity in cheese properly prepared. Milk, when examined by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, appears composed of numerous globules <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in a transparent fluid. It boils in nearly the same degree of heat with common water; some sorts rather sooner, and some a little later: after boiling, it is less disposed to grow four than in its natural state. It is coagulated by acids both mineral and vegetable, and by alkalies both fixed and volatile. The coagulum made by acids falls to the bottom of the serum; that made by alkalies swims on the surface, commonly forming (especially with volatile alkalies) a thick coriaceous skin. The serum, with alkalies, proves green or fuscous; with acids, it differs little in appearance from the whey that separates spontaneously. The coagulum formed by acids is dissolved by alkalies, and that formed by alkalies is re-dissolved by acids; but the milk does not in either case resume its original properties. It is coagulated by most of the middle salts, whose basis is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or a metallic body; as solution of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, fixed sal ammoniac, sugar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, green and blue vitriol: but not by the chalybeate or purging mineral waters, nor by the bitter salt extracted from the purging waters. Among the neutral salts that have been tried, there is not one that produces any coagulation. They all dilute the milk, and make it less disposed to coagulate with acids or alkalies: Nitre seems to have this effect in a greater degree than the other neutral salts. It is instantly coagulated by highly-rectified spirit of wine, but feebly by a phlegmatic spirit. It does not mingle with expressed oils. All the coagula are dissolved by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>. Milk of Lime. Milk of Sulphur. The name of milk is given to substances very different from milk properly Milk, so called, and which resemble milk only in colour. Such is water in which quicklime has been flaked, which acquires a whiteness from the small particles of lime being suspended in it, and has hence been called the milk of lime. Such also is the solution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> of sulphur, when an acid is mixed with it, by which white particles of sulphur are made to float in the liquor. Milk of Vegetables. For the same reason that milk of animals may be considered as a true animal-emulsion, the emulsive liquors of vegetables may be called vegetable milks. Accordingly emulsions made with almonds are commonly called milk of almonds. But besides this vegetable milk, which is in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, many plants and trees contain naturally a large quantity of emulsive or milky juices. Such are lettuce, spurge, fig-tree, and the tree which furnishes the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> American resin. The milky juices obtained from all these vegetables derive their whiteness from an oily matter, mixed and undissolved in a watery or mucilaginous liquor. Most resinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> were originally such milky juices, which afterwards become solid by the evaporation of their most fluid and volatile parts. These natural milky juices have not been examined by any chemist. Such an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> would, however, procure much essential knowledge concerning vegetable economy. We should probably find examples of all kinds of oils reduced into milky juices; and this knowledge cannot fail of throwing much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the nature of resins and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-resins. Milk-Powder. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, Chap. XX.

MILL

Pages 224-224

a very learned divine, was born at Shap in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, about the year 1655; and became a servitor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. On his entering into orders he became an eminent preacher, and was made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. In 1681, he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; about the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was made chaplain in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and in 1685 he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of St Edmund's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in Oxford. His edition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever render his name memorable, was published about a fortnight before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1707. Dr Mill was employed 30 years in preparing this edition.

MILLENIARIES

Pages 224-224
or CHILIASTS, a name given to those, in the primitive ages, who believed that the saints will reign on earth with Christ 1000 years. The Millenarians held, that after the coming of Antichrist, and the destruction of all nations which shall follow, there shall be a first resurrection of the just alone: that all who shall be found upon earth, both good and bad, shall continue alive; the good, to obey the just who are risen, as their princes; the bad, to be conquered by the just, and to be subject to them: that Jesus Christ will then descend from heaven in his glory: that the city of Jerusalem will be rebuilt, enlarged, embellished, and its gates stand open night and day. They applied to this new Jerusalem what is said in the Apocalypse, chap. xxi. and to the temple all that is written in Ezekiel xxxvi. Here, they pretended, Jesus Christ will fix the seat of his empire, and reign 1000 years with the saints, patriarchs, and prophets, who will enjoy perfect and uninterrupted felicity. This reign of our Saviour on earth is usually styled the millennium, or reign of 1000 years.

MILLEPEES

Pages 224-224
or WOOD-LOUSE, in zoology; a species of Oniscus. These insects are found in cellars, under stones, and in cold moist places; in the warmer countries they are rarely met with. Millepedes have a faint disagreeable smell, and a somewhat pungent, sweetish, nauseous taste. They have been highly celebrated in suppressions of urine, in all kinds of obstructions of the bowels, in the jaundice, weaknesses of sight, and a variety of other disorders. Whether they have any just title to these virtues is greatly to be doubted: thus much is certain, that their real effects come far short of the character usually given them.

MILLET

Pages 219-219

millet; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable is the panicum <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> millet. This is a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, but is now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> cultivated in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> as an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESCULENT">esculent</a> grain. It rises, with a reed-like stalk, three or four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and channelled; at every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> there is one reed-like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, which is joined on the top of the sheath, and embraces and covers that joint of the stalk below the leaf; this sheath is closely covered with soft hairs, but the leaf which is expanded has none. The top of the stalk is terminated by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> loose panicle, which hangs on one side, having a chaffy flower, which is succeeded by a small round seed. There are two varieties; one with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and the other with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> seeds; but they do not differ in any other particular. This plant is greatly cultivated in the oriental countries, and from whence we are annually furnished with it. It is seldom cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> but in small gardens, for feeding of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, where the seeds generally <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> very well. It is used as an ingredient in puddings, and is by some people greatly esteemed. The seeds must be sown in the beginning of April, upon a warm dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, but not too thick, because the plants divide into several branches, and should have much room. When they come up they should be cleaned from weeds; after which they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> get the better of them, and prevent the future growth. In August the seeds will ripen, when the plant must be cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the seeds beaten out as is practised for other grain; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is not protected from birds, they will devour it as soon as it begins to ripen.

MILLION

Pages 224-224

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the sum of ten hundred thousand, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a thousand times a thousand. See ARITHMETIC.

MILLO

Pages 224-224

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of mount <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZION">Zion</a> at its extremity; and therefore called Millo, of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, (2 Chron. xxii.) taken in with the wall that encompassed mount Zion. Uncertain whether Beth-Millo, (Judges ix. 20.) denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did, it lay near Sechem.

MILO

Pages 224-224

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, about 50 miles in circumference, with a harbour, which is one of the largest and best of the Mediterranean, and which serves for a retreat for all the ships that go to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> return from the Mediterranean. The inhabitants are all Greeks, except the eadi, or judge, who is a Turk. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> is so cheap, that they sell 67 pounds for sevenpence. There are two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, the one of the Greek, and the other of the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and there are 13 monasteries in this island. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the whole island is like a carpet thick set with anemones of all sorts and colours. There are public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> at the foot of a small hill going from the town to the harbour; they are in a cavern, with a very narrow entrance of 50 paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. When a person is got in, the sweat gushes out in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> drops; and this sweating is effectual good for the palsy, rheumatism, and other diseases. Below these baths, near the shore, there are many little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, so hot as to scald one's fingers. Four miles from the town, in a very steep <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is a grotto, 15 paces deep, which is all crusted over with plume-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in some places as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as snow, and reddish in others. Some paces from this cavern, on the sea-shore, is another grotto, whose bottom is filled with sulphur, which burns continually. Those who are troubled with the itch go and sweat here, and are generally cured. Near the chapel of St Surriacus is a spot of ground continually <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; and the fields about it are always smoking, and yet they are all covered with marigolds. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Milo is very unwholesome, yet the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a merry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and regale themselves very cheap; but the women are not very famous for chastity. They have partridges, turtle doves, quails, wheat-caps, wood-pigeons, and ducks, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty; as also good figs, melons, excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and very delicate fish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is of the same name as the island, and contains near 5000 inhabitants. It is prettily built, but abominably nasty; the houses are two stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with flat roofs, and are built with a sort of pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is hard, blackish, and yet very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This island is 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Candia, and the town is situated in E. Long. 25. 15. N. Lat. 36. 27.

MILT

Pages 224-224
or MILY, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, the soft roe in fishes; thus called by reason it yields, by expression, a whitish juice resembling milk. See ROS. The milt is properly the seed or spermatic part of the male fish. The milt of a carp is reckoned a choice bit. It consists of two long whitish irregular bodies, each included in a very thin fine membrane. M. Petit considers them as the testicles of the fish wherein the seed is preserved; the lower part, next the anus, he takes for the vesicula seminalis.

MILTIADES

Pages 224-224

a celebrated Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, who, with 12,000 men, routed above 300,000 Persians at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>, and, pursuing them, took many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Archipelago: but returning to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> without taking Paros, his fellow-citizens, forgetting the important services he had rendered them, sentenced him to pay a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fine. Being unable to advance the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, he was thrown into prison, where he languished.

MILTON

Pages 224-226

the most illustrious of the English poets, was defended of a genteel family, seated at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their own name, viz. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He was born <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 9, 1608, and received his first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of his parents, assisted by a private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. He afterwards passed some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> at St Paul's School, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> his father had settled, being engaged in the business of a scrivener. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17, he was sent to Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in all parts of academical learning; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> delight was in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. In 1624, he proceeded bachelor of arts, having performed his exercises for it with great applause. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> was so strong, that it became impossible to engage him in any other pursuits. In 1632, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and having now spent as much time in the university as became a person who determined not to engage in any of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, he left the college, greatly regretted by his acquaintance, but highly displeased with the usual method of training up youth there for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and being much out of humour with the public administration of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs, he grew dissatisfied with the established form of church-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and disliked the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education practised in the university. His parents, who now dwelt at Horton, near Colnbrook, in Buckinghamshire, received him with unabated affection, notwithstanding he had thwarted their views of providing for him in the church, and they amply indulged him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of retirement; wherein he enriched his mind with the choicest stores of Grecian and Roman literature; and his poems of Comus, L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas, all wrote at this time, would have been sufficient, had he never produced anything more considerable, to have transmitted his fame to latest posterity. However, he was not so absorbed in his studies as not to make frequent excursions to London; neither did so much excellence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed among his neighbours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with the most distinguished of whom he sometimes chose to relax his mind, and improve his acquaintance with the world as well as with books. After five years spent in this manner, he obtained his father's permission to travel for farther improvement.—At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he became acquainted with the celebrated Hugo Grotius; and from thence travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was everywhere cared for by persons of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and learning. Upon his return home, he set up a genteel academy in Aldersgate Street.—In 1641, he began to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Presbyterian party; and the next year he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Richard Powell, Esq., of Forest-Hill in Oxfordshire. This lady, however, whether from a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> on account of party, her father being a zealous royalist, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> some other cause, soon thought proper to return to her relations; which so incensed her husband, that he resolved never to take her again, and wrote and published several tracts in defence of the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of divorce. He even made his addresses to another lady; but this incident proved the means of a reconciliation with Mrs Milton. In 1644, he wrote his Tract upon Education; and the restraint on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the press being <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he wrote boldly and nobly against that restraint. In 1645, he published his juvenile poems; and about two years after, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he took a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Holborn, the back of which opened into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn Fields.—Here he quietly prosecuted his studies, till the fatal catastrophe and death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.; on which occasion he published his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">Tenure</a> of Kings and Magistrates, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of the fact. He was now taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the commonwealth, and made Latin secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state, who resolved neither to write to others abroad, nor to receive any answers, except in the Latin tongue, which was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. The famous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">Error</a> of State coming out about the same time, our author, by command, wrote and published his Iconoclaste the same year. It was also by order of his masters, backed by the reward of 100l. that, in 1651, he published his celebrated piece, entitled Pro Populo Anglicano Defensio, "A Defence of the People of England," in answer to Salmahus's Defence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>;" which performance spread his fame over all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.—He now dwelt in a pleasant house, with a garden, in Petty France, Westminster, opening into St James's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">Park</a>. In 1652, he buried his wife, who died not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the delivery of her fourth child; and about the same time he also lost his eye-sight, by a guita ferena, which had been growing upon him many years. Cromwell took the reins of government into his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the year 1653; but Milton still held his office. His leisure-hours he employed in prosecuting his studies, wherein he was so far from being discouraged by the loss of his sight, that he even conceived hopes this misfortune would add new vigour to his genius; which, in fact, seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>.—Thus animated, he again ventured upon matrimony: his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> lady was the daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Woodcock of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>: she died in childbirth about a year after. On the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of the protector, Richard Cromwell, and on the return of the long parliament, Milton being still continued secretary, he appeared again in print; pleading for a farther reformation of the laws relating to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and, during the anarchy that ensued, he drew up several schemes for re-establishing the commonwealth, exerting all his faculties to prevent the return of Charles II. England's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, however, and Charles's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, prevailing, our author chose to consult his safety, and retired to a friend's house in Bartholomew-Clothe. A particular prosecution was intended against him; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> esteem to which his admirable genius and extraordinary accomplishments entitled him, had raised him to many friends, even among those of the opposite party, that he was included in the general amnesty. This storm over, he married a third wife <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Mr Minshall a Cheshire gentleman; and not long after he took a house in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> Walk, leading to Bunhill-Fields.—This was his last stage; here he sat <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for a longer continuance than he had been able to do anywhere; and though he had lost his fortune, (for every thing belonging to him went to wreck wreck at the Restoration), he did not lose his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature; but continued his studies with almost as much ardour as ever; and applied himself particularly to the finishing his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the *Paradise Lost*; one of the noblest poems that ever was produced by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> genius.—It was published in 1667, and his *Paradise Regained* came out in 1670.—This latter work fell short of the excellence of the former production; although, were it not for the transcendent merit of the Paradise Lost, the second <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> would doubtless have stood foremost in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of English epic poems.—After this he published many pieces in prose; for which we refer our readers to the edition of his Historical, Poetical, and Miscellaneous Works, printed by Millar, in 2 vols. 4to. in 1753. In 1674, this great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> paid the last debt to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, at his house in Bunhill-Fields, in the 66th year of his age; and was interred on the 12th of November, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St. Giles's, Cripplegate.—A decent monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, in 1737, in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, by Mr. Benson, one of the auditors of the imprest.—As to his person, it was remarkably handsome; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was tender, and by no means equal to his incessant application to his studies.—Though greatly reduced in his circumstances, yet he died worth £500l. in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, beside his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods.—He had no son; but left behind him three daughters, whom he had by his first wife.

MILVIUS

Pages 226-226

Motivius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> *Maelius Pontis*, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Tiber, built by *Emilius Scaurus* the censor, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Sylla, at two miles distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, on the Via Flaminia, and repaired by Augustus. From this bridge the ambassadors of the Allobroges were brought back to Rome, by Cicero's management, and made a discovery of Catiline's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> (Sallust.) Near it Maxentius was defeated by Constantine, (Eutropius.) Now called *Ponte <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>*. **Milvius**, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Falco.

MIMESIS

Pages 226-226

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, the imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and gestures of another person.

MIMNERMUS

Pages 226-226

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet and musician, flourished about the beginning of the 6th century B.C. He was of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Solon. Athenaeus gives him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of pentameter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. His elegies, of which only a few fragments are preserved, were so much admired in antiquity, that Horace preferred them to those of Callimachus. He composed a poem of this kind, as we learn from Pausanias, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the people of Smyrna, and the Lydians, under Gyges. He likewise was author of a poem in elegiac verse, quoted by Strabo, which he intitled *Nanna*, and in which we may suppose he chiefly celebrated a young and beautiful girl of that name, who, according to Athenaeus, was a player on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, with whom he was enamoured in his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. With respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-matters, according to Propertius, his verses were more valuable than all the writings of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. *Plur in amore <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALET">valet</a> Mimnermi verbor Homero.* Lib. i. Eleg. 9. v. 11. And Horace bears testimony to his abilities, in describing that seducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: *Si Mimnermum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> coelos, sine amore poecilae Nil est facundum, utrae in amore poecilae.* Epist. VI. Lib. i. v. 65. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, as wise Mimnermus said, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> unbless'd with love and joy, Ranks us with the senseless dead, Let these gifts each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> employ. Alluding to some much admired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of this Greek poet, which have been preserved by Stoebus. *Tu si vis, mi te sequere, aut juvenis *Appollinis*, &c.* What is life and all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, If love and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> be denied? Smile, snatch me hence, ye fates, where'er The amorous bliss I come to share. Oh! let me crop each fragrant flow'r, While youth and vigour give us pow'rs; For frozen age <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon destroy The force to give <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> take a joy: And then, a prey to pain and care, Detested by the young and fair, The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s blest beams will hateful grow, And only shine on scenes of woe!

MIMOSA

Pages 226-228

the sensitive plant; a genus of the monoeica order, belonging to the polygamy class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. This genus comprises shrubby and herbaceous plants, but mostly of the shrub kind, some trailing, others erect, all natives of the Indies, &c. retained here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosities, particularly for the very singular <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of the leaves of some sorts, which on being touched, suddenly recede, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a very wonderful manner; all of them garnished with pinnated leaves, and monopetalous, funnel-shaped, five-parted, polygamous flowers at the axillas and ends of the branches in clusters and spikes. The name *mimosa* of this genus, signifies mimic, originating from the sensibility of the leaves, which, by their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, mimic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> imitate, as it were, the motions of animals. To this genus Linnæus joins many of the *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACACIAS">acacias</a>*, and it comprises upwards of 40 different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; tho' not more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of them are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the English gardens, or possess any particular merit either for curiosity or ornament, and none for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Of the sorts cultivated here in our flowers, &c. some are of the shrub and tree kind, and two or three are herbaceous perennials and annuals; are mostly of the sensitive kinds, except the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a> sorts, which are motionless, as expressed under their proper heads, i.e. sensitive and humble kinds, and sentelefs kinds. The former of which are exceedingly curious plants in the very singular circumstance of their leaves receding rapidly from the touch; the leaves are winged, each composed of numerous small lobes, all of which on being touched, hastily run up <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together; and in some sorts the footstalks and all are affected, so as instantly to fall downward, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> fastened by hinges. **Shrubby, Sensitive, and Humble Kinds.** They have all winged leaves, each wing consisting of many small pinnae; some only contract the lobes of the leaves and pinnae at the touch; others not only contract every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their leaves, but their footstalks also suddenly drop downward; and for distinction sake, the former are called sensitive mimosas, and the latter humble sensitives; but the leaves of both sorts soon recover their usual position. The most remarkable species are, 1. Sen- MIMOSA 1. Sensitiva, or common sensitive humble plant. Rises with an underbrushy prickly stem, branching six or eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, armed with crooked spines; conjugated, pinnate leaves, with bifurcated partial lobes, or wings, having the inner ones the least, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> footstalk; and at the sides and ends of the branches many purple flowers in roundish heads; succeeded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat, jointed pods, in radiated clusters. This is somewhat of the humble sensitive kind; the leaves, footstalks and all, recede from the touch, though not with such facility as in some of the following sorts. 2. The pudica, or bashful humble plant. Rises with an underbrushy, declinate, prickly stem, branching two or three feet around, armed with hairy spines; pinnate, digitate leaves, each leaf being of five or more long foliicles, attached by their base to a long footstalk, and spread out above like the fingers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and at the sides and ends of the branches roundish heads of greenish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flowers, succeeded by small, jointed, prickly pods. This is truly of the humble sensitive kind; for by the least touch the leaves instantly recede, contract close, and, together with the footstalk, quickly decline downward, as if ashamed at the approach of the hand. 3. The pernambucana, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERNAMBUCO">pernambuco</a> slothful mimosa. Hath underbrushy, procumbent, unarmed stems, branching two or three feet around; bipinnate leaves, of three or four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of short, winged foliicles; and at the axillas drooping spikes of pentandrous flowers, the lower ones castrated. This sort recedes very slowly from the touch, only contracting its pinnae a little when smartly touched; hence the name slothful mimosa. 4. The asperata, or rough sensitive mimosa, hath a shrubby, upright, prickly, hairy, rough stem, branching four or five feet high, armed with short, broad, whitish spines; bipinnate, prickly leaves, of five or six pair of foliicles, or wings, arranged opposite, having two thorns between each pair; and at the upper axillas globular heads of purple flowers, succeeded by short, flat, jointed pods, in clusters, spreading each way like a radius. This is only moderately sensitive in its foliicles, but not in the footstalks. 5. The punctata, or punctated sensitive mimosa, rises with a shrubby, upright, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a>, punctated, or spotted, unarmed stem, branching erectly five or six feet high; bipinnate leaves, of four or five pair of long, winged foliicles, having each about 20 pair of pinnae; and at the axillas and termination of the branches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spikes of yellowish decandrous flowers, the inferior ones castrated; succeeded above by oblong seed-pods. This sort, though naturally shrubby and perennial in its native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, yet in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> it sometimes decays in winter. It is only sensitive in the foliicles, but quick in the motion. Herbaceous Sensitive and Humble Kinds. Of these sorts two are perennial of the trailing kind; and one is annual, of somewhat erect growth; have all winged leaves, with the wings formed of many small pinnae. 6. The vivax, — perennial, or lively sensitive mimosa, bath herbaceous, trailing, unarmed, repent stems, very branchy, spreading widely around, rooting at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> as they advance; conjugated pinnate leaves, with quadrifurcated, roundish, partial lobes, or wings; and at the axillas globular heads of yellowish flowers; succeeded by short, flat, jointed pods. This species is only sensitive in the foliicles; but is the most lively of that kind, it being so susceptible that all the foliicles recede rapidly from the least touch, whereby it has the distinctive appellation of vivacious, or lively mimosa. 7. The quadrivalvis; — perennial, or quadrivalve humble mimosa, bath herbaceous slender, quadrangular, prickly stems, branching and spreading all around, armed with recurved spines; bipinnate leaves of two or three pair of winged lobes, having each many pinnae; and at the axillas globular heads of purple flowers, succeeded by quadrivalcular pods. This is the humble sensitive kind, both leaves and footstalks recede from the touch. 8. The plena, — annual, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-flowered sensitive annual mimosa, rises with an herbaceous, erect, round, unarmed stem, closely branching and spreading every way, three or four feet high; bipinnate leaves of four or five pair of winged lobes, of many pairs of pinnae; and at the axillas and termination of the branches spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> pentandrous flowers, the lower ones double; succeeded by short broad pods. This annual is only sensitive in the foliicles, but extremely sensible of the touch or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Shrubby Insensible Kinds. There are of the acacia kind, formerly a distinct genus, but now all species of Mimosa; but their leaves are destitute of motion or sensibility at the touch; there are about three noted species in the English gardens, all for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>. 9. The cornigera, or horned Mexican mimosa, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called great horned acacia, hath a shrubby, upright, deformed stem, branching irregularly, armed with very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, horned-like white spines, by pairs, connated at the base; bipinnate leaves thinly placed; and flowers growing in spikes. This species is esteemed a curiosity for the oddity of its large spines, resembling the horns of animals, and which are often variously wreathed, twisted, and contorted. 10. The farnesiana, or farnesian fragrant acacia, hath a shrubby stem, branching many feet high, armed with dilating spines; bipinnate leaves, having eight pair of partial lobes, or wings; and globular, clove-scented spikes of yellow sweet-scented flowers. 11. The nilotica, or nilotic true Egyptian acacia, hath an upright tree-stem, branching many feet high, armed with spreading spines; bipinnate leaves; and globular spikes of flowers, having footstalks. From the exudation of the leaves of this sort is procured the drugs called succus acaciae and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-arabic. Propagation, &c. These 11 species of mimosa are the most noted sorts in the English gardens; all the shrubby kinds are durable in root, stem, and branches; those of the perennial herbaceous kinds are also often abiding; but the annual sort always perish, root and branch, at the approach of winter. They are all natives of the Indies; and in this country require the continual shelter of a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or of a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of similar lar temperature under frames and glasses; though they can hardly be supported alive in winter unless placed in a stove; so all the forts must constantly be kept in pots, and placed principally in that department, especially during the winter; nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> they succeed well in the open air in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, except about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> during the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; but the sensitive and humble kinds, if exposed to the open air, even in the hottest days, will be deprived of their sensibility during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they remain so exposed, therefore should always be kept under glasses, in a stove if possible; or in default of such a convenience, the plants might be raised from seed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> in any common hot-bed under frames, &c., as directed for tender annuals, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> constantly under the glasses, and thereby will afford <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> all summer by the oddity of their sensitive foliage; however, to have them to remain in perfection the year round, some must be continued always in a stove, as before observed; for the warmer they are kept, the stronger will be their sensible <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>: but for a particular account of this quality, see the article Sensitive Plant. The propagation of all the forts, both sensitives and acacias, is by seed in spring in a hot-bed, or in the bark-bed in the stove; and some of the sensitive kinds also by layers and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>.

MINDANOA

Pages 228-228

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the East Indies, and one of the Philippines; 180 miles in length, and 120 in breadth. It is a very mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, full of hills and valleys, and the mould is generally deep, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and fruitful. The sides of the hills and valleys are stony, and yet there are tall trees of kinds not known in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> yield very good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and the valleys are watered with variety of rivulets. The palm-trees produce the sago, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people eat, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, three <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> four months in the year. They have here all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> proper to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, besides plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; some affirm that there are nutmegs and cloves, but none of the trees that bear them appear near the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. They have horses, beves, buffaloes, goats, deer, monkeys, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">lizards</a>, and snakes; but they have neither lions nor tygers. Their hogs are very ugly creatures, having all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knobs growing over their eyes; however, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is sweet. Their fowls are ducks, hens, pigeons, parrots, paroquets, turtle-doves, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a> as large as kites, besides many small birds. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, they having breezes by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and cooling <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-winds at night. The winds are easterly one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year, and westerly the other: while the former blow, it is fair <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; but while the latter, it is rainy, stormy, and tempestuous. The inhabitants are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> low stature, with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> and little heads. Their faces are oval, with flat foreheads, black small eyes, short low noses, and pretty large mouths. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is black and frizzy, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> tawny, but more inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> than that of other Indians. The women are very desirous of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of strangers, especially <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trades are goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and carpenters; and they can build pretty good vessels for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Their distempers are as in other places, except the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, which is very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> here. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, besides 20 other women, and all the men have several wives; for their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is Mahometanism. Their houses are built on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, from 14 to 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and they have ladders to go up out of the streets. They have but one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which is divided into several rooms; and the roofs are covered with palmetto leaves. Those that have been far up in the country say, that the people are all blacks, and go quite naked. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, of the same name, is pretty large, and is seated on the eastern coast.

MINDELHEIM

Pages 228-228

a district of Germany, in Swabia, lying between the bishopric of Augsburg and the abbacy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEMPTEN">Kempten</a>, which is 20 miles in length and 16 in breadth.

MINDEN

Pages 228-228

a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name; seated on the river Weser, which renders it a trading-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, who has secularized the bishopric. It is 27 miles east-by-south of Osnaburg, and 37 west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 5'. N. Lat. 52° 22'. Minden (the principality of), in Germany, lies in the circle of Westphalia, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Ravensberg, and along each side of the river Weser. It is about 22 miles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and Minden and Petershagen are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places. It was formerly a bishopric, but is now secularized; and was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Westphalia.

MINDORA

Pages 228-228

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, and one of the Philippines, 50 miles in circumference, and separated from Luzon by a narrow channel. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which abound in palm-trees and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The inhabitants are idolaters, and pay tribute to the Spaniards, to whom this island belongs.

MINERAL

Pages 230-232

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is used in general for all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies, whether simple <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, dug out of a mine; from whence it takes its denomination. Mineral Waters. All waters naturally impregnated with any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which they have dissolved within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> may be called mineral waters, in the most general and extensive meaning of that name; in which are therefore comprehended almost all those that flow within or upon the surface of the earth, for almost all these contain some earth or selenites. But waters containing only earth or selenites are not generally called mineral, but hard or crude waters. Hard waters, which are simply selenitic, when tried by the chemical proofs, show no marks of an acid or of an alkali, nor of any volatile, sulphurous, or metallic matters. Waters which contain a disengaged calcareous earth, change the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of syrup of violets to a green; and those that contain selenites, being mixed with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> in nitrous acid, form a turbid mineral; and when a fixed alkali is added, they are rendered turbid, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sediment is precipitated. These waters also do not dissolve <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> well. From these we may know, that any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> which produces these effects is a hard, earthy, or selenitic water. The waters impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a> are also hard. Although the waters of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and saline <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> be not generally enumerated amongst mineral waters, they might nevertheless be justly considered as such; for besides earthy and selenitic matters, they also contain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mineral salts. We shall therefore consider them as such in this article. Mineral waters, properly so called, are those in which gas, or sulphurous, saline, or metallic substances, are discovered by chemical trials. As many of these waters are employed successfully in medicine, they are also called medicinal waters. Mineral waters receive their peculiar principles by passing through earths containing salts, or pyritous substances that are in a state of decomposition. Some of these waters are valuable from the quantity of useful salts which they contain, particularly of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of which are obtained from these waters; and others are chiefly valued for their medicinal qualities. The former kind of mineral waters is an object of manufacture, and from them is chiefly extracted that salt only which is most valuable in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. See Salt. Many of these waters have been accurately analysed by able chemists and physicians. But notwithstanding these attempts, we are far from having all the certainty and knowledge that might be desired on this important subject; for this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> is perhaps the most difficult of any in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>.—Almost all mineral waters contain several different substances, which being united with water may form with each other numberless compounds. Frequently some of the principles of mineral waters are in so small quantity, that they can scarcely be perceived; although they may have some influence on the virtues of the water, and also on the other principles contained in the water. The chemical operations used in the analysis of mineral waters, may sometimes occasion essential changes in the substances that are to be discovered. And also, these waters are capable of suffering very considerable changes by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, by rest, and by exposure to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Probably also the variations of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, subterranean changes, some secret junction of a new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of mineral or of pure water, lastly the exhaustion of the minerals whence waters receive their peculiar principles, are causes which may occasionally change the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of mineral waters. We need not therefore wonder that the results of analyses of the same mineral waters made by different chemists, whose skill and accuracy are not questioned, should be very different. The consequences of what we have said on this subject are, That the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of mineral waters is a very difficult task; that it ought not to be attempted but by profound and experienced chemists; that it requires frequent repetitions, and at different times; and lastly, that no fixed general rules can be given concerning these analyses. As this matter cannot be thoroughly explained without entering into details connected with all the parts of chemistry, we shall here mention only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> results, and the most essential rules, that have been indicated by the attempts hitherto made on this subject. We may admit the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> or arrangement of mineral waters into certain classes, proposed by some of the best chemists and naturalists. Some of these waters are called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, because they are not naturally hotter than the atmosphere. Some of them are even colder, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Those are called hot mineral waters, which in all seasons are hotter than the air. They are of various degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and some of them are almost as hot as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water. In some mineral waters certain volatile, spirituous, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> principles may be perceived, by a very sensible piquant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; this principle is called the gas or the spirit of waters. The waters which contain this principle are generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than pure water. They sparkle and emit bubbles, at their spring, but especially when they are shook, and poured from one vessel into another. They sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the bottles containing them, when these are well corked, as fermenting wines sometimes do. When mixed with ordinary wine, they give it the piquancy and sparkling quality of Champagne wine. This volatile principle, and all the properties of the water dependent upon it, are lost merely by exposure to air, or by agitation. The waters containing this principle are distinguished by the name of spirituous mineral waters, or acidulous waters. Other divisions of mineral waters may be made relatively to some of their predominant principles. Hence some waters are called acidulous, alkaline, martial, neutral, &c. When a mineral water is to be examined, we may observe the following rules: Experiments ought to be made near the spring, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible. The situation of the spring, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and the neighbouring rising grounds, ought to be examined. Its sensible qualities, as its smell, taste, colour, are to be observed. Its specific gravity and heat are to be ascertained by the hydrometric <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> and the thermometer. From the properties above-mentioned of spirituous mineral waters, we may discover whether it be one of this class. For greater certainty we may make the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Let the neck of a wet bladder be tied to the neck of a bottle containing some of this water. By shaking the water, any gas that it may contain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be disengaged, and will swell the bladder. If the neck of the bladder be then tied with a string above the bottle, and be cut below this string, so as to separate the bladder from the bottle, the quantity and nature of the contained gas may be further examined. Lastly, we must observe the changes that are spontaneously produced upon the water in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and in open vessels, and with different degrees of heat. If by these means any matter be crystallized or deposited, it must be set apart for further examination. These <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> experiments and observations will almost certainly indicate, more or less sensibly, something concerning the nature of the water, and will point out the method to be followed in our further inquiry. We must then proceed to the decomposition of the water, either without addition, and merely by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, or with the addition of other substances, by means of which the matters contained in the water may be precipitated and discovered. It is not material which of these two methods be first practiced, but it is quite necessary that the one should succeed the other. If we begin by evaporating and distilling, these operations must be sometimes interrupted, that the several principles which rise at different times of the distillation may be obtained and examined separately, and also to allow the several salts that may be contained to crystallize by the evaporation and by cold. The substances generally found in mineral waters, are almost always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of vitriolic acid, and those of marine acid, together with the several matters that these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> are capable of dissolving. The following combinations of vitriolic acid are found in mineral waters: 1. Volatile sulphurous acid. This is seldom found, both because it easily loses its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>, and because it must almost always meet with some substance that it is capable of dissolving. 2. Sulphur. This is found sometimes singly, but generally in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> of sulphur. In these waters, sulphur is formed into a heap by means of calcareous earth or of mineral alkali. 3. Vitriolic salts with earthy bases. These salts are frequently selenitic, that is, their acid is combined with a calcareous earth; or they are of the nature of Epsom salt, the basis of which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>. Sometimes, but not so frequently, they are aluminate, when their acid happens to be united with an argillaceous earth. 4. Vitriols. Martial vitriol is frequently contained in mineral waters; vitriol of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> is sometimes, but seldom, and vitriol of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> is still more rarely found in these waters. The vitriols of other metallic substances are scarcely ever, but in very singular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, found in water. 5. Lastly, vitriolic salts with basis of fixed alkali. This is always Glauber's salt. Neither vitriolated tartar nor vitriolic ammoniacal salt are ever found, unless by some singular accident, in mineral waters. The combinations of marine acid that are contained in mineral waters are common salts, and marine salt with earthy basis. For no combinations of this acid with phlogiston are known, and it is very seldom found united with any metallic substance. Compounds formed of the nitrous acid with an earthy basis are very common in waters in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, inasmuch that some have thought that nitre might be extracted from them advantageously in the way of trade. See Chemistry, n° 178. In France, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> seems to be otherwise; for Mr. Mosquer determines, in his Chemical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, that the nitrous acid is not (nay that it cannot) be found in waters except by accident. These are the principal substances that form almost all these waters. We shall now show the proofs by means of which they may be discovered in water, without decomposing the water by evaporation or by distillation. If any portion of disengaged acid or alkali be contained in water, it may be known by the taste, by changing the colour of violets or of turpentine, and by adding the precise quantity of acid or of alkali that is necessary for the saturation of the contained disengaged saline matter. Sulphur, and liver of sulphur, may be discovered in waters by their singular smell, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour which these substances give to white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> or to their precipitates, but especially to silver. Vitriolic salts with earthy basis may be discovered in water by two proofs: 1. By adding some fixed alkali, which decomposes all these salts, and precipitates their earthy basis; and, 2.
