Ceruus by fire takes the colour of citron, and is often called masticot. Observe, that yellow ochre heated, becomes more tender than it was, and softer than brown red. Likewise brown red heated becomes softer than fine yellow ochre. Both are very proper. The finest and truest ultramarine, heated upon a red-hot hot iron, becomes more glittering; but it wastes, and is coarser and harder to work with in miniature. All these colours are diluted in little cups of ivory, made on purpose, or in sea shells, with water in which gum-arabic and sugar-candy are put. For instance, in a glass of water put a piece of gum as big as a walnut, and half that quantity of sugar-candy. This last hinders the colours from sealing when they are laid on, which they generally do when they want it, or the vellum is greasy. This gum-water must be kept in a neat bottle corked; and you never must take any out of it with a pencil that has colour upon it, but with a quill or some such thing. Some of this water is put in the shell with the colour you would temper, and diluted with the finger till it be very fine. If it be too hard, you must let it soften in the shell with the said water before you dilute it. Afterwards let it dry: and do thus with every colour, except lily-green, pop-green, and gamboge, which must be tempered with fair water only. But ultramarine, lake, and bitre, are to be more gummed than other colours. If you make use of sea-shells, you must let them steep two or three days beforehand in water: then cleanse them in boiling-hot water, mixed with vinegar, in order to carry off a certain salt, which otherwise sticks to them, and spoils the colours that are put to them. To know whether colours are sufficiently gummed, you have nothing to do but to give a stroke of the pencil upon your hand when they are diluted, which dries immediately: if they chap and scale, there is too much gum; if they rub out by passing the finger over them, there is too little. It may be seen likewise when the colours are laid on the vellum, by passing the finger over them. If they stick to it like a powder, it is a sign there is not gum enough, and more must be put to the water with which you temper them: but take care you do not put too much; for that makes the colour extremely hard and dry. It may be known likewise by their glistening and brightness: so the more they are gummed, the darker they paint; and when you have a mind to give a greater strength to a colour than it has of itself, you have nothing to do but to give it a great deal of gum. Provide yourself with an ivory pallet, very smooth, as big as your hand; on one side of which the colours for the carnation, or naked parts of a picture, are to be ranged in the following manner. In the middle put a great deal of white, pretty largely spread; because it is the colour most made use of: and upon the edge, from the left to the right, place the following colours at a little distance from the white. Masticot. Dutch pink. Orpiment. Yellow-ochre. Green; composed of verditer, Dutch pink, and white, in equal quantities. Blue; made of ultramarine, Indigo, and white, to a great degree of paleness. Vermilion. Carmine. On the other side of the pallet, spread some white in the same manner as for the carnation. And when you have a mind to paint draperies, or other things, place near the white the colour you would make them of, in order to work as shall be shewn hereafter. The use of good pencils is a great matter. In order to make a good choice, wet them a little; and if the hairs keep close together as you turn them upon the finger, and make but one point, they are good: but if they close not together, but make several points, and some are longer than others, they are good for nothing. When they are too sharp-pointed, with only four or five hairs longer than the rest, yet clotting all together, they are, notwithstanding, good; but they must be blunted with a pair of scissors, taking care at the same time you do not clip away too much. It is proper to have two or three sorts of them; the largest for laying the grounds and dead-colouring, and the smallest for finishing. To bring the hairs of your pencil to join close together and make a good point, you must often put the pencil just between your lips when you are at work; moistening and pressing it close with the tongue, even when there is colour upon it; for if there be too much, some of it is taken off by this means, and enough left for giving fine and equal touches. You need not apprehend this will do you any harm. None of the colours for miniature, except orpiment, when they are prepared, have either ill taste or ill quality. This expedient must especially be used for dotting, and for finishing, particularly the naked parts of a picture, that the touches may be neat and fair, and not too much charged with colour. As for draperies and other things, as well in dead-colouring as in finishing, it is sufficient, in order to make the hairs of your pencil join well, and to unload it when it has too much colour, to draw it upon the edge of the shell, or upon the paper you must put upon your work to rest your hand on, giving some strokes upon it before you work upon your piece. To work well in miniature, you must do it in a room that has but one window, and fix yourself very near it, with a table and desk almost as high as the window; placing yourself in such a manner, that the light may always come in on the left side, and never forward or on the right. When you would lay a colour on all parts equally strong, as for a ground, you must make your mixtures in shells, and put in enough for the thing you design to paint; for if there be not enough, it is a great chance but the colour you mix afterwards is too dark or too light. Sect. III. Of Working. After having spoke of vellum, pencils, and colours, let us now shew how they are to be employed. In the first place, then, when you would paint a piece, be it carnation, drapery, or any thing else, you must begin by dead-colouring; that is to say, by laying your colours on with liberal strokes of the pencil, in the smoothest manner you can, as the painters do in oil; not giving it all the force it is to have for a finishing:

MINIMS

Pages 299-299

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, founded by St Francis de Paula, towards the end of the 15th century. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> woollen stuff, with a woollen girdle, of the same colours, tied in five knots. They are not permitted to quit their habit and girdle night nor <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Formerly they went bare-footed, but are now allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of shoes.

MINIMUM

Pages 299-299

in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the least <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> attainable in a given <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

MINISTER

Pages 299-299

a person who preaches, performs <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship in public, administers the sacraments, &c. Minister of State, a person to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> intrusts the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. See Counsellor. Foreign Minister, is a person sent into a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to manage the affairs of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of the state to which he belongs. Of these there are two kinds; those of the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are ambassadors, and envoys extraordinary, who represent the persons of their sovereigns; the ministers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rank are the ordinary residents.

MINIUM

Pages 299-300
or RED-LEAD. See Chemistry, p. 402. The general method of preparing that colour is there described; but the following more accurate and particular one hath appeared in the last edition of the Chemical Dictionary. "The furnace in which miniun is made is of the reverberatory kind, with two fire-places at the ends; each fire-place being separated from the area, or body of the furnace, by a wall 12 inches high. The fire-places are 15 inches broad, and their length is equal to the breadth of the whole furnace, which is about eight or nine feet. The length of the area from one fire-place to the other is 9 or 10 feet. The quantity of lead used in one operation is about 1500 pounds, of which nine parts are lead obtained from furnaces where the ore is melted, and one part is lead extracted from the scoria which is formed in melting the ore. This latter kind is said to be necessary, as the former could not alone be reduced into powder. All the lead is at once put into the area, the bottom of which is level. The calx, as fast as it is formed, is drawn to one side by means of a rake suspended by a chain before the mouth of the furnace. In four or five hours the whole quantity of the lead is calcined, or, if any pieces remain uncalcined, they are separated, and kept for the next operation. The heat employed is that of a cherry-red; and the fire-places and mouth are kept open, that the air may accelerate the calcination. The powder or calx is to be frequently stirred to prevent its concreting; and when this operation has been continued about 24 hours, the matter is taken out of the furnace, and laid on a flat pavement. The cold water is thrown on it, to give it weight, as the workmen say; but rather, as some think, to make it friable. It is then to be ground in a mill, and the Miner, finer part is separated by washing, while the coarser part, referred for some following operation, is to be placed at the mouth of the furnace in order to retain the melted lead. The fine powder, which is now of a yellow colour, is again put into the same or a similar furnace, and exposed to a very moderate fire from 36 to 48 hours; during which time it is stirred frequently to prevent its concreting; and the powder gradually acquires its proper red colour. The minium is then to be taken out of the furnace, cooled, and sifted through an iron sieve placed in a cask."

MINNOW

Pages 303-303

a very small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus, so well known that it needs no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>.

MINOR

Pages 300-300

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, n° clxi. Minor, in logic, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> proposition of a regular syllogism. See Logic.

MINORCA

Pages 300-302

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, situated between 39 and 40 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Latitude, and near four degrees of East <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a>. It is about 33 miles in length from north-west to south-east, in breadth from eight to twelve, but in general about ten miles; so that in size it may nearly equal the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Huntingdon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>. The form is very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; and the coasts are much indented by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little creeks and inlets, some of which might be very advantageous. This island is one of those called by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Baleares, which arose from the dexterity of the inhabitants in using the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLING">sling</a>. It fell under the power of the Romans, afterwards of the northern barbarians, who destroyed that empire. From them it was taken by the Arabs, who were subdued by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, and he by the king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The English subdued it in 1708, and the French in the late <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; but it was restored to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1763. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this island is much more clear and pure than in Britain; being seldom darkened with thick fogs; yet the low valleys are not free from mists and unwholesome vapours; and in windy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the spray of the sea is driven over the whole island. Hence it happens that utensils of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are extremely susceptible of rust, in spite of all endeavours to preserve them; and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture becomes mouldy. The summers are dry, clear, calm, and excessively hot; the autumns moist, warm, and unequal; at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> perfectly serene, at another cloudy and tempestuous. During the winter there are sometimes violent storms, though neither frequent nor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; and whenever they cease, the weather returns to its usual serenity. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is always variable, but resembles the winter more than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The changes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> are neither so great nor so sudden in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> as in many others. In the compass of a year, the thermometer seldom rises much above the 80th, or falls below the 48th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. In summer there is scarcely ever a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of four or five degrees between the heat of the air at noon and at night; and in winter the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> is still less considerable. But this must be understood of a thermometer shaded from the influence of the solar beams; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exposed to them it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> often rise 12, 14, or 16 degrees higher than what we have mentioned; and in other seasons the difference between the heat of the air in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> is much greater. Yet, even in the dog-days, the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, at least in open places, seldom surpasses that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood. The winds are very boisterous about the equinoxes, and Minorca sometimes during during the winter. At other times they are generally moderate, and, according to the observations of seamen, they rarely blow in the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> near the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> adjacent to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Lyons as in the open sea. During the summer there is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a perfect calm in the mornings and evenings; but the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> is cooled by refreshing breezes which come from the east, and, following the course of the sun, increase gradually till two or three in the afternoon; after which they insensibly die away, as night approaches. This renders the heat of the sun less dangerous and inconvenient; and if these breezes intermit for a day or two, the natives grow languid and inactive from the heat. The northerly winds in general are clear and healthy, dispel the mists, and make a clear blue sky; whilst those which blow from the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> render the air warm, moist, and unhealthy. The north <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is superior in power to all the rest; which appears from hence, that the tops of all the trees incline to the south, and the branches on the north side are bare and blasted. The next to it in force is the north-west. Both are frequent towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of winter, and in the spring; and, being dry and cold, they shrivel up the leaves of the vegetables, destroy their tender shoots, and are often excessively detrimental to the vineyards and rising corn. The piercing blasts at that season from the north-east, as they are more moist, and more frequently attended with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, are less prejudicial. The south and south-east winds are by much the most unhealthy. In whatever seasons they blow, the air is foggy, and affects the breathing; but in the summer season they are sultry and suffocating. An excessive dejection of spirits is then a universal complaint; and on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the thermometer to the rays of the sun, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> has frequently risen above the 100th degree. The west wind is usually drier than the south; the east is cold and blustering in the spring, and sultry in the summer. The weather in Minorca is generally fair and dry; but when it rains, the showers are heavy, though of short continuance, and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> most commonly in the night. The sky in summer is clear, and of a beautiful azure, without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or rain; but moderate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a> descend regularly after sunset. In autumn the weather becomes less serene; whirlwinds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> become frequent; and in the night-time <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and those meteors called falling stars, are very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-sprouts also are often seen at that season, and frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> upon the shore. A sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the weather takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> about the autumnal equinox; the skies are darkened with clouds, and the rains fall in such quantities, that the torrents thereby occasioned, pouring <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills, tear up trees by the root, carry away cattle, break down fences, and do considerable mischief to the gardens and vineyards. But these anniversary rains are much more violent than lasting; always falling in sudden and heavy showers, with intervals of fair weather. They are accompanied with thunder, lightning, and squalls of wind, most commonly from the north. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a> and snow are often intermixed with the rains which fall in winter and in spring; but the snow, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, dissolves immediately; and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a> is here an uncommon The whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Minorca lies low; and there are only a few hills near the centre, of which the most considerable, named Toro by the inhabitants, may be seen at the distance of 12 or 14 leagues from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The surface of the island is rough and unequal; and in many places divided by long narrow vales of a considerable depth, called barrancos by the natives. They begin towards the middle of the island, and after several windings terminate at the sea. The south-west side is more plain and regular towards the north-east; where the hills are higher, with low, marshy valleys betwixt them; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> less fruitful, and the whole tract unhealthy to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. Near the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages the fields are well cultivated, and inclosed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-walls; but the rest, for the most part, are rocky, or covered with woods and thickets. There are some pools of standing water, but very few rivulets; which is the greatest defect about the island, as the inhabitants have scarcely any wholesome water excepting what is saved from the clouds. The soil is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, thin, and very stony, with a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of sea-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and, in some places, of calcareous nitre intermixed. In most places there is so little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, that the island appears to be but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> irregular rock covered here and there with mould, and an infinite variety of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Notwithstanding this, however, it is not only extremely proper for vineyards, but produces more wheat and barley than could at first sight be imagined; and, if the peasants may be credited, it would always yield a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn and wine sufficient for the natives, did not the violence of the winds, and the excessive drought of the weather, frequently spoil their crops. The fields commonly <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> fallow for two years, and are sown the third. About the latter end of winter, or the beginning of spring, they are first broke up; and next autumn, as soon as the rains fail, they are again ploughed and prepared for receiving the proper seeds. The tillage is very easily performed; for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> so light as to be transported from place to place on the ploughman's shoulder, and to be drawn by an heifer, or an ass sometimes assisted by an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, is sufficient for opening so thin a soil. The later the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> happens, the more plentiful it proves. The barley is usually cut down about the 20th of May N.S., and the wheat is reaped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>; so that the whole harvest is commonly got in by midsummer-day. The grain is not threshed with flails as in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but trodden out on a smooth piece of rock by oxen and asses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the eastern nations. The natives of Minorca are commonly lean, thin, and well-built, of a middle stature, and olive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>; but their character is by no means agreeable. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> impetuosity of their temper, that the slightest cause provokes them to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>; and they seem to be incapable of forgiving or forgetting an injury. Hence quarrels break out daily, even among neighbours and relations; and family-disputes are transmitted from father to son; and thus, though lawyers and pettifoggers are very numerous in this country, there are still too few for the clients. Both sexes are, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, extremely amorous: they are often betrothed to each other while children, and marry at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14. The women have easy labours, and commonly return in a few days to their usual <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> business; but, lest the family should become too numerous for their income, it is a practice among the poorer sort to keep their children at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> for two or three years, that by this means the mothers may be hindered from breeding. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> of the finest wheat-flour, well fermented and well baked, is more than half the diet of people of all ranks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, vermicelli, herbs and roots from the garden, summer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, pickled olives, and pods of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, make up almost all the other half; so that scarce a fifth of their whole food is furnished from the animal-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and of this fish makes by much the most considerable portion. On Fridays, and other fast-days, they abstain entirely from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; and during <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they live altogether on vegetables and fish, excepting Sundays, when they are permitted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of eggs, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Most of their dishes are highly-seasoned with pepper, cloves, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, and other spices; and garlic, onions, or leeks, are almost constant ingredients. They eat a great deal of oily, and that none of the sweetest or best flavoured; using it not only with salads, but also with boiled and fried fish, greens, pulse, &c. instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. A slice of bread soaked in boiled water, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and salt, is the common breakfast of the peasants, well known by the name of alaquas. Their ordinary meals are very frugal, and consist of very little variety; but on festivals and other solemn occasions, their entertainments are to the last degree profuse and extravagant, insomuch that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of fare of a country <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s wedding-dinner would scarce be credited. With regard to other matters, the Minorquins are accused of prodigious indolence in the way of business, and neglect of the natural advantages they possess. In the bowels of the earth are iron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-ores, of none of which any use hath been made except the last. A lead-mine was worked to advantage some time ago, and the ore sent into France and Spain for the use of the potters in those countries. The proprietor discontinued his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on some small discouragement; and indeed it is said, that these people are of all mankind the most easily put out of conceit with an undertaking that does not bring them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, or that admits of the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of disappointing their most sanguine expectations; nor will their purse admit of many disappointments; and thus their poverty co-operating with their natural despondence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of ease, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of their backwardness to engage in projects, though ever so promising, for the improvement of their private fortune, and the advantage of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of their country. This lead-ore went under the name of vermis among the natives, as it was wholly used by the potters in varnishing and glazing their earthen vessels. There are few exports of any account, and they are obliged to their neighbours for near one-third of their corn, all their oil, and such a variety of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of less consideration, that nothing could preserve them from a total bankruptcy, but the English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> circulated by the troops, which is exchanged for the daily supplies of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, increased by the multiplication of vineyards, the breeding of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and the production of vegetables, in a proportion of at least five to one since the island has been in our possession. It will not require many words to enumerate their exports: they make a sort of cheese, little liked by the English, which sells in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> at a very great price; this, perhaps, to the amount of 800 l. per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> they send abroad may produce 900 l. more. Some wine is exported; and, if we add to its value that of the home-consumption, which has every merit of an export, being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parts in ten taken off by the troops for ready money, it may well be estimated at 16,000 l. a-year. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and salt, their yearly exports may be about 400 l. and this comes pretty near the sum of their exports, which we estimate together at 18,100 l. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a> per annum. A vast <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> lies against them, if we consider the variety and importance of the articles they fetch from other countries, for which they must pay ready cash. Here it may be necessary to withdraw some things from the heap, such as their cattle, sheep, and fowls, on which they get a profit; for the country does not produce them in a sufficient abundance to supply them, especially when we have a fleet of men of war stationed there. Their imports are, corn, cattle, sheep, fowls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, oil, rice, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, spices, hard-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and tools of all kinds; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; chocolate, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a> to make it; tobacco, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, plank, boards, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, tobacco-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, playing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, turnery ware, seeds, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, saddles; all manner of cabinet-makers work, iron spikes, nails, fine earthen-ware, glass, lamps, bric-a-brac, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> wares; copperas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, dye-fluffs, painters brushes, and colours; musical instruments, music, and strings; watches, wine, fruit, all manner of fine and printed linens, muslins, cambrics, and laces; bottles, corks, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, fans, trinkets, toys, ribbands, tape, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, pins, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, mohair, lanthorns, cordage, tar, pitch, rosin, drugs, gloves, fire-arms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and lead; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, caps, velvet, cotton stuffs, woollen cloths, stockings, capes, medals, vestments, pictures, images, ignus Dei's, books, pardons, bulls, relics, and indulgences. The island is divided into what they style terminos, of which there were anciently five, now reduced to four, and resemble our counties. The termino of Ciutadella, at the north-western extremity of the island, is so styled from this place, which was once a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Minorca. It makes a venerable and majestic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, even in its present state of decay, having in it a large Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, some other churches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, which is no contemptible pile. There are in it 600 houses, which, before the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> were removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, were fully inhabited; and there are still more gentlemen's families here than in all the rest of the island. It hath a port commodious enough for the vessels employed in the trade of this country, which, though in the possession of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power, is less than it formerly was. It is still, in the style of our officers, the best <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> (and there are none bad), in the country; and if there was a civil government, and the place made a free port, the best judges are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it would very soon become a flourishing place again; and the fortifications, if it should be found necessary, might then also be easily restored and improved. The termino of Fenerias is the next, a narrow slip reaching across from sea to sea, and the country little cultivated; it is therefore united to Mercadal. In this last termino stands Mont-toro in the very centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>, and the highest ground, some say the only mountain in it; on the summit of which there is a convent, where, even in the hottest months, the monks enjoy a cool air, and at all times a most delightful prospect. About six miles north from Mont-toro stands the castle that covers Port Fornelles, which is a very spacious harbour on the east side of the island. There are in it shoals and foul ground, which, to those who are unacquainted with them, render it difficult and dangerous; yet the packets bound from Mahon to Marseille frequently take shelter therein; and while the Spaniards were in possession of the isle, large ships and men of war frequented it. At a small distance from this lies another harbour called Alaior, which runs far into the land; but being reputed unsafe, and being so near Fornelles, is at present useless. The country about it is, however, said to be the pleasantest and wholesomest spot in the island, and almost the only one plentifully supplied with excellent spring-water, so that the gardens are well laid out, and the richest and finest fruits grow here in the highest perfection. Alaior is the next termino, in which there is nothing remarkable but the capital of the same name, well situated on an eminence, in a pleasant and tolerably cultivated country. The termino of Mahon, at the south-east end of the island, is at present the most considerable of them all, containing about 60,000 English acres, and nearly one-half of the inhabitants in Minorca. The town of Mahon derives its name from the Carthaginian general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a>, who is universally allowed to be its founder. It stands on an eminence on the west side of the harbour, the ascent pretty steep. There are in it a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, three convents, the governor's palace, and some other public edifices. It is larger; but the streets are winding, narrow, and ill-paved. The fortres of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> stands near the entrance of the harbour, which it covers, is very spacious, of great strength, with subterranean works to protect the garrison from bombs, large magazines, and whatever else is necessary to render it a complete fortification, and hath a numerous and well-disposed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. Port Mahon is allowed to be the finest harbour in the Mediterranean, about 90 fathoms wide at its entrance, but within very large and safe, stretching a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> or more into the land. Beneath the town of Mahon there is a very fine quay, one end of which is reserved for the ships of war, and furnished with all the accommodations necessary for careening and refitting them; the other serves for merchantmen. On the other side the harbour is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLA">Mola</a>, where it is generally agreed a fortres might be constructed which would be impregnable, as the castle of St Philip was esteemed before we took it, and bestowed so much money upon it, that, though some works were erected at Cape Mola, it was not judged proper to proceed in the fortifications there at a fresh expense; at least this is the only reason that hath been assigned.

MINOS

Pages 302-303

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, was Rhadaman- Minotaur the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>. He is said to have built several cities in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Crete; to have given laws to the Cretans; and to have had a son, from whom sprung Minos II., king of Crete, Sarpedon, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>, who distributed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> with such severity, that they were, according to the poets, constituted judges of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, where the most difficult <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> were referred to Minos, who was distinguished from the rest by his holding a sceptre of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>.

MINOTAUR

Pages 303-303

in antiquity, a fabulous monster much talked of by the poets, feigned to be half <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and half bull. The minotaur was brought forth by Pasiphaë, wife of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. It was shut up in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and at last killed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>. Servius gives the explanation of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>: he says that a secretary of king Minos, named Taurus, "bull," having an intrigue with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> (Pasiphaë) in the chamber of Daedalus, she was at length delivered of twins; one of whom resembled Minos, and the other Taurus. This occasioned the production to be reputed monstrous.

MINSTREL

Pages 303-304

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> for a singer and instrumental performer. The word minstrel is derived from the French minstrelier, and was not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> here before the Norman conquest. It is remarkable, that our old monkish historians do not use the word citharodus, cantator, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, to express a minstrel in Latin; but either viarius, bistris, joculator, or some other word that implies jesture. Hence it should seem that the minstrels set off their singing by mimicry, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; or, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, united the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, poem, and dance. The Saxons, as well as the ancient Danes, had been accustomed to hold men of this profession in the highest reverence. Their skill was considered as something divine; their persons were deemed sacred; their attendance was solicited by kings, and they were everywhere loaded with honours and rewards. In short, poets and their art were held among them in that rude admiration which is ever shewn by an ignorant people to such as excel them in intellectual accomplishments. When the Saxons were converted to Christianity, in proportion as letters prevailed among them, this rude admiration began to abate, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was no longer a peculiar profession. The poet and the minstrel became two persons. Poetry was cultivated by men of letters indiscriminately, and many of the most popular rhymes were composed amidst the leisure and retirement of monasteries. But the minstrels <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a distinct order of men, and got their livelihood by singing verses to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> at the houses of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. There they were still hospitably and respectfully received, and retained many of the honours shewn to their predecessors the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">Bards</a> and Scalds. And indeed, though some of them only recited the compositions of others, many of them still composed songs themselves; and all of them could probably invent a few stanzas on occasion. There is no doubt but most of the old heroic ballads were produced by this order of men. For although some of the larger metrical romances might come from the minstrel <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of the monks or others, yet the smaller narratives were probably composed by the minstrels who sung them. From the amazing variations which occur in different copies of these old pieces, it is evident they made no scruple to alter each other's productions, and the reciter added or omitted whole stanzas, according to his own fancy or convenience. In the early ages, as is hinted above, this profession was held in great reverence among the Saxon tribes, as well as among their Danish brethren. This appears from two remarkable facts in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which show that the same arts of music and song were equally admired among both nations, and that the privileges and honours conferred upon the professors of them were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both; as it is well known their customs, manners, and even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, were not in those times very dissimilar. When <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Alfred the Great was desirous to learn the true situation of the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, which had invaded his realm, he assumed the dress and character of a minstrel; and taking his harp, and only one attendant, (for in the earliest times it was not unusual for a minstrel to have a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to carry his harp,) he went with the utmost security into the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. And though he could not but be known to be a Saxon, the character he had assumed procured him a hospitable reception; he was admitted to entertain the king at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and stood among them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to contrive that assault which afterwards destroyed them. This was in the year 878. About 60 years after, a Danish king made use of the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to explore the camp of king Athelstan. With his harp in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and dressed like a minstrel, Anlaf, king of the Danes went among the Saxon tents, and taking his stand near the king's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, began to play, and was immediately admitted. There he entertained Athelstan and his lords with his singing and his music; and was at length dismissed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reward, though his songs must have discovered him to have been a Dane. Athelstan was saved from the consequences of this stratagem by a soldier, who had observed Anlaf <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which had been given him, from some scruple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. This occasioned a discovery. From the uniform procedure of both these kings, it is plain that the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of entertainment prevailed among both people, and that the minstrel was a privileged character among both. Even as late as the reign of Edward II., the minstrels were easily admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence, as appears from a passage in Stow, which also shows the splendour of their appearance. "In the year 1316, Edward the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> did solemnize his feast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a> at Westminster, in the great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>: where sitting royally at the table with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> about him, there entered a woman adorned like a minstrel, sitting on a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> trapped, as minstrels then used, who rode round about the tables, shewing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>; and at length came up to the king's table, and laid before him a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and forthwith <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> her horse, saluted every one, and departed." The subject of this letter was a remonstrance to the king on the favours heaped by him on his minions, to Minstrel—neglect of his knights and faithful servants. The messenger was sent in a minstrel's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, as what would <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an easy admission; and was a woman concealed under that habit, probably to disarm the king's resentment: for we do not find that any of the real minstrels were of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and therefore conclude this was only an artful contrivance peculiar to that occasion. In the 4th year of Richard II., John of Gaunt erected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TETBURY">Tetbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of minstrels, with a full power to receive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> from the men of this profession within five neighbouring counties, to exact laws, and determine their controversies; and to apprehend and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> such of them as should refuse to appear at the said court, annually held on the 16th of August. For this they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, by which they were empowered to appoint a king of the minstrels, with four officers, to preside over them. These were every year elected with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; the whole form of which is described by Dr. Plot: in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, they seem to have become <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> musicians. Even so late as the reign of king Henry VIII., the reciters of verses or moral speeches learnt by heart, intruded without ceremony into all companies; not only in taverns, but in the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> themselves. This we learn from Erasmus, whose argument led him only to describe a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of these men who did not sing their compositions; but the others that did, enjoyed without doubt the same privileges. We find that the minstrels continued <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; in whose time they had lost much of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and were sinking into contempt and neglect. Yet still they sustained a character far superior to any thing we can conceive at present of the singers of old ballads. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Elizabeth was entertained at Killingworth castle by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> in 1575, among the many devices and pageants which were exhibited for her entertainment, one of the personages introduced was that of an ancient minstrel, whose appearance and dress are so minutely described by a writer there present, and gives us so distinct an idea of the character, that we shall quote the passage at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. "A person very meet seemed he for the purpose, of a xlv. years old, apparelled partly as he would himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> off: his head seemingly rounded monsterwise: fair-kembed, that, with a sponge daintily dipped in a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPON">capon</a>'s grease, was finely smoothed, to make it shine like a mallard's wing. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> fmugly shaven: and yet his shirt after the new trink, with ruffs fair starched, flecked and glittering like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of new shoes, marshalled in good order with a setting slick, and strut, 'that' every ruff stood up like a wafer. A side [i.e. long] <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> of Kendale green, after the freshness of the year now, gathered at the neck with a narrow gorget, fastened afore with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> clasp and a keeper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> up to the chin; but easily, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to undo when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>. Seemingly begirt in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> caddis girdle: from that a pair of capped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> knives hanging at two sides. Out of his bosom drawn from a lappet of his napkin edged with a blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, and marked with a D for Damian; for he was but a bachelor yet. "His gown had side [i.e. long] sleeves down to mid-leg, slit from the shoulder to the hand, and lined with white cotton. His <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOUBLET">doublet</a>-sleeves of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> worsted: upon them a pair of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of tawny-chamlet laced along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> with blue threaden pointes. A west towards the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of fulsian-a-napes. A pair of red neather flecks. A pair of pumps on his feet, with a crofs cut at his toes for corns; not new indeed, yet cleanly blackt with foot, and shining as a shining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. "About his neck a red ribband suitable to his girde. His harp in good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> dependent before him. His wreft tyed to a green lace and hanging by: under the gorget of his gown a fair flaggon chain, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> for) silver, as a squire Minstrel of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, that travelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, unto fair and worshipful mens houses. From his chain hung a leutecheon, with metal and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, resplendent upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, of the ancient arms of Ilington." This minstrel is described as belonging to that village. We suppose such as were retained by noble families, wore their arms hanging down by a silver chain as a kind of badge. From the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of Squire Minstrel above, we may conclude there were other inferior orders, as Yeomen Minstrels, or the like. This minstrel, the author tells us a little below, "after three lowly courtesies, cleared his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> with a hem ... and wiped his lips with the hollow of his hand for 'kiling his napkin; tempered a string or two with his wreft'; and, after a little warbling on his harp for a prelude, came forth with a solemn song, warranted for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> out of king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s acts, &c." Towards the end of the 16th century, this class of men had lost all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, and were sunk so low in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that in the 39th year of Elizabeth a statute was passed by which "minstrels, wandering abroad" were included among "rogues, vagabonds, and sturdy beggars," and were adjudged to be punished as such. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> seems to have put an end to the profession, for after this time they are no longer mentioned.

MINT

Pages 304-305

the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is coined. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COINAGE">COINAGE</a>. There were anciently mints in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England; but the only mint at present in the British dominions is that in the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The officers of the mint are, 1. The warden of the mint, who is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; he oversees the other officers, and receives the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-worker, who receives the bullion from the warden, causes it to be melted, delivers it to the moneyers, and, when it is coined, receives it again. 3. The comptroller, who is the overseer of all the inferior officers, and sees that all the money is made to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> assize. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a>-master, who weighs the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and sees that it is according to the standard. 5. The auditor, who takes the accounts. 6. The surveyor of the melting; who, after the assay-master has made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the bullion, sees that it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out, and not altered after it is delivered to the melter. 7. The engraver; who engraves the stamps and dyes for the coinage of the money. 8. The clerk of the irons; who fees that the irons are clean and fit to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> with. 9. The melter; who melts the bullion before it be coined. 10. The provost of the mint; who provides for and oversees MIN oversees all the moneyers. 11. The blanchers, who anneal and cleanse the money. 12. The moneyers; some of whom forge the money, some shear it, some round and mill it, and some stamp and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> it. 13. The porters, who keep the gate of the mint. Mint-Marks. It hath been usual, from old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to oblige the masters and workers of the mint, in the indentures made with them, "to make a privy mark in all the money that they make, as well of gold as of silver, so that another time they might know, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> need were, and witte which moneys of gold and silver among other of the same moneys, were of their own making, and which not." And whereas, after every trial of the pix at Westminster, the masters and workers of the mint, having there proved their moneys to be lawful and good, were immediately entitled to receive their quietus under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, and to be discharged from all suits <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> actions concerning those moneys, it was then usual for the said masters and workers to change the privy mark before used for another, that so the moneys from which they were not yet discharged might be distinguished from those for which they had already received their quietus; which new mark they then <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to stamp upon all their moneys, until another trial of the pix gave them all their quietus concerning those. The pix is a strong box with three locks, whose keys are respectively kept by the warden, master, and comptroller of the mint; and in which are deposited, sealed up in several parcels, certain pieces taken at random out of every journey, as it is called; that is, out of every 15 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of gold, or 60 pounds weight of silver, before the same is delivered to the proprietors. And this pix is, from time to time, by the king's command, opened at Westminster, in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the lord-commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, the justices of the several benches, and the barons of the exchequer; before whom a trial is made, by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of goldsmiths impaneled and sworn for that purpose, of the collective weights of certain parcels of the several pieces of gold and silver taken at random from those contained in the pix; after which those parcels being feverishly melted, assays are then made of the bullion of gold and silver so produced, by the melting certain small quantities of the same against equal weights taken from the respective trial-pieces of gold and silver that are deposited and kept in the exchequer for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. This is called the trial of the pix; the report made by the jury upon that trial is called the verdict of the pix for that time; and the indented trial-pieces just above-mentioned, are certain plates of standard gold and standard silver, made with the greatest care, and delivered in upon oath, from time to time as there is occasion, by a jury of the most able and experienced goldsmiths, summoned by virtue of a warrant from the lords of the treasury to the wardens of the mystery of goldsmiths of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London for that purpose; and which plates being so delivered in, are divided each, at this time, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts by indentures, one of which parts is kept in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of exchequer at Westminster, another by the said <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of goldsmiths, and two more by the officers of his majesty's mint in the tower; the remaining three being for the use of the mint, &c. in Scotland. The pix has sometimes been tried every year, or even oftener, but sometimes not more than once in several years: and from hence is understood how it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that, among the pieces that are dated as well as marked, three or more different dates are sometimes found upon pieces impressed with the same mark; and again, that different marks are found upon pieces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>. These marks are first observable upon the coins of king Edward III.; the words above quoted concerning those marks are from the indentures made with the lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, master and worker to king Edward IV., and the marks themselves continued to be stamped very conspicuously upon the moneys, till the coinage by the mill and press was introduced and settled after the Restoration, in the year 1662: since which time, the moneys being made with far greater regularity and exactness than before, these marks have either been totally laid aside, or such only have been used as are of a more secret <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and only known to the officers and engravers concerned in the coinage: and indeed the constant practice that has ever since prevailed, of dating all the several pieces, has rendered all such marks of much less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> than before.

MINUET

Pages 305-305

a very graceful kind of dance, consisting of a couple, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> step, and a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>: it begins with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>; and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is triple. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the minuet seems generally to be ascribed to the French, and particularly to the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Poitou. The word is said by Menage and Furetiere to be derived from the French menue <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> menu, "small, or little;" and in strictness signifies a small pace. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of this dance consists of two strains, which, as being repeated, are called repeats, each having eight or more bars, but never an odd <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> is three crotchets in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and is thus marked $\frac{3}{4}$, though it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> performed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> $\frac{4}{4}$. Walther speaks of a minuet in Lully's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of Roland, each strain of which contains ten bars, the sectional number being 5; which renders it very difficult to dance.

MINUM

Pages 310-311

MARSHMOSS; a genus of the order of musci, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 18 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; but none have any remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> except the two following. 1. The fontana is an elegant moss, frequent in bogs, and on the borders of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. It is from two to four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: the stalks are simple at the base, and covered with a rusty <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but higher up are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, and divided into several veral round, single, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> branches, which proceed nearly from the same point. The leaves are not more than \( \frac{1}{4} \) of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, lanceolate and acute, of a whitish green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and so thinly set, that the red stalk appears between them. This moss, as it may be seen at a considerable distance, is a good mark to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the discovery of clear and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> springs. Linnaeus informs us, that the Laplanders are well acquainted with this sign. Mr Withering informs us, that wherever this moss grows, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> may be found without much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>. 2. The hygrometricum grows in woods, heaths, garden-walks, walls, old trees, decayed wood, and where coals <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cinders have been laid. It is stemless, hath tips inversely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped, nodding, and bright <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the fruit-stalk is moistened at the base with a little water or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, the head makes three or four revolutions; if the head is moistened, it turns back again.

MINUTE

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the 60th <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of a circle. Minute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">Time</a>, the 60th part of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Minute, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, usually denotes the 60th, sometimes the 30th, part of a module. See Architecture. Minute is also used for a short memoir, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sketch of a thing taken in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. MINUTIUS Felix. See Felix.

MIQUELETS

Pages 305-305

a name given to the Spaniards who inhabit the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the frontiers of Arragon and Catalonia, and live by robbing.

MIQUELON

Pages 305-305

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to the southwest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> May in Newfoundland, ceded to the French by the peace of 1763, for drying and curing their fish. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54° 30'. N. Lat. 47° 22'.

MIRABILIS

Pages 305-306

Marvel <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Pox; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The jalappa, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, hath a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, thick, fleshy root; an upright, thick, jointed stalk, dividing and branching numerously, widely, Mirabilis, and erectly, a yard or more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, opposite leaves; and all the branches and shoots terminated by numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in clusters, of different colours in the varieties. Of this there are varieties with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flowers—with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flowers—with purple flowers—with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> flowers—with white and yellow flowers—white and purple flowers—purple and yellow flowers—red and yellow flowers. Several other varieties often rise from seed; and it is remarkable that although several of the above colours and variegations are sometimes common to the same plant, yet it is rare that a plant of this species produces flowers of one of those colours alone; sometimes, however, the same plant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> exhibit only white and purple flowers separate, and sometimes both colours in the same flowers, intermixed with the plain ones: the same is also observable in the red and yellow; others have plain flowers of several different colours, and sometimes variegated flowers also on the same plants. The root of this species was supposed to be the true officinal jalap, but which is since discovered to be the root of a species of convolvulus. 2. The longiflora, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-flowered mirabilis, hath a large, thick, fleshy root; a thick stalk, dividing low into many declinated spreading branches, extending two or three feet every way; large, heart-formed, hairy, viscid leaves, in opposite pairs; and all the branches and shoots terminated by white flowers in clusters, having very long tubes, nodding downward. 3. The dichotoma, dichotomous, or forked mirabilis; hath a thick fleshy root; an upright, thick, swollen, jointed stem, branching forkedly two or three feet high; oblong opposite leaves; and smallish red flowers at the axillas, singly and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting. All these plants flower in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, continuing in plentiful succession until October, very conspicuous and elegant. They have the singularity of being shut all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and expanding towards the evening when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> declines; hence the inhabitants of the Indies, where they grow naturally, called them four o'clock flowers: their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of opening here, however, depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> cloudy, or that the sun is not very vehement, they often open <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the day. They are naturally perennial in root, which, however, if not preserved here in winter, prove but of one year's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; but if sheltered from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> and wet during the winter season, they will remain alive, and shoot out strongly again in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>: in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, however, the plants are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> considered as annuals; because they rise from seed in the spring, and the same year produce flowers and perfect seed; and if left to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, totally perish in winter, at the first attack of frost or excessive wet; but, as aforesaid, if in autumn, when the stalks begin to assume a state of decay, the roots are taken up, and preserved in sand in a dry room all winter, and planted again in spring, they shoot out afresh stronger than at first, and sometimes obtain four or five feet stature, with very spreading heads; or if plants growing in pots, having the stems cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in autumn, and the pots placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or garden-frames under glasses, the roots may also be preserved <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and will shoot out again in spring as above. The roots generally become large, tuberous, and fleshy, covered with a dark rind. All the species are of a tender nature, scarcely able to endure the open air here fully day and night, until May or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>; that is, they being raised from seed in spring, chiefly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a> under glasses, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and forwarded there until the beginning of June, then fully exposed in the borders or pots, they become large branchy plants in July and August, and continue flowering until October or November, till prevented by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. They are all elegant furniture for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> compartments of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>-ground, they being both very ornamental in their large branchy growth, closely garnished with leaves; and, by flowering so numerously, seem as if entirely covered with flowers, in constant plentiful succession from July till the beginning of winter, as aforesaid. The roots of all these plants is a strong purgative, and given in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> operate equal to the true jalap. The propagation of all the species is by seed in the spring, either in a warm border, or in a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>; but the latter will forward the plants to considerably the earliest and greatest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection.

MIRACLE

Pages 306-307

is defined by Dr Samuel Clarke, to be a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> effected in a manner different from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and regular method of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, by the interposition either of God himself, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> some intelligent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> superior to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. It has been much controverted, whether true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> can be worked by any less power than the immediate power of God; and whether to complete the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of a miracle, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the doctrine pretended to be proved by it is necessary to be taken into the consideration. The above learned author undertakes to set this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as follows. In respect to the power of God, and the nature of the things themselves, all things that are possible at all, are equally easy to be done: it is at least as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of power to cause the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to move at all, as to cause it at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to stand still; yet this latter we call a miracle, the former not. What degrees of power God may reasonably be supposed to have communicated to created beings or subordinate intelligences, is impossible for us to determine; therefore a miracle is not rightly defined to be such an effect as could not have been produced by any less power than the divine omnipotence. There is no instance of any miracle in scripture, which to an ordinary spectator would necessarily imply the immediate operation of original, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, and undervived power.
