All things that are done in the world, are done either immediately by God himself, or by created intelligent beings, matter not being at all capable of any laws or powers whatsoever; so that all those things which we say are the effects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> powers of matter and laws of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, are properly the effects of God acting upon matter continually and every moment, either immediately by himself, or mediately by some created intelligent beings. Consequently it is no more against the course of nature for an angel to keep a man from sinking in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, than for a man to hold a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> from falling in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, by overpowering the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>; and yet the one is a miracle, the other not so. The only possible ways by which a spectator may certainly certainly and infallibly distinguish whether miracles be the works either immediately of God himself, or of some good angel employed by him; or whether, on the contrary, they are the works of evil spirits, are these: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the doctrine attested by miracles, be in itself impious, or manifestly tending to promote vice; then, without all question, the miracles, how great forever they may appear to us, are neither worked by God himself, nor by his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. If the doctrine itself be indifferent, and at the same time there be worked other miracles more and greater than the former, then that doctrine which is attested by the superior power must necessarily be believed to be divine: this was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Moses and the Egyptian magicians. If, in the last <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the doctrine attested by miracles tends to promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of God, and the practice of righteousness among men; and yet nevertheless be not in itself demonstrable, nor could without a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> be discovered to be actually true, and there is no pretence of more and greater miracles to contradict it, which is the case of the doctrine and miracles of Christ; then the miracles are unquestionably divine, and the doctrine must, without all controversy, be acknowledged as an immediate and infallible revelation from God. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> observes, that a miracle was never wrought by God to convert an atheist, because the light of nature might have led him to confess a God: but miracles, says he, are designed to convert idolaters and the superstitious, who have acknowledged a deity, but erred in the manner of adoring him; because no light of nature extends so far as fully to declare the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> and true worship of God. Acosta inquiring into the cause why miracles are not wrought by the present missionaries for the conversion of heathen nations, as they were by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the primitive ages, gives this as one reason: That the Christians at first were ignorant men, and the Gentiles learned; but now, on the contrary, all the learning in the world is employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the gospel; and there is nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> to oppose it; and there can be no need of farther miracles in so good a cause, when it is in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of such able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> against such weak adversaries. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">ABRIDGMENT</a>.

MIRANDA-DE-EBRO

Pages 307-307

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in Old Castile, with a strong castle; seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that produces excellent wine. The town is divided into two parts by the river, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 42. 52.

MIRANDE

Pages 307-307

a town of Gascogne in France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Astarac; seated on a mountain near the river Baute. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 21. N. Lat. 42. 53. MIRANDO-DE-Douro, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Duero, a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tras-os-Montes, with a bishop's see. It is well fortified, and seated on a rock near the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Douro and Trefna. W. Long. 5. 40. N. Lat. 41. 30.

MIRANDOLA

Pages 307-307

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, situate between the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, well fortified, and has also a strong citadel and fort. It has been several times taken and retaken; the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in 1742. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 5. N. Lat. 44. 52. MIRANDULA. See Picus.

MIRIAM

Pages 307-307

sister of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and Moses, makes two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three remarkable appearances in scripture. It was owing to her that her mother was employed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> as nurse to Moses. She put herself at the head of the women of Israel after their passage through the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in order to sing the song which the men had sung before. She joined with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Aaron in murmuring against Moses, and was severely chastised for that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; for she became leprous, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> separate from the rest without the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. She died before her brothers, though in the same year with them, and was buried at the public expense.

MIRROR

Pages 307-307

a name for a looking-glass, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any polished body, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to form the images of distant objects by reflexion of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. See REFLEXION. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">Mirrors</a> are either plain, convex, or concave. They reflect the rays of light in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> exactly similar to that in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon them, and therefore represent bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> magnitude. The convex ones make the rays diverge much more than before reflexion, and therefore greatly diminish the images of those objects which they show: while the concave ones, by collecting the rays into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, not only magnify the objects they show, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> burn very fiercely when exposed to the rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and hence they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mirrors. See BURNING-MIRRORS. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the mirrors were made of some kind of metal; and from a passage in the Mosaic writings we learn that the mirrors used by the Jewish women were made of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. The Jews certainly had been taught to use that kind of mirrors by the Egyptians; from whence it is probable, that brazen mirrors were the first kind used in the world. Any kind of metal indeed, when well polished, will reflect very powerfully; but of all others silver reflects the most, though it hath been in all countries too expensive a material for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> also is very powerful; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, or even wood, gilded and polished, will <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> very powerfully as burning mirrors. Even polished <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or straw nicely plaited together, will form mirrors capable of burning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of glass, and the application of quicksilver to it, became generally known, it hath been universally employed for those plain mirrors used as ornaments to houses; but in making reflecting telescopes, they have been found much inferior to metallic ones. It doth not appear that the same superiority belongs to the metallic burning mirrors, considered merely as burning-glasses; since the mirror with which Mr Maquier melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, though only 22 inches diameter, and which was made of quicksilvered glass, produced much greater effects than M. Villette's metallic speculum, which considerably exceeded it in size. It is very probable, however, that this mirror of M. Villette's was by no means so well polished as it ought to have been; as the art of preparing the metal for taking the finest polish hath but lately been discovered and published in the Philosophical Transactions by Mr Mudge. See Glass-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">Grinding</a>.

MISADVENTURE

Pages 308-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, has an especial signification for the killing a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> partly by negligence, and partly by chance. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMICIDE">HOMICIDE</a>.

MISCHNAH

Pages 308-308
or Misnah, the code or collection of the civil law of the Jews. The Jews pretend, that when God gave the written law to Moses, he gave him also another which was not written; and which was preserved by tradition among the doctors of the synagogue, till Rabbi Judah, surnamed the Holy, seeing the danger they were in, through their dispersion, of departing from the traditions of their fathers, judged it proper to reduce them to writing. The misnah is divided in six parts: the first relates to the distinction of seeds in a field, to trees, fruits, tythes, &c.; the second regulates the manner of observing festivals; the third treats of women, and matrimonial cases; the fourth, of losses in trade, &c.; the fifth is on obligations, sacrifices, &c.; and the sixth treats of the several sorts of purification.

MISDEMEANOUR

Pages 308-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a crime. Every crime is a misdemeanor; yet the law has made a distinction between crimes of an higher and a lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; the latter being denominated misdemeanours, the former felonies, &c. For the understanding of which distinction, we shall give the following <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> from Blackstone's Commentaries, vol. iv. 5. "A crime, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanor, is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> committed or omitted, in violation of a public law, either forbidding or commanding it. This general definition comprehends both crimes and misdemeanours; which, properly speaking, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; tho' in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> usage, the word crime is made to denote such offences as are of a deeper and more atrocious dye; while smaller faults, and omissions of less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, are comprised under the gentler name of misdemeanours only."

MISE

Pages 308-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, is used in various senses; thus it sometimes signifies costs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> expenses, in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in entering of judgments in actions personal. It is also used for the issue to be tried on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> assize; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, joining of the mise upon the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, is putting in issue between the tenant and defendant, who has the best or clearest right.

MISE ALSO

Pages 308-308

e also signifies a tax <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tallage, &c. An honorary gift, or customary present from the people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> to every new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales, anciently given in cattle, wine, and corn, but now in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, being £5000l. or more, is denominated a mise: so was the usual tribute or fine of 3000 merks paid by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, at the change of every owner of the said charters, for enjoying their liberties. And at Chester they have a mise-book, wherein every town and village in the county is rated what to pay towards the mise. The 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26. ordains that lords shall have all such mises and profits of their lands as they had in times past, &c. Mise, is sometimes also corruptly used for misse, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> French meer, "a messuage;" as a mise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in some manors, is such a messuage or tenement as answers the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> a heriot at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of its owner. 2 Inst. 528.

MISERICORDIA

Pages 308-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an arbitrary fine imposed on any person for an offence: this is called misericordia, because the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a> ought to be but small, and less than that required by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person be outrageously amerced, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> that is not of record, the writ called moderata misericordia lies for moderating the amercement according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the fault. MISFORTUNE. An unlucky accident. Misfortune, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> chance, in law, a deficiency of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>; or committing of an unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> by misfortune or chance, and not by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. In such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the will observes a total neutrality, and does not cooperate with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>; which therefore wants one main ingredient of a crime. See Crime. Of this, when it affects the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of another, we have spoken under the article <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMICIDE">Homicide</a>; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> have only occasion to observe, that if any accidental mischief happens to follow from the performance of a lawful act, the party stands excused from all guilt: but if a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> be doing anything unlawful, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> ensues which he did not foresee or intend, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a man or the like, his want of foresight shall be no excuse; for, being guilty of one offence, in doing antecedently what is in itself unlawful, he is criminally guilty of whatever consequence may follow the first misbehaviour.

MISNOMER

Pages 308-308

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a misnaming <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mistaking a person's name. The Christian name of a person should always be perfect; but the law is not so strict in regard to surnames, a small mistake in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be dispensed with to make good a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and support the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the party. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>. MISO. See Dolichos.

MISPRISIONS

Pages 308-309

(a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> derived from the old French, mispris, a neglect <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> contempt,) are, in the acceptation of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, generally understood to be all such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> offences as are under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, but nearly bordering thereon: and it is said, that a misprision is contained in every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> and felony whatsoever; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> so please, the offender may be proceeded against for the misprision only. And upon the same principle, while the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR_CHAMBER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>-chamber subsisted, it was held that the king might remit a prosecution for treason, and cause the delinquent to be censured in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, merely for a high misdemeanor: as happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Roger <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Rutland, in 43 Eliz. who was concerned in the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>'s rebellion. Misprisions are generally divided into two sorts; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, which consist in the concealment of something which ought to be revealed; and positive, which consist in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of something which ought not to be done. 1. Of the first, or negative kind, is what is called misprision of treason; consisting in the bare knowledge and concealment of treason, without any degree of assent thereto: for any assent makes the party a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Misprision pal traitor; as indeed the concealment, which was considered aiding and abetting, did at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; in like manner as the knowledge of a plot against the state, and not revealing it, was a capital crime at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and other states of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. But it is now enacted by the statute 1 & 2 Ph. & Mar. c. 10, that a bare concealment of treason shall be only held a misprision. This concealment becomes criminal, if the party apprised of the treason does not, as soon as conveniently may be, reveal it to some judge of assize or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace. But if there be any probable circumstances of assent, as if one goes to a treasonable meeting, knowing beforehand that a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> is intended against the king; or, being in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> once by accident, and having heard such treasonable conspiracy, meets the same company again, and hears more of it, but conceals it; this is an implied assent in law, and makes the concealer guilty of actual high treason. Misprision of felony is also the concealment of a felony which a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> knows, but never assented to; for, if he assented, this makes him either principal or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a>. And the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of this, in a public officer, by the statute Westm. 1. 3 Edw. I. c. 9, is imprisonment for a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; in a common person, imprisonment for a less discretionary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and, in both, fine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: which pleasure of the king must be observed, once for all, not to signify any extra-judicial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the sovereign, but such as is declared by his representatives, the judges in his courts of justice; voluntas regis in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>, non in camera. 2. Misprisions, which are merely positive, are generally denominated contempt or high misdemeanor; of which the principal is the mal-administration of such high officers as are in public trust and employment. This is usually punished by the method of parliamentary impeachment: wherein such penalties, short of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, are inflicted, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> shall seem proper; consisting usually of banishment, imprisonment, fines, or perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a>. Either also may be referred the offence of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, called among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> peculatus; which the Julian law punished with death in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and with deportation, or banishment, in a private person. With us it is not a capital crime, but subjects the committer of it to a discretionary fine and imprisonment.—Other misprisions are, in general, such contempts of the executive magistrate as demonstrate themselves by some arrogant and undutiful behaviour towards the king and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; for a detail of which, vide Blackstone's Comment, iv. 22.

MISSAL

Pages 309-309

the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>-book, containing the several masses to be said on particular days. It is derived from the Latin word missa, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, signified every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

MISSIONARIES

Pages 309-309

such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> as are sent by any Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> into Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFIDEL">Infidel</a> countries, to convert the natives, and establish the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> among them. There are in France, and other Popish countries, several congregations of missionaries, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> end is to be employed on missions, and to inspire into the young clerks that spirit of piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> which is necessary for the worthy discharge of their ministry. Such are the congregations of the priests of the mission, the Euchits, the missionaries of Lyons, and some others. The most remarkable of these congregations is that of the priests of the mission, which consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy; who nevertheless make four simple vows, of poverty, chastity, obedience, and perseverance. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is distinguished from that of other ecclesiastics only by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-collar four fingers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and by their wearing a little tuft of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>.

MISSISSIPPI

Pages 309-309

also called the river of St <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, is one of the largest in the world. Its source is unknown; for it has not been navigated higher than 300 miles below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cataract of St Anthony; and there it is 50 fathoms deep, though at the distance of 2400 miles from its mouth. It discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by three mouths; and, like the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, has periodical inundations, by the melting of snow in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, so that in May it overflows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on each side, from 60 to 90 miles, and the inundation continues till near the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. In the lowest parts of the country there are morasses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, along the banks, which are generally covered with trees, and in some places the course of the river is confined between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> precipices. Its inundations always leave a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mud upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and sometimes carry <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> trees to the river's mouth, where they form new <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and render the entrance difficult.

MISSON

Pages 309-309

whose pleadings before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in favour of the reformers bear genuine marks of eloquence and ability, retired into England after the revocation of the edict of Nantz, and became a strenuous adherer of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In the years 1687 and 1688, he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> as governor to an English nobleman; in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he published at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, "A new voyage to Italy," 3 vols 12mo; which has been translated into English with many additions. He published also the "Sacred <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a> at Cevennes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> an account of Prophecies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> performed in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>," <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1707. "Observations and remarks of a traveller," 12mo, Hague. He died at London in 1721.

MISTAKE

Pages 309-309

any wrong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> committed, not through an evil <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, but through an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of judgment.

MISUSER

Pages 309-309

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an abuse of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> benefit; as "He shall make fine for his misuser." Old Nat. Br. 149. By misuser a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of a corporation may be forfeited; so also an office, &c.

MISY

Pages 309-309

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the chalcantia, a fossil very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the Turkish dominions, and sometimes found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Cremaitz in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It is a considerably firm sublance, of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture, not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>; much resembling some of our more gaudy marcasites, but wanting in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. It is of no determinate shape <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> size; but is often found in small detached masses, which are usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat, and very rugged at the edges. As to its medical virtues, they are no other than those of the green vitriol.

MITELLA

Pages 310-310
BASTARD AMERICAN SANICLE; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the decandra class of plants. There are two species, both natives of North America, rising with annual herbaceous stalks from five or six to eight or nine inches in height, and producing spikes of small whitish flowers, whose petals are fringed on their edges. They are easily propagated by parting their roots; and should be planted in a shady situation, and in a soft loamy soil. The fruit of one of the species is the achiotte, or arnotto.

MITHRIDATE

Pages 310-310

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>; an antidote, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in form of an electuary, supposed to serve either as a remedy or a preservative against poisons. See Pharmacy, n° 892.—894. It takes its name from the inventor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pontus; who is said to have so fortified his body against poisons with antidotes and preservatives, that when he had a mind to dispatch himself, he could not find any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> that would take effect. The receipt of it was found in his cabinet, written with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and was carried to Rome by Pompey. It was translated into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by Damocrates, a famous physician; and was afterwards translated by Galen, from whom we have it: though there is room to imagine it has undergone considerable alterations since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> prescriber.

MITHRIDATES

Pages 310-310
king of Pontus, a renowned general, and at first successful against the Romans; but being finally conquered by Pompey, and his son Pharnaces raised to the throne, who treated him with unnatural barbarity, he took poison; but this proving ineffectual, owing to a salutary medicine which he had almost constantly employed, he was slain at his own request by one of his attendants, 63 B.C., aged 72. He was a prince of extraordinary courage, capable of forming and executing the greatest designs. He had travelled a great deal, was learned, fond of men of letters, and spoke many languages. He composed a treatise De Arcanis Morborum; which Pompey caused to be carried to Rome, and which his freedman Lærus translated into Latin. It was he who composed that counter-poison which from his name is still called mithridate; but his sanguinary temper darkened the lustre of his most amiable perfections. See Pontus.

MITRE

Pages 310-310

a sacred ornamental worn on the head by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and certain abbots on solemn occasions; being a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, pointed and cleft at top. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> among the Jews wore a mitre <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> on his head. The inferior priests of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had likewise their mitres; but in what respect they differed from that of the high priest, is uncertain. Some contend that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bishops wore mitres; but this is by no means certain.

MITTAU

Pages 310-310

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>. It is strongly fortified; but was taken by the Swedes in 1701, and by the Muscovites in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 51. N. Lat. 56. 44.

MITTIMUS

Pages 310-310

as generally used, hath two significations. 1. It signifies a writ for removing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> transferring of records from one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> to another. 2. It signifies a precept, or command in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, directed to the gaoler or keeper of some prison, for the receiving and safe keeping of an offender <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with any crime, until he be delivered by due course of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

MITYLENE

Pages 310-310

(anc. geogr.), a celebrated, powerful, and affluent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>; nor was it less famous for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and eloquence. It suffered much in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> from the Athenians; and in the Mithridatic war from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, being taken and destroyed; but it soon rose again, having recovered its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by the favour of Pompey, (Velleius, Plutarch). It remained a free city and in power 1500 years. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Pittacus, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wise men of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; of Alceus, and of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>. Mytilenaei, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Mytilenenses, the people; who at stated times celebrated poetical contests, (Plutarch). Cicero calls it a city ennobled by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and situation, especially by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its edifices, and by its plains, which are pleasant and fertile. It is sometimes by the poets joined with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, (Horace, Martial). Mityleneus, the epithet, (Lucan). It now gives name to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and this as early as the days of Euathus; and is itself called Caffro.

MIXTURE

Pages 310-310

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of several different bodies in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Simple mixture, consists only in the simple <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPOSITION">apposition</a> of parts of different bodies to each other. Thus, when powders of different kinds are rubbed together, the mixture is only simple, and each of the powders retains its particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In like manner, when <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> are mixed together, though the parts of both are confused, so that the liquor may appear to be homogeneous, we cannot say that there is any more than a simple apposition of the parts, as the oil and water may very easily be again separated from each other. But the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> is very different when bodies are chemically mixed; for then one or both bodies assume new properties, and can by no means be discovered in their proper form without a particular chemical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> adapted to this purpose. Hence chemical mixture is attended with many phenomena which are never observed in simple mixtures; such as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, effervescence, &c. To chemical mixture belongs the union of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol4.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, the amalgamation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, solution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, &c. and upon it depend many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> operations of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. See that article pafsim.

MIZEN

Pages 310-310

in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a particular mast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sail. The mizen-mast stands in the sternmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship. In some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ships there are two of these; when that next the main-mast is called the main-mizen, and that next the poop the bonaventure mizen.

MIZRAIM

Pages 310-310
or MISRAIM, the dual name of Egypt, used in scripture to denote the Higher and Lower Egypt, which see. It sometimes occurs singular, Mizra: 2 Kings xix. Isaiah xix. Micah vii.

MOAB

Pages 311-311

(anc. geogr.), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea; so called from Moab the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, to whose posterity this country was allotted by divine appointment, Deut. xi. 9. It was anciently occupied by the Emims, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of giants exterminated by the Moabites, ibid. Moab anciently lay to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, before Sihon the Amorite divided both nations of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their territory, afterwards occupied by the Israelites, Numb. xxi.; and then Moab was bounded by the river Arnon to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Lacus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a> to the west, the brook Zared to the south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Abarim to the east.

MOAT

Pages 311-311
or Ditch, in fortification, a deep trench dug round the rampart of a fortified place, to prevent surprizes. The brink of the moat, next the rampart, is called the scarpe; and the opposite one, the counter-scarpe. A dry moat round a large place, with a strong garrison, is preferable to one full of water; because the passage may be disputed inch by inch, and the besiegers, when lodged in it, are continually exposed to the bombs, grenades, and other fire-works, which are thrown incessantly from the rampart into their works. In the middle of dry moats, there is sometimes another small one, called cunette; which is generally dug so deep, till they find water to fill it. The deepest and broadest moats are accounted the best; but a deep one is preferable to a broad one; the ordinary breadth is about 20 fathoms, and the depth about 16. To drain a moat that is full of water, they dig a trench deeper than the level of the water, to let it run off; and then throw hurdles upon the mud and slime, covering them with earth or bundles of rushes, to make a sure and firm passage.

MOCHO

Pages 311-312

Moco, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Mocha; by some supposed to be the Mufa or Muza of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, is a port and town on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, of considerable trade; contains about 10,000 inhabitants, Jews, Armenians, and Mohammedans, is surrounded with walls after the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner, and has four gates and four towers, the last mounted with cannon, but no ditch. It gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> extending along the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; of which that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> which lies next the sea is a dry barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, in some places 10 or 12 leagues over; but bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which being well watered, enjoy an almost perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and besides coffee, the peculiar produce of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, yields corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, frankincense, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CALAMUS">calamus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> of several sorts, mangos, dates, pomegranates, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> here is so hot and sultry in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, especially when the south <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, that it would be un-supportable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not mitigated by the cool breezes that generally blow from the mountains on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, or the Red and Arabian Seas on the west and east. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in winter is equal to that of our warmest summers; and it is very seldom that either <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> are seen. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mocha is now the emporium for the trade of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> to the Red-Sea. The trade was removed hither from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the prophecy of a sheik, much revered by the people; who foretold, that it would soon become a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, notwithstanding its disadvantageous situation. It stands <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the sea, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, dry, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain, that affords no good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> within 20 miles of the city; what they drink comes from Mocha, and cools as dear as small-beer in England. The water near the town, as it is thought, produces a worm, which the naturalists call the dracunculus, which is about two feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, very slender, and breeds in the fleshy parts of the body; in extracting it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care must be used, the consequence being dangerous if any part of it remains in the body. The buildings here are lofty, and tolerably regular, having a pleasant aspect from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. The steeples of several mosques are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, presenting themselves to view at a great distance. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well stored with beef, mutton, lamb, kid, camels, and antelopes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fowls, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> hens, partridges, and pigeons. The sea affords plenty of fish, but not savoury; which some think proceeds from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> saltness of the water, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their aliment. The markets are also stocked with fruit, such as grapes, peaches, apricots, quinces, and nectarines; although neither shrub nor tree is to be seen near the town, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>-trees. Frequently no rain falls here in two or three years, and seldom more than a shower or two in a year; but in the mountains, at the distance of about 20 miles from Mocha, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is watered with a gentle shower every morning, which makes the valleys fertile in corn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The Arab inhabitants, though remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and superstitious, are said to be extremely covetous and hypocritical; robbing, thieving, and committing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, without the least scruple or remorse. The English and Dutch companies have handsome houses here, and carry on a great trade in coffee, olibanum, myrrh, aloes, liquid thorax, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> arsenic, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, mummy, balm of Gilead, and other drugs. One inconvenience, however, they suffer from the violence and exactions of the Arabian princes; but the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s customs are easy, being fixed at three per cent. to Europeans. Of the coins at Mocha, the most current is the camaille, which rises and falls in value at the banker's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: they are from 50 to 80 for a current dollar, which is but an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, being always reckoned one and a half per cent. lower than Spanish dollars. As to their weights, they are almost infinite. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">MODE</a> Mocking infinite, according to the nature of the thing to be weighed; they have the baniain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the magnet; the ambergrise; the agala; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver weights, &c.

MODE

Pages 312-313

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, denotes the manner of a thing's existence. See METAPHYSICS, n° 50. 51. 55.—86. Mode, in music; a regular disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> and accompaniments relative to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sounds upon which a piece of music is formed, and which are called the essential sounds of the mode. There is this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the mode and the tone, that the latter only determines the principal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and indicates the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which is most proper to be occupied by that system which ought to constitute the basis of the air; whereas the former regulates the thirds, and modifies the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> agreeably to its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> sounds. Our modes are not, like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, characterized by any sentiment which they tend to excite, but result from our system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> alone. The sounds essential to the mode are in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> three, and form together one perfect chord. 1. The tonic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">key</a>, which is the fundamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> both of the tone and of the mode. (See TONE and TONIC). 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>, which is a fifth from the tonic. (See DOMINANT). 3. The mediant, which properly constitutes the mode, and which is a third from the same tonic. As this third may be of two kinds, there are of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> two different modes. When the mediant forms a greater third with the tonic, the mode is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; when the third is lesser, it is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. The major mode is immediately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the resonance of sounding bodies, which exhibit the third major of the fundamental sound: but the minor mode is not the product of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; it is only found by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a>. This is equally true upon the system of Sig. Tartini as upon that of M. Rameau. This last author, in his various and successive publications, has explained the origin of this minor mode in different ways, of which his interpreter M. D'Alembert was satisfied with none. It is for this reason that he has founded this origin on a different principle which cannot be better explained than in the words of that eminent geometrician. See MUSIC, Art. 28, 29, 30 and 31. When the mode is once determined, every note in the scale assumes a name expressive of its relation to the fundamental sound, and peculiar to the place which it occupies in that particular mode. We subjoin the names of all the notes significant of their relative values and places in each particular mode, taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> of ut as an example of the major mode, and of la as an example of the minor. Major, ut re mi fa sol la si ut, Minor, la si ut re mi fa sol la. It is necessary to remark, that when the seventh note is only a semitone distant from the highest in the octave, that is to say, when it forms a third major with the dominant, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> in the major mode, or sol sharp in the minor, that seventh sound is then called a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSIBLE_NOTE">sensible note</a>, because it discovers the tonic and renders the tone appreciable. Nor does each gradation only assume that name which is suitable to it; but the nature of each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is determined according to its relation to the mode. The rules established for this are as follow: 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> note must form a second major above the tonic, the fourth note and the dominant should form a fourth and fifth exactly true; and this equally in both modes. 2. In the major mode, the mediant or third, the sixth and the seventh from the tonic, should always be major; for by this the mode is characterized. For the same reason these three intervals ought always to be minor in the minor mode: nevertheless, as it is necessary that the sensible note should likewise there be perceived, which cannot be effectuated without a false relation whilst the fifth note still remains minor; this occasions exceptions, of which in the course of the air or harmony care must be taken. But it is always necessary that the clef, with its transpositions, should preserve all the intervals, as determined with relation to the tonic, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the mode. For this a general rule <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found at the word Clef in Rousseau's Musical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. As all the natural chords in the octave of ut give, with relation to that tonic, all the intervals prescribed for the major mode, and as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the same with the octave of la for the minor mode, the preceding example, which was only given that we might have an opportunity of naming the notes, may likewise serve as a formula for the rule of the intervals in each mode. This rule is not, as one might imagine, established upon principles that are merely arbitrary: it has its source in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of harmony, at least in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you give a perfect major chord to the tonic, to the dominant, and the sub-dominant, you will have all the sounds of the diatonic scale for the major mode: to obtain that of the minor, leaving still its third major to the dominant, give a third minor to the two other chords. Such is the analogy of the mode. As this mixture of major and minor chords introduces into the minor mode a false relation between the sixth and the sensible note, to avoid this false relation, they sometimes give the third major to the fourth note in ascent, or the third minor to the dominant in descending, chiefly by inverting the chords; but these in this case are licences. There are properly no more than two modes, as we have seen: but as there are twelve different sounds in the octave which may be made fundamental sounds, and of consequence form as many keys or tones; and as each of these tones are susceptible of the major or minor mode, music may be composed in twenty-four modes or manners. Nay, in the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> music, there are even thirty-four passable modes: but in practice ten are excluded, which when thoroughly examined are nothing else but a repetition of the other ten, under relations much more difficult, in which all the chords must change their names, and where it must cost any one some trouble to know what he is about. Such is the major mode upon a note raised above its natural pitch by a semitone, and the minor mode upon a note depressed by a semitone. Thus, instead of composing upon sol sharp with a third major, it is much more eligible to operate upon la flat, which will give you an opportunity to employ the same tones; and instead of composing upon re flat with a third minor, you will find it more convenient to choose ut sharp for the same reason; viz. on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to avoid a fa with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> sharp, which would be <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a sol natural; and on the other hand a si with a double flat, which would become a la natural. The composer does not always continue in the same mode, nor in the same key, in which he has begun an air; but, whether to alter the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> or introduce variety, modes and keys are frequently changed, according to the analogy of harmony; yet always returning to those which have been first heard: this is called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>. From thence arises a new <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of modes into such as are principal and such as are relative: the principal is that in which the piece begins and ends; the relative modes are such as the composer interweaves with the principal in the flow of the harmony. (See MODULATION). Others have proposed a third species, which they call a mixed mode, because it participates the modulation of both the others, or rather because it is composed of them; a mixture which they did not reckon an inconvenience, but rather an advantage, as it increases the variety, and gives the composer a greater latitude both in air and harmony. This new mode, not being found by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of the three chords like the two former, is not determined, like them, by harmonics essential to the mode, but by an entire scale which is peculiar to itself, as well in rising as descending; so that in the two modes above-mentioned the scale is investigated by the chords, and in this mixed mode the chords are investigated by the scale. The following notes exhibit the form of this scale in succession, as well rising as descending: mi fa sol la si ut re mi. Of which the essential difference is, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, in the position of the two semitones; of which the first is found between the first and the second note, and the last between the fifth and sixth: and, with respect to the harmony, the difference consists in this, that upon its tonic it carries a third minor in the beginning, and major in ending, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a> of this scale, as well in rising as descending, such as it has been given by those who proposed it, and executed at a spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>, May 30, 1751. They object to its inventor, That his mode has neither chords nor harmony essential to itself, nor cadences which are peculiar to it, and which sufficiently distinguish it from the major or minor mode. He answers to this, That the distinction of his mode is less in harmony than in melody, and less even in the mode itself than in the modulation; that in its beginning it is distinguished from the major mode by its third minor, and in its end from the minor mode by its plagal cadence. To which his opponents reply, That a modulation which is not exclusive cannot be sufficient to establish a mode; and that his mode inevitably occurs in the two other modes, and above all in the minor: and, as to his plagal cadence, that it necessarily takes place in the minor mode as often as transition is made from the chord of the tonic to that of the dominant, as has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the case in practice, even upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> notes, in plagal modes, and in the tone proper to the fourth. From whence it is concluded, that his mixed mode is not so much a particular species, as a new denomination for the manner of interweaving and combining the major and minor modes, as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as harmony, practised at all periods: and this appears to be so true, that, even when he begins his scale, its author will neither venture to give the fifth nor the sixth to his tonic, for fear lest by the first the tonic should be determined in the minor mode, or the mediant in the major mode by the second. He leaves the harmony equivocal by not filling up his chord. But whatever objections may be made against the mixed mode, whose name is rather rejected than its practice, this will not prevent the author from appearing as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius, and a musician profoundly learned in the principles of his art, by the manner in which he treats it, and the arguments which he uses to establish it. MODE MAJOR. See INTERVAL.

MODE MINOR

Pages 313-313
MODEL, in a general sense, an original pattern, proposed for any one to copy or imitate. This word is particularly used, in building, for an artificial pattern made in wood, stone, plaster, or other matter, with all its parts and proportions, in order for the better conducting and executing some great work, and to give an idea of the effect it will have in large. In all great buildings, it is much the surest way to make a model in relief, and not to trust to a bare design or draught. There are also models for the building of ships, &c. and for extraordinary staircases, &c. They also use models in painting and sculpture; whence, in the academies, they give the term model to a naked man or woman, disposed in several postures, to give an opportunity to the scholars to design him in various views and attitudes.

MODENA

Pages 313-314

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> and the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, on the east by the Bolognese and the territories of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and on the west by the duchy of Parma; extending in length from south to north about 56 English miles, and in breadth between 24 and 36, and yielding plenty of corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, with mineral waters. In some places also <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a> is skimmed off the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of deep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> made on purpose; and in others is found a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tophus, which, when pulverised, is said to be an excellent remedy against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, fevers, dysenteries, and hypochondriac disorders. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of La Salfa affords several kinds of petrifications. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Crostolo, Secchia, and Panaro. The family of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, dukes of Modena, is very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. They had their name from Este, a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the district of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. MOD In 1753, the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> was appointed imperial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>-general, field-marshal, and governor of the Milanese during the minority of the archduke <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Leopold, who was declared governor-general of the Aulician <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>. The duke, though a vassal of the empire, hath an unlimited power within his own dominions. Modena, an ancient city, in Latin Mutina, which gives name to a duchy of Italy, and is its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It stands 28 miles east of Parma, 44 almost south of Mantua, and 20 west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; and is a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous, but not a handsome city. It is much celebrated by Roman authors for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and opulence; but was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sufferer by the siege it underwent during the troubles of the triumvirate. It hath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the usual residence of the dukes; and is also the see of a bishop, who is suffragan to the archbishop of Bologna. Mr Keyser says, that when Decius Brutus was besieged here by Mark Antony, Flirius the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>-pigeons; and that, even at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, pigeons are trained up at Modena, to carry letters, and bring back answers. This city hath given birth to several celebrated persons, particularly Tasso the poet, Correggio the great painter, Sionius the civilian and historian, da Vignola the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, and Montecucculi the imperial general. The tutelary saint of it is named Geminius. The ducal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a very noble edifice, in which, among the other fine pictures, the birth of Christ by Correggio, called la Notte Felice, is much celebrated. The only manufacture for which this city is noted, is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>, of which great numbers are exported. The churches of the Jesuits, of the Theatines, and of St Dominic, are well worth viewing. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St Carlo Borromeo between 70 and 80 young noblemen are continually maintained, and instructed both in the sciences and genteel exercises. St Bentrix, who was of the family of Este, is said to knock always at the gate of the palace three days before any of the family die. Before most of the houses are covered walks, or porticos, as at Bologna. The city is fortified, and on its south side stands the citadel.

MODERATOR

Pages 314-314

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, the person who presides at a dispute, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in a public <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the annual assembly of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland is styled moderator.

MODERN

Pages 314-314

something new, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in opposition to what is antique, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. MODERN Authors, according to Naudé, are all those who have wrote since Boëthius. The modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> commences with Galileo; the modern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> with Copernicus.

MODIFICATION

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, that which modifies a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> gives it this or that manner of being. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> are accidents, which modify all bodies. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">Decree</a> of Modification, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a decree ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a minister's stipend, without proportioning it among the persons liable in payment.

MODILLIONS

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, ornaments in the corniche of the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite columns.

MODIUS

Pages 314-314

in antiquity, a kind of dry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, for several sorts of grain.

MODREVIVS

Pages 314-314

secretary to Sigismund Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, acquired considerable reputation by his learning and works. He broke off from the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, favoured the Lutherans and Anti-trinitarians, and took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains in order to unite all Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> under the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Grotius has placed him in the class of the reconcilers of the different schemes of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is intitled, De republica emendanda.

MODULATION

Pages 314-316

in music, derived from the Latin modulare. This word in our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is susceptible of several different significations. It frequently means no more than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of musical sounds properly connected and arranged. Thus it answers to what Mr Malcolm understands by the word tune, when he does not expressly treat concerning the tuning of instruments. Thus likewise it expresses the French word chant; for which reason, in the article Music, we have frequently expressed the one word by the other. But the precise and technical acceptation to which it ought to be confined, is the art of composing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> agreeably to the laws prescribed by any particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">key</a>; that of changing the key, or of regularly and legitimately passing from one key to another. In what remains to be said upon the subject we follow Rousseau. Modulation (says he) is properly the manner of ascertaining and managing the modes; but at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the word most frequently signifies the art of conducting the harmony and the air successively through several modes, in a manner agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> and conformed to rules. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the different modes be produced by harmony, from thence likewise must <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the laws of modulation. These laws are simple in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, but difficult in practice. We proceed therefore to shew in what they consist. To modulate properly in the same tone, it is necessary, 1. To run through all the sounds of it in an agreeable air, frequently repeating the sounds which are most essential to it, and dwelling upon these sounds with the most remarkable emphasis; that is to say, that the chord containing the sensible notes, and that of the tonic, should frequently be heard in it, but under different appearances, and obtained by different procedures to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>. 2. That repose or cadences should only be established upon these two chords: the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, however, which ought to be taken with the rule is, that a cadence or repose may be established on the chord of the subdominant. 3. In short, that none of the sounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> ought ever to be altered; for without quitting it, we cannot introduce a sharp or a flat which does not belong to it, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> any one which in reality does belong to it. But passing from one mode to another, we must consult <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, we must consider the relations which a key bears to the other notes in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, and to the num- If we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from a mode <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, whether we consider the fifth from the key as having the most simple relation with it except that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>, or whether we consider it as the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> which enters into the harmonies of the same key, we shall always find, that this fifth, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a> of the mode, is the chord upon which we may establish the modulation most analogous to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> key. This dominant, which constituted one of the harmonies of the first key, makes also one of its own peculiar key, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> sound. There is then a connection between these two chords. Besides, that same dominant carrying, as well as the tonic, a perfect chord major upon the principle of resonance, these two chords are only different one from the other by the dissonance, which passing from the key to the dominant is the sixth superadded, and when reascending from the dominant to the key is the seventh. Now these two chords, thus distinguished by the dissonance which is suitable to each, by the sounds which compose them when ranged in order, form precisely the octave, or the diatonic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, which we call a gamme, which determines the mode. This same series of the key, altered only by a sharp, forms the scale belonging to the mode of the dominant; which shows how striking the analogy is between these two tones, and gives the easiest opportunity of passing from one to the other by means of one single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> alone. The mode then of the dominant is the first which presents itself after that of the key in the order of modulations. The same simplicity of relations which we find between a tonic and its dominant, is likewise found between the same tonic and its sub-dominant; for that fifth, in ascending, which is formed by the dominant with the tonic, is likewise formed by the sub-dominant in descending; but that sub-dominant does not form a fifth with the tonic except by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a>; it is directly a fourth, if we take that tonic below, as it ought to be; and which fixes the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of their relations: for in this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the fourth, whose ratio is as 3 to 4, immediately follows the fifth, whose ratio is as 2 to 3. So that, if that sub-dominant does not enter into the chord of the tonic, in return the tonic enters into its perfect chord.
