When the Dutch war broke out in 1664, and the duke of York took upon himself the command of a fleet as high-admiral, his lordship commanded the blue squadron, and by his industry and care abundance of the enemies' ships were taken; and in the great battle fought on the third of June 1665, in which the Dutch lost admiral Opdam, and had 18 men of war taken and 14 destroyed, a large share of the honour of the victory was justly given to the conduct of the earl of Sandwich. On the return of the English navy, the command of the whole fleet was given to the earl of Sandwich, which he was ordered to put as speedily as possible in a condition to return to the coast of Holland. Accordingly the earl sailed on the fifth of July with 60 men of war to the Dutch coast; when finding that their East India and Smyrna fleets were to return home north about, he steered for the coast of Norway, and found they had taken shelter in the port of Bergen, where the fleet were attacked; but leaving them there, and failing back towards the coast of Holland, he met with four Dutch East Indiamen, with several other merchant-ships, under a good convoy, and took eight men of war, two of their East India ships, and 20 sail of merchant-men; and a few days after, a part of the fleet falling in with 18 of the Hollanders, the greatest part of them were also taken, with four Dutch men of war, and above 1000 prisoners. On his return he was received by the king with distinguished marks of favour; and soon after, he was sent ambassador-extraordinary to the court of Madrid, to mediate a peace between the crowns of Spain and Portugal; when he had the happiness to conclude a peace between the two nations to their mutual satisfaction. On the breaking out of the last Dutch war, his lordship went to sea with the duke of York, and commanded the blue squadron; the French admiral, count d'Estrées, commanding the white. The fleet was at sea in the beginning of the month of May, and coming to an anchor in Southwold-bay in order to take water, we are told, that on the 27th many officers and seamen were permitted to go on shore, and were at Southwold, Dunwich, and Aldborough; when, the weather being hazy, the earl gave it as his opinion, that the wind standing as it did, the fleet rode in danger of being surprized by the Dutch; and indeed, between two and three the next morning, they were informed of their approach, upon which his royal highness made the signal for weighing anchor. The blue squadron was out first, the red next, and the white was much a-fern. The earl of Sandwich in the Royal James, which carried 100 guns, began the fight, and fell furiously on the squadron of Van Ghent, in order to give the rest of his fleet time to form; when captain Brakel, in the Great Holland, attacked the Royal James; but was soon disabled, as were several other men of war, and three fire-ships sunk. By this time most of his men were killed; and the hull of the Royal James was so pierced with shot, that it was impossible to carry her off. In this distress he might have been relieved by Montague by his vice-admiral Sir Joseph Jordan, had not that gentleman been more solicitous about afflicting the duke. When therefore he saw him fail by, heedless of the condition in which he lay, he said to those who were about him, "There is nothing left for us now, but to defend the ship to the last man." Being at length grappled by a fourth fire-ship, he begged his captain Sir Richard Haddock, and all his servants, to get into the boat and save themselves, which they did; yet some of the sailors refused to quit the admiral, and staying endeavoured to extinguish the fire, but in vain; the ship blew up about noon. His lordship's body was found about a fortnight after, and was interred with great state in Henry VII.'s chapel. We have of his lordship's writing, 1. The Art of Metals, in which is declared the manner of their generation, translated from the Spanish of Alvaro Alonso Barba, 8vo. 2. Several letters during his embassy to Spain, published with Arlington's letters. 3. A letter to secretary Thurloe. 4. Original letters and negotiations of Sir Richard Fanshaw, the earl of Sandwich, the earl of Sunderland, and Sir William Godolphin, wherein divers matters between the three crowns of England, Spain, and Portugal, from the year 1663 to 1678, are set in a clear light, 2 vols 8vo. Montague (Lady Mary Wortley,) eminent by her Letters, was daughter of the first duke of Kingston, and died in 1762. Montague (Edward Wortley), son of the former, passed through such variegated scenes, that a bare recital of them would favour of the marvellous. From Westminster school, where he was placed for education, he ran away three several times. He exchanged clothes with a chimney-sweep, and he followed for some time that footy occupation. He next joined himself to a fisherman, and cried flounders in Rotherhithe. He then sailed as a cabin-boy to Spain; where he had no sooner arrived, than he ran away from the vessel, and hired himself to a driver of mules. After thus vagabondizing it for some time, he was discovered by the consul, who returned him to his friends in England. They received him with a joy equal to that of the father of the prodigal son in the gospel. A private tutor was employed to recover those rudiments of learning which a life of dissipation, of blackguardism, and of vulgarity, might have obliterated. Wortley was sent to the West-Indies, where he remained some time; then returned to England, acted according to the dignity of his birth, was chosen a member, and served in two successive parliaments. His expenses exceeding his income, he became involved in debt, quitted his native country, and commenced that wandering traveller he continued to the time of his death. Having visited most of the eastern countries, he contracted a partiality for their manners. He drank little wine; a great deal of coffee; wore a long beard; smoked much; and, even whilst at Venice, he was habited in the eastern style. He sat crook-legged in the Turkish fashion through choice. With the Hebrew, the Arabic, the Chaldaic, and the Persian languages, he was as well acquainted as with his native tongue. He published several pieces. One on the "Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire." Another an exploration of "The Causes of Earthquakes."—As this gentleman was remarkable for the uncommon incidents which attended his life, the close of that life was no less marked with singularity. He had been early married to a woman, who aspired to no higher a character than that of an industrious washerwoman. As the marriage was solemnized in a frolic, Wortley never deemed her sufficiently the wife of his bosom to cohabit with her. She was allowed a maintenance. She lived contented, and was too submissive to be troublesome on account of the conjugal rites. Mr Montague, on the other hand, was a perfect patriarch in his manners. He had wives of almost every nation. When he was with Ali Bey in Egypt, he had his household of Egyptian females, each striving who should be the happy who could gain the greatest ascendancy over this Anglo-Eastern bashaw. At Constantinople, the Grecian women had charms to captivate this unsettled wanderer. In Spain a Spanish brunette, in Italy the olive-complexioned female, were solicited to partake the honours of the bridal-bed. It may be asked what became of this group of wives? Mr Montague was continually shifting the place, and consequently varying the scene. Did he travel with his wives, as the patriarchs did with their flocks and herds? No such thing. Wortley, considering his wives as bad travelling companions, generally left them behind him. It happened, however, that news reached his ears of the death of the original Mrs Montague the washerwoman. Wortley had no issue by her; and without issue male, a very large estate would revert to the second son of lord Bute. Wortley, owing the family no obligations, was determined, if possible, to defeat their expectations. He resolved to return to England and marry. He acquainted a friend with his intentions, and he commissioned that friend to advertise for any young decent woman who might be in a pregnant state. Several ladies answered it. One out of the number was selected, as being the most eligible object. She waited with eagerness for the arrival of her expected bridegroom; but, behold, whilst he was on his journey, death very impertinently arrested him in his career. Montague (Charles), earl of Halifax, fourth son of George Montague of Harton in Northamptonshire, Esq; son of Henry the first earl of Manchester, was born in 1661. He was educated at Westminster-school and Cambridge, showed very early a most pregnant genius, and quickly made great progress in learning. In 1684, he wrote a poem on the death of king Charles II. in which he displayed his genius to such advantage, that he was invited to London by the earl of Dorset; and upon his coming thither he soon increased his fame, particularly by a piece which he wrote in conjunction with Prior, published at London in 1687, under the title of The Hind and the Panther transferred to the Story of the Country-mouse and the City-mouse. Upon the abdication of king James II. he was chosen one of the members of the convention, and recommended by the earl of Dorset to king William, who immediately allowed him a pension of £500. per annum. Having given proofs of his great abilities in the house of commons, he was made one of the commissioners of the treasury, and soon after chancellor of the exchequer; in which post he brought about that great work of recovering all the current money of the nation. In 1698, he was appointed first commissioner of the treasury; and in 1679, was created a peer of England, by the title of Baron Halifax in the county of Montaigne, of York. In 1701, the house of commons impeached him of six articles, which were dismissed by the house of Lords. He was attacked again by the house of commons in 1702, but without success. In 1705, he wrote, An answer to Mr Bromley's speech in relation to the occasional Conformity-bill. In 1706, he was one of the commissioners for the union with Scotland; and upon passing the bill for the naturalization of the illustrious house of Hanover, and for the better security of the succession of the crown in the Protestant line, he was made choice of to carry that act to Hanover. Upon the death of Queen Anne, when the king had taken possession of his throne, his lordship was appointed first commissioner of the treasury, and created earl of Halifax and knight of the garter. He died in 1715. His lordship wrote several other pieces besides those abovementioned; all which, with some of his Speeches, were published together in 1716, in an octavo volume.

MONTAIGNE

Pages 359-359

a French <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was born in Perigord in 1533. His father educated him with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care, and made him learn Latin as other children learn their mother-tongue. His tutors were Nicholas Gronchi, who wrote De Comititis Romanorum; William Guerenti, who wrote on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; George Buchanan; and M. Anthony <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a>. He was also taught Greek by way of recreation; and because some think that starting children out of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> spoils their understanding, he was awakened every morning with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of music. He was counsellor for a while in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Bordeaux; afterwards made mayor of Bordeaux. He published his Essays, so much known in the world, in 1580. Montaigne had a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and subtlety, but no small share of conceit and vanity. The learned and ingenious are much divided in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> about his works. He died in 1592.

MONTANISTS

Pages 359-359

Christian heretics, who sprung up about the year 171, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius. They were so called from their leader, the hierarch Montanus, a Phrygian by birth; whence they are sometimes styled Phrygians and Cataphyrgians. Montanus, it is said, embraced Christianity in hopes of rising to the dignities of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He pretended to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; and gave out, that the Holy Ghost had instructed him in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which had not been revealed to the apostles. Priscilla and Maximilla, two enthusiastic women of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, presently became his disciples; and in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being assembled together, condemned his prophecies, and excommunicated those who dispersed them. Afterwards they wrote an account of what had passed to the western churches, where the pretended prophecies of Montanus and his followers were likewise condemned. The Montanists, finding themselves exposed to the censure of the whole church, formed a schism, and set up a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those who called themselves prophets. Montanus, in conjunction with Priscilla and Maximilla, was at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. These sectaries made no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the creed. They only held, that the Holy Spirit made Montanus his organ for delivering a more perfect form of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> than what was delivered by the apostles. They refused <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> for ever to those who were guilty of Montanist crimes, and believed that the bishops had no authority to reconcile them. They held it unlawful to fly in time of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. They condemned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages, allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and observed three lents. The Montanists became separated into two branches; one of which were the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, and the other of Eschines. The latter are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with following the heterodoxy of Praxias and Sabellius concerning the Trinity.

MONTANUS

Pages 359-359

a most learned Spanish theologian, born in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BADAJOZ">Badajoz</a>, about the year 1528. He assisted at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; and his merit and writings recommended him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, who employed him in publishing a new polyglot <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> after the Complutensian edition, which was printed by the care of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Ximenes. This bible was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, whither Montanus went in 1571; and on his return to Spain he refused the bishopric which Philip offered him for his reward, but spent the rest of his days at Sevilla, where he died about the year 1598. Montanus had not only vast erudition, but great good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; he loved solitude, was very laborious, never drank wine, and seldom ate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>.

MONTECUCULI

Pages 359-361
generalissimo of the emperor's army, and one of the greatest commanders of his time, was born in the duchy of Modena, of a distinguished family in 1608. Ernest Montecuculi his uncle, who was general of the artillery in the Imperial army, resolved that he should serve first as a common soldier, and that he should pass through all the military degrees, before he was raised to command. This the young Montecuculi did with applause. In 1644, when he was at the head of 2000 horse, he surprised by a precipitate march 10,000 Swedes, who laid siege to Nemefiau in Silea, and obliged them to abandon their artillery and baggage; but a short time after, he was defeated and taken prisoner by the general Banier. Having obtained his liberty at the end of two years, he joined his troops to those of John de Wert; and defeated general Wrangel in Bohemia, who was killed in the battle. In 1657, the emperor made him general marshal de camp; and sent him to the assistance of John Casimir, king of Poland. Montecuculi vanquished Ragotzi prince of Transilvania, drove out the Swedes, and distinguished himself in an extraordinary manner against the Turks in Transilvania and Hungary. In 1673, he commanded the Imperial army against the French, and took Bonne; he then proceeded with feint marches in order to deceive Turenne, in which he obtained great honour. However, the command of that army was taken from him the next year; but it was restored to him in 1675, in order that he might make head against the great Turenne. All Europe had their eyes fixed on these two able warriors, who then made use of all the stratagems which genius and military knowledge were capable of effecting. The marshal de Turenne was obtaining the superiority, when he was taken off by a cannon-ball. Montecuculi wept at the death of so formidable an enemy, and bestowed upon him the greatest praises. The great prince of Conde was the only French general that could deprive Montecuculi of the superiority he had obtained by Turenne's death. That prince Montesquieu was therefore sent to the Rhine, and stopped the Imperial general; who considered this last campaign as the most glorious of his life, not for his being conqueror, but for his not being conquered, when he was opposed by a Turenne and a Conde. He spent the rest of his life at the Imperial court; and died at Linz, in 1680. He wrote Memoirs; the best edition of which is that of Strasbourg, in 1735. Montesquieu (Charles de Secondat) baron, a most illustrious Frenchman descended from an ancient and noble family of Guienne, was born at the castle of La Brede, near Bordeaux, in 1689. The greatest care was taken of his education; and at the age of 20, he had actually prepared materials for his Spirit of Laws, by well-digested extracts from those immense volumes of civil law which he had studied, not barely as a civilian, but as a philosopher. He became a counsellor of the parliament of Bordeaux in 1714, and was received president à mortier two years after. In 1721 he published his Persian Letters; in which, under the screen of Oriental manners, he satirized those of France, and treated of several important subjects by delicate transient glances: he did not avow this publication; but was no sooner pointed out as the author, than zeal without knowledge, and envy under the mask of it, united at once against the Persian Letters. He was received into the French academy in 1728; and having previously quitted his civil employments, he entirely devoted himself to his genius, and was no longer a magistrate but a man of letters. Having thus set himself at liberty, he travelled through Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Holland, and England, in which last country he resided three years, and contracted intimacies with the greatest men then alive; for Locke and Newton were dead. The result of his observations was, "that Germany was fit to travel in, Italy to sojourn in, England to think in, and France to live in." On his return he retired for two years to his estate at La Brede, where he finished his work On the Causes of the Grandeur and Declension of the Romans; which appeared in 1734. The reputation acquired by this last work only cleared the way for his greater undertaking, the Spirit of Laws, which was printed at Geneva in 2 vols. 4to. 1750. This was immediately attacked by the adversaries of his Persian Letters, in a multitude of anonymous pamphlets containing all the reproaches to which a liberal mind is exposed from craft and ignorance. M. Montesquieu drew up a defence of this work; which, for truth, moderation, and delicacy of ridicule, may be regarded as a model in its way. This great man was peaceably enjoying that fulness of esteem which his great merits had procured him, when he fell sick at Paris, and died on the 10th of February 1755.—The following character of this great man is drawn by Lord Chesterfield. "His virtues did honour to human nature, his writings justice. A friend to mankind, he asserted their undoubted and unalienable rights with freedom, even in his own country; whose prejudices in matters of religion and government he had long lamented, and endeavoured, not without some success, to remove. He well knew, and justly admired, the happy constitution of this country, where fixed and known laws equally restrain monarchy from tyranny, and liberty from licentiousness. His works will illustrate his name, and survive him, as long as right reason, moral obligation, and the true spirit of laws, shall be understood, respected, and maintained."—As to his personal qualities, we are told by his elogist M. d'Alembert, that "he was of a sweet, gay, and even temper. His conversation was spirited, agreeable, and instructive. Nobody told a story in a more lively manner, or with more grace and less affectation. He had frequent absence of mind; but always awakened from it by some unexpected stroke that re-animated the languishing conversation. Though he lived with the great, he retired whenever he could to his estate in the country, and there met his books, his philosophy, and his repose. Surrounded at his leisure-hours with peasants, after having studied man in the commerce of the world, he studied him in those simple people solely instructed by nature. With them he cheerfully conversed; he endeavoured, like Socrates, to find out their genius, and appeared as happy with them as in the most brilliant assemblies; especially when he reconciled their differences, and by his benevolence relieved them from their distresses." Besides the works already mentioned, M. Montesquieu wrote several small pieces, as the Temple of Genius, Lycurgus, and Essay upon Taste, which is left unfinished. His works have been collected since his death, and printed at Paris in a splendid edition, in quarto. They have likewise all of them been translated into English. Montfaucon (Bernard de), a very learned Benedictine of the congregation of St Maur, singularly famous for his knowledge in Pagan and ecclesiastical antiquities, was born of an ancient and noble family in Languedoc, in 1655. He served for some time in the army; but the death of his parents mortified him so with regard to the world, that he commenced Benedictine monk in 1675, and applied himself intensely to study. Though Montfaucon's life was long, healthy, retired, and laborious, his voluminous publications seem sufficiently to have employed the whole; exclusive of his greatest undertaking, for which he will be always memorable. This was his Antiquité expliquée, written in Latin and French, illustrated with elegant plates, in 10 vols folio, to which he added a supplement of 5 vols more. He died at the abbey of St Germain in 1741. Montferrat, a province of Italy, with the title of a duchy; bounded on the east by the duchy of Milan, and part of the territory of Genoa; on the north, by the Vercellese and Canavesi; on the west, by Piedmont properly so called; and on the south by the territory of Genoa, from whence it is separated by the Appenine mountains. It contains 200 towns and villages; and is very fertile and well cultivated, abounding in corn, wine, oil, and silk. It belongs to the king of Sardinia. Casal is the capital town. Montgomery, the capital of a county of the same name in North Wales, took its name from Roger de Montgomery earl of Shrewsbury, who built the castle; but it is called by the Welsh Tre Vallovin, that is, Baldwin's town; having been built by Baldwin, lieutenant of the marches of Wales, in the reign of William I. The Welsh, after having put the garrison to the sword, demolished it in 1095; but Henry III. rebuilt it, and granted it the privileges of a free borough, with other liberties. It is a large and tolerably well built town, in a healthful situation and fertile soil. It sends a member to parliament, and has Montgomeryshire, a county of North Wales, 35 miles in length and 34 in breadth; bounded on the north by Merionethshire and Denbighshire, on the east by Shropshire, on the south by Radnor and Cardiganshire, and on the west by another part of Merionethshire. It contains about 34,000 inhabitants, and between 5000 and 6000 houses. The county is full of high hills, with a few valleys and meadows fit for corn and pasture. The air is sharp and cold on the mountains, but is more mild in the valleys.

MONTH

Pages 361-361

the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a year. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, p. 136.

MONTMORENCY

Pages 361-361

a town of France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, remarkable for the tombs of the dukes of this name. It is seated on a hill, near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> valley, fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, especially excellent cherries. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 24. N. Lat. 48. 59. Montmorency (<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> de), a peer, marshal, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, of France, and one of the greatest generals of the 16th century, defended, in 1512, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEZIERES">Mezieres</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. and obliged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> to raise the siege. The following year he was made marshal of France; and in 1525 following <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Francis I. into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was taken with that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, which was fought contrary to his advice. The important services he afterwards rendered the state were rewarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of constable of France, with which he was presented by the king on the 10th of February 1538. He afterwards underwent various revolutions of fortune both at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> and in the field. At last, being wounded at the battle of St Denis, which he gained on the 10th of November 1567, he died of his wounds two days after, at 74 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It is said, that a cordelier attempting to prepare him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when he was covered with blood and wounds, after the battle of St Denis, he replied in a firm and steady <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>: "Do you think that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has lived near 80 years with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, has not learnt to die for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>?"

MONTPELIER

Pages 361-361

one of the handsomest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, and the most considerable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> excepting Thoulouse, is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 20. N. Lat. 45. 58. It hath a citadel, a bishop's see, a famous university where the art of medicine is taught, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of sciences, and a mint. The streets are very narrow and crooked; but always clean, because lying on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. The inhabitants are reckoned about 30,000 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, among whom are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of physicians and apothecaries. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is celebrated for its medicinal compositions, which are distributed all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; particularly <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-HUNGARY_WATER"><a class="xre</a>f" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of lavender, syrup of capillaire, essences, and perfumes. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is extremely healthy, for which reason valetudinarians come hither from all parts for their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. It is seated on a hill, on the river Merdanson, which passes into several parts of the town through subterranean vaults.

MONTREAL

Pages 361-361

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the river St Lawrence, about 28 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> wholesome. It belonged to the French; but was taken by the generals <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a> and Murray on the 8th of September 1760, without firing a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>. According to the terms of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, all the French forces were to be sent to Old Montreal-France; and, consequently, all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> became subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>: this cession was confirmed by the peace of 1763. The town is pretty well fortified; and has a pleasant situation, with wide open streets. It is built on the side of the river, from whence there is a gradual easy ascent to what is called the Upper Town. The Hôtel Dieu, the magazines, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of arms, are in the Lower Town; which is also the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The seminary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> school, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the monks called Recollets, the Jesuits, and the nuns, are in the Upper; where likewise the late governor, and most of the officers, resided. There are also a general <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a church belonging to the Jesuits, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well-built. The inhabitants carry on a trade with the savages in skins and furs. It is 120 miles south-west of Quebec, and 110 north of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>. W. Long. 72. 4. N. Lat. 45. 35.

MONTROSE

Pages 361-361

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, situated at the mouth of the river Esk, on the German Ocean, 46 miles north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">Steel</a> spaws are very numerous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round Montrose. Besides these, there is a well near this town, whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and faintly discovering a mineral <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and is of a different <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> from the steel one. It is universally diuretic; and has been found useful in stranguries, scrofulous disorders, flatulencies, &c. Montrose (Marquis of). See Graham; and Batin, p. 137, 138, 143, 165.

MONTSERRAT

Pages 361-362

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Catalonia, on which is a famous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> and chapel, dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, whose image is said to perform many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; so that numbers of pilgrims <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> hither. It is inhabited by monks of several nations, who entertain all that come out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> curiosity, for three days gratis. This mountain is said to be 10 miles in circumference, and five high, from the top of which there is a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the distance of 150 miles. It is 25 miles N. W. of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 35. N. Lat. 41. 40. Montserrat, one of the Caribbee Isles belonging to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is a very small, but very pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, so called by Columbus from its resemblance to a famous mountain near Barcelona in Catalonia. It lies in W. Long. 61. 0. N. Lat. 16. 50., having Antigua to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, St Christopher's and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a> to the north-west, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a> lying south south-east at the distance of about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues. In its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it is nearly round, about nine miles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> every way, 27 in circumference, and is supposed to contain about 40,000 or 50,000 acres. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is warm, but less so than in Antigua, and is esteemed very healthy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is mountainous, but with pleasant valleys, rich and fertile, between them; the hills are covered with cedars and other fine trees. Here are all the animals as well as vegetables and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> that are to be found in the other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and not at all inferior them in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The inhabitants raised formerly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, which was none of the best, but which they cut four times a-year. The present product is cotton, rum, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. There is no good harbour, but three tolerable Montserrat, tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, Old Harbour, and Ker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, where they ship the produce of the island. Public affairs are administered here as in the other isles, by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, composed of no more than eight members, two from each of the four districts into which it is divided. The wonderful effects of industry and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in meliorating the gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> have been nowhere more conspicuous than in these islands, and particularly in this, by gradually improving their produce, more especially of late years, since the art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> hath been reduced to a regular system, and almost all the defects of soil so thoroughly removed by proper management and manure, that, except from the failure of seasons, or the want of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, there is seldom any fear of a crop. In 1770 there were exported from this island to Great Britain 167 bags of cotton, 1670l.; 740 hogheads of rum, 7400l. To <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> 133 <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>, 1330l.; 4338 hogheads 232 tierces 202 barrels of sugar, 79,507l.; in the whole 89,907l. To North <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> 12,633l. There are a few ships employed in trading to this island from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. As to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, according to the most probable accounts, they consist of between 1200 and 1500 whites, and from 10,000 to 12,000 <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, tho' some say not so many.

MONUMENT

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> destined to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, &c. of the person who raised it, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the person for whom it was raised; such are a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, &c.

MOORE

Pages 362-362
or **MORE**, (Edward), a late ingenious writer, was bred a linen-draper, but quitted business to join the retinue of the mutes; and he certainly had a very happy and pleasing talent for poetry. In his Trial of Selim the Persian, he complimented lord Lyttelton in an elegant kind of panegyric, couched under the appearance of accusation: and his Fables for the female sex, for easy verification, poignant satire, and striking morals, approach nearer to the manner of Gay, than any other of the numerous imitations of that author. He wrote also three dramatic pieces; The Gamester, a tragedy; The Foundling, and Gil Blas, comedies. The success of these was not such as they merited; the first of them having met with a cold reception, for no other apparent reason but because it too nearly touched a favourite and fashionable vice; and the second having been condemned for its supposed resemblance to Sir Richard Steele's Conscious Lover, but to which good judges have been inclined to give it greatly the preference. Mr Moore married a lady of the name of Hamilton, daughter to Mr Hamilton table-decker to the princesses; who had herself a very poetical turn, and has been said to have assisted him in the writing of his tragedy. One specimen of her poetry, however, was handed about before their marriage, and has since appeared in print in different collections of songs, particularly in one called the Goldfinch. It was addressed to a daughter of the famous Stephen Duck; and begins with the following stanza: Would you think it, my Duck, for the fault I must own, Your Jenny, at last, is quite covetous grown: Tho' millions if Fortune should lavishly pour, I still think I be wretched, if I had not More. And after half a dozen stanzas more, in which, with great ingenuity and delicacy, and yet in a manner that expresses a sincere affection, she has quibbled on our author's name, she concludes with the following lines: You will wonder, my girl, who this dear one can be, Whose merit can boast such a conquest as me: But you shan't know his name, tho' I told you before, It begins with an M, but I dare not say More. In the year 1753, Mr Moore commenced a weekly miscellaneous paper, intitled The World, by Adam Fitz-Adam; in which undertaking he was assisted by lord Chesterfield with some essays. This paper was collected into volumes, and Mr Moore died soon after.

MOORING

Pages 362-362

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of confining and securing a ship in a particular station, by chains <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, which are either fastened to the adjacent shore, or to anchors in the bottom. A ship may be either moored by the head, or by the head and stern: that is to say, she may be secured by anchors before her, without any behind; or she may have anchors out, both before and behind her; or her cables may be attached to polls, rings, or moorings, which answer the same purpose. When a ship is moored by the head with her own anchors, they are disposed according to the circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where she lies, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> she is to continue therein. Thus wherever a tide ebbs and flows, it is usual to carry one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> out towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and another towards the ebb, particularly where there is little room to range about; and the anchors are laid in the same manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the vessel is moored head and stern in the same place. The situation of the anchors, in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, is usually opposed to the reigning winds, or those which are most dangerous; so that the ship rides therein with the effort of both her cables. Thus if she rides in a bay, or road, which is exposed to a northerly <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and heavy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, the anchors passing from the opposite bows ought to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> east and west from each other; hence both the cables <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> retain the ship in her station with equal effort against the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the wind and sea.

MOOT

Pages 362-362

a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> argued by the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">barristers</a> and students at the inns of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, the better to qualify them for practice, and to defend the causes of their clients. This, which is called meeting, is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> exercise of the inns of court. Particular times are appointed for the arguing moot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this exercise is performed was anciently called moot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> surveyor of the moots, annually chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, to appoint the moot-men for the inns of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and to keep an account of the performance of exercises.—The word is formed either from the Saxon *mootan*, *genetan*, "meeting;" or from the French *mot*, "word." **MORAL**

MORAL PHILOSOPHY

Pages 398-400

tion as before, that he is destined for that after-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, and is to be produced upon a more august and solemn stage, where his sublimer powers shall have proportioned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> attain its completion? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we attend to that curiosity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> prodigious thirst of knowledge, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the mind in every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its progress, and consider withal the endless round of business and care, and the various hardships to which the bulk of mankind are chained <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; it is evident, that in this present state it is impossible to expect the gratification of an appetite at once so insatiable and so noble. Our senses, the ordinary organs by which knowledge is let into the mind, are always imperfect, and often fallacious; the advantages of afflicting or correcting them are possessed by few; the difficulties of finding out <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> amidst the various and contradictory opinions, interests, and passions of mankind, are many; and the wants of the creature, and of those with whom he is connected, numerous and urgent: so that it may be said of most men, that their intellectual organs are as much shut up and secluded from proper nourishment and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> in that little circle to which they are confined, as the bodily organs are in the womb. Nay, those who to an aspiring genius have added all the assistances of art, leisure, and the most liberal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, what narrow prospects can even they take of this unbounded <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of things from that little eminence on which they stand? and how eagerly do they still grasp at new discoveries, without any satisfaction or limit to their ambition? But should it be said, that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is made for action, and not for speculation, or fruitless searches after knowledge, we ask, For what kind of action? Is it only for bodily exercises, or for moral, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ones? Of all these he is capable; yet, by the unavoidable circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, he is tied down to the former, and has hardly any leisure to think of the latter, or, if he has, wants the proper instruments of exerting them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue, of one's friends and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the generous sympathy with mankind, and heroic zeal of doing good, which are all so natural to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and good minds, and some traces of which are found in the lowest, are seldom united with proportioned means or opportunities of exercising them: so that the moral <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the noble energies and impulses of the mind, can hardly find proper scope even in the most fortunate condition; but are much depressed in some, and almost entirely restrained in the generality, by the numerous clogs of an indigent, sickly, or embarrased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Were such mighty powers, such godlike affections, planted in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to be folded up in the narrow womb of our present existence, never to be produced into a more perfect life, nor to expatiate in the ample <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>? Let it be considered, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that no possession, no enjoyment within the round of mortal things, is commensurate to the desires, or adequate to the capacities, of the mind. The most exalted condition has its abatements; the happiest conjunction of fortune leaves many wishes behind; and, after the highest gratifications, the mind is carried forward in pursuit of new ones without end. Add to all, the fond desire of immortality, the secret dread of non-existence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> for perfection, joined to the improbability or the impossibility of attaining it here; and then judge whether this elaborate structure, this magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of inward powers and organs, does not plainly point out an hereafter, and intimate eternity to man? Does nature give the finishing touches to the lesser and ignoble instances of her skill, and raise every other creature to the maturity and perfection of his being; and shall she leave her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> workmanship unfinished? Does she carry the vegetative and animal life in man to their full vigour and highest destination; and shall she suffer his intellectual, his moral, his divine life to fade away, and be forever extinguished? Would such abortions in the moral world be congruous to that perfection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness which upholds and adorns the natural? We must therefore conclude from this detail, that the present state, even at its best, is only the womb of man's being, in which the noblest principles of his mortal nature are in a manner fettered, or secluded from a correspondent sphere of action; and therefore destined for a future and unbounded state, where they shall emancipate themselves, and exert the fulness of their strength. The most accomplished mortal, in this low and dark apartment of nature, is only the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of what he shall be when he takes his ethereal flight, and puts on immortality. Without a reference to that state, man were a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, a rude unfinished embryo, a monster in nature. But this being once supposed, he still maintains his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the masterpiece of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; his latent powers are all suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and progression of nature; his noble aspirations, and the pains of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, are his efforts towards a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> birth, the pangs of his delivery into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and perfection; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his discharge from goal, his separation from his fellow-prisoners, and introduction into the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of those heroic spirits who are gone before him, and of their great eternal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">Parent</a>. The fetters of his mortal coil being loosed, and his prison-walls broke down, he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be bare and open on every side to the admission of truth and virtue, and their fair attendant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; every vital and intellectual spring will evolve itself with a divine elasticity in the free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of heaven. He will not then peep at the universe and its glorious Author through a dark grate or a grofs medium, nor receive the reflections of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> through the strait openings of sensible organs; but will be all eye, all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, all ethical and divine feeling*. Let one part, however, of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> be attended to: That as in the womb we receive our original <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, form, and the essential framing of our being, which we carry along with us into the light, and which greatly affect the succeeding periods of our life; so our temper and condition in the future life will depend on the conduct we have observed, and the character we have formed, in the present life. We are here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> what we shall be at full length hereafter. The first rude sketch or outlines of reason and virtue must be drawn at present, to be afterwards enlarged to the stature and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. This, if duly attended to, must prove not only an immediate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, but an admirable incentive to virtue. For he lays a guard who faithfully and ardently follows the lights of knowledge, and pants after higher improvements in virtue, will... will be wonderfully animated and inflamed in that pursuit by a full conviction that the scene does not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with life—that his struggles, arising from the weakness of nature and the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, will be turned into triumphs—that his career in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of wisdom and goodness will be both swifter and smoother—and those generous ardours with which he glows towards heaven, i.e., the perfection and immortality of virtue, will find their adequate object and exercise in a sphere proportionally enlarged, incorruptible, immortal. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, what an inexpressible damp must it be to the good man, to dread the total extinction of that light and virtue, without which life, nay, immortality itself, were not worth a fingle wish? Many writers draw their proofs of the immortality of the soul, and of a future state of rewards and punishments, from the unequal distribution of these here. It cannot be dissembled that wicked men often escape the outward <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to their crimes, and do not feel the inward in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their demerit seems to require, partly from the callousness induced upon their nature by the habits of vice, and partly from the dilution of their minds abroad by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or business—and sometimes good men do not reap all the natural and genuine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their virtue, through the many unforeseen or unavoidable calamities in which they are involved. This, no doubt, upon the supposition of an all-wise and good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, were an argument, and a strong one too, for a future state, in which those inequalities shall be corrected. But unless we suppose a prevalent good order in the present scene of things, we weaken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the divine administration, and the presumption of any better order in any future period of it. Virtue has present rewards, and vice present punishments, annexed to it; such rewards and punishments as make virtue, in most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> that happen, far more eligible than vice; but, in the infinite variety of human contingencies, it may sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out, that the inflexible practice of virtue shall deprive a man of considerable advantages to himself, his family, or friends, which he might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by a well-timed piece of roguery; suppose by betraying his trust, voting against his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, selling his country, or any other crime, where the security against discovery shall heighten the temptation. Or, it may happen, that a strict adherence to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, to the cause of liberty and virtue, shall expose him, or his family, to the loss of every thing, nay, to poverty, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, death itself, or to torments far more intolerable. Now what shall secure a man's virtue in circumstances of such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>? What shall enforce the obligations of conscience against the allurements of so many interests, the dread of so many and so terrible evils, and the almost unsurmountable aversion of human nature to excessive pain? The conflict is the greater, when the circumstances of the crime are such as easily admit a variety of alleviations from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, natural affection, love to one's family or friends, perhaps in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>; these will give it even the air of virtue. Add to all, that the crime may be thought to have few bad consequences,—may be easily concealed,—or imagined possible to be retrieved in a good measure by future good conduct. It is obvious to which side most men will lean in such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>; and how much need there is of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, from the consideration of a God, of a Providence, and of an immortal state of retribution, to keep the mind firm and uncorrupt in those or like instances of singular trial or distress. But without supposing such peculiar instances, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of a governing Mind, and a persuasion that virtue is not only befriended by him here, but will be crowned by him hereafter with rewards suitable to its nature, will in themselves, and immortal in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, must be not only a mighty support and incentive to the practice of virtue, but a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against vice. The thoughts of an Almighty Judge, and of an impartial future reckoning, are often alarming, inexpressibly so, even to the stoutest offenders. On the other hand, how supporting must it be to the good man, to think that he acts under the eye of his friend, as well as judge! How improving, to consider the present state as connected with a future one, and every relation in which he stands as a school of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> for his affections; every trial as the exercise of some virtue; and the virtuous deeds which result from both, as introductory to higher scenes of action and enjoyment! Finally, how transporting is it to view death as his discharge from the warfare of mortality, and a triumphant entry into a state of freedom, security, and perfection, in which knowledge and wisdom shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> upon him from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; where each <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> shall have its proper object; and his virtue, which was often damped or defeated here, shall be enthroned in undisturbed and eternal empire! On reviewing this short system of morals, and the advantages which support and enforce it, and comparing of both with the Christian scheme, what light and encouragement do they borrow from thence! How clearly and fully does Christianity lay open the connections of our nature, both material and immaterial, and future as with natural as present! What an ample and beautiful detail does it present of the duties we owe to God, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and ourselves, promulgated in the most simple, intelligible, and popular manner; divested of every partiality of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and adapted to the general state of mankind! With what bright and alluring examples does it illustrate and recommend the practice of those duties; and with what mighty sanctions does it enforce that practice! How strongly does it describe the corruptions of our nature; the deviations of our life from the rule of duty, and the causes of both! How marvellous and benevolent a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> does it unfold, by which those corruptions may be remedied, and our nature restored from its deviations to transcendent heights of virtue and piety! Finally, what a fair and comprehensive prospect does it give us of the administration of God, of which it represents the present state only as a small period, and a period of warfare and trial! How solemn and unbounded are the scenes which it opens beyond it! the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead, the general judgment, the equal distribution of rewards and punishments to the good and the bad; and the full completion of divine wisdom and goodness in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> establishment of order, perfection, and happiness! How glorious then is that scheme of religion, and how worthy of affection as well as of admiration, which, by making such discoveries, and affording such affluence, has disclosed the unfading fruits and triumphs of virtue, and secured its interests beyond the power of time and chance!

MORAL SCIENCE

Pages 400-401

that whereby we perceive what is good, virtuous, and beautiful, in actions, manners, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">PHILOSOPHY</a>. MORALITY. See MORAL PHILOSOPHY.

MORASS

Pages 401-401

a low and moist <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which receives the waters from the higher grounds without having any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to carry them off.

MORATA

Pages 401-401

an Italian lady, distinguished for her learning, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, in 1526. Her father, after teaching the belles lettres in several cities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, was made preceptor to the two young princes of Ferrara, the sons of Alphonso I. The uncommon abilities he discovered in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> determined him to give her a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Meanwhile the princess of Ferrara studying polite literature, it was judged expedient that she should have a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in the same pursuit; and Morata being called, she was heard by the astonished courtiers to declaim in Latin, to speak Greek, and to explain the paradoxes of Cicero. Her father dying, she was obliged to return home, to take upon her the management of family-affairs, and the education of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; both which she executed with the greatest diligence and success. In the meantime Andrew Gruntzler, a young German, who had studied physic, and taken his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> at Ferrara, fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with her, and married her. She now went with her husband to Germany, taking her little brother with her, whom she instructed in the Latin and Greek tongues; and after staying a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Augsburg, went to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCHWEINFURT">Schweinfurt</a> in Franconia, where her husband was born: but they had not been there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before that town was unhappily besieged and burnt; however, escaping the flames, they fled in the utmost distress to Hammelburg. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they were also obliged to quit, and were reduced to the last extremities, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> palatine invited Gruntzler to be professor of physic at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, and he entered on his new office in 1554; but they no sooner began to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> the sweets of repose, than a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, occasioned by the distresses and hardships they had suffered, seized upon Morata, who died in 1555, in the 29th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and her husband and brother did not long survive her. She composed several works, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which were burnt with the town of Schweinfurt; the remainder, which consist of orations, dialogues, letters, and translations, were collected and published under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a> Fulviae Moratae, faminae deliciosa, et <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> divina, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> omnia qua balteos inventae fuerint; quibus Celti secundi curiosi epistle ac orationes accesserunt; which has had several editions in octavo.

MORAVIA

Pages 401-402

a marquisate of Germany, derives the name of Mahern, as it is called by the Germans, and of Moravia, as it is called by the natives, from the river of that name which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Glatz, and passes through the middle of it. It is bounded to the south by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Glatz and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, to the west by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and to the east by Silesia and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; being about 120 miles in length, and 100 in breadth. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is over-run with woods and mountains, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but much wholesome than in the low grounds, which are full of bogs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The mountains, in general, are barren; but the more champaign parts tolerably fertile, yielding corn, with plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, good saffron, and pasture. Nor is it altogether destitute of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and garden-stuff. Moravia also abounds in horses, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and goats. In the woods and about the lakes there is plenty of wild fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, venison, bees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, hare, foxes, wolves, beavers, &c. In this country are likewise quarries of marble, baltard diamonds, amethysts, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-petre, and vitriol, with wholesome mineral-waters, and warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; but salt is imported. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, Morawa, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Morau, are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, abound with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, crayfish, barbels, eels, perch, and many other sorts of fish. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the inhabitants is a dialect of the Slavonic, differing little from the Bohemian; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and citizens speak German and French. Moravia was anciently inhabited by the Quadi, who were driven out by the Scavi. Its kings, who were once powerful and independent, afterwards became dependent on, and tributary to, the German emperors and kings. At last, in the year 908, the Moravian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was parcelled out among the Germans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, and Hungarians. In 1086, that part of it properly called Moravia was declared a marquisate by the German <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry IV. and united with Bohemia, to whose dukes and kings it hath ever since been subject. Though it is not very populous, it contains about 42 greater or walled <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 17 smaller or open towns, and 198 market-towns, besides villages, &c. The states of the country consist of the clergy, lords, knights, and burgesses; and the diets, when summoned by the regency, are held at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRUNN">Brunn</a>. The marquisate is still governed by its own peculiar constitutions, under the directorium in publicis & cameralibus, and the supreme judicatory at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. It is divided into five circles, each of which has its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, and contributes to its sovereign about one-third of what is exacted of Bohemia. Towards the expenses of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment of the whole Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> countries, its yearly quota is 1,856,490 florins. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> regiments of foot, one of cuirassiers, and one of dragoons, are usually quartered in it. Christianity was planted in this country in the 9th century; and the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome till the 15th, when they espoused the doctrine of John Huss, and threw off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>; but after the defeat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, whom they had chosen king, as well as the Bohemians, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II. re-established popery. However, there are still some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in Moravia; and here it was that the Herrnhutters, or Moravian Brethren, first made their appearance. See MORAVIANS. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OLMUTZ">Olmutz</a>, who stands immediately under the pope, is at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> in this country. The supreme <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction, under the bishop, is vested in a consistory. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this country is inconsiderable. Of what they have, Brunn enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGLAU">Iglau</a> and Trebitz are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder, &c. There are also some iron-works and glass-houses in the country. The inhabitants of Moravia in general are open-hearted, not easy to be provoked or pacified, obedient to their masters, and true to their promises; but credu- Moravians, lovers of old prophecies, and much addicted to drinking, though neither such sots or bigots as they are represented by some geographers. The boors, indeed, upon the river Hanak, are said to be a thievish, unpolished, brutal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>. The sciences now begin to lift up their heads a little among the Moravians, the university of Olmutz having been put on a better footing; and a riding academy, with a learned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, have been lately established there.

MORAVIANS

Pages 402-402

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, who have been settled for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> past at Herrnhuth in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, and have of late years spread themselves over most of our American colonies, as well as in several parts of England, where they are permitted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, by a late <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. They have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> peculiar to themselves; and are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of Unitas Fratrum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> The Brethren. They profess the utmost veneration for our blest Saviour, whom they consider as their immediate head and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>; enjoin the most implicit obedience to the rulers of their church; and are said to practise much brotherly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> amongst one another; but from many of their tenets, it would appear, that obscenity makes no small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. See ZINZENDORFF.

MORBID

Pages 402-402

among physicians, signifies "disposed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> corrupt;" a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied either to an unsound <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, or to those parts or humours that are affected by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

MORBUS SACER

Pages 402-402

MORDAUNT

Pages 402-402
earl of Peterborough, a celebrated commander both by sea and land, was the son of John Lord Mordaunt, viscount Avalon, and was born about the year 1658. In 1675 he succeeded his father in his honours and estate. While young he served under the admirals Torrington and Narborough in the Mediterranean, against the Algerines; and in 1680 embarked for Africa with the earl of Plymouth, and distinguished himself at Tangier when it was besieged by the Moors. In the reign of James II. he voted against the repeal of the test-act; and disliking the measures of the court, obtained leave to go to Holland to accept the command of a Dutch squadron in the West Indies.
