He afterwards accompanied the prince of Orange into this kingdom; and upon his advancement to the throne, was sworn of the privy-council, made one of the lords of the bedchamber to his majesty, also first commissioner of the treasury, and advanced to the dignity of earl of Monmouth. But, in November 1690, he was dismissed from his post in the treasury. On the death of his uncle Henry earl of Peterborough in 1697, he succeeded to that title; and, upon the accession of queen Anne, was invested with the commission of captain-general and governor of Jamaica. In 1705 he was sworn of the privy-council; and the same year declared general and commander in chief of the forces sent to Spain, and joint admiral of the fleet with Sir Cloudley Shovel, of which the year following he had the sole command. His taking Barcelona with a handful of men, and afterwards relieving it when greatly distressed by the enemy; his driving out of Spain the Duke of Anjou, and the French army, which consisted of 25,000 men, though his own troops never amounted to 10,000; his gaining possession of Catalonia, of the kingdoms of Valencia, Arragon, and the isle of Majorca, with part of Murcia and Castile, and thereby giving the earl of Galway an opportunity of advancing to Madrid without a blow; are astonishing instances of his bravery and conduct. For these important services his Lordship was declared general in Spain by Charles III. afterwards emperor of Germany; and on his return to England he received the thanks of the House of Lords. His Lordship was afterwards employed in several embassies to foreign courts, installed knight of the garter, and made governor of Minorca. In the reign of George I. he was general of all the marine forces in Great Britain, in which post he was continued by king George II. He died in his passage to Lisbon, where he was going for the recovery of his health, in 1735. His Lordship was distinguished by his possessing various shining qualities: for, to the greatest personal courage and resolution, he added all the arts and address of a general; a lively and penetrating genius; and a great extent of knowledge upon almost every subject of importance within the compass of ancient and modern literature; hence his familiar letters, inserted among those of his friend Mr Pope, are an ornament to that excellent collection.

MORE

Pages 402-404
lord high chancellor of England, the son of Sir John More, knight, one of the judges of the king's-bench, was born in the year 1480, in Milk-street, London. He was first sent to a school at St Anthony's in Threadneedle-street; and afterwards introduced into the family of cardinal Morton, who, in 1497, sent him to Canterbury college in Oxford. During his residence at the university he constantly attended the lectures of Linacre and Grocious, on the Greek and Latin languages. Having in the space of about two years made considerable proficiency in academical learning, he came to New-inn in London, in order to study the law; whence, after some time, he removed to Lincoln's-inn, of which his father was a member. Notwithstanding his application to the law, however, being now about 20 years old, he was so bigotted to monkish discipline, that he wore a hair-thirt next his skin, frequently fasted, and often slept on a bare plank. In the year 1503, being then a burgess in parliament, he distinguished himself in the house, in opposition to the motion for granting a subsidy and three fifteenths for the marriage of Hen.VII.'s eldest daughter, Margaret, to the king of Scotland. The motion was rejected; and the king was so highly offended at this opposition from a beardless boy, that he revenged himself on Mr More's father, by sending him on a frivolous pretence to the Tower, and obliging him to pay 100l. for his liberty. Being now called to the bar, he was appointed law-reader at Furnival's val's inn, which place he held about three years; but about this time, he also read a public lecture in the church of St Lawrence, Old Jewry, upon St Austin's treatise De civitate Dei, with great applause. He had indeed formed a design of becoming a Franciscan friar, but was dissuaded from it; and, by the advice of Dr Colet, married Jane, the eldest daughter of John Colt, Esq., of Newhall in Essex. In 1508 he was appointed judge of the sheriff's court in the city of London, was made a justice of the peace, and became very eminent at the bar. In 1516 he went to Flanders in the retinue of bishop Tonstal and Dr Knight, who were sent by king Henry VIII. to renew the alliance with the archduke of Austria, afterwards Charles V. On his return, cardinal Wolsey would have engaged Mr More in the service of the crown, and offered him a pension, which he refused. Nevertheless, it was not long before he accepted the place of master of the requests, was created a knight, admitted of the privy s="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council, and in 1520 made treasurer of the exchequer. About this time he built a house on the bank of the Thames, at Chelsea, and married a second wife. This wife, whose name was Middleton, and a widow, was old, ill-tempered, and covetous; nevertheless Erasmus says he was as fond of her as if she were a young maid. In the 14th year of Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More was made speaker of the house of commons; in which capacity he had the resolution to oppose the then powerful minister, Wolsey, in his demand of an oppressive subsidy; notwithstanding which, it was not long before he was made chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, and was treated by the king with singular familiarity. The king having once dined with Sir Thomas at Chelsea, walked with him near an hour in the garden, with his arm round his neck. After he was gone, Mr Roper, Sir Thomas's son-in-law, observed how happy he was to be so familiarly treated by the king: to which Sir Thomas replied, "I thank our lord, Jon Roper, I find his grace my very good lord indeed, and believe he doth as singularly favour me as any subject within this realm: howbeit, I must tell thee, I have no cause to be proud thereof; for, if my head would win him a castle in France, it would not fail to go off." From this anecdote it appears, that Sir Thomas knew his grace to be a villain. In 1526 he was sent, with cardinal Wolsey and others, on a joint embassy to France, and in 1529 with bishop Tonstal to Cambrai. The king, it seems, was so well satisfied with his services on these occasions, that in the following year, Wolsey being disgraced, he made him chancellor; which seems the more extraordinary, when we are told that Sir Thomas had repeatedly declared his disapprobation of the king's divorce, on which the great defender fidei was so positively bent. Having executed the office of chancellor about three years, with equal wisdom and integrity, he resigned the seals in 1533, probably to avoid the danger of his refusing to confirm the king's divorce. He now retired to his house at Chelsea; dis- (a) This last disposition, we are told, he could not restrain even at his execution. The day being come, he ascended the scaffold, which seemed so weak, that it was ready to fall; whereupon, "I pray (said he) see me safe up, and for my coming down let me shift for myself." His prayers being ended, he turned to the executioner, and with a cheerful countenance said, "Pluck up thy spirits, man, and be not afraid to do thy office; my neck is very short, take heed therefore thou strike not awry for saving thy honesty." Then laying his head upon the block, he bid him stay until he had put aside his beard, saying, "That had never committed any treason." Vol. VII. His English works were collected and published by order of queen Mary, in 1557; his Latin, at Basil in 1563, and at Louvain in 1566. More (Henry), an eminent English divine and philosopher, in the 17th century, was educated at Eton school, and in Christ-college in Cambridge, of which he became a fellow, and spent his life in a retired way, publishing a great number of excellent works. He refused bishoprics both in Ireland and England. He was an open-hearted, sincere Christian philosopher, who studied to establish men in the belief of providence against atheism. Mr Hobbes was used to say, that if his own philosophy was not true, there was none that he should sooner like than our philosopher's. His writings have been published together in Latin and English, folio.

MOREA

Pages 404-404

formerly called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, to which it is joined by the isthmus of Corinth. Its form resembles a mulberry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and its name is derived from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mulberry-trees which grow there. It is about 180 miles in length, and 130 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> fertile, except in the middle, where it is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and is watered by a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is divided into three provinces; Scania, Belvedera, and Brazzo-di-Maina. It was taken from the Turks by the Venetians in 1687; but they lost it again in 1715. The sovereign of the Morea resides at Modon. See GREECE and PELOPONNESUS.

MOREAU

Pages 404-404

an eminent French physician, born at Chalons-sur-Saone, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and friend of the famous Guy Patin. He drew upon himself the jealousy and hatred of the old physicians by the public theses he maintained, and afterwards vindicated in his writings. He died in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in 1729. He wrote in French, 1. Consultations on the Rheumatism. 2. A chemical treatise on Fevers. 3. A physical dissertation on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">Dropsy</a>; and other works which are esteemed.

MOREL

Pages 404-404

a very eminent antiquary, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. Having a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medals, he travelled through several countries, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> collections: in 1683 he published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 8vo, Specimen universae rei nummariae antiquae; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of which this was the specimen, was to be a complete collection of all <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> medals, of which he had at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> 20,000 exactly designed. Soon after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> appeared, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in his cabinet of antiques, in which capacity he brought himself into great danger by speaking too freely of M. Louvois on account of the neglect in paying his salary, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on some other private account; as he was committed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>, where he lay for three years: nor was he released until the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Louvois, nor till the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Berne had interceded in his favour. He afterward accepted an invitation from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Schwartzenberg at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARNSTADT">Arnstadt</a> in Germany, with whom he lived in the capacity of antiquary, and was furnished with every thing necessary for carrying on his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> work. In 1703 he died; and in 1734 came out at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this collection, in 2 vols folio, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Theatrum Morellianum, sive familiarum Romanorum manifesta omnia, diligentissime undique cognita, &c. Nunc primum edit & commentarius perpetuo illustravit Sigibertus Harvercambus. These volumes contain an explication of 3539 medals, engraved, with their reverses.

MORELLA

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of the coleoptera class of insects. The antennae are thread-shaped and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>; the head is deflected under the neck; the pappi are elevated, compressed, and obliquely blunted; and the elytra are bent backwards near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a>. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all natives of different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

MORENA

Pages 404-404

(anc. geog.), a district <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Mytia, in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a>, formerly at the head of a band of robbers; but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Abrettensis, and enriched with possessions, first by Antony, and then by Cesar.

MORESK

Pages 404-404
or Morisco, is a kind of painting, carvings, &c. done after the manner of the Moors; consisting of several grotesque pieces and compartments, promiscuously mingled, not containing any perfect figure of a man, or other animal; but a wild resemblance of birds, beasts, trees, &c.

MORGAGNI

Pages 404-405
doctor of medicine, first professor of anatomy in the university of Padua, and member of several of the most eminent societies of learned men in Europe, was born in the year 1682, at Forli, a town in the district of La Romagna in Italy. His parents, who were in easy circumstances, allowed him to follow that course in life his genius dictated. He began his studies at the place of his nativity; but soon after removed to Bologna, where he obtained the degree of Doctor of Medicine, when he had but just reached the 16th year of his age. Here his peculiar taste for anatomy found an able preceptor in Valdivia, who bestowed on him the utmost attention; and, such was Morgagni, the progress he made under this excellent master, that at the age of 20 he himself taught anatomy with high reputation. Soon, however, the fame of his predictions, and the number of his pupils, excited the jealousy of the public professors, and gave rise to various persecutions. But his abilities and prudence gained him a complete triumph over his enemies; and all opposition to him was finally terminated from his being appointed by the senate of Bologna to fill a medical chair, which soon became vacant. But the duties of this office, although important, neither occupied the whole of his time, nor satisfied his anxious desire to afford instruction. He still continued to labour in secret on his favourite subject, and soon after communicated the fruits of these labours to the public in his *Adversaria Anatomica*, the first of which was published in the year 1706, the second and third in 1717, and the three others in 1719. The publication of this excellent work spread the fame of Morgagni far beyond the limits of the state of Bologna. Such was his reputation, that the wise republic of Venice had no hesitation in making him an offer of the second chair of the theory of medicine in the university of Padua, then vacant by the death of Mr Moliatti; and, to ensure his acceptance, they doubled the emoluments of that appointment. While he was in this department, he published his treatise, entitled *Nova institutionum medicarum idea*, which first appeared at Padua in the year 1712. From this work his former reputation suffered no diminution. And soon after he rose, by different steps, to be first professor of anatomy in that celebrated university. Although Morgagni was thus finally settled at Padua, yet he gave evident proofs of his gratitude and attachment to Bologna, which he considered as his native country with respect to the sciences. He exerted his utmost efforts in establishing the academy of Bologna, of which he was one of the first associates; and he enriched their publications with several valuable and curious papers. Soon after this, the royal societies of London and Paris received him among their number. Not long after the publication of his *Adversaria Anatomica*, he began, much upon the same plan, his *Epistle Anatomica*, the first of which is dated at Padua in the beginning of April 1726. The works of Morgagni which have already been mentioned, are to be considered, in a great measure, as strictly anatomical; but he was not more eminent as an anatomist, than as a learned and successful physician. In the year 1760, when he was not far distant from the 80th year of his age, he published his large and valuable work *De causis et sedibus morborum per anatomen indagatis*. This last and most important of all his productions will afford convincing evidence of his industry and abilities to late posterity. Besides these works, he published, at different periods of his life, several miscellaneous pieces, which were afterwards collected into one volume, and printed under his own eye at Padua, in the year 1765. It does not appear that he had in view any future publications; but he intended to have favoured the world with a complete edition of all his works, which would probably have been augmented with many new observations. In this he was engaged, when, on the 5th of December 1771, after he had nearly arrived at the 90th year of his age, death put a period to his long and glorious career in the learned world.

MORHOFF

Pages 405-405

a very learned German, born at Wilmar in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Mecklenburgh, in 1639. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, when he founded an university at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KIEL">Kiel</a>, made him professor of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> there in 1665; to which was afterwards added the professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and in 1680 the office of librarian to the university. He was the author of many works of a small kind; as orations, dissertations, theses, and poems: but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was his *Polyhistor, sive de notitia auctorum rerum commentarii*; first published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a> in 1688; which has been greatly enlarged since his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1691, and gone through several successive editions.

MORIAH

Pages 405-405

one of the eminences of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; on which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> went to offer his son, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> wanted to build the temple, which was afterwards executed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>: The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of Araunah; originally narrow, so as scarce to contain the temple, but enlarged by means of ramparts; and surrounded with a triple wall, so as to add <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength to the temple, (Josephus). It may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, to which it was joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> and gallery, (Id.)

MORIN

Pages 405-406

a very learned Frenchman, born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>, of Protestant parents, in 1591; but converted by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> du Perron to the catholic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He published, in 1626, some Exercitations upon the original of patriarchs and primates, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> usages of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> censures; dedicated to pope Urban VIII. In 1628 he undertook the edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, with Nobilius's version; and placed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> before it, in which he treats of the authority of the Septuagint, and prefers the version in the edition made at Rome by order of Sixtus V., to the present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text, which he affirms has been corrupted by the Jews. About the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he gave a French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the deliverance of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine; and of the temporal greatness conferred on the Roman church by the kings of France. He afterwards published Exercitations upon the Samaritan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>; and took the care of the Samaritan Pentateuch, for the Polyglot then preparing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He was greatly carefree at Rome; where, after living <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, at the invitation of cardinal Barini, MORINUS barini, he was recalled by cardinal Richlieu, and died at Paris in 1659. His works are very numerous; and some of them as much valued by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> as Papists for the oriental learning they contain.

MORINUS

Pages 406-406

a learned French Protestant, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> in 1625. He became minister of two churches near Caen, and in 1664 was chosen minister of Caen; but on the revocation of the edict of Nantes, was obliged to take refuge in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. He was soon called to be professor of the oriental tongues at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, to which employment was afterwards joined that of minister in ordinary: he died in 1700. He was the author of several works: and his fondness for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> made him run into some extravagancies concerning it; for in his Lettre sur l'origine de la langue Hebraïque, he endeavours to prove that language as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and that God himself inspired it into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>. This was answered by Huet.

MORISON

Pages 406-406

physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, was born at Aberdeen in 1620, bred at the university there, and taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it; but having a strong inclination to botany, made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in it. The civil wars obliged him to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which, however, he did not do till he had first signalized his zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, and his courage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the inhabitants of Aberdeen and the Presbyterian troops on the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Aberdeen, in which he received a dangerous wound on the head. As soon as he was cured of it, he went into France; and fixing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he applied assiduously to botany and anatomy. He was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. He exercised the office till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and afterwards went over to England in 1660. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., to whom the duke of Orleans had presented him at Blois, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his physician, and that of professor regal of botany, with a pension of 200l. per annum. The Prodromus Botanicum, which he published in 1669, procured him so much reputation, that the university of Oxford invited him to the professorship of botany in 1669; which he accepted, and acquitted himself in it with great ability. He died at London in 1683, aged 63. He published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, in 2 vols. folio; with this title Plantarum Historia Oxoniensis Universalis. The first part of this excellent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> has not been printed; and it is not known what has become of it.

MORLACHIA

Pages 406-411

a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The inhabitants are called Morlacchi <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Morlacchis; and inhabit the pleasant valleys of Koter, along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Kerka, Cettina, Narenta, and among the inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Dalmatia. The inhabitants are by some said to be of Walachian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, as (according to these authors), is indicated even by their name; Morlachia being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Maur-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> Walachia; and the Walachians are said to be descendents of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman colonies planted in these countries. This however is denied by the abbe Fortis, who hath published a volume of travels into that country. He informs us, that the origin of the Morlacchi is involved in the darkness of barbarous ages, together with that of many other nations, resembling them so much in customs and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that they may be taken for one people, Morlacchi dispersed in the vast tracks from the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the frozen ocean. The emigrations of the various tribes of the Slavi, who, under the names of Scythians, Geti, Goti, Hunni, Slavini, Croats, Avari, and Vandals, invaded the Roman empire, and particularly the Illyrian provinces during the decline of the empire, must have strangely perplexed the genealogies of the nations which inhabited it, and which perhaps removed thither in the same manner as at more remote periods of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The remainder of the Ardaii, Autariati, and other Illyrian people anciently settled in Dalmatia, who probably could not reconcile themselves to a dependence on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, might nevertheless naturally enough form an union with foreign invaders not unlike themselves in dialect and customs; and, according to our author, it seems no ill-founded conjecture, that many families, driven out of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> by the irruption of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> under Jenghiz Khan and his successors, might people the deserted valleys between the mountains of Dalmatia. This conjecture is also somewhat confirmed by the traces of the Calmuck Tartars, which are still to be found in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of that country called Zara. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, the abbe observes, that the Morlacchi generally call themselves, in their own language, Vlasi; a national <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, of which no vestige is found in the records of Dalmatia till the 13th century. It signifies powerful men, or men of authority, and the denomination of Moro-Vlasi, corruptly Morlacchi, as they are now called, may perhaps point out the original of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This word may possibly signify the conquerors that came from the sea; Moor, in all the dialects of the Sclavonian language, signifying the sea. The Morlacchi are so different from the inhabitants of the sea-coasts in dialect, dress, dispositions, and customs, that they seem clearly to be of a different original, or at least the colonies must have settled at such distant periods from each other, that they have had time to alter in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their national character. There is also a remarkable diversity among the Morlacchi themselves in several districts, probably on account of the different countries from whence they came. With regard to the character of these people, we are informed that they are much injured by their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> neighbours. The inhabitants of the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Dalmatia tell many frightful stories of their avarice and cruelty; but these, in our author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, are all either of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any have happened in latter times, they ought rather to be ascribed to the corruption of a few individuals, than to the bad disposition of the nation in general; and though thieves tricks are frequent among them, he informs us, that a stranger may travel securely through their country, where he is faithfully escorted, and hospitably treated. The greatest danger is from the Haiduks or Banditti, of whom there are great numbers among the woods and caves of these dreadful mountains on the confines. There, says our author, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> ought to get himself escorted by a couple of these "honest fellows;" for they are not capable of betraying him, although a bandit; and their situation is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> more apt to raise compassion than dislike. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> among among the wolves, wandering from one precipice to another, exposed to the severity of the seasons, and frequently languish in want of the necessaries of life, in the most hideous and solitary caverns. Yet they very seldom disturb the tranquillity of others, and prove always faithful guides to travellers; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> objects of their rapine being sheep and oxen, to supply themselves with food and shoes. Sometimes it happens, that, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, the Haiduks go in parties to the shepherds cottages, and rudely demand something to eat; which they do not fail to take immediately by force if the least hesitation is made. It is seldom indeed that they meet with a refusal, or with resistance, as their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and fury are well known to be equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> life they lead. Four Haiduks are not afraid to assail a caravan of 15 or 20 Turks, and generally plunder and put them to flight. The greatest part of the Haiduks look upon it as a meritorious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to shed the blood of the Turks; to which cruelty they are easily led by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> ferocity, inflamed by a mistaken zeal for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and the discourses of their fanatic priests. As to the Morlacchi themselves, they are represented as open and sincere to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they would be taken for simpletons in any other country; and by means of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they have been often duped by the Italians, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of an Italian, and the faith of a dog, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> among the Morlacchi. They are very hospitable to strangers, and their hospitality is equally conspicuous among the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The rich prepares a roasted lamb or sheep, and the poor with equal cordiality offers whatever he has; nor is this generosity confined to strangers, but generally extends itself to all who are in want. When a Morlack is on a journey, and comes to lodge at a friend's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the family, or the newly-married <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> if there happens to be one, receives and kisses him when he alights from his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or at the door of the house; but a foreigner is rarely favoured with these <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> civilities; on the contrary, the women, if they are young, hide themselves, and keep out of his way. The Morlacchi in general have little notion of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy, and readily consume in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as much as would be sufficient for several months, whenever any occasion of merriment presents itself. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the holiday of the faint, protector of the family, the arrival of relations or friends, or any other joyful incident, consumes of course all that there is to eat and to drink in the house. Yet the Morlack is a great economizt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his wearing-apparel; for, rather than spoil his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, he takes it off, let it <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> ever so hard, and goes bareheaded in the storm. In the same manner he treats his shoes, if the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is dirty and they are not very old. Nothing but an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> impossibility hinders a Morlack from being punctual; and if he cannot repay the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he borrowed at the appointed time, he carries a small present to his creditor, and requests a longer term. Thus it happens sometimes, that, from term to term, and present to present, he pays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> what he owed, without reflecting on it. Friendship, that among us is so subject to change on the slightest motives, is lasting among the Morlacchi. They have even made it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point, and tie the sacred bond at the foot of the altar. The Slavonian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> contains a particular benediction for the solemn union of two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> or two female friends in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>. The male friends thus united are called Pobratimi, and the female Polifreme, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> half-brothers and half-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. Friendships between those of different sexes are not at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> bound with so much solemnity, though perhaps in more ancient and innocent ages it was also the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. From these consecrated friendships among the Morlacchi and other nations of the same origin, it should seem that the sworn brothers arose, a denomination frequent enough among the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these and the Pobratimi of Morlacchia consists not only in the want of the ritual <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the union itself. For, among the Morlacchi, the sole view is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage; but such a brotherhood among the Italians, is generally commenced by bad men, to enable them the more to hurt and disturb <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The duties of the Pobratimi are, to assist each other in every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of need or danger, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> mutual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a>, and such like. The enthusiasm is often carried so far as to risk and even to lose their life for the Pobratimi, although these savage friends are not celebrated like a Pyradyes. If <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> happens to arise between two friends, it is talked of over all the country as a scandalous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>; and there has been some examples of it of late years, to the great affliction of the old Morlacchi, who <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the depravation of their countrymen to their intercourse with the Italians. Wine and strong liquors, of which the nation is beginning to make daily abuse, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of course produce the same bad effects as among others. But as the friendships of the Morlacchi are strong and sacred, so their quarrels are commonly unextinguishable. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from father to son; and the mothers fail not to put their children in mind of their duty to revenge their father if he has had the misfortune to be killed, and to shew them often the bloody skirt and arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>. And so deeply is revenge rooted in the minds of this nation, that all the missionaries in the world would not be able to eradicate it. A Morlack is naturally inclined to do good to his fellow-creatures, and is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the smallest benefit; but implacable if injured or insulted. A Morlack who has killed another of a powerful family, is commonly obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight, and to keep out of the way for several years. If during that time he has been fortunate enough to escape the search of his pursuers, and has got a small sum of money, he endeavours to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and peace; and, that he may treat about the conditions in person, he asks and obtains a safe conduct, which is faithfully maintained, through only verbally granted. Then he finds mediators; and, on an appointed day, the relations of the two hostile families are assembled, and the criminal is introduced, dragging himself along on his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, the musket, pistol, or cutlass, with which he committed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, hung about his neck; and while he continues in that humble posture, one or more of the relations recites a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on the the dead, which sometimes rekindles the flames of revenge, and puts the poor prostrate in no small danger. It is the custom in some places for the offended party to threaten the criminal, holding all kind of arms to his throat, and, after much intreaty, to consent at least to accept of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. These pacifications cost dear in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>; but the Morlacchi make up matters sometimes at a small expense; and everywhere the business is concluded with a feast at the offender's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The Morlacchi, whether they happen to be of the Roman or of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, have very singular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> about religion; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of their teachers daily augments this monstrous evil. They are as firmly persuaded of the reality of witches, fairies, enchantments, nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>, and fortigies, as if they had seen a thousand examples of them. Nor do they make the least doubt about the existence of vampires; and attribute to them, as in Transylvania, the sucking the blood of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. Therefore, when a man dies suspected of becoming a vampire, or *vukodak*, as they call it, they cut his hams, and prick his whole body with pins; pretending, that after this operation he cannot walk about. There are even instances of Morlacchi, who, imagining that they may possibly thirst for children's blood after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, intreat their heirs, and sometimes oblige them, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to treat them as vampires when they die. The boldest Haiduk would fly trembling from the apparition of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a>, ghost, phantom, or such like goblins as the heated imaginations of credulous and prepossessed people never fail to see. Nor are they ashamed, when ridiculed for this terror; but answer, much in the words of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>: "Fear that proceeds from spirits, causes even the sons of the gods to fly." The women, as may be naturally supposed, are a hundred times more timorous and visionary than the men; and some of them, by frequently hearing themselves called *witches*, actually believe they are so. A most perfect discord reigns in Morlachia, as it generally does in other parts, between the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, which their respective priests fail not to foment, and tell a thousand little scandalous stories of each other. The churches of the Latins are poor, but not very dirty; those of the Greeks are equally poor, and shamefully ill kept. Our author has seen the curate of a Morlack village sitting on the ground in the church-yard, to hear the confession of women on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> by his side: a strange posture indeed! but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the innocent manners of those good people, who have the most profound veneration for their spiritual pastors, and a total dependence upon them; who, on their part, frequently make use of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and correct the bodies of their offending flock with the cudgel. Perhaps this particular is carried to an abuse as well as that of public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, which they pretend to inflict after the manner of the ancient church. They moreover, thro' the silly credulity of those poor mountaineers, draw illicit profits, by selling certain superstitious ferrols and other scandalous merchandise of that kind. They write in a capricious manner, on the ferrols called *zapiz*, sacred names which ought not to be trifled with, and sometimes adding others very improperly joined. The virtues attributed to these *zapiz* are much of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as those which the Basilians attributed to Morlachia, their monstrously cut <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The Morlacchi use to carry them sewed to their caps, to cure or to prevent diseases; and they also tie them for the same purpose to the horns of their oxen. The composers of this trumpery take every method to maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of their profitable trade, in spite of its absurdity, and the frequent proofs of its inutility. And so great has their success been, that not only the Morlacchi, but even the Turks near the borders, provide themselves plentifully with *zapiz* from the Christian priests, which not a little increases their income, as well as the reputation of the commodity. The Morlacchi have also much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and many of the ignorant people in Italy have little less, to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and silver coins of the low empire; or to Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> pieces, which pass among them for medals of St Helen; and they think they cure the epilepsy and such like. They are equally fond of an Hungarian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> called *prizza*, which has the virgin and child on the reverse; and one of these is a most acceptable present to a Morlack. The bordering Turks not only keep with devotion the superstitious *zapiz*, but frequently bring presents and cause masses to be celebrated to the images of the Virgin; which is doubtless in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">alcoran</a>; yet when saluted, in the usual manner in that country, by the name of *Jesu*, they do not answer. Hence, when the Morlacchi, or other travellers, meet them on the confines, they do not say, *Hagian Iesus*, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> be praised;" but, *Hagian Bog*, "God be praised." Innocence, and the natural <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of pastoral ages, are still preserved among the Morlacchi, or at least many traces of them remain in the places farthest distant from our settlements. Pure cordiality of sentiment is not there restrained by other regards, and displays itself without any distinction of circumstances. A young handsome Morlack girl, who meets a man of her district on the road, kisses him affectionately, without the least malice or immodest thought; and our author has seen all the women and girls, all the young men and old, kissing one another as they came into the church-yard on a holiday; so that they looked as if they had been all belonging to one family. He hath often observed the same thing on the road, and at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the maritime <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the Morlacchi came to sell their commodities. In times of feasting and merriment, besides the kisses, some other little liberties are taken with the hands, which we would not reckon decent, but are not minded among them; and when they are told of it, they answer, it is only toying, and means nothing. From this toying, however, their amours often take their beginning, and frequently end seriously when the two lovers are once agreed. For it very rarely happens, in places far distant from the coast, that a Morlacco carries off a girl against her will, or dishonours her: and were such attempts made, the young woman would, no doubt, be able to defend herself; the women in that country being generally very little less robust than the men. But the custom is for the woman herself to appoint the time and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of being carried off; and she does so in order to extricate herself from other suitors, from whom she may have received some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-token, such as a brais <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, a little The Morlack women keep themselves somewhat neat till they get a husband; but after marriage they abandon themselves totally to a loathsome dirtiness, as if they intended to justify the contempt with which they are treated. Indeed it cannot be said that even the young women have a grateful odour, as they are used to anoint their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, which soon becoming rancid exhales no agreeable effluvia. The dress of the unmarried women is the most complex and whimsical, in respect to the ornaments of the head; for when married they are not allowed to wear any thing else but a handkerchief, either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or coloured, tied about it. The girls use a scarlet cap, to which they commonly hang a veil falling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the shoulders, as a mark of their virginity. The better sort adorn their caps with strings of silver coins, among which are frequently seen very ancient and valuable ones; they have moreover <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings of very curious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and small silver chains with the figures of half moons fastened to the ends of them. But the poor are forced to content themselves with plain caps; or if they have any ornaments, they consist only of small exotic shells, round glass beads, or bits of tin. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merit of these caps, which constitute the good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as well as vanity of the Morlack young ladies, is to attract and fix the eyes of all who are near them by the multitude of ornaments, and the noise they make on the least <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of their heads. Hence half-moons of silver, or of tin, little chains and hearts, false stones and shells, together with all kind of splendid trumpery, are readily admitted into their head-dress. In some districts, they fix tufts of various coloured feathers, resembling two horns on their caps; in others, tremulous plumes of glass; and in others, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which they purchase in the sea-port towns; and in the variety of those capricious and barbarous ornaments, sometimes a fancy not inelegant is displayed. Their holiday-thicts are embroidered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and sometimes with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which they work themselves while they attend their flocks; and it is surprising to see how nicely this work is executed. Both old and young women wear about their necks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> strings of round glass-beads of various size and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and many rings of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, tin, or silver, on their fingers. Their bracelets are of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covered with wrought tin or silver; and they embroider their stomachers, or adorn them with beads or shells. But the use of flays is unknown, nor do they put whalebone or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in the stomacher. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> woollen girdle surrounds their petticoat, which is commonly decked with shells, and of blue colour, and therefore called medrina. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, as well as petticoat, is of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>; and both reach near to the ankle: the gown is bordered with scarlet, and called sadak. They use no medrina in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and only wear the sadak without sleeves over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> petticoat or shift. The girls always wear red stockings; and their shoes are like those of the men, called spanels. The sole is of undressed ox-hide, and the upper part of sheep-skin thongs knotted, which they call apates; and these they fasten above the ankles, something like the ancient cothurnus. The unmarried women, even of the richest females, are not permitted to wear any other sort of shoes; tho' after marriage they may, if they will, lay aside the o-Morlacki panke, and use the Turkish slippers. The girls keep their hair trifled under their caps, but when married they let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dishevelled on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; sometimes they tie it under the chin; and always have medals, beads, or bored coins, in the Tartar or American <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, twisted amongst it. An unmarried woman, who falls under the imputation of want of chastity, runs the risk of having her red cap torn off her head publicly in church by the curate, and her hair cut by some relation, in token of infamy. Hence, if any of them happen to have fallen into an illicit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>, they commonly of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> lay aside the badge of virginity, and remove into another part of the country. Nothing is more common among the Morlacki than marriages concluded between the old people of the respective families, especially when the parties live at a great distance, and neither see nor know each other; and the ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of these alliances is the ambition of being related to a numerous and powerful family, famous for having produced valiant men. The father of the future bridegroom, or some other near relation of mature <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, goes to ask the young woman, or rather a young woman of such a family, not having commonly any determinate choice. Upon this, all the girls of the house are thrown to him, and he chooses which pleases him best, though generally respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of seniority. A denial in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is very rare; nor does the father of the maid inquire much into the circumstances of the family that asks her. Sometimes a daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is given in marriage to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> or tenant, as was usual in patriarchal times; so little are the women regarded in this country. On these occasions, however, the Morlacki girls enjoy a privilege which ours would also wish to have; as in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> they certainly ought. For he who acts by proxy, having obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, is obliged to go and bring the bridegroom; and if, on seeing each other, the young people are reciprocally content, the marriage is concluded, but not otherwise. In some parts it is the custom for the bride to go to see the house and family of the proposed husband, before she gives a definitive answer; and if the place or persons are disagreeable to her, she is at liberty to annul the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. But if she is contented, she returns to her father's house, escorted by the bridegroom and nearest relations. There the marriage-day is appointed; on which the bridegroom comes to the bride's house, attended by all his friends of greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, who on this occasion are called svati, and are all armed, and on horseback, in their holiday-cloaths, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather in their cap, which is the distinctive ornament used by those who are invited to weddings. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> goes armed, to repulse any attack or ambush that might be intended to disturb the feast; for in old times these encounters were not unfrequent, according to the records of many national heroic songs. The bride is conducted to a church, veiled, and surrounded by the svati on horseback; and the sacred ceremony is performed amidst the noise of mulets, pistols, barbaric shouts and acclamations, which continue till she returns to her father's house, or to that of her husband if not far off. Each of the svati has his parti- particular inspection, as well during the cavalcade, as at the marriage feast, which begins immediately on their return from church. The parvinaz precedes all the rest, singing such songs as he thinks suitable to the occasion. The bariaetar brandishes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> with a silken banner fastened to it, and an apple stuck on the point; there are two bariaetars, and sometimes four, at the more noble marriages. The flari-fvat is the principal personage of the brigade, and the most respectable relation is commonly invested with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The flacheo's duty is to receive and obey the orders of the flari-fvat. The two diversi, who ought to be the bridegroom's brothers when he has any, are appointed to serve the bride. The knum corresponds to our sponsors; and the komorgia, or fekfa-na is deputed to receive and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the dowery. A ciaous carries the mace, and attends to the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, as master of the ceremonies; he goes singing aloud, Breberi, Davori, Dobrofriboia, Jara, Pico, names of ancient propitious deities. Bukhia is the cup-bearer of the company, as well on the march as at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; and all these offices are doubled, and sometimes tripled, in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the company. The first day's entertainment is sometimes made at the bride's house, but generally at the bridegroom's, whether the fvati haften immediately after the nuptial benediction; and at the same time, three or four men run on foot to tell the good news; the first who gets to the house has a kind of towel, embroidered at the ends, as a premium. The domachin, or head of the house, comes out to meet his daughter-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and a child is handed to her, before she alights, to caress it; and if there happens to be none in the house, the child is borrowed from one of the neighbours. When she alights, she kneels down, and kisses the threshold. Then the mother-in-law, or, in her place, some other female relation, presents a corn-sieve, full of different kinds of grain, nuts, almonds, and other small fruit, which the bride scatters upon the fvati, by handfuls behind her back. The bride does not sit at the great table the first day, but has one apart for herself, the two diversi, and the flacheo. The bridegroom sits at table with the fvati; but in all that day, consecrated to the matrimonial union, he must neither unloosen or cut anything whatever. The knum carves his meat, and cuts his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. It is the domachin's business to give the toast; and the flari-fvat is the first who pledges him. Generally the bukkara, a very large wooden cup, goes round, first to the saint protector of the family; next to the prosperity of the holy faith; and sometimes to a name the most sublime and venerable. The most extravagant abundance reigns at these feasts; and each of the fvati contributes, by sending a share of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The dinner begins with fruit and cheese; and the soup comes last, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> contrary to our custom. All sorts of domestic fowls, kid, lamb, and sometimes venison, are heaped in prodigious quantities upon their tables; but very rarely a Morlacchi eats veal, and perhaps never, unless he has been persuaded to do it out of his own country. This abhorrence to calves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is very ancient among the Morlacchi. St Jerom, against Jovinian, takes notice of it; and Tomo Marnavich, a Bosnian writer, who lived in the beginning of the last age, says, that the Dalmatians, uncorrupted by the vices of strangers, abstained from Morlacchi eating calves-flesh, as an unclean food, even to his days. The women-relations, if they are invited, never dine at table with the men, it being an established custom for them to dine by themselves. After dinner, they pass the rest of the day in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, singing ancient songs, and in games of dexterity, or of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and fancy; and in the evening, at a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, the three ritual heads having first gone round, the knum accompanies the bridegroom to the matrimonial apartment, which commonly is the cellar or the stable, whither the bride is also conducted by the diversi and the flacheo; but the three last are obliged to retire, and the knum remains alone with the newly-married couple. If there happens to be any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> prepared better than straw, he leads them to it; and having untied the bride's girdle, he cautes them both to undress each other reciprocally. It is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since the knum was obliged to undress the bride entirely; but that custom is now out of use; and, instead of it, he has the privilege of killing her as often as he pleases, wherever he meets her; which privilege may possibly be agreeable for the first months, but must soon become very disagreeable. When they are both undressed, the knum retires, and stands listening at the door, if there be a door. It is his business to announce the consummation of the marriage, which he does by discharging a pistol, and is answered by many of the company. The next day, the bride, without her veil and virginal cap, dines at table with the fvati, and is forced to hear the coarse equivocal jests of her indelicate, and sometimes intoxicated, company. These nuptial-feasts, called sfavize by the ancient Huns, are by our Morlacchi called sfavizze, from whence our Italian word sfavizzze is undoubtedly derived. They continue three, six, eight, or more days, according to the ability or prodigal disposition of the family where they are held. The new-married wife gets no inconsiderable profit in these days of joy. And it usually amounts to much more than all the portion she brings with her, which often consists of nothing but her own cloaths, and perhaps a cow; nay, it happens sometimes that the parents, instead of giving money with their daughter, get something from the bridegroom by way of price. The bride carries <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> every morning, to wash the hands of her guests, as long as the feasting lasts; and each of them throws a small piece of money into the basin, after performing that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, which is a very rare one among them excepting on such occasions. The brides are also permitted to raise other little contributions among the fvati, by hiding their shoes, caps, knives, or some other necessary part of their equipage, which they are obliged to ransom by a piece of money, according as the company <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a> it. And, besides all these voluntary or extorted contributions already mentioned, each guest must give some present to the new married wife at taking leave the last day of the sfavizze; and then she also distributes some trifles in return, which commonly consist in shirts, caps, handkerchiefs, and such like. The nuptial-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> are almost precisely the same thro' all the vast country inhabited by the Morlacchi; and those in use among the peasants and common people of the sea-coast of Dalmatia, Itria, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, differ differ but little from them. Yet among these particular varieties, there is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Zlarine, near Sebenico, remarkable enough; for there the tarifvat (who may naturally be supposed drunk at that hour) malt, at one blow, with his naked broad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, strike the bride's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of flowers off her head, when she is ready to go to bed. And in the island of Pag, in the village of Novoglia, (probably the Gilla of ancient geographers), there is a custom more comical, and less dangerous, but equally savage and brutal. After the marriage-contract is settled, and the bridegroom comes to conduct his bride to church; her father or mother, in delivering her over to him, makes an exaggerated enumeration of her ill qualities: "Know, since thou wilt have her, that she is good for nothing, ill-natured, obdurate, &c." On which the bridegroom, afflicting an angry look, turns to the young woman, with an, "Ah! since it is so, I will teach you to behave better;" and at the same time regales her with a blow or a kick, or some piece of similar gallantry, which is by no means figurative. And it seems in general, that the Morlack women, and perhaps the greatest part of the Dalmatians, the inhabitants of the cities excepted, do not dislike a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>, either from their husbands or lovers. In the neighbourhood of Dernish, the women are obliged, during the first year after marriage, to kiss all their national acquaintances who come to the house; but after the first year they are dispensed from that compliment; and indeed they become so intolerably nasty, that they are no longer fit to practise it. Perhaps the mortifying manner in which they are treated by their husbands and relations, is, at the same time, both the cause and effect of this shameful neglect of their persons. When a Morlack husband mentions his wife, he always premises, by your leave, or begging your pardon. And when the husband has a bedhead, the wife must <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> near it. Our author often lodged in Morlack houses, and observed that the female <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> is universally treated with contempt: it is true, that the women are by no means amiable in that country; they even deform and spoil the gifts of nature. The pregnancy and births of those women would be thought very extraordinary among us, where the ladies suffer so much, notwithstanding all the care and circumspection used before and after labour. On the contrary, a Morlack woman neither changes her food nor interrupts her daily fatigue, on account of her pregnancy; and is frequently delivered in the fields, or on the road, by herself; and takes the infant, washes it in the first water she finds, carries it home, and returns the day after to her usual labour, or to feed her flock. The little creatures, thus carelessly treated in their tenderest moments, are afterwards wrapped in miserable rags, where they remain three or four months, under the same ungentle management; and when that term is elapsed, they are set at liberty, and left to crawl about the cottage and before the door, till they learn to walk upright by themselves; and at the same time acquire that singular degree of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> with which the Morlacki are endowed, and are able, without the least inconvenience, to expose their naked breasts to the severest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> and snow. The infants are allowed to suck their mother's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> while she has any, or till she is with child again; and if that should not happen for three, four, or six years, they continue all that time to receive nourishment from the breast. The prodigious length of the breasts of the Morlackian women is somewhat extraordinary; for it is very certain, that they can give the teat to their children over their shoulders, or under their arms. They let the boys run about, without breeches, in a shift that reaches only to the knee, till the age of 13 or 14, following the custom of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, subject to the Porte, where no haraz or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>-tax is paid for the boys till they wear breeches, they being considered before that time as children, not capable of labouring, or of earning their bread. On the occasion of births, and especially of the first, all the relations and friends send presents of eatables to the woman in childbed, or rather to the woman delivered; and the family makes a supper of all those presents together. The women do not enter the church till 40 days after child-birth. The Morlacki pass their youth in the woods, attending their flocks and herds, and in that life of quiet and leisure they often become dexterous in carving with a simple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; they make wooden cups, and whistles adorned with fanciful bas-reliefs, which are not void of merit, and at least show the genius of the people.

MORLEY

Pages 411-411

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, was the son of Francis Morley, Esq., and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1597. He was educated at Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, of which he had the canonry in 1641, and the next year was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He had also several church-preferments, of which he was deprived by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> visitors in the beginning of the year 1648. After this, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. sent for him to assist at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight. After the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Capel at his execution, and then retired to Charles II. at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, on whom he constantly waited till his majesty went to Scotland, when he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, where he read the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the church of England, as he afterwards did at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>. At the Restoration he was first made <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Christ-church, and in 1660 was consecrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, and soon after was made dean of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> chapel. In 1662 he was translated to the bishopric of Winchester, when he bestowed considerable sums on that see, in repairing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARNHAM">Farnham</a>-castle and his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Westminster, and in purchasing Winchester-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Chelsea. He died at Farnham-castle in 1684. He was a Calvinist, and before the wars was thought a friend to the Puritans; but after his promotion, he took care to free himself from all suspicions of that kind. He was a pious and charitable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, of a very exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but extremely passionate. He published, 1. Epistle apologetica et paradoxa <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> theologum quendam Belgam scripta, in 4to. 2. The sum of a short conference between Father Darcey a Jesuit, and Dr Morley at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>. 3. An argument drawn from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> and certainty of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> against the doctrine of Transubstantiation. 4. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>. 5. Several sermons, and other pieces.

MORNAY

Pages 411-412
lord of Pleissi-Marly, governor of Saumur, and one of the best Protestant generals of France, was born of a noble family at Buhy. Morning, in 1549. He became well skilled in polite literature, divinity, and the learned languages. Having embraced the Protestant religion, he travelled to Italy, Germany, the Netherlands, and to England; and at length engaged himself in the interest of the king of Navarre, who was afterwards Henry the Great. That prince relied greatly on his judgment, and in 1590 made him counsellor of state. De Puffis performed the most important services for him, and was one of the lords who contributed most to his ascending the throne. He was in a manner the head and soul of the Protestants: he had their entire confidence, and acquired great reputation amongst them on account of his learning, valour, and probity; which occasioned his being called the Pope of the Huguenots. He opposed king Henry IV.'s embracing the Roman religion to the utmost of his power; and soon after that event retired from court, and laboured at his famous work on the Eucharist. He continued to support the Calvinists party by his writings; and Lewis XIII., taking from him the government of Saumur in 1621, he retired to his barony at Forêt-sur-Sevre in Poitou, where he died in 1623, aged 74. He also wrote, 1. A treatise on the truth of the Christian religion. 2. The mystery of iniquity; and other works.

MORNING

Pages 412-412

the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the first appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> from midnight till noon.

MOROCCO

Pages 412-416

an empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, comprehending a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, is bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>; on the east by the river Muluya, which separates it from Algiers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and on the south by mount <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather by the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>, which divides it from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tafilet. Its greatest length is from the north-east to the south-west, amounting to above 590 miles; its breadth is not above 260 where broadest, and in the most narrow places is not above half that breadth. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Morocco hath been already given under the article Mauritania.
