It <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> upwards of 400 years. On the decline of that empire it fell under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who held it till about the year 600, when the Goths were driven out by the Vandals, the Vandals by the Greeks, and they in their turn by the Saracens, who conquered not only this empire, but we may say the whole continent of Africa; at least their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, one way or other, is to be found in all parts of it. The Saracen empire did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> united under one head, and many princes set up for themselves in Africa as well as elsewhere, through whose divisions the Almoravides were at length raised to the sovereignty, as related under the article Algiers, n° 2. Yulef, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> monarch of that line, built the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Morocco, conquered the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and the Moorish dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; all which were lost by his grandson Abu Hali, who was defeated and killed by the Spaniards. On this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> passed to the Mohedians, or Almohedes, with whom it had not continued above three generations, when Mohammed the son of Al Manfur lost the famous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sierra Morena, in which 200,000 Moors were slain, and in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which Alphonso X. retook Morocco, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of the Moorish conquests immediately after. Mohammed died soon after this disgrace, and left several sons, between whom a civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> ensued, during which the viceroys of Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and Tremelen, found means to establish themselves as independent princes. At length one of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood of Tremelen having defeated the Almoheds, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the kingdoms of Morocco and Fez, and entailed them on his own family. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, this family was expelled by the Merinoi, the Merinoi by the Oataxes, and these by the Sharifs of Hafzen, who have kept the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> ever since. This happened about the year 1516; and since that time the history of the empire affords nothing remarkable. What we have under that name is indeed nothing else than a catalogue of the enormous vices and excesses of the emperors and people. Nothing indeed can be conceived more unjust and despotic than the government of Morocco, and nothing more degenerate than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is allowed to have not only an uncontrollable power over the lives and fortunes of his subjects, but in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> over their consciences, such as they are; in as much as he is the only person who, as the successor of the prophet, hath a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to interpret the Koran; and appoints all the judges under him, of whom those of Morocco and Fez are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, whose business it is to explain and dispense all matters relating to their religion; and, being his creatures and dependents, dare not steer otherwise than as he directs. Whenever therefore the laws are enacted by him, and proclaimed by his governors in all the provinces, as is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> done, that none may plead <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they are everywhere received with an implicit and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> submission. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the subjects are bred up with a notion, that those who die in the execution of his command are entitled to an immediate admittance into paradise, and those who have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to die by his hand to a still greater <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in it. After this we need not wonder at finding so much cruelty, oppression, and tyranny on the one side, and so much submission, passiveness, and misery on the other. This latter, however, extends no farther than the Moors; for as to the Arabs, the subjection and tribute they pay to those tyrants was always involuntary, and altogether forced; and as for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, their zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> is owing merely to the great sway and power which they have gained in the government, both on account of their being better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> than the Moors, and from a particular regard which Muley Ishmael a late emperor had for them on account of his mother being a negro; so that, being now grown in a manner too strong to be supprelled, their loyalty and affection to those monarchs, whom they strive to imitate in all their vices, must be supposed to rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> according to the favour and encouragement they receive from them. And they are now the only ones to whom those tyrants entrust their persons, their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, and their concubines; whom they raise to the highest posts of authority and trust; and whom they suffer, not to say encourage by their their own example, to tyrannize and oppress their native, as well as their most faithful and submissive subjects. These negroes, ever since their adhering so closely to Muley Ishmael, have been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> request with his successors, and make the main branch of the footmen both of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot. They are brought to young out of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, that they quickly lose the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of it; and having no relations or friends, nor dependence but on the emperor's favour, are the more ready to obey his orders in all things. They are at first brought up to be foot-soldiers; and after so many years <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in it, or sooner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their behaviour deserve it, are advanced to the cavalry, which is a great honour in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They are taught little else except the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of arms, and to obey the emperor's orders; and, by the readiest compliance with his views, politics, and inclination, advance themselves to the highest posts under him. But we shall perhaps find less reason to wonder at this connivance, if we consider, that, sooner or later, all the extortions of those blood-thirsters come in course into their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, either by the heavy fines they impose upon them upon any complaint preferred against them, or upon any other, whether real or pretended, mal-administrations, or by seizing on all their ill-gotten wealth at their deaths. For the emperors here have found means to establish another branch of despotism, which renders them still more powerful and formidable to their subjects; viz., their making themselves their sole heirs, and, in virtue of that, seizing upon all their effects, and making only such provision for their families as they think proper; and often, on some frivolous pretence, leaving them destitute of any, according to the liking or dislike they bear to the deceased: so that, upon the whole, they are the only makers, judges, and interpreters, and in many instances likewise the executioners, of their own laws, which have no other limits than their own arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. To preserve, however, some specious show or shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, they allow their mufti a kind of superiority in spirituals, and a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to the meanest subject to summon them before his tribunal. But the danger which such an attempt would bring upon a plaintiff, perhaps no less than death and destruction, is of itself sufficient to deter any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> from it; especially considering the little <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> there is that the judges of it would run the risk of declaring themselves against a monarch whose creatures they are, and on whom their lives and fortunes so absolutely depend. The titles which the emperors of Morocco assume, are those of "Most glorious, mighty, and noble emperor of Africa, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Fez and Morocco, Taphilet, Suz, Darba, and all the Algarbes, and its territories in Africa; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Sharif (or, as others write it, Xarif), that is, "successor, or vicegerent," of the great prophet Mohammed, &c." The judges or magistrates that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> immediately under him, are either spiritual or temporal, or rather ecclesiastic and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The mufti and the kadi are judges of all religious and civil affairs; and the bashas, governors, alcaldes, and other military officers, of those that concern the state or the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. All of them the most obsequious creatures and slaves of their prince, and no less the rapacious tyrants of his subjects, and from whom neither justice nor favour can be obtained but by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> dint of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and extortionate bribery, from the highest to the lowest. Neither can it indeed be otherwise in such an arbitrary government, where the highest posts must not only be bought of the prince at a most extravagant price, and kept only by an exorbitant tribute, which is yearly paid to him, but where no one is sure to continue longer than he can bribe some of the courtiers to insinuate to the monarch that he pays to the utmost of his power, and much beyond what was expected from him. Add to this, that those bashas, governors, &c. are obliged to keep their agents and spies in constant pay at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to prevent their being supplanted by higher bidders, flatterers, or other artful underminers. From what hath been said under this head, it may be reasonably concluded that this branch of the imperial revenue must be very considerable, though there is no possibility to make any other conjecture of its real amount, than that it must be an immense one. Another considerable branch is the piratical trade, which brings the greater income into his treasury, as he is not at any expense either for fitting of corsair vessels out, or maintaining their men: and yet hath the tenth of all the cargo, and of all the captives; besides which, he appropriates to himself all the rest of them, by paying the captors 50 crowns per head; by which means he engrosses all the slaves to his own service and advantage. This article is indeed a very considerable addition to his revenue, not only as he sells their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at a very high rate, but likewise as he hath the profit of all their labour, without allowing them any other maintenance than a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, nor any other assistance when sick than what medicines a Spanish convent, which he tolerates there, gives them gratis; and which, notwithstanding, is forced to pay him an annual present for that toleration, besides furnishing the court with medicines, and the slaves with lodging and diet when they are not able to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Another branch of his revenue consists in the tenth part of all cattle, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and other products of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is exacted of the Arabs and Berbers, as well as of the natives; and these are levied, or rather farmed, by the bashas, governors, alcaldes, &c. with all possible severity. The Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> likewise pay an income or capitation, the former of six crowns per head on all males from 15 years and upwards, besides other arbitrary imposts, fines, &c. That on the Christians, for the liberty of trading in his dominions, rises and falls according to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> they drive; but which, whatever it may bring yearly into his coffers, is yet detrimental to trade in general, seeing it discourages great numbers from settling there, notwithstanding the artful invitations which the emperors and their ministers make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to invite them to it; for, besides those arbitrary exactions, there is still another great hardship attending them, viz., that they cannot leave the country without forfeiting all their debts and effects to the crown. The duties on all imports and exports is another branch of his income, the amount of which, communibus annis, no author hath yet given us any account of; only <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HATFIELD">Hatfield</a> hath computed the whole yearly revenue, Morocco, venue, including ordinaries and extraordinaries, to amount to 500 quintals of silver, each quintal, or 100 lb. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, valued at somewhat above £30l. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>; so that the whole amounts to no more, according to him, than £65,000l.; a small revenue indeed for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> an empire, if the calculation may be depended upon. But St Olan, though he doth not pretend so much as to guess at the yearly amount of it, doth in general represent it as so considerable, that Muley Ishmael was reckoned to have amassed out of it a treasure in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver of about 50 effective millions; but whether of crowns or livres he doth not tell us, nor how he came by his knowledge of it; because that politic prince, even by his own confession, not only caused all his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to be buried in sundry places under-ground, his gold and silver to be melted into great lumps, and laid in the same privacy underground, but likewise all those whom he entrusted with the secret to be as privately murdered. However that be, we shall, upon the whole, have the least cause to wonder at these exorbitant exactions which he extorts from Christian princes and states, whenever they are obliged either to seek his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, or to obtain some redress in favour of their trading subjects; much less at the shameful delays, insults, extortions, indignities, and injustice, which their ambassadors must be content to put up with, to obtain the least favour from their rapacious ministers. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this country, though hot and dry, is pleasant and healthy, the winds from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and mount Atlas refreshing the inhabitants in the hottest season. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is neither so mountainous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, or barren, as many other parts of Africa; but produces, or would produce if duly cultivated, vast quantities of corn, wine, and oil. No country affords better wheat, barley, or rice: both the French and Spaniards fetch these from the Barbary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, when they have a scarcity at home; and our garrisons of Gibraltar and Port-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a> are often supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> from thence. The plains of Fez and Morocco are well planted with olives; and there are no better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> for making wine in the world, as the Jews at Tetuan <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; though the cultivation of vines is not encouraged among the Mahommedans, in consequence of the precept in the Koran, forbidding the drinking of wine. Here are also other fruits, as dates, figs, raisins, almonds, apples, pears, cherries, plums, citrons, lemons, oranges, pomegranates, with plenty of roots and herbs, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, honey, and wax; but they have not many forest-trees, and scarce any good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; possibly their soil is not proper for timber, or they take no care to preserve it, having little occasion for any. The animals of this part of Africa, whether wild or tame, are much the same we meet with to the southward; except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">elk</a>, the elephant, and the rhinoceros, which no travellers pretend to meet with in the empire of Morocco: and as they want these, so they have some others not to be found in the south of Africa, particularly camels, dromedaries, and that fine breed of horses called barbs, which for their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and swiftness can scarce be paralleled in the world. Nor are their horses to be admired only for their beauty and speed, but their use in war, being extremely ready to obey their riders upon the least sign, in charging, wheeling, or retiring; so that the trooper has his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> very much at liberty, and can make the best use of his arms. As to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the chief are that chain which goes under the name of Mount Atlas, and runs the whole length of Barbary from east to west, passing through Morocco, and abutting upon that ocean which separates the eastern from the western continent, and is from this mountain called the Atlantic Ocean. This mountain, as the poets feigned, sustained the universe; hence we see Atlas represented with the world upon his shoulders, and descriptions of the globe or sets of maps dignified with the name of Atlas. Dr Shaw, however, assures us, that this chain cannot stand in competition either with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> or Appennines for height. Near the Straits stands the mountain anciently called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYLA">Abyla</a>, and now, if we are not mistaken, by our countrymen styled the Aperill. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides the Malva or Mulvia above-mentioned, which rises in the deserts, and running from south to north divides Morocco from the kingdom of Algiers, are the Suz, Ommiribili, Rabbatta, Larache, Darodt, Sebon, Gueron, and Tensift, which rise in Mount Atlas, and fall into the Atlantic Ocean. The chief capes are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Threecorfs on the Mediterranean, Cape Spartel at the entrance of the straits, Cape Cantin, Cape None, and Cape Rajador, on the Atlantic Ocean. Of the bays the most considerable are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Tetuan in the Mediterranean, and the bay of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a> in the straits of Gibraltar. There are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of very fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> in this empire; but if there are any of gold and silver, as some writers tell us, they have never been opened, as far as we can find. The traffic of the empire by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> is either with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> or Negroland: to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> they send <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, consisting of several thousand camels, horses, and mules, twice every year, partly for traffic, and partly upon a religious account; for numbers of pilgrims take that opportunity of paying their devotions to their great prophet. The goods they carry to the east are woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, very fine Morocco skins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, and ostrich feathers; and they bring back from thence, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, muslins, and drugs. By their caravans to Negroland, they send <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, silk, and woollen manufactures, and bring back gold and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> in return, but chiefly negroes: for from hence it is that their emperor chiefly recruits his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cavalry, though there are also great numbers born in the country; for they bring those of both sexes very young from Negroland, the females for breeders, and the males for soldiers. As they grow up, they first carry a musket, and serve on foot, and after some time are preferred to be cavaliers: and as they have no other hopes or dependence but the favour of the emperor, they prove much the most dutiful and obsequious of all his subjects, and indeed support his tyranny over the rest. The caravans always go strong enough to defend themselves against the wild Arabs in the deserts of Africa and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; though, notwithstanding all their vigilance, some of the stragglers and baggage often fall... fall into their hands; they are also forced to load one half of their camels with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to prevent their perishing with drought and thirst in those inhospitable deserts. And there is still a more dangerous enemy, and that is the sand itself; when the winds rise, the caravan is perfectly blinded with dust; and there have been instances both in Africa and Asia, where whole caravans, and even armies, have been buried alive in the sands. There is no doubt also, but both men and cattle are sometimes surprized by wild beasts, as well as robbers, in those vast deserts; the hot winds also, blowing over a long tract of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sand, are equal almost to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of an oven, and destroy abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and pilgrims. If it was not for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of very great gains, no man would undertake a journey in these deserts; great are the hazards and fatigues they must of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> undergo; but those that go to Mecca assure themselves of paradise if they die, and have uncommon honours paid them at home if they survive. People crowd to be taken into the eastern caravans; and the gold that is found in the south, make them no less eager to undertake that journey. The natives have hardly any trading vessels, but are seldom without some caravans. These, and European merchant-ships, bring them whatever they want from abroad; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen cloth, stuffs, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wrought and unwrought, arms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and the like; for which they take in return, copper, wax, hides, Morocco <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, (which is very fine) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, dates, almonds, and other fruits. The coins of this empire are a fluce, a blanquil, and ducat. The fluce is a small copper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, twenty whereof make a blanquil, of the value of two-pence Sterling. The blanquil is of silver, and the ducat of gold, not unlike that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and worth about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings. Both these pieces are so liable to be clipped and filed by the Jews, that the Moors always carry scales in their pockets to weigh them; and when they are found to be much diminished in their weight, they are recoined by the Jews, who are masters of the mint, by which they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a considerable profit; as they do also by exchanging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pieces for those that are full weight. Merchants accounts are kept in bounces, ten of which make a ducat; but in payments to the government, it is said they will reckon seventeen one-half for a ducat. With respect to religion, the inhabitants of Morocco are Mohammedans, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>; and have a mufti, or high-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who is also the supreme civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in all causes <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and civil. They have a great veneration for their hermits, and for idiots and madmen; as well as for those who by their tricks have got the reputation of wizards; all whom they look upon as inspired persons, and not only honour as saints while they live, but build tombs and chapels over them when dead; which places are not only devoutly visited by their devotees far and near, but are esteemed inviolable sanctuaries for all sorts of criminals, except in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Notwithstanding the natives are zealous Mohammedans, they allow foreigners the free and open protection of their religion, and their very slaves have their priests and chapels in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city, though it must be owned that the Christian slaves are here treated with the utmost cruelty. Here, as in all other Mohammedan countries, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">alcoran</a> and their comments upon it are their only written laws; and though in some instances their cadi's, and other civil magistrates, are controlled by the arbitrary determinations of their princes, bailiffs, generals, and military officers, yet the latter have generally a very great deference and regard for their laws. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>, theft, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, are commonly punished with death; and their punishments for other crimes, particularly those against the state, are very cruel; as impaling, dragging the prisoner through the streets at a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MULE">mule</a>'s heels, till all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is torn off; throwing him from a high tower upon iron hooks; hanging him upon hooks till he die; crucifying him against a wall; and, indeed, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of criminals is in a manner arbitrary. The emperor, or his bailiffs, frequently turn executioners; shoot the offender, or cut him to pieces with their own hands, or command others to do it in their presence. In regard to the character of the Moors, they are said to be a covetous inhospitable people, intent upon nothing but heaping up riches, to obtain which they will be guilty of the meanest things, and stick at no manner of fraud. The Arabs also, who are almost as numerous as the Moors, have always had the character of a pilfering <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. The people who inhabit the hills, and who have the least to do with the court and with traffic, are much the honestest people among them, and still retain a good share of liberty, the government using them rather as allies than subjects, lest they should entirely disown their authority. The Moors, however, with all their bad qualities, are observed to be very dutiful to their parents, their princes, and superiors. A plurality of wives is allowed here, as in other Mohammedan countries; nor do they confine themselves to women, but keep boys, as they do in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. The woman who commits adultery is punished with death; but it is not difficult for them to obtain a divorce, if ill used. The dead are carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> in their usual dress, the priests singing before them, La illa ill illa, Mahomet Rasul Allah, i.e. God is a great God, and Mahomet his prophet. The Moors, or natives of the country, are of much the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> as the Spaniards on the opposite shore; but such multitudes of negroes have been brought from Guinea, that you see almost as many black as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people, especially about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEQUINEZ">Mequinez</a>, where the court resides. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a Moor is a linen frock or shirt next his skin, a vest of silk or cloth tied with a sash, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of drawers, a loose coat, his arms bare to the elbow, as well as his legs, sandals or slippers on his feet, and sometimes people of condition wear buckles; they shave their heads, and wear a turban, which is never pulled off before their superiors, or in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; they express their reverence both to God and man by pulling off their slippers, which they leave at the door of the mosque or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; and, when they attend their prince in the city, they run bare-foot after him, if the streets are ever so dirty. Their turbans are of fine silk, or fine linen. The habit of the women is not very different from from that of the men, except that they wear a fine linen cloth or caul on their heads, instead of a turban, and their drawers are much larger and longer than the mens. The women also, when they go abroad, have a linen cloth over their faces, with holes in it for their eyes, like a mask. Morocco, the capital city of the kingdom of Morocco, in Barbary; seated in a very large plain, 250 miles south by west of Fez, 125 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, and 15 from Mount Atlas. It was surrounded by a strong wall, fortified with towers and some bulwarks, and encompassed with deep ditches. The number of houses were reckoned formerly to be 100,000, all with flat roofs; but they are now greatly diminished, inasmuch that the greatest part of the city is unoccupied. The irruptions and robberies of the Arabs hinder them from cultivating the lands about it, inasmuch that there is nothing but vines, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>-trees, and some other fruits. There were three temples or mosques in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, of a prodigious size; and the emperor's palace was so large, and took up so much ground, that it resembled a small city. A late traveller affirms, that the inhabitants now are not above 25,000, and that the houses go to ruin every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, without being rebuilt. This may happen partly from the removal of the court, which is now at Mequinez. W. Long. 6. 45. N. Lat. 30. 32. Morocco, or Turkey-leather. See Leather.

MOROCHTHUS

Pages 416-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an indurated clay called by us French chalk; serving tailors and others to mark with. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> esteemed it as an astringent, prescribing it in the colic, hemorrhages, and other fluxes.

MORON

Pages 416-416

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, seated in a pleasant fertile plain, and in the neighbourhood is a mine of precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. It is 30 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. N. Lat. 37. 0.

MORPETH

Pages 416-416

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The most remarkable particular concerning it is a story of its being reduced to ashes by its own inhabitants on the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> John in 1215, out of pure hatred to their monarch, that he might find no shelter there.

MORPHEUS

Pages 416-416

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, one of the ministers of Somnus. He caused sleepiness, and represented the forms of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>. Ovid styles him the kindest of the deities; and he is usually described in a recumbent posture, and crowned with poppies.

MORRERI

Pages 404-404

author of the Historical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, was born at Bargemont in Provence 1643. He learned <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Lyons. At 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he wrote a small piece, intitled Le Pays d'<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMOUR">Amour</a>; and a collection of the finest French poems, intitled Deux plaisirs de la Poésie. He learned Spanish and Italian; and translated out of Spanish into French, the book intitled La Perfection Chrétienne de Rodriguez. He then refined the Saints Lives to the purity of the French tongue. Being ordained <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, he preached at Lyons; and undertook, when he was but 30 years of age, a new Historical Dictionary, printed at Lyons in one vol. folio, 1673. But his continual labour impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; so that he died in 1680, aged 37. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume was published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and four more volumes have since been added. He left some other works behind him.

MORTALITY

Pages 416-416
or Bills of Mortality, properly denote lists of the persons who die in any place. See Annuities. Brief of MORTANCESTRY, in Scots law; anciently the ground of an action at the instance of an heir, in the special case where he had been excluded from the possession of his ancestor's estate by the superior, or other person pretending right.

MORTAR

Pages 416-416

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of lime and sand mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which serves as a cement, and is used by masons and bricklayers in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> walls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and brick. Under the article Cement, we have already given the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of mortar, as delivered by Mr Anderson; which hath now received a farther <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> by a recent discovery, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the lime is flaked, and the mortar made up with lime-water instead of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> water, the mortar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be much better. The reason of this is, that in common water, especially such as is drawn from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, there is always a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which, mingling with the mortar previous to its being used, spoils it by reducing the quicklime in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> to an inert calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> like chalk; but when it is built up in a perfectly caustic state, it attracts the air so slowly, that it hardens into a kind of stony <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> as hard as was the rock from whence the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> was taken. Mortar, a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> very useful for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of bodies, partly by percussion, and partly by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>. Mortars have the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. The matter intended to be pounded is to be put into them, and there it is to be struck and bruised by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> instrument called a pestle. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> given to the pestle ought to vary according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the substances to be pounded. Those which are easily broken, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> which are apt to fly out of the mortar, or which are hardened by the stroke of the pestle, require that this instrument should be moved circularly, rather by grinding or bruising, than by striking. Those substances which are softened by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> occasioned by rubbing and percussion, require to be pounded very slowly. Lastly, those which are very hard, and which are not capable of being softened, are easily pounded by repeated strokes of the pestle. They require no bruising but when they are brought to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness. But these things are better learnt by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and practice than by any directions. As mortars are instruments which are constantly used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, they ought to be kept of all sizes and materials; as of marble, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, glass, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, gritstone, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>. The nature of the substance to be pounded determines the choice of the kind of mortar. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and dissolving power of that substance are particularly to be attended to. As copper is a soft metal, soluble by almost all menstrums, and hurtful to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, good artists have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago prohibited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this metal. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inconveniences of pulverization in a mortar proceeds from the fine powder which rises abundantly from some substances during the operation. If these substances be precious, the loss will be considerable; and if they be injurious to health, they may hurt the operator. These inconveniences may be remedied, either by covering the mortar with a skin, in the middle of which is a hole, thro' which the pestle passes; or by moistening the matter with a little water, when this addition does not injure it; or, lastly, by covering the mouth and nose of the operator with a fine cloth, to exclude this powder. Some substances, as corrosive sublimate, arsenic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a>, euphorbium, &c. are so noxious, that all these precautions ought to be used, particularly when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of them is pounded. Large mortars ought to be fixed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that the mortar shall be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the middle of the operator. When the pestle is large and heavy, it ought to be suspended by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a> or chain fixed to a moveable pole, placed horizontally above the mortar: this pole considerably relieves the

MORTGAGE

Pages 416-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, (mortuum nadium, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dead-pledge,) is where a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> borrows of another a specific sum (e.g., 200 l.) and grants him an estate in fee, on condition that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he, the mortgagor, shall pay the mortgagee the said sum of 200 l. on a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, that then the mortgagor may re-enter on the estate so granted in pledge; or, as is now the more usual way, that the mortgagee shall reconvey the estate to the mortgagor: in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> which is so put in pledge, is by law, in case of nonpayment at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> limited, for ever dead and gone from the mortgagor; and the mortgagee's estate in the lands is then no longer conditional, but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>. But, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it continues conditional, that is, between the time of lending the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the time allotted for payment, the mortgagee is called tenant in mortgage. But as it was formerly a doubt, whether, by taking such estate in fee, it did not become liable to the wife's dower, and other incumbrances, of the mortgagee, (though that doubt has been long ago overruled by our courts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>), it therefore became usual to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> only a long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, by way of mortgage; with condition to be void on repayment of the mortgage-money: which course has been since <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, principally because on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the mortgagee such term becomes vested in his personal representatives, who alone are entitled in equity to receive the money <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a>, of whatever <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> the mortgage may happen to be. As soon as the estate is created, the mortgagee may immediately enter on the lands; but is liable to be dispossessed, upon performance of the condition by payment of the mortgage-money at the day limited. And therefore the usual way is to agree that the mortgagor shall hold the land till the day assigned for payment; when, in case of failure, whereby the estate becomes absolute, the mortgagee may enter upon it and take possession, without any possibility at law of being afterwards evicted by the mortgagor, to whom the land is now for ever dead. But here again the courts of equity interpose; and though a mortgage be thus forfeited, and the estate absolutely vested in the mortgagee at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, yet they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> consider the real value of the tenements compared with the sum borrowed. And if the estate be of greater value than the sum lent thereon, they will allow the mortgagor at any reasonable time to recall or redeem his estate; paying to the mortgagee his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and expenses: for otherwise, in strictness of law, an estate worth 1000 l. might be forfeited for non-payment of 100 l. or a less sum. This reasonable advantage, allowed to mortgagors, is called the equity of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and this enables a mortgagor to call on the mortgagee, who has possession of his estate, to deliver it back, and account for the rents and profits received, on payment of his whole debt and interest; thereby <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the mortuum into a kind of vivum nadium; (see Vadium). But, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the mortgagee may either compel the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the estate, in order to get the whole of his money immediately; or else call upon the mortgagor to redeem his estate presently, or, in default thereof, to be for ever foreclosed from redeeming the same; that is, to lose his equity of redemption without possibility of recall. And also, in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of fraudulent mortgages, the fraudulent mortgagor forfeits all equity of redemption whatsoever. It is not, however, usual for mortgagees to take possession of the mortgaged estate, unless where the security is precarious, or small; or where the mortgagor neglects even the payment of interest: when the mortgagee is frequently obliged to bring an ejectment, and take the land into his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, in the nature of a pledge, or the pignus of the Roman law: whereas, while it remains in the hands of the mortgagor, it more resembles their hypotheca, which was where the possession of the thing pledged remained with the debtor. But, by statute 7 Geo. II. c. 20, after payment or tender by the mortgagor of principal, interest, and costs, the mortgagee can maintain no ejectment; but may be compelled to re-align his securities. In Glanvil's time, when the universal method of conveyance was by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> of seizin or corporal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the lands, no gage or pledge of lands was good unless possession was also delivered to the creditor; si non sequatur ipsius cadui traditio, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> dominis regis baiulam praetor conveniunt tueri non solent: for which the reason given is, to prevent subsequent and fraudulent pledges of the same land; cum in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALI">tali</a> caesi positis cadum res pluribus aliis creditoribus tum primum tum posterium invadantur. And the frauds which have arisen, since the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of these public and notorious conveyances for more private and secret bargains, have well evinced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law.

MORTIER

Pages 417-417

an ensign of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, borne by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> presidents of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of France. That borne by the chancellor is a piece of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, edged and turned up with ermine; and that of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> is a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> velvet edged with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row of gold <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, while that of the other presidents is only edged with a single row. They formerly carried on their heads, as they still do in grand ceremonies, such as the entry of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; but ordinarily they carry them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

MORTISE

Pages 417-417
or Mortoise, in carpentry, &c. a kind of joint wherein a hole of a certain depth is made in a piece of timber, which is to receive another piece called a tenon.

MORTMAIN

Pages 417-418
or Alienation in Mortmain, (in mortua manu,) is an alienation of lands or tenements to any corporation, sole or aggregate, ecclesiastical or temporal: but these purchases having been chiefly made by religious houses, in consequence whereof the lands became perpetually inhered in one dead hand, this hath occasioned the general appellation of mortmain to be applied to such alienations, and the religious houses themselves to be principally considered in forming the statutes of mortmain: in deducing the history of which statutes, it will be matter of curiosity to observe the great address and subtle contrivance of the ecclesiastics in eluding from time to time the laws in being, and the zeal with which successive parliaments have pursued them through all their finesse: how new remedies were still the parents of new evasions; till the legislature at last, though with difficulty, hath Mortmain hath obtained a decisive victory. By the common law any man might dispose of his lands to any other private man at his own discretion, especially when the feudal restraints of alienation were worn away. Yet in consequence of these it was always, and is still necessary, for corporations to have a licence of mortmain from the crown, to enable them to purchase lands: for as the king is the ultimate lord of every fee, he ought not, unless by his own consent, to lose his privilege of escheats and other feudal profits, by the vesting of lands in tenants that can never be attainted or die. And such licences of mortmain seem to have been necessary among the Saxons, above 60 years before the Norman conquest. But, besides this general licence from the king as lord paramount of the kingdom, it was also requisite, whenever there was a mesne or intermediate lord between the king and the alienor, to obtain his licence also (upon the same feudal principles) for the alienation of the specific land. And if no such licence was obtained, the king or other lord might respectively enter on the lands so alienated in mortmain, as a forfeiture. The necessity of this licence from the crown was acknowledged by the constitutions of Clarendon, in respect of advowsons, which the monks always greatly coveted, as being the groundwork of subsequent appropriations. Yet such were the influence and ingenuity of the clergy, that notwithstanding this fundamental principle we find that the largest and most considerable donations of religious houses happened within less than two centuries after the conquest. And (when a licence could not be obtained) their contrivance seems to have been this: That as the forfeiture for such alienations accrued in the first place to the immediate lord of the fee, the tenant who meant to alienate first conveyed his lands to the religious house, and instantly took them back again to hold as tenant to the monastery; which kind of instantaneous seisin was probably held not to occasion any forfeiture: and then, by pretext of some other forfeiture, surrender, or escheat, the society entered into those lands in right of such their newly acquired signory, as immediate lords of the fee. But when these donations began to grow numerous, it was observed that the feudal services, ordained for the defence of the kingdom, were every day visibly withdrawn; that the circulation of landed property from man to man began to flagitate; and that the lords were curtailed of the fruits of their signories, their escheats, wardships, reliefs, and the like: and therefore, in order to prevent this, it was ordained by the second of king Henry III.'s great charters, and afterwards by that printed in our common statute-books, that all such attempts should be void, and the land forfeited to the lord of the fee. But as this prohibition extended only to religious houses, bishops and other sole corporations were not included therein; and the aggregate ecclesiastical bodies (who, Sir Edward Coke observes, in this were to be commended, that they ever had of their counsel the best learned men that they could get) found many means to creep out of this statute, by buying in lands that were bona fide holden of themselves as lords of the fee, and thereby evading the forfeiture; or by taking long leases for years, which first introduced those extensive terms, for a thousand or more years, which are now frequent in conveyances. This produced the statute Mortmain de religiosis, 7 Edward I.; which provided, that no person, religious or other whatsoever, should buy, or sell, or receive, under pretence of a gift, or term of years, or any other title whatsoever, nor should by any art or ingenuity appropriate to himself any lands or tenements in mortmain; upon pain that the immediate lord of the fee, or, on his default for one year, the lords paramount, and, in default of all of them, the king, might enter thereon as a forfeiture. This seemed to be a sufficient security against all alienations in mortmain: but as these statutes extended only to gifts and conveyances between the parties, the religious houses now began to set up a fictitious title to the land, which it was intended they should have, and to bring an action to recover it against the tenant; who, by fraud and collusion, made no defence, and thereby judgment was given for the religious house, which then recovered the land by a sentence of law upon a supposed prior title. And thus they had the honour of inventing those fictitious adjudications of right, which are since become the great assurance of the kingdom, under the name of common recoveries. But upon this the statute of Westminster the second, 13 Edw. I. c. 32., enacted, that in such cases a jury shall try the true right of the demandants or plaintiffs to the land; and if the religious house or corporation be found to have it, they shall still recover seisin; otherwise it shall be forfeited to the immediate lord of the fee, or else to the next lord, and finally to the king, upon the immediate or other lord's default. And the like provision was made by the succeeding chapter, in case the tenants set up crosses upon their lands (the badges of knights templars and hospitallers) in order to protect them from the feudal demands of their lords, by virtue of the privileges of those religious and military orders. And so careful was this provident prince to prevent any future evasions, that when the statute of quia emptores, 18 Edward I., abolished all sub-feudations, and gave liberty for all men to alienate their lands to be holden of their next immediate lord, a proviso was inserted that this should not extend to authorize any kind of alienation in mortmain. And when afterwards the method of obtaining the king's licence by writ of ad quod damnum was marked out, by the statute 27 Edward I. ft. 2., it was farther provided by statute 34 Edward I. ft. 3., that no such licence should be effectual without the consent of the mesne or intermediate lords. Yet still it was found difficult to set bounds to ecclesiastical ingenuity: for when they were driven out of all their former holds, they devised a new method of conveyance, by which the lands were granted, not to themselves directly, but to nominal feoffees to the use of the religious houses; thus distinguishing between the possession and the use, and receiving the actual profits, while the seisin of the land remained in the nominal feoffee; who was held by the courts of equity (then under the direction of the clergy) to be bound in conscience to account to his feoffee for the rents and emoluments of the estate. And it is to these inventions that our practisers are indebted for the introduction of uses and trusts, the foundation of modern conveyancing. But, unfortunately for the inventors themselves, they did not long enjoy

MORTON

Pages 418-419

a learned English bishop in the 17th century, was bred at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and was logic-lecturer of the university. After several preferments he was advanced to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> in 1615; and translated to that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a> in 1618: at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he became acquainted with Antonio de Dominis archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>, whom he endeavoured to dissuade from returning to Rome. While he was bishop of Litchfield and Coventry, in which see he sat 14 years, he educated, ordained, and presented to a living, a youth of excellent parts and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, who was born <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>; and detected the imposture of the famous boy of Bilston in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, who pretended to be possessed with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. In 1632 he was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, in which he sat with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation till the opening of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which met in 1640; when he received great insults from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, and was committed twice to custody. The parliament, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of bishoprics, voted him £800 per annum, of which he received but a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>. He died in 1659, in the 95th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and 44th of his episcopal consecration. He published Apologia Catholicæ, and several other works; and was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of extensive learning, great piety, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>.

MORTUARY

Pages 419-420

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> heriot*, being a customary gift claimed by and due to the minister in very many parishes on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his parishioners. They seem originally to have been only a voluntary bequest to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; being intended, as Lyndewode informs us from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of archbishop Langham, as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> and amends to the clergy for the personal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, and other ecclesiastical duties, which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> might have neglected <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> forgotten to pay. For this purpose, after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s heriot or best good was taken out, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> best chattel was referred to the church as a mortuary. And therefore in the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Canute this mortuary is called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>-feast, or symbolum animæ. And, in pursuance of the same principle, by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where no personal tithes have been paid du- MOR <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> the life of the party, they are paid at his death out of his merchandise, jewels, and other moveables. So also, by a similar policy, in France, every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> that died without bequeathing a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his estate to the church, which was called dying without confession, was formerly deprived of Christian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he died intestate, the relations of the deceased, jointly with the bishop, named proper arbitrators to determine what he ought to have given to the church, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> he had made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in 1409, redressed this grievance. It was anciently usual in England to bring the mortuary to church along with the corpse when it came to be buried; and thence it is sometimes called a corse-present: a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> which bespeaks it to have been once a voluntary donation. However, in Bracton's time, so early as Henry III., we find it riveted into an established <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>: insomuch that the bequests of heriots and mortuaries were held to be necessary ingredients in every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> of chattels. Insprimit autem debet quilibet, qui testamentum fecerit, dominum suum de meliori re quam habuerit recognoscere; et postea ecclesiam de alia meliori: the lord must have the best good left him as an heriot; and the church the second best as a mortuary. But yet this custom was different in different places: in quibusdam locis habet ecclesia melius animal de confestitudine; in quibusdam secundum, vel tertium melius; et in quibusdam nihil: et idem conferenda est confestudo loci. This custom still varies in different places, not only as to the mortuary to be paid, but the person to whom it is payable. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> a mortuary or corse-present was due upon the death of every clergyman to the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; till abolished, upon a recompense given to the bishop, by the statute 12 Ann. st. 2. c. 6. And in the archdeaconry of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> a custom also prevailed, that the bishop, who is also archdeacon, should have, at the death of every clergyman dying therein, his best <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or mare, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, saddle, and spurs, his best <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> or cloak, hat, upper garment under his gown, and tippet, and also his best <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a> or ring. But by statute 28 Geo. II. c. 6. this mortuary is directed to cease, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> has settled upon the bishop an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> in its room. The king's claim to many goods, on the death of all prelates in England, seems to be of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; though Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> apprehends, that this is a duty upon death, and not a mortuary: a distinction which seems to be without a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. For not only the king's ecclesiastical character, as supreme ordinary, but also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the goods claimed, which bear so near a resemblance to those in the archdeaconry of Chester, which was an acknowledged mortuary, puts the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> out of dispute. The king, according to the record vouched by Sir Edward Coke, is entitled to fix things; the bishop's best horse or palfrey, with his furniture; his cloak or gown, and tippet; his cup and cover; his basinet and ewer; his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> ring; and lastly, his muta canum, his mew or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a> of hounds. This variety of customs with regard to mortuaries, giving frequently a handle to exactions on the one side, and frauds or expensive litigations on the other, it was thought proper by statute 21 Henry VIII. c. 6. to reduce them to some kind of certainty. For this purpose it is enacted, that all mortuaries, or corse-presents to parsons of any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, shall be taken in the following manner, unless where by custom less or none at all is due: viz. for every person who does not leave goods to the value of ten marks, nothing: for every person who leaves goods to the value of ten marks and under 30 pounds, 3l. 4d. if above 30 pounds, and under 40 pounds, 6l. 8d. if above 40 pounds, of what value forever they may be, 10l. and no more. And no mortuary shall throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> be paid for the death of any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>; nor for any child; nor for any one of full <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that is not a housekeeper; nor for any wayfaring man; but such wayfaring man's mortuary shall be paid in the parish to which he belongs. And upon this statute stands the law of mortuaries to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

MORUS

Pages 420-421

the mulberry-tree; a genus of the tetrandria order, belonging to the monocota class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The nigra, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-fruited mulberry-tree. It rises with an upright, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rough <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, dividing into a large, branchy, and very spreading head, rising 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, or more; large, heart-shaped, rough leaves, and monoecious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; succeeded in the females by large succulent black-berries. There is a variety with jagged leaves and smaller fruit. This species is the proper mulberry-tree for general cultivation in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for its fruit; the tree being a plentiful bearer, and the fruit <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in good perfection in August and September. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> mulberry-tree, rises with an upright trunk, branching 20 or 30 feet high; garnished with large, oblique, heart-shaped, smooth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-green, shining leaves, and monoecious flowers, succeeded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>-whitish fruit. There is a variety with purple fruit. 3. The papaverifera, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> mulberry-tree of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, grows 20 or 30 feet high, with large palmated leaves, some trilobate, others quinqulobed, and monoecious flowers, succeeded by small black fruit. In the countries where this tree grows naturally, the inhabitants make paper of the bark. 4. The rubra, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> mulberry-tree, grows 30 feet high, with very large, heart-shaped, rough leaves, hairy underneath, and monoecious flowers, succeeded by large reddish berries. All these trees are very hardy, and succeed in any common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation. The black mulberry is the only sort proper to cultivate as a fruit-tree for its fruit; the others are principally employed here to form variety in our ornamental plantations, of which the white and paper mulberry are the most common, the red sort being very scarce in the English gardens; the black and the white-fruited kinds are also eminent for their leaves to feed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, they being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of these valuable insects; but the white mulberry-leaves are in the most esteem for this purpose; and abroad, in France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, &c. vast plantations of the trees are made solely for their leaves to feed silk-worms, which amply reward the possessors with the annual supply of silk they spin from their bowels: plantations of the same trees has formerly been recommended in this country for the purpose of silk-worms, to introduce the manufacturing of raw silk, since it is observable that where the trees thrive, the silk-worms <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> also prosper; all recommendations, however, have proved fruitless, although it. The leaves of these trees are generally late before they begin to come out; the buds seldom beginning to open till the middle or towards the latter end of May, according to the temperature of the season; and when these trees in particular begin to expand their foliage, it is a good sign of the near approach of fine warm settled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; the white mulberry, however, is generally forwarder in leafing than the black. The flowers and fruit come out soon after the leaves; the males in *amentum*, and the females in small roundish heads; neither of which are very conspicuous, nor possess any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, but for observation; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or fruitful flowers always rise on the extremity of the young shoots, on short spurs; and with this singularity, the calyxes of the flowers become the fruit; which is of the berry kind, and being composed of many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>, each of these furnishes one seed. The fruit ripens here gradually from about the middle of August until the middle of September; which in dry warm seasons ripen in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection; but when it proves very wet weather they ripen but indifferently, and prove devoid of flavour. Considered as fruit-trees, the black-fruited kind is the only proper sort to cultivate, the trees being not only the most plentiful bearers in this country, but the fruit are larger and much finer-flavoured than the white kind, which is the only sort, besides the black mulberry, that bears fruit in this country.

MOSAIC

Pages 421-422
or Mosaic-work, an assemblage of little pieces of glass, marble, precious stones, &c. of various colours, cut square, and cemented on a ground of stucco, in such a manner as to imitate the colours and gradations of painting. The critics are divided as to the origin and reason of the name. Some derive it from *mosaicum*, a corruption of *musaicum*, as that is of *musaicum*, as it was called among the Romans. Scaliger derives it from the Greek *μασίς*, and imagines the name was given to this sort of works as being very fine and ingenious. Nebricius is of opinion it was so called, because *ex illis picturis eramabantur mosiaci*. 1. Method of performing Mosaic-work of glass is this: They provide little pieces of glass, of as many different colours and sizes as possible. Now, in order to apply these several pieces, and out of them to form a picture, they in the first place procure a cartoon or design to be drawn; this is transferred to the ground or plaster by calking, as in painting in fresco. See Fresco. As this plaster is to be laid thick on the wall, and therefore will continue fresh and soft a considerable time, so there may be enough prepared at once to serve for as much work as will take up three or four days. This plaster is composed of lime, made of hard stone, with brick-dust very fine, gum tragacanth, and whites of eggs: when this plaster has been thus prepared and laid on the wall, and made the design of what is to be represented, they take out the little pieces of glass with a pair of pliers, and range them one after another, still keeping strictly to the light, shadow, different tints, and colours, represented in the design before; pressing or flattening them down with a ruler, which serves both to sink them within the ground, and to render the surface even. Thus in a long time, and with a great deal of labour, they finish the work, which is still the more beautiful, as the pieces of glass are more uniform, and ranged at an even height. Some of these pieces of mosaic-work are performed with that exactness, that they appear as smooth as a table of marble, and as finished and masterly as a painting in fresco; with this advantage, that they have a fine lustre, and will last ages. The finest works of this kind that have remained till our time, and those by whom the moderns have retrieved the art, which was in a manner lost, are those in the church of St Agnes, formerly the temple of Bacchus, at Rome; and some at Pisa, Florence, and other cities of Italy. The most esteemed among the works of the moderns are those of Joseph Pine and the Chevalier Lanfranc, in the church of St Peter at Rome; there are also very good ones at Venice. 2. Method of performing Mosaic-work of marble and precious stones is this: The ground of Mosaic-works, wholly marble, is usually a massive marble, either white or black. On this ground the design is cut with a chisel, after it has been first calked. After it has been cut of a considerable depth, i.e., an inch or more, the cavities are filled up with marble of a proper colour, first fashioned according to the design, and reduced to the thickness of the indentures with various instruments. To make the piece thus inserted into the indentures cleave fast, whose several colours are to imitate those of the design, they use a stucco, composed of lime and marble-dust; or a kind of mastic, which is prepared by each workman, after a different manner peculiar to himself. The figures being marked out, the painter or sculptor himself draws with a pencil the colours of the figures not determined by the ground, and in the same manner makes strokes or hatchings in the place where shadows are to be; and after he has engraved with the chisel all the strokes thus drawn, he fills them up with a black mastic, composed partly of Burgundy-pitch poured on hot; taking off afterwards what is superfluous with a piece of soft stone or brick, which, together with water and beaten cement, takes away the mastic, polishes the marble, and renders the whole so even that one would imagine it only consisted of one piece.
