This is the kind of Mosaic-work that is seen in the pompous church of the invalids at Paris, and the fine chapel at Versailles, with which some entire apartments of that palace are incrustated. As for Mosaic-work of precious stones, other and finer instruments are required than those used in marble; as drills, wheels, &c. used by lapidaries and engravers on stone. As none but the richest marbles and stones enter this work, to make them go the farther, they are fawn into the thinnest leaves imaginable, scarce exceeding half a line in thickness; the block to be fawn is fastened firmly with cords on the bench, and only raised a little on a piece of wood, one or two inches high. Two iron pins, which are on one side the block, and which serve to fasten it, are put into a vice contrived. Mosaic—contrived for the purpose; and with a kind of saw or bow, made of fine brass-wire, bent on a piece of spongy wood, together with emery steeped in water, the leaf is gradually fashioned by following the stroke of the design, made on paper, and glued on the piece. When there are pieces enough fastened to form an entire flower, or some other part of the design, they are applied to the ground. The ground which supports this Mosaic-work is usually of free-stone. The matter with which the stones are joined together, is a mastic, or kind of stucco, laid very thin on the leaves as they are fashioned; and this being done, the leaves are applied with pliers. If any contour, or side of a leaf, be not either squared or rounded sufficiently, so as to fit the place exactly into which it is to be inserted, when it is too large, it is to be brought down with a brass file or rasp; and if it be too little, it is managed with a drill and other instruments used by lapidaries. Mosaic-work of marble is used in large works, as in pavements of churches, basilicas, and palaces; and in the incrustation and vancing of the walls of the same edifices. As for that of precious stones, it is only used in small works, as ornaments for altar-pieces, tables for rich cabinets, precious stones being so very dear. 3. Manner of performing Mosaic-work of gypsum. Of this stone calcined in a kiln, beaten in a mortar, and sifted, the French workmen make a sort of artificial marbles, imitating precious stones; and of these they compose a kind of Mosaic-work, which does not come far short either of the durability or the vivacity of the natural stones; and which besides has this advantage, that it admits of continued pieces or paintings of entire compartments without any visible joining. Some make the ground of plaster of Paris, others of free stone. If it be of plaster of Paris, they spread it in a wooden frame, of the length and breadth of the work intended, and in thickness about an inch and a half. This frame is to contrive, that the tenons being only joined to the mortises by single pins, they may be taken asunder, and the frame be dismounted, when the plaster is dry. The frame is covered on one side with a strong linen-cloth, nailed all round, which being placed horizontally with the linen at the bottom, is filled with plaster passed through a wide sieve. When the plaster is half dry, the frame is set up perpendicularly, and left till it is quite dry; then it is taken out, by taking the frame to pieces. In this mosaic, the ground is the most important part. Now in order to the preparation of this sifted gypsum, which is to be applied on this ground, it is dissolved and boiled in the best English glue, and mixed with the colour that it is to be of; then the whole is worked up together into the usual consistence of plaster, and then is taken and spread on the ground five or six inches thick. If the work be such, as that mouldings are required, they are formed with gouges and other instruments. It is on this plaster, thus coloured like marble or precious stone, and which is to serve as a ground to a work, either of lapis, agate, alabaster, or the like, that the design to be represented is drawn; having been first pounced or calqued. To hollow or impress the design, they use the same instruments that sculptors do; the ground whereon they are to work not being much less hard than the marble itself. The cavities being thus made in the ground, are filled with the same gypsum boiled in glue, only differently coloured, and thus are the different colours of the original represented. In order that the necessary colours and tints may be ready at hand, the quantities of the gypsum are tempered with the several colours in pots. After the design has been thus filled and rendered visible, by half-polishing it with brick and soft stone, they go over it again, cutting such plates as are either to be weaker or more shadowed, and filling them with gypsum; which work they repeat, till all the colours being added one after the other, represent the original to the life. When the work is finished, they scour it with soft stone, sand, and water; after that, with a pumice-stone; and in the last place polish it with a wooden mullet and emery. Then, lastly, they gave it a lustre, by smearing it over with oil, and rubbing it a long time with the palm of the hand, which gives it a lustre no ways inferior to that of natural marble.

MOSAMBIQUE

Pages 422-422

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying south of Quilon, and taking its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, which is situated on an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, at the mouth of a river of the same name, in 15° S. Lat. The island is thirty miles in circumference, and very populous, though the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be very hot, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general dry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and barren; yet they have most of the tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, hogs, and sheep. There is a kind of fowl here, both the feathers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which are black, inasmuch that, when they are boiled, the broth looks like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INK">ink</a>; and yet their flesh is very delicate, and good food. The town of Mosambique is regularly fortified, and has a good harbour, defended by a citadel, with several churches and monasteries. The Portuguese shipping to and from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> touch here for refreshments. As the island abounds in cattle, the Portuguese slaughter and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> up a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of beef, which they afterwards send to the Brazils, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sell to the European shipping. They also <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> European goods with the natives for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, elephant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and slaves. There is another town, called Mongale, situated also on an island, and garrisoned by the Portuguese, being their chief <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for European goods. The gold they receive from the natives is found near the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; no gold-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, or at least very few, being at present wrought in Africa.

MOSCHUS

Pages 422-423

as well as Bion to have lived later than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, upon the authority of Suidas; while others again suppose him to have been the scholar of Bion, and probably his successor in governing the poetic school; which, from the elogy of Moschus, does not seem unlikely. Their remains are to be found in all the editions of the Poetica minores. Moschus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> of the order of pecora, having no horns; the canine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the upper jaw are foliary and exerted. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The moschiferus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a> animal, hath been considered by some authors as a stag, a roebuck, a goat; and by others as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cherrontain, a species of antelope; but M. Buffon hath determined it to be an ambiguous animal, partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of all these, but differing effectually from every one of them, and from all other animals. It is of the size of a small roebuck, but has no horns; it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> coarse <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, a sharp muzzle, and tusks like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>. From the nose to the tail, the animal is about a yard and half a foot long; the head above half a foot; the neck is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a yard; the fore-head three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the nose end scarce three-fourths of an inch, being very sharp, like that of a greyhound. The ears are like those of a rabbit, about three inches long, and erect; as is also the tail, which exceeds not two inches; the fore-legs are a foot and two inches long, taking in the foot and thigh. The foot is deeply cloven; with two fore-hoofs, an inch and a quarter long, each a quarter of an inch over; and two heels almost as big, and therefore conspicuous. The hair on the head and legs is about half an inch long, and rather small; on the belly it is an inch and an half in length, and somewhat thicker; on the back and buttocks it is three inches long, thicker in proportion than in any other animal, excepting perhaps some of the deer-kind, viz. three or four times as thick as hog's bristles; consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> portions alternately from the root to the top. On the head and legs it is brown; on the belly, and under the tail, whitish, and as it were frizzled, especially on the back and belly, by a kind of undulation. The hair of the mink is softer than in most animals, and exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and rare; for, being split, they appear to be made up of little bladder-like those in the plumage or stalk of a quill; so that it is something betwixt a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hair and a quill. On each side of his lower chops, almost under the corner of his mouth, there is a peculiar tuft, (about three-fourths of an inch long), of short, thick, and hard hairs, or rather bristles, of equal length, as in a scrubbing-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The musk-bladder or bag which holds the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>, is on the belly near the navel. It is about three inches long, and two over; standing out from the belly one and a half, and before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROIN">groin</a> as much. The creature hath 26 teeth, 16 in the lower chop; of which there are eight little cutters before; behind four grinders on each side, rugged and continuous, with as many grinders in the upper jaw. About an inch and an half from the nose end in the same jaw, is on each side a tuft two inches and an half long, hooked downward and backward, and ending in a point. This tuft is not round, but flat; the breadth of half an inch; thin, and having a sharp edge behind; so that it hath a considerable resemblance of a scythe.—From the testimony of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of travellers it appears that the perfume is produced only in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> hath indeed a pouch of the same kind near the navel, but the humour secreted in it has not the same odour; and this tumour of the male is not filled with musk except in the rutting season; at other times the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of this humour is smaller, and its odour weaker. See Musc. 2. The grimmia, grimm, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> antelope, is a most beautiful animal, with stout <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> horns, slender and sharp-pointed, not three inches long, and slightly annulated at the base. Its height is about 18 inches; the ears are large, and the eyes dusky; below the eyes is a large cavity, into which exudes a strong-scented oily liquid; between the horns is a tuft of black hair. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the neck and body is brown, mixed with an ash-colour, and a tinge of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; the belly is white; the tail short, white beneath, and black above. M. Volfmaer tells us, that these animals are extremely timid, and easily frightened with any noise, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>; when surprised, they express their fear by blowing suddenly and with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force through their noses. He describes one which was kept in the menagerie of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. "This one (says he) was at first wild, but afterwards became pretty tame. It listens when called by its name Tofes; and when gently approached with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it allows its head and neck to be stroked. It is so cleanly, that it suffers not the smallest particle of dirt to remain on any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of its body; and for this purpose it often scratches itself with one of its hind-feet. This is the reason why it has received the appellation of teftes, from teftes, which signifies neat or clean. However, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person continues for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to rub its body, a white powder adheres to his fingers like that which proceeds from horses when they are curried. This animal is extremely agile; and, when reposting, it frequently keeps one of its fore-feet in an elevated and bended position, which gives it a very agreeable appearance. It is fed with bread, rye, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>; it likewise spontaneously eats potatoes; it is a ruminating animal, and discharges its excrements in small balls, the size of which is considerable in proportion to the magnitude of the creature."—Dr. Herman Grimm tells us, that the fat, viscid, yellow humour, which is secreted in the cavities above the eyes of this animal, has an odour that participates of musk and causticum; but M. Volfmaer remarks, that in his live subject this viscid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> has no odour of any kind. 3. The pygmaeus has feet narrower than a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s finger, and is found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>.

MOSCOW

Pages 423-425

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of Russia, deriving its name from the river Moikva, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Molka, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is situated. It was from this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> that the czars of old took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dukes of Moscow. The province is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchies of Tver, Roitow, Sudfal, and Wodlomir; on the south by Rezan, from which it is separated by the river Occa; on the east by the principality of Cachein, and the same river Occa parting it from Nifinovgorod; and on the west by the duchies of Rzeva, Biela, and Smolensko. It extends about 200 miles in length, and about 100 in breadth; and... Moscow is watered by the Moskva, Occa, and Clefma, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Wolga; nevertheless, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is not very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, however, though sharp, is salubrious; and this consideration, with the advantage of its being situated in the midst of the best provinces in the empire, induced the czars to make it their chief residence. In the western <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Moscow is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forest, from whence flows the celebrated river Nieper, or Borysthenes, which, traversing the duchy of Smolensko, winds in a serpentine course to Ukrainia, Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. The capital, Moscow, or Moskova, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> and largest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Russian empire, situated in a spacious plain on the banks of the river Moskova; over which the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Gafichin built a stately <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, consisting of 12 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of prodigious height, breadth, and solidity, because the river is so apt to overflow its banks: it was designed by a Polish monk, and is the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-bridge in all Russia. Moscow is seated on a wholesome gravelly soil, and divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, each surrounded with a distinct wall. These districts are known by the names of Cataigorod, Czarigorod, Skorodum, and Streletz-faboda. The Cataigorod, surrounded with a brick-wall, is the middle of the city; in which stands the citadel, about two miles in circuit, fortified with a triple wall, flanked with towers and a fosse. It contains two imperial palaces, the one of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and the other of stone, built after the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; the patriarchal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which is a large <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> edifice; the exchequer, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and other offices; two noble monasteries; five large churches, including that of St Michael, famous for its fabric and ornaments, as well as for the monuments of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> dukes and czars who have been here interred; the grand <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, and many other stately buildings. Without the citadel-gate stands that noble edifice the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, finished by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> John Basilides, who ordered the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> to be deprived of his eye-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that he might never contrive, or at least behold, its equal. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> market that fronts the citadel we see the stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, supposed to be the largest in the whole world. It was hung in a tower built for the purpose, which tower was consumed by fire in the beginning of the present century. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the bell amounts to 336,000 pounds. It is in height 19 feet, in diameter 23, in circumference 70, and the sides are two feet in thickness. One hundred men were employed in moving this monstrous machine, which was only rung on extraordinary occasions: for example, when the Czar condescended to show himself to his people, and when he conversed with his wife, that the subjects might know when to petition heaven that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> child should be the issue of the conjugal embrace. This district is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Negliga and Moskva; and is called Cataigorod, from catai, the Russian name for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, because here the merchandises of that empire are chiefly sold. The Czarigorod, or ducal city, encompassed the Cataigorod, and is itself fortified with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-flower wall, called Bielagena; whence it has acquired the appellation of Bielagored, or the white city. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is the great arsenal. The Skorodum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> stands to the north-west of the Czarigorod; and is chiefly inhabited by timber-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and carpenters, who fell wooden houses ready made. It is surrounded with a mud-wall, and distinguished by the name of Moscow, Scordum, which signifies done in haste; because, on an alarm from the Tartars, it was finished in four days, tho' it is 15 miles in circuit, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is everywhere supported by planks and beams of timber. It is absolutely necessary that there should be such a magazine of houses ready made, to supply the loss of those that perish almost every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> by conflagrations, owing to the carelessness, rage, and intoxication, of the inhabitants. On the east and south-east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> of the Cataigorod and citadel stands the Streletz-fabodo, so called from the guards of that name, who were formerly lodged in this quarter, which is fortified with wooden ramparts, and divided from the other parts of the city by the river Moskva. The houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> are no better than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> wooden huts, without neatness and furniture: but the merchants secure their commodities in vaults of stone or brick, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the accidents of fire. There are 3000 stone or brick houses in the city of Moscow; but they stand at such distances from one another, are so intermingled with rows of wooden houses, and such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them stand detached from, and as it were behind the streets, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls, that the effect of them is almost lost in the general prospect. The streets, instead of being paved with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, are boarded with fir-planks; so that in conflagrations the ground seems to burn, and it becomes impossible to approach the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of disaster. Among the churches and chapels of this city, which are said to amount in number to 1500, that in the Kremlin, or palace of the citadel, is a very ancient and remarkable edifice. On the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> side of the altar is the Czar's throne, and on the left is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>. The body of the church is lighted by a silver chandelier of immense weight and value. The jewels and ornaments belonging to an image of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> are valued at half a ton weight in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; but ineffable is the value of an infinite number of chalices, pixes, patens, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and other church-utensils of gold and silver, curiously wrought and enriched with precious stones, a prodigious number of rich priestly vestments, besides innumerable donations, and presents offered to the relics of three eminent Russian saints interred in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In a word, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> contained in this church is said to equal, at least, that of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Hard by the church of St Michael, which we have mentioned above, is the stately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of nuns, called trudofmonaster: here the bodies of the princesses of the blood are interred; and in a separate chapel we see the tombs of those princes who never ascended the throne. Nothing can be more rich and magnificent than the palls with which their coffins are covered on holidays. Of the several monasteries that appear in Moscow and its neighbourhood, the most remarkable is the Deiwitz-monaster, about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the city, where <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> confined his ambitious foster the princess Sophia, who had hatched so many conspiracies against his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, which is situated in an extensive plain, contains 300 nuns, who are kept under severe restrictions, contrary to the freedom with which other Muscovite nuns are indulged. The only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> these enjoy is in holiday-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, when they are permitted to walk on the terraces of the garden, which overlook Peter the Great founded at Moscow three colleges, and selected for them able professors. In the first they taught <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and in the third, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. To these colleges he added a dispensatory, which is one of the noblest structures in Moscow, completely furnished with all sorts of drugs and medicines, under the care of some Germans well skilled in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. The yearly revenue of this dispensatory amounts to 2000 rubles, allotted for fresh supplies of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>; and from hence not only the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, but likewise all the chief cities of the empire, are furnished. The courts of judicature, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, goals, and other public edifices, are built of stone, large, strong, and masonry. The city of Moscow was founded in the year 1334, and in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time gradually enlarged itself to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that it is said to have contained 80,000 houses; but in the sequel it suffered greatly, both from the enemy and successive conflagrations. Nevertheless, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. of England, while <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Carlisle was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the city was 12 miles in compass, and the number of houses computed at 40,000. Notwithstanding the severity and vigilance of the magistracy in Moscow, the city swarms with sturdy-beggars and vagabonds, who render it very unsafe to walk through the streets in the dark. Some of these, being armed with short truncheons, lurk in obscure corners, from whence they throw their weapons at the heads of passengers with such dexterity that they seldom fail to knock them <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; then they rob and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> them, and make off with the booty. The body of the person thus murdered is exposed in public for a certain time; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not owned, the magistrates order it to be thrown into a large deep pit, dug on purpose for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of all those who lose their lives in this manner: thither some priests repair on Whitewash-holidays, to say <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> for the souls of the deceased. The ancient splendour and opulence of Moscow was greatly diminished by the building of Petersburg, and the removal of the court to that city. Nevertheless the place is still populous; and there is plenty of all kinds of provision, extremely good, and surprisingly cheap; except the article of fish, for which there is a very great demand, occasioned by the four great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> and weekly fairs observed by the Russians. The canal between Moscow and Petersburg is one of the most stupendous works of the czar Peter: it begins at the Neva, and is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from lake to lake, and river to river, for near 100 leagues, until it reaches Moscow. What is properly deemed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> canal, commences at the city of Novgorod, and is carried on with incredible labour and expense through the territories of Brognitz, Chrititz, Chilojova, Witcheno, Volofcha, Torfchock, the province of Tvere, and the district of Klin. The city of Moscow stands about 650 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a>, the capital of Crim-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>; 950 miles from Constantinople; 720 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in Poland; 660 from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>; and 1320 from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in 55 degrees 42 minutes of north latitude.

MOSELLE

Pages 425-425

a river of Germany, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Vauge in Lorraine, and running thro' that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Triers, falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>.

MOSKITO COUNTRY

Pages 425-425

is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, between 85 and 88 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 13 and 15 degrees of north latitude; having the north <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north and east; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NICARAGUA">Nicaragua</a> on the south; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a> on the west; and indeed the Spaniards esteem it a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the principality of Honduras, though they have no colonies in the Mosquito <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When the Spaniards first invaded this part of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, they massacred the greatest part of the natives, which gave those that escaped into the inaccessible part of the country an unutterable aversion to them; and they have always appeared ready to join any Europeans that come upon their coasts against the Spaniards, and particularly the English, who frequently come hither; and the Mosquito-men being excellent marksmen, the English employ them in striking the maratee fish, &c. and many of the Mosquito Indians come to Jamaica, and sail with the English in their voyages. These people are so situated between morasses and inaccessible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> full of rocks and shoals, that no attempts against them by the Spaniards, whom they mortally hate, could ever succeed. Nevertheless, they are a mild inoffensive people, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> morality and virtue, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> never trust a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has once deceived them. They have so great a veneration towards the English, that they have spontaneously put themselves and their lands under the protection and dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England. This was first done when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a> was governor of Jamaica, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Moskitos received a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; since which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they have not only been ready in their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the English, but warm in their affections, and very useful to them on many occasions. When their king dies, the next <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> heir goes to Jamaica, to certify that he is next in blood, and receives a commission in form from the governor of Jamaica to be king of the Moskitos, till which he is not acknowledged as such by his countrymen. So fond are these people of every thing that is English, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people are proud of every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> given them by our seamen, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men with the titles of some of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>.

MOSQUE

Pages 425-426

a temple <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship among the Mahometans. All mosques are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, generally constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gate there is a square <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> paved with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and low galleries round it, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by marble pillars. In these galleries the Turks walk themselves before they go into the mosque. In each mosque there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lamps; and between these hang many crystal rings, ostriches eggs, and other curiosities, which, when the lamps are lighted, make a fine show. As it is not lawful to enter the mosque with stockings or shoes on, the pavements are covered with pieces of fluff sewed together, each being wide enough to hold a row of men kneeling, sitting, or prostrate. The women are not allowed to enter the mosque, but stay in the porches without. About every mosque there are six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers, called minarets, each of which has three little open galleries, one above another; these towers, as well as the mosques, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and adorned with gilding and other ornaments; and from thence, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, the people are called to prayers by certain officers appointed for that purpose. Most of the mosques have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> belonging to them, in which travellers, of what <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> ever, are entertained three days. Each mosque has also a place called tarbe, which is the burying-place of its founders; within which is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> fix or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with green velvet or satinn; at the ends of which are two tapers, and round it several seats for those who read the koran, and pray for the souls of the deceased.

MOSS

Pages 426-426
dean of Ely, was bred in Benet-college Cambridge, of which he was chosen a fellow. He acquired the reputation of one of the most ingenious performers of any about his time, of all kinds of public exercises, whether in classical or academical learning. His sermons at St Mary's were much crowded. He published sermons, and some poems; and he is supposed to be the author of a pamphlet intitled, A defense of my lords the bishops, as well as the clergy of the lower house of Convocation; in a letter from a member of that house to the prosecutor, concerning the late consultations about the bishop of Bangor's writing. He died in 1729, aged 63.

MOSTRA

Pages 428-428

in the Italian music, a mark at the end of a line <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> space, to show that the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the next line is in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this note be accompanied with a sharp or flat, it is proper to place these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> along with the motra.

MOTACILLA

Pages 428-431

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus of birds of the order of passerines distinguished by a straight beak of a subulated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and a lacerated tongue. There are 49 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> belonging to this genus; the most remarkable are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wagtail, frequents the sides of ponds and small streams, and feeds on insects and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The head, back, and upper and lower side of the neck, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; in some the chin is white, and the throat marked with a black <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>: the breast and belly are white; the quill-feathers are dusky; the coverts black, tipped and edged with white. The tail is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and always in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Mr Willoughby observes, that this species shifts its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in the winter; moving from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to the south of England during that season. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn it is a constant attendant on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, for the sake of the worms thrown up by that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. 2. The flavo, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> wagtail, migrates in the north of England, but in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> continues the whole year. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>: the breast, belly, thighs, and vent-feathers, being of a most vivid and lovely yellow: the throat is marked with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> black spots; above the eye is a bright yellow line: beneath that, from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, across the eye, is another of a dusky hue; and beneath the eye is a third of the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: the head and upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body is of an olive-green, which brightens in the coverts of the tail; the quill-feathers are dusky; the coverts of the wings olive-coloured; but the lower rows dusky, tipped with yellowish white; the two outmost feathers of the tail half white; the others black, as in the former. The colours of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> are far more obscure than those of the male: it wants also those black spots on the throat. It makes its nest on the ground, in corn-fields: the outside is composed of decayed stems of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots; the inside is lined with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>: it lays five eggs. 3. The regulus, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-coloured wren, is a native Plate of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and of the corresponding latitudes of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is the least of all the European birds, weighing only a single drachm. Its length is about four inches and an half; and the wings, when spread out, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> little more than six inches. On the top of its head is a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured spot called its crest, which it can hide at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the margins... margins of the crest are yellow, and it ends in a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> black line; the sides of the neck are of a beautiful yellowish green; the eyes surrounded with a white circle; the neck and back of a dark green mixed with yellow; the breast of a dirty white; the tail composed of 12 feathers of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour, an inch and an half long, but not forked. In America it associates with the titmice, running up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the bark of lofty oaks with them, and collecting its food in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were all of one brood. It feeds on insects lodged in their winter dormitories in a torpid state. 4. The sialis, or blue-bird, is a native of most parts of North America; and is about the bigness of a sparrow. The eyes are large; the head and upper part of the body, tail, and wings, are of a bright blue, excepting that the ends of the feathers are brown. The throat and breast are of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. The belly is white. It flies swiftly, having very long wings; so that the hawk generally pursues it in vain. It makes its nest in holes and trees; resembles our robin-red breast in its disposition, and feeds only on insects. 5. The sutoria, or taylor-bird, is a native of the East-Indies. It is remarkable for the art with which it makes its nest, seemingly in order to secure itself and its young in the most perfect manner possible against all danger from voracious animals. It picks up a dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and sews it to the side of a living one; its slender bill is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, and its thread is formed of some fine fibres; the lining is composed of feathers, gossamer, and down; its eggs are white, the colour of the bird <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-yellow; its length three inches; and its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> only three sixteenths of an ounce, so that the materials of the nest and its own size are not likely to draw down a habitation depending on so slight a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>.

MOTHER

Pages 431-431

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation, denoting a woman who hath born a child. Mother of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>. See Pearl.

MOTION

Pages 431-434

is defined to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and successive change of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There are three general laws of motion. 1. That a body always perseveres in its state of rest, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of uniform motion in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line, till by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force it be made to change its state: for as body is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> in receiving its motion, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of its motion; so it retains them, or perseveres in them without any change, till it be acted on by something external. From this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> it appears why we inquire not, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, concerning the cause of the continuation of the motion or rest in bodies, which can be no other than their <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a motion begin, or if a motion already produced is either accelerated or retarded, or if the direction of the motion is altered, an inquiry into the power or cause that produces this change is a proper subject of philosophy. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> general law of motion is, The change of motion is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the force impressed, and is produced in the right line in which that force acts. When a fluid acts upon a body, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> upon the vanes of a mill, or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> upon the sails of a ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a> of the motion is not proportional to the whole force of those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, but to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> only which is impressed upon the vanes or sails, which depends upon the excess of the velocity of the fluid above the velocity which the vane or sail has already acquired; for if the velocity of the fluid be only equal to that of the vane or sail, it <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> keeps up with it, but has no effect either to advance or retard its motion. Regard must always be had to the direction in which the force is impressed, in order to determine the change of motion produced by it: thus, when the wind acts obliquely with respect to the direction of a ship, the change of her motion is first to be estimated in the direction of the force impressed; and thence, by a proper application of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> and geometrical principles, the change of the motion of the ship in her own direction is to be deduced. 3. The third general law of motion is, That <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> are equal, with opposite directions, and are to be estimated always in the same right line. Body not only never changes its state of itself, but resists by its inertia every action that produces a change in its motion: hence when two bodies meet, each endeavours to persevere in its state, and resists any change; the one acquires no new motion, but what the other loses in the same direction; nor does this last lose any force, but what the other acquires: and hence, though, by their collision, motion passes from the one to the other; yet the sum of their motions, estimated in a given direction, is preserved the same, and is unalterable by their mutual actions upon each other. All motion may be considered absolutely or relatively. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">Absolute</a> or real motion, says Mr Maclaurin, is when a body changes its place in absolute space; and relative motion, is when a body changes its place only with relation to other bodies. From the observation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, every one knows that there is motion; that a body in motion perseveres in that state, till by the action of some power it is necessitated to change it; that it is not in relative or apparent motion in which it perseveres in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its inertia, but in real or absolute motion. Thus the apparent diurnal motion of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and stars would... Motion ceases, without the least power or force acting upon them, if the motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was stopt; and if the apparent motion of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> was destroyed by a contrary motion impressed upon it, the other celestial bodies would still appear to persevere in their course. To make this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> still plainer, Mr Martin observes, that space is nothing but an absolute and infinite void, and that the place of a body is that part of the immense void which it takes up or possesses; and this place may be considered absolutely, or in itself, in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is called the absolute place of the body; or else with regard to the place of some other body, and then it is called the relative or apparent place of the body. Now, as a motion is only the change of place in bodies, it is evident that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> come under the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of absolute and relative, or apparent. All motion is in itself absolute, or the change of absolute space; but when the motions of bodies are considered and compared with each other, then are they relative and apparent only: they are relative, as they are compared to each other; and they are apparent only, in so much that not their true or absolute motion, but the sum or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the motions only is perceivable to us. In comparing the motions of bodies, we may consider them as moving both the same way, or towards contrary parts: in the first case, the difference of motion is only perceived by us; in the latter, the sum of the motions. Thus, for example; suppose two ships, A and B, set sail from the same port upon the same thumb, and that A sails at the rate of five miles per <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and B at the rate of three; here the difference of the velocity (viz. two miles per hour) is that by which the ship A will appear to go from the ship B forwards, or the ship B will appear at A to go with the same velocity backwards, to a spectator in either respectively. If the two ships, A and B, move with the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of velocity, then will the difference be nothing, and so neither ship will appear to the other to move at all. Hence it is, that though the earth is continually revolving about its axis; yet as all objects on its surface partake of the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> motion, they appear not to move at all, but are relatively at rest. If two ships, A and B, with the degrees of velocity as above, meet each other, the one will appear to the other to move with the sum of both velocities, viz. at the rate of eight miles per hour; so that in this case the apparent motion exceeds the true, as in the other it fell short of it. Hence the reason why a person, riding against the wind, finds the force of it much greater than it really is; whereas if he rides with it, he finds it less. The reason of all these phenomena of motion will be evident, if we consider that we must be absolutely at rest, if we would discern the true or real motion of bodies about us. Thus a person on the strand will observe the ships sailing with their real velocity. A person standing still will <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the true strength and velocity of the wind; and a person placed in the regions between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> will view all their true motions, which he cannot otherwise do, because in all other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the spectator's own motion must be added to or subtracted from that of the moving body. Motion is either equable or accelerated. Equable motion is that by which a body passes over equal spaces in equal times. Accelerated motion is that which is continually augmented or increased, as retarded motion is that which continually decreases; and if the increase or decrease of motion be equal in equal times, the motion is then said to be equally accelerated or retarded. Equable motion is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by a single impetus or stroke: thus the motion of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> from a cannon is produced by the single action of the powder in the first moment; and therefore the velocity it first sets out with would always continue the same, were it void of gravity, and to move in an unresisting medium; which therefore would be always equable, or such as would carry it through the same length of space in every equal part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Hence we may determine the theorems for the expressions of the time (T) the velocity (V) and the space (S) passed over in equable or uniform motion very easily thus: If the time be given, or the same, the space passed over will be as the velocity, viz. \( S : V \); that is, with twice the velocity, twice the space; with three times the velocity, three times the space, will be passed over in the same time; and so on. If the velocity be given, or remain the same, then the space passed over will be as the time, viz. \( S : T \); that is, it will be greater or less, as the time is so. But if neither the time nor velocity be given or known, then will the space be in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> ratio of both, viz. \( S : TV \). Hence, in general, since \( S : TV \), we have \( V = \frac{S}{T} \); that is, the velocity is always directly as the space, and inversely as the time. And also \( T : V \); that is, the time is as the space directly, and as the velocity inversely; or, in other words, it increases with the space, and decreases with the velocity. If, therefore, in any rectangle, one side represent the time, and the other side the velocity, it is evident that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of the said rectangle will represent the space passed over by an uniform motion in that time, and with that velocity. Accelerated motion is produced by a constant impulse or power, which keeps continually acting upon the body, as that of gravity which produces the motion of falling bodies; which sort of motion is constantly accelerated, because gravity every moment adds a new impulse, which generates a new degree of velocity; and the velocity thus increasing, the motion must be quickened each moment, or the body must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> faster and faster the lower it falls. In like manner a body thrown perpendicularly upward, as a ball from a cannon, will have its motion continually retarded, because gravity acts constantly upon it in a direction contrary to that given it by the powder; so that its velocity upwards must be continually diminished, and so its motion as continually retarded, till at last it be all destroyed. The body has then attained its utmost height, and is for a moment motionless; after which it begins to descend with a velocity in the same manner accelerated, till it comes to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface. Since the momentum (M) of a body is compounded of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter (Q), and the velocity (V), we have this general <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> \( M = QV \), for the force force of any body A; and suppose the force of another body B be represented by the same letters in Italics, viz. \( Q = Q' \). Let the two bodies A and B in motion impinge on each other directly; if they tend both the same way, the sum of their motions towards the same part will be \( QV + Q'V \). But if they tend towards contrary parts, or meet, then the sum of their motions towards the same part will be \( QV - Q'V \); for since the motion of one of the bodies is contrary to what it was before, it must be connected by a contrary sign. Or thus; because, when the motion of B conspires with that of A, it is added to it; so, when it is contrary, it is subtracted from it, and the sum or difference of the absolute motions is the whole relative motion, or that which is made towards the same part. Again, this total motion towards the same parts, is the same both before and after the stroke, in case the two bodies A and B impinge on each other; because, whatever change of motion is made in one of those bodies by the stroke, the same is produced in the other body towards the same part; that is, as much as the motion of B is increased or decreased towards the same part by the action of A, just so much is the motion of A diminished or augmented towards the same part by the equal reaction of B, by the third law of motion. In bodies not <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, let \( x \) be the velocity of the bodies after the stroke (for, since we suppose them not elastic, there can be nothing to separate them after collision; they must therefore both go on together, or with the same celerity). Then the sum of the motions after collision will be \( Qx + Q'x \); whereas, if the bodies tend the same way, we have \( QV + Q'V = Qx + Q'x \); or if they meet, \( QV - Q'V = Qx + Q'x \); and accordingly \( \frac{QV + Q'V}{Q + Q'} = x \), or \( \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} = x \). If the body (B) be at rest, then \( V = 0 \), and the velocities of the bodies after the stroke will be \( \frac{QV}{Q + Q'} \). Thus if the bodies be equal (viz. \( Q = Q' \)) and A with 10 degrees of velocity impinge on B at rest; then \( \frac{QV}{Q + Q'} = \frac{10}{5} = x \). If \( Q = Q' \), and \( V : V' :: 10 : 6 \) we have \( \frac{QV + Q'V}{Q + Q'} = \frac{16}{8} = x \), the velocity after the stroke. If the bodies are both in motion, and tend the contrary way; then when \( Q = Q' \) and \( V = V' \), it is plain \( \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} = x \); that is, the bodies which meet with equal bulks and velocities will destroy each other's motion after the stroke, and remain at rest. If \( Q = Q' \) but \( V : V' :: 6 : 14 \), then \( \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} = \frac{-8}{2} = -4x \); which shews that equal bodies meeting with unequal velocities, they will, after meeting the stroke, both go on the same way which the most prevalent body moved before. If the velocity \( \frac{QV + Q'V}{Q + Q'} \) be multiplied by the quantities of matter \( Q \) and \( Q' \), we shall have \( \frac{QV + Q'V}{Q + Q'} = \) the momentum of A after the stroke; and \( \frac{QV + Q'V}{Q + Q'} = \) the momentum B; therefore \( QV + Q'V = Q + Q' \times V = V \); the quantity of the motion lost in A after the stroke, and consequently is equal to what is gained in B, as may be shown in the same manner. But since a part of this expression (viz. \( \frac{Q}{Q + Q'} \)) is constant, the loss of motion will ever be proportional to the other part \( V = V' \). But this loss or change of motion in either body is the whole effect, and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> the magnitude or energy of the stroke. Therefore any two bodies, not elastic, strike each other with a stroke always proportionable to the sum of their velocities \( (V + V') \) if they meet, or to the difference of their velocities \( (V - V') \) if they tend the same way. Hence, if one body (B) be at rest before the stroke, then \( V = 0 \); and the magnitude of the stroke will be as \( V \); that is, as the velocity of the moving body A; and not as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of its velocity, as many philosophers (viz. the Dutch and Italians) maintain. In bodies perfectly elastic, the restituent power or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> by which the parts displaced by the stroke restore themselves to their first situation, is equal to the force impressed, because it produces an equal effect; therefore, in this sort of bodies, there is a power of action twice as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as in the former non-elastic bodies; for these bodies not only strike each other by impulse, but likewise by repulse, they always repelling each other after the stroke. But we have shewn, that the force with which non-elastic bodies strike each other is as \( V = V' \); therefore the reaction of elastic bodies is the same; that is, the velocity with which elastic bodies recede from each other after the stroke, is equal to the velocity with which they approached each other before the stroke. Whence if \( x \) and \( y \) be the velocities of two bodies A and B, tending the same way after the stroke, since \( V - V' = x - y \), we have \( x + V = V' - y \); whence the motion of A after the stroke will be \( Qx \), and that of B will be \( Qx + QV - Q'V \); and the sum of these motions will be equal to the sum of the motions before the stroke, viz. \( Qx + Qx + QV - Q'V = QV + Q'V \). Whence, by reducing the equation, it will be \( Qx + Q'x = QV - Q'V + 2Q'V \); and \( x = \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} = \) the velocity of the body A. Again, the velocity of B is \( x + V = V' - y \); \( \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} + V - V' = \frac{2QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} \). Here we suppose the bodies tend the same way before the stroke; and it is evident from the equation above, that so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as \( QV + 2Q'V \) is greater than \( Q'V \), the velocity \( (x) \) of A after the stroke will be affirmative, or the body A will move the same way after the stroke as before; but when \( Q'V \) is greater than \( QV + 2Q'V \), the velocity \( (x) \) will be <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, or the body A will be reflected back. If the body B be at rest, then \( V = 0 \); and \( x = \frac{QV - Q'V}{Q + Q'} \), which shews the body A will go forwards or backwards, as \( QV \) is greater or lesser than \( Q'V \), or A greater or lesser than B. If \( Q = 3 \), \( Q = V = 10 \), and \( V = 5 \); then after the stroke the velocity of \( A \) will be \[ x = \frac{QV - 2V}{Q + 2} = \frac{30 - 20}{5} = 2, \] and the velocity of \( B \) will be \[ y = \frac{2QV - 5Q}{Q + 2} = \frac{60 - 30}{5} = 6. \] If the bodies are both in motion, and \( V = 5 \), the rest is the same as before; then \[ \frac{QV - 2QV + 2V}{Q + 2} = \text{velocity of } A \text{ after the stroke}, \quad \frac{2QV - QV + QV}{Q + 2} = \text{velocity of } B \text{ after the stroke}. \] If the bodies \( A \) and \( B \) move towards contrary parts, or meet each other, then will the relative velocity, to which the force of the stroke is proportional, be \[ V + V', \] and so the velocities of \( A \) and \( B \) after the stroke will be \[ x = x + V + V', \quad y = y + V + V'. \] If \( QV + 2QV \) be greater than \( QV \), the motion of the body \( A \) will be backwards; otherwise it will go forwards as before. If \( Q = 3 \), \( Q = 2 \), \( V = 10 \), and \( V = 5 \); then will the velocity of \( A \) be \[ \frac{QV - 2QV + 2V}{Q + 2} = \frac{10}{5} = 2; \] so the velocity of the body \( A \) will go back with two degrees of velocity. The velocity of \( B \), after the stroke, will be \[ \frac{2QV - QV + QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{4 \times V}{4}. \] If the bodies are equal, that is, if \( Q = Q \), then \[ x = \frac{-2QV}{2V} = -V; \] which shews, that when equal bodies meet each other, they are reflected back with interchanged velocities; for in that case also the velocity of \( B \) becomes \[ \frac{2QV}{Q} = V. \] If the bodies are equal, and one of them at rest, as \( B \), then since \( Q = Q \), and \( V = 0 \), we have the velocity of \( A \) after the stroke \[ x = 0; \text{ or the body } A \text{ will abide at rest, and the velocity of } B \text{ will be } -V, \text{ the velocity of } A \text{ before the impulse, as appears by the example in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> referred to.} \] If several bodies \( B, C, D, E, F \) are contiguous in a right line, and another equal body \( A \) strike \( B \) with any given velocity, it shall lose all its motion, or be quiescent after the stroke; the body \( B \) which receives it will communicate it to \( C \), and \( C \) to \( D \), and \( D \) to \( E \), and \( E \) to \( F \); and because action and re-action between the bodies \( B, C, D, E, F \) are equal, as they were quiescent before, they must continue so; but the body \( F \), having no other body to re-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon it, has nothing to obstruct its motion; it will therefore move on with the same velocity which \( A \) had at first, because it has all the motion of \( A \), and the same quantity of matter by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. Let there be three bodies \( A, B, C \), and let \( A \) strike \( B \) at rest; the velocity generated in \( B \) by the stroke will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q} = 2QV; \] and so the momentum of \( B \) will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{QV}{Q + 2}. \] With this momentum \( B \) will strike \( C \) at rest and contiguous to it; the velocity generated in \( C \) will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{QV}{Q + 2}; \] and its momentum will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{QV}{Q + 2}. \] If now we suppose \( B \) a variable quantity, while \( A \) and \( C \) remain the same, we shall find what proportion it must have to each of them, in order that the momentum of \( C \) may be a maximum, or the greatest possible, by putting the flexion thereof equal to nothing; that is, \[ 4Q \frac{QV}{Q + 2} = 4Q \frac{QV}{Q + 2}. \] Witn this momentum \( B \) will strike \( C \) at rest and contiguous to it; the velocity generated in \( C \) will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{QV}{Q + 2}; \] and its momentum will be \[ \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} = \frac{QV}{Q + 2}. \] If the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> \( n \) of bodies in a geometrical ratio \( r \) to each other, and the first be \( A \), the second will be \( Dr \), the third \( Dr^2A \), and so on to the last, which will be \( Dr^{n-1}A \). Allo, the velocity of the first being \( V \), that of the second will be \[ \frac{2V}{1+r} \quad \text{(for } \frac{2QV}{Q + 2} \text{ here)} = \frac{AV}{r+1}, \] that of the third \( \frac{AV}{1+r^2} \), that of the fourth \( \frac{AV}{1+r^3} \), and so on to the last, which will be \( \frac{AV}{1+r^n} \). The momentum of the first will be \( AV \), that of the second \( \frac{4AV}{1+r} \), that of the third \( \frac{8AV}{1+r^2} \), that of the fourth \( \frac{8AV}{1+r^3} \), and so on to the last, which will be \( \frac{16AV}{1+r^n} \). To give an example of this theorem; if \( n = 100 \), and \( r = 2 \), then will the first body \( A \) be to the last \( \frac{r^n}{r} = 10241 \), nearly; and its velocity to that of the last nearly as 2710621000000000 to 1; laffly, the momentum of the first to that of the last will be nearly as 1 to 233848000000. If the number \( n \) of bodies be required, and the ratio of the momenta of the first and last be given as 1 to \( M \), and the ratio of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> \( r \) given also; then, putting \( \frac{r^n}{r} = R \), we have the momentum of the last body expressed by \( \frac{r^n}{r} = R = R^{n-1} \); therefore the logarithm of \( M \) (i.e., \( M \)) is equal to the logarithm of \( R \) (i.e., \( R \)) multiplied by the power \( n-1 \); that is, \[ M = I \times R; \] consequently \( I/M + 1 = n \), the number of bodies required.

MOTTE

Pages 431-431

an ingenious Frenchman, greatly distinguished by his writings in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and by his literary contests with many eminent persons, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1672. He wrote with very different success, no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> having been more praised <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> more criticised than he was: his literary paradoxes, his singular systems, in all branches of polite learning, and above all, his judgment upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which, like those of Perrault, were thought disrespectful and detracting, raised him up formidable adversaries. Racine, Boileau, Rousseau, and Madam Dacier, were among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those who made it their business to avenge antiquity on a man who, with more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> than genius or learning, assumed a kind of dictatorial authority in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of belles lettres. He became <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> in the latter years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and died in 1731: a complete edition of all his works was published in 11 vols., 8vo. in 1754; though, as has been said of our Swift, his reputation had been better consulted by reducing them to three or four.

MOTTEUX

Pages 434-435

a French <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, born and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in Normandy. Coming over to England on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, he became a considerable trader in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, kept an East-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> warehouse in Leadenhall-street, and had a genteel <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>-office, relating to foreign letters, being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of several languages. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and humour; and acquired so perfect a mastery of the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that he not only was qualified to oblige the world with a very good translation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, but also wrote several songs, prologues, epilogues, &c. and what was still more extraordinary, became a very eminent dramatic writer in a language to which he was not a native. He was at last, in the year 1718, found dead in a disorderly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, on his birth-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when he completed his 58th year.

MOULD

Pages 435-435

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, a loose kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, everywhere obvious on the surface of the ground, called also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mother earth; by some also loam. For an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and properties of this earth, see AGRICULTURE, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> I.

MOULDINESS

Pages 435-435

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to bodies which corrupt in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, from some hidden principle of humidity therein; and whose corruption shews itself by a certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> lanugo on their surface, which, viewed through a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, appears like a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, out of which arise herbs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, some only in the bud, others full-blown, and others decayed; each having its root, stalk, and other parts. Moulding See MUCOR.

MOULDING

Pages 435-435

anything <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in a mould, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that seems to have been so though in reality it were cut with a chisel or the ax.

MOULDINGS

Pages 435-435

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, projections beyond the naked wall, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, wainscot, &c. the assemblage of which forms cornices, door-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and other decorations of ARCHITECTURE. See that article.

MOULIN

Pages 435-435

a Protestant divine, believed to be of the same family with the former, was born in 1568. He taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; and afterwards became chaplain to the princess of Navarre. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of England's desire he came hither in 1615, and prepared a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for the union of the Protestant churches. The university of Leyden offered him a professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in 1619; but he refused it, and presided at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> held by the Calvinists at Alais in 1620. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, being informed by Mr Drelincourt that the French king resolved to have him thrown into prison, he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Bouillon made him professor of divinity, and minister in ordinary. He was employed by the Calvinists in the most important affairs; and died at Sedan in 1658. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. The anatomy of Arminianism. 2. A treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, and the keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. 3. The Capuchine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of those monks. 4. The buckler of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the reformed churches. 5. The judge of controversies and traditions. 6. The anatomy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> du Moulin, his eldest son, was chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. of England, and prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, where he died in 1684, aged 84.
