He wrote, 1. The peace of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, in French. 2. Clamor religii sanguinis; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, by mistake, attributed to Alexander Morus. 3. A defence of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, in English.

MOULINET

Pages 435-435

is used, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, which, being crossed with two levers, is usually applied to cranes, capstans, and other sorts of engines of the like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, to draw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and heave up <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c. MOULINET is also a kind of turnstile, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wooden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, which turns horizontally upon a stake fixed in the ground; usually placed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> to keep out horses, and to oblige passengers to go and come one by one. These moulinets are often let near the outworks of fortified places at the sides of the barriers, through which people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on foot.

MOUND

Pages 435-435

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> globe with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> upon it, such as our kings are usually drawn with, holding it in their left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as they do the sceptre in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

MOUNT

Pages 435-436

an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, called also mountain. See Mountain. Mount of Piety, certain funds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> establishments in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a> out on some small security. There were also mounts of piety in England, raised by contribution for the benefit of people ruined by the extortions of the Jews.

MOUNTAIN

Pages 436-439

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> rising to a considerable height above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the surface thereof. The origin of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> is variously assigned by philosophers: some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them coeval with the world, and created along with it; others, among whom is Dr Burnet, will have them to take their rise from the deluge, urging that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> irregularity and disorder visible in them, plainly shews they do not come immediately out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God, but are the wrecks of the old world, broken into the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. See Deluge. Others again allege from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that the roots of many hills being eaten away, the hills themselves have subsided and sunk into plains; whence they conclude, that where the corruption is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> is so too. It appears certain to many, that some mountains must have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> gradually, and have grown up in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shells, &c. found in them, which they suppose may be accounted for from a violent <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blowing the sand, &c. into huge heaps, which were made into mafs by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, &c. The origin of mountains, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Mr Ray, seems to have been from explosions by means of subterraneous fires; and he thinks it very probable, that they all have vast hollows beneath them; and that this might have been the means used at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> to make the dry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> appear, he thinks no way dissonant to reason, since history proves that fires have raged in subterraneous caverns under the seas; and there is no natural impossibility in fire's subsiding in such caverns, even when the earth was all over covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as at the first creation. Mountains appear to many to be defects and blemishes in the earth; but they are truly of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> to the well-being both of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and other animals. They serve as screens to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and nipping blasts of the northern and eastern winds; they serve for the production of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vegetables and minerals, which are not found in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ridges and chains of lofty and topping mountains, being generally found to run from east to west, serve to stop the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the vapours towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, without which they would all run from the hot countries, and leave them destitute of rain. Mr Ray adds, that they condense these vapours, like alembic heads, into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>; and so, by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, give origin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and by amassing, cooling, and constituting them, turn them into rain, and by that means render the fervid region of the torrid zone habitable. He farther adds, that many creatures cannot live but in particular situations; and even the tops of the highest and the coldest mountains are the only places where some creatures, as well birds as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, will live. Mr Buffon remarks, that the highest mountains of the world, as well as the largest, are situated in the torrid zone; and the nearer we approach the equator, the greater are the inequalities on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface. "A short enumeration of mountains and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> (says he) will be sufficient to establish this point.—In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the Cordilleras, which are the highest mountains in the world, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> precisely under the equator; and they extend on both sides a considerable way beyond the tropic circles. The highest mountains of the Moors, of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, and the great and little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lie either under <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> very near the equator. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, the chain of which, under different names, runs into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and through this whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, lies nearer the equator than the poles. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the Pyrenees, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, which form one chain, are still less distant from the equator than the pole. "These chains of mountains of which we have given an enumeration, are higher and of greater extent, both in length and breadth, than those of more northern countries. With regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, the Alps form a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> chain which runs across the whole continent from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to China. They commence on the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, join the Pyrenees, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> France by Vivares and Auvergne, run through <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and stretch into Germany above <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, until they reach <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; from thence they join the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, the Caucasus, the Taurus, the Imaus, and at last terminate on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. Mount Atlas in the same manner traverses the whole continent of Africa, from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> to the Straits of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea. The mountains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> have likewise the same direction; but the mountains of America have an opposite direction. The vast chains of Cordilleras, and other mountains, run more from south to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> than from east to west." This <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> concerning the magnitude and height of mountains, is no doubt necessary for the support of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the earth*; but it is by no means agreeable to fact. The mountains of the moon, though much nearer the equator than the Alps, are not, by all accounts, equal to them in size; one of the peaks of the Alps, named Mont Blanc, being reckoned the highest point of land in Europe, Asia, or Africa. According to some late computations, this peak is more than 800 feet higher than mount Aetna would be with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> set on its top; so that we may reckon it little inferior to the highest mountains even in America. In Mr Forster's account of the Southern <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THULE">Thule</a> also, he tells us of an exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain seen on that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and which was thought to be little less than two miles perpendicular; and yet this island lies in a very considerable south latitude: so that the height of mountains seems by no means to be in proportion to the vicinity of the equator or torrid zone. The most remarkable mountain in the world for shape, is that called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> mountain, or the inaccessible mountain, in Dauphiny.—This is a vast hill, placed as it were bottom upwards, or set on its summit on the earth, with its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> base elevated in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; it is but about 1000 paces in circumference at bottom, and above 2000 at the top. On the centre of the plain at the top there stands another small and very narrow, but very high hill. It obtained its name from from the supposed impossibility of ascending it, on account of its projection outwards. Some hardy persons, however, once ventured to climb it; and found at the top a number of the chamois, animals by no means qualified for climbing, and which doubtless had never either ascended or descended the mountain, and which must be supposed to have bred there for many ages; though it is very difficult to account for their coming there. The difficulty and danger of ascending to the tops of mountains, proceeds not from the thinness of the air as has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reported; but the reason is, that they rise with such a rugged and precipitate ascent, that they are utterly inaccessible. In some places they appear like a great wall of 600 or 700 feet high; in others, there stick out enormous rocks, that hang upon the brow of the steep, and every moment threaten destruction to the traveller below. In this manner almost all the tops of the highest mountains are bare and pointed. And this naturally proceeds from their being so continually assaulted by thunders and tempests. All the earthy substances with which they might have been once covered, have for ages been washed away from their summits; and nothing is left remaining but immense rocks, which no tempest has hitherto been able to destroy. Nevertheless, time is every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> and every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> making depredations; and huge fragments are seen tumbling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the precipice, either loosened from the summit by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> or rains, or struck down by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. Nothing can exhibit a more terrible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> than one of these enormous rocks, commonly larger than an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, falling from its height with a noise louder than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, and rolling down the side of the mountain. Dr Plot tells us of one in particular, which being loosened from its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, tumbled down the precipice, and was partly shattered into a thousand pieces. Notwithstanding, one of the largest fragments of the same, still preserving its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, travelled over the plain below, crossed a rivulet in the midst, and at last stopped on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>! These fragments, as was said, are often struck off by lightning, and sometimes undermined by rains; but the most usual manner in which they are disunited from the mountain, is by frost: the rains infilling between the interstices of the mountain, continue there until there comes a frost; and then, when converted into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, the water swells with an irresistible force, and produces the same effect as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder, splitting the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rocks, and thus shattering the summits of the mountain. But not rocks alone, but whole mountains, are, by various causes, disunited from each other. We see, in many parts of the Alps, amazing clefts, the sides of which to exactly correspond with the opposite, that no doubt can be entertained of their having been once joined together. At Cjjeta, in Italy, a mountain was split in this manner by an earthquake; and there is a passageway opened through it, that appears as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> elaborately done by the industry of man. In the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a> these breaches are frequently seen. That at Thermopylae, in Greece, has been long famous. The mountain of the Troglodytes, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, has thus a passageway through it; and that in Savoy, which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> began, and which Victor Amadeus completed, is an instance of the same kind. We have accounts of some of these disruptions, immediately after their happening. "In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, in the year 1714, a part of the mountain of Diableret, in the district of Valais, in France, suddenly fell down, between two and three o'clock in the afternoon, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> being very calm and serene. It was of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and destroyed 55 cottages in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Fifteen persons, together with about 100 beasts, were also crushed beneath its ruins, which covered an extent of a good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The dust it occasioned instantly covered all the neighbourhood in darkness. The heaps of rubbish were more than 300 feet high. They stopped the current of a river that ran along the plain, which now is formed into several new and deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. There appeared, through the whole of this rubbish, none of those substances that seemed to indicate that this disruption had been made by means of subterraneous fires. Most probably, the base of this rocky mountain was rotted and decayed; and thus fell, without any extraneous violence." In the same manner, in the year 1618, the town of Pleurs, in France, was buried beneath a rocky mountain, at the foot of which it was situated. These accidents, and many more that might be enumerated of the same kind, have been produced by various causes: by earthquakes, as in the mountain at Cjjeta; or by being decayed at the bottom, as at Diableret. But the most general way is, by the foundation of one part of the mountain being hollowed by waters, and thus wanting a support, breaking from the other. Thus it generally has been found in the great chasms in the Alps; and thus it almost always is known in those disruptions of hills which are known by the name of land-slips. These are nothing more than the sliding down of an higher piece of ground, disrooted from its situation by subterraneous inundations, and settling itself upon the plain below. There is not an appearance in all nature that so much astonished our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> as these land-slips. In fact, to behold a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> upland, with its houses, its corn, and cattle, at once loosened from its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and floating as it were upon the subjacent water; to behold it quitting its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> situation, and travelling forward like a ship, in quest of new adventures; this is certainly one of the most extraordinary appearances that can be imagined; and, to a people ignorant of the powers of nature, might well be considered as a prodigy. Accordingly, we find all our old historians mentioning it as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> of approaching calamities. In this more enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, however, its cause is very well known; and, instead of exciting ominous apprehensions in the populace, it only gives rise to some very ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits among them, about whose the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> shall be; whether the land which has thus slipped, shall belong to the original possessor, or to him upon whose grounds it has encroached and settled. What has been the determination of the judges is not so well known; but the circumstances of the slips themselves have been minutely enough and exactly described. In the lands of Slatberg, in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, there stood a declivity gradually ascending for near half a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. In the year 1713, and on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the inhabitants perceived a crack on its side, somewhat like a furrow made with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, which they imputed to the effects of lightning, as there had been thunder the night before. However, on the evening of the same day, they were surprised to hear an hideous confused noise issuing all round from the side of the hill; and their curiosity being raised, they repaired to the place. There, to their amazement, they found the earth for near five acres all in gentle motion, and sliding down the hill upon the subjacent plain. This motion continued the remaining part of the day, and the whole night; nor did the noise cease during the whole time; proceeding, probably, from the attrition of the ground beneath. The day following, however, this strange journey down the hill ceased entirely; and above an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> below was found covered with what before composed a part of the declivity. However, these slips, when a whole mountain's side seems to descend, happen but very rarely. There are some of another kind, however, much more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; and, as they are always sudden, much more dangerous. These are snow-slips, well known, and greatly dreaded by travellers. It often happens, that when snow has long been accumulated on the tops and on the sides of mountains, it is borne down the precipice either by means of tempests or its own melting. At first, when loosened, the volume in motion is but small; but it gathers as it continues to roll, and, by the time it has reached the habitable parts of the mountain, it is generally grown of enormous bulk. Wherever it rolls, it levels all things in its way; or buries them in unavoidable destruction. Instead of rolling, it sometimes is found to slide along from the top; yet even thus it is generally as fatal as before. Nevertheless, we have had an instance, a few years ago, of a small family in Germany that lived for above a fortnight beneath one of these snow-slips. Although they were buried during that whole time in utter darkness, and under a bed of some hundred feet deep, yet they were luckily taken out alive, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the snow being supported by a beam that kept up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>; and nourishment being supplied them by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of a sheep that was buried under the same ruin. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a> of Mountains. This is a late discovery, and a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's theory of universal gravity. According to the Newtonian system, an attractive power is not only exerted between those large masses of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which constitute the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; but likewise between all comparatively smaller bodies, and even between the smallest particles of which they are composed. Agreeably to this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, a heavy body, which ought to gravitate or tend toward the centre of the earth, in a direction perpendicular to its surface, supposing the said surface to be perfectly even and spherical, ought likewise, though in a less <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to be attracted and tend towards a mountain placed on the earth's surface: so that a plumb-line, for instance, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, hanging in the neighbourhood of such a mountain, ought to be drawn from a perpendicular situation, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the attractive power of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter of which it is composed, acting in a direction different from that exerted by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of matter in the earth, and with a proportionably inferior degree of force. Though Sir Isaac Newton had long ago hinted at an experiment of this kind; and had remarked, that "a mountain of an hemispherical figure, three miles high and six broad, would not, by its attraction, draw the plumb-line two minutes out of the perpendicular (A):" yet no attempt to ascertain this matter, by actual experiment, was made till about the year 1738; when the French academicians, particularly Meflis Bouguer and Condamin, who were sent to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a degree under the equator, attempted to discover the attractive power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a>, a mountain in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Quito. According to their observations, which were however made under circumstances by no means favourable to an accurate solution of so nice and difficult a problem, the mountain Chimborazo exerted an attraction equal to eight seconds. Though this experiment was not perhaps sufficient to prove satisfactorily even the reality of an attraction, much less the precise quantity of it; yet it does not appear that any steps had been since taken to repeat it. Through the munificence of his Britannic majesty, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> were enabled to undertake the execution of this delicate and important experiment; the astronomer royal was chosen to conduct it. After various inquiries, the mountain Schehallien, situated nearly in the centre of Scotland, was pitched upon as the most proper for the purpose that could be found in this island. The observations were made by taking the meridian zenith distances of different fixed stars, near the zenith, by means of a zenith <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> of ten feet radius; first on the south, and afterwards on the north side of the hill, the greatest length of which extended in an east and west direction. It is evident, that if the mass of matter in the hill exerted any sensible attraction, it would cause the plumb-line of the sector, through which an observer viewed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the meridian, to deviate from its perpendicular situation, and would attract it contrary ways at the two stations, thereby doubling the effect. On the south side the plummet would be drawn to the northward, by the attractive power of the hill placed to the northward of it; and on the north side, a contrary and equal deflection of the plumb-line would take place, in consequence of the attraction of the hill, now to the southward of it. The apparent zenith distances of the stars would be affected contrarywise; those being increased at the one station which were diminished at the other: and the correspondent quantities of the deflection of the plumb-line would give the observer the sum of the contrary attractions of the hill, acting on the plummet at the two stations; the half of which will of course indicate the attractive power of the hill. The various operations requisite for this experiment lasted about four months; and from them it appears, that the sum of the two contrary attractions of the mountain Schehallien, in the two temporary observations which were successively fixed half-way up the hill (where the effect of its attraction would be greatest) was equal to 11". 6.—From a rough computation, founded on the known law of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, and By a very easy calculation it is found that such a mountain would attract the plumb-line 1' 18" from the perpendicular. and on an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> that the density of the hill is equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> density of the earth; it appears that the attraction of the hill should amount to about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of this quantity. From thence it was inferred, that the density of the hill is only about half the mean density of the earth. It does not appear, however, that the mountain Schehallien has ever been a volcano, or is hollow; as it is extremely solid and dense, and seemingly composed of an entire rock. The inference drawn from these experiments may be reduced to the following: 1. It appears, that the mountain Schehallien exerts a sensible attraction; therefore, from the rules of philosophizing, we are to conclude, that every mountain, and indeed every particle of the earth, is endowed with the same property, in proportion to its quantity of matter. 2. The law of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of this force, in the inverse ratio of the squares of the distances, as laid down by Sir Isaac Newton, is also confirmed by this experiment. For if the force of attraction of the hill had been only to that of the earth as the matter in the hill to that of the earth, and had not been greatly increased by the near approach to its centre, the attraction thereof must have been wholly insensible. But now, by only supposing the mean density of the earth to be double to that of the hill, which seems very probable from other considerations, the attraction of the hill will be reconciled to the general law of the variation of attraction in the inverse duplicate ratio of the distances, as deduced by Sir Isaac Newton from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the motion of the heavenly bodies with the force of gravity at the surface of the earth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of nature will be preserved. 3. We may now, therefore, be allowed to admit this law, and to acknowledge, that the mean density of the earth is at least double of that at the surface; and consequently that the density of the internal parts of the earth is much greater than near the surface. Hence also, the whole quantity of matter in the earth will be at least as great again as if it had been all composed of matter of the same density with that at the surface; or will be about four or five times as great as if it were all composed of water.—This conclusion, Mr Maseleyne adds, is totally contrary to the hypothesis of some naturalists, who suppose the earth to be only a great hollow shell of matter; supporting itself from the property of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, with an immense vacancy in the midst of it. But, were that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the attraction of mountains, and even smaller inequalities in the earth's surface, would be very great, contrary to experiment, and would affect the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the degrees of the meridian much more than we find they do; and the variation of gravity, in different latitudes, in going from the equator to the poles, as found by pendulums, would not be near so regular as it has been found by experiment to be. 4. As mountains are, by these experiments, found capable of producing sensible deflections of the plumb-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of astronomical instruments; it becomes a matter of great importance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of degrees in the meridian, either to choose places where the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> attractions of the elevated parts may be small; or where, by their situation, they may compensate or counteract the effects of each other. For measuring the heights of mountains, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">BAROMETER</a>, and the same in the Appendix.

Mouse-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See Hierachium. Mouse-Tail. See Myosurus. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DOR">Dor</a>-Mouse. See Sorex.

MOUSUL

Pages 439-439
or Mosul, a town of Turkey in Asia, seated on the western bank of the river Tigris, nearly opposite to the place where Nineveh formerly stood. It is a large place, surrounded with high walls; but the houses are ill-built, and in several places gone to ruin; however, it has a strong castle and a citadel. It is a place of great trade, particularly in cloth and all sorts of cottons and silks. At some distance from Mosul is a mosque, in which they pretend the prophet Jonah lies. The inhabitants are generally Mahometans; but there are a great number of Nestorian Christians. It was besieged in vain by the Persians in 1743. E. Lon. 41° 45'. N. Lat. 35° 30'.

MOUTH

Pages 439-439

in anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, consisting of the lips, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, the inside of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, the palate, the salivary glands, the os hyoides, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UVULA">uvula</a>, and the tonsils; which see under the article ANATOMY. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> observes, that the mouth in the several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals is nicely adapted to the uses of such a part, and well sized and shaped for the formation of speech, the gathering and receiving of food, the catching of prey, &c. In some creatures it is wide and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, in others little and narrow; in some it is formed with a deep incisure into the head, for the better catching and holding of prey, and more easy commination of hard, large, and troublesome food; and in others with a shorter incisure, for the gathering and holding of herbaceous food. In birds, it is neatly shaped for piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; hard and horny, to supply the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; hooked, in the rapacious kind, to catch and hold their prey; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and slender in those that have their food to grope for in moorish places; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and long in those that search for it in the mud. Nor is the mouth less remarkable in insects: in some it is forcipated, to catch, hold, and tear the prey; in others aculeated, to pierce and wound animals, and suck their blood; in others, strongly rigid, with jaws and teeth, to gnaw and scrape out their food, carry burdens, perforate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, nay the hardest wood, and even <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> themselves, for houses and nests for their young.

MOVEABLE

Pages 435-435

in general, denotes any thing capable of being moved. MOVEABLE Subject, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, any thing that moves itself, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> can be moved; in contradistinction to immoveable or heritable subjects, as lands, houses, &c.

MOVEMENT

Pages 435-435

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, a machine that is moved by clock-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. See CLOCK and WATCH. Perpetual Movement. Many have attempted to find a perpetual movement, but without success; and there is reason to think, from the principles of mechanics, that such a movement is impossible: for tho', in many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of bodies acting upon one another, there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, yet the gain is always equal in opposite directions; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> motion is never increased. To make a perpetual movement, it appears necessary that a certain system of bodies, of a determined <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and quantity, should move in a certain space for ever, and in a certain way and manner; and for this there must be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of actions returning in a circle, otherwise the movement <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be perpetual; so that any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by which the absolute quantity of force is increased, of which there are several sorts, must have its corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-action, by which the gain is destroyed, and the quantity of force restored to its first state. Thus by these actions there will never be any gain of direct force to overcome the friction and resistance of the medium; so that every motion being diminished by these resistances, they must at length languish and cease. MOVING <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">PLANTS</a>. See HEDYSARUM, TREMELLA, and MIMOSA.

MOXA

Pages 439-439

also called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTEMISIA">artemisia</a> Chinensis. Moxa, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mugwort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. It is a soft lanuginous substance, prepared in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> from the young leaves of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mugwort, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them together when thoroughly dried, and rubbing them betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, till only the fine fibres are left. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the leaves of mullein, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, &c., do as well as moxa. In the Eastern countries it is used by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> it on the skin: a little cone of the moxa is laid upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, previously moistened, and set on fire at the top; it burns down with a temperate glowing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and produces a dark-coloured spot, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXFOLIATION">exfoliation</a> of which is promoted by applying a little garlic; the ulcer is left to discharge, or is soon healed, according to the intention in using the moxa. See Artemisia.

MOYLE

Pages 439-440

a learned English writer in the 18th century, descended of a good family in Cornwall, where he was born in 1672. He was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and thence removed to the temple; where he applied himself chiefly to the general, and more noble parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, such as led him to the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In 1697 he had a share with Mr Trenchard in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a pamphlet, intitled, "An argument shewing that a standing <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> is inconsistent with a free government, and absolutely destructive to the constitution of the English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>." He translated Xenophon's discourse upon improving the state of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> member of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in which he always acted an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; applying himself to the improvement and regulation of trade, and the employment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, which has so near a connection with trade. He afterwards retired to his seat at Bake in Cornwall, where he applied himself with vigour to his studies, and died in 1721. In 1726, his works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 2 vols 8vo.

MUCILAGE

Pages 440-440

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, is in general any viscid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> glutinous liquor. Mucilage, also imports the liquor which principally serves to moisten the ligaments and cartilages of the articulations; and is supplied by the mucilaginous glands.

MUCOR

Pages 440-440

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the order of fungi, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 12 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which are, 1. The sporocephalus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> grey round-headed mucor, growing upon rotten wood, and sometimes upon decayed plants and mosses. The stalks of this are generally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; about a line in height, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> each at the top a spherical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> about the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head; its coat or rind is covered with a grey powder, and containing within a black or fulvous spongy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The coat bursts with a ragged, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> margin. 2. The lichenoides, or little, black, pin headed mucor. This species grows in groups near to each other, in chinks of the barks of old trees, and upon old <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>-pales. The stalks are black, about two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in height; bearing each a single head, sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> or treble one, of the size of mustard or poppy seeds, of a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> at first, but when burst often flattish or truncated, and of a black <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The internal powdered down is black, with a tinge of green. 3. The mucodo, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> grey mould, grows on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, plants, and other substances in a putrid state. It grows in clusters; the stalks a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, pellucid, hollow, and cylindrical; supporting each a single globular head, at first transparent, afterwards dark grey; which bursts with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> force, and ejects small round seeds discoverable by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. 4. The glaucus, or grey cluster-headed mould, is found on rotten apples, melons, and other fruits; as also upon decayed wood, and the stalks of wheat. These are of a pellucid grey colour; the stalks generally single, supporting a spherical ball, which, when magnified, appears to be compounded of numerous, fine, moniliform, necklace-like radii. 5. The crustaceus, or fingered mould, is frequent upon corrupted food of various kinds. It is of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> aqueous colour; the stalks single, each supporting at the top four or five necklace-like radii, diverging from the same point or centre. 6. The septicus, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> frothy mucor, is found on the leaves of plants, such as ivy and beech, &c., sometimes upon dry sticks, and frequently upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> or bark in hot-houses. It is of no certain size or figure, but of a fine yellow colour, and a substance resembling at first cream <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a>. In the space of 24 hours it acquires a thin filmy coat, becomes dry, and full of a footy powder adhering to downy threads. The seeds under the microscope appear to be globular. Haller ranks it under a new genus, which he terms fuligo; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, that the plants contained under it are soft, and like <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> at first, but soon change into a black footy powder.

MUCUS

Pages 440-441

a mucilaginous liquor secreted by certain glands, and serving to lubricate many of the internal cavities of the body. In its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state it is generally limpid and colourless; but, from certain causes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> often assume a thick consistence and whitish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like pus. As it is sometimes of very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance in medicine to distinguish these two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> from each other, this was lately proposed as the subject of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-disputation by the Medical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The prize was gained by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Darwin student of medicine from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>. The conclusions drawn from his experiments were, 1. Pus and mucus are both soluble in the vitriolic acid, though in very different proportions, pus being by far least soluble. 2. The addition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> to either of these compounds decomposes it. The mucus thus separated, either swims in the mixture, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> forms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocculi in it; whereas the pus falls to the bottom, and forms, on agitation, an uniform turbid mixture. 3. Pus is diffusible through a diluted vitriolic acid, though mucus is not. The same also occurs with water, or with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. 4. Nitrous acid dissolves both pus and mucus. Water added to the solution of pus produces a precipitate, and the fluid above becomes clear and green, while water and the solution of mucus form a turbid dirty-coloured fluid. 5. Alkaline lixivium dissolves, though sometimes with difficulty, mucus, and generally pus. 6. Water precipitates pus from such a mixture, but does not mucus. 7. Where alkaline lixivium does not dissolve pus, it still distinguishes it from mucus, as it then prevents its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> through water. 8. Coagulable lymph is neither soluble in concentrated nor diluted vitriolic acid. 9. Water produces no change on a solution of serum in alkaline lixivium, until after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> standing, and then only a very slight sediment appears. 10. Corrosive sublimate coagulates mucus, but does not pus. From the above experiments it appears, that strong vitriolic acid and water, diluted vitriolic acid, and caustic alkaline lixivium and water, will serve to distinguish pus from mucus; that the vitriolic acid can separate it from coagulable lymph, and alkaline lixivium from serum. Hence, when a person has any expectorated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of which he wishes to ascertain, let him dissolve it in vitriolic acid, and in caustic alkaline line lixivium. And let him add pure water to both solutions. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there be a fair precipitation in each, he may be assured that some pus is present. But if there be a precipitation in neither, it is a certain test that the mixture is entirely mucus. If the matter cannot be made to dissolve in alkaline lixivium by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> and titration, we have also reason to believe that it is pus.

MUD-INGUANA

Pages 441-441

the American name of a remarkable kind of two-footed amphibious animal found in South Carolina, first observed by Dr Garden of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a>, and afterwards described by John Ellis, F.R.S., in the Phil. Transf. p. 189. "It is found (says he) in swampy and muddy places, by the side of pools, under the trunks of old trees that hang over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. "The lesser one B, which is preserved in spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> about 9 inches in length; and appears to be a very young state of the animal, as we may observe from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> of the tail, and the opercula <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> coverings of the gills being not yet extended to their full size. These opercula, in their present state, consist each of three indented lobes, hiding the gills from view, and are placed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the two feet. These feet appear like little arms and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, each furnished with four fingers, and each finger with a claw. "In the specimen A, which is 31 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, the head is something like an eel, but more compressed; the eyes are small, and placed as those of the eel are. In this they are scarcely visible. This smallness of the eye best suits an animal that lives so much in mud. The nostrils are very plainly to be distinguished; these, with the gills, and remarkable length of the lungs, shew it to be a true amphibious animal. The mouth is small in proportion to the length of the body; but its palate and inside of the lower jaw (see fig. C) are well provided with many rows of pointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>: with this provision of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, added to the sharp exterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> edges of both the upper and under jaw, the animal seems capable of biting and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the hardest kind of food. The skin, which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and full of small scales, resembles thagreen. These scales are of different sizes and shapes, according to their situation; but all appear sunk into its gelatinous surface: those along the back and belly are of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> oval form, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> set together; in the other parts they are round, and more distinct. Both the sides are mottled with small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots, and have two distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> composed of small white streaks <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> along from the feet to the tail. The fin of the tail has no rays, and is no more than an adipose membrane like that of the eel; this fin appears more distinctly in the dry animal than in those that have been preserved in spirits. "The opercula, or coverings to the gills, in dry specimens, appear shrivelled up; but yet we may plainly see that they have been doubly pennated. Under these coverings are the openings to the gills, three on each side, agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the opercula. In the plate, at fig. F, the fins are represented as they appear when just taken out of the water and put into the spirits of wine. "The form of these pennated coverings approach very near to what I have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago observed in the larva, or aquatic state of our English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACERTA">lacerta</a>, known by the name of eel or water-newt, (see fig. D and E), which serve them for coverings to their gills, and for fins to swim with during this state; and which they lose, as well as the fins of their tails, when they change and become <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-animals; as I have observed by keeping them alive for some time myself. "Recollecting these observations on the changes of our lizard, and at the same time the many remarkable changes in frogs, I began to suspect whether this animal might not be the larva state of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kind of lizard; and therefore requested the favour of Dr Solander to examine with me the lacertas in the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, that we might see whether any of the young ones had only two feet; but after carefully going through many kinds, we could plainly discover four feet perfectly formed, even in those that were but just coming out of their eggs. "During this state of uncertainty, I forwarded to Dr Linnaeus of Upsal, at Dr Garden's request, his account of the largest specimen, and at the same time sent him one of the smaller specimens preserved in spirits; desiring his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, for my own as well as Dr Garden's satisfaction. "About the end of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> last I was favoured with an answer from the professor, dated Upsal, Dec. 27th 1765; wherein he says, "I received Dr Garden's very rare two-footed animal with gills and lungs. The animal is probably the larva of some kind of lacerta, which I very much desire that he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> particularly inquire into. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it does not undergo a change, it belongs to the order of nantes, which have both lungs and gills; and if so, it must be a new and very distinct genus, and should most properly have the name of sirex. I cannot possibly describe to you how much this two-footed animal has exercised my thoughts; if it is a larva, he will no doubt find some of them with four feet. It is not an easy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to reconcile it to the larva of the lizard tribe, its fingers being furnished with claws; all the larvas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">lizards</a> that I know are without them, (digestis mutatis). Then, also the branchiae, or gills, are not to be met with in the aquatic salamanders, which are probably the larvas of lizards. Further, the croaking noise or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> it makes, does not agree with the larvas of those animals; nor does the situation of the anus. So that there is no creature that ever I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, that I long so much to be convinced of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, as what this will certainly turn out to be. "P.S. In a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> lately received from Dr Garden, he mentions one remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this animal, which is, that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> endeavouring to kill one of them by dashing it against the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, it broke into three or four pieces: he further says, that he has had an opportunity of seeing many of them lately of a much larger size, and that he never saw one with more than two feet; so that he is fully convinced that it is quite a new genus of the animal-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>."

MUFFLE

Pages 441-441

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a vessel much used in some metallurgic operations. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it represents an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> vault, the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is closed by a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, and the lower part, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of which, is a rectangular plane. It is a little oven that is placed horizontally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> and enamelling furnaces, so that its open side corresponds with the door of the fire-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. Under this arched oven small cupels, or crucibles, are placed; and the substances contained are thus exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without contact.

MUG

Pages 441-442

the mullet; in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominates. The lips are membranaceous, the inferior one being carinated inwards; they have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the branchiostegal membrane has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> crooked rays; the opercula are smooth and round; and the body is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rays in the back-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a>. The mullet is justly ranked by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> among the piscis litterales, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> those that prefer the shores to the full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; they are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty on several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> coasts of our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and haunt in particular those small bays that have influxes of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They come in great shoals, and keep rooting like hogs in the sand or mud, leaving their traces in form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round holes. They are very cunning; and when surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>, the whole shoal frequently escapes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> over it; for when one takes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, the others are sure to follow. This circumstance is observed by Oppian; who also informs us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these fishes fail to get over at the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, they never attempt a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> as if they resigned themselves to their fate. Mr Pennant says he is uncertain whether this last observation holds good or not; however, Oppian had good opportunity of examining those fish, as they sometimes swarm on the coasts of the Mediterranean. Near Martegues, in the south of France, abundance of mullets are taken in weirs made of reeds placed in the shallows. Of the tails of the males, which are there called allantons, and of the roes of females, which are called botaris, is made botargo. The materials are taken out entire, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> for four or five hours, then pressed a little between two boards or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, washed, and at last dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> for 13 or 14 days. This fish was sometimes made the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of a horrible <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for unfortunate gallants. It was used both at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome; but it is very doubtful whether it was a legal punishment or not. By Horace it is mentioned in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: Difficile tenacem fugitum efi, et pede nudo: No nummi percunt, sed Pyga, et demoque fuma. Satyr. II. lib. i. 131. The mullet is an excellent fish for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, but at present not a fashionable one.

MUGWORT

Pages 442-442

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a>. An infusion of this plant in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a bath made of it, has been always esteemed an emmenagogue, and useful in difficult parturition. The leaves, when young and tender, are frequently made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the Highlanders of Scotland as a pot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-people in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> drink a decoction of them for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>.

MUID

Pages 442-442

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the French, for things dry. The muid is no real vessel used as a measure, but an ellimation of several other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; as the septier, mine, minot, bulbel, &c. Muid, is also one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> casks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> regular vessels used in France, to put wine and other liquors in. The muid of wine is divided into two demi-muids, four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> muids, and eight half-quarter muids, containing 36 septiers.

MULATTO

Pages 442-442

a name given in the Indies to those who are begotten by a negro <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> on an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> woman, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by an Indian man on a negro woman.

MULE

Pages 442-443

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a mongrel kind of quadruped, usually <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> between an ass and a mare, and sometimes between a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and a she-ass; but the signification of the word is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> extended to every kind of animal produced by a mixture of two different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. There are two kinds of these animals; one from the he-ass and mare, the other from the horse and the she-ass. We call them indifferently mules, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> distinguished them by proper appellations. The first kind are the best and most esteemed; as being larger, stronger, and having least of the ass in their disposition. The largest and stoutest asses, and the fairest and finest mares, are chosen in those countries where these creatures are most in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; as in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. In the last especially, they succeeded in having very stately mules from the size of their mares, some of them 16, and some 17 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which are very serviceable as sumpter-mules in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But, since the Low Countries are no longer under the dominion of Spain, they breed fewer mules. These creatures are very much commended for their being stronger, faster footed, going easier, being more cheaply maintained, MULE tained, and lasting longer than horses. They are commonly of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> quite black, with that shining lilt along the back and across the shoulders, which distinguishes asses. In former times they were much more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than at present; being often brought over in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> by the Italian prelates. They <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> longest in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of millers; and are yet in use among them in some places, on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> loads they carry on their back. As they are capable of being trained for riding, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> burdens, and for draught, there is no doubt that they might be usefully employed in many different services. But they are commonly found to be vicious, stubborn, and obdurate to a proverb; which whether it occasions or is produced by the ill usage they meet with, is a point not easily settled. Whatever may be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of asses, it is allowed that mules are larger, fairer, and more serviceable in mild than in warm climates. In the British American colonies, both on the continent and in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, but especially in the latter, they are much used and esteemed; so that they are frequently sent to them from hence, suffer less in the passage, and die much seldom than horses, and commonly yield, when they arrive, no considerable profit. It hath commonly been asserted, that animals produced by the mixture of two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> species, are incapable of generating, and thus perpetuating the monstrous breed; but this, we are informed by M. Buffon, is now discovered to be a mistake. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> says he, tells us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> engenders with the mare, and that the junction produces an animal which the Greeks call himur, or ginnaus. He likewise remarks, that the she-mule easily conceives, but seldom brings the foetus to perfection. But the most remarkable and well attested instance of this fact, is mentioned in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> read by M. d'Alembert before the academy of sciences, which informed him that a she-mule in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Domingo had brought forth a foal. The fact was attested by persons of the most unquestionable veracity; and other instances, though not so well authenticated, are adduced by our author. We may therefore, continues M. Buffon, consider it as an established fact, that the he-mule can <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a>, and the she-mule produce. Like other animals, they have a seminal liquor, and all the organs necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. But mongrel animals are always less fertile and more tardy than those of a pure species. Besides, mules have never produced in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> climates, seldom in warm regions, and still more seldom in temperate countries. Hence their barrenness, without being <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, may be regarded as positive; since their productions are so rare, that a few examples can only be collected. The translator of Buffon's works, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> on the passage above-quoted, hath given a remarkable and well authenticated instance of the prolific powers of a she-mule in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scotland. Having heard that a mule, belonging to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Tullo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in Auchtertyre, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Forfar, had some years ago brought forth a foal, he transmitted a few queries to be put to Mr Tullo; and requested that his answers might be legally attested before a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. This request was cheerfully complied with; and the following is an exact copy of the queries, answers, and attestations. Interrogatories to be put to Mr Tullo tenant in Auchtertyre, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Newtyle, and county of Forfar, with his answers thereto. 1st. Had you ever a she-mule? At what <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>? Is it true that the mule had a foal? At what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> was she covered; and when did the foal? Answered by Mr Tullo: That he bought a she-mule about 20 years ago; that she was constantly in season for a horse; that, about some years thereafter, he gave her a horse; and that she thereafter gave him a foal, about the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The mule's price was £1.5s. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>. 2nd. What was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the foal? Was there any thing particular in its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>? Answer: The foal was exactly the colour of its mother, inclined to black, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> head, big ears, and small tail; and the declarant thinks, had its head been weighed when foaled, it would have weighed nearly as much as its body. 3rd. How <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> was the animal allowed to live? Answer: The next <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the mule foaled, it was sent, with its mother, to the Loch of Lundie, in order to let the foal die, as the declarant could not want the mule's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and the mother seemed not fond of the foal: That it was accordingly left, and next day came to Auchtertyre, about two miles distance, over a hill, with the cattle of Auchtertyre, that had been grazing near to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and was drowned in a ditch the day following. 4th. Was its skin preserved, or the head, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the skeleton? Could any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof be still found? Answered: Neither the skin, nor any part of the skeleton was preserved, nor can now be had; though the declarant has often regretted the not preserving the foal, as its mother always performed any work that a horse of £1. value could do. 5th. Is the mother still alive? What is her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>? Answer: The mother died about eight years ago, of an epidemic cold that was raging among the horses in this country: The mule had little or no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> after foaling, and the foal got some cow's milk: And this is all that he remembers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. David Tullo. Auchtertyre, 4th February 1780. We James Small tenant in Burnmouth, and Robert Ramsay tenant in Newtyle, hereby certify, That we have often seen the mule above described; and we know that she had a foal, as is narrated by David Tullo. James Small. Rob. Ramsay. Ballantyne <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, 4th February 1780. The within interrogatories were put to David Tullo tenant in Auchtertyre, asent he mule he had, and the foal she produced; to which he gave the answers subjoined to each query, and signed them; as did James Small and Robert Ramsay, attesting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> thereof, in presence of George Watson, J.P. The original attestation is in the possession of the translator; and he lately transmitted notarial or authenticated copies of it to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Buffon, and to Thomas Pennant, Esq; of Downing, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>.

MULIER

Pages 443-443

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies the lawful issue born in wedlock, though begotten before. The mulier is

MULL

Pages 443-444

one of the Western <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of Scotland, about 24 Scots miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and as much in breadth. It is in general rocky and barren, not producing a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn for the inhabitants; but about 1800 head of cattle are annually exported. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was originally <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the dominions of the Lords of the Isles; but in after-times it became part of the possessions of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and valiant family of Macleans, who still retain one-half. The other is the litigated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, whose ancestor possessed himself of it in 1674, on account of a debt; but after the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> had made an adjudication in his favour, he was obliged to support their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> by force of arms. Mull of Cantire, the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cantire or Mull, in the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, in the west of Scotland. Mull of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, the south cape or promontory of all Scotland, in the county of Galloway, on the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>.

MULLER

Pages 444-444
or Regiomontanus (John), a celebrated astronomer of the 15th century, was born at Koningshoven in Franconia in 1436, and acquired great reputation by publishing an abridgment of Ptolemy's Almagest, which had been begun by Parback. He went to Rome to perfect himself in the Greek tongue, and to see the cardinal Basso; but finding some faults in the Latin translations of George de Trebizond, that translator's son assassinated him in a second journey he made to Rome in 1476, where Pope Sixtus IV. had provided for him the archbishopric of Ratibon, and had sent for him to reform the calendar. Others say that he died of the plague.

MULLERAS

Pages 444-444

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, seated 38 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, upon a canal which joins the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> and the Spree. This canal is 15 miles in length, 10 yards in breadth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in depth. It was eight years in making; and since that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> have carried on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 50'. N. Lat. 52° 21'.

MULLET

Pages 444-444
or Mellet, in heraldry, a bearing in form of the rowel of a spur, which it originally represented. See Plate CXLIV.

MULLUS

Pages 444-444
