in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. The barbus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> mullet, was highly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and bore an exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price. The capricious epicures of Horace's days valued it in proportion to its size; not that the larger were more delicious, but that they were more difficult to be got. The price that was given for one in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Juvenal and Pliny, is a striking <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and extravagance of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>: \[ \text{Mullum <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> millibus emit} \] \[ \text{Aquaeum fons milibus sellaria libit.} \] \[ \text{Juv. Sat. IV.} \] The lavish flares Six thousand pieces for a mullet gave, A sestertius for each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. But Asinius Celcr, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of consular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, gave a still more unconceivable sum; for he did not scruple bestowing 8000 nummi, or 64l. 11s. 8d. for a fish of so small a size as the mullet: for, according to Horace, a mullet trilobris, or one of 3 lb., was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rarity; so that Juvenal's spark must have had a great bargain in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what Celcr had. But Seneca says, that it was not worth a farthing except it died in the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of your guest: that such was the luxury of the times, that there were flows even in the eating-rooms, so that the fish could at once be brought from under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and placed on it: that they put the mullets in transparent vases, that they might be entertained with the various changes of its rich <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> while it lay expiring. Apicius, a wonderful genius for luxurious inventions, first <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon the method of suffocating them in the exquisite Carthaginian pickle, and afterwards procured a rich sauce from their livers. This is the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> whom Pliny, in another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, honours with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Nepotum omnium altissimus gurges; an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> too forcible to be rendered in our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Mr Pennant has heard of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> being taken on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland, but had no opportunity of examining it; and whether it is found in the west of England with the other species or variety, we are not at this time informed. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALVIANUS">Salvianus</a> makes it a distinct species, and says that it is of a purple colour, striped with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and that it did not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> exceed a palm in length: no wonder then that such a prodigy as one of 6 lb. should so captivate the fancy of the Roman epicure. Mr Ray establishes some other distinctions, such as the first dorsal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> rays, and the colour of that fin, the tail, and the pectoral fins, being of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> purple.

MULTCT

Pages 442-442

a fine of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> laid upon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has committed some fault <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanor.

MULTIPLE

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which comprehends some other several times: thus 6 is a multiple of 2, and 12 is a multiple of 6, 4, and 3; comprehending the first twice, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> thrice, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">Action</a> of MULTIPLEPOINDING, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, n° cxxxiii. 24.

MULTIPLICATION

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, is a rule by which any given <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> may be speedily increased, according to any proposed number of times.

MULTIPLICATOR

Pages 444-444
or MULTIPLIER, in arithmetic, the number by which any other is multiplied, or the number of times it is supposed to be taken. See ARITHMETIC, n° 10.

MULTIPLICATUS FLOS

Pages 444-445

a luxuriant flower, whose petals are multiplied so as to exclude a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stamina. A multiplied luxuriant flower differs from a full one, the highest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of luxuriance, in that the petals of the latter are so multiplied as to exclude all the stamens; whereas those of the former are only repeated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> multiplied, two, three, or four times, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of only a small part of the essential organs.

MULTIPLYING-GLASS

Pages 445-445

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, a glass wherewith objects appear increased in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. See (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> subjoined to) Optics.

MULTPLICAND

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to be multiplied by another. See there, n° 10.

MULTURE

Pages 445-445

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of grain paid to the proprietor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tacksmen of a mill, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>.

MULVIA

Pages 445-445

a river of Barbary in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, and divides the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> from that of Algiers, and then falls into the Mediterranean, to the westward of Marjalquivir.

MUM

Pages 445-445

a kind of malt-liquor much drunk in Germany, and chiefly brought from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for making it. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> mum, as recorded in the town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is as follows: Take 63 gallons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> that has been boiled till one-third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is consumed, and brew it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> bushels of wheaten malt, one bushel of oat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and one bushel of ground beans. When it is tunned, the hoghead must not be filled too full at first: as soon as it begins to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, put into it three pounds of the inner rind of fir, one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the tops of fir and beach, three handfuls of cardus benedictus, a handful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> two of the flower of rosa folis: add burnet, betony, marjoram, avena, pennyroyal, and wild thyme, of each an handful and an half; of elder-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, two handfuls or more; seeds of cardamom bruised, 30 ounces; barberries bruised, one ounce: when the liquor has worked a while, put the herbs and seeds into the vessel; and, after they are added, let it work over as little as possible; then fill it up: lastly, when it is stopped, put into the hoghead ten new-laid eggs unbroken; stop it up <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it at two years end. The brewers of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, instead of the inner rind of fir, use cardomom, ginger, and saffraan; and also add elicampane, madder, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> sanders. Mum, on being imported, pays for every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> £1.5s.

MUMMY

Pages 445-445

among gardeners, a kind of wax used in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the roots of trees, made in the following manner: Take one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> pitch, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound of turpentine; put them together into an earthen pot, and let them on fire in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, holding something in your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to cover and quench the mixture in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which is to be alternately lighted and quenched till all the nitrous and volatile parts be evaporated. To this a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wax is to be added; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is then to be set by for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. MUMPS. See MEDICINE, no 526.

MUNICH

Pages 445-446

furnished and adorned in the most magnificent manner, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, gilding, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and paintings. It contains an amazing collection of jewels, antiquities, and curiosities. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is 118 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 52 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and the stair-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> leading to it, from top to bottom, of marble and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. In the hall of antiquities are 345 busts and statues of jasper and porphyry, bronzes and marble. In this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> also is a library, containing a vast collection of books, and many valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, in most languages, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>; and a chamber of rarities, among which is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of a brave, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> affable, who is said to have committed 345 murders with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and to have been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> in, or privy to, 400 more. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> in the chapel contains also a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pictures, precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, medals, vessels of gold and silver, &c. Among other curiosities, here is a cherry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> with 140 heads distinctly engraved upon it. The gardens of the palace are also very fine, and it is said a secret passage leads from it to all the churches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> in the town. There is a great number of other fine buildings in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, public and private, particularly the riding-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, town-house, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>-room, the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice for tournaments, the churches, convents, fountains, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, particularly velvet, woollen cloths, and tapestry; and it has two annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, at which great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, wine, &c. are sold. The streets are broad and regular; and most of the houses well built, and painted on the outside. The market-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is extremely beautiful. Mr Keyser says, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>-maids at the great inns here, on holidays, wear a silver chain round their necks, consisting of three rows; and that their breasts are likewise laced with two other chains of the same metal. He further observed, that it was a general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to place a green garland, on a bundle of straw, before every house containing the corpse of an unmarried person. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salutation here, and in the other catholic countries of Germany, is, Praised be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; and the answer returned, For ever amen: two popes having granted an <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of 100 days each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it. Not far from Munich are four other palaces, with fine gardens, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, viz., those of Schleissheim, Nymphenburg, Dauchau, and Starnberg. The first and last are about three leagues from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> about half a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>; and the third about two, at a market-town of the same name.

MUNICIPAL

Pages 446-446

among us, is applied to the laws that obtain in any particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. And those are called municipal officers who are elected to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of cities, to maintain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges, and to preserve order and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> among the citizens; such as mayors, sheriffs, consuls, &c.

MUNITION

Pages 446-446

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> with which a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is furnished, in order for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that which follows a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for its subsistence.

MUNITION SHIPS

Pages 446-446

are those that have stores on board in order to supply a fleet of men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In an engagement, all the munition-ships and victuallers attending the fleet take their station in the rear of all the rest; they are not to engage in the fight, but to attend such directions as are sent them by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>.

MUNSTER

Pages 446-447

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bishopric of the same name and of all Westphalia, stands at the conflux of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> with the Ems, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 49'. N. Lat. 52° 0. It is of a circular form, Munychia, form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and well fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. It hath a fine citadel called the Brille, erected by a bishop named Bernard van Galen in order to awe the burghers. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> now elect the bishop; but till the beginning of the 13th century he was nominated by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. This city has been rendered famous by three remarkable transactions: 1. By the peace concluded here in 1648, which put an end to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 30 years; occasioned by the persecuting spirit of bigotted papists, who chose rather to plunge their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> into all the calamities of war than allow <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. By this peace, however, they consented, much against their inclinations, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a toleration. 2. By the disorders and disturbances occasioned here in 1553, by a parcel of enthusiasts called the Munster <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, who, headed by a taylor, called John of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, turned out the magistrates, and took possession of the city, where they perpetrated the most horrid villanies and cruelties. 3. For the noble, though unsuccessful, efforts it made in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of its liberties against the tyranny and usurpation of the above-mentioned turbulent and bloody-minded bishop, Bernard van Galen. In this city are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, many of them stately piles, and surrounded with beautiful gardens.

MUNYCHIA

Pages 447-448
or Munychius Portus (anc. geogr.) a village and port of Athens, nearer to the city, less than and fortified in the same manner with the Piraeus, to the east of which it lay, or between it and the promontory Sunium, at the mouth of the Ilissus. Strabo says it was an eminence in form of a peninsula, at the foot of which stood three harbours, anciently encompassed with a wall, taking within its extent the Piraeus and other harbours, full of docks, with the temple of Diana Munychia, (Pausanias); taking its name from Mynichus, the founder of the temple, (Strabo, Plutarch). MURÆNA, or Eel, in ichthyology; a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of apodes. The head is smooth; there are ten rays in the membrane of the gills; the eyes are covered with a common skin; and the body is cylindrical and slimy. There are seven species, distinguished by their fins, tail, &c. The most remarkable are, 1. The anguilla, or common eel, is very frequent in all our fresh waters, ponds, ditches, and rivers; according to Mr Pennant, it is the most universal of fish, yet is scarce ever found in the Danube, though very common in the lakes and rivers of Upper Austria. The eel is very singular in many things relating to its href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, and in some respects borders on the nature of the reptile tribe. It is known to quit its element, and during night to wander along the meadows, not only in order to change its habitation, but also for the sake of prey, feeding on snails as it passes along. During winter it beds itself deep in the mud, and continues in a state like the serpent-kind. It is very impatient of cold, and will eagerly take shelter in a wisp of straw flung into a pond in severe weather, which has sometimes been practised as a method of taking them. Albertus affirms, that he has known eels to take shelter in a hay-rick; yet all perished through excess of cold. It has been observed in a river of England called Munro, the Nyme, there is a variety of small eel, with a lesser head and narrower mouth than the common kind, that is found in clutters in the bottom of the river, and is called the bed-eel; these are sometimes roused up by the violent floods, and are never found at that time with meat in their stomach. There is scarce any animal the generation of which has puzzled the learned more than this. Aristotle first broached an opinion that eels were of no sex, nor did propagate their species like other animals, but were equivocally gendered of the mud; and as wild and absurd a system as this is, there have not been wanting many, even in these latter and more enlightened times, who have given into it. But there is now no room to doubt that all animals are produced by the copulation of parents like themselves; and the finding of eels in new ponds is easily accounted for from the above-mentioned circumstance of their migration. Dr Plot, and many others, have given accounts of whole droves of them leaving one ditch or pond to go to another. Though the learned world at this time generally allows that eels are produced like other animals, by parents of their own kind, yet there remain many doubts about the manner in which the generation is performed. Some allow the eels to be, like the generality of other animals, of different sexes in the different individuals; and others affirming that they are all hermaphrodites, each having the parts of generation of both sexes. Rondeletius affirms that they are of both sexes; and Mr Allan, who has given a very curious paper concerning them in the Philosophical Transactions, is of the same opinion; and both say, that the parts of the sexes may be discovered on a careful inspection; and some are found to be males, and others females; but these parts are, in both sexes, they say, buried in a large quantity of fat; and they are of opinion, that hence proceeded the mistake of Aristotle and his followers, who, not being able to find those parts, concluded that they did not exist at all. Among those who allow the eel to be produced, like other animals, from animal-parents which have the sexes, some are of opinion that they are viviparous, and others that they are oviparous: but Mr Chartwynd seems to have determined this controversy by observing, that if the aperture under the belly of the eel, which looks red in the month of May, be cut open at that time, the young eels will be seen to come forth alive after the operation. Mr Lewenhoeck says, that he found an uterus in every eel he examined; and therefore concludes, that they are hermaphrodites: and he supposes that they have no male parts of generation like those of other animals; but that the office of these is performed by a liquor analogous to the male seed of animals, which is contained in certain glands, situated on the inside of the uterus itself. Eels have sometimes been met with in recent ponds, made at such a distance from any other water that we cannot reasonably suppose them to have migrated thither over land. But in these cases there is reason to believe, that the ponds have been supplied with them by the aquatic fowl of prey, in the same manner as vegetation is spread by many of the land-birds, either These fish are extremely voracious, and destructive to the fry of others. No fish lives so long out of water as the eel; and it is extremely tenacious of life, inasmuch that its parts will move a considerable time after they are flayed and cut in pieces. They vary much in their colours, from a footy hue to a light olive green; and those which are called silver eels have their bellies white, and a remarkable clearness throughout. Besides these, there is a variety of this fish known in the river Thames by the name of grigs, and about Oxford by that of grigs or glats. There are scarce ever seen near Oxford in the winter; but appear in spring, and bite readily at the hook, which common eels in that neighbourhood will not. They have a larger head, a blunter nose, thicker skin, and less fat, than the common sort; neither are they so much esteemed, nor do they often exceed three or four pounds in weight.—Common eels grow to a large size, sometimes weighing 15 or 20 pounds; but that is extremely rare. Mr Dale indeed, in the Philosophical Transactions, and some others, bring instances of eels much exceeding that size; but Mr Pennant suspects them to have been congers, since the enormous fish they describe have all been taken at the mouths of the Thames or Medway. The Romans held eels very cheap, probably on account of their likeness to snakes. On the contrary, the luxurious Sybarites were so fond of these fish, as to exempt from tribute of every kind those persons who sold them. 2. The conger, or conger-eel, grows to a vast size. Dr Borlase informs us, that they are sometimes taken near Mount's-bay of 100 lb. weight; and Mr Pennant assures us, that he has heard of some taken near Scarborough that were 10 feet and a half long, and 18 inches in circumference in the thickest part. They differ from the common eel in the following particulars: 1. Their colour in general is more dark. 2. Their eyes much larger in proportion. 3. The irides of a bright silvery colour. 4. The lower jaw is rather shorter than the upper. 5. The side-line is broad, whitish, and marked with a row of small spots. 6. The edges of the dorsal and anal fins are black. 7. They have more bones than the common eel, especially along the back quite to the head. 8. They grow to a much larger size. As to the distinction that Mr Ray and other writers make of the small beards at the end of the nose, Mr Pennant thinks it not to be depended on, being sometimes found in both kinds, and sometimes entirely wanting. Probably they generate like the fresh-water species. Innumerable quantities of what are supposed to be their fry, come up the Severn about the month of April, preceding the thads, which it is conjectured migrate into that river to feed on them; they are called elvers. They swarm during their season, and are taken in a kind of sieve made of hair-cloth, fixed to a long pole; the fisherman standing on the edge of the water during the tide, puts in his net as far as he can reach, and drawing it out again, takes multitudes at every sweep, and will take as many during one tide as will fill a buttel. They are dressed, and reckoned very delicate. Congers are extremely voracious, preying on other fish, and on crabs at the time they have lost their shell and are in a soft state. They and eels in general are also particularly fond of carcases of any kind, being frequently found lodged in such as are accidentally taken up. These fish are an article of commerce in Cornwall; numbers are taken on that coast, and exported to Spain and Portugal, particularly to Barcelona. Some are taken by a single hook and line, but (because that way is tedious, and does not answer the expense of time and labour) they are chiefly caught by butlers, which are strong lines 500 feet long, with 60 hooks, each eight feet asunder, baited with pilchards or mackerel; the butlers are sunk to the ground by a stone fastened to them: sometimes such a number of these are tied together as to reach a mile. The fishermen are very fearful of a large conger, lest it should endanger their legs by clinging round them; they therefore kill them as soon as possible by striking them on the navel. They are afterwards cured in this manner: They are slit, and hung on a frame till they dry, having a considerable quantity of fat, which it is necessary should exude before they are fit for use. It is remarkable that a conger of 100 weight will waste by drying to 24 lb.; the people therefore prefer the smallest, possibly because they are sooner cured. During the process there is a considerable stench; and it is said, that in the fishing villages the poultry are fed with the maggots that drop from the fish. The Portuguese and Spaniards use those dried congers after they have been ground into a powder, to thicken and give a relish to their soups. They are sold for about 40 shillings the quintal, which weighs 126 lb. A fishery of congers, says Mr Pennant, would be of great advantage to the inhabitants of the Hebrides. Perhaps they would at first undertake it with repugnancy, from their absurd aversion to the eel kind. MURAL CROWNS. See Crown.

MURATORI

Pages 448-452

a learned and celebrated Italian writer, born at Vignoles, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, in 1672. He early discovered an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> fondness for the learned languages and sciences; and this was seconded by an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. After having completed his first studies, he embraced the state of an ecclesiastic; and applied himself to polite literature, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, antiquities, and other sciences; by which means he became in a manner universally learned. He was scarce 22 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> when he was made librarian of the Ambrosian library at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. In 1700 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, his sovereign, recalled him, and made him his librarian, and keeper of the archives of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. Muratori discharged this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> employment during the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and had no other benefit than the provostship of Santa <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> del Pompis. He acquired the esteem of the learned throughout <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who had recourse to him for the lights they wanted. He became an associate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a> of the Ar- The killing may be by poisoning, striking, slaying, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DROWNING">drowning</a>, and a thousand other forms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> may be overcome. Of these the most detestable of all is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>; because it can of all others be the least prevented, either by manhood <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> forethought. And therefore, by the flat, 22 Hen. VIII, c. 9, it was made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; and a more grievous and lingering kind of death was inflicted on it than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law allowed; namely, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> to death; but this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> did not live <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, being repealed by 1 Edw. VI, c. 12. There was also, by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> common law, one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of killing held to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, which may be dubious at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as there hath not been an instance wherein it has been held to be murder for many ages past, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> false witness against another, with an express premeditated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to take away his life, so as the innocent person be condemned and executed. The Gothic laws punished in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> both the judge, the witnesses, and the prosecutor; and among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the lex Cornelia de fictitiis, punished the false witness with death, as being guilty of a species of assassination. And there is no doubt but this is equally murder in furo conscientiae as killing with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; though the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> law (to avoid the danger of deterring witnesses from giving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> prosecutions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it must be at the peril of their own lives) has not yet punished it as such. If a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, however, does such an act, of which the probable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> may be, and eventually is, death; such killing may be murder, although no stroke be struck by himself, and no killing may be primarily intended: as was the case of the unnatural son who exposed his sick father to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> against his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, by reason whereof he died; and of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a>, who laid her child under leaves in an orchard, where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a> struck it, and killed it. So too, if a man hath a beast that is used to do mischief; and he, knowing it, suffers it to go abroad, and it kills a man; even this is manslaughter in the owner: but if he had purposely turned it loose, though barely to frighten people, and make what is called sport, it is with us (as in the Jewish law) as much murder as if he had incited a bear or a dog to worry them. If a physician or surgeon gives his patient a potion or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> to cure him, which, contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, kills him, this is neither murder nor manslaughter, but misadventure; and he shall not be punished criminally, however liable he might formerly have been to a civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for neglect or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>; but it hath been holden, that if it be not a regular physician or surgeon who administers the medicine, or performs the operation, it is manslaughter at the least. Yet Sir Matthew Hale very justly questions the law of this determination; since physic and salves were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before licensed physicians and surgeons: wherefore he treats this doctrine as spurious, and fitted only to gratify and flatter licentiates and doctors in physic; though it may be of use to make people cautious and wary how they meddle too much in so dangerous an employment. In order also to make the killing murder, it is requisite that the party die within a year and a day after the stroke received, or cause of death administered; in the computation of which the whole day upon which the hurt was done shall be reckoned the first. Further: The person killed must be "a reasonable..." Murderable creature in being, and under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s peace," at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the killing. Therefore to kill an alien, a Jew, or an outlaw, who are all under the king's peace or protection, is as much murder as to kill the most regular-born Englishman; except he be an alien enemy, in time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. To kill a child in its mother's womb, is now no murder, but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> misprision: but if the child be born alive, and die by reason of the potion or bruises it received in the womb, it seems, by the better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, to be murder in such as administered or gave them. As to the murder of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>-children, see Bastard. 4. Lastly, the killing must be committed "with malice aforethought," to make it the crime of murder. This is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> criterion which now distinguishes murder from other killings: and this malice prepense, malitia praecogitata, is not so properly spite or malevolence to the deceased in particular, as any evil design in general; the dictate of a wicked, depraved, and malignant heart; an disposition à faire un <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> chose: and it may be either express, or implied, in law. Express malice is when one, with a sedate deliberate mind and formed design, doth kill another: which formed design is evidenced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances discovering that inward intention; as lying in wait, antecedent menaces, former grudges, and concerted schemes to do him some bodily harm. This takes in the case of deliberate duelling, where both parties meet avowedly with an intent to murder: thinking it their duty, as gentlemen, and claiming it as their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, to wanton with their own lives and those of their fellow-creatures; without any warrant or authority from any power either divine or human, but in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the laws both of God and man: and therefore the law has justly fixed the crime and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of murder on them, and on their seconds also. Yet it requires such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> valour to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> the dread of even undeserved contempt, arising from the false notions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> too generally received in Europe, that the strongest prohibitions and penalties of the law will never be entirely effectual to eradicate this unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, till a method be found out of compelling the original aggressor to make some other satisfaction to the affronted party, which the world shall esteem equally reputable as that which is now given at the hazard of the life and fortune, as well of the person insulted, as of him who hath given the insult. Also, if even upon a sudden provocation one beats another in a cruel and unlawful manner, so that he dies, tho' he did not intend his death, yet he is guilty of murder by express malice; i.e., by an express evil design, the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of malitia. As when a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>-keeper tied a boy that was stealing wood to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s tail, and dragged him along the park; when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> corrected his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> with an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and a schoolmaster flamed on his scholar's belly, so that each of the sufferers died; these were justly held to be murders, because the correction being excessive, and such as could not proceed but from a bad heart, it was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a deliberate act of slaughter. Neither shall he be guilty of a less crime who kills another in consequence of such a wilful act as shews him to be an enemy to mankind in general; as going deliberately, and with an intent to do mischief, upon a horse used to strike, or coolly discharging a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> among a multitude of people. So if a man resolves to kill the next man he meets, and does kill him, it is murder, although he knew him not; for this is universal malice. And if two or more come together to do an unlawful act against the king's peace, of which the probable consequence might be bloodshed; as to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> a man, to commit a riot, or to rob a park, and one of them kills a man; it is murder in them all, because of the unlawful act, the malitia praecogitata, or evil intended beforehand. Also in many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where no malice is expressed, the law will imply it: as, where a man wilfully poisons another, in such a deliberate act the law presumes malice, though no particular enmity can be proved. And if a man kills another suddenly, without any, or without a considerable provocation, the law implies malice; for no person, unless of an abandoned heart, would be guilty of such an act upon a slight or no apparent cause. No affront, by words, or gestures only, is a sufficient provocation, so as to excuse or extenuate such acts of violence as manifestly endanger the life of another. But if the person so provoked had unfortunately killed the other, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> him in such a manner as showed only an intent to chastise and not to kill him, the law so far considers the provocation of contumelious behaviour, as to adjudge it only manslaughter, and not murder. In like manner, if one kills an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, either civil or criminal, in the execution of his duty, or any of his affiants endeavouring to conferve the peace, or any private person endeavouring to suppress an affray or apprehend a felon, knowing his authority or the intention with which he interferes, the law will imply malice, and the killer shall be guilty of murder. And if one intends to do another felony, and undesignedly kills a man, this is also murder. Thus it one shoots at A and misses him, but kills B, this is murder; because of the previous felonious intent, which the law transfers from one to the other. The same is the case, where one lays poison for A; and B, against whom the prisoner had no malicious intent, takes it, and it kills him; this is likewise murder. So also, if one gives a woman with child a medicine to procure <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, and it operates so violently as to kill the woman, this is murder in the person who gave it. It were endless to go through all the cases of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>, which have been adjudged, either expressly or impliedly, malicious: these therefore may suffice as a specimen; and we may take it for a general rule, that all homicide is malicious, and of course amounts to murder, unless where justified by the command or permission of the law; excused on a principle of accident or self-preservation; or alleviated into manslaughter, by being either the involuntary consequence of some act, not strictly lawful, or (if voluntary) occasioned by some sudden and sufficiently violent provocation. And all these circumstances of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>, excuse, or alleviation, it is incumbent upon the prisoner to make out, to the satisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a>: the latter of whom are to decide whether the circumstances alleged are proved to have actually existed; the former, how far they extend to take away or mitigate the guilt. For all homicide is presumed to be malicious, until the contrary appeareth upon evidence. The punishment of murder, and that of manslaughter, slaughter, were formerly one and the same; both having the benefit of clergy: so that none but unlearned persons, who least knew the guilt of it, were put to death for this enormous crime. But now, by several statutes, the benefit of clergy is taken away from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> through malice prepense, their abettors, procurers, and counsellors. In atrocious cases it was frequently usual for the court to direct the murderer, after execution, to be hung upon a gibbet in chains near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the fact was committed; but this was no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the legal judgment; and the like is still sometimes practised in the case of notorious thieves. This, being quite contrary to the express command of the mafial law, seems to have been borrowed from the civil law; which, besides the terror of the example, gives also another reason for this practice, viz. that it is a comfortable sight to the relations and friends of the deceased. But now, in England, it is enacted by statute 25 Geo. I. c. 37. that the judge, before whom any person is found guilty of wilful murder, shall pronounce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> immediately after conviction, unless he sees cause to postpone it; and shall in passing sentence direct him to be executed on the next day but one (unless the same shall be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, and then on the Monday following), and that his body be delivered to the surgeons to be dissected and anatomized; and that the judge may direct his body to be afterwards hung in chains, but in no wise to be buried without dissection. And, during the short but awful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between sentence and execution, the prisoner shall be kept alone, and sustained with only <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. But a power is allowed to the judge, upon good and sufficient cause, to respite the execution, and relax the other restraints of this act. See further, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">Parricide</a>, and Petit Tresou. Murderers, or Murdering Pieces, in a ship, are small pieces of ordnance, either of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or iron, which have chambers put in at their breeches. They are used at the bulk-heads of the fore-castle, half-deck, or steerage, in order to clear the deck, on the ship's being boarded by an enemy. Murena. See Murena. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURENGERS">Murengers</a>, two officers of great antiquity in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, annually chosen out of the aldermen, to see that the walls are kept in repair, and to receive a certain toll and custom for the maintenance thereof. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a> (Mark Anthony Francis) in Latin Muretus, was born at Muret, near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIMOGES">Limoges</a>, in 1526. He acquired a perfect knowledge of the Greek and Latin tongues without any instructor, and became one of the most learned men of his time. After having taught some time in Provence, he was made a professor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> with Turnebus and Buchanan. In 1554, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and in 1563 was professor of law, philosophy, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, at Rome, where he died in 1585. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Excellent notes on Terence, Horace, Catullus, Tacitus, Cicero, Sallust, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Xenophon, &c. 2. Orations. 3. Varia Lectiones, Poemata, Hymni Sacri. 4. Disputationes in Lib. I. Pandectarum, de Origine Juris, &c. 5. Epistolae, Juvenilia Carmina, &c. Most of Muret's works have been printed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> edition of 1737; in 5 vols 8vo. Murex, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes testacea. This animal is of the snail-kind: the shell consists of one spiral <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, rough, with membranaceous furrows; and the aperture terminates in an entire canal, either straight, or somewhat ascending. There are 60 species, particularly distinguished by peculiarities in their shells, &c. From a species of murex was obtained the famous Tyrian dye so much valued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. This, however, has long been superseded by the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>. One of the shells producing the dye was a kind of buccinum; but the finest, or Tyrian purple, was got from the murex. These species of shells are found in various parts of the Mediterranean. Immense heaps of them are to be seen about Tarentum to this day, evincing one place where this precious liquor was extracted. See Plate CLXXVI. fig. 1. In the accounts of a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> it is mentioned, that on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUAYAQUIL">Guayaquil</a> and Guatemala in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> the murex is also found. The shell which contains it adheres to the rocks that are washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: it is of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> walnut. The liquor may be extracted two ways; some kill the animal after they have drawn it out of the shell; then press it with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> from head to tail; separate from the body the part where the liquor is collected, and throw away the rest. When this operation, after being repeated on several snails, has afforded a certain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fluid, the thread intended to be dyed is dipped in it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is finished. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which is at first of the whiteness of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, becomes afterwards green, and is not purple till the thread is dry. Those who disapprove of this method, draw the fish partly out of the shell, and, squeezing it, make it yield a fluid which serves for dying: they repeat this operation four times at different intervals, but always with less success. If they continue it, the fish dies. No colour at present known, says the abbé Raynal, can be compared to this, either as to lustre, liveliness, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. It succeeds better on cotton than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. Muria, Alimentary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. See Salt. Murrain, or Gargle, a contagious <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> among cattle. The symptoms are, a hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and swelling of the head, abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> in the eyes, rattling in the throat, a short breath, palpitation at the heart, staggering, a hot breath, and a shining tongue. In order to prevent this disease, the cattle should stand cool in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and have plenty of good water: all carrion should be speedily buried; and as the feeding of cattle in wet places, on rotten grass and hay, often occasions this disease, dry and sweet fodder should be given them. Murray, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, extending by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> from the river Spey on the east to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAULY">Beauly</a> on the west, which is the boundary of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ross; and comprehending the countries of Strathspey, Badenoch, Strathern, Strathnaver, and Stratherrick. According to the account of the reverend Mr Shaw minister of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>, in answer to some queries of Mr Pennant, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces wheat, barley, oats, rye, peas, and beans. Of these, in plentiful years, upwards of 20,000 bolls are exported, besides serving the Murray, the country itself and some of the Highland countries. Some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> is also cultivated, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>; of which linen is made, not only for home-consumption, but a considerable quantity of linen-yarn is exported. Great quantities of potatoes are also cultivated. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle also are exported from the Highlands of Murray, but few or none from the Lowlands.—Peculiar to this province is a kind of wood, called <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> laugh, or felloe; which is no less beautiful than mahogany. It is much more firm and tough than mahogany, and resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>-colored kind of that wood. It receives a fine polish, but is very scarce, growing on rocks. But there are great forests of fir and birch, which our author thinks are the remains of the Sylva <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>. Here also is found a remarkable root, called by the natives carmel; it grows in heaths and birch-woods to the bigness of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>; and sometimes there are four or five roots joined together by fibres. It has a green stalk, and small red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Dio, speaking of the Caledonians, says, Certain cibi genus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> omnium, quem si copertum quantum est unius sibis magnitudi, minime efiuire aut fitire solent. Cæsar also tells us of a root called chara, which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> mixed with milk and made into bread when in want of provision, which greatly relieved them. This root, Mr Shaw thinks, is the same with the carmel, or finest root of Murray. He informs us, that he hath often seen it dried, and kept for journeys through hills where no provision was to be had; he has likewise seen it pounded and infused; the liquor makes a more agreeable and wholesome liquor than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAD">mead</a>. It grows in such plenty, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CART">cart</a>-load of it can easily be gathered. Murray is intersected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Spey, Lossie, Findern, Nairn, Ness, and Beauly. The river of Spey, rising on the borders of Lochaber, is more than 60 Scots, or 100 English miles long, but too rapid to be navigable. Upon this river great floats of fir and birch-wood are carried down to the Firth; the float is guided by a man sitting on a coracle. This vessel is of an oval shape, about four feet long and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> from head to stern; a few ribs <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the keel, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of pliable wood round the lip of it; the whole covered with the rough hide of an ox or horse. The rower sits on a transverse seat in the middle, and holds in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a rope, the end of which is tied to the float, and with the other hand he manages a paddle, keeps the float in deep water, and brings it to shore when he pleases. In this province, also, is Loch Ness, remarkable for its never freezing. There are many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in this country, of which one called Duntelchaig is remarkable in that it is never covered with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; but after that time one night's strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> covers it all over. On the east side of Loch Ness, a large <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> above the loch, is the waterfall of Fother, where the river Feach-Len falls over a steep rock about 80 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and a thick fog rises from the place where it falls, occasioned by the violent dashing of the water. There is a considerable salmon-fishery on the rivers Spey, Findern, Ness, and Beauly, which serves the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and country, besides exporting to the value of 12,000l. annually. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> caves in the hills of this country, which formerly were the receptacles of thieves and robbers, and now afford shelter to hunters and shepherds in stormy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The most remarkable mountain is Carnochan, in Strathpey. In it are found a particular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> well known to the lapidaries. They are of blue, green, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> colours; some so large as to make snuff-boxes, or small cups; some of hexagonal or pentagonal figures, and tapering to a point at each end. The mountain of Benalas, in Badenoch, is by Mr Shaw reckoned to be the highest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> in Scotland, as waters flowing from it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the sea at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERLOCHY">Inverlochy</a>, and Garroch in Murray.

MUS

Pages 452-464

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, belonging to the order of glires; the genuine character of which is, that the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the lower jaws are furred. There are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The porcellus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>-pig, so called from its being supposed to come only from Guinea, is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> as well as Guinea. It is about the size of a young pig; and hath erect <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> not unlike it. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or white varied with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> blotches; hath no tail, but very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ears rounded at the sides. These animals are of such a hot <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, that they copulate five or six weeks after birth. They acquire not, however, their full growth before the eighth or ninth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. But this increase of size consists only of fat; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> parts are fully unfolded before the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of six months. The females go with young only three weeks; the first litter consists of four or five; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of five or six; and the succeeding ones of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight, and sometimes of 10 or 12. The mother suckles her young 12 or 15 days; she banishes them as soon as she receives the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>, which happens at farthest three weeks after her delivery; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of them persist in following her, they are maltreated and killed by the male. As they breed so fast, their multitudes would be innumerable, if there were not so many enemies which destroy them. They cannot resist either <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or moisture; when cold, they assemble and crowd <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> they often all perish together. They are also devoured in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers by cats, and many are killed by the males. Though perpetually throwing out urine, they never drink. They feed on all kinds of herbs; but especially on parsley, which they prefer to grain or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and they are likewise fond of apples and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. They eat precipitately like the rabbit, little at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but very often; make a grunting noise like a little pig, and are very restless. No mention is made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> historians of the manners of this animal in a wild state. Their skin is hardly of any value; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, though eatable, is not so good as to be much demanded; but it might be improved by keeping them in warrens, where they would have the benefit of the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of choosing herbs agreeable to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Those kept in houses have nearly the same bad taste with warren-rabbits; and those kept in gardens during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, have an insipid, but lefs disagreeable flavour. 2. The aguti, is about the size of a hare, has a short tail; four toes on the fore-feet, three on the hind ones; and a yellowish belly. According to M. Buffon, it is an animal peculiar to the southern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, being ing never found in the old world. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Brazil, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, St Domingo, and all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and seems to require a warm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in order to subsist and multiply. However, they can live in France, if kept in a dry <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and sheltered from winter frosts. The aguati is a very mischievous animal, and bites cruelly: he grunts like a pig; is very voracious; sits on his hind-legs, and holds his food with the fore-feet when he eats; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> what he cannot consume; hops like a hare, and runs very fast both on plain and rising grounds; but as his fore-legs are much shorter than the hind-ones, he would tumble headlong if he did not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> his course in descending. Both his eye and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> are fine; he stops and listens to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of music: the flesh of those which are fat and well-fed is not very bad, though it be hard, and not very agreeable to the taste. They scald the aguati, and make him ready in the same manner as a pig. He is hunted with dogs. When forced among the cut <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, he is soon taken; because these grounds being generally covered a foot thick with straw and leaves, at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> he sinks in this litter, so that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> may overtake and slay him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a>. He <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> runs very nimbly before the dogs; and when he gains his retreat, he lies squat, and remains obstinately in his concealment. The hunters are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> him out by filling his hole with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. The animal, half suffocated, utters mournful cries; but never issues forth, unless when pushed to the last extremity. His cry, which he often repeats when disturbed or irritated, resembles that of a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>. If taken young, he is easily tamed, and goes out and returns of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>. These animals commonly reside in the woods and hedges; where the females choose a place well covered and bushy, and there prepare a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of leaves and hay for their young. They annually produce two or three, but generally two. Like the cats, they transport their young, two or three days after birth, into the hollows of trees, where they suckle them for a short time; the young are soon in a condition to follow their mother, and to search for food. 3. The leporinus, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> hare, is about the size of an ordinary hare: the hair of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour; the head small in proportion to the body; the eyes large and prominent; the ears like those of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAT">rat</a>; in other respects the head resembles both a deer and hare; the hind-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body and thighs remarkably big; the legs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; four toes on the fore-feet, and three on the hind-feet: is a native of Java and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>. The above <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> was taken from an animal of this kind in the possession of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>. It was very tame and inoffensive, and fed only on fruit and other vegetables. 4. The citellus, or earless marmot, hath a short tail, an ash-coloured body, and no ears. It inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. It hath been confounded with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRICETUS">cricetus</a>, or hamster; but, according to M. Buffon, the differences between them are very conspicuous, chiefly in the want of ears in the citellus; for though the ears of the hamster are short, they are broad, and very observable; the citellus also never copulates with the hamster, which is sufficient to remove every doubt with regard to the diversity of their species. This creature burrows, and forms its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of corn, nuts, &c. for its winter-food. It sits up like a squirrel. By Gmelin's account, some inhabit the fields in Siberia, others penetrate into granaries; the former make holes in the ground with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> entrance, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> during winter in the centre of their lodge: those which inhabit the granaries are in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> during the whole of the cold season. They couple in the beginning of May, and bring from five to eight young, which they bring up in their burrows, and cover with hay. They whistle like the marmot; are very irascible, and bite very severely: their furs were once used by the ladies of Bohemia to make cloaks. 5. The lemmus, or lemming, hath a short tail, five toes on both fore and hind feet, and the body is variegated with green and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. This creature, which is one of the most singular that we know of, is said to be a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Kolin in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>. They appear not every year; but at certain unforeseen periods they come in such numbers, that they spread everywhere, and cover the whole surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The arrival of the lemmings is considered as a terrible scourge, the effects of which it is impossible to avoid. They make dreadful devastations in the fields; lay waste the gardens; ruin the crops; and leave nothing, except what is shut up in houses, where they never enter. They bark nearly like small dogs. When attacked, they neither fear clubs nor halberds, but dart against those who strike them, outrageously biting, and fixing upon the weapons employed to kill them. When struck at with a stick, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> it so forcibly with their teeth, that they allow themselves to be carried to a considerable distance without quitting their hold. They dig holes in the earth, and make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> like the moles, in quest of roots. They sometimes make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and divide themselves into two armies along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and meadows. Their enemies are foxes and ermines, who devour great numbers of them. Grass that has been eaten <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> again, is said to kill them; and they seem likewise to commit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>; for they are often found suspended on the branches of trees; and they probably throw themselves in troops into the waters like the swallows. It would also appear, that the lemmings, like the rats, mutually destroy and eat each other, when pasture fails them; and that this is the reason why their destruction is as sudden as their multiplication. At particular times they assemble together, and the whole die in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. They are very courageous, and defend themselves against other animals. It is not certainly known whence they come. The vulgar believe that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> along with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. Upon the renewal of the grass they infallibly die. In fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> they take to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> in vast multitudes; but when a breeze of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> arises, they are all drowned. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these animals is so prodigious, that when they die the air is infected, and produces many diseases. They even seem to infect the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which they gnaw; for the pasture then kills the cattle. The flesh of the lemmings is not good to eat; and their skin, though the hair be fine, does not answer for making furs, because it is too thick. 6. The paca, or spotted cavy, is an animal peculiar to the new world, particularly Brazil. It has a short tail, five toes on each foot, and three yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on each side. It resembles a pig of two months old; and its flesh is fat, and makes excellent food. Even the skin is eat, like that of a pig. For these reasons this animal is in perpetual request. It is difficult for the hunters to take him alive. When surprized in his hole, which they lay open both before and behind, he defends himself, and even bites fiercely. His skin, though covered with coarse short hair, makes a very good fur, because it is regularly spotted on both sides. These animals produce often and in great numbers; many of them are destroyed by men and beasts of prey, and yet the species is always numerous. When kept in a wooden cage or box, this animal remains perfectly tranquil during the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, especially when plentifully supplied with food. He seems even to have an affection for his retreat as long as the day lasts; for, after feeding, he retires spontaneously into it. But when night approaches, by perpetual restlessness and agitation, and by tearing the bars of his prison with his teeth, he discovers a violent desire of getting out. Nothing of this kind happens during the day, unless he has occasion for some natural evacuation; for he cannot endure the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of dirtiness in his little apartment; and when about to void his excrements, always retires to the most distant corner he can find. When his straw begins to smell, he often throws it out, as if he meant to demand fresh litter. This old straw he pushes out with his muzzle, and goes in quest of rags or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> to replace it. In a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> cavy, the following extraordinary instance of cleanliness was observed. A large male rabbit being shut up with her when she was in season, she took an aversion to him the moment he voided his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a> in their common apartment. Before this she was very fond of him; licked his nose, ears, and body; and allowed him to take almost the whole food that was given her. But as soon as the rabbit had infected the cage with his ordure, she retired into the bottom of an old press, where she made a bed with paper and rags, and returned not to her old lodging, till she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it neat, and freed from the unclean guilt which had been presented to her. The spotted cavy is easily accustomed to a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Unless indolently irritated, he is gentle and tractable. He is fond of adulation, and licks the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the person who caresses him. He knows those who take care of him, and readily distinguishes their voices. When gently stroked on the back, he stretches himself out, lies down on his belly, by a small cry expresses his acknowledgment, and seems to ask a continuance of the favour. When seized in a rough manner, however, he makes very violent efforts to escape. 7. The marmota, or marmot, has a short hairy tail, round ears, and gibbous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. It is found only on the tops of the highest mountains, and is more subject to be rendered torpid by cold than any other. In the end of September, or beginning of October, he retires into his hole, from which he comes not out till the beginning of April. His retreat is capacious, broader than long, and very deep, so that it can contain several marmots, without any danger of corrupting the air. With their feet and claws, which are admirably adapted for the purpose, they dig the earth with surprising quickness, and throw it behind them. It is not a hole, or a straight or winding tube, but a species of gallery made in the form of a Y, each branch of which has an aperture, and both terminate in one where the animal lodges.
