SHORT-SIGHTEDNESS, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vision wherein objects are seen only at small distances. See Medicine, p. 178.

MYOSOTIS

Pages 549-549

SCORPION-CRASS; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the scorpioides, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mouse-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. This is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, growing naturally in dry fields, and on the margins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and rills. It hath naked seeds, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the leaves callous. It varies considerably in different situations. In dry places the plant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are smaller; in moist ones both are larger, and sometimes hairy. The blossoms vary from a full blue to a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> one, and sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; and appear in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> spirally twisted spike. When it grows in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell is thereby rendered less observable, sheep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes eat it; but it is generally fatal to them. Cows, horses, swine, and goats, refuse it.

MYRICA

Pages 549-550
GALE, or SWEET-WILLOW, in botany; a genus of the tetrandria order, belonging to the dioica clas of plants. Species. 1. The gale, or sweet-willow, grows naturally in many places both of Scotland and England. It rises near four feet high, with many shrubby stalks, which divide into several slender branches, garnished with stiff spear-shaped leaves of a light yellowish green, smooth, and a little sawed at their points; and emit a fragrant odour when bruised. The female flowers or catkins are produced from the sides of the branches, growing upon separate plants from the female, which are succeeded by clusters of small berries, each having a single seed. It flowers in July, and ripens in autumn. 2. The cerifera, or candleberry gale, is a native of North America. It is a small tree or shrub about twelve feet high, with crooked stems branching forth near the ground irregularly. The leaves are long, narrow, and sharp-pointed. Some trees have most of their leaves serrated, others not. In May, the small branches are alternately and thick set with oblong tufts of very small flowers, resembling in form and size the catkins of the hazel-tree, coloured with red and green. These are succeeded by small clusters of blue berries close connected, like bunches of grapes. The kernel is inclosed in an oblong, hard stone, incrusted over with an unctuous mealy substance, from which the wax is procured in the following manner: in November and December, when the berries are ripe, a man with his family will remove from home to some island or sand-bank near the sea, where these trees most abound, taking with them kettles to boil the berries in. He builds a hut with palmetto-leaves for the shelter of himself. himself and family during his residence there, which is commonly for four or five weeks. The man cuts down the trees, while the children strip off the berries into a porridge-pot; and having put water to them, they boil them till the oil floats, which is then skimmed off into another vessel. This is repeated till no more oil appears. When cold, this hardens to the consistence of wax, and is of a dirty green colour. Then they boil it again, and clarify it in brass kettles; which gives it a transparent greenness. These candles burn a long time, and yield a grateful smell. They usually add a fourth part of tallow, which makes them burn clearer.

MYRMECOPHAGA

Pages 550-550
or Ant-bear, in zoology; a genus of quadrupeds, belonging to the order of bruta; the characters of which are these: There are no teeth in the mouth; the tongue is long and cylindrical; the head terminates in a long snout or muzzle; and the body is covered with pretty long hair. There are four species, viz. 1. The didactyla, or little ant-eater, hath a conic nose bending a little down; ears small, and hid in the fur; two hooked claws on the fore-feet, the exterior being much the largest; four on the hind-feet; the head, body, limbs, and upper part and sides of the tail, covered with long soft silky hair, or rather wool, of a yellowish brown colour: from the nose to the tail it measures seven inches and an half; the tail eight and an half; the last four inches of which on the under side are naked. It is thick at the base, and tapers to a point. Inhabits Guinea, climbs trees in quest of a species of ants which build their nests among the branches: has a prehensible power with its tail. 2. The tridactyla, tamandua-guaca, or tamanioir, has three toes on the fore-feet, five on the hind-feet, and long hair on the tail. This animal is about four feet long; and the head and snout about 15 inches: it is a native of the East Indies, and feeds on ants, &c., in the same manner as the former. 3. The jubata, or great ant-eater, hath a long slender nose, small black eyes; short round ears; a slender tongue two feet and an half long, which lies double in the mouth; the legs slender; four toes on the fore-feet, five on the hind-feet; the two middle claws on the fore-feet very large, strong, and hooked; the hair on the upper part of the body is half a foot long, black mixed with grey; the fore-legs are whitish, marked above the feet with a black spot; the tail is clothed with very coarse black hair a foot long: the length from the nose to the tail about four feet; the tail, two feet and an half. 4. The tetradactyla, or middle ant-eater, has four toes on the fore-feet, and five on the hind, with a tail naked at the extremity; the length from the nose to the tail is one foot seven inches, and the tail ten inches. These animals have many properties in common with each other, both in their structure and manners. They all feed upon ants, and plunge their tongues into honey and other liquid or viscid substances. They readily pick up crumbs of bread, or small morsels of flesh. They are easily tamed, and can subsist for a long time without food. They never swallow all the liquor which they take for drink; for a part of it falls back through their nostrils. They run so slowly that Myrmidons a man may easily overtake them in an open field. Their flesh, though its taste be very disagreeable, is eaten by the savages.—At a distance the great ant-eater has the appearance of a fox; and for this reason some travellers have given him the name of the American fox. He has strength sufficient to defend himself from a large dog, or even from the jaguar or brasilian cat. When attacked, he at first fights on end, and, like the bear, annoys his enemy with the claws of his fore-feet, which are very terrible weapons. He then lies down on his back, and uses all the four feet; in which situation he is almost invincible; and continues the combat to the last extremity. Even when he kills his enemy, he quits him not for a long time after. He is enabled to resist better than most other animals; because he is covered with long bushy hair; his skin is remarkably thick; his flesh has little sensation; and his principle of life is very tenacious.

MYRMIDONS

Pages 550-550

MYRMIDONES, in antiquity; a people of Thessaly, said to have arose from ants <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pitheciæ, upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> put up for that purpose by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Æacus to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, after his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> had been depopulated by a severe pestilence.—In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, the Myrmidons are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

MYROBALANS

Pages 550-550

a kind of medicinal fruit brought from the Indies, of which there are five kinds. 1. The citrine, of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, hard, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and the size of an olive. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> myrobalan, of the bigness of an acorn, wrinkled, and without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. 3. Chebulic myrobalans, which are of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>, pointed at the end, and of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. 4. Emble, which are round, rough, the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>, and of a dark brown. 5. Balleric, which are hard, round, of the size of an ordinary prune, less angular than the rest, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. They are all slightly purgative and astringent. The word comes from the Greek ἀπόρος, "ointment;" and ἀπόρος, "acorn;" as being in the form of acorns, and used in medicine.

MYRON

Pages 550-550

an excellent Grecian statuary, flourished 442 B.C. The cow he represented in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> was an admirable piece of workmanship, and was the occasion of many fine epigrams in Greek.

MYRRH

Pages 550-550

in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, a concrete, gummy, resinous juice, brought from the East Indies in globes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> drops, of various colours and magnitudes. The best sort is of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> reddish or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, somewhat transparent; of a lightly pungent bitter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, with an aromatic flavour, though not sufficient to prevent its proving nauseous to the palate; and a strong disagreeable smell. The medical effects of this aromatic bitter are, to warm and strengthen the visceræ, and dissolve thick tenacious juices; it frequently occasions a mild diaphoresis, and promotes the fluid secretions in general. Hence it proves serviceable in languid <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; diseases arising from a simple inactivity; those <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> disorders which proceed from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, mucous, sluggish indisposition of the humours; suppressions of the uterine discharges; cachectic disorders, where the lungs and thorax are oppressed by viscid phlegm. Myrrh is likewise supposed in a peculiar manner to retit <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> in all parts of the body; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> stands recommended in malignant, putrid, and pettential fevers, and in the smallpox;

MYRTIFORM

Pages 550-551

in anatomy, an appellation given to several parts, from their resembling myrtle-berrys.

MYRTUS

Pages 551-552

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, the MYRTLE; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the icofandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are: 1. The communis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> myrtle-tree, rises with a shrubby, upright, firm stem, branching numerously all around into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> full head, rising eight or ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; very closely garnished with oval-lanceolate, entire, mostly opposite leaves, from half an inch to an inch and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, on short footstalks; and numerous, small, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> from the axillae, singly on each footstalk, having diphylloous involucrums; each flower succeeded by a small, oval, dark-purple berry. The most material varieties are, Broad-leaved Roman myrtle, with oval, shining, green leaves, an inch and an half long, and one broad; and is remarkably floriferous. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>-striped broad-leaved Roman myrtle. Broad-leaved Dutch myrtle, with spear-shaped, sharp-pointed, dark-green leaves, an inch long, and about three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of one broad. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a>-flowered Dutch myrtle. Broad-leaved Jews myrtle, having the leaves placed by three at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>; by which particular circumstance this species is in universal estimation among the Jews in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, particularly in decorating their tabernacles; and for which purpose many gardeners about <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> cultivate this variety with particular care, to sell to the above people, who are often obliged to purchase it at the rate of sixpence or a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> for a small branch: for the true sort, having the leaves exactly by threes, is very scarce, and is a curiosity; but by care in its propagation, taking only the perfectly ternate-leaved shoots for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, it may be increased fast enough; and is worth the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the curious, and particularly those who raise myrtles for the London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>-leaved Spanish myrtle, with oval spear-shaped leaves, an inch and a half long or more, and one broad, in clusters round the branches, and resemble the shape and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of orange-tree leaves. Gold-striped-leaved orange myrtle. Common upright Italian myrtle, with its branches and leaves growing more erect, the leaves oval, lanceolate-shaped, acute-pointed, and near an inch long, and half a one broad. Silver-striped upright Italian myrtle. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-berried upright Italian myrtle. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> acute-leaved myrtle, with spear-shaped, oval, acute-pointed leaves, about an inch long. Box-leaved myrtle, with weak branches, small, oval, obtuse, lucid-green, closely-placed leaves. Striped box-leaved myrtle. Rosemary-leaved myrtle, hath erect branches, small, narrow, lanceolate, acute-pointed, shining, green, very fragrant leaves. Silver-striped rosemary-leaved myrtle. Thyme-leaved myrtle, with very small closely-placed leaves. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTMEG">Nutmeg</a>-myrtle, with erect branches and leaves; the leaves oval, acute-pointed, and finely scented like a nutmeg. Broad-leaved nutmeg-myrtle. Silver-striped leaved <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>. Crifated or cock's comb myrtle, frequently called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>'s-nest myrtle, hath narrow, sharp-pointed leaves, crifated at intervals. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> varieties of the myrtus communis; but of which sorts there are several intermediate varieties of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; and more may still be obtained from seed, though the plants are rarely raised from seed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but mostly by slips and cuttings. They are all beautiful ever-green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> of exceeding fragrance; exotics originally of the southern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and consequently in this country require shelter of a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in winter; all of which, though rather of the small-leaved kind, have their foliage closely placed, and remain all the year, and are very floriferous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; and when there is a collection of the different sorts, they afford an agreeable source of variety with each other. They therefore claim universal esteem as principal greenhouse plants, especially as they are all so easily raised from cuttings, and of such easy culture as to be attainable in every garden, where there is any sort of greenhouse, or garden-frames furnished with glasses for protecting them in winter from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>: but some of the broad-leaved sorts are so hardy as to succeed in the full ground, against a south wall and other warm exposures, all the year, by only allowing them shelter of mats occasionally in severe frothy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>: so that a few of these sorts may also be exhibited in a warm situation in the shrubbery: observing, however, all the sorts are principally to be considered as greenhouse plants, and a due portion of them must always remain in pots to move to that department in winter. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STOVE">Stove</a>-kinds.—There are several species of the flore-temperature, as being natives of the Indies: but there are not more than the four following sorts <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> met with in the British gardens, all of which are beautiful ever-greens, with larger leaves than the myrtus communis; and are mostly strong aromatics. 2. The zelanica, or Ceylon white-berried myrtle, hath a shrubby upright stem, branching erectly six or eight feet high; oval, shining-green, opposite, very odoriferous leaves, on short footstalks; and all the branches terminated by pedunculi, each fulfilling many flowers; succeeded by snowy-white berries, but rarely in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. 3. The pimenta, pimento, or Jamaica all-spice-tree, rises with an upright tree-stem, branching regularly 20 or 30 feet high, having a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> bark; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>-oval, stiff, shining, very odoriferous leaves, like those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>; and at the sides and termination of the branches large loose bunches of greenish flowers; succeeded by round, dusky, hard, spicy fruit, called all-spice, or Jamaica-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>. —This species is an excellent aromatic; its leaves are remarkably fine-scented; and its fruit is that valuable spice, Jamaica pepper, or all-spice, so called, because it is supposed to partake of the odour and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of most other spices. The tree grows in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Jamaica, where its fruit is made a considerable branch of trade. It is generally gathered a little before before it acquires full growth, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> 10 or 12 days; and is then packed up ready for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> to Europe. 4. The dioica, or dioecious American myrtle, rises with an upright tree-stem, branching many feet high; oblong, thick, opposite, odoriferous leaves; and at the axils and ends of the branches pedunculi dividing into trichotomous panicles of dioecious flowers; succeeded by small, globular, spicy berries. Every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tree is a strong aromatic. 5. The brasiliaca, or Brazilian inodorus myrtle, rises with a branching stem, having a whitish bark; broad, oval, shining, opposite, inodorous or scentless leaves, and naked pedunculi, sustaining solitary flowers, with ciliated petals; succeeded by large oval fruit. All these five species of myrtus are exotics of the shrub and tree kind; though in this country, as being confined in pots, the largest of them assume only the growth of moderate shrubs. The first species, common myrtle, is considerably the most noted species of this genus in this country; where in most of our greenhouse collections one or other of the varieties is found in tolerable plenty; but all the varieties of it highly merit notice. The other four species are rare in Britain; they, however, are retained in many curious gardens, in the stove-collection; more particularly the pimento, which is a very beautiful odoriferous evergreen, and exhibits a fine variety in the stove at all seasons. In short, all the species, both greenhouse and stove-kinds, have a pretty effect as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>; and some of the sorts flower very ornamentally, particularly of the common myrtle. With respect to flowering, all the varieties of the myrtus communis flower here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, most of which are very floriferous: the broad-leaved Roman kind, in particular, is often covered with flowers, which in some of the sorts are succeeded here by berries ripening in winter. Some of the stove kinds also flower here, but are rarely succeeded by fruit in England. The flowers, however, of most of the sorts are small, but numerous; and are all formed each of five oval petals, and many stamina. As all the species require occasional shelter here, they must be kept always in pots, for moving to the proper places of shelter, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; the myrtus communis and varieties to the greenhouse in winter; the others to the stove, to remain all the year; therefore let all the sorts be potted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and, as they advance in growth, shift them into larger pots, managing the myrtles as other greenhouse shrubs, and the stove-kinds as other woody exotics of the stove. But, as we before observed, the broad-leaved myrtus communis, being hardier than the smaller-leaved kinds, some of them may also be turned out into the full ground in a warm situation against a wall, &c., allowing them shelter of mats in frosty weather, and mulch the ground over their roots; they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> frequently succeed tolerably, and effect a good variety in such places. They may all be propagated by slips, cuttings, or layers. The leaves and flowers of common upright myrtle have an astringent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and are used for cleansing the skin, and strengthening the fibres. From the flowers and young tops is drawn a distilled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> that is detergent, astringent, cosmetic, and used in gargles. A decoction of the flowers and leaves is applied in fermentations. The berries have a binding detergent quality; and the chemical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> obtained from them is excellent for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and used in pomatums and most other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> beautifiers of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> and skin. As an internal medicine, these berries have little or no merit.

MYSIA

Pages 552-552

(anc. geog.), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which Strabo makes two-fold; the one called Olympus, near mount Olympus, whence its name; the other near the river Caicus and Pergamene, as far as Teuthrania, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the mouth of the Caicus; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was afterwards called Rhodi, from the Eolians, (Mela, Pliny); by which means this Mysia was greatly contracted in its limits.—There were also two other Mysias, called Abrettene and Meroe; which see. Strabo mentions a small district, called Mysia Combustia, famous for generous wines; which, whether to be allotted to Mysia <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Lydia, he is doubtful: it was in length 500 stadia, in breadth 400: and he observes, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of difficulty to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the limits of the Bithynians, Mysians, Phrygians, Mygdonians, and Trojans, being so intermixed and blended; which gave rise to a proverb, denoting the difficulty of distinguishing things, though really distinct. Mysii, or Mysia, the people, were held in the utmost contempt; so that Mysorum ultimus denotes a person highly desppicable, (Cicero): and because the being made a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of is generally the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of contempt, this gave rise to another proverb, Μυσική λογία, (<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>). The name Mysia is said to denote the beech-tree, which grows plentifully about Olympus; and hence the country took its name.

MYSTERY

Pages 552-552

something secret <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> concealed, impossible or difficult to comprehend. All religions, true or false, have their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>. The pagan <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> was remarkably full of them. Ovid reckons it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> crime to divulge the mystic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and Juno. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELEUSINIA">eleusinia</a>, or sacred rites of Ceres, solemnized at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, were called, by way of eminence, the mysteries; and so superstitiously careful were they to conceal these sacred rites, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any person divulged any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, he was thought to have called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some divine judgment on his head, and it was accounted unsafe to abide under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> with him; and Horace declares, that he would not put to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in the same ship with one who revealed the mysteries of Ceres. The pagan mysteries, it is true, were generally mysteries of iniquity, and concealed only because their being published would have rendered their religion ridiculous and odious. Thus the sacred writings often speak of the infamous mysteries of the pagan deities, in which the most shameful crimes were committed under the specious veil of religion. The whole religion of the Egyptians was mysterious from the beginning to the end, and both their doctrine and worship wrapped up in symbols and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. The religion of the Jews is supposed to be full of mysteries. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, according to St Augustine, was a mystery, as it represented or was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of the people of Christ, and the Christian religion. Whatever was commanded or forbidden them was figurative;

MYSTICAL

Pages 552-553

something mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> allegorical. Some of the commentators on the sacred writings, besides a literal, find also a mystical meaning. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of scripture, say they, is either that immediately signified by the words and expressions in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; or it is mediate, sublime, typical, and mystical. The literal sense they again divide into proper literal, which is contained in the words taken simply and properly; and metaphorical literal, where the words are to be taken in a figurative and metaphorical sense. The mystical sense of scripture they divide into three kinds: the first corresponding to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and called allegorical; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to hope, called analogical; and the third to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, called the tropological sense. And sometimes they take the same word in scripture in all the four senses: thus the word <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, literally signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Judea; allegorically, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> militant; tropologically, a believer; and analogically, heaven. So that passage in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, let there be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and there was light, literally signifies corporeal light; by an allegory, the Messiah; in the tropological sense, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; and analogically, beatitude, or the light of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>.

MYSTICS

Pages 553-559

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, distinguished by their professing a pure, sublime, and perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, with an entire disinterested <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of God, free from all selfish considerations, and by their aspiring to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">MYTHOLOGY</a>. The word mythology is a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, that signifies a discourse on fables; and comprehends, in a collective <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, all the fabulous and poetical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of pagan antiquity. It follows therefore, that this science teaches the history of the gods, demi-gods, and fabulous heroes of antiquity; the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the pagans, the principles of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, metamorphoses, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, &c. By this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, it appears sufficiently what are the objects of which we are to treat in this article. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we well consider the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, we shall find, that there were, in pagan antiquity, three different religions. First, That of the philosophers, who treated metaphysically of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the attributes, and of the works of the Supreme Being. They endeavoured to discover the true God, and the manner in which he ought to be worshipped. It is not wonderful, that these men of exalted genius should in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, in their works, the two other positive religions, and those gods on whom they were founded; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that they outwardly professed the established religion, in order to preserve the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and to avoid the persecutions of the legislature, and the insults of the populace. For in fact, was it possible for them to believe the pagan fables? Must they not foresee, that their religion would one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> give <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, while their own works would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with their names to the latest posterity? And could they suffer the thought, that their reputation would be tarnished in the eyes of that posterity, by having it imagined they believed such idle tales as were broached by the priests of their times? Could <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, Seneca, and Cicero, be unconcerned for their fame among future generations and future philosophers? And what should we at this day have said of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, had they been so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> hypocritical, as to have entirely concealed their sentiments with regard to these matters? The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> religion was that of paganism, which was the established religion of all the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nations except the Jews. This was the doctrine that was taught by the priests, and protected by the sovereigns. Its dogmas were demonstratively false, but not always so absurd as may at first appear; especially if we annex to the divinities, and to the religious ceremonies of the pagans, a sense that is frequently mystic, and always allegoric; if we remember, that the first heathens deified those great men to whom the rest of mankind were indebted for any signal benefits, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, Esculapius, &c. in order to induce others, as well of the present as future ages, to reverence and to imitate them. Would not an ancient pagan, if he were to return upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, have specious arguments, at least, to support his religion, when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> weak mortals beatify or canonize, merely by their own authority, other weak mortals (frequently <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> pedants), and place them in heaven, without the permission or approbation of the Supreme Being? Happy is it for mankind, when at different times faggot pontiffs purge the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, and the brains of the people, from a herd of pretended saints, and prevent them, at least after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, from doing injury to society, by interrupting the industry of the laborious inhabitants with keeping their festivals. The third religion was idolatry, or the religion of the populace. For the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, born to be deceived in every thing, confounding in their imaginations the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the gods, the idols of their divinities, the emblems of their virtues and of religious worship, with the gods, divinities, virtues, and worship themselves, adored these images, and proceeded to extravagancies the most ridiculous, and frequently most criminal, in their ceremonies, texts, libations, sacrifices, &c. It is to be feared, that, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as there are upon the earth men of our limited capacities, this triple religion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> constantly subsist under different forms; and we are much deceived, if it may not be found under the empire of Christianity itself, notwithstanding the purity of its doctrine. It will be easily conceived, that it is not of the religion of philosophers, nor that of the populace, of which we are to treat in this article of Mythology; but of that which subsisted Mythology subsisted under the authority of the magistracy and the priesthood, and consequently of paganism in general. As far as we are able to judge by all the ancient authors we have read, the pagans adored the sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of the universe under the name of Fate or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">Destiny</a>, which we must not confound with Fortune, who was regarded as a subordinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Jupiter himself, all the gods, every animated being, the heavens, the earth, the whole frame of nature, was subservient to Destiny, and nothing could reverse its decrees. This divinity was so highly adorable, as to be above all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; and was regarded as too supreme to be represented under any sensible image or statue, or to have any temple erected for its worship. We do not remember to have read, that ever any sacrifice was offered to this Destiny, or that any temple or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> was ever dedicated to its name. We are almost inclined to think, that the pagans were sensible, that the temple and the worship of the God of gods ought to be in the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Mention is made, indeed, of a temple that was dedicated to the Unknown God; but we are ignorant whether or not Destiny were thereby meant. We must not confound this Destiny, moreover, with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of chance, of which there are some antique statues that represent her in a recumbent posture, and playing with little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; for this was nothing more than an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of some statuary. After this general and philosophical idea of the Supreme Being, comes the positive religion of the pagans. This was entirely founded on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, which took its rise either from ancient traditions, or historical events, altered or augmented by the imaginations of the poets, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, or by the credulity of the people; or else it consisted of allegoric or moral fictions. A crowd of writers, and among the rest Noel le Comte, (Natalis Comes), the abbots Banner and Pluche, &c. have made many researches into the origin of fable: and they think they have discovered its source, 1. In the vanity of mankind; 2. In the want of letters and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; 3. In the defective eloquence of orators; 4. In the relations of travellers; 5. In the fictions of poets, painters, flutuaries, and dramatic writers; 6. In the diversity and uniformity of names; 7. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; 8. In the foundation of colonies, and the invention of arts; 9. In the desire of having gods for our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; 10. In the imperfect or false interpretation of the holy scriptures; 11. In the ignorance of ancient history; 12. In a like ignorance of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>; 13. In that of foreign languages; 14. In the translation of the religion of the Egyptians and Phoenicians into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; 15. In the ignorance of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>; and, 16. In the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> which the first people had of the intercourse of gods with men. It is certain, that all these matters taken together are sufficient to produce many thousands of fables; are more than sufficient to enable us to deceive ourselves and others, and to give rise to infinite reveries. But we should take care how we draw from these sources demonstrations that might be used, by irreligious, as arguments to overthrow the history of the Jews; a people the most stupid, most credulous, and ostentatious of all others. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the pagan philosophers themselves asserted, that it was a god who invented the fable: so much they were convinced of its ingenuity, and of its strong tendency to instruct mankind in their duty. Mythology therefore, when properly treated, begins with making learned researches into the real origin of fable, of paganism, and of that idolatry which was its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. It recurs for this purpose even to the beginning of the world: and after finding that Laban, the father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, was a maker of idols, and that he had his little images, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> gods, which he formed of baked earth, and which shews that idolatry existed in the greatest antiquity; it then explains cosmogony, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEOGONY">theogony</a>, or the belief that the first inhabitants of the earth entertained of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the universe, and what the pagan theology taught of the genealogy of their false gods. It begins with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the Chaldeans, a people so ancient, that Nimrod was their first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>; but at the same time so credulous and superstitious, that we may regard them as the authors of all those fables, and the propagators of all those visions, that have since blinded <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason. According to this tradition, a monster named <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OANNES">Oannes</a>, or Oo, half fish and half man, sprung from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> was completely dispersed, and gave laws to the Chaldeans. A woman called Omorpha, reigned over all the earth. Bel cut her in two, and made of one moiety the heavens, and of the other the earth. They likewise invented the two primitive beings; of which the good one, who was named Orphiagelos, had the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of heaven; and the other, called Arimanus, that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. The science of mythology then teaches the theogony of the Phoenicians; concerning whom it draws great lights from Sanchoniathon, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Beryte, who lived before the Trojan wars, more than 400 years before <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, and of whom Eusebius has preserved considerable fragments. From thence it passes to the theogony of the Egyptians; of whom Thot or Thoth, the founder of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, was likewise, they say, their first historian; that Sanchoniathon even copied from him; and of whom we find many relations in the Greek historians, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Diodorus Siculus, and in Eusebius of Cesarea. It then examines the theogony of the Atlantides, who dwelt on the western <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and of whom Diodorus alone has preserved any account. From thence it proceeds to the theogony of the Greeks, which is far better known to us, as we find accounts of it, more or less particular, in numberless Greek and Latin writers. This theogony had the same foundation as that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; the latter having only extended it, by adding to the Greek divinities certain gods or demi-gods, formed of their heroes, and certain symbolic and allegoric divinities, which mythology explains at the same time: and it is on this occasion that it enters into a particular explication of the cosmogony and theogony of Orph; whose book of metamorphoses contains as copious descriptions as we could desire of the fables of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: what was their belief concerning the habitations of the blessed after their death, or of the Elysian fields; as well as of their hell or Tartarus; of the dog Cerberus; of the ferryman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a>; of the fires; of the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, Cocytus, Lethe, Phlegethon, and Styx, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> the Tartarian regions, &c. Mythologists then continue their researches into the time, the epoch, and place, of the real origin of paganism and idolatry; and they prove that the pagans began <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVINATION">Divination</a>, or the prediction of future events, a weakness that has at all times possessed the human mind, forms also an important article of pagan theology. It is therefore in this place that mythology considers the nature of oracles, and in what manner these oracles gave their answers; the ceremonies that were observed in consulting them; the frantic emotions of the priestess Pythia on her tripod, and those of other priests. See Divination and Oracles. It then endeavours to investigate the history of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a>, and of their prophecies. See Sibyls. It next passes to the examen of the nature of auguries, auspices, haruspices, prodigies, &c.; of expiations and ablutions; of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> and astrology of the ancients, &c. See Augury, &c. It then proceeds to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the nature of the pagan divinities themselves. The celebrated treatise of Cicero De natura Deorum will here furnish great lights; but <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors who have treated on these matters, have not been contented with this alone: they have, so to say, extracted the essence of all antiquity, of which they have formed systems; but unluckily these scarce ever agree with each other. As philosophers, it is of very little importance for us to know what was the nature of these gods, seeing we know that they were merely fabulous; but as historians and antiquaries, it concerns us to know what was the nature that was attributed to them in general; and, in particular, what were the origin, genealogy, rank, functions, authority, and operations, that were attributed to each divinity; and it is on these matters that we have still some remarks to make. The gods of the ancient Greeks and Romans were all either Dii majorum gentium, or Dii minorum gentium; that is, of the first or second order. The former were also called consentes, magni consentes, &c. According to Ennius, they were 12 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and are included in these verses: Juno, Vesta, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, Ceres, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Mercurius, Jovis, Neptunus, Vulcanus, Apollo. To these were added eight others, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Selecti, which were Sol, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>, Tellus, Genius, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, Saturnus, Liber, and Pluto. The second order, or minorum gentium, were called Adscriptiti, Medioximi, Minucularii, Patatitii, Indigeter, Semones, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which were Elenapius, Bacchus, Caltor, Fauna, Hercules, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LARES">Lares</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENATES">Penates</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, Quirinus. See these under their several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, &c. According to the second <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, all their divinities were clasped into, 1. Celestial gods; 2. Terrestrial gods; 3. Sea gods; and, 4. The infernal deities, or inferi. The celestial gods were Jupiter, Juno, Apollo, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>, Cupid, Cybele, the Graces, Hebe, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>, Luna, Mars, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, Minerva, Nemesis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, Themis, Venus, &c. The terrestrial gods were Æolus, Mythology, Africa, Ceres, Diana, the Fauni, Feronia, Flora, Janus, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOMUS">Momus</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, Pales, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, Pomona, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIAPUS">Priapus</a>, the Satyrs, Silenus, the god Terminus, Vella or Rhea, Vulcanus, &c. The sea-gods were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, Thetis, Canopus, Glaucus, Ino, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a>, Oceanus, Palaeemon, Triton, &c. The infernal gods were Pluto, Proserpine, Charon, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, Æacus, Rhadamantus, the Furies, Death, Night, the Fates, Plutus, &c. See these articles. The third division ranged the divinities according as they precluded, 1. Over the pregnancy of women, (Pregnantiam); 2. At parturition (Parturientiam); 3. At births, (Nasciuntiam); 4. At adulteries; 5. At marriages: to which they added, 7. Dii morales, or moral gods; and, 7. Funeral gods. The gods of pregnancy were Plutus, Intercidona, and Deverra: the gods of parturition, Juno, Lucina, Diana, Egerio, Proa, Polliwta, Menagenata, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, the gods that were called Nixi, or of labour, &c. The gods of birth were Janus, Opis, Naftion, Cumina, Carmenta, Vagianus, Levana, Rumia, Potina, Educa, Offilago, Carnea, Nundina, Statilius, Fabulius, Parentia, &c. The gods of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> were Juventas, Agenoria, Strema, Stimula, Horta, Quies, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, Adeona, Abeona, Voluptas, Orbona, Pellonia, Numeria, Cambena, Sentia, Angeronia, Heres, Martea, Laverna, the god Averruncus, Confus, Catius, Volumnus and Volumna, Honorius, Alias Locutius, &c. The nuptial gods were Diana, Domiduca, Domitius, Hymenetus or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYMEN">Hymen</a>, Jugatius, Jupiter perfectus, Juno perfecta, Juno cinxia, Juno unxia, Lucina, Manturna, Mutinus, Dea Mater prima, Suada, Thalassius, Venus, &c. The moral gods were called Virtus, Honos, Fides, Spes, Justitia, Pietas, Misericordia, Clementia, Pacificia, Veritas, Mens, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONCORDIA">Concordia</a>, Pax, Salus, Felicitas, Libertas, Pecunia, Ritus, Invicta, Continencia, Impudentia, Calumnia, Fraus, Discordia, Furore, Fama, Fortuna, with all their epithets good or bad, Febris, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVOR">Pavor</a> and Pavor, Paupertas, Necessestas, Tempestas, Silentium, &c. The funeral gods were Pluto, Libitina, Nenia, Death, the Fates, &c. Hesiod indeed pretends, that all these gods derived their origin from chaos; but we have already pointed out more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> sources. It is almost incredible to what a prodigious number the superstition and weakness of the Greeks and Romans multiplied these divinities; there have been 30,000 of them enumerated. It will not be expected that we should here attempt to describe them, nor will it be remarkable if we have forgotten to mention even some of the first rank: although, vast as this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of gods is, mythology does not omit to trace the history of the greatest part of them, as is taught by paganism; and they who are desirous of particular information in these matters may consult with advantage the theogony of Hesiod, the catalogue of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, the metamorphoses of Ovid, the fables of Hygina, Lylii Gregorii Gyraldi Syntagma de diis Gentilium, the mythology of Natalis Comes, the books of Gerard Vossius de idolatria Gentilium, Johannis Boccati Genealogia deorum, the Pantheon of Pompey, the history of heaven by Abbé Pluche, the historic explanation of fables by Abbé Banier, and Bryant's Mythology. There were still many other distinctions, of which the pagans made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to mark the rank, the functions, and nature of their several divinities. For example, the goddess Vesta, or the mother of all the gods, was adored by all people in general. Mars, Bellona, Victoria, Fortunata, &c., afflicting all parties. The topical gods, on the contrary, were adored in particular countries only; as Astarte in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Derceto and Semiramis among the Assyrians, Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> by the Egyptians, Quirinus at Rome, &c. The title Semiones, which was given to a certain class of divinities, was doubtless derived from Semi-homines, that is, demi-men; and signified the same as semi-dii, or demi-gods. These were monarchs and illustrious heroes, or those great men who were the founders of cities and nations, that were deified by way of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> had taught the Chaldeans the doctrine of transmigration; and that, after their death, those who were virtuous would be elevated to the rank of divinities. This doctrine was adopted by all the pagan world. The apotheosis, after they had erected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and altars to the new gods, was celebrated with much solemnity. In the last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, an eagle was fixed on the catafalque, or funeral pile, on which was placed the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; and when the pile began to burn, the eagle was let loose, who, mounting into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> with the flames, seemed to carry the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the departed hero up to heaven. Mythology informs us also who those persons were that antiquity regarded as the children of the gods, such as Thelens, Hippolytus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, &c., what the pagans believed with regard to the nature of their genii and demons, of their dryades, hamadryades, nymphs, tritons, sirens, fauns, sylvans, centaurs, and other subterranean divinities; and in this manner it explains all the systems of the polite religion of the Greeks and Romans. They who are desirous of extending their knowledge of paganism still further, of knowing the dogmas of each particular people, what were their gods, and the various manners in which they were worshipped, such as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>, Isis, Osiris, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of crocodiles and onions, &c., among the Egyptians, must <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the different theologies of these people; and notwithstanding all the informations which ancient and modern authors afford, this study is yet boundless, and attended with many difficulties and uncertainties: though it appears demonstrative, that the origin of paganism, and of idolatry in general, was derived from the Chaldeans, from whom the Egyptians drew that doctrine which they after transmitted to all other nations; and consequently that the primordial divinities were the same, under different denominations, among all the idolatrous nations of the earth. The nature of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> will not permit us to descend to further particulars. But to give our readers an idea of the manner in which mythology treats its subjects, and of the method that should be observed in studying fable, or the history of the gods of antiquity, we shall here give, by way of example, a cursory <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> and its inhabitants. Parnassus was a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, that had two summits, one of which was called Titoreus, and the other Hyampoeus. Others say, that one of these hills was named <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and the other Cytheron; and that it is an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> to imagine, that Helicon was a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>. However that be, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> hill was consecrated to Apollo and the muses, who there held their usual residence. According to fable, there had been a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> on this hill, between Helicon and Cytheron. Whoever slept on Parnassus, when he waked, became a poet. Apollo had there a temple. There also was the fountain Castalia, into which Apollo had metamorphosed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> that he loved, and had given to its waters the power of making all who drank of them poets. At the foot of Parnassus flowed the river Hippocrene, that had the same virtue; and the source of which was opened by a stroke of the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Pegasus. This river nourished a great number of swans, that were regarded as sacred. Pegasus was a winged horse, that belonged to Apollo, and grazed on the summit of Parnassus. He sprang from the blood of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>, when Perseus cut off her head, which was placed among the stars. Such was the delicious abode of Apollo, the son of Jupiter and Latona, who was born, with his twin sister Diana, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Delos. He killed the Cyclops, who forged the thunderbolts with which Jupiter had overthrown his son Æsculapius; but for that presumption he was forced to leave heaven, and became an inhabitant of the earth. He guarded the oxen of Admetus; he aided Neptune to build the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and Alcides in forming the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>. He killed the dragon or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> Python. He invented music and physic; and was honoured as the god of poets and physicians. He was represented as a young man without a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, his head surrounded with rays, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a bow, or a lyre. As the ancients denoted the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> by the name of Apollo, they sometimes represented him also as seated in a chariot, drawn by two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> horses, preceded by Aurora and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> Venus: Phaeton his son, being desirous of conducting these horses, was thrown into the sea. Apollo was also called Phebus, Titan, and Sol. He is known to have had amours with Arinoe, Corycia, Melene, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, Mantho, Sinope, Calliope, and others; by whom he had Delphic, Naxic, Nileus, Arabe, Garamas, Sirius, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, and other children. He had peculiar honours paid him in the Pythian games at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR_GAMES"><a class="xre</a>f" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> games at Rome. The muses were the companions of Apollo in his rural abode. They were likewise called the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; as also the Cumaenion, Heliconian, Parnassian, Anionian, Pierian, Pegalian, Agamippian, Thebian, Libethrian, and Calliopean sisters. They were the daughters of Jupiter and Macmolynae, and were regarded as the godesses of sciences and arts in general. There were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of these muses; to whom they attributed: 1. To Clio, history; 2. To Melpomene, tragedy; 3. To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THALIA">Thalia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>; 4. To Euterpe, flutes and other pneumatic instruments of music; 5. To Terpsichore, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> and the dance; 6. To Erato, the lyre and the lute; 7. To Calliope, heroic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; 8. To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; and 9. To Polyhymnia, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and eloquence. The Graces also sometimes quitted Venus to pay their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> to Apollo. Such was the idea they entertained of Parnassus and its inhabitants. There is no doubt but that, under these fabulous representations, these sensible images, Mythology, were concealed allegoric and moral meanings; nor can it be denied but that their method of cultivating the arts and sciences, by this manner of expressing their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, was as ingenious and pleasing as it is possible to imagine. Every other subject that paganism embraced, it treated with the same genius, and in a manner equally pleasing; and though that religion was altogether fallacious, yet we must allow that it was extremely well calculated to promote the polite arts, by those refined, noble, graceful, brilliant images, by those charming subjects, which it constantly presented, and which it still offers to the poet, painter, sculptor, and every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. But this was not a power sufficiently strong to secure paganism against that vicissitude, that decline and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, which finally attends all the productions of this world. This religion, which had subsisted near 3000 years, and almost from the origin of the human <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>, gradually declined in proportion as the lights of Christianity and philosophy illumined the minds of mankind. For though the pagan religion, and the fables on which it was founded, were pleasing and favourable to the polite arts, they were not however calculated to satisfy the minds of philosophers, nor to promote the real good of mankind, by securing their temporal and eternal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. It is even surprising that so great a genius as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian should attempt to revive the embers of paganism, which insensibly declined, and had received a mortal blow at the beginning of the fourth century by the emperor Constantine the great. Julian employed all the resources of his imagination, of his eloquence, of his power, and even of his own fatal example, to revive it; but in vain. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of paganism was arrived, and nothing could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it from destruction. The furious Theodosius, to whom bigotted priests and historians have assigned the name of great, totally overthrew it toward the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the same century, destroyed those temples and altars which yet subsisted, dispersed its colleges, and exterminated its priests. From that dire epoch, nothing of paganism has remained, except some ruins dispersed in the remote parts of the earth, and among people wretched and almost unknown; where this religion, once so flourishing and universal, is now degenerated into grofs and delirious idolatry. **Mytilus**, the Muscles, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>; a genus of animals, belonging to the order of vermes tellacea. The animal is an acidia: the shell bivalve; often affixed to some substance by a beard; the hinge without a tooth, marked by a longitudinal hollow line. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The rugosus, or rugged muscle, with a brittle shell, very rugged, and in shape very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; usually <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and round at the ends. Its length is near an inch; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> whitish. It is always found lodged in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>; the outside appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-combed; but the apertures are too small for the shell to pass through, without breaking into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a> they are lodged in. Multitudes are found in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but each has a separate apartment, with a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> spiracle. 2. The edulis, or edible muscle, has a strong shell, slightly incurved on one side, and angulated on the other. The end near the hinge is pointed; the other rounded. When the epidermis is taken off, it is of a deep blue colour. Mytilus. It is found in immense beds, both in deep water, and above low-water mark. The finest muscles are those called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> hookers, from a village called Humbleton in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. They are taken out of the sea, and placed in the river Wier, within reach of the tide, where they grow very fat and delicious. 3. The incurvatus, or crooked muscle, is very crooked on one side near the end; then greatly dilated, and covered with a thick rough epidermis. Within it has a violet tinge. It is found on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Anglesea, near Prietholme; usually an inch and an half long. 4. The pellucidus, or pellucid muscle, hath a delicate transparent shell, most elegantly rayed lengthwise with purple and blue; like the former in shape, but more oval; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shorter than two inches. It is found in Anglesea, sometimes in oyster-beds, sometimes in trawling over flutty bottoms. 5. The umbilicatus, or umbilicated, muscle, is nearly of an oval form, the length sometimes five inches. It is a rare and new species; sometimes dredged up off Prietholme island, Anglesea; discovered by the reverend Mr Hugh Davies. 6. The curtus, or short muscle, with a short, ventricose, obtuse shell, of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, length about an inch. 7. The modiolus, or great muscle, with a strong shell, blunted at the upper end; one side angulated near the middle; from thence dilating towards the end, which is rounded. It is the greatest of British muscles, being from six to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches in length; it lies at great depths; often seizes the baits of ground-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and is taken up with the hooks. 8. The cygnus, or swan muscle, with a thin brittle shell, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and convex, marked with concentric striae; attenuated towards one end, dilated towards the other; decorticated about the hinge; the colour a dull green; the length six inches, breadth three and a half; inhabits fresh waters. 9. The anatinus, or duck muscle, hath a shell more oblong and less convex than the last; is very brittle and semitransparent; the space round the hinges like the last; the length about five inches, breadth two and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; inhabits fresh waters. Crows feed on these muscles, and also on different shell-fish. It is diverting to observe, that when the shell is too hard for their bills, they fly with it to a great height, drop the shell on a rock, and pick out the meat when the shell is fractured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The common sea or edible muscle has, from its being always found fastened to the rocks, been supposed by many wholly incapable of progressive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; but this is an erroneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. It is a common practice in France, at such seasons of the year as do not afford sun enough to make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, to throw the common sea-muscles, which the fishermen catch about the coasts, into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRINE">brine</a>-pits. They have an opinion that this renders their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> the more tender and delicate, as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> which falls at these seasons makes the water of the pits much less salt than the common seawater. The muscles are on this occasion thrown carelessly in, in several different parts of the pits; yet, at whatever distances they have been thrown in, the fishermen when they go to take them out, always find them in a clutter together; and as there is no current of water in these places, nor any other power of motion which can have brought the muscles together, it seems seems very evident that they must voluntarily have marched from the places where they were at first, to have met thus together. This progressive motion is wholly performed by means of what we call the tongue of the muscle, from its shape; but, from its use in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, appears rather to merit the name of a leg, or an arm, as by laying hold of any distant substance, and then forcibly contracting itself again, it draws along the whole body of the fish; the same part, when it has moved the animal to a proper place, serves also to fix it there, being the organ by which it spins the threads which we call its beard, by which it is held to a rock, or to another muscle. The motion of the muscle, by means of this part, is just the same with that of a man laid flat on his belly, who would draw himself along by laying hold of any thing with one hand, and then <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> himself to it. Muscles are well known to have a power of fastening themselves either to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, or to one another's shells, in a very strong and firm manner; but the method of doing this was not well understood till the observations of Mr Reamur explained it. Every one who opens and examines a common muscle, will find, that in the middle of the fish there is placed a little blackish or brownish body resembling a tongue. This in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> muscles is near half an inch long, and a little more than a fifth of an inch in breadth, and is narrower at the origin than at the extremity: from the root of this tongue, or that part of it which is fastened to the body of the fish, there are produced a great number of threads, which, when fixed to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance, hold the muscle firmly in its place: these threads are usually from an inch to two inches in length, and in thickness from that of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s bristle. They issue out of the shell in that part where it naturally opens, and fix themselves to any thing that lies in their way, to stones, to fragments of shells, or, which is the most common case, to the shells of other muscles; whence it happens that there are usually such large parcels of muscles found together. These threads are expanded on every side, and are usually very numerous, having been found issuing from one shell: they serve the office of so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>; and, each pulling in its proper direction, they keep the muscle fixed against any force that can be offered from whatever part it come. The filaments are well known to all who eat muscles, who ever carefully separate them under the name of the beard; and Mr Reamur has found, that while the animal is living in the sea, if they are all torn away by any accident, the creature has a power of substituting others in their room: he found, that if a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of muscles were detached from one another and put into a vessel of any kind, and in that plunged into the sea, they in a little time fastened themselves both to the sides of the vessel, and to one another's shells; the extremity of each thread seemed in this case to serve in the manner of a hand to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon any thing that it would fix to, and the other part which was slenderer and smaller to do the office of an arm in conducting it. To know the manner of the muscles performing this operation, this diligent observer put some muscles into a vessel in his chamber, and covered them with seawater; he there saw that they soon began to open their shells, and each put forth that little body before described by its resemblance to a tongue, and at the root of which these threads grow; they extended and shortened this part several times, and thrust it out every way, often giving it not less than two inches in length, and trying before, behind, and on every side with it, what were the proper places to fix their threads at: at the end of these trials they let it remain fixed for some time on the spot which they chose for that purpose, and then drawing it back into the shell with great quickness, it was easy to see that they were then fastened by one of these threads to the spot where it had before touched and remained fixed for a few minutes; and in repeating this workmanship the threads are increased in number one at every time, and being fixed in different places they sustain the fish at rest against any common force. The several threads were found to be very different from one another; the new formed ones being ever whiter, more glossy, and more transparent than the others: and it appeared on a close examination, that it was not, as might have been most naturally supposed, the office of the tongue to convey the old threads one by one to the new places where they were now to be fixed, but that these in reality were now become useless; and that every thread we see now formed, is a new one made at this time; and in fine, that nature has given to some sea-fishes, as well as to many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-insects, a power of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> those threads for their necessary uses; and that muscles and the like fish are under water, what caterpillars and spiders are at land. To be well assured of this, however, Mr Reamur cut off the beard or old threads of a muscle as close as he could, without injuring the part; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the opinion of their spinning new ones at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> was now brought to this easy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, whether these muscles, so deprived of their old ones, could fix themselves as soon as others which were possessed of theirs, and could throw out their threads to as considerable distances.
