The experiment proved the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the conjecture; for those whose beards or old threads were cut off, fixed themselves as soon as those in which they were left, and spread their threads to as great a distance every way. When the mechanism of this manufacture was thus far understood, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> desire to inquire into the nature of the part by which it was performed: this has hitherto been mentioned under the name of the tongue, from its shape; but it is truly the arm of the fish; and whenever it happens to be loosened from its company, or fixed in a wrong place, it serves the animal to drag its whole body shell and all along, and to perform its several motions. It fixes itself to some solid body; and then strongly contracting its length, the whole fish must necessarily follow it, and be pulled toward the place where it is fixed. This is an use, however, that this part is so rarely put to, that it is not properly to be esteemed a leg or an arm, for this; but, according to its more frequent employment, may much better be denominated the organ by which the threads are spun. Though this body is flat in the manner of a tongue for the greater part of its length, it is however rounded or cylindric about the base or insertion, and it is much smaller there than in any other part: there are several several muscular ligaments fastened to it about the root or base, which hold it firmly against the middle of the back of the shell; of these ligaments there are four which are particularly observable, and which serve to move the body in any direction. There runs all along this body a slit or crack, which pierces very deeply into its substance, and divides it as it were into two longitudinal sections; this is properly a canal, and along this is thrown the liquor which serves to form the threads; and it is in this canal or slit that these threads are moulded into their form. Externally, this appears only a small crack or slit, because the two fleshy sections of the parts almost meet and cover it, but it is rounded and deep within, and is surrounded with circular fibres. This canal is carried regularly on from the tip of the tongue, as it is called, to its base, where it becomes cylindric; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> in this part being no other than a close tube or pipe, in which this open canal terminates. The cylindric tube contains a round elongated body, of the nature of the threads, except that it is much larger; and from the extremity of this all the threads are produced, this serving as a great cable to which all the other little cordages differ, towards different parts are fixed. The tube or pipe in which this large thread is lodged, seems the reservoir of the liquor of which the other threads are formed; all its internal surface being furnished with glands for its secretion. The muscle, like many other sea-fishes, abounds in this liquor; and if at any time one touch with a finger the base of this spinning organ, one draws away with it a viscous liquor in form of several threads, like those of the caterpillar, spider, and the other spinning land-animals. The threads fix themselves with equal ease to the most smooth and glossy, as to rougher bodies; if the muscles are kept in glass jars of sea-water, they as firmly fasten themselves to the glass as to any other body. Muscles, be they ever so young, have this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of spinning; and by this means they fasten themselves in vast numbers to any thing which they find in the sea. Mr Reaumur has seen them when as small as millet seeds, spin plentifully; tho' their threads, proportioned to their own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, are much finer and smaller than those of larger muscles. It is a question yet undetermined, whether the muscle has a power of breaking or otherwise getting rid of its threads, in order to its removing from the place where it is once fixed; but it appears probable that they have not, and that they must remain where they have once fastened themselves, tho' their destruction be the consequence of it. Mr Reaumur tried this experiment in his jars: when they had well fixed themselves to the sides of them, he poured off part of the salt-water, so that it became the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the fish to leave their hold and go lower <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, but they seemed to have no power to effect this. The common muscle affords the curious observer a very pleasing object of examination by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. The transparent membrane, which immediately appears on opening the shell, shews the circulation of the blood for a long time together through an amazing number of vessels. And Mr Lewenhoeck, in several which he dissected, discovered numbers of eggs or embryo muscles in the ovarium, appearing as plainly as if he had seen them by the naked eye, and all lying with their sharp ends fastened to the string of vessels by which they receive nourishment. The minute eggs, or embryos, are by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> placed in due order, and in a very close arrangement on the outside of the shell, where, by means of a gluey matter, they adhere very fast, and continually increase in size and strength, till becoming perfect muscles, they fall off and shift for themselves, leaving the holes where they were placed, behind them. This abundance of muscle-shells very plainly shew when examined by the microscope, and sometimes they are in the number of 2000 or 3000 on one shell: but it is not certain that these have been all fixed there by the muscle within; for these fish usually lying in great numbers near one another, the embryos of one are often affixed to the shell of another. The fringed edge of the muscle, which Lewenhoeck calls the beard, has in every the minutest part of it such variety of motions as is inconceivable; for being composed of longish fibres, each <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> has on both sides a vast many moving particles. From the common muscles abundance of small pearls, called seed-pearls, were, till of late, procured for medical purposes; but they are now disused since it became generally known, that the cheaper terebrate powders were equally efficacious with these. Pearls are also found in the two last species.—Muscles sometimes disagree with those who eat them, bringing on swellings, difficulty of breathing, blotches, and sometimes even death. The cure is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> mixed with salt water.

MYUS

Pages 559-559

(anc. geog.), one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>; seated on the Meander, at the distance of 30 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was incorporated with the Milesians, on account of the paucity of its inhabitants, from its being formerly overwhelmed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; for which reason the Ionians configned its suffrage and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> allotted this town to Themistocles, in order to furnish his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The town now lies in ruins.

MYXINE

Pages 559-560

the HAG; a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes intestini. It hath a slender body, carinated beneath; mouth at the extremity, ciliated; the two jaws pinnated; an adipose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rayless <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> round the tail and under the belly. The only remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the glutinosa, about eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It inhabits the ocean; enters the mouths of fish when on the hooks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> that remain a tide under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and totally devours the whole, except skin and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a> fishermen often take it in the robbed fish, on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up their lines. Linnaeus attributes to it the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> water into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. N, A liquid consonant, and the 13th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek, Latin, English, &c. alphabets. The n is a nasal consonant; its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is that of a d, passed through the nose; so that when the nose is stopped by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, or the like, it is usual to pronounce d for n. M. L'Abbé de Dangeau observes, that in the French, the n is frequently a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nasal vowel, without any thing of the consonant in it. He calls it the Slavonic vowel. The Hebrews call their n <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUN">nun</a>, which signifies child, as being supposed the offspring of m; partly on account of the resemblance of sound, and partly on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Thus from the m, by omitting the last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, is formed n; and thus from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> N, by omitting the first column, is formed the Greek minuscule n. Hence for binnius, &c. the Latins frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> binus, &c. and the same people convert the Greek i, at the end of a word into an n, as ἀπολαμβάνειν, pharmacum, &c. See M. N before p, b, and m, the Latins change into m, and frequently into l and r; as in in-ludeo, illudo; in-rigo, irrego, &c.; in which they agree with the Hebrews, who, in lieu of nun, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the following <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>; and the Greeks do the same; as when for Manlius, they write Μανλίους, &c. The Greeks also, before κ, γ, χ, changed the v into γ; in which they were followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; who, for Angulus, wrote Aggulus; for ancus, agcus, &c. The Latins retrench the n from Greek <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> ending in -os; as Λέων, Leo; Δράκων, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>: on the contrary, the Greeks add it to the Latin ones ending in -us; as Κατός, Nero, for Cato, Nero. N, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was a numeral letter, signifying 900; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Barionus, N, quaeque nongentos numeros defigent habebant. And when a line was struck over it, N̄, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> thousand. Among the ancient lawyers N. L. stood for non liquet, i.e. the cause is not clear enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon. N., or N°, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c. is used as an abbreviation of numero, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

NABIS

Pages 560-560
tyrant of Sparta, reigned about 204 B.C.; and is reported to have exceeded all other tyrants so far, that, upon comparison, he left the epithets of gracious and merciful to Dionysius and Phalaris. He is said to have contrived an instrument of torture in the form of a statue of a beautiful woman, whose rich dress concealed a number of iron spikes in her bosom and arms. When any one therefore opposed his demands, he would say, "If I have not talents enough to prevail with you, perhaps my woman Apega may persuade you." The statue then appeared; which Nabis taking by the hand, led up to the person, who, being embraced by it, was thus tortured into compliance. He reigned 14 years, and was slain in battle.

NABOB

Pages 560-560

a viceroy, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> governor of one of the provinces of the Mogul's empire.

NABONASSAR

Pages 560-560

first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Chaldeans, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Babylonians; memorable for the Jewish era which Nabopolassar bears his name, which is generally fixed in 3257, beginning on Wednesday February 26th in the 3967th of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 747 years before Christ. The Babylonians revolting from the Medes, who had overthrown the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, did, under Nabonassar, found a dominion, which was much increased under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. It is probable, that this Nabonassar is that Baladan in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Kings xx. 12, father of Merodach, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah. See 2 Chron. xxxii.

NABOPOLASSAR

Pages 560-560
king of Babylon: he joined with Assyriaces the Mede, to destroy the empire of Assyria; which having accomplished, they founded the two empires of the Medes under Assyriaces, and the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar, 627 B.C.

NABUCHADNEZZAR

Pages 560-560
or Nabuchodonosor II: king of Assyria, son of Nabopolassar, and styled the Great, was associated by his father in the empire, 607 B.C. and the following year he took Jehoiakim king of Judah prisoner, and proposed to carry him and his subjects in captivity into Babylon; but upon his submission, and promising to hold his kingdom under Nabuchodonosor, he was permitted to remain at Jerusalem. In 603 B.C. Jehoiakim attempted to shake off the Assyrian yoke, but without success; and this revolt brought on the general captivity. Nabuchadnezzar having subdued the Ethiopians, Arabians, Idumeans, Philistines, Syrians, Persians, Medes, Assyrians, and almost all Asia; being puffed up with pride, caused a golden statue to be set up, and commanded all to worship it; which Daniel's companions refusing to do, they were cast into the fiery furnace. But as he was admiring his own magnificence, by divine sentence, he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, that is, he imagined himself to be one. At the end of seven years his reason returned to him, and he was restored to his throne and glory. He died 562 B.C. in the 43rd year of his reign; in the 5th of which happened that eclipse of the sun mentioned by Ptolemy, which is the surest foundation of the chronology of his reign.

NADIR

Pages 560-560

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, that point of the heavens which is diametrically opposite to the zenith, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> point directly over our heads.

NAERDEN

Pages 560-560

a strong town of the United Provinces in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, seated at the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The foundations of it were laid by William of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, in 1350. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1572, and by the French in 1672; but it was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> the next year. It stands at the south end of the Zuider-Zee, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 3. N. Lat. 51. 22.

NAEVUS

Pages 560-561

a famous poet of Campania, was bred a soldier, but quitted the profession of arms, in order to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which he prosecuted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence; and composed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of comedies. But it is said, that that his first performance of this last kind so displeased Metellus, on account of the satyrical strokes it contained, that he procured his being banished from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>; on which he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, where he at length died, 202 B.C. We have only some fragments left of his works. NÆVUS, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> on the skin, generally called a mother's mark; also the tumour known by the name of a wen. All preternatural tumours on the skin, in the form of a wart <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tubercle, are called excrescences; by the Greeks they are called acrotymias; and when they are born with a person, they are called nevi materni, or marks from the mother. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tumour depending from the skin is denominated sarcoma. These appear on any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body: some of them differ in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest of the skin; whilst others are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, &c. Their shapes are various; some resembling strawberries, others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, &c. Healer advises their removal by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a>, a cautery, or a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, as circumstances best <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. As to the tumour called a wen, its different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are distinguished by their contents. They are encysted tumours; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the first three following is infusorial lymph, and that in the fourth is only fat. Mons. Littre is the first who hath particularly described the fourth kind; and to the following purpose he speaks of them all. A wen is said to be of three sorts, according to the kind of matter it contains: those whose contents resemble boiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, or curds, or a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-poultice, is called athetoma; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it resembles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, it is named melicaria; and if it is like suet, it is denominated steatoma; but there is a fourth sort, which may be called lipoma, because of its fat contents resembling grease. He says that he hath seen one on the shoulders of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, which was a thin bag, of a tender texture, full of a soft fat, and that it had all the qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> grease. And though the fat in the lipoma resembles that in the steatoma, yet they cannot be the same; for the matter of the steatoma is not inflammable, nor does it melt; or if it does, it is with great difficulty and imperfectly; whereas it is the contrary with the lipoma. When the man who had the above-named lipoma was fatigued, or had drank freely of strong liquors, his lipoma was inflamed for some days after, and its contents rarefying increased the size of the tumour. The lipoma seems to be no other than an enlargement of one or more of the cells of the adipose membrane, which is filled only with its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> contents. Its softness and largeness distinguish it in general from the other species, though sometimes the fatty contents <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be so hard as to deceive. As this kind of wen does not run between the muscles, nor is possessed of any considerable blood-vessels, it may always be cut off with ease and safety. As to the other kind of wens, their extirpation may or may not be attempted, according as their situation is with respect to adjacent vessels, the wounding of which would endanger the patient's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

NAGERA

Pages 561-561
or NAGARA, a town of Spain, in Old Castile, and the territory of Rioja, with the title of a duchy and fortress; famous for a battle fought in its neighbourhood in 1369. It is situated in a fertile country, on a brook called Nafrilla. W. Long. 2° 20'.

NAGRACUT

Pages 561-561

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, with a rich temple to which the Indians go in pilgrimage. It is seated on the river Ravi. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 10'. N. Lat. 33° 12'.

NAHUM

Pages 561-561
or the Prophecy of Nahum, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Nahum, the seventh of the 12 lesser prophets, was a native of Elkofhai, a little village of Galilee. The subject of his prophecy is the destruction of Nineveh, which he describes in the most lively and pathetic manner; his style is bold and figurative, and cannot be exceeded by the most perfect masters of oratory. This prophecy was verified at the siege of that city by Assyrians, in the year of the world 3378, 622 years before Christ.

NAIADES

Pages 561-561

in pagan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the nymphs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and fountains, who were adored by the pagans as a kind of inferior deities, and were represented as young and beautiful virgins.

NAIANT

Pages 561-561

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, when borne in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> posture, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>.

NAILS

Pages 561-561

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c. Small spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c. which being drove into wood, serve to bind several pieces together, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to fasten something upon them. Nail, is also a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, containing the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a yard. Nailing of Cannon. When circumstances make it necessary to abandon cannon, or when the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> is seized, and it is not however possible to take them away, it is proper to nail them up, in order to render them useless; which is done by driving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nail or iron spike into the vent of a piece of artillery, to render it unserviceable. There are various contrivances to force the nail out, as also sundry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> invented for that purpose, but they have never been found of general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; so that the best method is to drill a new vent. One Gasper Vimercatus was the first who invented the nailing of cannon. He was a native of Bremen, and made use of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> first in nailing up the artillery of Sigismund Malatesta.

NAIRN

Pages 561-562

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, comprehending the west <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Murray. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Murray frith, on the west and south by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, and on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>. The length of it amounts to 20 miles, and the breadth to 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and salubrious, and the winters are remarkably mild. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rough and mountainous; yet there are some fruitful traths, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> valleys, which produce good crops of oats and barley; but in general the country is much better adapted for pasture. Here are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> woods of fir, and other trees, that afford shelter to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, of which there is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. A thath is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, narrow valley, with a ri- ver running through the bottom. Of these, the most remarkable in this county, are Strath-nairn, on the river of that name, in the south-west part of the shire; and on the south-east side, Strath-erin, on both sides of Findhorn river. Nairn is well watered with streams, rivulets, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, abounding with fish. In the southern part there is a small lake, called Moy, surrounding an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, on which there is a castle belonging to the laird of M'Intosh; but the greater part of the shire is peopled by the Frasers, a warlike Highland clan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lovat, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on a scaffold, for having been concerned in the late rebellion. Here is a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; but no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, except Nairn, supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAURIS">Tauris</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, situated at the mouth of the river which bears the same name; a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, which gave a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lord to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, forfeited in the rebellion of 1715. The harbour, which opened in the Murray frith, is now choked up with sand; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the town is too inconsiderable to deserve notice. The people in general subsist by feeding sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. About four miles from Nairn stands the castle of Calder, on the river of that name, belonging to a branch of the family of Campbell. In this neighbourhood we find a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of freestone, and many signs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. About six miles to the north-west of Nairn, a new fort hath been lately built by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Ardrossan, a small isthmus upon the Murray frith, which it is intended to command.

NAISSANT

Pages 562-562

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and shewing only his head, shoulders, fore-feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail; the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it; in which it differs from issuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge. NAKED seeds, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, those that are not inclosed in any pod or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

NAME

Pages 562-563

denotes a word whereby men have agreed to express some idea; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or subject spoken of. See Word. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. See Noun. Seneca, Lib. II. de Beneficiis, observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name; and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Ingens est, says he, rerum copia sine nomine, quas eum propriis appellationibus signare non possumus, alienis accommodatis utimur; which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, we frequently give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper Names, are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or General Names, are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, &c. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; or surnames: The first imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen: The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the women of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymicum of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name; as among the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, &c. among the Egyptians, Bafris; among the Chaldees, Nimus; the Medes, Abysses; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Divitiacus; the Germans, Arvicius; the Britains, Cassibelan; the English, Hengist, &c. And thus of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonymous, "nameless." The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth: the Romans, to females the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nominalia. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; except our English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, till of late, baptized and gave the name on the birth-day. The first imposition of names was founded on different views, among different people; the most common was to mark the good wishes of the parents, or to entitle the children to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> a happy name seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. Hence, Vittor, Caeser, Faustus, Statius, Probus, &c. Accordingly, we find such names, by Cicero called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONA">bona</a> nomina, and by Tacitus fausta nomina, were first enrolled and ranged in the Roman muster; first called to serve at the sacrifices, in the foundation of colonies, &c.—And, on the contrary, Livy calls Atrius Umbert, abominandi omnis nomen; and Plautus, on occasion of a person named Lyco, i.e. "greedy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>," says: Vosque nomen facite confesturam exterum Quid id sit benevoli, sed Lyco nomen fit. Hence, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> recommends it to men to be careful in giving happy names; and the Pythagoreans taught expressly, that the minds, actions, and successes of men, were according to their names, genius, and fate. Thus Panormitan, ex bono nomine ortur bona praesumptio; and the common proverb, Bonum nomen bonum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; and hence the foundation of the onomantia. See ONOMANTIA. Hence Camden takes it for granted, that the names, in all nations and languages, are significative, and not simple sounds for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> distinction sake. This holds not only among the Jews, Greeks, Latins, &c. but even the Turks; among whom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDALLA">Abdalla</a> signifies God's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>; Soliman, peaceable; Mahomet, glorified, &c. And the savages of Hispaniola, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who, in their languages, name their children, Glittering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> Bright, Fine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, &c.; and they of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, by the names of precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. To suppose names given without any meaning, however by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of languages their signification may be lost, that learned author thinks is to reproach our ancestors; and that contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Porphyry notes, that the barbarous names, as he calls them, were very emphatical, and very concise; and accordingly, it was esteemed a duty to be strenuous, or sui nominis homines; as Severus, Probus, It was the usual way of giving names, to wish the children might discharge their names.—Thus when Gunthram <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France named Clotharius at the font, he said, *Crescat puer, &c.* butus fit homines executor. The ancient Britons, Camden says, generally took their names from colours, because they painted themselves; which names are now lost, or remain hid among the Welsh. When they were subdued by the Romans, they took Roman names, some of which still remain, corrupted; though the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> became extinct upon the admission of the English Saxons, who introduced the German names, as *Gridda*, *Penda*, *Oswald*, *Edward*, &c.—The Danes, too, brought with them their names; as *Swyn*, *Harold*, *Knute*, &c. The Normans, at the Conquest, brought in other German names, as originally using the German tongue; such as *Robert*, *William*, *Richard*, *Henry*, *Hugh*, &c. after the same manner as the Greek names: *Alphius*, *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>- thius*, *Synnachus*, &c. were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire. After the Conquest, our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which had ever been averse to foreign names, as deeming them unlucky, began to take <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> names; as *Matthew*, *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>*, *Samson*, &c. The various names anciently or at present obtaining among us, from what <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> or people forever borrowed, are explained by Camden in his Remains. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when names began to be multiplied, and surnames introduced, &c. see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">Surname</a>. Of late years it has obtained among us to give surnames for Christian names; which some dislike, on account of the confusion it may introduce. Camden relates it as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the practice first began in the reign of Edward VI. by such as would be godfathers, when they were more than half fathers. Upon which some were prevailed to change their names at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>; which, it seems, is usual in other countries.—Thus, two sons of Henry II. of France, christened Alexander and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, changed them at confirmation into Henry and Francis. In monasteries, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assume new names at their admittance, to show they are about to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and have renounced the world, their family, and even their name: e.g. sister <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of the Incarnation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry of the holy Sacrament, &c. The popes also changed their name at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> to the pontificate; a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> first introduced by Pope Sergius, whose name till then, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> informs us, was *Sergius*. But Omophrius refers it to John XII or XIII.; and at the same time adds a different reason for it from that of Platina, viz. that it was done in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, who were first called Simon and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, those deified by the Heathen confraternities, had new names given them; as Romulus was called *Quirinus*; Melicertes, *Portunus* or *Portunus*, &c. New names were also given in adoptions, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>: thus L. *Emilius*, adopted by Scipio, took the name of *Scipio Africanus*; and thus Augustus, who at first was called *G. Octavius Thurinus*, being adopted by the testament of Julius Caesar into his name and family, took the name of *<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Julius Caesar Othoianus*. Names were also changed at enfranchisements into new cities. Thus Lucumo, at his first being made free of Rome, took the name *Lucius Tarquinius Priscus*, &c.; and slaves, when made free, usually assumed their masters' names. Those called to the equitatus order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had base names, were always new named, *nomine ingeniorum veterumque Romanorum*. And among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was the practice to change the names of the catechumens: Thus the renegade Lucius, till his baptism, was called *Lucius*.

NAMUR

Pages 563-563

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Sambre and Maas; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Brabant, on the east and south by the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, and on the west by Hainault. It is pretty fertile; has several forests, marble quarries, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and pit-coal; and is about 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Namur is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. Namur, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and very strong town of the Netherlands, capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Namur, with a strong castle, several forts, and a bishop's see. The most considerable forts are, Fort-William, Fort-Maese, Fort Coquetel, and Fort-Espinor. The castle is built in the middle of the town, on a craggy rock. It was besieged by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> William in 1695, who took it in the sight of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 French, though there were 60,000 men in garrison. Namur is now a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>-town, and has a Dutch garrison. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> in 1713, but taken by the French in 1746; and restored by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. It is situated between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, at the confluence of the rivers Maas and Sambre, in E. Long. 4° 57'. N. Lat. 50° 25'.

NANCI

Pages 563-563

a town of France, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Lorraine, is situated on the river Meuse, in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It is divided into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. The first, though irregularly built, is very populous, and contains the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the streets of the New Town are as straight as a line, adorned with handsome buildings, and a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The primatial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a magnificent structure, and in that of the Cordeliers are the tombs of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. The two towns are separated by a canal; and the new town was very well fortified, but the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France has demolished the fortifications. It has been taken and retaken several times; particularly by the French, to whom it was ceded in 1736, to enjoy it after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Stanislaus.

NANKING

Pages 563-563

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kiang-nan. It is the largest in China, being 17 miles in circumference, and about three miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river Yang-tse Chiang, from which there are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> cut; so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> that vessels may enter the town. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is greatly fallen from its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour, for it had a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which is quite destroyed, as well as many ancient monuments, and a third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city itself is desolate. The streets are narrow, but handsome and well paved, and on each side are shops neatly furnished. The public buildings are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, the city-gates, and a tower of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. They have several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants are said to be 1,000,000, without

NANSIO

Pages 563-564

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the island of Santorino, 16 miles in circumference; but has no harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are nothing but bare rocks, and there are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> the fields. There are a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of partridges, whose eggs they delivory every year to preserve the corn, and yet vast numbers of them are always produced. The ruins of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> are yet to be seen, and consist chiefly of marble columns. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 20. N. Lat. 36. 15.

NANTES

Pages 564-564

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and very considerable town of France, in Bretagne, with a bishop's see, an university, and a mint. It is one of the most considerable places in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; contains the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and was formerly the residence of the dukes of Bretagne, where they built a very strong castle on the side of the river, and which is strongly fortified. There are several parishes, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> contains the tombs of the ancient dukes. There are several fine bridges over the river <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, which is navigable. The suburbs are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people that come from all parts to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> here, that they exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Spaniards trade here with wine, fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, oranges, and lemons; and they carry back cloth, stuffs, corn, and hard-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. The Dutch send <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fish, and all sorts of spices; and in return have wine and brandy. The Swedes bring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; and the English, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, and pit-coal. It was in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> that Henry IV. promulgated the famous edict in 1598, called the Edict of Nantes, and which was revoked in 1685. The territory of Nantes lies on both sides the Loire, and feeds a great number of cattle. Large vessels can come no higher than Port Launay, which is 12 miles from Nantes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 31. N. Lat. 47. 13.

NANTUEIL

Pages 564-564

the celebrated designer and engraver to the cabinet of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1630. Though his father was but a petty shopkeeper, he gave his son a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; who, having a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, cultivated it with such success, that he became the admiration of the whole town: but marrying young, and not being able to maintain his family, he took a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he made his talents known by a stratagem.—Seeing several abbés at the door of an eating-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he asked the mistress for an ecclesiastic of Rheims, whose name he had forgot, but that he might easily know him by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of him which he shewed: the abbés crowding round, were so charmed with it, that he seized the opportunity of offering to draw any of their pictures for a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Customers came so fast that he soon raised his price, and brought his family to Paris, where his reputation was quickly established. He applied himself particularly to taking portraits in crayons, which he afterward engraved for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of academical theses; and in this way he did the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, and afterward engraved it as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; a thing never before attempted. The king was so pleased with it, that he created the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of designer and engraver to the cabinet for him, with a pension of 1000 livres. He died in 1678; and an entire collection of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> amounts to upwards of 240. NAPÆA, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>; a genus of the polygynia order, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; both of them with perennial roots, composed of many thick fleshy fibres, which strike deep into the ground, and are connected at the top into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heads; the stalks grow to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, producing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, tubulous at bottom, but spreading open at top, and dividing into five obtuse segments. Both these plants are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; from the bark of some of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> kinds a sort of fine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> might be procured, capable of being woven into very strong cloth. They are easily propagated by seed, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive in any situation.

NAPHTHA

Pages 564-564

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a fluid mineral body, of a thin consistence, bright and pellucid, of a strong smell, very readily inflammable, and, when pure, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> away without leaving any residuum. The naphtha is found in considerable quantities floating on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, principally breaking out at the sides of hills in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and some parts of the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> be held near the surface, it takes fire and overspreads the surface of the water for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and emits a very disagreeable smell. The genuine naphtha is very rare in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; it is not known to be anywhere naturally produced here, and what we see of it is generally sophicated. Distilled by the retort, it yields an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> somewhat thinner than it was originally, and of a weaker smell. The substance remaining at the bottom of the retort, has much the resemblance of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>; and Dr Hill thinks it highly probable, that the origin of all the amber is from the same sort of principle; may, he tells us that he has succeeded so far in an attempt to make amber by this fluid and an acid drawn from the crude pyrites, that he has produced a friable, somewhat pellucid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, having all the properties of amber except the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and clearness, and yielding a true <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and oil of amber on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The medicinal virtues of the naphtha are the same with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, but in a lower <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. It is used externally on many occasions in Persia; and is taken inwardly, a few drops for a dose, in colics. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it, however, is for burning in lamps; and for this it is extremely well adapted.

NAPHTHALI

Pages 564-564
or NEPTHALI, (Joth. xix.) one of the tribes of Israel; having Zabulon on the south, Asher on the west, the Jordan on the east, and on the north Antilibanus. NAPIER. See NEPER.

NAPLES

Pages 564-575

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, comprehending the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> countries of Samnium, Campania, Apulia, and Magna Graecia. It is bounded on all sides by the Mediterranean and Adriatic, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, where it terminates on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> state. Its greatest length from south-east to north-west is about 280 English miles; and its breadth from north-east to south-west, from 96 to 120. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> falls under the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> ROME and ITALY; the present state of it, as well as of the rest of Italy, is owing to the conquests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. When that monarch put an end to the kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, he obliged the dukes of Friuli, Spoleto, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, to acknowledge ledge him as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy; but allowed them to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the same power and authority which they had enjoyed before his conquest. Of these three dukedoms Benevento was by far the most powerful and extensive, as it comprehended almost all the present kingdom of Naples; that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of farther <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Savuto and Peto, a few <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities in Hither Calabria, with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Acripoli, and the promontory in its neighbourhood called Capo di Lezza; and lastly, the dukedoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, Naples, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a>, which were very inconsiderable, and extended along the shore only about 100 miles, and were interrupted by the Gaetaldate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>. This flourishing and extensive dukedom was at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed by Arechis, who had married one of the daughters of the last king of the Lombards, and had submitted, and taken the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. However, a few years after, he renounced his allegiance to the Franks, declared himself an independent sovereign, and was acknowledged as such by all the inhabitants of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. To strengthen himself against Pepin king of Italy, who resided at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, he enlarged and fortified the city of Benevento, and likewise built Salerno on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, surrounding it with a very strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall. He engaged in several wars with the Greeks, whom he sometimes obliged to give him hostages; but having invaded the territories of the pope, whom Pepin could not assist, Charlemagne was prevailed on to return to Italy. Arechis, unable to oppose such a formidable enemy, sent his eldest son, Romuald, to Rome, with an offer of submission; but, at the instigation of the pope, Charles refused the offer, and detained his son prisoner; after which he ravaged the country, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Capua. Other deputies, however, proved more successful; and, in the year 787, a peace was concluded on these conditions: That Arechis and the Beneventans should renew their allegiance to the Franks; that he should pay a yearly tribute to Pepin; deliver up all his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and give his son Grimoald and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Adelgifa, with twelve others, as hostages for his fidelity: however, after many intrigues, Adelgifa was restored to her father. Charles had no sooner left Italy, than Arechis forgot all his engagements, and began to negotiate with Irene, empress of Constantinople, and her son Constantine, for expelling the Franks out of Italy. For himself, he desired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of patriciate, and the dukedom of Naples with all its dependencies; and, in return, promised to acknowledge the Greek emperor as his sovereign, and to live after the manner of the Greeks. He required, however, to be supported by a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> Adalgiso, son to Desiderius the last king of the Lombards, should be sent over into Italy, to raise a party among his countrymen. These conditions were readily accepted, on condition that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Romuald should be sent as an hostage; ambassadors were sent to Naples with the ensigns of the patrician order, namely the mantle of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, the comb, and the sandals: but before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> could be performed, prince Romuald died, and soon after him his father; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was supposed to have been hastened by that of his son. After the death of Arechis, the Beneventans sent a most submissive embassy to Charlemagne, intreating him to send them Grimoald, the late king's son, and only lawful heir to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; threatening at the same time to revolt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their prince was denied them. Charles readily granted their request, and allowed Grimoald to depart; after he had agreed to the following terms: viz. That he should oblige the Lombards to shave their beards; that, in writings, and on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, the name of the king should be put before that of the prince; and that he should cause the walls of Salerno, Accerenza, and Conisa, to be entirely demolished. The new king was received by his subjects with the utmost joy; and for some time <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> faithful to his engagements, excepting only the last article, which he either neglected or eluded. So far, however, was he from afflicting the Greeks, that he gave notice of their machinations to Pepin king of Italy; raised an army to oppose his uncle Adalgiso; and being joined by Hildebrand <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Spoleto, and Vinigilo the general of Pepin, he attacked the Greeks in Calabria soon after they had landed, entirely defeated and took his uncle prisoner, and, as is said, put him to a cruel death. Yet in a short time Grimoald contracted an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Greek emperor by marrying his niece Wanzia; and in the fifth year of his reign, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out between him and Pepin, which continued for twelve years; at the end of which time a truce was concluded. Grimoald survived this pacification only three years, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Grimoald II., who submitted to Charlemagne after the death of Pepin, and from this time the Beneventans were looked upon as tributaries of the western emperors. As yet, however, the city of Naples did not own allegiance to the dukes of Benevento, but was held by the eastern emperors; and frequent wars took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Beneventans and Neapolitans. This happened to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> when Grimoald II. ascended the throne. He concluded a peace with them; which however, was of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; for Theodore, governor of Naples, having granted protections to Dauferius a noble Beneventan, who had been concerned in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against his prince, Grimoald marched against the city of Naples, and invested it by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Theodore still refused to deliver up the traitor, and a general engagement both by land and sea was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; in which the Neapolitans were defeated with so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter, that the sea was stained with their blood for more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. Theodore then consented to deliver up Dauferius, with 8000 crowns for the expenses of the war; and Grimoald not only pardoned Dauferius, but received him into favour: the traitor, however, reflecting on the heinousness of his crime, was seized with remorse; and went a pilgrimage to the holy land, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in his mouth, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, which he never took out but at his meals. In the year 821, Grimoald was murdered by Radclis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Conisa, and Sico gaufalo of Accerenta, aided by the latter of whom succeeded to the dukedom of Benevento. Radclis being soon after seized with remorse, became a monk; while Sico associated his son Sicardo with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and both, being of an ambitious and restless disposition, sought a pretence for attacking the Neapolitans. This was Naples soon found, and the city was invested by sea and land. The walls were furiously battered; and part of them being <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, Sico prepared for a general assault. Stephen, at that time duke of Naples, pretended to submit; but, that he might prevent the city from being pillaged, intreated Sico to put off his entry till the morning, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time sent out his mother and his two children as hostages. Sico consented to his request; but next morning found the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> built up, and the Neapolitans prepared for their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Exasperated at their presidy, he renewed his attacks with vigour, but without any success; the besieged defending themselves with the utmost obstinacy. At last, perceiving that they should not be able to hold out much longer, they consented to a peace on the following conditions, viz. That the Neapolitans should pay an annual tribute to the princes of Benevento, and consent to the transporting of the body of St Januarius from his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> without the walls of Naples to Benevento. These conditions being ratified, Sico returned with great honour to Benevento; but soon after renewed the war, under pretence that the Neapolitans had neglected to pay the stipulated sum; and hostilities continued till his death, which happened in 833. Sico was succeeded in the government of Benevento by his son Sicardo, who had married the daughter of Daufurius; and being influenced by the evil counsels of Roffrid his wife's brother, opprest his subjects to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that they conspired against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He besieged Naples with a powerful army, and took possession of Accera and Atella, both of which he fortified. But Bonus, the Neapolitan duke, defended himself so vigorously, that the Beneventans were obliged to retire, and even to abandon Accera and Atella, the fortifications of which were immediately demolished. At last Sicardo agreed to a peace for five years, on the intercession of Lothaire, emperor and king of Italy; but his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> was thought to have been the fear of the Saracens, whom the duke of Naples had called over from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> to his alliance; for no sooner were they sent back, than Sicardo attempted to delay the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>; but the emperor interposing his authority, a peace was concluded in the year 836, after the war had continued, with very little intermission, for 16 years. Soon after the conclusion of this peace, the Saracens landed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRINDISI">Brindisi</a>; and having made themselves masters of the place, ravaged all the neighbouring country. Sicardo marched against them with a numerous army; but the Saracens having dug a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ditches which they slightly covered over, found means to draw the Beneventans among them, whereby they were repulsed with great loss. However, Sicardo, having reinforced his army, marched again to attack them; but the Saracens, despairing of success, pillaged and burnt Brindisi, and then retired with their booty, and a great many captives, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Sicardo then, without any apparent provocation, attacked the city of Amalfi, levelled its walls with the ground, carried off all its wealth, and the body of its tutelar saint Triphomen. A great many of the inhabitants were transported to Salerno; and by promoting alliances between the inhabitants of both places, he endeavoured to unite Amalfi to his own principality as firmly as possible. During all these transactions, Sicardo had tyrannized over his subjects in such a manner, that at last he became intolerable. Among other acts of injustice, he imprisoned his own brother Siconolphilus; compelled him to turn <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and afterwards sent him Sicardo bound to Tarento, where he caused him to be shut up murdered in an old tower that had been built for a cistern. By such acts of tyranny his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> were provoked to conspire against him; and in the year 839 he was murdered in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. On the death of Sicardo, Radelchis, his secretary or treasurer, was unanimously elected prince of Benevento; but Siconolphilus, the last king's brother, having regained his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, formed a great party against the new prince. Radelchis did not fail to oppose him with a formidable army; and a most ruinous civil war ensued. Both parties by turns called in the Saracens; and these treacherous allies acted sometimes against one, and sometimes against the other; or turned their arms against both, as seemed most suitable to their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Thus the war continued with the utmost animosity for 12 years, during which time the principality was almost entirely ruined; till at last the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> interposed, and obliged the competitors to agree to a partition of the principality: by this treaty, Radelchis promised to acknowledge Siconolphilus and his successors as lawful princes of the principality of Salerno, which was declared to contain Tarento, Latiniano, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASSANO">Cassano</a>, Costenzo, Laino, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, Conisa, Montella, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROTA">Rota</a>, Salerno, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SARNO">Sarno</a>, Ciraterium, Forcilo, Capua, Feano, Sora, and the half of the Gaufaldate of Accerenza, where it joins Latiano and Conisa. The boundary betwixt Benevento and Capua was fixed at St Angelo <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Cerros; Alli Pergerini was made the boundary betwixt Benevento and Salerno, and Staffilo betwixt Benevento and Conisa. The monasteries of Monte Cassino and St Vincent were declared to be immediately under the protection of the emperor; both princes stipulated that no hostilities should be committed by either, against the subjects of each other; and promised to join their forces, in order to drive out the Saracens. Soon after this pacification, however, both Radelchis and Siconolphilus died; the former appointing his son Radelgarus, or Radelcar, to succeed him; and the latter leaving an infant son, Sico, to the care of his godfather, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The war with the Saracens proved very unsuccessful; neither the united efforts of the princes, nor the assistance of the emperor Lewis himself, being able to expel the infidels; and, in 844, Arechis, the son and successor of Radelchis, was obliged to pay them an annual subsidy. Two years after, Lando, count of Capua, revolted from the prince of Salerno, and could not be reduced. In the mean time, Sico, the lawful prince of Salerno, had been poisoned by count Lando, and the principality usurped by Ademarius, the son of Peter above-mentioned; but, in 861, Ademarius himself was seized and imprisoned by Guafurius, the son of Daufurius formerly mentioned. This was occasioned by his cruelty and rapaciousness, which entirely alienated the hearts of his subjects from him, and encouraged Guafurius to become the head of the conspirators. The Saracens in the mean time committed terrible terrible ravages throughout the Beneventan territories which at last obliged Adelgide to enter into an alliance with Guasterius, and both together sent a most humble embassy to the emperor Lewis, requesting him to take them under his protection. About the same time an embassy arrived from Constantinople, proposing a junction of the forces of the eastern and western empires against the infidels; upon which Lewis gave orders for assembling a formidable army. But in the mean time Adelgide fell off from his alliance, and made peace with the Saracens; nay, according to some, he encouraged them in their incursions, and it was at his desire that they invaded the duchy of Capua, and afterwards that of Naples, which they ravaged in a most barbarous manner. The Neapolitans, in conjunction with the duke of Spoleto and the count of Marti, endeavoured to oppose them; but being defeated, the Saracens continued their ravages with redoubled fury, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, which was their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city, with an immense booty. In 866, Lewis arrived at Sora with his army; and having marched to Capua, was there joined by Landolph, the bishop and count, with a body of Capuans: but Landolph soon after persuading his countrymen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, Lewis marched against that city, which he took after a siege of three months, and almost totally destroyed. In the end of the year he was joined by Guasterius with his quota of troops, having ordered the eyes of Ademarius to be put out in his absence. Lewis confirmed him in the principality, and marched with his army to Benevento, where Adelgide received him with great respect. Having reduced some inconsiderable places belonging to the Saracens, Lewis soon after invested Bari; but as the Saracens received continual supplies from their countrymen settled in Sicily, and besides were protected by the Neapolitans, he could not reduce the place till the year 871, tho' he had received considerable assistance from his brother Lotharius, and the Greek emperor had sent him a fleet of 200 sail. The expulsion of the Saracens was completed the same year by the taking of Tarento; after which the emperor returned with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to Benevento, resolving next to carry his arms into Sicily, and expel the infidels from thence also. But his future schemes of conquest were frustrated by a quarrel between him and Adelgide. The latter, pretending to have been insulted by the empress, and opprobried by the French, seized the emperor himself, and kept him prisoner for 40 days. His imprisonment would probably have been of much longer continuance, had not a body of Saracens arrived from Africa, who, being joined by such of their countrymen as had concealed themselves in Italy, laid siege to Salerno with an army of 30,000 men, ravaging the neighbouring country at the same time with the utmost barbarity. By this new invasion Adelgide was so much alarmed, that he set the emperor at liberty, but first obliged him to swear that he would not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the insult that had been offered him, and that he would never return to Benevento. Lewis having then joined his forces to those of the prince of Salerno, soon obliged the Saracens to raise the siege of Salerno; but tho' they were prevented from taking that city, they entirely destroyed the inhabitants of Calabria, leaving it, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of one of the historians of that time, "as desolate as it was at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>."
