Concerning Currents, and how to make proper allowances. 1. Currents are certain settings of the stream, by which all bodies (as ships, &c.) moving therein, are compelled to alter their course or velocity, or both; and submit to the motion impressed upon them by the current. Case I. If the current sets just with the course of the ship, i.e. moves on the same rhumb with it; then the motion of the ship is increased, by as much as is the drift or velocity of the current. Example. Suppose a ship sails SE&S at the rate of 6 miles an hour, in a current that sets SE&S 2 miles an hour: Required her true rate of sailing. Here it is evident that the ship's true rate of sailing will be 8 miles an hour. Case II. If the current sets directly against the ship's course, then the motion of the ship is lessened by... Example. Suppose a ship sails SSW at the rate of 10 miles an hour, in a current that sets NNE 6 miles an hour: Required the ship's true rate of sailing. Here it is evident that the ship's true rate of sailing will be 4 miles an hour. Hence it is plain, Cox. I. If the velocity of the current be less than the velocity of the ship, then the ship will get so much a-head as is the difference of these velocities. Cox. II. If the velocity of the current be greater than that of the ship, then the ship will fall so much a-tern as is the difference of these velocities. Cox. III. Lastly, If the velocity of the current be equal to that of the ship, then the ship will stand still; the one velocity destroying the other. Case III. If the current thwarts the course of the ship, then it not only lessens or augments her velocity, but gives her a new direction compounded of the course she steers, and the setting of the current, as is manifest from the following Lemma. If a body at A (No. 26.) be impelled by two forces at the same time, the one in the direction AB capable to carry that body from A to B in a certain space of time, and the other in the direction AD capable to carry it from A to D in the same time; complete the parallelogram ABCD, and draw the diagonal AC; then the body at A, agitated by these two forces together, will move along the line BC, and will be in the point C at the end of the time in which it would have moved along AD or AB with the forces separately applied. Hence the solution of the following examples will be evident. Example I. Suppose a ship sails (by the compass) directly south 96 miles in 24 hours, in a current that sets east 45 miles in the same time: Required the ship's true course and distance. Geometrically. Draw AD (see No. 26.) to represent the south and north line of the ship at A, which make equal to 96; from D draw DC perpendicular to AD, equal to 45; and join AC. Then C will be the ship's true place, AC her true distance, and the angle CAD the true course. To find which, By Calculation: First, For the true course DAC, it will be, (by rectangular trigonometry), As the apparent distance AD = 96 = 1.9827 is to the current's motion DC = 45 = 1.6532 so is radius = 10.00000 to the tangent of the true course DAC = 25° 07' 9.67094 consequently the ship's true course is S 25° 07' E, or SSE 2° 37' easterly. Then for the true distance AC, it will be, (by rectangular trigonometry), As the fine of the course A = 25° 07' = 9.62784 is to the departure DC = 45 = 1.65321 so is radius = 10.00000 to the true distance AC = 106 = 2.02537 Example. Suppose a ship sails SE 120 miles in 20 hours, in a current that sets WNW at the rate of 2 miles an hour: Required the ship's true course and distance sailed in that time. Geometrically. Having drawn the compass NESW (No. 27.) let C represent the place the ship sails from; draw the SE line CA, which make equal to 120; then will A be the place the ship caped at. From A draw AB parallel to the WNW line CD, equal to 40, the motion of the current in 20 hours, and join CB; then B will be the ship's true place at the end of 20 hours, CB her true distance, and the angle SCB her true course. To find which, By Calculation: In the triangle ABC, are given CA 120, AB 40, and the angle CAB equal to 34° 45', the distance between the EAS and SE lines, to find the angles B and C, and the side CB. First, For the angles C and B, it will be, (by oblique trigonometry), As the sum of the sides CA and AB 160 = 2.20412 is to their difference = 80 = 1.90309 so is the tang. of half the sum = 73° 07' 10.51783 of the angles B and C = 59° 45' 10.21680 to the tang. of half their diff. = 131° 52' 9.87198 consequently the angle B will be 131° 52', and the angle ACB 14° 23'. Hence the true course is S 30° 37' E, or SSE 2° 07' easterly. Then for the true distance CB, it will be, (by oblique trigonometry), As the fine of B = 131° 52' = 9.87198 is to AC = 120 = 2.07918 so is the fine of A = 33° 45' = 7.94744 to the true distance CB = 89.53 = 1.95194 Example III. Suppose a ship coming out from sea in the night, has sight of Scilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, bearing NE4N distance 4 leagues, it being then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> tide setting ENE 2 miles an hour, and the ship running after the rate of 5 miles an hour: Required upon what course and how far the most sail to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> the Lizard, which bears from Scilly E1S distance 17 leagues. Geometrically. Having drawn the compass NESW (No. 28.) let A represent the ship's place at sea, and draw the NE4N line AS, which make equal to 12 miles; so S will represent Scilly. From S draw SL equal to 51 miles, and parallel to the E1S line; then L will represent the Lizard. From L draw LC parallel to the ENE line, equal to 2 miles, and from C draw CD equal to 5 miles meeting AL in D; then from A draw AB parallel to CD meeting LC produced in B; and AB will be the required distance, and SAB the true course. To find which, By Calculation: In the triangle ASL are given the side AS equal to 12 miles, the side SL equal to 51, and the angle ASL equal to 118° 07', the distance between the NE4N and WNW lines; to find the angles SAL and SLA. Consequently, (by oblique trigonometry), it will be, As the sum of the sides AS and SL = 63 = 1.79934 is to their difference = 39 = 1.59166 so is the tang. of half the sum = 30° 56' 9.77763 of the angles SAL and SLA = 20° 21' 9.56935 to the tang. of half their diff. = 51° 17' 9.56935 consequently the angle SAL, will be 51° 17'; and to the direct bearing of the Lizard from the ship will be N 85° 02' E, or E6N 6° 17' E; and for the distance AL, it will be, (by oblique trigonometry), 30 H 2 As As the fine of SAL - 51° 17' - 9.89223 is to SL - 51° - 1.70757 so is the fine of ASL - 118° 07' - 9.49546 to AL - 57° 65' - 1.76080 the distance between the ship and the Lizard. Again, in the triangle DLC, are given the angle L equal to 17° 32', the distance between the ENE and N 85° 02' E lines; the side LC, equal to 2 miles, the current's drift in an hour; and the side CD, equal to 5 miles, the ship's run in the same time. Hence for the angle D, it will be, (by oblique trigonometry), As the ship's run in 1 hour DC - 5° - 0.69897 is to the fine of L - 17° 32' - 9.47894 so is the current's drift LC - 2° - 0.30103 to the fine of D - 6° 55' - 0.08100 consequently, since by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> the angle LAB is equal to the angle LDC, the course the ship must steer is S 88° 03' E. Then for the distance AB, it will be, (by oblique trigonometry), As the fine of B - 155° 33' - 9.61689 is to AL - 57° 65' - 1.76080 so is the fine of L - 17° 32' - 9.47894 to AB - 41° 96' - 1.62285 consequently, since the ship is failing at the rate of 5 miles an hour, it follows, that in failing 8° 24' S 88° 03' E, she will arrive at the Lizard. Example IV. A ship from a certain headland in the latitude of 34° 00' north, sails SE 88° 12 miles in 3 hours, in a current that sets between north and east; and then the same headland is found to bear WNW, and the ship to be in the latitude of 33° 52' north: Required the setting and drift of the current. Geometrically. Having drawn the compass NESW (No. 29.) let A represent the place of the ship, and draw the SE 88° line AB, equal to 12 miles, also the ESE line AC. Set off from A upon the meridian AD, equal to 8 miles, the difference of latitude, and through D draw DC parallel to the east and west line WE, meeting AC in C. Join C and B with the right line BC; then C will be the ship's place, the angle ABC the setting of the current from the SE 88° line, and the line BC will be the drift of the current in 3 hours. To find which, By Calculation: In the triangle ABC, right-angled at D, are given the difference of latitude AD equal to 8 miles, the angle DAC equal to 67° 30'. Whence for AC, the distance the ship has failed, it will be As radius - 10.00000 is to the diff. of latitude AD - 8 - 0.90309 so is the secant of the course? - 67° 30' - 10.41716 DAC - 20° 9' - 1.32025 Again, in the triangle ABC, are given AB equal to 12 miles, AC equal to 20° 9', and the angle BAC equal to 30° 45', the distance between the SE 88° and ESE lines. Whence, for the angle at B, it will be, As the sum of the sides AC and AB - 32° 29' - 1.51720 is to their difference - 8° 9' - 0.94930 so is the tang. of half the? - 73° 07' - 10.51806 sum of the angles Band C - 41° 43' - 9.95025 consequently the angle B is 114° 51' and so the setting of the current will be N 81° 06' E, or ENE 2°. Then for BC, the current's drift in 3 hours, it will be, As the fine of B - 114° 51' - 9.92700 is to the distance run AC - 20° 9' - 1.32025 so is the fine of A - 33° 45' - 9.74474 to BC - 12° 8' - 1.10719 the current's drift in 3 hours; and consequently the current sets ENE 2° 21' E 4.266 miles an hour. § 9. Concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a> of the Compass, and how to find it from the true and observed Amplitudes or Azimuths of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. 1. The variation of the compass is how far the north or south point of the needle stands from the true north or north point of the horizon towards the east or west; or it is an arch of the horizon intercepted between the meridian of the place of observation and the magnetic meridian. 2. It is absolutely necessary to know the variation of the compass at sea, in order to correct the ship's course; for since the ship's course is directed by the compass, it is evident that if the compass be wrong, the true course will differ from the observed, and consequently the whole reckoning differ from the truth. 3. The sun's true amplitude is an arch of the horizon comprehended between the true east or west point thereof, and the centre of the sun at rising or setting; or it is the number of degrees, &c. that the centre of the sun is distant from the true east or west point of the horizon, towards the south or north. 4. The sun's magnetic amplitude is the number of degrees that the centre of the sun is from the east or west point of the compass, towards the south or north point of the same at rising or setting. 5. Having the declination of the sun, together with the latitude of the place of observation, we may from thence find the sun's true amplitude, by the following astronomic proposition, viz. As the co-fine of the latitude is to the radius So is the fine of the sun's declination to the fine of the sun's true amplitude which will be north or south according as the sun's declination is north or south. Example. Required the sun's true amplitude in the latitude of 41° 50' north, on the 23rd day of April 1731. First, I find (from the tables of the sun's declination) that the sun's declination the 23rd of April is 15° 54' north; then for the true amplitude, it will be, by the former <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, As the co-fine of the lat. 41° 50' - 9.87221 is to radius - 10.00000 so is the fine of the decl. 15° 54' - 9.43769 to the fine of the ampl. 21° 35' - 9.56548 which is north, because the declination is north at that time; and consequently, in the latitude of 40° 50' north, the sun rises on the 23rd of April 21° 35' from the east part of the horizon towards the north, and sets so much from the west the same way. 6. The sun's true azimuth is the arch of the horizon intercepted between the meridian and the vertical circle passing through the centre of the sun at the time of observation. 7. The sun's magnetic azimuth is the arch of the horizon, intercepted between the magnetic meridian and the vertical, passing through the sun. 8. Having the latitude of the place of observation, together with the sun's declination and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> at the time of observation, we may find his true azimuth after the following method, viz. Make it, As the tangent of half the complement of the latitude is to the tangent of half the sum of the distance of the sun from the pole and complement of the altitude. So is the tangent of half the difference between the distance of the sun from the pole and complement of the altitude To the tangent of a fourth arch which fourth arch added to half the complement of the latitude will give a fifth arch, and this fifth arch lessened by the complement of the latitude will give a sixth arch. Then make it, As the radius is to the tangent of the altitude so is the tangent of the fifth arch to the co-sine of the sun's azimuth which is to be counted from the south or north, to the east or west, according as the sun is situated with respect to the place of observation. If the latitude of the place and declination of the sun be both north or both south, then the declination taken from 90° will give the sun's distance from the pole; but if the latitude and declination be on contrary sides of the equator, then the declination added to 90° will give the sun's distance from the nearest pole to the place of observation. Example. In the latitude of 51° 32' north, the sun having 19° 39' north declination, its altitude was found by observation to be 38° 18': Required the azimuth. By the first of the foregoing analogies, it will be As the tangent of \( \frac{1}{2} \) the complement of the latitude \( 19°, 14' \cdot 9\cdot54269 \) is to the tangent of \( \frac{1}{2} \) the sum of the distance of the sun from the pole and complement of the altitude \( 61°, 01' 10.25655 \) so is the tangent of half their difference \( 9°, 19' 7.21499 \) to the tangent of a 4th arch \( 40°, 20' 9.92885 \) which fourth arch \( 40°, 20' \), added to \( 19°, 14' \), half the complement of the latitude, gives a fifth arch \( 59°, 34' \); and this fifth arch lessened by \( 38°, 28' \), the complement of the latitude, gives the sixth arch \( 21°, 06' \); then for the azimuth, it will be, by the second of the preceding analogies, As radius \( 10.00000 \) is to the tangent of the altitude \( 38°, 18' \cdot 9\cdot89749 \) so is the tangent of the fifth arch \( 21°, 06' \cdot 9\cdot58644 \) to the cosine of the azimuth \( 72°, 15' \cdot 9\cdot48393 \) which, because the latitude is north and the sun fourth of the place of observation, must be counted from the fourth towards the east or west; and consequently, if the altitude of the sun was taken in the morning, the azimuth will be \( S\ 72°, 15' \ E \), or \( ESE\ 4°, 45' \ E \); but if the altitude was taken in the afternoon, the azimuth will be \( S\ 72°, 15' \ W \), or \( WSW\ 4°, 45' \ W \). 9. Having found the sun's true amplitude or azimuth by the preceding analogies, and his magnetic amplitude or azimuth by observation, it is evident, if they agree, there is no variation; but if they disagree, then if the true and observed amplitudes at the rising or setting of the sun be both of the same name, i.e., either both north, or both south, their difference is the variation; but if they be of different names, i.e., one north and the other south, their sum is the variation. Again, if the true and observed azimuth be both of the same name, i.e., either both east or both west, their difference is the variation; but if they be of different names, their sum is the variation: And to know whether the variation is easterly, observe this general rule, viz. Let the observer's face be turned to the sun: then if the true amplitude or azimuth be to the right-hand of the observed, the variation is easterly; but if be to the left, westerly. To explain which, Let NESW (No. 3c.) represent Plate CCIII a compass, and suppose the sun is really ESS at the time of observation, but the observer sees him off the east point of the compass, and so the true amplitude or azimuth of the sun is to the right of the magnetic or observed; here it is evident that the ESS point of the compass ought to lie where the east point is, and so the north where the NWS is; consequently the north point of the compass is a point too far east, i.e., the variation in this case is easterly. The same will hold when the amplitude or azimuth is taken on the west side of the meridian. Again, let the true amplitude or azimuth be to the left-hand of the observed. Thus, suppose the sun is really ESN at the time of observation, but the observer sees him off the east point of the compass, and so the true amplitude or azimuth to the left of the observed: Here it is evident that the ESN point of the compass ought to stand where the east point is, and so the north where the NWS point is; consequently the north point of the compass lies a point too far westerly; so in this case the variation is west. The same will hold when the sun is observed on the west side of the meridian. Example I. Suppose the sun's true amplitude at rising is found to be \( E\ 14°, 20' \ N \), but by the compass it is found to be \( E\ 26°, 12' \): Required the variation, and which way it is. Since they are both the same way, therefore From the magnetic amplitude \( E\ 26°, 12' \ N \) take the true amplitude \( E\ 14°, 20' \ N \) and there remains the variation \( 11°, 52' \ E \) which is easterly, because in this case the true amplitude is the right of the observed. Example II. Suppose the sun's true amplitude at setting is \( W\ 34°, 26' \ S \), and his magnetic amplitude \( W\ 23°, 13' \ S \): Required the variation, and which way it is. Since they lie both the same way, therefore From the sun's true amplitude \( W\ 34°, 26' \ S \) take his magnetic amplitude \( W\ 23°, 13' \ S \) there remains the variation \( 11°, 13' \ W \) which which is westerly, because the true amplitude, in this case, is to the left-hand of the observed. **Example III.** Suppose the sun's true altitude at rising is found to be $13^\circ 24' N$, and his magnetic $E 12^\circ 32' S$: Required the variation, and which way it lies. Since the true and observed amplitudes lie different ways, therefore To the true amplitude $E 13^\circ 24' N$ add the magnetic amplitude $E 12^\circ 32' S$ the sun is the variation $25^\circ 56' W$, which is westerly, because the true amplitude is, in this case, to the left of the observed. **Example IV.** Suppose the sun's true altitude at setting is found to be $W 8^\circ 24' N$, but his magnetic amplitude is $W 10^\circ 13' S$: Required the variation. To the true amplitude $W 8^\circ 24' N$ add the magnetic $W 10^\circ 13' S$ the sun is the variation $18^\circ 37' E$, which is easterly, because the true amplitude is to the right of the observed. **Example V.** Suppose the sun's true azimuth at the time of observation is found to be $N 86^\circ 40' E$, but by the compass it is $N 75^\circ 24' E$: Required the variation, and which way it lies. From the sun's true azimuth $N 86^\circ 40' E$ take the magnetic $N 73^\circ 24' E$ there remains the variation $13^\circ 16' E$, which is easterly, because the true azimuth is to the right of the observed. **Example VI.** Suppose the sun's true azimuth is $S 3^\circ 24' E$, and the magnetic $S 4^\circ 36' W$: Required the variation, and which way it lies. To the true azimuth $S 3^\circ 24' E$ add the magnetic $S 4^\circ 36' W$ the sun is the variation $8^\circ 00' W$, which is westerly, because the true azimuth is, in this case, to the left of the observed. 10. The variation of the compass was first observed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the year 1580, to be $11^\circ 15'$ easterly, and in the year 1622 it was $6^\circ 05'$ E.; also in the year 1634, it was $4^\circ 05'$ E. still decreasing, and the needle approaching the true meridian, till it coincided with it; and then there was no variation; after which, the variation began to be westerly; and in the year 1672, it was observed to be $2^\circ 30' W.$; also in the year 1683, it was $4^\circ 30' W.$; and since that time the variation still continues at London to increase westerly; but how far it will go that way, time and observations will probably be the only means to discover. Again, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in the year 1640, the variation was $9^\circ 00' E.$; and in the year 1666, there was no variation; but in the year 1681, it was $2^\circ 30' W.$ and still continues to go westerly. In short, from observations made in different parts of the world, it appears, that in different places the variation differs both as to its quantity and denomination, it being east in one place, and west in another; the true cause and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of which, for want of a sufficient number of observations, has not as yet been fully explained. § 10. The Method of keeping a Journal at sea; and how to correct it, by making proper allowance for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>-way, Variation, &c. 1. Lee-way is the angle that the rhumb-line, upon which the ship endeavours to sail, makes with the rhumb she really sails upon. This is occasioned by the force of the wind or surge of the sea, when she lies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a>, or is close-hauled, which causes her to fall off and glide sideways from the point of the compass she capes at. Thus let NESW (No. 31.) represent the compass; and suppose a ship at C capes at, or endeavours to sail upon, the rhumb Ca; but by the force of the wind, and surge of the sea, she is obliged to fall off, and make her way good upon the rhumb Cb: then the angle acb is the lee-way; and if that angle be equal to one point, the ship is said to make one point lee-way; and if equal to two points, the ship is said to make two points lee-way, &c. The quantity of this angle is very uncertain, because some ships, with the same quantity of sail, and with the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a>, will make more lee-way than others; it depending much upon the mould and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> of the ship, and the quantity of water that she draws. The common allowances that are generally made for the lee-way, are as follow: 1. If a ship be close hauled, has all her sails set, the water smooth, and a moderate gale of wind, she is then supposed to make little or no lee-way. 2. If it blow so fresh as to cause the small sails be handed, it is usual to allow one point. 3. If it blow so hard that the top-sails must be close reefed, then the common allowance is two points for lee-way. 4. If one top-sail must be handed, then the ship is supposed to make between two and three points lee-way. 5. When both top-sails must be handed, then the allowance is about four points for lee-way. 6. If it blows so hard as to occasion the fore-course to be handed, the allowance is between 5½ and 6 points. 7. When both main and fore-courses must be handed, then 6 or 6½ points are commonly allowed for lee-way. 8. When the mizen is handed, and the ship is trying a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a>, she is then commonly allowed about 7 points for lee-way. 3. Though these rules are such as are generally made use of, yet since the lee-way depends much upon the mould and trim of the ship, it is evident that they cannot exactly serve to every ship; and therefore the best way is to find it by observation. Thus, let the ship's wake be set by a compass in the poop, and the opposite rhumb is the true course made good by the ship; then the difference between this and the course given by the compass in the binnacle, is the lee-way required. If the ship be within sight of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; then the lee-way may be exactly found by observing a point on the land which continues to bear the same way, and the distance between the point of the compass... error in the course to make any considerable error in practice. The difference of latitude by account is to the true difference of latitude, So is the departure by account to the true departure, And so is the direct distance by account to the true direct distance. The reason of this is plain: for let AB (No. 33.) denote the meridian of the ship at A, and suppose the ship sails upon the rhumb AE near the meridian, till by account she is found in C, and consequently her difference of latitude by account is AB; but by observation she is found in the parallel ED, and so her true difference of latitude is AD, her true distance AE; and her true departure DE; then, since the triangles ABC ADE are similar, it will be AB : AD :: BC : DE, and AB : AD :: AC : AE. Example. Suppose a ship from the latitude of 45° 20' north, after having sailed upon several courses near the meridian for 24 hours, her difference of latitude is computed to be upon the whole 95 miles southerly, and her departure 34 miles easterly; but by observation she is found to be in the latitude of 43° 10' north, and consequently her true difference of latitude is 130 miles southerly; then for the true departure, it will be, As the difference of latitude by account 95 is to the true difference of latitude 130; so is the departure by account 34 to the true departure 46.52, and so is the distance by account 100.9 to the true distance 138. 2dly, If the courses are for the most part near the parallel of east and west, and the direct course be within 5° or 6 points of the meridian; then if the latitude by account differs from the observed latitude, it is most probable that the error lies in the course or distance, or perhaps both; for in this case it is evident, the departure by account will be very nearly true; and thence by the help of this, and the true difference of latitude, may the true course and direct distance be readily found by Case 4. of Plane Sailing. Example. Suppose a ship from the latitude of 45° 50' north, after having sailed upon several courses near the parallel of east and west, for the space of 24 hours, is found by dead reckoning to be in the latitude of 42° 45' north, and to have made 160 miles of westing; but by a good observation the ship is found to be in the latitude of 42° 35' north. Required the true course, and direct distance sailed. With the true difference of latitude 75 miles, and departure 160 miles, we shall find (by Case 4. of Plane Sailing) the true course to be S. 64° 53' W. and the direct distance 176.7 miles. 3dly, If the courses are for the most part near the middle of the quadrant, and the direct course within 2° and 6 points of the meridian; then the error may be either in the course or in the distance, or in both, which which will cause an error both in the difference of latitude and departure; to correct which, having found the true difference of latitude by observation, with this, and the direct distance by dead reckoning, find a new departure (by Case 3. of Plane Sailing); then half the sum of this departure, and that by dead reckoning, will be nearly equal to the true departure; and consequently with this, and the true difference of latitude, we may (by Case 4. of Plane Sailing) find the true course and distance. **EXAMPLE.** Suppose a ship from the latitude of 44° 38' north, sails between south and east upon several courses, near the middle of the quadrant, for the space of 24 hours, and is then found by dead reckonings to be in the latitude of 42° 15' north, and to have made of sailing 136 miles; but by observation she is found to be in the latitude of 42° 04' north: Required her true course and distance. With the true distance of latitude 154 miles, and the direct distance by dead reckoning 197.4, you will find (by Case 3. of Plane Sailing) the new departure to be 123.4, and half the sum of this and the departure by dead reckoning will be 123.7 the true departure; then with this, and the true difference of latitude, you will find (by Case 4. of Plane Sailing), the true course to be S. 39° 00' E. and the direct distance 198.2 miles. 7. In keeping a ship's reckoning at sea, the common method is to take from the log-book the several courses and distances sailed by the ship last 24 hours, and to transfer these together with the most remarkable occurrences into the log-book, into which also are inserted the courses corrected, and the difference of latitude and difference of longitude made good upon each; then the whole day's work being finished in the log-book, if the latitude by account agree with the latitude by observation, the ship's place will be truly determined; if not, then the reckoning must be corrected according to the preceding rules, and placed in the journal. The form of the Log-book and Journal, together with an example of 2 days work, you have here subjoined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, to express the days of the week, they commonly use the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> by which the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are expressed, viz. ⊙ denotes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, ☉ Monday, ♡ Tuesday, ♢ Wednesday, ♣ Thursday, ♠ Friday, and ♦ denotes Saturday. ### § II. The Form of the Log-Book, with the Manner of working Days Work at Sea. #### The Log-Book. | Courses | Correct. Dist. | Diff. Lat. | Diff. NAVY

Pages 668-668

the fleet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> shipping of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state. See Marine. The management of the British navy-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is entrusted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers and commissioners of the navy, who hold their places by patent. The principal officers of the navy are four, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, whose business it is to receive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> out of the exchequer, and to pay all the charges of the navy, by warrant from the principal officers: comptroller, who attends and controls all payment of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, is to know the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of stores, to examine and audit all accounts, &c.: surveyor, who is to know the states of all stores, and see wants supplied; to estimate repairs, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> boatwains, &c., with what stores they receive, and at the end of each voyage to state and audit accounts: clerk of the acts, whose business it is to record all orders, contracts, bills, warrants, &c. The commissioners of the navy are five: the first executes that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the comptroller's duty which relates to the comptrolling; the victualler's accounts; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, another part of the said comptroller's duty relating to the account of the storekeepers of the yard; the third has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the navy at the port of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>; the fourth has the same at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>; and the fifth at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. There are also other commissioners at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> more or less

NAX NAXUS

Pages 668-669

the most remarkable of the Cyclades, 18 miles to the east of Delos; called Strongyle, then Dia, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIONYSIA">Dionysia</a>. Some have called it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> the Left. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NAXIA">Naxia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Naxos. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26.5. N. Lat. 36.30. Naxus (anc. geogr.), a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a> Naxius. Another of Sicily, built by the Chalcidian; situate on the south side of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a> Mount Taurus, destroyed by Dionysius the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>; from whose ruins Tauromenium, built by Timoleon, either arose or was recreated, (Plutarch).

NAZARENES

Pages 669-669

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name originally given to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in general, on account that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a>; but afterwards restrained to a set of heretics, whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> consisted of a strange jumble of Judaism and Christianity, observing at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic <a </a>class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the Christian religion.

NAZARETH

Pages 669-669

a town of Galilee near mount Tabor, situate on an eminence; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the annunciation <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of our Saviour, and of his residence till he entered on his public ministry at 30 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

NAZARITES

Pages 669-669

among the Jews, persons who, either of themselves, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by their parents, were dedicated to the observance of Nazarite ship. They were of two sorts; namely, such as were bound to this observance only for a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; or those who were bound to it all their lives. All that we find peculiar in the latter's way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is, that they were to abstain from wine and all intoxicating liquors, and never to shave or cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of their heads. The first sort of Nazarites were, moreover, to avoid all defilement; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they chanced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> any pollution before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> was expired, they were obliged to begin afresh. Women as well as men might bind themselves to this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a>. NAZIANZEN. See Gregory Nazianzen.

NEALED

Pages 669-669

among seamen, is used when the sounding is deep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the shore; as also when the shore is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, clayey, oozy, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> foul and rocky ground.

NEALING

Pages 669-669
or rather Annealing, a term used for the preparing of several matters, by heating or baking them in the oven, or the like. NEAPED. When a ship wants water, so that she cannot get out of the harbour, off the ground, or out of the dock, the seamen say she is neaped, or beheaded.

NEAPOLIS

Pages 669-670

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the Nomos Panopolitanus, between Thebes to the south, and Panopolis to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, on the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Otherwise called Carne.—A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, situate near the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, on the south side.—A third of Campania, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, and a colony from Carne, called at first Parthenope, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the sire of that name, (Velleius, Pliny, Strabo); accounted a Greek city, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flicker for Greek usages, (Livii, Tacitus). Its hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> were in nothing inferior to those of Baiae, according to Strabo: at two miles distance from it stands the monument of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, held in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration by learned posterity. The Younger Pliny relates, that Virgil's birthday was more religiously observed by Silius Italicus than his own, especially at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, where he resorted to his tomb as to a temple. The city is washed by river Sebethus. Virgil feigns the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Sebethus to preside over the stream. Now Naples, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of that name; E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15.12. N. Lat. 41.6.—A fourth, Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, near the Maeander, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).—A fifth, an inland town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, situate between <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a> and Arinoss, (Ptolemy); NEC Necesse. A sixth, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, (Strabo); which belonged first to the Ephesians, but afterwards to the Samians, who exchanged Marathusium, a more distant city, for a nearer.—A seventh, Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> Adjecta, situate at the distance of 12 miles to the east of Philippi, (Antonine).—An eighth, Neapolis of Paphlagonia, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, situate between Ambracia and Pappa, (Ptolemy).—A ninth, of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, the ancient Sichem, which see; so called upon its restoration by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>, Pliny, Josephus).—A tenth, of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, situate on the south-west side of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 30 miles to the north of Metalla: now called Neapolis.—An eleventh, of the Regio Syrtica, called also Lepcis.—A twelfth, of Zeugitana on the Mediterranean, to the east of Clypea, and south of the Promontorium Mercuri. NEAT <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">NET</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">WEIGHT</a>, the weight of a commodity alone, clear of the cask, bag, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, or even filth. See NET.

NEBIO

Pages 670-670
or NERIO, a ruined city of Italy, on the north side of the island of Corsica, with a bishop's see, whose bishop resides at San Fiorenzo, from which it is a mile distant.

NEBO

Pages 670-670

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Abarim, and their highest top, whither Moses was ordered to ascend to take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, and there die. Situated in the land of Moab, over-against <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>: with a cognominal town at its foot (Isaiah) belonging to the Reubenites, which afterwards returned to the Moabites; in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> desolate; eight miles to the south of Heshbon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">NEBUCHADNEZZAR</a>. See Nabuchadnezzar.

NEBULY

Pages 670-670
or Nebulee, in heraldry, is when a coat is charged with several little figures, in form of words running within one another, or when the outline of a bordure, ordinary, &c. is indented or waved.

NECHO

Pages 671-671
king of Egypt, began his reign 69 B.C. and was killed eight years after by Sabacon king of Ethiopia. Plammiticus his son succeeded him, and was the father of Necho II., who reigned in the 616 B.C. This Necho II. is celebrated in history for attempting, though in vain, to cut a canal from the Nile to the Arabian gulf. He sent the Phoenicians to sail round Africa by sea, defeated Jollas and the Babylonians, and gained many victories; but he was conquered in his turn by Nebuchadnezzar, who confined him within his ancient kingdom.

NECROMANCY

Pages 671-671
or Necromancy, a species of divination performed by raising the dead, and extorting answers from them. See Divination.

NECTAR

Pages 671-671

among <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, the drink of the fabulous deities of the heathens; in contradistinction from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, which was called ambrosia.

NECTARINE

Pages 671-671

a fruit differing in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peach, of which it is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, than in having a smoother rind and a firmer pulp. See Persica.

NECTARIUM

Pages 671-672

from *<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>*, the fabled "drink of..." Nectarium of the gods;" defined by Linnæus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the corolla, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> appendage to the petals, appropriated for containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> under a fluid form, that oozes from the plant, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of bees and other insects. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which seems to consider the nectarium as necessary a part of the corolla as the petals; it is certain that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are not provided with this appendage, neither indeed is it essential to fructification. There is, besides, a manifest impropriety in terming the nectarium a part of the corolla. Linnæus might, with equal propriety, have termed it a part or appendage of the stamens, calyx, or pointal, as the appearance in question is confined to no particular part of the flower, but is as various in point of situation as of form. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> nectarium is exceedingly vague; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any determinate meaning can be affixed to it, is expressive of all the singularities which are observed in the different parts of flowers. The tube, or lower part of flowers with one petal, Linnæus considers as a true nectarium, because it is generally found to contain the sweet liquor formerly mentioned. This liquor Pontedera compares to that called amnios in pregnant animals, which enters the fertile or impregnated seeds: but that this is not at least its sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is evident from this circumstance, that the honey or liquor in question is to be found in flowers where there are either no seeds, or those, from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, cannot be impregnated. Thus the male flowers of nettle and willow; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side laurel, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bryony; the male and female flowers of clutia, kiggelaria, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, all abound with the honey or nectar alluded to. Dr Vaillant was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the nectarium was an essential part of the corolla; for which reason he distinguished the singular appearances in fennel-flower and cumbine, by the name of petals; the coloured leaves which are now termed the petals, he denominates the flower-cup. That the nectarium, however, is frequently distinct from the petals, is evident, both from the well-known examples <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, as likewise from the flowers of monkshood, heliobore, ifopryum, fennel-flower of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, barrenwort, gras of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, chocolate-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, cherleria, and sauvagelia. These general observations being premised, we proceed to take a nearer and more particular view of the principal diversities, both in form and situation, of this striking appendage to the flower. 1. In many flowers the nectarium is shaped like a spur or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and that either in flowers of one petal, as valerian, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-milfoil (articulata), <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-wort, and calves'-foot; or in such as have more than one, as lark-spur, violet, fumitory, balsam, and orchis. 2. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the nectarium is properly a part of the corolla, as lying within the substance of the petals: ranunculus, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-imperial, water-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, mouse-tail, ananas or pine-apple, dog's-tongue violet, piperidge bush, wallflower, hemmannia, urvalis, and fertia. 3. The nectarium is frequently placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or row within the petals, though entirely unconnected with their substance. In this situation it often resembles a cup, as in narcissus. A nectarium of this kind is said by Linnæus to crown the corolla. The following are examples: daffodil, sea-daffodil, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, viscos campion, swallow-wort, tapelia, cynanchum, nepenthes, cherleria, balsam-tree, African spirea, witch-hazel, olax, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>-flower. 4. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, buckler multard, Barbadoes cherry, and monotropa, the nectarium is situated upon or makes part of the calyx. 5. The nectarium in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> flower-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is seated upon the antherae or tops of the stamens; whence the name adenanthera, or glandular antera, which has been given to this genus of plants. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> it is placed upon the filaments: bean-caper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, fraxinella, marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-flower, leadwort, rocilla, and commelina. 6. In hyacinth, flowering-ruth, stock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>-flower, and rocket, the nectarium is placed upon the seed-bud. 7. In honey-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, buck-wheat, collinsonia, lathrea, navel-wort, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, clutia, kiggelaria, sea-side laurel, and African spirea, it is attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> receptacle. Lastly, in ginger, nettle, dyer's weed, heart-seed, costus, turmeric, grewia, bastard orange, vanellus, skrewtree, and willow, the nectarium is of a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and cannot properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any of the foregoing heads. In discriminating the genera, the nectarium often furnishes an essential character. Plants which have the nectarium distinct from the petals, that is, not lodged within their substance, are affirmed by Linnæus to be generally poisonous. The following are adduced as examples: monk's hood, heliobore, cumbine, fennel-flower, gras of Parnassus, barren-wort, oleander, marvel of Peru, bean-caper, succulent swallow-wort, fraxinella, and honey-flower.

NECYDALIS

Pages 672-672

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. The feelers are taceous; the elytra are shorter and narrower than the wings; the tail is simple. There are 11 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, chiefly distinguished by the size and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their elytra.

NEEDLE

Pages 672-674

a very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> utensil, made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, pointed at one end, and pierced at the other, used in sewing <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a> make a very considerable article in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, though there is scarce any commodity cheaper, the consumption of them being almost incredible. The sizes are from No. 1, the largest, to No. 25, the smallest. In the manufacture of needles, German and Hungarian steel are of most repute. In the making of them, the first thing is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the steel through a coal-fire, and under a hammer, to bring it out of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> into a cylindrical one. This done, it is drawn through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole of a wire-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and returned into the fire, and drawn thro' a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hole of the iron, smaller than the first; and thus successively from hole to hole, till it has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness required for that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of needles; observing every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is to be drawn, that it be greased over with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to render it more manageable. The steel thus reduced to a fine wire, is cut in pieces of the length of the needles intended. These pieces are flattened at one end on the anvil, in order to form the head and eye: they are then put into the fire, to soften them farther; and thence taken out and pierced at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of the flat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> on the anvil, by force of a puncheon of well-tempered steel, and laid on a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> to bring out, with another puncheon, The corners are then filed off the square of the heads, and a little cavity filed on each side of the flat of the head; this done, the point is formed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and the whole filed over: they are then laid to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow iron, crooked at one end, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire; and when taken out thence, are thrown into a basin of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> to harden. On this operation a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> depends; too much heat burns them, and too little leaves them soft; the medium is learned by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. When they are thus hardened, they are laid in an iron shovel on a fire more or less brisk in proportion to the thickness of the needles; taking care to move them from time to time. This serves to temper them, and take off their brittleness; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care here too must be taken of the degree of heat. They are then straightened one after another with the hammer, the coldness of the water used in hardening them having twisted the greatest part of them. The next <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is the polishing them. To do this, they take 12,000 or 15,000 needles, and range them in little heaps against each other on a piece of new buckram sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>-dust. The needles thus disposed, emery-dust is thrown over them, which is again sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; at last the whole is made up into a roll, well bound at both ends. This roll is then laid on a polishing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it a thick plank loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which two men <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> backwards and forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half, or two days, successively; by which means, the roll thus continually agitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the plank over it, the needles withinside being rubbed against each other with oil and emery, are infallibly polished. After polishing, they are taken out, and the filth washed off them with hot water and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>: they are then wiped in hot bran, a little moistened, placed with the needles in a round box, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which is kept stirring till the bran and needles be dry. The needles thus wiped in two or three different brans, are taken out and put in wooden vessels, to have the good separated from those whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or eyes have been broke either in polishing or wiping; the points are then all turned the same way, and smoothed with an emery-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned with a wheel. This operation finishes them, and there remains nothing but to make them into packets of 250 each. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">Dipping</a> Needle, or Inclinatory Needle, a magnetic needle, so hung, as that, instead of playing horizontally, and pointing out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south, one end dips, or inclines to the horizon, and the other points to a certain degree of elevation above it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING_NEEDLE">dipping-needle</a> was invented in the year 1576, by one Robert Norman a compass-maker at Wapping. The occasion of the discovery, according to his own account was, that it being his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to finish and hang the needles of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> before he touched them, he always found, that immediately after the touch, the north-point would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> or incline downward, under the horizon; insomuch that, to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the needle again, he was always forced to put a piece of wax on the south-end as a counterpoise. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of this effect led him at length to observe the precise <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the dip, or to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the needle would make with the horizon; and this at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> he found to be $71^\circ 50'$. In 1723 Mr Graham made a great many observations on the dipping-needle, and found the angle to be between 74 and 75 degrees. Mr Nairne, in 1772, found it to be somewhat above $72^\circ$. It is not certain whether the dip varies, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The trifling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Mr Forman and Mr Nairne, would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to imagine that the dip was unalterable; but Mr Graham, who was a very accurate observer, makes the difference more considerable. It is certain, however, from a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments and observations, that the dip is variable in different latitudes, and that it increases in going northwards. It appears from a table of observations made with the marine dipping-needle in a voyage towards the north pole, in 1773, that in lat. $60^\circ 18'$ the dip was $75^\circ$; and in lat $70^\circ 45'$ it was $77^\circ 52'$; in lat. $80^\circ 12'$ it was $81^\circ 52'$; and in lat. $80^\circ 27'$ it was $82^\circ 25'$. Several authors have endeavoured to apply this discovery of the dip to the finding of the latitude; and Mr Bond attempted to apply it to the finding of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> also; but for want of observations and experiments, he could not make any progress. The affair was farther prosecuted by Mr Whitton, who published a treatise on the longitude, and for some time imagined it was possible to find it exactly by means of the dip of the needle; yet he at last despaired of it, for the following reasons. 1. The weakness of the magnetic power. 2. The concussion of the ship, which he found it exceeding difficult to avoid so much as was necessary for the accuracy of the experiments. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objection was an irregularity in the motions of all magnetic needles, both horizontal and dipping, by which they, within the compass of about a degree, vary uncertainly backward and forward; even sometimes, in a few hours time, without any evident cause. For a particular account of these variations both of the horizontal and dipping needle, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a>. Mr Nairne, an ingenious instrument-maker in London, made a dipping-needle in 1772 for the board of longitude, which was used in the voyage towards the north-pole. This is represented Plate CCIV. fig. 1. The needle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a> is 12 inches long, and its axis, the ends BB of which are made of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> alloyed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, rests on friction-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> CCCC, of four inches diameter, each end on two friction-wheels; which wheels are balanced with great care. The ends of the axes of the friction-wheels, are likewise of gold alloyed with copper, and moved in small holes made in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-metal; and opposite to the ends of the axes of the needle, and the friction-wheels, are flat agates, set in at DDD, finely polished. The magnetic needle vibrates within a circle of bell-metal, EEE, divided into degrees and half degrees; and a line, passing through the middle of the needle to the ends, points to the divisions. The needle of this instrument was balanced, before it was made magnetic; but by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, the ends of which are FFFF, (contrived by the reverend Mr Mitchell) fixed on the axis of the needle, on the arms of which are cut very fine screws to receive small buttons, that may be screwed nearer or farther from the axis, the needle may be adjusted both ways to a great nicety, after being made magnetic, by reversing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and changing the sides of the needle. GG are two levels, by which the line of 0 degrees of the instrument... Instrument is set horizontal, by means of the four adjusting screws LLLL; H is the perpendicular axis, by which the instrument may be turned, that the divided <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the circle may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the call or well; to this axis is fixed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> I, which points to an opposite line on the horizontal plate K when the instrument is turned half round; MMMM are screws which hold the glass-cover to keep the needle from being disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. When this needle is constructed for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is suspended by an universal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> on a triangular stand, and adjusted vertically by a plumb-line and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> above the divided circle and the dovetail work at the upper go; and the divisions on the circle are adjusted so as to be perpendicular to the horizon by the same plumb-line, and an adjoining screw; and when it is adjusted, a pointer annexed to a screw, which serves to move the divided circle, is fixed at the lowest go. Whenever the instrument is used to find the dip, it must be so placed that the needle may vibrate exactly in the magnetic meridian. Magnetical Needle, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, a needle touched with a loadstone, and sustained on a pivot or centre; on which playing at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, it directs itself to certain points in or under the horizon; whence the magnetical needle is of two kinds, viz. horizontal and inclinatory. See the article Magnet. Horizontal needles are those equally balanced on each side the pivot that sustains them; and which, playing horizontally with their two extremes, point out the north and south points of the horizon. For their application and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, see the article Compass. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the horizontal needle, a piece of pure steel is provided; of a length not exceeding six inches, lest its weight should impede its volatility; very thin, to take its verticity the better; and not pierced with any holes, or the like, for ornament sake, which prevent the equable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the magnetic virtue. A perforation is then made in the middle of its length, and a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> or head soldered on, whose inner cavity is conical, so as to play freely on a style or pivot headed with a fine steel point. The north point of the needle in our hemisphere is made a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the southern; the touch always destroying the balance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well adjusted before, and rendering the north end heavier than the south, and thus occasioning the needle to dip. The method of giving the needle its verticity or directive <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, has been shewn already under the article Magnet; but if, after touching, the needle be out of its equilibrium, something must be filed off from the heavier side, till it balance evenly. Needles in sea compasses are usually made of a rhomboïdal or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form: we have given their structure already under the article Compass. The needle is not found to point precisely to the north, except in very few places; but deviates from it more or less in different places, and that too at different times; which deviation is called its declination or variation from the meridian. See the article Variation. Needle-Fish. See Synaptus. Needles, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, two capes or headlands at the west end of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, which it is very difficult to pass on account of the sands and rocks.

NEGATION

Pages 674-674

in logic, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind affirming one thing to be different from another; as that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. See Logic.

NEGATIVE

Pages 674-674

in general, something that implies a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>: thus we say, negative quantities, negative powers, negative signs, &c. NEGATIVE <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. See the article Electricity. See also Positive Electricity.

NEGOMBO

Pages 674-674

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ceylon. It has a fort built by the Portuguese, which was taken from them by the Dutch in 1640. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 25. N. Lat. 17. 6. NEGRIL point, the most westerly promontory of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Jamaica.

NEGROES

Pages 674-674

properly the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIGRITIA">Nigritia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Negroland in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, called also Blacks and Moors; but this name is now given to all the Blacks. The origin of the Negroes, and the cause of this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> from the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, has much perplexed the naturalists. Mr Boyle has observed, that it cannot be produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>: for though the heat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> may darken the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the skin, yet <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> does not show that it is sufficient to produce a new blackness like that of the Negroes. In Africa itself, many nations of Ethiopia are not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; nor were there any blacks originally in the West Indies. In many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, under the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the African region inhabited by the blacks, the people are but tawny. He adds, that there are Negroes in Africa beyond the southern tropic; and that a river sometimes parts nations, one of which is black, and the other only tawny. Dr Barriere alleges, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a> of Negroes is black, and being mixed with their blood is deposited between the skin and scarf-skin. However, Dr Mitchel of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, in the Philosophical Transactions no 476, has endeavoured by many learned arguments to prove, that the influence of the sun in hot countries, and the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of their inhabitants, are the remote causes of the colour of the Negroes, Indians, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, no 48—51, and Colour of the Human Species. Negroes are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and other coasts of Africa, and sent to the colonies in America, to cultivate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, &c. and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> to dig in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, however indefensible on the foot of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, is now carried on by all the nations that have settlements in the West Indies. Those Negroes make the best slaves who are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Verd, the river <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>, the kingdoms of Jolofics, &c. There are various ways of procuring them: some, to avoid famine, sell themselves,

NEGROLAND

Pages 674-677
or NIGRITIA, a country of Africa, lying next to Guinea towards the north, and extending from 18° of west to 150° of east longitude, and from 10° to 20° of north latitude. On the north it is bounded by Zara or the Desert; on the east, by countries unknown; on the south, by Guinea; and on the west, by the Atlantic Ocean; and is watered by the great river Niger or Senegal, which runs through it from east to west. The Europeans have settlements on the coasts of this country, especially near the mouths of the Niger and Gambia, which last is supposed to be a branch of the former. A great many nations inhabit the banks of the rivers; some Pagans, some Mohammedans, of different languages, and independent of one another. The country is fruitful, especially along the rivers; abounding in rice, Guinea grain, and Indian corn, where it is cultivated; and with cocoa-nuts, plantains, pulle, palm-trees, and tropical fruits; nor is it destitute of cattle, and a variety of other animals, particularly such as abound in Guinea. Negroland is fertilized by the overflowing of its rivers the Senegal and Gambia, as Egypt is by the Nile. It hath not yet been ascertained whether the Gambia is a branch of the Senegal or not. As far as the Europeans have penetrated up the country, they appear to be distinct; and the Mundingo Negroes report that the Gambia has a different origin. The entrance into the Niger or Senegal river is narrow and somewhat difficult, by reason of its immoveable bar and sandy shoals, as well as the several islands at the mouth of it, and the several canals and marshes that clog it; but after sailing up eight or ten leagues, it is found broad and deep, and fit to carry large vessels; and, excepting about five or six leagues on each side above the mouth, which is sandy and barren ground, the banks are covered with flatly trees and villages, and the country in general is fertile and well watered; for, like the Nile, this river overflows its banks for many leagues, and enriches the land to a great degree, though, for want of skill, the inhabitants do not reap the advantages which they might obtain from its fertility. The people on both sides of the river live as near to it as they can, and feed great herds of cattle, sowing large and small millet, the former of which is called by us Turkey wheat, in great quantities, and with great increase. If the river fails of overflowing at its usual season, a great scarcity, if not a downright famine, never fails to ensue in the adjacent country; and, even when it overflows regularly, it breeds such vast flights of grasshoppers and insects, as quite darken the air, and frequently eat up all the produce of the earth; in which case the only remedy the people have is to kill those insects and eat them; which they do either by pounding in leathern bags, and then boiling them in milk, or, which is reckoned the more delicious method, by frying or broiling them over a light blaze, in a frying-pan full of holes. Thus the legs and wings of the insects are burnt off, and the rest of the body is sufficiently roasted to be eaten as a Negroland dainty, which they look upon to be very wholesome and nourishing. To the east, north-east, and south-east of the island of Senegal, the country, as far as it is known, is over-run with woods and marshes; the Senegal, Gambia, and Sherbro, which are looked upon by some as branches of one immense river, passing through it in their way to the Atlantic Ocean. During the rainy months, which begin in July, and continue to October, they lay the whole country under water; and indeed the sudden rise of these rivers is incredible to such as are not acquainted with the violent rains that fall between the tropics. At Galam, 900 miles from the mouth of the Senegal, the waters rise 150 feet perpendicular from the bed of the river. At the island of Senegal, the river rises gradually, during the rainy season, above 20 feet perpendicular over part of that flat coast; which of itself so refreshes the water, that ships lying at anchor, at the distance of three leagues from its mouth, generally make use of it, and fill their water there for their voyage home. When the rains are at an end, which usually happens in October, the intense heat of the sun soon dries up those flagging waters which lie on the higher parts, and the remainder from lakes and marshes, in which are found all sorts of dead animals. At last, those too are quite dried up; and then the effluvia that arise are almost quite insupportable. At this season the winds blow so hot from the land, that they may be compared to the heat proceeding from the mouth of an oven, and they bring with them an intolerable smell. The wolves, tigers, lions, and other wild beasts, then resort to the river, keeping their body under water, and only their snout above it for the sake of breathing. The birds soar to an immense height in the air, and fly a vast way over the sea, where they continue till the wind changes, and comes from the west. See SENEGAL, GUINEA, GOLD-COAST, and SLAVE-COAST. NEGROMANCY. See Necromancy.

NEGROPONT

Pages 677-678

anciently Euboea, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, stretching along the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Achaia <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a>, from which it is separated by a narrow channel called the Euripus. This strait is so narrow, that the island is joined to the continent by a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> thrown over it; and, here it is thought, there was formerly an isthmus. The irregularity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> in the Euripus hath from the remotest antiquity been very remarkable, and this irregularity is found to be connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. From the three last days of the old moon to the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new moon, and from the 14th to the 20th day inclusive, they are regular; but on the other days they are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, flowing 12, 13, or 14 times in the space of 24 hours, and ebbing as often. The island is 90 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; and produces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, and cattle, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance.
