The only <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the island worth notice is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which is also called Negropont; and which is walled, and contains about 15,000 inhabitants; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> are said to be much more numerous than the Turks. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, who is also governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the island, and the adjacent continent of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, resides here; and the harbour, which is very safe and spacious, is seldom without Nehemiah without a fleet of galleys, ready to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against the pirates and the Maltese. A part of the bridge between the city and the coast of Greece, consists of a drawbridge no longer than <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> to let a galley <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through.

NEHEMIAH

Pages 678-678

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, so called from the name of its author. Nehemiah was born in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and succeeded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Judah and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. He was a Jew, and was promoted to the office of cup-bearer to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimanus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; when the opportunities he had of being daily in the king's presence, together with the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, procured him the favour of being authorised to repair and fortify the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Jerusalem in the same manner as it was before its destruction by the Babylonians. On his going to Jerusalem, he finished the rebuilding of the walls in 52 days, and dedicated the gates of the city with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity. He then reformed some abuses which had crept in among his countrymen, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a> of the usurers, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> were so oppressed as to be forced to sell their lands and children for support; after which he returned to Persia, and came back again with a new <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, by virtue of which he regulated every thing relating both to the state and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Jews. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these transactions is the subject of this book.

NEISSE

Pages 678-678

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> in Germany, and the residence of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, who has a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very wholesome, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are cheap; the inhabitants carry on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> suffered greatly by an inundation and fire in 1729. It was taken by the Prussians in 1741, who augmented the fortifications after the peace in 1742, and built a citadel to which they gave the name of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is situated on a river of the same name; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 17° 35'. N. lat. 50° 32'.

NELSON

Pages 678-679

a learned and pious English <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was the son of Mr John Nelson a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> merchant, and was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1656. He had the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at St Paul's school, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part was under a private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, after which he studied at Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. In 1680 he was chosen a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; being probably inclined to receive that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> out of respect to his friend and school-fellow Dr Edmund Halley, for whom he had a particular regard, and in whose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> he set out on his travels abroad the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the remarkable comet which gave rise to the comical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton; and our author, apparently by the advantage of his fellow-traveller's instructions, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it to Dr, afterwards archbishop, Tillotson, by whom he was very much esteemed. From Paris he went with his fellow-traveller to Rome, where he fell into the acquaintance of Lady Theophila Lucy, widow of Sir Kingmill Lucy of Broxburne in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, bart., and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of George <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Berkeley, who soon discovered a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for him; this concluded in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, after his arrival in England in 1682. But it was some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before she confessed to Mr Nelson the change of her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; which was owing to her conversations at Rome with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Howard, who was grandson of the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, the collector of the Arundelian marbles, &c., and had been raised to the purple by pope Clement X. in May 1675. Nor was this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sentiments confined to her own mind, but involved in it her daughter by her first husband, whom she drew over to her new religion; and her zeal for it prompted her even to engage in the public controversy then depending. She is the supposed authoress of a piece written in 1686, 4to, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of, "A discourse concerning a judge of controversy in matters of religion, shewing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of such a judge." This misfortune touched her husband very nearly. He employed not only his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, but those of his friends Dr Tillotson and Dr Hickes, to recover her; but all proved ineffectual; and she <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome till her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. She was a person of fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and understanding. Dr Tillotson particularly laments her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> on that account; and even seems not to be entirely free from all apprehensions of the influence she might have upon her husband in this important affair. But Mr Nelson's religion was too much the result of his learning and reason to be shaken by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, which was equally steady and inviolable. Her change of religion made no change in his affections for her; and when she relapsed into such a bad state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> as obliged her to go and drink the waters at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>, he attended her thither in 1688; and not liking the prospect of the public affairs at home, he proceeded to make a second trip to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, taking his lady, together with her son and daughter by her former husband, along with him. He returned through Germany to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, where he laid some time with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Durlcy, who was married to his wife's sister. From the Hague he arrived in England, in the latter end of 1691; where, being adverse to the Revolution, he declared himself a nonjuror, and left the communion of the church of England. In this last point he had consulted Dr Tillotson, and followed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, who thought it no better than a trick, detestable in any thing, and especially in religion, to join in prayers where there was any petition which was held to be sinful. Thus, notwithstanding their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of opinion in this case, the friendship between them remained the same; and the good archbishop expired in his friend's arms in 1694. Our author's new character unavoidably threw him into some new connections. Among these we find mentioned particularly Mr Kettlewell, who had resigned his living at Coleshill in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> on account of the new <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, and afterwards resided in London. This pious and learned divine also agreed with him in leaving the communion of the established church; yet at the same time persuaded him to engage in the general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; observing to him, that he was very able to compose excellent books of that kind, which would be apt to do more good as coming from a layman. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> corresponded with the truly catholic spirit of our author; who accordingly published many works of piety, which are deservedly esteemed. At the same time, he engaged zealously in every public public scheme for the honour and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, as well as for propagating the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and promoting the practice of true Christianity, both at home and abroad; several proposals for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, repairing, and endowing churches, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> particularly. Upon the death of Dr William Lloyd, the deprived bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, in the end of the year 1799, he returned to the communion of the church of England. Dr Lloyd was the last surviving of the deprived <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> by the Revolution, except Dr Kenn, by whose advice Mr Nelson was determined in this point. Mr Nelson's tutor, Dr George Bull, bishop of St <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, dying before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of this year, he was easily prevailed upon by that prelate's son, to draw up an account of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and writings, as he had maintained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and intimate friendship with his Lordship, which gave him an opportunity of being acquainted with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and substantial worth. The life was published in 1733; and, as our author had long before laboured under a constitutional weakness, which had brought on an asthma and dropy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, the distemper grew to such a height soon after the publication of that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that, for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, he retired at length to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a>, where he expired on the 16th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1741-15. He left his whole estate to pious and charitable uses; particularly to charity-schools.

NEMAUSUS

Pages 679-679
or NEMEAUSUS, (anc. geog.) the capital of the Arecumici in Gallia Narbonensis; a colony, (Coin), with the surname Augusta, (Inscription). In it stands a Roman amphitheatre, which is still almost entire. Now Nîmes in Languedoc.

NEMEA

Pages 679-679

(anc. geog.), situated between Cleone and Philus in Argolis; whether town, district, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing, uncertain: there a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> stood in which the Argives celebrated the Nemean games, and there happened all the fabulous circumstances of the Nemean lion. The district Nemea is called Bembinadia, (Pliny); a village, Bembinia, standing near Nemea, (Strabo). Stephanus places Nemea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; though not in, but on, the borders of Elis; Pliny, erroneously, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. In the adjoining mountain is still shown the den of the lion, distant 15 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Nemea, (Pausanias); in which stands a considerable temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Nemetus and Cleoneus, from the vicinity of these two places. This place gave name to the Nemean games, celebrated every third year.

NEMEAN GAMES

Pages 679-679

so called from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEMEA">Nemea</a>, a village between the cities of Cleone and Philus, where they were celebrated every third year. The exercises were chariot-races, and all the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATHLON">Pentathlon</a>. These games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Opheltes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Archemorus, the son of Euphates and Creusa, who was nursed by Hypsipyle; who leaving him in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> while she went to slay the besiegers of Thebes a fountain, at her return found him dead, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> twined about his neck: whence the fountain, before called Langia, was named Archemorus; and the captains, to comfort Hypsipyle, instituted these games. Others ascribe their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, after his victory over the Nemean lion. Others allow, that they were instituted first in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemorus; Nemeanus but intermitted, and revived again by Hercules. The victors were crowned with parsley, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> used at funerals, and feigned to have sprung from Archemorus's blood.

NEMESIANUS

Pages 679-679

a Latin poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, who wrote a poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, intitled Cyngeeticon, and four eclogues, which are still extant. This poet lived under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a> and his sons Carinus and Numerianus, about the year 281. People were so fond of his poem in the eighth and ninth centuries, that young men were obliged to read it in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>.

NEMESIS

Pages 679-679

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Necesis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Oceanus and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOX">Nox</a>, had the care of revenging the crimes which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> left unpenished. She was also called Adrasta, because Adrastus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> first raised an altar to her; and Rhamnusia, from her having a magnificent temple at Rhamnus in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. She had likewise a temple at Rome in the Capitol. She is represented with a stern countenance, holding a whip in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales in the other.

NEMINE CONTRADICENTE

Pages 679-679

"none contradicting it;" a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> when anything is carried without opposition.

NEMOURS

Pages 679-679

a town of the Ile de France in the Gatinois, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is seated on the river Loing, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 2. 45. N. lat. 48. 15.

NENIA

Pages 679-679
or NENIA, in the ancient poetry, a kind of funeral song sung to the music of flutes at the obsequies of the dead. Authors represent them as forry compositions, sung by hired women-mourners called Proceres. The first rise of these Nenia is ascribed to the physicians. In the heathen antiquity the goddess of tears and funerals was called Neela; whom some suppose to have given that name to the funeral song, and others to have taken her name from it.

NEOMAGUS

Pages 679-679

(<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a town of Galia Narbonensis, on the confines of the Tricallini. Now Nyons in Dauphiné.

NEOMENIA

Pages 679-680
or Noumenia, a festival of the ancient Greeks, at the beginning of every lunar month, which, as the name imports, was observed upon the day of the new moon, in honour of all the gods, but especially Apollo, who was called Neomenios, because the sun is the fountain of light, and whatever distinction of times and seasons may be taken from other planets, yet they are all owing to him as the original of those borrowed rays by which they shine. The games and public entertainments at these festivals were made by the rich, to whose tables the poor flocked in great numbers. The Athenians at these times offered solemn prayers and sacrifices for the prosperity of their country during the ensuing month. See Games. The Jews had also their neomenia, or feast of the new moon, on which peculiar sacrifices were appointed; and on this day they had a sort of family entertainment and rejoicing. The most celebrated neomenia of all others was that at the beginning of the civil year, or first day of the month Tisri, on which no servile labour was performed: they then offered particular burnt-sacrifices, and sounded the trumpets of the temple. The modern Jews keep the neomenia only as a feast of devotion, which any one may observe or not as he pleases.

NEOPHYTES

Pages 680-680

"new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>;" a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, to those heathens who had newly embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; such persons being considered as regenerated, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> born anew by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> neophyte has been also used for new priests, or those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> admitted into orders, and sometimes for the novices in monasteries. It is still applied to the converts made by the missionaries among the infidels.

NEPER

Pages 680-681
or NAPIER (John), baron of Merchiston in Scotland, whose high attainments in many branches of useful literature render his memory valuable, was born in 1550. He had a peculiar turn to mathematical investigations and useful inventions: among the latter may be ranked that instrument called Neper's Rods or Bones, to facilitate the multiplication and division of large numbers; and his invention of logarithms have spread his fame throughout the world. This discovery was contained in his Canon mirabilis Logarithmorum, dedicated to prince Charles, and published in 1614. In his Rabdologia, published in 1616, he mentions another species of those numbers; when, finding his health declining, he engaged Mr Briggs to prosecute that useful laborious scheme. Besides his abilities in these calculations, he is said to have wrote an Exposition on the Revelation: an undertaking in which his rare talents in reason and computation could however afford him no advantages; nor is he remembered by it. He died in 1622. Neper's Rods, or Bones, an instrument invented by J. Neper, baron of Merchiston in Scotland, whereby the multiplication and division of large numbers is much facilitated. As to the construction of Neper's Rod: Suppose the common table of multiplication to be made upon a plate of metal, ivory, or pasteboard, and then conceive the several columns (standing downwards from the digits on the head) to be cut afiunder; and these are what we call Neper's rods for multiplication. But then there must be a good number of each; for as many times as any figure is in the multiplicand, so many rods of that species (i.e., with that figure on the top of it) must we have; though six rods of each species will be sufficient for any example in common affairs: there must be also as many rods of o's. But before we explain the way of using these rods, there is another thing to be known, viz., that the figures on every rod are written in an order different from that in the table. Thus the little square space or division in which the several products of every column are written, is divided into two parts by a line across from the upper angle on the right to the lower on the left; and if the product is a digit, it is set in the lower division; if it has two places, the first is set in the lower, and the second in the upper division; but the spaces on the top are not divided: also there is a rod of digits, not divided, which is called the index rod, and of this we need but one single rod. See the figure of all the different rods, and the index, separate from one another, in Plate CCI. fig. 1. Multiplication by Neper's Rods. First lay down the index-rod; then on the right of it set a rod, whose top is the figure in the highest place of the multiplicand; next to this again, set the rod, whose top is the next figure of the multiplicand; and so on in order, to the first figure. Then is your multiplicand tabulated for all the nine digits; for in the same line of squares standing against every figure of the index rod, you have the product of that figure; and therefore you have no more to do but to transfer the products and sum them. But in taking out these products from the rods, the order in which the figures stand obliges you to a very easy and small addition: thus, begin to take out the figure in the lower part, or unit's place, of the square of the first rod on the right; add the figure in the upper part of this rod to that in the lower part of the next, and so on; which may be done as fast as you can look on them. To make this practice as clear as possible, take the following example. Example: To multiply 4768 by 385. Having set the rods together for the number 4768 (ibid. n° 2.) against 5 in the index, I find this number, by adding according to the rule, | Against 5, this number | 23840 | |-----------------------|-------| | Against 8, this number | 38144 | | Against 3, this number | 14304 | Total product 1835680 To make the use of the rods yet more regular and easy, they are kept in a flat square box, whose breadth is that of ten rods, and the length that of one rod, as thick as to hold six (or as many as you please) the capacity of the box being divided into ten cells, for the different species of rods. When the rods are put up in the box (each species in its own cell distinguished by the first figure of the rod set before it on the face of the box near the top) as much of every rod stands without the box as shows the first figure of that rod; also upon one of the flat sides without and near the edge, upon the left hand, the index rod is fixed; and along the foot there is a small ledge; so that the rods when applied are laid upon this side, and supported by the ledge, which makes the practice very easy; but in case the multiplicand should have more than nine places, that upper face of the box may be made broader. Some make the rods with four different faces, and figures on each for different purposes. Division by Neper's Rods. First tabulate your divisor; then you have it multiplied by all the digits, out of which you may choose such convenient divisors as will will be next left to the figures in the dividend, and write the index answering in the quotient, and so continually till the work is done. Thus $2179788$, divided by $6123$, gives in the quotient $356$. Having tabulated the divisor $6123$, you see that $6123$ cannot be had in $2179$; therefore take five places, and on the rods find a number that is equal or next left to $21797$, which is $18369$; that is, 3 times the divisor; wherefore set 3 in the quotient, and subtract $18369$ from the figures above, and there will remain $3428$; to which add 8, the next figure of the dividend, and seek again on the rods for it; or the next left, which you will find to be five times; therefore set 5 in the quotient, and subtract $30615$ from $34288$, and there will remain $36738$; to which add 8, the last figure in the dividend, and finding it to be just 6 times the divisor, let 6 in the quotient. $$\begin{array}{c} 6123 \div 2179788 = 356 \\ 18369 \\ \hline 34288 \\ 30615 \\ \hline 36738 \\ 36738 \\ \end{array}$$

NEPETA

Pages 681-681

Catmint, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Nep; a genus of the gymnospermia order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 14 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable is the cataria, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> nep, or catmint. This is a native of many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, growing about hedges and in waste places. The stalk is a yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and branched; the leaves are hoary; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-coloured, growing verticillate in spikes at the tops of the branches; the middle segment of the lower lip is spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. The plant has a bitter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and strong smell, not unlike pennyroyal. An infusion of this plant is reckoned a good cephalic and emmenagogue; being found very efficacious in chlorotic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Two ounces of the expressed juice may be given for a dose. It is called catmint, because cats are very fond of it, especially when it is withered; for then they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> roll themselves on it, and tear it to pieces, chewing it in their mouths with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Mr Ray mentions his having transplanted some of the plants of this sort from the fields into his garden, which were soon destroyed by the cats; but the plants which came up from seeds in his garden escaped: this verifies an old proverb, viz. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you set it, the cats will eat it; if you sow it, the cats will not know it." Mr Withering is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of plants growing together, the cats will not meddle with them; but Mr Millar assures us, that he has frequently transplanted one of these plants from another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the garden, within two feet of which, some came up from seeds; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the latter have remained unhurt, when the former have been torn to pieces and destroyed: he acknowledges, however, that, where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> growing together, they will not meddle with it. This plant is very hardy, and is easily propagated by seeds. If sown upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, the plants will not grow too <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, but will continue longer, and appear much handsomer, than in rich ground, where they grow too luxuriant, and have not so strong a scent.

NEPHEW

Pages 681-681

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> relative to uncle and aunt, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sister's son; who, according to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is in the third <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>, but according to the canon in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>.

NEPHRITIC

Pages 681-682

something that relates to the kidneys. See Kidney. **Nephritic Wood**, (lignum nephriticum), a wood of a very dense and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, and of a fine grain, brought to us from New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in small blocks, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, and covered with its bark. It is to be chosen of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and firm, and such as has not lost its acid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the furred tell of it is the infusing it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>: for a piece of it infused only half an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, gives it a changeable colour, which is blue <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, as variously held to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the vial it is in be held between the eye and the light, the tincture appears yellow; but if the eye be placed between the light and the vial, it appears blue. We often meet with this wood adulterated with others of the same pale colour; but the dullish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> hue of the bark is a striking character of this. The tree is the coatl of Hernandez. It grows to the height of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-tree, and its wood while fresh is much of the same texture and colour; the leaves are small and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, not exceeding half an inch in length, or a third of an inch in breadth; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are small, of a pale-yellow colour, and oblong shape, standing in spikes: the cups they stand in are divided into five segments at the edge, and are covered with a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. This is the best <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the tree that can be collected from what has been hitherto written of it; nobody having yet had an opportunity of taking its true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. This wood is a very good diuretic, and is said to be of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with the Indians in all diseases of the kidneys and bladder, and in suppression of urine, from whatever cause. It is also recommended in fevers, and in obstructions of the viscera. The way of taking it among the Indians is only an infusion in cold water. **Nephritic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>**, a soft, brittle, opaque stone, not susceptible of a good polish; smooth, and, as it were, unctuous to the touch; variegated with several colours, of which green is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Spain, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>; and from the imaginary virtues ascribed to it in nephritic disorders, has been ranked among the precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, but differs exceedingly from them in all its sensible qualities. Neumann finds fault with some authors for referring this stone to the jaspers, agates, or marbles; from all of which, he says, it widely differs: it wants the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> specks of the jaspers, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and compactness of the others, and all of them want its unctuosity or soapiness. Out of 60 grains of nephritic stone, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> dissolved three; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; spirit of vitriol 14; spirit of nitre 16; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia 18; and spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> 20. The spirit of salt acquired a greenish-yellow tincture; aqua regia a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> yellow; oil of vitriol a dark-brownish; the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> remained colourless. Both the marine acid and aqua regia left the undissolved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> whitish; the nitrous acid greyish; the diluted vitriolic acid brownish-yellow; the concentrated light reddish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; the acetic acid... Nephritics tous, unchanged. An ounce of this substance powdered, and distilled in a retort in an open fire, yielded about a drachm and an half of phlegm, which had a penetrating empyreumatic smell, but made no change in the colour of the syrup of violets. On distilling four ounces together, there was an appearance of an actual empyreumatic oil, with a saline <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which was found to be sal ammoniac. The matter remaining in the retort was of a reddish-brown colour. An ounce of the powdered stone, mixed with an equal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fixed alkaline salt, and urged with a strong fire, did not melt, but formed a quite porous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, in colour inclining to reddish-grey, and weighing two drachms less than the mixture did at first. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> tells us, that the nephritic stone is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the indurated clays, called, from their unctuousity, fleatisse. With these it agrees, not only in its obvious properties, but likewise in its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> hard, the peculiar characteristic of argillaceous earths. Its green colour seems to proceed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. Pott relates, that on fusion with an equal quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, it yielded a beautiful red mass resembling an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, with a grain of copper at the bottom. The nephritic stone is considerably the hardest of all the substances of this class.

NEPHRITICS

Pages 682-682

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, medicines proper for diseases of the kidneys, especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.—Such particularly are the roots of althea, dog's-grass, asparagus, lago, pellitory of the wall, mallows, pimpinella, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> chick-peas, peach-kernels, turpentine, &c.

NEPOS

Pages 682-682

a celebrated Latin historian, born at Hoftia near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus. He was the friend of Cicero and Atticus; and composed several excellent works, of which there are only extant the lives of the most illustrious Greek and Roman captains.

NEPTUNE

Pages 682-682

in Pagan worship, the god of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Vesta, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Ops, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Pluto. He assisted Jupiter in his expeditions; on which that god, when he arrived at the supreme power, assigned him the sea and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> for his empire. He was, however, expelled from heaven with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, for conspiring against Jupiter, when they were both employed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAOMEDON">Laomedon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> dismissing Neptune without a reward, he sent a sea-monster to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on which he was obliged to expose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Helen. He is said to have been the first inventor of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and chariot-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RACING">racing</a>; on which account <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> king of Pontus threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> drawn by four horses into the sea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this god; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> instituted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> at his festival, during which all other horses left working, and the mules were adorned with wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. In a contest with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> he produced a horse by striking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; and on another occasion, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of skill with Minerva and Vulcan, produced a bull, whence that animal was sacrificed to him. His favourite wife was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> courted in vain, till sending the dolphin to intercede for him, he met with success; on which he rewarded the dolphin by placing him among the stars. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a> He had also two other wives, one of whom was called Salacia, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the other Venilia, from the ebbs and flows of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. He had likewise many concubines, by whom he had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children. He is represented with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with a garment of an azure or sea-green, holding his trident in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> shell drawn by sea-horses, attended by the sea-gods Palemon, Glauceus, and Phorcys, and the sea goddesses Thetis, Melita, and Panopea, and a long train of tritons and sea-nymphs.

NEREIDS

Pages 682-682

in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-nymphs, daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris.—The Nereids were esteemed very handsome; inasmuch that Calliope, the wife of Cepheus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, having triumphed over all the beauties of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and daring to vie with the Nereids, they were so enraged that they sent a prodigious sea-monster into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and, to appease them, she was commanded by the oracle to expose her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>, bound to a rock, to be devoured by the monster. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, the Nereids are represented riding upon sea-horses; sometimes with an entire <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, and at other times with the tail of a fish.

NEREUS

Pages 682-682

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a marine deity, was the son of Oceanus and Thetis. He settled in the Ægean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, was considered as a prophet, and had the power of assuming what form he pleased. He married his sister Doris, by whom he had 50 daughters called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, who constantly attended on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and when he went abroad surrounded his chariot. NERO (Domitian) <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Domitius Aenobarbus, and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a>, who married Claudius, whom Nero succeeded, A.D. 54, aged 18. He professed he would follow the example of Augustus, and at first he did; and as they once presented him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of a person condemned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, "I wish," said he, "that I could not write." But after five years reign he fell into the most extravagant crimes that ever entered the imagination of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. He would appear upon the stage in woman's dress. He committed sodomy with the greatest debauchees, and particularly Sporus, whom he kept in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of his wife, and caused to be dressed like a woman; which gave occasion to that pleasant saying, "That the world had been happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his father Domitian had had such a wife." He caused his mother to be murdered, his wife to be put to death, and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Seneca to lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, &c. and wished that mankind had but one head, that he might have the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it off. To have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of rebuilding Rome, he set it on fire, laid the blame upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and began the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against them.

NERVA

Pages 682-683
emperor after Domitian. He recalled those who had been banished for their religion, and forgot nothing that might contribute to the restoring of the empire to its former lustre; but finding his age would not suffer him to finish it, he adopted Trajan, and died A.C. 98.

NERVES

Pages 683-683

in anatomy; certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glistering cords, proceeding from the brain and spinal marrow, and dividing into very small branches, which are sent off throughout all parts of the body; and which are found to be the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See ANATOMY, n° 400. NERVOUS FLUID. See ANATOMY, n° 400, l. NEST. See NIDUS. Nestable Birds-Nests. See BIRDS-NESTS.

NESTOR

Pages 683-683

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos, and the son of Nestus and Chloris. He subdued the Eleans, and conquered the Centaurs, who would have carried off Hippodamia. He afterwards went to the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> with Agamemnon, who had a particular esteem for him on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and eloquence. He was then, according to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, so old, that he had seen three generations of men.

NESTORIANS

Pages 683-683

a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, the followers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NESTORIUS">Nestorius</a> bishop and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Constantinople; who, about the year 520, taught that there were two persons in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, the divine and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>, which are united not hypostatically <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> substantially, but in a mythical manner; whence he concluded, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> was the mother of Christ, and not the mother of God. For this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Nestorius was condemned and deposed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Ephesus; and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of this council was confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius, who banished the bishop to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>.

NET

Pages 683-683

Neat, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, something pure, and unadulterated with any foreign mixture. Thus, wine is said to be neat when not falsified <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> balderdashed; and coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c., are neat when the fifth and ordure are separated from them. See NEAT. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> is said to be neat when it has no stains or flaws; a crystal, when transparent throughout. Net is also used for what remains after the tare has been taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of any merchandise; i.e., when it is weighed clear of all package. See TARE. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> weighs 450 pounds; the tare is 50 pounds, and there remains neat 400 pounds. NET Produce, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express what any commodity has yielded, all tare and charges deducted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Italian words netto prodotto, for net produce.

NETHERLANDS

Pages 683-683

anciently called Belgia, but since denominated Low Countries <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Netherlands, from their low situation, are situated between 2° and 7° of east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 50° and 53° 30' of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude; and are bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north, Germany on the east, by Lorraine and France on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of France and the British seas on the west; extending near 300 miles in length from north to south, and 200 miles in breadth from east to west. They consist of 17 provinces; 10 of which are called the Austrian and French Netherlands, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> the United Provinces. The Austrian Netherlands consist of the greatest part of the duchies of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBURG">Limburg</a>, and Luxemburg, with a part of that of Gueldres; and of the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Hennegau, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>. The Netherlands formerly made a part of the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the whole of which once belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. devolved to the Burgundian Spanish line of that house; but was all afterwards lost, except the abovementioned countries, which, on the death of Charles II., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, fell to the German line of the Austrian family. These Austrian Netherlands are still considered as a circle of the empire, of which the archducal house, as being sovereign of the whole, is the sole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> and summoning <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. This circle contributes its share to the imposts of the empire, and sends an envoy to the diet; but is not subject to the judicatories of the empire. It is wholly Catholic, and under a governor-general appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. The French Netherlands consist of a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Luxemburg, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hainault, of the earldom of Flanders, the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, the Cambrefis, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Namur; and this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the greatest part of which belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, comprehends French Flanders, the

NETSCHER

Pages 683-684

an eminent painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in 1639. His father dying while he was an engineer in the Polish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, his mother was obliged, on account of her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, suddenly to leave Prague with her three sons. When she had proceeded three leagues, she stopped at a castle; which being soon after besieged, two of her sons were starved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but she herself found means to escape out of the fortress by night, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her only remaining child. Carrying him in her arms, she reached <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARNHEM">Arnhem</a> in Guelderland, where she found means to support herself, and breed up her son. At length a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic took young Netscher into his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, with the view of giving him an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> proper for a physician; but Netscher's genius leading him to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he could not forbear crawling out designs upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on which he wrote his themes; and it being found impossible to conquer his fondness for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, he was sent to a glazier, who was the only person in the town that understood drawing. Netscher soon finding himself above receiving any farther assistance from his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>, to a painter named Terburg, who was an able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> and burgomaster of the town; and having acquired under him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> command of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he worked a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for the dealers in pictures, who paid him very little for his pieces, which they sold at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price. Disgusted at this ungenerous treatment, he resolved to go to Rome, and for that purpose embarked on board a vessel bound for Bordeaux. But his marrying in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> prevented his travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and therefore, returning into Holland, he settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>; where observing that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>-painting was the most profitable, he applied himself solely to it, and acquired such reputation, that there is not a considerable family in Holland that has not some of his portraits; and besides, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foreign ministers could not think of quitting Holland without carrying with them one of Netscher's portraits, whence they are to be seen all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He died at the Hague, in 1684; leaving two sons, Theodore and Constantine Netscher, both of them good portrait-painters.

NETTINGS

Pages 684-684

in a ship, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> made of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> fixed together with rope-yarn <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> twine, and fixed on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> and in the tops; they are sometimes stretched upon the ledges from the waste-trees to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>-trees, from the top of the forecastle to the poop, and sometimes are laid in the waist of a ship to serve instead of gratings.

NETTLE

Pages 684-684

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See URTICA. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Nettle. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>; and Animal-Flower. Nettle-Tree. See Celtis.

NETTUNO

Pages 684-684

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome. It is but thinly peopled, though seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The inhabitants are almost all hunters. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 57'. N. Lat. 41° 30'.

NEUFCHATEAU

Pages 684-684

a town of France, in Lorraine, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the chartellie of Chateau. It is an handsome, populous, trading town; having an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of the nuns of St Clair, a commandery of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of monks and nuns. It is seated in a bottom, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile in corn, wine, and all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on the river Mouzon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 45'. N. Lat. 48° 20'.

NEUFCHATEL

Pages 684-684

an handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ruins near it, which shew its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> churches, besides a castle where the governor resides. It is seated on a lake of the same name, 17 miles in length and five in breadth, and the side of the harbour is the usual walk of the inhabitants. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: the first is composed of 40 persons, with two masters of the keys; the little council consists of 24 members, comprehending the mayor, who is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. These two councils assemble regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> likewise assemble every month, to consult on affairs belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and to fill up the places of ministers that die. They choose a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> every year, who is president of the general assemblies, which are called classes; and sometimes he is confirmed in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 10'. N. Lat. 47° 5'.

NEUROGRAPHY

Pages 685-685

signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the nerves. See Anatomy, no. 400. **NEUROPTERA**. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>.

NEUTER

Pages 685-685

a person indifferent, who has espoused neither party, and is neither friend nor foe. A judge ought to be neuter in the causes he judges; in questions, where reason appears neuter, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> should ever incline to the side of the unhappy. **Neuter**, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, denotes a sort of gender of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, which are neither masculine nor <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>. See Gender. The Latins have three kinds of genders, masculine, feminine, and neuter. In English, and other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues, there is no such thing as neuter nouns. See Noun. Verbs Neuter, by some grammarians called intransitive verbs, are those which govern nothing, and that are neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. See Verb. When the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> expressed by the verb has no object to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon, but the verb alone supplies the whole idea of the action; the verb is said to be neuter; as, I <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, thou yawnest, he sneezes, we walk, ye run, they stand still. Some divide verbs neuter into, 1. Such as do not signify any action, but a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; as aluit, "it is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>;" <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a situation, as sedet, "he sits;" or have some relation to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; as adeit, "he is present;" or to some other state or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, as regnat, "he rules," &c. And, 2. Those that do signify actions, though those such as do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into any subject different from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>; as to dine, to sup, to play, &c. But this latter kind sometimes cease to be neuter, and commence active; especially in Greek and Latin, when a subject is given them: as, vivere vitam, ambulare viam, pugnare pugnam. Thus the old French poets say, Soupirer son tourment; the English, to sigh his woes, &c. But this is observed only to obtain where something particular is to be expressed, not contained, in the verb: as, vivere vitam beatam, to live a happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; pugnare bonam pugnam, to fight a good fight, &c. According to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> de Dangeau, verbs neuter may be divided into active and passive; the first, those that form their tenses in English, by the auxiliary verb to have; in French, by avoir. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, those that form them in English with the verb to be; in French être.—Thus, to sleep, to yawn, dormir and sternuer, are neuters active.—To come, and to arrive, are neuters passive. **Neutral Salts**, among chemists, those <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> ed of an acid with any other substance capable of uniting with it and destroying its acidity. Those in which the acid is saturated with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or a metal are called imperfect, but those in which a pure alkali is employed are called perfect, neutrals. **Neutrality**, the state of a person or thing that is neuter, or that takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> with neither side.

NEVERS

Pages 684-684

a considerable town of France, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Nivernais, in Orleansois, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle, and a bishop's see. It is built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and contains several fine buildings. It is seated on the river Loir, over which there is an handsome <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and at the end of it a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> causeway reaching to the town. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 14'. N. Lat. 46° 59'.

NEVIS

Pages 684-685

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Montferrat, and separated from St Christopher's by a narrow channel. It makes a beautiful appearance from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> com- cal mountain covered with fine trees, of an easy ascent on every side, and entirely cultivated. The circumference is about 21 miles, with a considerable tract of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground all around. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is reckoned to be warmer than Barbadoes, but it is more temperate towards the summit. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fine in the lower part, but grows coarser as we ascend. The productions are nearly the same with those of St Christopher. There are three pretty good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bays, with small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in their vicinity; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>-town, Moreton-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. This pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was settled under the auspices of Sir Thomas Warner from St Christopher's. His successor, governor Lake, was considered as the Solon of this little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which he disposed of everything with such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as procured him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation with the French as well as English. In the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> they met with some disturbance from the French; but by being covered by an English squadron, the enemy were obliged to desist from their intended invasion, after a smart engagement in sight of the island. Sir William Stapleton sometimes resided here, and Sir Nathaniel Johnston constantly, at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the inhabitants of Nevis were computed at 30,000. In the war immediately after the revolution, they exerted themselves gallantly, and had two regiments of 300 men each. In that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> they behaved equally well, tho' they were less fortunate; for the French landing with a superior force, and having inveigled most of their slaves, they were forced to capitulate. About 4000 of these slaves the French carried away and sold to the Spaniards, to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, after making due inquiry into the losses they had sustained, voted them about a third part of the sum in which they had suffered. These losses by war, an epidemic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and repeated hurricanes, exceedingly diminished the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the people. They are now thought not to exceed 2000 or 3000 whites, and 6000 blacks. There is here a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, which is composed of three members from each of the five parishes into which the island is divided. The commodities are cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; and about 20 sail of ships are annually employed in this trade.

NEWBURG

Pages 684-684

the name of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Germany, two of which are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns of duchies of the same name; one in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and the other in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>.

NEWCASTLE

Pages 685-686

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in England, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and flourishing town, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Tyne, about 300 miles to the northward of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is connected, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with the suburbs of Gateshead, which, being on the southern side of the river, is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>. Near the spot where the town now stands, there was of old a fort called Moncaster; and Robert, son of William the Conqueror, having built another to overawe the Scots, bestowed upon it the name of Newcastle, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the old fortress. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> monasteries and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> being raised around it, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, swelled into a town; and the walls of it were begun in the reign of Edward I. by a rich burgher, who had been taken by the Scots, and paid a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. It is at present surrounded by a strong wall, in which there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates and as many turrets, with some casemates said to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. It was created a borough by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Richard II. who granted permission to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> before the mayor; and king Henry VI. erected it into a town and county incorporate, independent of Northumberland. The magistracy consists of a mayor, 19 aldermen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, a recorder, a town-clerk, a clerk of the chambers, two coroners, eight chamberlains, a sword-bearer, with a NEWCASTLE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of maintenance, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mace, and seven serjeants at mace. Newcastle has been exposed to frequent incursions and sieges of the Scots before the union of the two crowns; and in the great rebellion, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, under the command of Leslie, took it by storm: but it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago retrieved all its losses, and become the great emporium of the north of England for coal and other merchandise. The town is built upon the declivity of a hill, which renders the streets steep and inconvenient. The houses are crowded together so as to exhibit but a disagreeable appearance: yet one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> two of the streets are large, spacious, and well paved. The town is overlooked by the old ruinous castle; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> are magnificent buildings, but too <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the river; along the bank of which there is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">key</a> or wharf faced with freestone, to which ships of ordinary burden can carry their broadsides to be loaded or unloaded. But the coal-ships are loaded at near Shields, seven miles farther <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the river; their lading being conveyed thither in lighters, which they call keels. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the keelmen who <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in these lighters, exceed 6000, who live in a suburb called Sandgate. They have, by a contribution among themselves, built a noble <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for such of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> brethren as are disabled by accident, or superannuated and past labour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Newcastle, called St Nicholas, is a stately old fabric, built by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> king of Scotland, with a fine fleecy of rare <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>: here are, besides, six churches or chapels. We may number among the public edifices, an elegant mansion-house for the mayor; a noble <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> for the surgeons, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; a stately infirmary on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; a library belonging to the corporation; a large prison called Newgate; several meeting-houses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> well endowed. The number of inhabitants amounts to above 40,000; and many of them are wealthy, and live with splendour. They are generally bold, rough, and industrious; enriching themselves with the coal-trade, and other branches of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and manufacture, such as ship-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, glass-making, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, and hardware or wrought <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The place is particularly famous for grind-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which are exported to all the countries in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The fashionable people live in the upper part of the town, at a distance from the river, where they possess elegant houses and gardens, and enjoy themselves at comedies, assemblies, and other polite diversions. The houses are chiefly built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some are of brick, and a very few of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. The revenue of the town, amounting to 8000l. a-year, is considerably larger than that of any other corporation-borough in England: and from this the mayor is indulged with an annual allowance of 600l. besides the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, barge, and mansion-house.
