First, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a>, such as absent themselves from divine worship in the established <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> through total irreligion, and attend the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of no other persuasion. These, by the Statute 1 Eliz. c. 2. 23 Eliz. c. 1. and 3 Jac. I. c. 4. forfeit one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> they so absent themselves, and 20l. to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they continue such default for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> together. And if they keep any innate thus irreligiously disposed in their houses, they forfeit 10l. per month. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of nonconformists are those who offend through a mistaken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> perverse zeal. Such were esteemed, by the English laws enacted since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Reformation, to be Papists and Protestant dissenters: both of which were supposed to be equally schismatics, in not communicating with the national church; with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the Papists divided from it upon material, though erroneous, reasons; but many of the dissenters upon matters of indifference, or, in other words, upon no reason at all. "Yet certainly (says Sir William Blackstone) our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were mistaken in their plans of compulsion and intolerance. The sin of schism, as such, is by no means the object of temporal coercion and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. If, through weakness of intellect, through misdirected piety, through perverseness and acerbity of temper, or (which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>) through a prospect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> advantage in herding with a party, men quarrel with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> establishment, the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> has nothing to do with it; unless their tenets and practice are such as threaten ruin or disturbance to the state. He is bound indeed to protect the established church; and if this can be better effected by admitting none but its genuine members to offices of trust and emolument, he is certainly at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> so to do; the disposal of offices being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of favour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. But, this point being once secured, all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> for diversity of opinions, however ridiculous or absurd they may be, is contrary to every principle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy and civil freedom. The names and subordination of the clergy, the posture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, the materials and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the minister's garment, the joining in a known or unknown form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and other matters of the same kind, must be left to the option of every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s private judgment. "With "With regard therefore to Protestant dissenters, although the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of their turbulent disposition in former times occasioned several disabilities and restrictions (which I shall not undertake to justify) to be laid upon them by abundance of statutes; yet at length the legislature, with a true spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, extended that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to these sectaries, which they themselves, when in power, had held to be countenancing schism, and denied to the church of England. The penalties are conditionally suspended by the statute 1 W. & M. II. c. 18. "for exempting their Majesties Protestant subjects, dissenting from the church of England, from the penalties of certain laws," <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the toleration <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; which declares, that neither the laws above-mentioned, nor the statutes 1 Eliz. c. 2. § 14. 3 Jac. I. c. 4. &c., nor any other penal laws made against Popish recusants (except the test acts) shall extend to any dissenters, other than Papists and such as deny the Trinity: provided, 1. That they take the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy, or make a similar <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a>, being <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and subscribe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. 2. That they repair to some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> certified to, and registered in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the bishop or archdeacon, or at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-sessions. 3. That the doors of such meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> shall be unlocked, unbarr'd, and unbolted; in default of which, the persons meeting there are still liable to all the penalties of the former acts. Dissenting teachers, in order to be exempted from the penalties of the statutes 13 & 14 Car. II. c. 4. 17 Car. II. c. 2. and 22 Car. II. c. 1. are also to subscribe the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> mentioned in the statute 13 Eliz. c. 12. (viz. those which only concern the confession of the true Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and the doctrine of the sacraments), with an express exception of those relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and powers of the church, and to infant-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. And by statute 10 Ann. c. 2. this toleration is ratified and confirmed; and it is declared, that the said act shall at all times be inviolably observed for the exempting such Protestant dissenters as are thereby intended, from the pains and penalties therein mentioned. Thus, though the offence of nonconformity is by no means universally abrogated, it is suspended, and ceases to exist with regard to these Protestant dissenters, during their compliance with the conditions imposed by the act of toleration: and, under these conditions, all persons, who <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> approve themselves no Papists or oppugners of the Trinity, are left at full liberty to act as their consciences shall <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them in the matter of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship. And if any person shall wilfully, maliciously, or contumaciously disturb any congregation, assembled in any church or permitted meeting-house, or shall misuse any preacher or teacher there, he shall (by virtue of the same statute) be bound over to the sessions of the peace, and forfeit 20l. But by statute 5 Geo. I. c. 4. no mayor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> magistrate must appear at any dissenting meeting with the ensigns of his office, on pain of disfavour to hold that or any other office: the legislature judging it a matter of propriety, that a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship, set up in opposition to the national, when allowed to be exercised in peace, should be exercised also with decency, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, and humility. Neither doth the act of toleration extend to enervate those clauses of the statutes 14 & 13 Car. II. c. 4. &c. Car. II. c. 2. which prohibit (upon pain of fine and imprisonment) all persons from teaching school, unless they be licensed by the ordinary, and subscribe a declaration of conformity to the liturgy of the church, and reverently frequent divine service established by the laws of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. As to Papists, what has been said of the Protestant dissenters would hold equally strong for a general toleration of them; provided their separation was founded only upon difference of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in religion, and their principles did not also extend to a subversion of the civil government. If once they could be brought to renounce the supremacy of the Pope, they might quietly enjoy their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments; their purgatory, and auricular confession; their worship of relics and images; nay, even their transubstantiation. But while they acknowledge a foreign power, superior to the sovereignty of the kingdom, they cannot complain if the laws of that kingdom will not treat them upon the footing of good subjects. The following are the laws that have been enacted against the Papists; who may be divided into three classes, persons professing Popery, Popish recusants convicted, and Popish priests. 1. Persons professing the Popish religion, besides the former penalties for not frequenting their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-church, are disabled from taking any lands either by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> or purchase, after 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, until they renounce their errors; they must at the age of 21 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> their estates before acquired, and all future conveyances and wills relating to them; they are incapable of presenting to any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a>, or granting to any other person any avoidance of the same; they may not keep or teach any school under pain of perpetual imprisonment; and, if they willingly say or hear <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, they forfeit the one 200, the other 100 marks, and each shall suffer a year's imprisonment. Thus much for persons who, from the misfortune of family-prejudices, or otherwise, have conceived an unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Romish church from their infancy, and publicly profess its errors. But if any evil industry is used to rivet these errors upon them; if any person sends another abroad to be educated in the Popish religion, or to reside in any religious house abroad for that purpose, or contributes to their maintenance when there; both the fender, the tenant, and the contributor, are disabled to sue in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, to be executor or administrator to any person, to take any legacy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of gift, and to bear any office in the realm; and shall forfeit all their goods and chattels, and likewise all their real estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. And where these errors are also aggravated by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a> or perversion; where a person is reconciled to the see of Rome, or procures others to be reconciled, the offence amounts to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. 2. Popish recusants, convicted in a court of law of not attending the service of the church of England, are subject to the following disabilities, penalties, and forfeitures, over and above those before-mentioned. They are considered as persons excommunicated; they can hold no office or employment; they must not keep arms in their houses, but the same may be seized by the justices of the peace; they may not come within 10 miles of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on pain of 100l.; they can bring no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at law or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> in equity; they are not permitted to travel above five miles from home, unless by license. Nonconformists, upon pain of forfeiting all their goods; and they may not come to court under pain of 100l. No <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of such recusant, or baptism of his child, shall be had otherwise than by the ministers of the church of England, under other severe penalties. A married woman, when recusant, shall forfeit two thirds of her dower or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a>, may not be executrix or administratrix to her husband, nor have any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his goods; and during the coverture may be kept in prison, unless her husband redeems her at the rate of 10l. a-month, or the third part of all his lands. And lastly, as a feme-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> recusant may be imprisoned, so all others must, within three months after conviction, either submit and renounce their errors, or, if required so to do by four justices, must abjure and renounce the realm: and if they do not depart, or if they return without the king's licence, they shall be guilty of felony, and suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as felons without benefit of clergy. There is also an inferior species of recusancy, (refusing to make the declaration against Popery enjoined by statute 30 Car. II. st. 2. when tendered by the proper magistrate;) which, if the party resides within ten miles of London, makes him an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> recusant convict; or, if at a greater distance, suspends him from having any seat in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, keeping arms in his house, or any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> above the value of 5l. 3. Popish priests are in a still more dangerous condition. By statute 11 & 12 W. III. c. 4. Popish priests, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, celebrating mass or exercising any part of their functions in England, except in the houses of ambassadors, are liable to perpetual imprisonment. And by the statute 27 Eliz. c. 2. any Popish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, born in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, who shall come over hither from beyond <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, (unless driven by fires of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and tarrying only a reasonable time,) or shall be in England three days without conforming and taking the oaths, is guilty of high treason: and all persons harbouring him are guilty of felony without the benefit of clergy. This is a short summary of the laws against the Papists; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Montesquieu observes, that they are so rigorous, though not professedly of the sanguinary kind, that they do all the hurt that can possibly be done in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood. But in answer to this it may be observed, (what foreigners who only judge from our statute-book are not fully apprized of) that these laws are seldom exerted to their utmost rigour: and indeed, if they were, it would be very difficult to excuse them. For they are rather to be accounted for from their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and the urgency of the times which produced them, than to be approved (upon a cool review) as a standing system of law. The reliefs machinations of the Jesuits during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, the turbulence and unquietness of the Papists under the new religious establishment, and the boldness of their hopes and wishes for the succession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots, obliged the parliament to counteract so dangerous a spirit by laws of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and then perhaps necessary, severity. The powder-treason, in the succeeding reign, struck a panic into James I. which operated in different ways: it occasioned the enacting of new laws against the Papists; but deterred him from putting them in execution. The intrigues of queen Henrietta in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. the prospect of a Popish successor in that of Char. II. the assassination-plot in the reign of king William, and the avowed claim of a Popish pretender to the crown in subsequent reigns, will account for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of these penalties at those several periods of our history." But now that all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> fears of a pretender may be said to have vanished; and the power and influence of the pope has become feeble, ridiculous, and desppicable, not only in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but in almost every kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and as in fact the British Catholics solemnly disclaim the dangerous principles ascribed to them by the British legislature, giving way to that liberality of sentiment becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, have lately repealed the most rigorous of the above edicts, viz. The punishment of Popish priests or Jesuits who should be found to teach or officiate in the services of that church, which acts were felony in foreigners, and high treason in the natives of this kingdom:—The forfeitures of Popish heirs, who had received their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> abroad; and whose estates went to the next Protestant heir:—The power given to the son, or other relation, being a Protestant, to take possession of the father's or other relation's estate, during the life of the real proprietor:—And the debarring Papists from the power of acquiring any legal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> by purchase.—In proposing the repeal of these penalties, it was observed, That, belied that some of them had now ceased to be necessary, others were at all times a disgrace to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. The imprisonment of a Popish priest for life, only for officiating in the services of his religion, was horrible in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: And although the mildness of government had hitherto softened the rigour of the law in the practice, it was to be remembered that the Roman Catholic priests constantly lay at the mercy of the basest and most abandoned of mankind—of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> informers; for on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of any of these wretches, the magisterial and judicial powers were of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> bound to enforce all the shameful penalties of the act. Others of these penalties held out the most powerful temptations for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of acts of depravity, at the very thought of which our nature recoils with horror: They seemed calculated to loosen all the bands of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; to dissolve all civil, moral, and religious obligations and duties, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> the sources of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> fidelity, and to annihilate every principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The encouragement given to children to lay their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the estates of their parents, and the restriction which debars any man from the honest acquisition of property, need only to be mentioned to excite indignation in an enlightened age. In order the better to secure the English established church against perils from non-conformists of all denominations, infidels, Turks, Jews, heretics, Papists, and sectaries, there are, however, two bulwarks erected; called the corporation and test acts: By the former of which, no person can be legally elected to any office relating to the government of any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> or corporation, unless, within a twelvemonth before, he has received the sacrament of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the church of England; and he is also enjoined to take the oaths of allegiance and supremacy at the same time that he takes the oath of office: or, in default of either of these requisites, such <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> shall be void. The other, called the test act, directs all officers civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> to take the oaths and make the declaration against transubstantiation, in any of the king's courts at Westminster, or at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>- sessions, within six <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> months after their admis- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>; and also within the same time to receive the fa- crament of the Lord's supper, according to the usage of the church of England, in some public church im- mediately after divine service and sermon, and to deli- ver into court a certificate thereof signed by the mi- nister and church-warden, and also to prove the same by two credible witnesses; upon forfeiture of £501, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a> to hold the said office. And of much the same nature with these is the statute 7 Jac. I. c. 2, which permits no persons to be naturalised or restored in blood, but such as undergo a like test: which test having been removed in 1753, in favour of the Jews, was the next session of parliament restored again with some precipitation. Non-Naturals, in medicine, so called, because by their abuse they become the causes of diseases. Physicians have divided the non-naturals into five classes, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, meats and drinks, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> and watching, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and rest, the passions of the mind, the retentions and excretions. See Medicine, no 147, &c. Non Obstante, (notwithstanding,) a clause frequent in statutes and letters-patent, importing a licence from the king to do a thing, which at common law might be lawfully done, but being restrained by act of par- liament cannot be done without such licence. Non Pres. See Nolle Prosequi. Non-Suit, signifies the dropping of a suit or action, or a renouncing thereof by the plaintiff or defendant; which happens most commonly upon the discovery of some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the plaintiff's proceedings when the cause is so far proceeded in, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> is ready at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to deliver in their verdict.

NONIUS

Pages 719-719

a grammarian and Peripate- tic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, wrote a treatise, in- titled De proprietate sermonum. This author is only valuable for his giving fragments of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors that are nowhere else to be found. The above treatise was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1614, with notes.

NONNIUS

Pages 719-719
or Nonius (Lewis), a learned phy- sician of Antwerp in the 17th century, wrote several works which are excellent; the principal of which are, 1. An excellent treatise intitled Ichthyophagia, seu de Pisium efa. 2. Hispania; which is of great use in understanding the ancient geography of Spain. 3. A commentary on the medals of Greece, and those of Julius Cæsar, Augustus, and Tiberius, in folio: it contains Goltzius's two works on the same subject. 4. A commentary on Goltzius's account of Greece, the islands, &c. 5. Poems, &c.

NONNUS

Pages 719-719

a Greek poet of the 5th century, and native of Panopolis in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the author of an heroic poem in 48 books, intitled Dionysiacorum, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of St John's Gospel, which may serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon it.

NORDEN

Pages 719-719

an ingenious travel- ler and naval officer in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, was born at Glückstadt in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in the year 1708. He was well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, ship-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and espe- cially in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; and in 1732 obtained a pension to enable him to travel for the purpose of studying the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of ships, particularly the galleys and other rowing vessels used in the Mediterranean. He spent near three years in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Christian VI. being desirous of obtaining a circumstantial account of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, Mr Norden at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> received an order to extend his travels to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. How he acquitted himself in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, appears from his Travels into Egypt and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a> in folio, 1756; and which were soon after translated in- to English by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Templeman. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> be- tween England and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, Mr Norden, then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, attended <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> Ulric Adol- phus, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, to England; and they went out volunteers under Sir John Norris, and afterwards un- der Sir Chaloner Ogle. During his stay in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Mr Norden was made a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and gave the public drawings of some ruins and colossal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> at Thebes in Egypt; with an account of the same, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the royal society, 1741. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> was declining; and taking a tour to France, he died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1742.

NORFOLK

Pages 719-721

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, so called from its northern situation in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, is bounded on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the German ocean; on the south by Suffolk, from which it is parted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Waveney, and the lesser Ouse; and on the west it is separated from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a> by the Greater Ouse, and from a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> by the washes. According to Templeman, it extends in length 57 miles, in breadth 35, and 140 in cir- cumference. It contains an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 1426 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 32 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 711 villages, ac- cording to the book of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a>; though some make them 1500, and 236000 inhabitants, as some have it, and 283000, according to others. It is divided into 31 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 164 vicarages, and 660 parishes. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> differs in different parts of the county, ac- cording to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which in some parts is marshy, especially on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and there the air is foggy and unwholesome; in others it is clayey and chalky, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, lean, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; and there the air is good. The county is almost all champaign, except in some places, Norfolk, where rise gentle hills. The marsh-lands yield rich pasture for cattle; the clay-grounds pease, rye, and barley; and the sandy-heaths feed vast flocks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sheep, of which some villages are said to keep 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 5000. These heaths abound also in rabbits of a silver-grey <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALSINGHAM">Walsingham</a> is noted for producing the best saffron. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> quantities of mackerel and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> are caught upon the coasts of this county, the former in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the latter in September; especially at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a>, where they are cured in a particular manner, and to great perfection. Wood and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> are also very plentiful in this shire; and on the coasts jet and ambergrise are sometimes found. The inhabitants are generally strong and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, sagacious and acute. That they are so robust, is the more to be wondered at, because the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people live much on puddings, Norfolk dumplings. They are for the most part in easy circumstances, and were formerly very quarrelsome and litigious. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this disposition, lawyers swarmed among them to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that a statute was made so early as the reign of Henry VI. to restrain their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the county, which is exceedingly populous, are chiefly woollen and worsted stuffs, and stockings, for which they are well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> from the vast flocks of sheep bred in it. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the elder branch of the family of Howard, lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and sends twelve members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two knights for the shire, two citizens for Norwich, and two burgesses for each of the boroughs of Lynn Regis, Great Yarmouth, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a>, and Cattle-rising. The county is well watered, and supplied with fish by the rivers Yare, Thurn, Waveney, the Greater and Lesser Ouse, and the Bure, besides rivulets. The Bure abounds in excellent perch, and the Yare has a fish peculiar to it called the ruffe. The latter rises about the middle of the county; and after being joined by the Waveney and Bure, falls into the sea at Yarmouth. At the equinoxes, especially the autumnal, the Ouse is subject to great inundations, being forced back by the sea that enters it with great fury. Norfolk, a county of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> contiguous to North Carolina. Normandy, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the north by the English channel; on the east by Picardy and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France; on the south by Perche and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, and one part of Bretagne; and on the west by the ocean. It is about 150 miles in length, 80 in breadth, and 600 in circumference. It is one of the most fertile, and brings in the largest revenue of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It abounds in all things except wine, but they supply that defect by cider and perry. There are vast meadows, fat pastures, and the sea yields plenty of fish. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and a great number of rivers and harbours. It carries on a great trade, is very populous, and comprehends a vast number of towns and villages. It is divided into the Upper and Lower; the Upper borders upon Picardy, and the Lower upon Bretagne. The inhabitants are ingenious, and capable of understanding arts and sciences, but they are very fond of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The Normans, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, having entered France under Rollo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Simple ceded this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to them in 912, which from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> was called Normandy. Rollo was the first duke, and held it as a fief of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France, and several of his successors after him, till William, the seventh duke, conquered England in 1066: from which time it became a province of England, till it was lost in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> John, and re-united to the crown of France; but the English still keep the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the coasts of Normandy. North (<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>), the third baron of that accomplished family, was one of the finest gentlemen in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of king James; but, in supporting that character, dissipated and gained away the greatest part of his fortune. In 1645, he appears to have acted with the parliament; and was nominated by them to be administrator of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, in conjunction with the great earls of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, and others. He lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 85, the latter part of which he passed in retirement; and wrote a small folio of miscellaneous, in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, under this title, A Forest promiscuous of several Scatons Productions, in four parts, 1659. North (Dudley, lord) son of the former, was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the bath in 1616, at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of Charles <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; and sat in many parliaments, till secluded by the prevailing party in that which condemned the king. From that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> lord North lived privately in the country, and towards the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> entertained himself with books, and, as his numerous issue required, with economy, on which he wrote a little tract, called Observations and advices economical, 12mo. His other works are, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">Passages</a> relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> parliament; The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the life of the lord Edward North, the first baron of the family, addressed to his eldest son; and a volume of essays. North (Francis lord Guilford, lord-keeper of the great-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> in the reigns of Charles II. and James II.) was a third son of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Dudley lord North, baron of Kerling; and studied at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, from whence he removed to Middle Temple. He acquired French, Italian, Spanish, and Dutch; and became not only a good lawyer, but was well versed in history, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and music. He was afterwards made the king's solicitor-general, and was chosen to represent the borough of Lynn in parliament. He succeeded Sir Heneage Finch in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>; and lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> Vaughan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of lord chief-justice of the common-pleas. He was afterwards made keeper of the great-seal; and in 1683 was created a baron, by the title of lord Guilford. He died at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Wroxton in 1685. He wrote a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on music; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, considered in the bladders of fishes, printed in Lowthorp's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the Philosophical Transactions; and some other pieces. North, one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. See Pole. North-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, the most northerly promontory in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, on the coast of Norway. E. Long. 21°. N. Lat. 78°. North-Foreland, a cape or promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the isle of Thanet, four miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARGATE">Margate</a>. Between this and the South-Foreland are the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>, through which all ships <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> that are bound to or from the the west. E. Long. 1. 25. N. Lat. 51. 25. North-West Passage, a passage to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a> through <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> or Davis's Straits, and which hath been frequently attempted without success; notwithstanding which, many people are still of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it is practicable. North-East Passage, a passage to the East Indies along the northern coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which, like the former, hath frequently been attempted, but hitherto without success. Concerning these passages an opinion hath lately been revived by the hon. Daines Barrington, namely, that they ought to be attempted by the pole itself; and he hath no doubt of the possibility of accomplishing them by that means. See North Pole.

NORTHAMPTON

Pages 721-721

a town of England, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 55. N. Lat. 52. 15. According to Camden, it was formerly called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a>-afandon, from its situation to the north of the river Nen, called anciently Aysford, by which and another lesser river it is almost enclosed. Dr Gibson says, that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon annals called both it and Southampton simply <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>; and afterwards, to distinguish them, called the one, from its situation, Southampton, and the other Northampton; but never North-afandon. Though it does not appear to be a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, yet here was a castle, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> dedicated to St Andrew, built by Simon de Sancto Licio, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Senlac, the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Northampton of that name. It is said to have been burnt <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> during the Danish depredations; but in the reign of St Edward it appears to have been a considerable place. It was besieged by the barons in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> John; at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> called Hanhill, is supposed to have been raised. In the time of Henry III. it sided with the barons, when it was besieged and taken by the king. Here the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought in which Henry VI. was taken prisoner; and several parliaments have been held in this town. It was entirely consumed by a most dreadful fire in 1675; yet, by the help of liberal contributions from all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, it hath so recovered itself, that it is now one of the neatest and best-built <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the kingdom. Among the public buildings, which are all lofty, the most remarkable are the church called All-hallows, the sessions and assize <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the George inn, which belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of the town. There was formerly a nunnery in the neighbouring meadows. A county-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> infirmary has been lately built here, after the manner of those of Bath, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, &c. It has a considerable manufacture of shoes and stockings; and its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are noted for horses both for draught and saddle; besides, it is a great thoroughfare for the north and west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the family of Compton.

NORTHAMPTONSHIRE

Pages 721-721

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, is situated in the very heart of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>: bounded on the east by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> and Huntingdon; on the south by those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, Rutland, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, which are separated from it by the Leffer Avon, and the Welland. Its greatest length is about 50 miles, its greatest breadth about 20, and its circumference about 130. It contains 33 parishes; in which are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a> one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 11 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 150,000 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> members are returned to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for this county, viz. two knights for the shire, two for the city of Peterborough, two for each of the towns of Northampton and Brockley, and one for Higham Ferrers. It lies in the Mid-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> circuit, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Peterborough. As this county is dry, well cultivated, free from marshes, except the fens about Peterborough, in the centre of the kingdom, and of course at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it enjoys a very pure and wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this it is very populous, and so full of towns and churches, that 30 spires <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> steeples may be seen in many places at one view; and even in the fens, the inhabitants seem to enjoy a good state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and to be little affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> which frequently overflows their grounds, especially in winter, but is never suffered to remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> upon it. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is exceeding fertile both in corn and pasture; but it labours under a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, as it doth not produce much wood, and, by lying at a distance from the sea, cannot be easily supplied with coal. Its commodities, besides corn, are sheep, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>, tammies, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, boots, and shoes. Besides many lesser brooks and streams, it is well watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Nen, Welland, Ouse, and Leam; the three first of which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> navigable.

NORTHUMBERLAND

Pages 721-722

the most northerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, and formerly a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west by the river Tweed, which divides it from Scotland, the Cheviot-hills, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; washed on the east by the German Ocean; and separated from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tyne and Derwent. This county, which gives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to a nobleman who married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Algernoon duke of Somerset, whose mother was heiress of the Piercy family, extends about 50 miles in length from north to south, and above 40 from east to west; and is remarkably populous, containing 11 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 280 villages, and 46 parishes. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, especially towards the west, is roughened with huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the most remarkable of which are the Cheviot-hills, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ridge called Ridefale; but the lands are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side and the borders of Durham. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, like that of every other mountainous country in the neighbourhood of the sea, is moist and disagreeable: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, however, is pure and healthy, as being well ventilated by breezes and strong gales of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and in winter mitigated by the warm vapours from the two seas, the Irish and the German Ocean, between which it is situated. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> varies in different parts of the county. Among the hills it is barren; though it affords good pasture for sheep, which cover those mountains. The low country, when properly cultivated, produces plenty of wheat, and all sorts of grain; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of it is laid out in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>-lands and rich enclosures. Northumberland is well watered with many rivers, rivulets, and fountains: its greatest rivers are the Tweed and the Tyne. The Tyne is composed of two streams called South and North Tyne: the first rises on the verge of Cumberland, near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>-moor; enters Northumberland, Northumberland, running north to Haltwefel; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> easterly, and receiving the two small rivers East and West Alon, unites above <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEXHAM">Hexham</a> with the other branch, taking its rise at a mountain called Fame-head in the western part of the county, thence called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">Time</a>-dale; is swelled in its course by the little river Shee; joins the Read near Billingham; and running in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line to the south-east, is united with the southern Tyne, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river that washes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and falls into the German Ocean near Tiamouth. In all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the mountains of Northumberland contain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-ore and other mineralized <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in their bowels, as they in all respects resemble those parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> and Scotland where lead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> have been found and prosecuted. Perhaps the inhabitants are diverted from inquiries of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by the certain profits and constant employment they enjoy in working the coal-pits, with which this county abounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the greatest part of England, are supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> from these stores of Northumberland, which are inexhaustible, enrich the proprietors, and employ an incredible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and shipping. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> woods of any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in this county; but many plantations belonging to the seats of noblemen and gentlemen, of which here is a great number. As for pot-herbs, roots, fallading, and every article of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden and orchard, they are here raised in great plenty by the usual means of cultivation; as are also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of more delicate flavour, such as the apricot, peach, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTARINE">nectarine</a>. The spontaneous fruits it produces in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, are the crab-apple, the sloe <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bullace, the hazel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, the acorn, hips, and haws, with the berries of the bramble, the juniper, wood-strawberries, cranberries, and bilberries. Northumberland raises a good number of excellent horses and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, and affords pasture for numerous flocks of sheep; both the cattle and sheep are of a large breed, but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is coarser than that which the more southern counties produce. The hills and mountains abound with a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> deer, foxes, hares, rabbits, heathcock, grouse, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>, plover, teal, and woodcock: indeed, this is counted one of the best sporting counties in Great Britain. The sea and rivers are well stocked with fish; especially the Tweed, in which a vast number of salmon is caught and carried to Tinmouth, where being pickled, they are conveyed by sea to London, and sold under the name of Newcastle salmon. The Northumbrians were anciently stigmatized as a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, barbarous people, addicted to cruelty, and inclined to rapine. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, before the union of the two crowns of England and Scotland, the borderers on each side were extremely licentious and ungovernable, trained up to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> from their infancy, and habituated to plunder by the mutual incursions made into each kingdom; incursions which neither truce nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> could totally prevent. People of a pacific disposition, who proposed to earn their livelihood by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, would not on any terms remain in a country exposed to the first violence of a bold and desperate enemy; therefore the lands lay uncultivated, and in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> deserted by every body but lawless adventurers, who subsisted by theft and rapine. There was a Northumberland tract 50 miles in length and 6 in breadth, between Berwick and Carlisle, known by the name of the Debateable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, to which both nations laid claim, tho' it belonged to neither; and this was occupied by a set of banditti who plundered on each side, and what they stole in one kingdom, they sold openly in the other: nay, they were so dexterous in their occupation, that by means of hot <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> applied to the noses of the cattle which they stole, they twisted them in such a manner, that, when the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> owners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them in the market, they did not know their own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Wardens were appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the marches or borders in each kingdom; and these offices were always conferred on noblemen of the first character for influence, valour, and integrity. The English border was divided into three marches, called the east, west, and middle marches; the gentlemen of the country were constituted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-wardens, who held <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>-courts, regulated the watches, disciplined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for assembling them in arms at the first alarm: but in the time of peace between the two nations, they were chiefly employed in suppressing the insolence and rapine of the borderers. Since the union of the crowns, however, Northumberland is totally changed, both with respect to the improvement of the lands, and the reformation of the inhabitants. The grounds, being now secure from incursion and infest, are settled by creditable farmers, and cultivated like other parts of the kingdom. As hostilities have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ceased, the people have forgot the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms, and exercised themselves in the more eligible avocations of peace; in breeding sheep and cattle, manuring the grounds, working at the coal-pits, and in different branches of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and manufacture. In their persons they are generally tall, strong, hardy, and fresh-coloured; and though less unpolished than their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, not quite so civilized as their southerneighbours. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> are well fed, lodged, and cloathed; and all of them remarkably distinguished by a kind of gibbeshch or awrle, being a particular way of pronouncing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> R, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they hawked it up from the wind-pipe, like the cawing of rooks. In other respects, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> they speak is an uncoth mixture of the English and Scottish dialects. There is no material distinction between the fashionable people of Northumberland, and those of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in other parts of the kingdom: the same form of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce the same effects in all countries. The gentlemen of Northumberland, however, are remarkable for their courage, hospitality, and hard drinking. A great number of Roman monuments have been found in this county; but the most remarkable curiosity of that kind consists in the remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>'s vallum and the wall of Severus. See Adrian's Wall, and Severus's Wall. The most noted towns in Northumberland, are Newcastle, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORPETH">Morpeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a>, Berwick, Hexham, and North Shields.

NORWAY

Pages 722-730

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, lying between the 57th and 72d degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between the 5th and 31st degrees of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> east from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; extending in length about 1000 miles, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line from Lindesnaes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Chri- Norway. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANSAND">Christiansand</a>, to the North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, at the extremity of Finnmark. Its breadth, from the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> westward to Cape Statt, may amount to about 300 miles; but from thence the country becomes gradually narrower towards the north. On the south it is bounded by the Schagen-rock, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Categate, the entrance into the Baltic; on the east it is divided from Sweden by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and on the west and north it is washed by the northern ocean. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Norway, extending above 300 leagues, is studded with a multitude of small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, affording habitation to fishermen and pilots, and pasture to a few cattle. They form an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of narrow channels, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> of rocks, which renders Norway inaccessible to the naval power of its enemies. Attempts of this kind are the more dangerous, as the shore is generally bold, steep, and impending; so that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the rocks the depth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> amounts to 100, 200, or 300 fathoms. The perils of the north sea are moreover increased by sudden storms, sunk rocks, violent currents, and dreadful whirlpools. The most remarkable vortex on this coast is called Moskorsfjord, from the small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Moske, belonging to the district of Lofoden in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Nordland. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, the stream runs up between Lofoden and Moskoe with the most boisterous rapidity; but in its ebb to the sea, it roars like a thousand cataracts, so as to be heard at the distance of many leagues. The surface exhibits different vortices; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in one of these any ship or vessel is absorbed, it is whirled <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bottom, and dashed in pieces against the rocks. These violent whirlpools continue without intervals, except for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, at high and low <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, in calm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> gradually returns as the flood or ebb advances. When its fury is heightened by a storm, no vessel ought to venture within a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of it. Whales have been frequently absorbed within the vortex, and howled and bellowed hideously in their fruitless endeavours to disengage themselves. A bear, in attempting to swim from Lofoden to Moskoe, was once hurled into this whirlpool, from whence he struggled in vain for deliverance, roaring so loud as to be heard on shore; but notwithstanding all his efforts, he was borne down and destroyed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> trees being absorbed by the current, are sucked down, and rise again all shattered into splinters. There are three vortices of the same kind near the islands of Fertoc. Norway is divided into the four governments of Aggerhus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRONTHEIM">Drontheim</a>, and Wardhus, besides that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAHUS">Bahus</a>, which is now subject to Sweden. The province of Aggerhus comprehends the south-east <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Norway, extending in length about 300 miles. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Christiania, the see of a bishop, suffragan to the metropolitan see of Drontheim, where the sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is held, in presence of the viceroy and the governor of the province; Aggerhus, about 15 miles to the south-west of Christiania; Frederickshall, or Frederickstadt, in the siege of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. of Sweden lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; Saltzberg, Tonberg, Alleen, Hammar, and Hollen. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Bergen lies in the most southerly and westerly part of Norway, including the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, which is an episcopal see, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">Staff</a>-hanger, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Buekenfior, about 80 miles to the south-west of Bergen. The third province, called Drontheim or Trondheim, extends about 500 miles along the coast; and is but thinly peopled. The chief town Drontheim, seated on a little gulph at the mouth of the river Nider, is the only Metropolitan see in Norway; and carries on a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, deals, tar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Leetstrand, Stromden, Sverdalen, Oppdal, Romfiald, and Solendael, are likewise places of some traffic. The northern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Drontheim, called the sub-government of Sallen, comprehends the towns of Melanger and Scheen. The province of Wardhus, extending to the North Cape, and including the islands, is divided into two parts; namely, Finnmark and Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>. The chief town, which is very inconsiderable, stands upon an island, called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, from whence the place and the government derive their name. The province of Bahus, though now yielded to the Swedes, is reckoned part of Norway, being a narrow track of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, about 90 miles in length, lying on the coast of the Categate. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chain of Norway mountains, running from north to south, called indifferently Rudfield, Sudefield, Skarsfield, and Scoreberg, is known in different parts by other appellations; such as Dofrefield, Lamfield, Sagmefield, Filefield, Halsfield, Hardangerfield, Yokefield, Biglefield, Hicklefield, and Hangfield. The height and breadth of this extensive chain likewise vary in different parts. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the mountain Hardanger, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> must travel about 70 English miles whereas Filefield may be about 50 over. This last rises about two miles and a half in perpendicular height; but Dofrefield is counted the highest mountain of Norway, if not of Europe. The river Drivane winds along the side of it in a serpentine course, so as to be met <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times by those who travel the winter-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the other side of the chain. The bridges are thrown over roaring cataracts, and but indifferently fastened to the steep rocks on either side; so that the whole exhibits a very dreadful appearance, sufficient to deter the traveller from hazarding such a dangerous passage; for which reason, people generally choose the road over Filefield, which is much more tedious. This, however, is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>-road used by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The way is distinguished by posts fixed at the distance of 200 paces from each other, that, in snowy or dark weather, the traveller may not be bewildered. For the convenience of resting and refreshing, there are two mountain-houses or huts maintained on Filefield, as well as upon other mountains, at the expense of the public, and furnished with fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-utensils. Nothing can be more dismal and dreary than these mountains covered with eternal snow, where neither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, tree, nor living creature is to be seen, but here and there a solitary rein-deer, and perchance a few wandering Laplanders. In travelling from Sweden to Nordenfields, there is only one way of avoiding this chain of mountains; and that is, where it is interrupted by a long deep valley, extending from Romfdale to Guldbrandfdale. In the year 1612, a body of 1000 Scots, commanded by Sinclair, and sent over as auxiliaries to the Swedes, were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in this defile, by the peasants of Guld- Guldbrand, who never give quarter. Besides this chain, there is a great number of detached mountains over all the country, that form valleys and ridges, inhabited by the peasants. Some of these are of incredible height, and others exhibit very remarkable appearances. In sailing up Jøring Creek on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the sight is astonished with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of mountains, resembling the prospect of a city, with old Gothic towers and edifices. In the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Oerfjord is the high mountain Skopshorn, the top of which represents the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a fortification, with regular walls and bastions. In the district of Hildesland appears a very high range of mountains, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pinnacles or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, known by the appellation of the Seven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a>, discernible a great way off at sea. To the southward of this range, though in the same district, rises the famous mountain Torghatten, so called because the summit resembles a man's head with a hat on, under which appears a single eye, formed by an aperture through the mountain, 150 ells high, and 3000 ells in length. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> may be seen through this surprising cavity, which is passable by the feet of travellers. On the top of the mountain we find a reservoir of water, as large as a moderate fish-pond; in the lower part is a cavern, through which a line 400 fathoms in length, being let down, did not reach the bottom. At Haroe in Sundmoor is another cavern called Delften, supposed to reach under the sea to Scotland; which, however, is no more than an idle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. In the year 1759, two clergymen entered this subterranean cavity, and proceeded a considerable way, until they heard the sea dashing over their heads; the passage was as wide and high as an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the sides perpendicular, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> vaulted. They descended one flight of natural stairs; but arriving at another, they were afraid to penetrate farther; they had gone so far, however, that two candles were consumed in their progress and return. A cavern of a very curious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, serving as a conduit to a stream of water, penetrates through the sides of the mountain Limur. In the district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">Rake</a>, in the neighbourhood of Fredericksball, are three cavities in a rock; one of which is so deep, that a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> dropped down, does not reach the bottom in less than two minutes; and then the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> it produces is pleasant and melodious, not unlike the sound of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. The vast mountains and rugged rocks that deform the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this country, are productive of numberless inconveniences. They admit of little arable ground; they render the country in some parts impassable, and everywhere difficult to travellers: they afford shelter to wild beasts, which come from their lurking holes, and make terrible havoc among the flocks of cattle: they expose the sheep and goats, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, to daily accidents of falling over precipices: they occasion sudden torrents, and falls of snow, which descend with incredible impetuosity, and often <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> away the labours of the husbandman; and they are subject to dreadful disruptions, by which huge rocks are rent from their sides, and, hurling down, overwhelm the plains below with inevitable ruin. The peasants frequently build their houses on the edge of a steep precipice, to which they must climb by ladders, at the hazard of their lives; and when a person dies, the corpse must be let down with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, before it can be laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>. In winter the mail is often drawn Norway-up the sides of steep mountains. Even in the king's road, travellers are exposed to the frequent risks of falling over those dreadful rocks; for they are obliged to pass over narrow pathways, without rails or ridges on the sides, either shored up with rotten posts, or suspended by iron bolts fastened in the mountains. In the narrow pass of Naerøya is a remarkable way of this kind, which, above 600 years ago, the famous king Sverre caused to be made for the passage of his cavalry; and even this would have been found impassable by any other horses than those of Norway, which are used to climb the rocks like goats. Another very difficult and dangerous road is that between Shoghtadt and Vang in Volders, along the side of a steep mountain, in some places so narrow, that if two travellers on horseback should meet in the night, they would find it impracticable either to pass each other, or turn back. In such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> their lives could not be saved, unless one of them should alight, and throw his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> headlong into the lake below, and then cling to the rock, until the other could pass. When a sheep or goat makes a false step to the projection of a rock, from whence it can neither ascend nor descend, the owner hazards his own life to preserve that of the animal.
