He directs himself to be lowered down from the top of the mountain, sitting on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> stick, tied to the end of a long rope; and when he arrives at the place where the creature stands, he fastens it to the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, and it is drawn up with himself. Perhaps the other end of the rope is held by one person only; and there are some instances, in which the assistant has been dragged down by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his friend, so that both have perished. When either man or beast has had the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> over very high precipices, they have not only been suffocated by the repercussion of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, but their bodies have been always buried before they reached the ground. Sometimes entire crests of rocks, many fathoms in length and breadth, have fallen down at once, creating such a violent agitation of the air, as seemed a prelude to the world's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. At Steenbroeck in Laerdale, a stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, larger than any castle in the universe, appears to have been severed and tumbled from the mountain in large, sharp, and ragged fragments, thro' which the river roars with hideous bellowing. In the year 1731, a promontory on Sundmoor, called Rammerfield, that hung over Nordal Creek, suddenly gave way, and plunged into the water; which swelled to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the church of Strand, tho' half a league on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, was overflowed: the creek, however, was not filled up; on the contrary, the fishermen declare they find no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the depth, which is said to exceed 900 fathoms. The remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Norway are these: The Nied, issuing from Tydalen, on the borders of Sweden, runs westward into the lake Selboe; and afterwards, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the northward, passes by the city of Drontheim, to which it anciently gave the name of Niderei and Nidroga: Sule <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, that descending from Sulefeld, runs with a rapid course thro' Nordale into the fen: Gulen, which rises near Sifarsfield in the north; and running 20 leagues westward, thro' Aalen, Hlotaalen, Storco, and Melhaus, discharges itself into the sea, about a league to the west of Drontheim. In the year 1344, this river buried itself under ground; from whence it again burst forth with such violence, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> thrown up by the eruption, filled the valley, and formed a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>; which, however, was soon broken and washed away by the force of the water. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> churches, 48 <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-houses, with 250 persons, were destroyed on this occasion. Otteren, a large river, taking its rise from the mountain Agde, runs about 30 leagues through Scettdale and Effe, and disembogues itself into the cataract of Wiland. The river Syre rises near the mountain Lang, and winds its course thro' the vale of Syre into the lake of Lunde in the diocese of Christiania; thence it continues its way to the sea, into which it discharges itself through a narrow strait formed by two rocks. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> augments its impetuosity, so that it shoots like an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> into the sea, in which it produces a very great agitation. Nid and Sleen are two considerable rivers, issuing out of Tillermark. Their water-falls have been diverted, with infinite labour, by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> cut through the rocks, for the convenience of floating down the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. Tyreford, or Dramme, is in the neighbourhood of Hanifolle, joined by two rivers from Oedale and Hadeland, and disembogues itself into the sea near Bragernes. Loven rises in the highest part of Nummedal, and runs through Konberg to the sea near Laurvig. Glaamen is the largest river of Norway, distinguished by the name of Stor-Elvin, or the great river. It derives its origin from the mountain Dofre, from whence it winds all along the plains of Oederdale and Soloe; then joins the Vorme, another considerable river rising out of Mioes and Guldbrandsdale. These being joined, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the lake Oeyeren; and thence issuing, run on to Sarp near Fredericksstadt. Norway abounds with fresh-water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, Ryvand in Nordland, Snasalen, Selboe, the Greater and Lesser Mioes, Slirewand, Spedille, Rand, Vein, Saren, Modum, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">Lund</a>, Norfoe, Huidsoe, Farivand, and Oeyevand; all these are well stocked with fish, and navigable for large vessels. Wars have been formerly carried on upon these inland seas; in some of which are small floating islands, or parcels of earth with trees on them, separated from the main land, and probably preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> masses by the roots of trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> and grass, interwoven in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. In the year 1702, the family-seat of Borge, near Fredericksstadt, being a noble edifice, with lofty towers and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, suddenly sunk into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> 100 fathoms deep, which was instantaneously filled by a piece of water 300 ells in length, and about half as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Fourteen persons, with 200 head of cattle, perished in this catastrophe, which was occasioned by the river Glaamen precipitating itself down a water-fall near Sarp, and undermining the foundation. Of all the water-falls in Norway this of Sarp is the most dangerous for its height and rapidity. The current drives 17 miles; and roars with such violence, that the water, being dashed and comminuted among the rocks, rises in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, where a beautiful rainbow may be always seen when the sun shines. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times this cataract was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for the execution of traitors and other malefactors: they were thrown down alive, that they might be dashed in pieces on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of rocks, and die in a dreadful commotion, analogous to those they had endeavoured to excite in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. Great part of Norway is covered with forests of wood, which constitute the principal article of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in this country. They chiefly consist of fir and pine, for which great sums are received from foreigners, who export an immense number of masts, beams, planks, and boards. Besides, an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is consumed at home, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, ships, bridges, piles, moles, and fences; over and above the vast demand for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> to the founderies, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> uses. Nay, in some places, the trees are felled for no other purpose but to clear the ground and to be burned into ashes for manure. A good quantity of timber is yearly exported to Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but this is inconsiderable when compared to the vast exports from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRAMMEN">Drammen</a>, Fredericksstadt, Fredericksstadt, Christiania, Skeen, Arendal, Christiania, Christian's-bay, and Drontheim. The masts and large beams are floated down the rivers, and the rest is divided into boards at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. These works supply a vast number of families with a comfortable subsistence. A tenth part of all sawed timber belongs to his Danish majesty, and makes a considerable branch of his revenue. The forests in Norway are so vast and thick, that the people seem to think there can never be a scarcity of wood, especially as the soil is peculiarly adapted for the production of timber; they therefore destroy it with a wasteful hand; inasmuch that more wood rots in Norway than is burned in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The best timber grows in the provinces of Saltan, Helleland, Romsdale, Guldbrandsdale, Osterdale, Soloe, Valders, Hallingdale, Sogniford, Telemark, and the lordship of Nedene. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Norway is very different in different parts of the kingdom. At Bergen the winter is so moderate, that the seas are always open and practicable both to mariners and fishermen, except in creeks and bays, that reach far up into the country towards Filefield, when the keen north-east <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the land. On the east side of Norway from the frontiers of Sweden to Filefield, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> generally sets in about the middle of October with great severity, and lasts till the middle of April; during which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> the waters are frozen to a very considerable thickness, and the face of the country is covered with snow. In the year 1719, 7000 Swedes, who intended to attack Drontheim, perished in the snow on the mountain of Ruden or Tydel, which separates Jemteland in Sweden from the diocese of Drontheim. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of 200 Norwegian fledge-men under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> Emahus, found them all frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> on the ridge of the mountain, where they had been surprised by a storm accompanied with snow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cold. Some of these unhappy victims appeared sitting, some lying, and others kneeling in a posture of praying. They had cut in pieces their muskets, and burned the little wood they afforded. The generals Labarre and Zoega lost their lives; and of the whole corps, consisting originally of 10,000, no more than 2500 survived this dreadful catastrophe. The cold is still more intense in that part of Norway called Finnmark, situated in the frigid zone near Norway. But if the winter is generally cold, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is often excessively hot, in Norway. The rays of the sun are reverberated from the sides of the mountains so as to render the weather close and sultry in the valleys; besides the sun's absence below the horizon is so short, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> and mountains have not time to cool. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so great, that vegetation is remarkably quick. Barley is sown, grows, ripens, and is reaped, in the space of six weeks or two months.—The longest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> at Bergen consists of 19 hours; the sun rising at half an hour after two, and setting at half an hour after nine. The shortest day does not exceed six hours; for the sun rises at nine in the morning, and sets at three in the afternoon. In the beginning of the year, the daylight increases with remarkable celerity; and, at the approach of winter, decreases in the same proportion. In summer one may read and write at midnight by the light of the sky. Christian V., while he resided at Drontheim, used to sup at midnight without candles. In the district of Tromsø, at the extremity of Norway, the sun is continually in view at midsummer. It is seen to circulate day and night round the north pole, contracting its orbit, and then gradually enlarging it, until at length it leaves the horizon. In the depth of winter, therefore, it is for some weeks invisible; and all the light perceived at noon is a faint glimmering for about an hour and a half, proceeding from the reflection of the sun's rays from the highest mountains. But the inhabitants of these provinces are supplied with other lights that enable them to follow their employments in the open air. The sky being generally serene, the moonshine is remarkably bright, and, being reflected from the mountains, illuminates the valleys. They are also assisted by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol10.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> Borealis, which is very frequent in the northern parts of Europe. The air of Norway is generally pure and salubrious. On the sea-coasts, indeed, it is rendered moist by vapours and exhalations; but in the midland parts of the country, towards the mountains, the climate is so dry, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> may be kept for many years without being worm eaten or damaged in the least. The inhabitants have no idea of sickness except what is occasioned by excesses. It is said that in the vale of Gudbrandsdal the inhabitants live to such extreme old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that they become weary of life, and cause themselves to be removed to a less salubrious climate, whereby they may have a chance of dying the sooner. In consumptions, however, the moist air on the sea-side is found to be most agreeable to the lungs in respiration. Norway, being a mountainous country intersected by creeks, abounding with lakes, rivers, and snow, must be subject to frequent rains; and from sudden thaws the inhabitants are sometimes exposed to terrible dilatations. Vast masses of snow falling from precipices, overwhelm men, cattle, boats, houses, nay even whole villages. About two centuries ago, a whole parish was covered and destroyed by an immense mass of snow; and several domestic utensils, as scissars, knives, and ladles, have been at different times brought to light by a rivulet that runs under the snow, which has been gradually hardened and increased by repeated frosts and annual accretions. The winds that chiefly prevail on the western coast are those that blow from the south; whereas, on the other side of Filefjeld, the winds that produce and continue the hard frosts are always northerly. In the summer, there is a kind of regular trade-wind on the coast of Bergen. In the forenoon the sea begins to be cooled with a westerly breeze, which continues till midnight. Then the land breeze begins from the east, and blows till about ten in the morning. The coast is likewise subject to sudden squalls and storms. Hurricanes sometimes rise at sea; and in these latitudes the phenomenon called a waterspout is not uncommon. One of these in the neighbourhood of Ferro is said to have sucked up with the water some tails of herrings, which were afterwards dropped on Kolster, a mountain 1200 feet high. The fresh-water of Norway is not very light or pure; but on the contrary is generally turbid, and deposits a sediment of adventitious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, being sometimes impregnated with oler, and particles of iron. Nevertheless it is agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and remarkably salubrious; as appears from the good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, who drink little or no other liquor. The soil of Norway varies in different places according to the situation of rock or valley. The mountains here, as in every other country, are bare and barren; but the earth washed down from them by the rains, enriches and fertilizes the valleys. In these the soil generally consists of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mould, sand, loam, chalk and gravel, lying over one another in unequal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, and sometimes in three or four successions; the mould that lies uppermost is very fine and mellow, and fit to nourish all sorts of vegetables. There is also clay found in different parts of this kingdom, of which the inhabitants begin to make earthen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; but bricks and tiles are not used in building. The face of the country is in many places deformed by large fens and marshes, very dangerous to the traveller. Near Leefoe in the diocese of Christiania, a wooden causeway is extended near a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> over a morass; and if a horse or any other animal should make a false step, he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> sink at once into the abyss never to rise again. In a cold country like Norway, roughened with rocks and mountains, interspersed with bogs, and covered with forests, we cannot expect to find <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in perfection. The ploughed lands, in respect to mountains, woods, meadows, and wastes, do not exceed the proportion of 1 to 80; so that the whole country does not produce corn to maintain above half the number of its inhabitants. The peasants are discouraged from the practice of husbandry by the frequency of accidents that seem peculiar to the climate. Even in the fruitful provinces of Gudbrandsdal, Osterdal, and Solør, as well as in other places, when the corn appears in the most flourishing condition, the whole hope of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is sometimes destroyed in one night by a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> that nips the blade and extinguishes the vegetation. The kingdom is moreover visited by some unfavourable years, in which the sun seems to have lost his genial power; the vegetables are stunted; the trees bud and bloom, yet bear no fruit; and the grain, though it rises, will yet produce nothing but empty ears and straw. This calamity, however, rarely occurs; and in general the cultivated parts of Norway yield plentiful crops of excellent Norway: excellent rye, barley, and oats. The most fruitful provinces are Nordland, Inderbarre, and Numedale, in the diocese of Drontheim; Sognfjord, and Vaas in that of Bergen; Jedderen, Ryefjell, Raabygdelag, and the lordship of Nedenes, in the diocese of Chilifantand; Hedemark in the diocese of Aggerhus; Hadeland, Toten, Romerige, Ringerge, and Gudbrandsdale; these territories not only produce grain enough for their own consumption, but likewise support their neighbours, and even supply part of Sweden. Pease are likewise propagated in this country, together with wheat, buck-wheat, hops, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, but not to any considerable advantage. The meadows are well stored with pastureage for sheep and cattle, and the fields are productive of those vegetables which are common in other northern countries. Within these 50 years the people of Norway have bestowed some <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the culture of gardens, which in former times was so neglected, that the cities and towns were supplied with leeks, cabbage, and roots, from England and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. At present, however, the Norwegians raise their own culinary and garden roots and vegetables, which thrive there as well as in any other country. The scurvy being a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that prevails along the sea-coast, Nature has scattered upon it a variety of herbs efficacious in the cure of that distemper; such as angelica, rose-root, gentian, creosote, trefoil, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, scurvy-grass, and a plant called eric's grass, that grows in great plenty on the islands of Northland; from whence the people of the continent fetch away <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>-loads of it, to be preserved in barrels as a succedaneum for cabbage. There are also a few noxious vegetables little known in any country but Norway. In Gudbrandsdale is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grass called selings; the root of which is so poisonous, that any beast which eats of it dies immediately, the belly bursting; nay, the carnivorous fowls that prey upon the carcass of the beast meet with the same fate; children have been more than once poisoned by this root which nevertheless is sometimes used externally as an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMULET">amulet</a> for arthritic disorders. Another vegetable pernicious to the cattle is the Gramm of fragrant Norway, which is said to mollify the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the cattle which feed upon it. Among the noxious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of Norway we may also reckon the igle-grass, fatal to sheep and goats; the tour-grass, which affects horses and cows with a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>; and the plant toboe, or hill-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, which produces nearly the same effect on horses, but is not at all prejudicial to cows, sheep, or any ruminating animals. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> turt, not unlike angelica, operates nearly in the same manner: yet the bears are said to feed upon it with peculiar relish; and when their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> begins to fall off by feeding upon this plant, they cure themselves by eating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of animals. The common fruit-trees thrive tolerably well in Norway, the inhabitants of which have plenty of cherries, apples, and pears. Some kinds of plums attain maturity; which is seldom the case with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, apricots, and peaches. But even the apples and pears that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> here are summer-fruit; that which grows till the winter seldom coming to perfection. Great variety of agreeable berries are produced in different parts of this kingdom; such as the hagberry, a kind flows; an infusion of which in wine makes a pleasant cooling liquor; juniper-berries, corinths <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, Norway, foobar or sun-berry, raspberries, gooseberries, blackberries, strawberries, &c., with many other species that seem to be natives of Norway and Sweden. Among these are the tranebar, the produce of the myrtillus repens, red and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, found in the spring in perfection under the snow, and much relished by the reindeer; crapebeer, resembling bilberries, deemed a powerful antiscorbutic; agerbeer, larger and blacker than bilberries, of a pleasant acid, ripened by cold, and used as cherries for an infusion in wine; and finally tyte-beer, a red pleasant berry growing on a short stem, with leaves like those of box; they are plucked off by handfuls, and sent to Denmark to be preserved for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, where they are eaten by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. Of the trees that grow wild in Norway, the principal are the fir and the pine. The first yield an annual revenue of 1,000,000 of rix-dollars, if we include the advantages resulting from the saw-mills and the masts; one of which last has been known to sell for 200 rix-dollars. The red fir-tree, which grows on the mountains, is rich in turpentine as to be almost incorruptible. Some of the houses belonging to the Norway peasants, built of this timber, are supposed to be above 400 years standing. In Gudbrandsdale the house is still to be seen standing in which king Olaf lodged five nights, above 700 years ago, when he travelled round the kingdom to convert the people to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Even 100 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the fir-tree has been cut down, the peasants burn the roots for tar, which is a very profitable commodity. In the fens, the resin of the fir-tree is by nature transformed into a substance which may be called Norway frankincense. The buds or pine-apples of this tree, boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STALE">stale</a> beer, make an excellent medicine for the scurvy; its unpleasant taste, though as efficacious, as tartar. The pine-tree is more tall and beautiful than the fir, though inferior to it in strength and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; for which reason the planks of it are sold at an inferior price, and the peasants waste it without remorse. Norway likewise produces some forests of oak, which is found to be excellent for ship-building. Here also grow plenty of elm-trees; the bark of which, being powdered, is boiled up with other food to fatten hogs, and even mixed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> among their meal; also the ash, from which the peasants distill a balsam used in certain disorders, and which is used both externally and internally. Many other trees flourish in this country, an enumeration of which would prove too tedious. Hazels grow here in such abundance, that 100 tons of the nuts are annually exported from Bergen alone. A great diversity of stones is found in Norway, some of which are of a surprising figure. Several mountains consist chiefly of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> pebble, which decays with age; nay, it sometimes dissolves, and drops into the sea, and, the cement being thus loosened, a terrible disruption ensues. In some places the grey and black pebbles are intermixed with iron, copper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The ground, in certain districts, is covered with the fragments of rocks that have been precipitated from the summits of mountains, and broken by their fall into innumerable shivers. Between 20 and 30 years ago, in the neighbourhood of Bergen, a Norway. man was suddenly overwhelmed with such a mass, which formed a kind of vault around him. In this dreadful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> he remained alive for several weeks. By his loud cries the place of his confinement was discovered; but it was found impossible to remove the huge stones by which he was inclosed. All that his friends could do for him was, to lower down meat and drink through some crevices; but at length the stones fell in, and crushed him to death. In Norway are inexhaustible quarries of excellent marble, black, white, blue, grey, and variegated; together with some detached pieces of alabaster, several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, chalk-stone, cement-stone, <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-stone</a>, mill-stone, basing-stone, slate, tale, magnets; and swine-stone, a production natural to Norway and Sweden, of a brown <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, fetid smell, in texture resembling crystal, and deriving its name from a supposed efficacy in curing a distemper incident to swine. Here also is found the amianthus or stone-flax, of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a> cloth may be made. Norway, however, affords no flints, but plenty of pyrites or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, beautiful crystals, granates, amethysts, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>-stones, and eagle-stones. Gold has formerly been found in a small quantity in the diocese of Christiania, and coined into ducats. There is at present a very considerable silver-mine wrought at Kongberg on the account and risk of his Danish majesty: the ore is surprisingly rich, but interrupted in such a manner, that the vein is often lost. Many masses of pure silver have been found; and, among the rest, one piece weighing 560 pounds, preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. Such is the richness of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, that the annual produce amounts in value to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a> and an half in gold. About 5000 people are daily employed, and earn their subsistence, in those stupendous works. Other silver-mines are prosecuted at Jarlberg, but not to the same advantage; and here the ore is mixed with lead and copper. In many parts of this country copper-mines have been discovered; but the principal, and perhaps the richest in all Europe, is at Rorans, about 100 English miles from Drontheim. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> yields annually about 1100 ship-pounds of pure copper: the founderies belonging to it consume yearly about 14,000 lasts of coal, and 500 fathoms of wood. The next in importance is the copper-work at Lykken, about 20 miles from Drontheim. A third mine is carried on at Indet, or Quickne, at the distance of 30 miles from the same place; and here they precipitate the copper from its menstruum, by means of iron. There is a fourth copper-work at Silboe, about 30 miles distant from Drontheim, though the least considerable of the four. Other copper-mines of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> are worked in different parts of the kingdom. Iron is still in greater plenty, and was the first metal wrought in this country. Many hundred thousand quintals are annually exported, chiefly in bars, and part of it in flares, pots, kettles, and cannon: the national profit arising from this metal is estimated at 300,000 rix-dollars. There is a species called moss-iron, found in large lumps among the mosses: of this the peasants make their own domestic tools and utensils, such as knives, scythes, and axes. The lead found mixed in the silver ore is an article of small importance in Norway; yet some mines of this metal have been lately opened in the district of Soloer, by the proprietors of the copper-work at Oudal. A vitriol work has been begun near Kongberg: the mines yield great plenty of sulphur; which, however, the Norwegians will not take the trouble to melt and depurate, because immense quantities are found at a cheaper rate in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">Alum</a> is found between the slate-flakes near Christiana in such plenty, that works have been set up for refining this mineral, though they have not yet brought it to any degree of transparency. His Danish majesty has established <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Valoe, about six English miles from Tonberg, where this mineral is extracted in large quantities from the sea-water. Besides the animals common to other countries, Norway is said to contain many of the uncommon and dubious kind; such as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KRAKEN">kraken</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERMAID">mermaid</a>, sea-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, &c. See these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Many Danish, English, Scotch, Dutch, and German families have settled in Norway, and now form no inconsiderable part of the trading people: but the original inhabitants are the descendants of those ferocious Normanni, who harassed almost all the coasts of Europe with piratical armaments in the 8th, 9th, and 10th centuries. They speak the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> that is used in Denmark, though their original tongue is the dialect now spoken in Iceland. They profess the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, under an archbishop established at Drontheim, with four suffragans; namely, of Bergen, Staffanger, Hammer, and Christiana. By the union of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALMAR">Calmar</a>, the two kingdoms of Norway and Denmark were united under one monarch; and then the people of both nations enjoyed considerable privileges: but the Danish government is now become <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>; and Norway is ruled despotically by a viceroy, who resides in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and presides in the supreme court, to which appeals are made from the subordinate courts of judicature. The Norwegians are generally well-formed, tall, sturdy, and robust, brave, hardy, honest, hospitable, and ingenious: yet <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, rash, quarrelsome, and litigious. The same character will nearly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the inhabitants of every mountainous country in the northern climates. Their women are well-shaped, tall, comely, remarkably fair and obliging. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Norway have been chiefly removed by the kings of Denmark, in order to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, and opposition to the court; or are long ago degenerated into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of peasants: some families, however, have been lately raised to that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Every freeholder in Norway enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of primogeniture, and power of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and it is very usual to see a peasant inhabiting the same house which has been possessed 400 years by his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The edels-gods, or freehold, cannot be alienated by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> or otherwise from the right heir, called edels-munde: if he is not able to redeem the estate, he declares his incapacity every 10th year at the sessions; and if he, or his heirs, to the third <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, should acquire wealth enough for that purpose, the possessor pro tempore must resign his possession. The mountaineers acquire surprising strength and dexterity by hard living, cold, laborious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, climbing rocks, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SKATING">skating</a> on the snow, and handling arms, which they carry from their youth to defend themselves against the wild beasts of the forests. Those who dwell Norway dwell in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> parts of Norway exercise the employments of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and become very expert mariners. The peasants of Norway never employ any handicraftsmen for necessaries to themselves and families: they are their own hatters, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>-makers, tailors, tanners, weavers, carpenters, smiths, and joiners: they are even expert at ship-building; and some of them make excellent violins. But their general turn is for carving in wood, which they execute in a surprising manner with a common <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> of their own forging. They are taught in their youth to wrestle, ride, swim, skate, climb, shoot, and forge iron. Their amusements consist in making verses, blowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, or playing upon a kind of guitarre, and the violin: this last kind of music they perform even at funerals. The Norwegians have evinced their valour and fidelity in a thousand different instances. The country was always distracted by intestine quarrels, which raged from generation to generation. Even the farmers stand upon their punctilio, and challenge one another to single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> with their knives. On such occasions they hook themselves together by their belts, and fight until one of them is killed or mortally wounded. At weddings and public feasts they drink to intoxication, quarrel, fight, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> generally ensues. The very common people are likewise passionate, ambitious of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and independence, and vain of their pedigree. The nobility and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Norway fare sumptuously; but the peasant lives with the utmost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and frugality, except at festivals: his common <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is made of oat-meal, rolled into broad thin cakes, like those used in Scotland. In time of scarcity, they boil, dry, and grind the bark of the fir-tree into a kind of flour which they mix with oat-meal: the bark of the elm-tree is used in the same manner. In those parts where a fishery is carried on, they knead the roes of cod with their oatmeal. Of these last, mixed with barley-meal, they make hasty-pudding, and soup, enriched with a pickled <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> or salted mackerel. Fresh fish they have in plenty on the sea-coast. They hunt and eat grouse, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, hare, red deer, and rein-deer. They kill cows, sheep, and goats, for their winter stock: these they pickle, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or dry for use. They make cheese of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and a liquor called fire of their four whey: this they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> drink mixed with water; but they provide a store of strong ale for Christmas, weddings, christenings, and other entertainments. From their temperance and exercise, joined to the purity and elasticity of their air, they enjoy good health, and often attain to a surprising degree of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a>. Nothing is more common than to see a hearty Norwegian turned of 100. In the year 1733, four couples danced before his Danish majesty at Fredericks-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>: their ages, when joined, exceeded 800 years. Nevertheless, the Norwegians are subject to various diseases; such as the scab, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, the scurvy, the catarrh, the rheumatism, gout, and epilepsy. The dress of the Norway peasants consists of a wide loose jacket made of coarse cloth, with waistcoat and breeches of the same. Their heads are covered with flapped <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, or caps ornamented with ribbons. They wear shoes without soles, and in the winter leatheren buskins. They have likewise snow-shoes and long skates, with which they travel at a great pace, either on the land or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. There is a corps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> thus accoutred, who can out-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> the swiftest horses. The Norwegian peasant never wears a neckcloth, except on extraordinary occasions: he opens his neck and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to the weather, and lets the snow <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> into his bosom. His body is girt round with a broad leathern belt, adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> plates, from which depends a brass chain that sustains a large knife, gimlet, and other tackle. The women are dressed in clofe-laced jackets, having leathern girdles decorated with ornaments of silver. They likewise wear silver chains round their necks, to the ends of which are fixed gilt medals. Their caps and handkerchiefs are almost covered with small plates of silver, brass, and tin, large rings, and buttons. A maiden <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> appears with her hair platted, and, together with her cloaths, hung full of such jingling trinkets. The churches, public edifices, and many private houses in Norway, are built of stone: but the people in general live in wooden houses, made of the trunks of fir and pine-tree laid upon each other, and joined by mortises at the corners. These are counted more dry, warm, and healthy, than stone or brick buildings. In the whole diocese of Bergen, one hardly sees a farm-house with a chimney or windows: they are generally lighted by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole in the top of the house, which lets in the light, and lets out the smoke. In summer this hole is left quite open: in the winter, it is covered with what they call a fag; that is, the membrane of some animal, stretched upon a wooden frame that fits the hole, and transmits the rays of light. It is fixed or removed with a long pole, occasionally. Every person that enters the house, upon business or courtship, takes hold on this pole, according to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. The ceiling is about eight feet high in the middle; and, being arched like a cupola, the smoke of the fire underneath rolls about, until it finds a vent at the hole, which is called liur. Under this opening stands a thick table with benches, and an high seat at the upper end for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the family: he has likewise a small cupboard for his own use, in which he locks up his most valuable effects. The boards of the roof are coated with the bark of birch-trees, which is counted incorruptible: this again is covered with turf, which yields a good crop of grass for goats and sheep, and is often mowed as hay by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>. The Norwegians carry on a considerable trade with foreign nations. The duty on the produce of their own country exported, amounts annually to 100,000 rix-dollars. These commodities are, copper wrought and unwrought; iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into cannon, staves, and pots, or forged into bars; lead, in small quantity; malts, timber, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>-boards, planks, marble, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, herrings, cod, ling, salmon, lobsters, flounders, cow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, goat-skins, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>-skins, the furs of bears, wolves, foxes, beavers, ermines, martens, &c., down, feathers, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, tallow, train-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, tar, juniper and other sorts of berries, and nuts; salt, alum, glaas, vitriol, and pot-ashes. All other commodities and articles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, the Norwegians import from different nations. The nature of the ground does not admit of much improvement in agriculture: nevertheless, the farmers are not deficient in industry, and skill. Norway, to drain marshes, and render the ground arable and fit for pasture. Many are employed in grazing and breeding cattle; but a much greater number is engaged in felling wood, floating timber, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> charcoal, and extracting tar from the roots of the trees which have been cut down; in the silver, copper, and iron mines; in the navigation and fishery. A considerable number of people earn a comfortable livelihood by hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-catching. Every individual is at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to pursue the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, especially in the mountains and commons; therefore every peasant is expert in the use of fire-arms; and there are excellent marksmen among the mountains, who make use of the bow to kill those animals whose skins, being valuable, would be damaged by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of fire-arms. Norway can produce above 14,000 excellent seamen. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of this country amounts to 30,000 effective men; and the annual revenue exceeds 800,000 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Norway-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAT">Rat</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>. See Mus.

NORWICH

Pages 730-731

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 26' N. Lat. 52° 40'. It is supposed to have had its name, which signifies "a castle to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>," from its situation in respect of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAISTOR">Caistor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Venta Icenorum, three <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> four miles to the south of it, out of whose ruins it seems to have risen. In its infancy, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>, it was plundered and burnt by Sueno the Dane, when he invaded England with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Afterwards it recovered; and in the reign of Edward the Confessor was a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, having 1320 burgurers. But it suffered again much in the reign of William I. by being the seat of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which Ralph, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of the East <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a>, raised against that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>. So much was it impaired by the siege it then underwent, that there were scarce 560 burgurers left in it, as appears from Doomsday-book. From that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> forward it began by little and little to recover, especially after bishop Herbert translated the episcopal see hither from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a> in the reign of William Rufus in 1096; and built a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, of which he himself laid the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, with this inscription, Dominus Herbertus posuit primum lapidem, in Nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, Amen, i.e. "<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> (bishop) Herbert laid the first stone, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost;" and by a licence from pope Paschal, declared it the mother-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Norfolk and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. After this, as Malmesbury has it, it became a town famous for merchandise and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants. Yet it was miserably barracked in the reign of Henry II. by Hugh Bigod, earl of Norfolk, who was an adherent of Henry's son, called the junior king. In the time of Edward I. it was walled round by the citizens, who had presented a petition to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to do it. Henry IV. allowed them, instead of bailiffs, which they had before, to elect a mayor yearly, and made the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> a county of itself. In the year 1348, near 58 persons were carried off by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>; and in 1507, the city was almost consumed by fire. For the flourishing state to which the city is now arrived, they are much indebted to the Flemings, who fled hither from the tyranny of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, and taught them the manufacture of those striped and flowered damasks, camlets, druggets, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> crepe, for which the place is now so noted, and which have been computed to yield sometimes 160,000 l. a-year. In the year 1583, the citizens, by the help of an engine, conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> thro' <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> to the highest parts of the city, which is pleasantly seated along the side of a hill, extending a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length from north to south; but the breadth is much less, and it contracts itself by degrees towards the south. It is now one of the most considerable cities in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> for wealth, populousness, neat buildings, beautiful churches, of which it had once 50, but now about 30, and the industry and civility of the inhabitants. The cathedral is a very venerable structure, with a curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, adorned with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in little images, carved to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and a lofty steeple 105 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The wall of flint-stone, beautified with 40 towers and 12 gates, finished in 1309, is now much decayed. The city, though there is a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of waste ground within the walls, was computed, upwards of 40 years ago, to contain 8000 houses, and 50,000 inhabitants. Besides the cathedral already mentioned, the most remarkable buildings are, the duke of Norfolk's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, one of the largest in England; the castle, which is now the county-gaol, and stands in the heart of the city, with a deep <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> round it, over which is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of one very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; the Town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; the Guild-hall, formerly the church belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Black-Friars; the house of correction; the shire-house, where the assizes are held; a lofty market-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, built after the manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>; the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the king's school, founded by Edward VI. the boys to be nominated by the mayor for the time being, with the consent of the majority of aldermen. There having been formerly many thatched houses, an order was made, that all houses that should hereafter be built should be covered with tiles. The city is interspersed with gardens, orchards, and trees, which make it both pleasant and healthful. It has four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, in which a great number of old men and women, boys and girls, are maintained; and a dozen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Here are two churches for the Dutch and French Flemings; who have particular privileges, and are very numerous. Some of the churches are thatched, and all of them crouded with flint stone curiously cut; which is the more wonderful, as Norwich stands in a clay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and has no flint within 20 miles of it. It is now governed by a mayor, recorder, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, two sheriffs, 24 aldermen, 60 <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, with a town-clerk, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and other inferior officers. The mayor is chosen on May-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the freemen, and (worn in on the Tuesday before Midsummer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>. The sheriffs are also chosen annually, on the first Tuesday in August, one by the freemen, the other by the aldermen, and sworn in on Michaelmas-day. The freemen of the several wards choose each their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. The common-council is chosen in Mid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. The mayor is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace and quorum, during his year (as are also the recorder and steward) within the city and liberties; and after his mayoralty, he is a justice during life. The trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the city are very considerable. At <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> they export large quantities of their manufactures, most of which are sent to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and import a great deal of wine, coal, fish, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c. All the city and country round are employed in the worsted manufacture, brought hither, as already observed, by the Flemings, in which they not only consume the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of their own county, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, &c., but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> many thousand packs of yarn, which they receive from other parts of England, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>. There are eight wardens of the weavers chosen annually, and sworn to take care that there be no frauds committed in spinning, weaving, or dying the stuffs. It is computed that there are not less than 120,000 people employed in and about the city in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and woollen manufactures. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are thought to be the greatest in England, and furnished with a surprising plenty and variety of goods and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. At a small village to the north of the city called St <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>'s, not less than 40,000 head of Scotch cattle are said to be yearly bought up by the Norfolk graziers, and fattened in their meadows and marshes. Its markets are on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. It has a great number of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the duke of Norfolk.

NOSE

Pages 731-731

in anatomy; see there, n° 20, &c. The uses of the nose are, its giving us the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of smelling*; its serving in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> office of respiration, and in modelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>; in receiving the abundant humours from the eyes, and in adding to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, the greatest beauties are those who have the least noses. Ruybroek mentions the wife of the great Jenghiz Khan as a celebrated beauty, because she had only two holes for a nose. In most other countries, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> excepted, great noses are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The Crim-Tartars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the noses of their children while young, as thinking it a great piece of folly to have their noses stand before their eyes.

NOSTOCH

Pages 731-731

the name of a vegetable substance which seems to differ from most of the other bodies of that kind in several particulars. It is a substance of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and somewhat transparent. It trembles at the touch, in the manner of a jelly; but it does not melt when held in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. It has therefore somewhat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of a vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, but it has neither veins nor fibres. It is found in all sorts of soils; but most frequently in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> ones, sometimes on the gravel of garden walks, and most usually makes its appearance after <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. It is found only in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-months; and retains its humidity and perfect figure as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it is a moist season, but immediately dries up and withers away on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>'s affecting it. Many people have supposed this not to be a plant. It appears all of a sudden, and, as it were, by a sort of miracle, either from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>; and some have called it flower of earth, others flower of heaven; and the obscurity of its origin occasioned its being held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem among the chemists; some of whom supposed it to contain an universal spirit, capable of converting other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Mr Magnol and Mr Tournefort were the first authors who affirmed its true origin, and ranged it among the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, however, was never perfectly discovered till Mr Reaumur took it under consideration. He found that it was a leaf which naturally imbibed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a very particular manner; that when it had enough of this liquor in it, it then appeared in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> flourishing state; and when it lost this again, it became thin, wrinkled, and was not to be known for the same substance, or, indeed, scarce to be seen at all. Hence appears the reason of its supposed production and sudden decay. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it has, ever so long, lain in the walks of a garden in its empty wrinkled state, it is never taken notice of; but, on a shower of rain, it swells out into its jelly-like state, and on the sun's evaporating that moisture it falls into its undistinguishable state again; and these changes may affect the same plant alternately for many days together. Mr Geoffroy imagined that he had found roots to the nostoch; but Mr Reaumur positively affirms that it has none. He observed indeed, at certain times, on the surface of certain specimens of this, a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of round <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> of different sizes, which appeared to be the seeds of the plant. These he regularly sowed in earthen pots of mould; and these produced young plants like the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> nostoch: But even these were never discovered to have any appearance of roots; and to try farther whether they had any, Mr Reaumur turned all the plants bottom upwards, and they received no harm from it, but grew <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> as vigorously as before. If the nostoch has truly no roots, as appears to be very evidently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it follows, that it imbibes its nourishment in the manner of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SEA_PLANTS"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-plants, which imbibe the water at all their pores. It should seem, that there are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this nostoch: the one a plain, flat, leaf; the other curled, wrinkled, and variously undulated: and it is on this last that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> which produce the young plants are principally found. It may be, however, that the one of these may be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of the same species, as in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plants; or possibly the being in the state of fructification alone may make the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>.

NOSTRADAMUS

Pages 731-731

an able physician and famous astrologer, born at St Remy, a small town, four leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, in 1503. He studied at Montpelier, and afterwards travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> and Bordeaux. At his return into Provence, he published, in 1555, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> first prophetic centuries. These were so highly valued by the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, Henry II., that he resolved to see the author; and having caused him to be brought to him, gave him 200 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> crowns, and sent him to see the princes his sons at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., in passing through Provence, also gave him public marks of his esteem. Nostradamus published his three last Centuries in 1566; and died at Salon in 1566. He wrote other works, and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was collected an 11th and 12th Century from his writings. The following distich, attributed to Stephen Jodelle, on Nostradamus's character, is well known. Nostre damus, cum falsa damus, non fallere segram est: Et cum falsa damus, nil sibi Nostre damus.

NOSTRE

Pages 731-732

comptroller of the buildings of the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, and designer of his gardens, distinguished himself by carrying the art of laying out gardens to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1631; and was near 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> when M. Fouquet superintendant of the finances gave him an an opportunity of becoming known by the fine gardens of Vaux-le-Vicomte. He was afterwards employed by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, Trianon, St Germain's, &c. and discovered an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in all his works. In 1678 he went to Rome, with the permission of the French king, to improve his skill; but he found nothing there comparable to what he himself had done. Pope Innocent XI. resolved to see Le Nostre, and gave him a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> audience; at the conclusion of which Le Nostre said, "I have seen the two greatest men in the world; your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, and the king my <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>." There is a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, answered the pope: "The king is a great victorious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and I am a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the servants of God." Le Nostre, charmed with this answer, and forgetting who he was with, clapped the pope on the shoulder, saying, "Reverend father, you look extremely well, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> live to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> all the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>." The pope laughed at his prediction. Le Nostre, charmed more and more at the goodness of the sovereign pontiff, and the singular esteem he showed for the king, threw his arms about the pope's neck and kissed him. It was his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to behave in the same manner to all who spoke in praise of Lewis XIV. and he even embraced the king himself whenever that prince returned from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Le Nostre had also a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. He preserved his good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and vivacity of mind to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and died at Paris in 1700, aged 87.

NOTARY

Pages 732-732

(notarius), signifies a person, usually some servitor, who takes notes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> frames short draughts, of contracts, obligations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-parties, or other writings. At present we call him a notary-public, who publicly attests deeds, or writings, in order to make them authentic in another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but he is principally employed in business concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; as making protests of bills of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, &c. And noting a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, is where he goes to take notice of a merchant's refusal to accept or pay the same.

NOTATION

Pages 732-732

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, the method of expressing numbers <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities by signs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> appropriated for that purpose. See Arithmetic and Algebra.

NOTION

Pages 732-732

in logic, an idea <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> representation of any thing in the mind. See Logic and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>.

NOTITIA

Pages 732-732

in literary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a book that gives an account of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; such is the Notitia Imperii Romani, Notitia Notomiae, Rome Antique, &c.

NOTONECTA

Pages 732-732

the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>-fly; a genus of insects belonging to the order of hemiptera. It generally inhabits the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and always swims on its back, and is very swift in its motions. Its belly, which it shows while in the water, is of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; its legs are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; when taken out of the water, it hops. It is indeed a very beautiful and very nimble little creature; and is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the ponds of water in Hyde-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>, and in several other places about <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has four wings, five legs, and no antennae; it is eight inches long, three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and two and a half thick. The body is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and of a very particular form, being flattened at the belly, and rising to a ridge on the middle of the back; so that when it swims, which is almost always on the back, its body resembles a boat in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The belly is jointed, striated, and hairy; and has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> opening at the tail, out of which, when hurt, it thrusts forth something resembling a fling. The head and shoulders are large, hard, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, without any spots; the eyes are large and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, and of a somewhat triangular form. The nose is a long, green, hollow proboscis, terminating in a hard and sharp <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> point; this, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> posture, is kept under the belly, and reaches to the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of legs. The outer pair of wings are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with spots of a dead white; these are long, narrow, and somewhat transparent; they terminate in a roundish point, and perfectly cover the whole body. The triangular piece which stands between the top of the wings is hard, and perfectly black; the inner wings are broader and shorter than the outer ones; they are thin and perfectly transparent, and are of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> colour. The legs are green and hairy; the foremost pair are shortest; the middle ones longer than these; but the hinder pair are greatly longer than all the rest, so that they serve as oars, and are tufted with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> at the end to that purpose. This creature mostly lives in the water, where it preys on small insects, killing them and sucking their juices with its proboscis, in the manner of the water-scorpion and many other aquatic insects; and it seizes its prey violently, and darts with incredible swiftness to a considerable distance after it. Though it generally lives in the water, it sometimes, however, crawls out in good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and drying its wings by expanding them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, takes flight, and becomes an inhabitant of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, not to be known for the same creature, unless to those who had accurately observed it before; when tired of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in danger of an enemy, it immediately plunges into the water. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it flings, and gives

NOTTEBURG

Pages 732-733

a town of Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ingria; seated on an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the lake <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LADOGA">Ladoga</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the river Neva proceeds from this lake. It is strong, has a good citadel, and was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the province before Petersburg was built. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 31° 40'. N. Lat. 60° 0'.

NOTTINGHAMSHIRE

Pages 733-733

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, on the south-east and south by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. It extends in length 43 miles, 24 in breadth, and 110 miles in compass; containing 560,000 acres, 8 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 9 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 168 parishes, 450 villages, about 17,500 houses, and 95,000 inhabitants. No county in England enjoys a pleasanter and healthier <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. As for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it differs widely in different parts of the county. Towards the west, where lies the forest of Sherwood, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; and therefore that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the county is called by the inhabitants, the Sand; but the south and east parts, watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> and the rivulets that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into it, are clayey; and for that reason are called by the inhabitants, the Clay. The latter is fruitful both in corn and pasture; but the former produces little besides wood, coal, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The county has a variety of commodities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, coal, marle, cattle, malt, liquorice, stockings, glaas, earthen-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and strong ale. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Trent and Idle. The Trent, whose name is supposed to be derived from the French <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Latin word signifying thirty, either because it receives thirty smaller rivers, or has thirty different sorts of fish in it, is inferior to no river in England, but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and Humber. It enters the county on the south-west, and passes through it to the north-east, where it enters Lincolnshire, and after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> course falls at last into the Humber. The Idle rises in Sherwood-forest; and after traversing the northern part of the county, falls into the Trent upon the borders of Yorkshire and Lincolnshire. The spacious forest of Sherwood lies in the west part of the county, and indeed takes up the greatest part of it. It was formerly so thick, that it was hardly passable; but now it is much thinner. It feeds an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of deer and hares; and has some towns in it, of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. It abounds in coal, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> lies through it for thirty miles together. Since the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward I., the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry have had grants of it.
