It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of officers under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield, chief forester; whose ancestor, Sir John Stanhope, had a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of it, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to destroy and kill at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, reserving only an hundred deer in the whole walk. The principal town is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, which gives name to the county. It is a handsome town, and a county of itself by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. The name is derived from the Saxon word Nottingham, which signifies caves, from the caves and apartments anciently dug in the rocks on which the town stands. These, being soft, easily yield to the spade and pickaxe; whence the townsmen have excellent cellars for storing the vast quantities of malt liquors made here, and hamper, as well as their malt, to most parts of England. The situation of the town is very pleasant, having meadows on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and hills of a gentle, easy ascent, on the other. It is well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, both wood and coal, from the forest; and with fish by the Trent, which runs about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> to the south of it, and has been made navigable for barges; so that they receive by it not only great quantities of cheese from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>; but all their heavy goods from the Humber, and even from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>. It is of great antiquity; and had anciently a very strong castle, where is now a fine seat belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. It is noted for its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races on a fine course on the north side of the town. The corporation is governed by a mayor, recorder, six aldermen, two coroners, two sheriffs, two chamberlains, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, eighteen of the senior-council, and six of the junior, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-bearer, and two pinders, one for the fields, and the other for the meadows. The town being within the jurisdiction of the forest, the former of these pinders is town-warden, and attends the forest courts. It has three neat churches, the chief of which is St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s; and an alm-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, endowed with 100 l. a-year, for twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people; with a noble town-house, surrounded with piazzas. A considerable trade is carried on in glaas and earthen-ware, and frame-flockings, besides the malt, and malt-liquors, mentioned above. Marshal Tallard, when a prisoner in England, was confined to this town and county. In the duke of Newcastle's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a> there is a ledge of rocks hewn into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, houses, chambers, dove-houses, &c. The altar of the church is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, and between that and the castle there is an hermitage of the like workmanship. Upon the side of a hill there is a very extraordinary fort of a house, where you enter at the garret, and ascend to the cellar, which is at the top of the house. Here is a noted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> founded by John Plumtree, Esq.; in the reign of Richard II., for thirteen poor old widows. There are four handsome bridges over the Trent and Lind. To keep these in repair, and other uses, the corporation has good estates. This town and Winchelsea both give <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the noble family of Finch. Here <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, king of Scots, when a prisoner in England, resided; and under-ground in a vault, called Mortimer's hole, because Roger Mortimer, earl of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, is said to have absconded in it, when he was taken and hanged by order of Edward III. NOVA-SCOTIA. See Nova-Scotia. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">NOVA ZEMBLA</a>. See Nova Zembla.

NOTUS

Pages 732-732

signifies spurious, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>; whence it is figuratively applied by physicians to such diseases as, though in a respect of a multitude of symptoms, &c. they have the same denomination as some others, yet are of a different origin, seat, or the like, from the same.

NOVALLE

Pages 733-733

a small, rich, and populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> and Trevigo. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 5'. N. Lat. 45° 35'.

NOVARA

Pages 733-733

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, well built, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Novarese, with a bishop's see; seated upon an eminence. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 35'. N. Lat. 45° 25'.

NOVATIANS

Pages 733-733

a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which sprung up in the third century, so called from Novatian a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Novatus. See Novatus.

NOVATION

Pages 733-733
or INNOVATION, in the civil law, denotes the change of one kind of obligation for another;

NOVATIUS

Pages 733-734

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, in the third century, who, to avoid being punished for a crime, joined with the deacon, named Felicissimus, against St Cyprian. He went to Rome in 251; and there found Novatian, a priest who had acquired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his eloquence; but who murmured at his not being raised to the see of Rome in preference to pope Cornelius. Novatus contracted a friendship with him; and afterwards, it is said, getting three ignorant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, made them drunk, and then obliged them to ordain Novatian bishop of Rome. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> ordination produced a very great schism; both Novatus and Novatian maintained, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> had not the power to receive those to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> who were fallen into idolatry. There are attributed to Novatian, the treatise on the Trinity, and the book on Jewish meats, which are among Tertullian's works; and it was he, and not Novatus, who gave his name to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called Novatians.

NOVEL

Pages 734-734

in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for the constitutions of several emperors, more particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. They were called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, either from their producing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> because they were made on new <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and after the revival of the ancient code.

NOVELLARA

Pages 736-736

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small district of the same name, with a handsome castle, where their sovereign resides. E. Lon.

NOVELTY

Pages 734-736
or Newness. Of all the circumstances that raise emotions, not excepting beauty, nor even greatness, says Lord Kames†, novelty hath the most powerful influence. A new object produceth instantaneously an emotion termed wonder, which totally occupies the mind, and for a time excludes all other objects. Conversation among the vulgar never is more interesting than when it turns upon strange objects and extraordinary events. Men tear themselves from their native country in search of things rare and new; and novelty converts into a pleasure, the fatigues and even perils of travelling. To what case shall we ascribe these singular appearances? To curiosity undoubtedly; a principle implanted in human nature for a purpose extremely beneficial, that of acquiring knowledge; and the emotion of wonder raised by new and strange objects, inflames our curiosity to know more of such objects. This emotion is different from admiration: novelty, wherever found, whether in a quality or action, is the cause of wonder; admiration is directed to the person who performs any thing wonderful. During infancy, every new object is probably the occasion of wonder, in some degree; because, during infancy, every object at first sight is strange as well as new: but as objects are rendered familiar by custom, we cease by degrees to wonder at new appearances, if they have any resemblance to what we are acquainted with; for a thing must be singular as well as new, to raise our wonder. To save multiplying words, we would be understood to comprehend both circumstances when we hereafter talk of novelty. In an ordinary train of perceptions where one thing introduces another, not a single object makes its appearance unexpectedly; the mind thus prepared for the reception of its objects, admits them one after another without perturbation. But when a thing breaks perception unexpectedly, and without the preparation of any connection, it raises an emotion, known by the name of surprize. That emotion may be produced by the most familiar object, as when one unexpectedly meets a friend who was reported to be dead; or a man in high life, lately a beggar. On the other hand, a new object, however strange, will not produce the emotion, if the spectator be prepared for the sight: an elephant in India will not surprize a traveller who goes to see one; and yet its novelty will raise his wonder: an Indian in Britain would be much surprized to stumble upon an elephant feeding at large in the open fields; but the creature itself, to which he was accustomed, would not raise his wonder. Surprise thus in several respects differs from wonder: unexpectedness is the cause of the former emotion; novelty is the cause of the latter. Nor differ they less in their nature and circumstances, as will be explained by and by. With relation to one circumstance they perfectly agree; which is, the shortness of their duration: the instantaneous production of these emotions in perfection, may contribute to that effect, in conformity to a general law, That things soon decay which soon come to perfection: the violence of the emotions may also contribute; for an ardent emotion, which is not susceptible of increase, cannot have a long course. But their short duration is occasioned chiefly by that of their causes: we are soon reconciled to an object, however unexpected; and novelty soon degenerates into familiarity. Whether these emotions be pleasant or painful, is not a clear point. It may appear strange, that our own feelings and their capital qualities, should afford any matter for a doubt: but when we are engrossed by any emotion, there is no place for speculation; and when sufficiently calm for speculation, it is not easy to recall the emotion with accuracy. New objects are sometimes terrible, sometimes delightful: the terror which a tyger inspires is greatest at first, and wears off gradually by familiarity: on the other hand, even women will acknowledge that it is novelty which pleases the most in a new fashion. It would be rash however to conclude, that wonder is itself neither pleasant nor painful, but that it assumes either quality according to circumstances. An object, it is true, that hath a threatening appearance, adds to our terror by its novelty: but from that experiment it doth not follow, that novelty is in itself disagreeable; for it is perfectly consistent, that we be delighted with an object in one view, and terrified with it in another. A river in flood swelling over its banks, is a grand and delightful object; and yet it may produce no small degree of fear when we attempt to cross it: courage and magnanimity are agreeable; and yet, when we view these qualities in an enemy, they serve to increase our terror. In the same manner, novelty may produce two effects clearly distinguishable from each other: it may, directly and in itself, be agreeable; and it may have an opposite effect indirectly, which is, to inspire terror; for when a new object appears in any degree dangerous, out, our ignorance of its powers and faculties affords ample scope for the imagination to dress it in the most frightful colours. The first sight of a lion, for example, may at the same instant produce two opposite feelings, the pleasant emotion of wonder, and the painful passion of terror; the novelty of the object produces the former directly, and contributes to the latter indirectly. Thus when the subject is analysed, we find, that the power which novelty hath indirectly to inflame terror, is perfectly consistent with its being in every circumstance agreeable. The matter may be put in the clearest light, by adding the following circumstances. If a lion be first seen from a place of safety, the spectacle is altogether agreeable without the least mixture of terror. If, again, the first sight puts us within reach of that dangerous animal, our terror may be so great as quite to exclude any sense of novelty. But this fact proves not that wonder is painful: it proves only, that wonder may be excluded by a more powerful passion. Every man may be made certain from his own experience, that wonder raised by a new object that is inoffensive, is always pleasant; and with respect to offensive objects, it appears, from the foregoing deduction, that the same must hold as long as the spectator can attend to the novelty. Whether surprise be in itself pleasant and painful, is a question not less intricate than the former. It is certain that surprise inflames our joy when unexpectedly we meet with an old friend; and not less our terror when we stumble upon anything noxious. To clear that question, the first thing to be remarked is, that in some instances an unexpected object overpowers the mind, so as to produce a momentary stupor; where the object is dangerous, or appears so, the sudden alarm it gives, without preparation, is apt totally to unhinge the mind, and for a moment to suspend all its faculties, even thought itself; in which state a man is quite helpless; and if he move at all, is as like to run upon the danger as from it. Surprise carried to such a height, cannot be either pleasant or painful; because the mind, during such momentary stupefaction, is in a good measure, if not totally, insensible. If we then inquire for the character of this emotion, it must be where the unexpected object or event produceth less violent effects. And while the mind remains sensible of pleasure and pain, is it not natural to suppose, that surprise, like wonder, should have an invariable character? It would appear, however, that surprise has no invariable character, but assumes that of the object which raises it. Wonder being an emotion invariably raised by novelty, and being distinguishable from all other emotions, ought naturally to possess one constant character. The unexpected appearance of an object, seems not equally intitled to produce an emotion distinguishable from the emotion, pleasant or painful, that is produced by the object in its ordinary appearance: the effect it ought naturally to have, is only to swell that emotion, by making it more pleasant or more painful than it commonly is. And that conjecture is confirmed by experience, as well as by language which is built upon experience: when a man meets a friend unexpectedly, he is said to be agreeably surprised; and when he meets an enemy unexpectedly, he is said to be disagreeably surprised. It appears, then, that the sole effect of surprise is to swell the emotion raised by the object. And that effect can be clearly explained: a tide of connected perceptions glide gently into the mind, and produce no perturbation; but an object breaking in unexpectedly, founds an alarm, routes the mind out of its calm state, and directs its whole attention to the object, which, if agreeable, becomes doubly so. Several circumstances concur to produce that effect: on the one hand, the agitation of the mind and its keen attention, prepare it in the most effectual manner for receiving a deep impression; on the other hand, the object, by its sudden and unforeseen appearance, makes an impression, not gradually as expected objects do, but as at one stroke with its whole force. The circumstances are precisely similar where the object is in itself disagreeable (a). The pleasure of novelty is easily distinguished from that of variety: to produce the latter, a plurality of objects is necessary; the former arises from a circumstance found in a single object. Again, where objects, whether coexistent or in succession, are sufficiently diversified, the pleasure of variety is complete, though every single object of the train be familiar; but the pleasure of novelty, directly opposite to familiarity, requires no diversification. There are different degrees of novelty, and its effects are in proportion. The lowest degree is found in objects surveyed a second time after a long interval; and that in this case an object takes on some appearance (a) What the Marechal Saxe terms le cœur humain, is no other than fear occasioned by surprise. It is owing to that cause that an ambush is generally so destructive: intelligence of it beforehand renders it perfectly harmless. The Marechal gives from Caesar's Commentaries two examples of what he calls le cœur humain. At the siege of Amiens by the Gauls, Caesar came up with his army, which did not exceed 7000 men; and began to intrench himself in such hurry, that the barbarians, judging him to be afraid, attacked his intrenchments with great spirit. During the time they were filling up the ditch, he issued out with his cohorts, and by attacking them unexpectedly struck a panic that made them fly with precipitation, not a single man offering to make a stand. At the siege of Alesia, the Gauls infinitely superior in number attacked the Roman lines of circumvallation, in order to raise the siege. Caesar ordered a body of his men to march out silently, and to attack them on the one flank, while he with another body did the same on the other flank. The surprise of being attacked when they expected a defence only, put the Gauls into disorder, and gave an easy victory to Caesar. A third may be added not less memorable. In the year 846, an obstinate battle was fought between Xamire king of Leon, and Abdoulrahman the Moorish king of Spain. After a very long conflict, the night only prevented the Arabians from obtaining a complete victory. The king of Leon, taking advantage of the darkness, retreated to a neighbouring hill, leaving the Arabians masters of the field of battle. Next morning, perceiving that he could not maintain his place for want of provisions, nor be able to draw off his men in the face of a victorious army, he ranged his men in order of battle, and, without losing a moment, marched to attack the enemy, resolving to conquer or die. The Arabians, astonished to be attacked by those who were conquered the night before, lost all heart: fear succeeded to astonishment, the panic was universal, and they all turned their backs without almost drawing a sword. ance of novelty, is certain from experience: a large building of many parts variously adorned, or an extensive field embellished with trees, lakes, temples, statues, and other ornaments, will appear new oftener than once; the memory of an object so complex is soon lost, of its parts at least, or of their arrangement. But experience teaches, that, even without any decay of remembrance, absence alone will give an air of novelty to a once familiar object; which is not surprising, because familiarity wears off gradually by absence: thus a person with whom we have been intimate, returning after a long interval, appears like a new acquaintance. And distance of place contributes to this appearance, not less than distance of time: a friend, for example, after a short absence in a remote country, has the same air of novelty as if he had returned after a longer interval from a place nearer home: the mind forms a connection between him and the remote country, and bestows upon him the singularity of the objects he has seen. For the same reason, when two things equally new and singular are presented, the spectator balances between them; but when told that one of them is the product of a distant quarter of the world, he no longer hesitates, but clings to it as the more singular: hence the preference given to foreign luxuries, and to foreign curiosities, which appear rare in proportion to their original distance. The next degree of novelty, mounting upward, is found in objects of which we have some information at second hand; for description, though it contribute to familiarity, cannot altogether remove the appearance of novelty when the object itself is presented: the first sight of a lion occasions some wonder, after a thorough acquaintance with the correctest pictures and statues of that animal. A new object that bears some distant resemblance to a known species, is an instance of a third degree of novelty: a strong resemblance among individuals of the same species, prevents almost entirely the effect of novelty, unless distance of place or some other circumstance concurs; but where the resemblance is faint, some degree of wonder is felt, and the emotion rises in proportion to the faintness of the resemblance. The highest degree of wonder arises from unknown objects that have no analogy to any species we are acquainted with. Shakespeare in a simile introduces that species of novelty: As glorious to the sight As is a winged messenger from heaven Into the eye of a furred wondering eye Of mortal, that fall back to gaze on him When he bestrides the lazy-pacing clouds And fills upon the bottom of the air. One example of that species of novelty deserves peculiar attention; and that is, when an object altogether new is seen by one person only, and but once. These circumstances heighten remarkably the emotion: the singularity of the spectator concurs with the singularity of the object, to inflame wonder to its highest pitch. In explaining the effects of novelty, the place a being occupies in the scale of existence, is a circumstance that must not be omitted. Novelty in the individuals of a low class is perceived with indifference, or with a very slight emotion: thus a pebble, however singular in its appearance, scarce moves our wonder. The emotion rises with the rank of the object; and, other circumstances being equal, is strongest in the highest order of existence; a strange insect affects us more than a strange vegetable; and a strange quadruped more than a strange insect. However natural novelty may be, it is a matter of experience, that those who relish it the most are careful to conceal its influence. Love of novelty, it is true, prevails in children, in idlers, and in men of shallow understanding; and yet, after all, why should one be ashamed of indulging a natural propensity? A distinction will afford a satisfactory answer. No man is ashamed of curiosity when it is indulged to acquire knowledge. But to prefer anything merely because it is new, shows a mean taste which one ought to be ashamed of: vanity is commonly at the bottom, which leads those who are deficient in taste to prefer things odd, rare, or singular, in order to distinguish themselves from others. And in fact, that appetite, as above mentioned, reigns chiefly among persons of a mean taste, who are ignorant of refined and elegant pleasures. One final cause of wonder, hinted above, is, that this emotion is intended to stimulate our curiosity. Another, somewhat different, is, to prepare the mind for receiving deep impressions of new objects. An acquaintance with the various things that may affect us, and with their properties, is essential to our well-being: nor will a slight or superficial acquaintance be sufficient; they ought to be so deeply engraved on the mind, as to be ready for use upon every occasion. Now, in order to a deep impression, it is wisely contrived, that things should be introduced to our acquaintance with a certain pomp and solemnity productive of a vivid emotion. When the impression is once fairly made, the emotion of novelty being no longer necessary, vanishes almost instantaneously; never to return, unless where the impression happens to be obliterated by length of time or other means, in which case the second introduction hath nearly the same solemnity with the first. Deigning wisdom is nowhere more eligible than in this part of the human frame. If new objects did not affect us in a very peculiar manner, their impressions would be so slight as scarce to be of any use in life: on the other hand, did objects continue to affect us as deeply as at first, the mind would be totally engrossed with them, and have no room left either for action or reflection. The final cause of surprise is still more evident than of novelty. Self-love makes us vigilantly attentive to self-preservation; but self-love, which operates by means of reason and reflection, and impels not the mind to any particular object or from it, is a principle too cool for a sudden emergency; an object breaking in unexpectedly, affords no time for deliberation; and in that case, the agitation of surprise comes in seasonably to rouse self-love into action: surprise gives the alarm; and if there be any appearance of danger, our whole force is instantly summoned to shun or to prevent it.

NOVEMVIRI

Pages 736-737
nine magistrates of Athens, whose government lasted but for one year. The first of whom was called archon, or prince; the second basileus, or king; the third polemarchus, or general of the army; the other six were called thephistarchus, or lawgivers. They took an oath to observe the laws; and in case of failure, obliged themselves to be thrown upon the commonwealth a statue of gold as big as themselves. Those who discharged their office with honour, were received into the number of the senators of Areopagus.

NOVI

Pages 737-737

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, on the confines of the Milanese. It was taken by the Piedmontese in 1746. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 43'. N. Lat. 44° 45'. Novi-Bazar, a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>, near the river Orefco. E. Long. 20° 24'. N. Lat. 43° 25'.

NOVICATE

Pages 737-737

a year of probation appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, whether <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> no they have a vocation, and the necessary qualities for living up to the rule; the observation whereof is to bind themselves to by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a>. The noviccate lasts a year at least; in some houses more. It is esteemed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a novice, who expires to the world by profession.

NOVICE

Pages 737-737

a person not yet skilled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> experienced in an art or profession. In the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, novicii, or novitii, were the young raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, distinguished by this appellation from the veterans. In the ancient orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, there were novices, or clerks in arms, who went through a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> ere they were admitted knights. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>. Novice is more particularly used in monasteries for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> yet in his, or her, year of probation, and who has not made the vows. In some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the sub-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the novices. In nunneries, the novices wear a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veil; the rest a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> one.

NOVIGRAD

Pages 737-737

a small but strong town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, with a good castle, seated on a mountain near the Danube. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18° 10'. N. Lat. 47° 50'. Novigrad, a small but strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, with a castle, and subject to the Turks; seated on a lake of the same name, near the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. Long. 16° 45'. N. Lat. 44° 30'. Novigrad, a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>, subject to the Turks; seated near the Danube. E. Long. 26° 5'. N. Lat. 45° 5'.

NOVIODUNUM

Pages 737-737

a town of the Aelui, commodiously seated on the Ligurian; the Noviomagus of Antonine. Now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a> in the Orléanais, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>.—A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Noviodunum of the Aulerci Dianites, in Gallia Celtica, (Antonine); called Noviodunum, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); and Nonnigentum Retradum by the moderns: Nogent le Retrou, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Perche.—A third, of the Bituriges, (Cæsar): Now Nauvè sur Baratons; a village 15 miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, towards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>.—A fourth, of Massia Inferior, (Ptolemy), situate on the Iltis: now Nivern, in Beauce.—A fifth, of Pannonia Superior, (Antonine); now Gurkfeld in Carinthia.—A sixth Novo-Novgorodum Suetonius, the same with Augusta Suetonius.—A seventh, Noviodunum of the Veromandui in Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, (Cæsar); now Noyon in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, on the borders of Picardy. NOVOGOROD Veliki, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Novgorod, a rich and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of the Russian empire, and capital of a duchy of the same name, with an archbishop's see, and a castle where the archbishop and the waiwode reside. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, because hither they bring their rich merchandizes that come from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. It contains 180 churches and monasteries, and carries on a great trade in Russian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. It is seated on the river Wolosoff, near the lake Honen. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33° 40'. N. Lat. 58° 23'. Novgorod Veliki, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, bounded on the north by Ingria; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the duchy of Belozero, and that of Tvera, which also bounds it on the south, with the province of Rzeva; and on the west by Plecnow. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and forests; however, there are some places which produce corn, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and wax. Novgorod Serpilow, a strong town of the Russian empire, and capital of a province of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> of the same name, seated on the river Dubica, in E. Long. 33° 20'. N. Lat. 52° 30'.

NOVOGORODECK

Pages 737-737

a town of Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the same name. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town, and situated in a vast plain, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 30'. N. Lat. 53° 45'. NOURISHMENT. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTRITION">Nutrition</a>. Nourishment of Vegetables. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. 1. and 2. and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>; also the article Composts.

NOWED

Pages 737-737

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, signifies "knotted," from the Latin nodatus; being applied to the tails of such creatures as are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and sometimes represented in coat-armour as tied up in a knot.

NUAYHAS

Pages 737-737

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUE">Ague</a>-tree; a name given by the Indians to a sort of Bamboo-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the leaves of which falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, are said to impregnate it with such virtue, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in it afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> cure the ague. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> also a decoction of the leaves to dissolve coagulated blood, giving it internally, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> rubbing the bruised <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> externally with it. It is said that this plant bears its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> only once in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; that it lives 60 years before these make their appearance; but that when they begin to show themselves, it withers away in about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> afterwards; that is, as soon as it has ripened the seed. There seems to be something of fiction in the account of many other particulars relating to this tree in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORUS">Horus</a> Malabaricus; but it seems certain, that the length of the stalks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, must be very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; for, in the gallery of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, there is preserved a cane of it 28 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and another not much shorter in the Ashmolean <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and which is more than eight inches in diameter; yet both these appear to be only parts of the whole trunk, they being nearly as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> at one end as at the other.

NUBECULA

Pages 737-738

little cloud, in medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> in the eye, wherein objects appear as through a cloud <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>. The nubecula seems to arise from certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> particles detained in the pores of the cornea, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in the aqueous humour, and thus intercepting the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. **Nubecula**, or **Nubes**, is also used for what we otherwise call **albugo**. See **Albugo**. **Nubecula** is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in form of a cloud, suspended in the middle of the urine.

NUBIA

Pages 738-738

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Abesh <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Abex, and on the west by Zara and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIGRITIA">Nigritia</a>. It is said to be 400 leagues in length, and 200 in breadth, and to be watered by a river which falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; but of these dimensions we have little certainty, and nothing can be depended upon concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the country or its inhabitants.

NUCLEUS

Pages 738-738

in general, denotes the kernel of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> even any seed inclosed within a husk. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> **nucleus** is also used for the body of a comet, otherwise called its **head**.

NUDITIES

Pages 738-738

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, those parts of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which are not covered with any drapery; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> those parts where the carnation appears.

NUISANCE

Pages 752-752

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a thing done to the annoyance of another. Nuisances are either public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> private.—A public nuisance is an offence against the public in general, either by doing what tends to the annoyance of all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects, or by neglecting to do what the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> good requires: in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, all annoyances and injuries to streets, highways, bridges, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, as also disorderly ale-houses, bawdy-houses, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>-houses, flags for rope-dancers, &c. are held to be common nuisances.—A private nuisance is, when only one person or family is annoyed by the doing of any thing; as where a person stops up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of another's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or builds in such a manner that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> falls from his house upon his neighbour's.

NULLITY

Pages 738-738

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies anything that is null <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> void: thus there is a nullity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, where persons marry within the degrees, or where <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> marry without consent of their parents or guardians.

NUMANTIA

Pages 738-738

a very noble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the ornament of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, (Florus); as appears from the Numantine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and though destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> under Scipio Emilianus, it was afterwards no doubt restored, because mentioned not only by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, but also by Antonine, who determines its situation between Uxama and Turiaso; and Strabo says, the Du-rus run by it, while still recent and near its source. With 4000 men it held out a siege of 14 years, against 40,000 Romans. And all this it did, like another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, without walls and without turrets; but this is doubtfully mentioned by authors.—Numantini, the people; who, after a tedious and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> siege, and after struggling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> with famine, at length destroyed themselves and their city by fire.

NUMERAL LETTERS

Pages 739-740

those letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> which are generally used for figures; as I, one; V, five; X, ten; L, fifty; C, a hundred; D, five hundred; M, a thousand, &c. It is not agreed how the Roman numerals originally received their value. It has been supposed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used M to denote 1000, because it is the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of millia, which is Latin for 1000; and C to denote 100, because it is the first letter of centum, which is Latin for 100. It has also been supposed, that D being formed by dividing the old M in the middle, was therefore appointed to stand for 500, that is, half as much as the M stood for when it was whole; and that L being half a C, was, for the same reason, used to denote 50. But what reason is there to suppose, that 1000 and 100 were the numbers which letters were first used to express? And what reason can be assigned why D, the first letter in the Latin word decem, ten, should not rather have been chosen to stand for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, than for 500, because it had a rude resemblance to half an M? But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these questions could be satisfactorily answered, there are other numeral letters which have never yet been accounted for at all. These considerations render it probable, that the Romans did not, in their original intentions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> letters to express numbers at all; the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> seems to be this: The Romans probably put <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a single stroke, I, for one, as is still the practice of those who score on a slate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> with chalk: this stroke, I, they doubled, trebled, and quadrupled, to express 2, 3, and 4; thus, II, III, IIII. So far they could easily number the minims, or strokes, with a glance of the eye. But they presently found, that if more were added, it would soon be necessary to tell the strokes one by one: for this reason, when they came to 5, they expressed it by joining two strokes together in an acute <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> thus, V; which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear the more probable, if it be considered, that the progression of the Roman numbers is from 5 to 9, i.e., from the fingers on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the fingers on the other.—Ovid has touched upon the original of this in his Fasti, lib. iii. and Vitruvius, lib. c. i. has made the same remark. After they had made this acute angle V, for five, they added the single strokes to it to the number of 4; thus, VI, VII, VIII, IX, and then as the minims could not be further multiplied without confusion, they doubled their acute angle, by prolonging the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> beyond their intersection thus, X, to denote two fives, or ten. After this they doubled, trebled, and quadrupled, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> acute angle thus, XX, XXX, XXXX. They then, for the same reason which induced them first to make a single and then to double it, joined two single strokes in another form, and instead of an acute angle, made a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> angle L, to denote fifty. When this 50 was doubled, they then doubled the right angle thus L, to denote 100, and having numbered this double right angle four times, thus LL, LL, LL, LL; when they came to the fifth number, as before, they reverted it, and put a single stroke before it thus D, to denote 500; and when this 500 was doubled, then they also doubled their double right angle, setting two double right <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> opposite to each other, with a single stroke between them, thus CCCC to denote 1000: when this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for 1000 had been four times repeated, then they put down XXXXXX for 10,000, and XXXXXX for 50,000, XXXXXXX for 100,000, XXXXXXX for 500,000, and XXXXXXXXX for one million. That the Romans did not originally write M for 1000, and C for 100, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as they are written above, we are expressly informed by Paulus Manutius; but the corners of the angles being cut off by the transcribers for dispatch, these figures were gradually brought into what are now numeral letters. When the corners of C, D, were made round, it stood thus CD, which is so near the Gothic c, that it soon deviated into that letter; so D having the corner made round, it stood thus DD, and then easily deviated into D. It also became a plain C by the same means; the single rectangle which denoted 50, was, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> L; the double acute angle was an X; the single acute angle a V consonant; and a plain single stroke, the letter I.; and thus these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> letters, M, D, C, L, X, V, I, became numerals.

NUMERATION

Pages 740-740
or NOTATION, in arithmetic, the art of expressing in characters any number proposed in words, or of expressing in words any number proposed in characters. See ARITHMETIC, p. 653.

NUMERICAL

Pages 740-740

NUMEROUS, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Numerical, something belonging to numbers; as numerical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a> is that which makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of numbers, instead of letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>.—Also numerical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is that by which one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is distinguished from another. Hence a thing is said to be numerically the same, when it is so in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word.

NUMIDA

Pages 740-740

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of gallinace. On each side of the head there is a kind of coloured fleshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and the beak is furnished with cere near the nostrils. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the meleagris, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>-hen; a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is of the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hen, but with a longer neck. Its body is sloped like that of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is all over a dark grey, very beautifully spotted with small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> specks; there is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> round the neck; its head is reddish, and it is blue under the eyes. They naturally herd together in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> numbers, and breed up their young in common; the females taking care of the broods of others, as well as of their own. Barthol informs us, that in Guinea they are in flocks of 200 or 300, that perch in trees, and feed on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and grasshoppers; that they are run <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and taken by dogs; and that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is tender and sweet, generally white, though sometimes black. They breed very well with us.

NUMIDIA

Pages 740-750

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; on the south by Gætulia, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior; on the west by the Mulucha, a river which separated it from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>; and on the east by the Tufca, another river which bounded it in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with Africa Propria. Dr Shaw has rendered it probable, that the river which formerly went under the denominations of Malwa, Numidia, Malca, Malvana, Mulucha, and Melochath, is the same with that now called Mullochia by the Algerians; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the kingdom of Numidia must have extended upwards of 500 miles in length: its breadth, however, cannot be so well ascertained; but supposing it to have been the same with that of the present kingdom of Algiers, in the narrowest part it must have been at least 40 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and in the widest upwards of 100. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> included two districts; one inhabited by the Massylii, and the other by the Massylii; the latter being also called in after-times, Mauritania Cæsarienis, and the former Numidia Propria. The country of the Massylii, or, as some call it, Terra Metagenitis, was separated from the proper territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> by its eastern boundary the river Tufca, and from the kingdom of the Massylii, or Mauritania Cæsarienis, by the river Ampsaga. It seems to correspond with that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Constantina lying between the Zaine and the Wed al Kibeer, which is above 130 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and more than 100 broad. The sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of this province is for the most part mountainous and rocky, answering to the appellation given to it by Abulafia, viz. El Edwan, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or lofty. It is far from being equal in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to the ancient country of the Massylii, which, Strabo informs us, was yet inferior to the country of the Massylii. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was Cirta, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The most celebrated antiquarians agree, that the tract, extending from the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a> to the lake Tritonis, was chiefly peopled by the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIZRAIM">Mizraim</a>; and that the posterity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Put, or Phut, spread themselves all over the country between that lake and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. To this notion <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> gives <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> countenance: for he tells us, that the Libyan Nomades, whose territories to the west were bounded by the Triton, agreed in their customs and manners with the Egyptians; but that the Africans from that river to the Atlantic Ocean, differed in almost all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> from them. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> called Putea near Adranemum; and Pliny, a river of Mauritania Tingitana, known by the name of Put, or Phut; and the district adjacent to this river was called Regio Phutenis, which plainly alludes to the name of Phut. That word signifies scattered, or dispersed, which very well agrees with what Mela and Strabo relate of the ancient Numidians; so that we may, without any scruple, admit the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a> of this country to have been the descendants of Phut. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Numidia, during many of the early ages, is buried in oblivion. It is probable, however, that as the Phoenicians were masters of a great part of the country, these transactions had been recorded, and generally known to the Carthaginians. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> Jarbas probably reigned here as well as in Africa Propria, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not in Mauritania, and other parts of Libya, when Dido began to build Byrsa. It appears from Justin, that about the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Herodotus, the people of this country were called both Africans or Libyans and Numidians. Justin likewise intimates, that about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Carthaginians vanquished both the Moors or Mauritians, and Numidians; in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they were excused from paying the tribute which had hitherto been demanded of them. After the conclusion of the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the African troops carried on a bloody contest against their masters the Carthaginians; and the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in this rebellion, according to Diodorus Siculus, were a part of the Numidian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> named Micatantani. This incensed the Carthaginians, that after <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> had either killed or taken prisoners all the mercenaries, he sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> to ravage the country of those Numidians. The commandant of that detachment executed his orders with the utmost cruelty, plundering the district in a terrible manner, and crucifying all the prisoners, without distinction, that fell into his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. This filled the rest with such indignation and resentment, that both they and their posterity ever afterwards bore an implacable hatred to the Carthaginians. In the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic war, Syphax, king of the Massylii, entered into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and gave the Carthaginians a considerable defeat. This induced Gala, king of the Massylii, to conclude a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Carthaginians, in consequence of which his son Masinissa marched at the head of a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to give Syphax <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The contest ended in favour of Masinissa; 30,000 of the Massylii were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and Syphax driven into Mauritania; and the like bad success attended Syphax in another engagement, where his troops were entirely defeated and dispersed. Gala dying whilst his son Masinissa was acting at the head of the Numidian troops sent to the assistance of the Carthaginians in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, his brother Defalces, according to the established rules of succession in Numidia, took possession of the Massylian throne. That <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> dying soon after his accession, Capusa his eldest son succeeded him. But he did not long enjoy his high <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; for one Mezetulus, a person of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood, but an enemy to the family of Gala, found means to excite a great part of his subjects to revolt. A battle soon took place between him and Capusa; in which the latter was slain with many of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and his army entirely defeated. But tho' Mezetulus thus became possessed of the sovereignty, he did not think proper to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king, but styled himself <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> to Lacumaces, the surviving son of Defalces, whom he graced with the royal title. To support himself in his usurpation, he married the dowager of Defalces, who was Hannibal's niece, and consequently of the most powerful family in Carthage. In order to attain the same end, he sent ambassadors to Syphax, to conclude a treaty of alliance with him. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Masinissa, receiving advice of his uncle's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>'s slaughter, and of Mezetulus's usurpation, immediately passed over to Africa, and went to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Bocechar king of Mauritania, to solicit succours. Bocechar, sensible of the great injustice done Masinissa, gave him a body of 4000 Moors to escort him to his dominions. His subjects, having been apprised of his approach, joined him upon the frontiers with a party of 500 men. The Moors, in pursuance of their orders, returned home, as soon as Masinissa reached the confines of his kingdom. Notwithstanding which, and the small body that declared for him having accidentally met Lacumaces at Thapsus with an escort going to implore Syphax's assistance, he drove him into the town, which he carried by assault, after a faint resistance. However, Lacumaces, with many of his men, found means to escape to Syphax. The same of this exploit gained Massinissa great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, in so much that the Numidians flocked to him from all parts, and, amongst the rest, many of his father Gala's veterans, who pressed him to make a speedy and vigorous push for his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions. Lacumaces having joined Mezentius with a reinforcement of Massylians, which he had prevailed upon Syphax to send to the assistance of his ally, the usurper advanced at the head of a numerous army to offer Massinissa battle; which that prince, though much inferior in numbers, did not decline. Hereupon an engagement ensued; which, notwithstanding the inequality of numbers, ended in the defeat of Lacumaces. The immediate consequence of this victory to Massinissa, was a quiet and peaceable possession of his kingdom; Mezentius and Lacumaces, with a few that attended them, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> into the territories of Carthage. However, being apprehensive that he should be obliged to sustain a war against Syphax, he offered to treat Lacumaces with as many marks of distinction as his father Gala had Decebalus; provided that prince would put himself under his protection. He also promised Mezentius <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and a restitution of all the effects forfeited by his treasonable conduct, if he would make his submission to him. Both of them readily complied with the proposal, and immediately returned home; so that the tranquillity and repose of Numidia would have been settled upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and lasting foundation, had not this been prevented by Afrubal, who was then at Syphax's court. He insinuated to that prince, who was disposed to live amicably with his neighbours, "That he was greatly mistaken, if he imagined Massinissa would be satisfied with his hereditary dominions. That he was a prince of much greater capacity and ambition, than either his father Gala, his uncle Decebalus, or any of his family. That he had discovered in Spain marks of a most rare and uncommon merit. And that, in fine, unless his rising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> was extinguished before it came to too great a head, both the Massylian and Carthaginian states would be infallibly consumed by it." Syphax, alarmed by these suggestions, advanced with a numerous body of forces into a district, which had long been in dispute between him and Gala, but was then in possession of Massinissa. This brought on a general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> between these two princes; wherein the latter was totally defeated, his army dispersed, and he himself obliged to fly to the top of mount Balbus, attended only by a few of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. Such a decisive battle at the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, before Massinissa was fixed in his throne, could not but put Syphax into possession of the kingdom of the Massylii. Massinissa in the mean time made nocturnal incursions from his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> upon mount Balbus, and plundered all the adjacent country, particularly that part of the Carthaginian territory contiguous to Numidia. This district he not only thoroughly pillaged, but likewise laid waste with fire and sword, carrying off from thence an immense booty, which was bought by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who had put into one of the Carthaginian ports for that purpose. In fine, he did the Carthaginians more damage, not only by committing such dreadful devastations, but by massacring and carrying into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> vast numbers of their subjects on this occasion, than they could have sustained in a pitched battle, or one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of a regular war. Syphax, at the pressing and reiterated instances of the Carthaginians, sent Bocchus, one of his most active commanders, with a detachment of 4000 foot, and 2000 horse, to reduce this pestilent gang of robbers, promising him a great reward if he could bring Massinissa either alive or dead. Bocchus, watching an opportunity, surprized the Massylians, as they were straggling about the country without any order or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; so that he took many prisoners, dispersed the rest, and pursued Massinissa himself, with a few of his men, to the top of the mountain where he had before taken post. Considering the expedition as ended, he not only sent many head of cattle, and the other booty that had fallen into his hands, to Syphax, but likewise all the forces, except 500 foot and 200 horse. With this detachment he drove Massinissa from the summit of the hill, and pursued him through several narrow passes and defiles, as far as the plains of Clupea. Here he surrounded him, that all the Massylians, except four, were put to the sword, and Massinissa himself, after having received a dangerous wound, escaped with the utmost difficulty. As this was effected by crossing a rapid river, in which attempt two of his four attendants perished in the fight of the detachment that pursued him, it was rumoured all over Africa, that Massinissa also was drowned; which gave inexplicable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to Syphax and the Carthaginians. For some time he lived undiscovered in a cave, where he was supported by the robberies of the two horsemen that had made their escape with him. But having cured his wound by the application of some medicinal herbs, he boldly began to advance towards his own frontiers, giving out publicly that he intended once more to take possession of his kingdom. In his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> he was joined by about 40 horse, and soon after his arrival amongst the Massylii, so many people flocked to him from all parts, that out of them he formed an army of 6000 foot, and 4000 horse. With these forces, he not only reestablished himself in the possession of his dominions, but likewise laid waste the borders of the Massylii. This so irritated Syphax, that he immediately assembled a body of troops, and encamped very commodiously upon a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> between Cirta and Hippo. His army he commanded in person; and detached his son Vermina, with a considerable force, to take a compass, and attack the enemy in the rear. In pursuance of his orders, Vermina set out in the beginning of the night, and took post in the place appointed him, without being discovered by the enemy. In the mean time Syphax decamped, and advanced towards the Massylii, in order to give them battle. When he had possessed himself of a rising ground that led to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and concluded that his son Vermina must have formed the ambuscade behind them, he began the fight. Massinissa being advantageously posted, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> distinguishing themselves in an extraordinary manner, the dispute was long and bloody. But Vermina unexpectedly falling upon their rear, and by this means obliging them to divide their forces, which were scarce able before to oppose the main body under Syphax, Numidia, they were soon thrown into confusion, and forced to betake themselves to a precipitate flight. All the avenues being blocked up, partly by Syphax, and partly by his son, such a dreadful slaughter was made of the unhappy Massylii, that only Massinissa himself, with 60 horse, escaped to the Lesser Syrtis. Here he remained, betwixt the confines of the Carthaginians and Garamantæ, till the arrival of Lælius and the Roman fleet on the coast of Africa. What happened immediately after this junction with the Romans, belongs to the article ROMÆ. It <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient therefore in this place to observe, that, by the assistance of Lælius, Massinissa at last reduced Syphax's kingdom. According to Zonaras, Massinissa, before the memorable battle of Zama, by a stratagem deprived Hannibal of some advantageous polls; which, with a solar eclipse happening during the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the action, and not a little intimidating the Carthaginian troops, greatly contributed to the victory the Romans obtained. At the conclusion therefore of the second Punic war, he was amply rewarded by the Romans for the important services he had done them. As for Syphax, after the loss of his dominions, he was kept in confinement for some time at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>; from whence being removed in order to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> Scipio's triumph, he died at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIBUR">Tibur</a> in his way to Rome. Zonaras adds, that his corpse was decently interred; that all the Numidian prisoners were released; and that Vermina, by the assistance of the Romans, took peaceable possession of his father's throne. However, part of the Massylian kingdom had been before annexed to Massinissa's dominions, in order to reward that prince for his singular fidelity and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Romans. This seems to be countenanced by the epitomizer of Livy, who gives us sufficiently to understand, that Syphax's family, for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> after the conclusion of the second Punic war, reigned in one part of Numidia. For he intimates, that Archobarzanes, Syphax's grandson, and probably Vermina's son, hovered with a powerful army of Numidians upon the Carthaginian frontiers a few years before the beginning of the third Punic war. This he seems to have done, either in order to cover them, or to enable the Carthaginians to make an irruption into Massinissa's territories. Cato, however, pretended that these forces, in conjunction with those of Carthage, had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to invade the Roman dominions, which he urged as a reason to induce the conscript fathers to destroy the African republic. Nothing is further requisite, in order to complete the history of this famous prince, than to exhibit to our readers view some points of his conduct towards the decline, and at the close, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; the wise dispositions made after his death by Æmilianus, in order to the regulation of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs; and some particulars relating to his character, genius, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body, drawn from the most celebrated Greek and Roman authors. By <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a line of circumvallation around the Carthaginian army under Afdrubal, posted upon an eminence, Massinissa cut off all manner of supplies from them; which introduced both the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> and famine into their camp. As the body of Numidian troops employed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> was not near so numerous as the Carthaginian forces, it is evident, that the line here mentioned must have been extremely strong, and consequently the effect of great labour and art. The Carthaginians, finding themselves reduced to the last extremity, concluded a peace upon the following terms, which Massinissa dictated to them: 1. That they should deliver up all deserters. 2. That they should recall their exiles, who had taken refuge in his dominions. 3. That they should pay him 5000 talents of silver within the space of 50 years. 4. That their soldiers should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under the jugum, each of them carrying off only a single garment. As Massinissa himself, though between 80 and 90 years of age, conducted the whole enterprise, he must have been extremely well versed in fortification, and other branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art. His understanding likewise he must have retained to the last. This happened a short time before the beginning of the third Punic war. See CARTHAGE. Soon after, the consuls landed an army in Africa, in Massinissa's order to lay siege to Carthage, without impairing to displeased Massinissa their design. This not a little chagrined him, as it was contrary to the former practice of the Romans; who in the preceding war had communicated their intentions to him, and consulted him on all occasions. When, therefore, the consuls applied to him for a body of his troops to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with their forces, he made answer, "That they should have a reinforcement from him when they stood in need of it." It could not but be provoking to him to consider, that after he had extremely weakened the Carthaginians, and even brought them to the brink of ruin, his pretended imperious friends should come to reap the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his victory, without giving him the least intelligence of it. However, his mind soon returned to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bias, which was in favour of the Romans. Finding his end approaching, he sent to Æmilianus, then a tribune in the Roman army, to desire a visit from him. What he proposed by this visit, was to invest him with full powers to dispose of his kingdom and estate as he should think proper, for the benefit of his children. The high idea he had entertained of that young <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s abilities and integrity, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and affection for the family into which he was adopted, induced him to take this step. But, believing that death would not permit him to have a personal conference with Æmilianus upon this subject, he informed his wife and children in his last moments, that he had impow-er ed him to dispose in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> manner of all his possessions, and to divide his kingdom amongst his sons. To which he subjoined, "I require, that whatever Æmilianus may <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, shall be executed as punctually as if I myself had appointed it by my will." Having uttered these words, he expired, at above 90 years of age. This prince, during his youth, had met with strange reverses of fortune. However, says Appian, being supported by the divine protection, he enjoyed an uninterrupted course of prosperity for a long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years. His kingdom extended from Mauritania to the western confines of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>; from whence it appears, that he was one of the most powerful princes of Africa. Many of the inhabitants of this vast tract he civilized in a wonderful manner, teaching them to cul- Numidia, tivate their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and to reap those natural advantages which the fertility of some parts of their country offered them. He was of a more robust habit of body than any of his contemporaries, being blessed with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour; which was doubtless owing to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and the toils he incessantly sustained. We are informed by Polybius, that sometimes he stood upon the same spot of ground from morning till evening, without the least <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and at others <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> as long in a sitting posture. He would remain on horseback for several days and nights together, without being sensible of the least fatigue. Nothing can better evince the strength of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, than his youngest son, named Sthenbal, Sthenba, or Sthenbomus, who was but four years old at his decease. Though 90 years of age, he performed all the exercises used by young men, and always rode without a saddle. Pliny tells us, that he reigned above 60 years. He was an able commander, and much facilitated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Carthage.
