Plutarch from Polybius observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after a great victory won over the Carthaginians, Massinissa was seen sitting at the door of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, eating a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. Suidas relates, that, to the last, he could mount his horse without any assistance. According to Appian, he left a numerous well-disciplined army, and an immense <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wealth, behind him. Massinissa, before his death, gave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> to his eldest son Micipsa; but left the distribution of all his other effects and possessions amongst his children, entirely to Aemilianus. Of 54 sons that survived him, only three were legitimate, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, Micipsa, Gulussa, and Massanabal. Aemilianus, arriving at Cirta after he had expired, divided his kingdom, or rather the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of it, amongst these three, though to the others he gave considerable possessions. To Micipsa, who was a prince of a pacific disposition, and the eldest son, he assigned Cirta, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, for the place of his residence, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the others. Gulussa, the next to him, being a prince of a military genius, had the command of the army, and the transacting of all affairs relating to peace or war, committed to his care. And Massanabal, the youngest, had the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, an employment suitable to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, allotted him. They enjoyed in common the immense treasures Massinissa had amassed, and were all of them dignified by Aemilianus with the royal title. After he had made these wise dispositions, that young nobleman departed from Cirta, taking with him a body of Numidian troops, under the conduct of Gulussa, to reinforce the Roman army, that was then acting against the Carthaginians. Massanabal and Gulussa died soon after their father, as appears from the express testimony of Sallust. We find nothing more remarkable of these princes, besides what has been already related, than that the latter continued to assist the Romans in the third Punic war; and that the former was pretty well versed in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Micipsa therefore became sole possessor of the kingdom of Numidia. In his reign, and the conflagration of M. Plautius Hypsaeus and M. Fulvius Flaccus, according to Orosius, a great part of Africa was covered with locusts, which destroyed all the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and even devoured dry wood. But at last they were all carried by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> into the African sea, out of which being thrown in vast heaps upon the Numidian shore, a plague ensued, which swept away an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of animals of all kinds. In Numidia only, perished 800,000 men, and in Africa Propria 200,000; amongst the rest, 30,000 Roman soldiers quartered in and about <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the last province. At Utica, in particular, the mortality raged to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that 1500 dead bodies were carried out of one gate in a day. Micipsa had two sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal, whom he educated in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, together with his nephew Jugurtha. That young prince was the son of Massanabal; but his mother having been only a concubine, Massinissa had taken no great notice of him. However, Micipsa considering him as a prince of the blood, took as much care of him as he did of his own children. Jugurtha possessed several eminent qualities, which gained him universal esteem. He was very handsome, Jugurtha, endowed with great strength of body, and adorned with the finest intellectual endowments. He did not devote himself, as young men <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> do, to a life of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and pleasure. He used to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> himself, with persons of his age, in running, riding, hurling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, and other manly exercises, suited to the martial genius of the Numidians; and though he surpassed all his fellow sportsmen, there was not one of them but loved him. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> was his only delight; but it was that of lions, and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> beasts. Sallust, to finish his character, tells us, that he excelled in all things, and spoke very little of himself. So conspicuous an assemblage of fine talents and perfections, at first charmed Micipsa, who thought them an ornament to his kingdom. However, he soon began to reflect, that he was considerably advanced in years, and his children in their infancy; that mankind naturally thirsted after power, and that nothing was capable of making men run greater lengths than a vicious and unlimited ambition. These reflections soon excited his jealousy, and determined him to expose Jugurtha to a variety of dangers, some of which, he entertained hopes, might prove fatal to him. In order to this, he gave him the command of a body of forces which he sent to assist the Romans, who were at that time besieging Numantia in Spain. But Jugurtha, by his admirable conduct, not only escaped all those dangers, but likewise won the esteem of the whole army, and the friendship of Scipio, who felt a high character of him to his uncle Micipsa. However, that general gave him some prudent advice in relation to his future conduct; observing, no doubt, in him certain sparks of ambition, which, if lighted into a flame, he apprehended might one day be productive of the most fatal consequences. Before this last expedition, Micipsa had endeavoured to find out some method of taking him off privately; but his popularity amongst the Numidians obliged Massinissa, that prince to lay aside all thoughts of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. After his return from Spain the whole nation almost adored him. The heroic bravery he had shewn there, his undaunted courage, joined to the utmost calmness of mind, which enabled him to preserve a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> medium between a timorous foresight and an impetuous rashness, a circumstance rarely to be met with in persons of his age, and above all the advantageous testimonials of his conduct given by Scipio, attracted an universal Namibia. versal esteem. Nay, Micipsa himself, charmed with the high idea the Roman general had entertained of his merit, changed his behaviour towards him; resolving, if possible, to win his affection by kindness. He therefore adopted him, and declared him <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> heir with his two sons to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Finding, some few years afterwards, that his end approached, he sent for all three to his bedside; where, in the presence of the whole court, he desired Jugurtha to recollect with what extreme tenderness he had treated him, and consequently to consider how well he had deserved at his hands. He then intreated him to protect his children on all occasions; who, being before related to him by the ties of blood, were now by their father's bounty become his brethren. In order to fix him the more firmly in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, he likewise complimented him upon his bravery, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and consummate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. He further intimated, that neither arms nor treasures constitute the strength of a kingdom; but friends, who are neither won by arms nor <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, but by real services, and an inviolable fidelity. "Now where," (continued he), "can we find better friends than in brothers? And how can that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> who becomes an enemy to his relations, repose any confidence in, or depend upon strangers?" Then addressing himself to Adherbal and Hiempfal, "And you," (said he), "I join always to pay the highest reverence to Jugurtha. Endeavour to imitate, and if possible surpass, his exalted merit, that the world may not hereafter obviate Micipsa's adopted son to have reflected greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> than his own children." Soon after, Micipsa, who, according to Diodorus, was a prince of an amiable character, expired. Though Jugurtha did not believe the king to speak his real sentiments with regard to him, yet he seemed extremely pleased with so gracious a speech, and made him an answer suitable to the occasion. However, that prince at the same time was determined within himself to put in execution the scheme he had formed at the siege of Numantia, which was suggested to him by some factious and abandoned Roman officers, with whom he there contracted an acquaintance. The purport of this scheme was, that he should extort the crown by force from his two cousins, as soon as their father's eyes were closed; which they intimated might easily be effected by his own valour, and the venality of the Romans. Accordingly, a short time after the old king's death, he found means to afflinate Hiempfal in the city of Thirmidha where his treasurers were deposited, and drive Adherbal out of his dominions. That unhappy prince found himself obliged to fly to Rome, where he endeavoured to engage the conscript fathers to espouse his quarrel; but, notwithstanding the justice of his cause, they had not virtue enough effectually to support him. Jugurtha's emissaries, by distributing vast sums of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> amongst the senators, brought them so far over, that a majority palliated his inhuman proceedings. This encouraged those ministers to declare, that Hiempfal had been killed by the Numidians on account of his excessive cruelty; that Adherbal was the aggressor in the late troubles, and that he was only chagrined because he could not make that havoc amongst his countrymen he would willingly have done. They therefore intreated the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> to form a judgment of Jugurtha's behaviour in Africa from his conduct at Numantia, rather than from the suggestions of his enemies. Upon which, by far the greatest part of the senate discovered themselves prejudiced in his favour. A few however, that were not lost to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, nor abandoned to corruption, insisted upon bringing him to condign <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. But as they could not prevail, he had the best part of Numidia allotted him, and Adherbal was forced to rely satisfied with the other. Jugurtha finding now by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that everything was venal at Rome, as his friends at Numantia had before informed him, thought he might pursue his Romans towering projects without any obstruction from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. He therefore, immediately after the last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Micipsa's dominions, threw off the mask, and attacked his cousin by open force. As Adherbal was a prince of a pacific disposition, and almost in all respects the reverse of Jugurtha, he was by no means a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for him. The latter therefore pillaged the former's territories, stormed several of his fortresses, and overran a good part of his kingdom without opposition. Adherbal, depending on the friendship of the Romans, which his father in his last moments assured him would be a stronger support to him than all the troops and treasures in the universe, dispatched deputies to Rome to complain of these hostilities. But whilst he lost his time in feeding thither fruitless deputations, Jugurtha overthrew him in a pitched battle, and soon after shut him up in Cirta. During the siege of this city, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> arrived there, in order to persuade both parties to an accommodation; but finding Jugurtha untractable, the commissioners returned home without so much as conferring with Adherbal. A second <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a>, composed of senators of the highest distinction, with Emilius Scaurus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the senate, at their head, landed some time after at Utica, and summoned Jugurtha to appear before them. That prince at first seemed to be under dreadful apprehensions, especially as Scaurus reproached him with his enormous crimes, and threatened him with the resentment of the Romans if he did not immediately raise the siege of Cirta. However, the Numidian by his address, and the irresistible power of gold, as was afterwards suspected at Rome, so mollified Scaurus, that he left Adherbal at his mercy. In fine, Jugurtha had at last Cirta surrendered to him; upon condition only, that he should spare the life of Adherbal. But the merciless <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, in violation of the laws of nature and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, when he had got possession of the town, ordered him to be put to a most cruel death. The merchants likewise, and all the Numidians in the place capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, he caused, without distinction, to be put to the sword. Every person at Rome inspired with any sentiments of humanity, was struck with horror at the news of this tragical event. However, all the venal senators still concurred with Jugurtha's malifiers in palliating his enormous crimes. Notwithstanding which, the people, excited thereto by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Memmius their tribune, who bitterly inveighed against the venality of the senate, resolved not to let so flagrant an instance of villany go unpunished. This disposition in them induced the conscript fathers likewise to declare their intention to chastise Jugurtha. In order to this, an army was levied to invade Numidia, and the command of it given to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Calpurnius Bertia, a person of good abili- abilities, but rendered unfit for the expedition he was to go upon by his insatiable avarice. Jugurtha being informed of the great preparations making at Rome to attack his dominions, sent his son Thiner to avert the impending storm. The young prince was plentifully supplied with money, which he had orders to distribute liberally amongst the leading men. But Belfia, proposing to himself great advantages from an invasion of Numidia, defeated all his intrigues, and got a decree passed, ordering him and his attendants to depart <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in ten days, unless they were come to deliver up the king himself, and all his territories, to the republic by way of dedition. Which decree being notified to them, they returned without so much as having entered the gates of Rome; and the consul soon after landed with a powerful army in Africa. For some time he carried on the war there very briskly, reduced several strongholds, and took many Numidians prisoners. But upon the arrival of Scaurus, a peace was granted Jugurtha upon advantageous terms. That prince coming from Vaece, the place of his residence, to the Roman camp, in order to confer with Belfia and Scaurus, and the preliminaries of the treaty being immediately after settled between them in private conferences, every body at Rome was convinced that the prince of the senate and the consul had to their avarice sacrificed the republic. The indignation therefore of the people in general, displayed itself in the strongest manner. Memmius also fired them with his speeches. It was therefore resolved to dispatch the praetor Caecilius, a person they could confide in, to Numidia, to prevail upon Jugurtha to come to Rome, that they might learn from the king himself which of their generals and senators had been seduced by the pestilent influence of corruption. Upon his arrival there, he found means to bribe one Bubius Salca, a man of great authority amongst the plebeians, but of insatiable avarice, by whose affiance he escaped with impunity. Nay, by the efficacy of gold, he not only eluded all the endeavours of the people of Rome to bring him to justice, but likewise enabled Bomilcar, one of his attendants, to get Mativa, an illegitimate son of Micipsa, affianced in the streets of Rome. That young prince was advised by many Romans of probity, well-wishers to the family of Mativissa, to apply for the kingdom of Numidia; which coming to Jugurtha's ears, he prevented the application by this execrable step. However, he was obliged to leave Italy immediately. Jugurtha had scarce set foot in Africa when he received advice, that the senate had annulled the shameful peace concluded with him by Belfia and Scaurus. Soon after, the consul <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> transported a Roman army into Numidia, flattering himself with the hopes of reducing Jugurtha to reason before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his consulate. In this, however, he found himself deceived; for that crafty prince, by various artifices so amused and imposed upon Albinus, that nothing of moment happened that campaign. This rendered him strongly suspected of having betrayed his country, after the example of his predecessors. His brother Aulus, who succeeded him in the command of the army, was still more unsuccessful; for after rising from before Suthul, where the king's treasures were deposited, he marched his forces into a defile out of which he found it impossible to extricate himself. He therefore was obliged to submit to the ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of passing under the jugum, with all his men, and to quit Numidia entirely in ten days' time, in order to deliver his troops from immediate destruction. The avaricious disposition of the Roman commander had prompted him to besiege Suthul, the possession of which place he imagined would make him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the wealth of Jugurtha, and consequently paved the way to such a scandalous treaty. However, this was declared void as soon as known at Rome, as being concluded without the authority of the people. The Roman troops retired into Africa Propria, which they had now reduced into the form of a Roman province, and there took up their winter-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. In the mean time Caius Mamilius Limetanus, tribune of the people, excited the plebeians to inquire into the conduct of those persons by whose affiance Jugurtha had found means to elude all the decrees of the senate. This put the body of the people into a great ferment; which occasioned a prosecution of the guilty senators, that was carried on, for some time, with the utmost heat and violence. Lucius Metellus, the consul, during these transactions, had Numidia assigned him for his province, and consequently was Jugurtha appointed general of the army destined to act against Jugurtha. As he perfectly disregarded wealth, the Numidian found him superior to all his temptations; which was a great mortification to him. To this he joined all the other virtues which constitute the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; so that Jugurtha found him in all respects inaccessible. That prince therefore was now forced to regulate his conduct according to the motions of Metellus, with the greatest caution, and to exert his utmost bravery, in order to compensate for that hitherto so favourable expedient which now began to fail him. Marius, Metellus's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, being likewise a person of uncommon merit, the Romans reduced Vacca, a large opulent city, and the most celebrated mart in Numidia. They also defeated Jugurtha in a pitched battle; overthrew Bomilcar, one of his generals, upon the banks of the Muthullus; and, in fine, forced the Numidian monarch to take shelter in a place rendered almost inaccessible by the rocks and woods with which it was covered. However, Jugurtha signalled himself in a surprising manner, exhibiting all that could be expected from the courage, abilities, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of a consummate general, to whom despair administers fresh strength, and suggests new lights. But his troops could not make head against the Romans; they were again worsted by Marius, though they obliged Metellus to raise the siege of Zama. Jugurtha therefore, finding his country every where ravaged, his most opulent cities plundered, his fortresses reduced, his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> burnt, vast numbers of his subjects put to the sword and taken prisoners, began to think seriously of coming to an accommodation with the Romans. His favourite Bomilcar, in whom he repose the highest confidence, tried but who had been gained over to the enemy by Metellus, observing this disposition, found it no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to persuade him to deliver up his elephants, money, arms, horses, and deserters, in whom the main strength of his army consisted, into the hands of the Romans. Some of these last, in order to avoid the punishment due to their crime, retired to Boeckus king of Mauritania, and enlisted in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. But Metellus ordering ordering him to repair to Tifidium, a city of Numidia, there to receive farther directions, and he refusing a compliance with that order, hostilities were renewed with greater fury than ever. Fortune now seemed to declare in favour of Jugurtha: he retaken Vaces, and massacred all the Roman garrison, except Turpilius the commandant. However, soon after, a Roman legion seized again upon it, and treated the inhabitants with the utmost severity. About this time, one of Massanabal's sons, named Ganda, whom Micipia in his will had appointed to succeed to the crown in case his two legitimate sons and Jugurtha died without issue, wrote to the senate in favour of Marius, who was then endeavouring to supplant Metellus. That prince having his understanding impaired by a declining state of health, fell a more easy prey to the base and infamous adulation of Marius. The Roman, soothing his vanity, assured him, that as he was the next heir to the crown, he might depend upon being fixed upon the Numidian throne, as soon as Jugurtha was either killed or taken; and that this must in a short time happen, when once he appeared at the head of the Roman army with an unlimited commission. Soon after, Bomilcar and Nabdalifa formed a design to assassinate Jugurtha, at the instigation of Metellus; but this being detected, Bomilcar and most of his accomplices suffered death. The plot however had such an effect upon Jugurtha, that he enjoyed afterwards no tranquillity or repose. He suspected persons of all denominations, Numidians as well as foreigners, of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> designs against him. Perpetual terrors sat brooding over his mind; insomuch that he never got a wink of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> but by stealth, and often changed his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> in a low plebeian manner. Starting from his sleep, he would frequently fetch his sword, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out into the most doleful cries: So strongly was he haunted by a spirit of fear, jealousy, and distraction! Jugurtha having deliroved great numbers of his friends on suspicion of their having been concerned in the late <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, and many more of them deserting to the Romans and Bocchus king of Mauritania, he found himself, in a manner, destitute of counsellors, generals, and all persons capable of afflicting him in carrying on the war. This threw him into a deep melancholy, which rendered him dissatisfied with every thing, and made him fatigue his troops with a variety of contradictory motions. Sometimes he would advance with great celerity against the enemy, and at others retreat with no small swiftness from them. Then he refused his former courage; but soon after despaired either of the valour or fidelity of the forces under his command. All his movements therefore proved unsuccessful, and at last he was forced by Metellus to a battle. That part of the Numidian army which Jugurtha commanded, behaved with some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; but the other fled at the first onset. The Romans therefore entirely defeated them, took all their standards, and made a few of them prisoners. Not many of them were slain in the action; since, as Sallust observes, the Numidians trusted more to their heels than to their arms for safety in this engagement. Metellus pursued Jugurtha and his fugitives to Thala. His march to this place being through vast deserts, was extremely tedious and difficult. But being supplied with leathern bottles and wooden vessels of all sizes taken from the huts of the Numidians, which were filled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought by the natives, who had submitted to him, he advanced towards that city. He had no sooner begun his march, than a most copious shower of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, a thing very uncommon in those deserts, proved a great and seasonable refreshment to his troops. This so animated them, that upon their arrival before Thala, they attacked the town with such vigour, that Jugurtha, with his family, and treasures deposited therein, thought proper to abandon it. After a brave defence, it was reduced; the garrison, consisting of Roman deserters, setting fire to the king's palace, and confining themselves, together with every thing valuable to them, in the flames. Jugurtha, being now reduced to great extremities, retired into Gætulia, where he formed a considerable corps. From thence he advanced to the confines of Mauritania; and engaged Bocchus king of that country, who had married his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, to enter into an alliance with him. In consequence of which, having reinforced his Gætulian troops with a powerful body of Mauritians, he turned the tables upon Metellus, and obliged him to keep close within his entrenchments. Sallust informs us, that Jugurtha bribed Bocchus's ministers to influence that prince in his favour; and that having obtained an audience, he intimated, that, should Numidia be subdued, Mauritania must be involved in its ruin, especially as the Romans seemed to have vowed the destruction of all the thrones in the universe. In support of what he advanced, he produced several instances very apposite to the point in view. However, the same author seems to intimate, that Bocchus was determined to assist Jugurtha against his enemies by the flight the Romans had formerly shewn him. That prince, at the first breaking out of the war, had sent ambassadors to Rome, to propose an offensive and defensive alliance to the republic; which, though of the utmost consequence to it at that juncture, a few of the most venal and infamous senators, who were abandoned to corruption, prevented from taking effect. This undoubtedly wrought more powerfully upon Bocchus in favour of Jugurtha, than the relation he stood in to him: For both the Moors and Numidians adapted the number of their wives to their circumstances, so that some had 10, 20, &c. to their share; their kings therefore were unlimited in this particular, and of course all degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> resulting to them from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> had little force. It is observable, that the posterity of those ancient nations have the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> prevailing amongst them at this day. Such was the situation of affairs in Numidia, when Marius and Metellus received advice of the promotion of Marius to the consulate. But, notwithstanding this injurious treatment, he generously endeavoured to draw off Bocchus from Jugurtha, though this would facilitate the reduction of Numidia for his rival. To this end ambassadors were dispatched to the Mauritanian court, who intimated to Bocchus, "That it would be highly imprudent to come to a rupture with the Romans without any cause at all; and that he had now a fine opportunity of concluding a most advantageous treaty with them, which was much preferable to a war. To which they added, that whatever dependence he might place upon his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, he ought not not to run the hazard of losing his dominions by embroiling himself with other states, when he could easily avoid this; that it was much easier to begin a war than to end it, which it was in the power of the victor alone to do; that, in fine, he would by no means consult the interest of his subjects if he followed the desperate fortunes of Jugurtha." To which Bocchus replied, "That for his part there was nothing he wished for more than peace; but that he could not help pitying the deplorable condition of Jugurtha; that if the Romans, therefore, would <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> that unfortunate prince the same terms they had offered him, he would bring about an accommodation." Metellus let the Mauritanian monarch know, that it was not in his power to comply with what he desired. However, he took care to keep up a private negotiation with him till the new consul Marius's arrival. By this conduct he served two wise ends. First, he prevented thereby Bocchus from coming to a general action with his troops; which was the very thing Jugurtha desired, as hoping that this, whatever the event might be, would render a reconciliation betwixt him and the Romans impracticable. Secondly, this inaction enabled him to discover something of the genius and disposition of the Moors; a nation, of whom the Romans, till then, had scarce formed any idea; which, he imagined, might be of no small service, either to himself or his successors, in the future protection of the war. Jugurtha, being informed, that Marius, with a numerous army, was landed at Utica, advised Bocchus to retire, with part of the troops, to some place of difficult access, whilst he himself took post upon another inaccessible spot with the remaining corps. By this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, he hoped the Romans would be obliged to divide their forces, and consequently be more exposed to his efforts and attacks. He likewise imagined, that seeing no formidable body appear, they would believe the enemy in no condition to make head against them; which might occasion a relaxation of discipline, the usual attendant of a too great security, and consequently produce some good effect. However, he was disappointed in both these views. For Marius, far from suffering a relaxation of discipline to take place, trained up his troops, which consisted chiefly of new levies, in so perfect a manner, that they were soon equal in goodness to any consular army that ever appeared in the field. He also cut off great numbers of the Gætulian marauders, defeated many of Jugurtha's parties, and had like to have taken that prince himself near the city of Cirta. These advantages, though not of any great importance, intimidated Bocchus, who now made overtures for an accommodation; but the Romans, not being sufficiently satisfied of his sincerity, gave no great attention to them. In the mean time Marius pushed on his conquests, reducing several places of less note, and at last resolved to besiege Capfa. That this enterprise might be conducted with the greater secrecy, he suffered not the least hint of his design to transpire, even amongst any of his officers. On the contrary, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> them, he detached A. Manlius, one of his lieutenants, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed cohorts, to the city of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LARES">Lares</a>, where he had fixed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, and deposited the military <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>. Before Manlius left the camp, that he might the more effectually amuse him, he intimated, that himself with the army should take the same route in a few days: but instead of that, he <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> his march towards the Tanais, and in six days' time arrived upon the banks of that river. Here he pitched his tents for a short time, in order to refresh his troops; which having done, he advanced to Capfa, and made himself master of it. As the situation of this city rendered it extremely commodious to Jugurtha, whose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of operations, ever since the commencement of the war, it had exceedingly favoured, he levelled it with the ground after it had been delivered up to the soldiers to be plundered. The citizens likewise, being more strongly attached to that prince than any of the other Numidians, on account of the extraordinary privileges he indulged them with, and of course bearing a more implacable hatred to the Romans, he put to the sword or sold for slaves. The true <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of the consul's conduct on this occasion seems here to be assigned; though we are told by Sallust, in conformity to the Roman genius, that neither avarice nor resentment prompted him to so barbarous an action, but only a desire to strike a terror into the Numidians. The Numidians, ever after this exploit, dreaded the very name of Marius; who now, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, had eclipsed the glory of all his predecessor's great achievements, particularly the reduction of Thala, a city, in strength and situation, nearly resembling Capfa. Following his blow, he gradually presented himself before most of the places of strength in the enemy's country; many of which either opened their gates, or were abandoned, at his approach, being terrified with what had happened to the unfortunate citizens of Capfa. Others taking by force, he laid in ashes; and in short, filled the greatest part of Numidia with blood, horror, and confusion. Then, after an obstinate defense, he reduced a castle that seemed impregnable, seated not far from Mulucha, where Jugurtha kept part of his treasures. In the mean time, Jugurtha not being able to prevail upon Bocchus, by his repeated solicitations, to advance into Numidia, where he found himself greatly pressed, was obliged to have recourse to his usual method of bribing the Mauritanian ministers, in order to put that prince in motion. He also promised him a third part of his kingdom, provided they could either drive the Romans out of Africa, or get all the Numidian dominions confirmed to him by treaty. So considerable a cession could not fail of engaging Bocchus to support Jugurtha with his whole power. The two African monarchs therefore, having joined their forces, surprized Marius near Cirta as he was going into winter-quarters. The Roman general was so perplexed on this occasion, that the barbarians thought themselves certain of victory, and doubted not but they should be able to extinguish the Roman name in Numidia. But their incursion and too great security enabled Marius to give them a total defeat; which was followed four days after by so complete an overthrow, entirely destroyed their numerous army, consisting of 92,000 men, foiled by the accession of a powerful corps of Moors, commanded by Bocchus's son Volux, was entirely ruined. Sylla, Marius's lieutenant, most eminently distinguished himself in the last action, which laid the foundation of Numidia of his future greatness. Bocchus, now looking upon Jugurtha's condition as desperate, and not being willing to run the risk of losing his dominions, shewed a disposition to clap up a peace with Rome. However, the republic gave him to understand, that he must not expect to be ranked amongst his friends, till he had delivered up into the consul's hands Jugurtha, the inveterate enemy of the Roman name. The Mauritanian monarch, having entertained an high idea of an alliance with that state, resolved to satisfy it in this particular; and was confirmed in his resolution by one Dabat, a Numidian prince, the son of Massinissa, and descended by his mother's side from Massinissa. Being closely attached to the Romans, and extremely agreeable to Bocchus on account of his noble disposition, he defeated all the intrigues of Apar, Jugurtha's minister. Upon Sylla's arrival at the Mauritanian court, the affair there seemed to be entirely settled. However, Bocchus, who was for ever projecting new designs, and, like the rest of his countrymen, in the highest degree perfidious, debated within himself, whether he should sacrifice Sylla or Jugurtha, who were both then in his power. He was a long time fluctuating with uncertainty, and combated by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of sentiments. The sudden changes, which displayed themselves in his countenance, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and his whole person, evidently shewed how strongly his mind was agitated. But at last he returned to his first design, to which the bias of his mind seemed naturally to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him. He therefore delivered up Jugurtha into the hands of Sylla, to be conducted to Marius; who, by that successful event, happily terminated this dangerous war. The kingdom of Numidia was now reduced to a new form: Bocchus, for his important services, had the country of the Massylii, contiguous to Mauritania, assigned him; which, from this time, took the name of New Mauritania. Numidia Propria, or the country of the Massylii, was divided into three parts; one of which was given to Hiempfal, another to Mandrepsal, both descendants of Massinissa; and the third the Romans annexed to Africa Propria, or the Roman province adjacent to it. What became of Jugurtha after he had grazed Marius's triumph, at which ceremony he was led in chains, together with his two sons, through the streets of Rome, our readers will find related at large in a former part of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Jugurtha's two sons survived him, but spent their lives in captivity at Venusia. However, one of them, named Oxyntas, was, for a short time, released from his confinement by Aponius, who besieged Accrae in the war between the Romans and the Italian allies. That general brought this prince to his army, where he treated him as king, in order to draw the Numidian forces off from the Roman service. Accordingly those Numidians no sooner heard that the son of their old king was fighting for the allies, than they began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> by companies; which obliged Julius Caesar the consul to part with all his Numidian cavalry, and send them back into Africa. Some few years after this event, Pompey defeated Cnælius Domitius Ahenobarbus, and Hiarbass, one of the kings of Numidia, killing 17,000 of their men upon the spot. Not satisfied with this victory, that general pursued the fugitives to their camp, which he soon forced, put Domitius to the sword, and took Hiarbass prisoner. He then reduced that part of Numidia which belonged to Hiarbass, who seems to have succeeded Mandrepsal above-mentioned; and gave it to Hiempfal, a neighbouring Numidian prince, descended from Massinissa, who had always opposed the Marian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>. Suetonius informs us, that a dispute happened between Hiempfal and one Massintha, a noble Numidian, whom, it is probable, he had in some respect injured when Julius Caesar first began to make a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the world. The same author adds, that Caesar warmly espoused the cause of Massintha, and even grossly insulted Juba, Hiempfal's son, when he attempted to vindicate his father's conduct on this occasion. He pulled him by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, than which a more unpardonable affront could not be offered to an African. In short, he screened Massintha from the insults and violence of his enemies; from whence a reason may be assigned for Juba's adhering so closely afterwards to the Pompeian faction. In consequence of the indignity Caesar had offered Juba, and the disputation it had occasioned, that prince of Carthage did Caesar great damage in the civil wars betwixt him and Pompey. By a stratagem he drew Curio, one of his lieutenants, to a general action, which it was his interest at that time to have avoided. He caused it to be given out all over Africa Propria and Numidia, that he was retired into some remote country at a great distance from the Roman territories. This coming to Curio's ears, who was then besieging Utica, it hindered him from taking the necessary precautions against a surprize. Soon after, the Roman general receiving intelligence that a small body of Numidians was approaching his camp, he put himself at the head of his forces in order to attack them, and, for fear they should escape, began his march in the night, looking upon himself as sure of victory. Some of their advanced posts he surprized asleep, and cut them to pieces; which still farther animated him. In short, about day-break he came up with the Numidians, whom he attacked with great bravery, though his men were then fasting, and vastly fatigued by their forced and precipitate march. In the mean time, Juba, who immediately after the propagation of the rumour abovementioned, had taken care to march privately, with the main body of the Numidian army, to support the detachment sent before to decoy Curio, advanced to the relief of his men. The Romans had met with a great resistance before he appeared; so that he easily broke them, killed Curio, with a great part of his troops, upon the spot, purposed thereof to their camp, which he plundered, and took many of them prisoners. Most of the fugitives, who endeavoured to make their escape on board the ships in the port of Utica, were either slain by the pursuers, or drowned. The remainder fell into the hands of Varus, who would have saved them; but Juba, who arrogated to himself the honour of this victory, ordered most of them to be put to the sword. This victory infused new life and vigour into the Pompeian faction, who thereupon conferred great honours upon Juba, and gave him the title of king of all Numidia. But Caesar and his adherents declared him an enemy to the state of Rome, adjudging to Bocchus and Bogud, two African princes entirely in their interest. terest, the sovereignty of his dominions. Juba afterwards, uniting his forces with those of Scipio, reduced Caesar to great extremities, and would in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> have totally ruined him, had he not been relieved by Publius Sittius. That general, having formed a considerable corps, consisting of Roman exiles, and Mauritonian troops sent him by Bocchus, according to Dio, or, as Caesar will have it, Bogud, made an irruption into Getaulia and Numidia, whilst Juba was employed in Africa Propria. As he ravaged these countries in a dreadful manner, Juba immediately returned with the best part of his army, to preserve them from utter destruction. However, Caesar knowing his horse to be afraid of the enemy's elephants, did not think proper to attack Scipio in the absence of the Numidian, till his own elephants, and a fresh reinforcement of troops, hourly expected, arrived from Italy. With this accession of strength, he imagined himself able to give a good account, both of the Roman forces with which he was to cope, and the barbarians. In the mean time Scipio dispatched reiterated express to Juba to hasten to his assistance; but could not prevail upon him to move out of Numidia, till he had promised him the possession of all the Roman dominions in Africa, if they could from thence expel Caesar. This immediately put him in motion; so that, having sent a large detachment to make head against Sittius, he marched with the rest of his troops to assist Scipio. However, Caesar at last overthrew Scipio, Juba, and Labienus, near the town of Thapsus, and forced all their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>. As Scipio was the first surprised and defeated, Juba fled into Numidia, without waiting for Caesar's approach; but the body of the Numidians detached against Sittius, having been broken and dispersed by that general, none of his subjects there would receive him. Abandoned therefore to despair, he fought death in a single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> with Petreius, and, having killed him, caused himself to be dispatched by one of his slaves. After this decisive action, and the reduction of Africa Propria, Caesar made himself master of Numidia, of which he reduced to a Roman province, appointing Crispus Sallustius to govern it in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of proconsul, with private instructions to pillage and plunder the inhabitants, and, by that means, put it out of their power ever to shake off the Roman yoke. However, Bocchus and Bogud still preferred a fort of sovereignty in the country of the Massylii and Mauritania, since the former of those princes, having deserted Caesar, sent an army into Spain to assist the Pompeians; and the latter, with his forces, determined victory to declare for Caesar at the ever memorable battle of Munda. Bogud, afterwards siding with Anthony against Otho, sent a body of forces to assist him in Spain; at which time the Tingitans revolting from him, Bocchus, with an army composed of Romans in the interest of Otho, who passed over from Spain into Africa, and his own subjects, possessed himself of Mauritania Tingitana. Bogud fled to Antony; and Otho, after the conclusion of the war, honoured the inhabitants of Tingi with all the privileges of Roman citizens. He likewise confirmed Bocchus king of Mauritania Caesariensis, or the country of the Massylii, in the possession of Tingitania, which he had conquered, as a reward for his important services. In this he imitated the example of his great predecessor <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUMIDA">Numida</a> Julius Caesar, who divided some of the fruitful plains of Numidia among the soldiers of P. Sittius, who had conquered great part of that country, and appointed Sittius himself sovereign of that district. Sittius, as has been intimated above, having taken Cirta, killed Sabura Juba's general, entirely dispersed his forces, and either cut off or taken prisoners most of the Pompeian fugitives that escaped from the battle of Thapsus, highly deserved to be distinguished in so eminent a manner. After Bocchus's death, Mauritania and the Massylian Numidia were, in all respects, considered as Roman provinces.

NUMISMATOGRAPHIA

Pages 750-750

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins and medals, whether of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. See Coins and Medals.

NUMITOR

Pages 750-750

the son of Procus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Amulius. Procus dying made him and Amulius <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> heirs to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, on condition of their reigning annually by turns; but Amulius, on getting possession of the throne, excluded Numitor, whose son Lautus he ordered to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and obliged Rhea Sylvia, Numitor's only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, to become a vestal. This princess becoming pregnant, declared that she was with child by the god <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>; and afterwards brought forth Rhenus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, who at length killed Amulius, and restored Numitor to the throne, 754 B.C.

NUN

Pages 750-751

a woman, in several Christian countries, who devotes herself, in a cloister <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> nunnery, to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. See the article Monk. There were women, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who made public profession of virginity, before the monastic life was known in the world, as appears from the writings of Cyprian and Tertullian. These, for distinction's sake, are sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> virgins, and were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> enrolled in the canon or matricula of the church. They differed from the monastic virgin chiefly in this, that they lived privately in their fathers' houses, whereas the others lived in communities; but their profession of virginity was not so strict as to make it criminal in them to marry afterwards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they thought fit. As to the consecration of virgins, it had some things peculiar in it: it was usually performed publicly in the church by the bishop. The virgin made a public profession of her <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and then the bishop put upon her the accustomed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of sacred virgins. One <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this habit was a veil, called the sacrum velamen; another was a kind of mitre or coronet worn upon the head. At present, when a woman is to be made a nun, the habit, veil, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of the candidate are carried to the altar; and she herself, accompanied by her nearest relations, is conducted to the bishop, who, after <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> and an anthem, the subject of which is, "that she ought to have her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> lighted, because the bridegroom is coming to meet her," pronounces the benediction; then she rises up, and the bishop consecrates the new habit, sprinkling it with holy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. When the candidate has put on her religious habit, she presents herself before the bishop, and sings, on her <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, Ancilla Christi sum, &c.; then she receives the veil, and afterwards the ring. Nuncio by which she is married to Christ; and lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of virginity. When she is crowned, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> is denounced against all who shall attempt to make her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> her vows.

NUNCIO

Pages 751-751
or Nuntio, an ambassador from the pope to some Catholic prince or state, or a person who attends on the pope's behalf at a congress, or an assembly of several ambassadors.

NUNCUPATIVE

Pages 751-751

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, something that is only nominal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> has no existence but in name. NUNCUPATIVE <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">Will</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, a will made verbally, and not put in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Will and Testament.

NUNDINA

Pages 751-751

a godess among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Heathens, supposed to have the care of the purification of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. And because <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>-infants were purified <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days after their birth, her name is derived from nonus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the ninth, though <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>-infants were purified the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; which purification was called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>.

NUNDINAL

Pages 751-751

(nundinalis,) a name which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave to the eight first letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, used in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, is placed and repeated successively from the first to the last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year; one of these always expressed the market-days, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the assemblies called nundinae, quasi mensendarum, because they returned every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people, after working eight days successively, came to town the ninth, to sell their several commodities, and to inform themselves of what related to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Thus the nundinal day being under A on the first, ninth, seventeenth, and twenty-fifth days of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> D <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the nundinal letter of the year following. These nundinals bear a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance to the dominal letters, which return every eight days, as the nundinals did every nine.

NUPTIAL RITES

Pages 751-751

the ceremonies attending the solemnization of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, which are different in different ages and countries.

NUREMBERG

Pages 751-751

an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° N. Lat. 49° 30'. It stands on the Regnitz, over which it has several bridges, both of wood and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, at the bottom of a hill, 60 miles from Augsburg, 87 from Munich, 46 from Wurtzburg, and 50 from Ratibon; and is thought by some to be the Segodunum, and by others the Castrum Noricum, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built, but not very populous. Its fortifications are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall, flanked with towers mounting cannon, and a deep ditch. The magistrates, and most of the inhabitants, are Lutherans. There are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many churches and chapels in it. In that of St Sebald is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> monument of the saint; and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world, by the celebrated Albert Durer, who was a native of the town; but the finest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the town is that of St Giles. In that of the Holy Ghost are kept most of the jewels of the empire, together with the pretended spear with which our Saviour's side was pierced, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THORN">thorn</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and a piece of the manger wherein he was laid. Here are also a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, one in particular for foundlings, and another for pilgrims; with a gymnasium, an anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a>, a fine Nuremberg public library, the old imperial fortress <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> castle, some remains of the old citadel of the burggraves of Nuremberg, several Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, an academy of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, a well furnished arsenal, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEUTONIC">teutonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in which the Roman-catholic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is tolerated, and a mint. Mr Keyler says, there are upwards of 500 streets in it, about 140 fountains, 16 churches, 44 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, 12 bridges, 10 market-places, and 25000 inhabitants; and that its territories, besides the capital and four other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, contains above 500 villages, and about 160 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> on the Regnitz. The trade of this city, though upon the decline, is still very great, many of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> being still exported to all parts of the world; among which may be reckoned a great variety of curious toys in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, wood, and metal. The city has also distinguished itself in the arts of painting and engraving. When the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Henry VI. assisted at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> in Nuremberg, he raised 38 burghers to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, the descendants of whom are called patricians, and have the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the city entirely in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; the whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, except eight masters of companies, who are summoned only on extraordinary occasions, consisting of them. Among the fine brass cannon in the arsenal, is one that is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> at the breech, and may be fired eight times in a minute; and two that carry balls of eighty pounds. The city keeps, in constant pay, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> companies, consisting each, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of peace, of 100 men, but, in time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, of 185; two troops of cuirassiers, each consisting of 85 men; and two companies of invalids. There are also 24 companies of burghers, well armed and disciplined. On the new <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which is said to have cost 100,000 guilders, are two pyramids, on the top of one of which is a dove with an olive branch in her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, and on the other an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eagle. Music also flourishes greatly in Nuremberg; and those who delight in mechanic arts and manufactures, cannot anywhere better gratify their curiosity. As an imperial city, it has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> at the diets of the empire and circle, paying to a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> one seventh <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> imposts of the circle, and to the chamber of Wetzlar 812 rix-dollars, each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>. The territory belonging to the city is pretty large, containing, besides two considerable forests of pine, called the Sibald and Laurence forests, several towns and villages.

NURSERY

Pages 751-752

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, is a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> set apart for raising and propagating all sorts of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to supply the garden and other plantations. NURSING OF CHILDREN. See Lactatio. The following observations are said to be the result of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. A child, when it comes into the world, is almost a round <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; it is the nurse's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> to assist <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in bringing it to a proper shape. The child should be laid (the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>) upon a thin matras, rather longer than the child, which the nurse <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep upon her lap, that the child may always <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> straight, and only fit up as the nurse flints the matras. To let a child quite upright before the end of the first month, hurts the eyes, by making the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> part of the eye appear below the upper eyelid. Afterwards the nurse will begin to set it up and dance it. NURSING The child must be kept as dry as possible. The clothing should be very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and not much longer than the child, that the legs may be got at with ease, in order to have them often rubbed in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> with a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, and in particular the inside of them. Rubbing a child all over takes off scurf, and makes the blood circulate. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> should be rubbed with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, one way, and the other the other way, night and morning at least. The ankle-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and inside of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> should be rubbed twice a-day; this will strengthen those parts, and make the child stretch its knees and keep them flat, which is the foundation of an erect and graceful person. A nurse ought to keep a child as little in her arms as possible, lest the legs should be cramped, and the toes turned inwards. Let her always keep the child's legs loose. The sooner the posture is changed, the better. Tossing a child about, and exercising it in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> in fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, is of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. In cities, children are not to be kept in hot rooms, but to have as much air as possible. Want of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> is the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heads, weak and knotted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, a contracted breast, which occasions coughs and stuffed lungs, an ill-shaped person, and waddling gait, besides a numerous train of other ills. The child's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is to be kept perfectly clean, by constantly washing its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, and likewise its neck and ears; beginning with warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, till by degrees it will not only bear, but like, to be washed with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Rising early in the morning is good for all children, provided they awake of themselves, which they generally do; but they are never to be waked out of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and as soon as possible to be brought to regular sleeps in the day. When laid in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> or cradle, their legs are always to be laid straight. Children, till they are two or three years old, they must never be suffered to walk long enough at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be weary. Girls might be trained to the proper management of children, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a premium were given in free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, workhouses, &c. to those that brought up the finest child to one year old. If the mother cannot suckle the child, get a wholesome cheerful woman, with a young <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, who has been used to tend young children. After the first six months, small broths, and innocent foods of any kind, may do as well as living wholly upon milk. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing to be always attended to is, to give young children constant exercise, and to keep them in a proper posture. With regard to the child's dress in the day, let it be a shirt; a petticoat of fine flannel, two or three inches longer than the child's feet, with a dimity top (<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a bodice-coat), to tie behind; over that a surcingle made of fine buckram, two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, covered over with fatin or fine ticken, with a ribbon fastened to it to tie it on, which answers every purpose of stays, and has none of their inconveniences. Over this put a robe, or a slip and frock, or whatever you like best; provided it is fastened behind, and not much longer than the child's feet, that their motions may be strictly observed. Two caps are to be put on the head, till the child has got most of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The child's dress for the night may be a shirt, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a> to tie on, and a thin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> to tie over the blanket.

NUTATION

Pages 752-752

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, a kind of tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the axis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereby, in each annual revolution, it is twice inclined to the ecliptic, and as often returns to its former position.

NUTMEG

Pages 752-753

the kernel of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fruit, not unlike the peach. The nutmeg, as we receive it, is of a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> oval <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, of a tolerably <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and firm texture, but easily cut with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and falling to pieces on a smart blow. Its surface is not smooth, but furrowed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wrinkles, running in various directions, though principally longitudinally. It is of a greyish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the outside, and of a beautiful variegated hue within, being marbled with brown and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> variegations, running in perfect irregularity through its whole substance. It is very unctuous and fatty to the touch, when powdered; and is of an extremely agreeable smell, and of an aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. There are two kinds of nutmeg in the shops; the one called by authors the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. The female is the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and is of the shape of an olive: the male is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and cylindric, and has less of the fine aromatic flavour than the other; so that it is much less esteemed, and people who trade largely in nutmegs <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> seldom buy it. The larger male nutmeg, as we <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, is called by the Dutch the wild nutmeg. It is always distinguishable from the others, as well by its want of fragrance, as by its shape: it is very subject to be worm-eaten; and is strictly forbid, by the Dutch, to be packed up among the other, because it will give occasion to their being worm-eaten too, by the insects getting from it into them, and breeding in all parts of the parcel. The largest, heaviest, and most unctuous of the nutmegs are to be chosen, such as are of the shape of an Nutmeg, an olive, and of the most fragrant smell. The Dutch import them from the East Indies. The tree which produces the nutmeg grows only in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANDA_ISLANDS">Banda <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It has a pithy wood, an ash-colored bark, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> branches. The leaves are produced in pairs upon one single stem; and, when bruised, emit an agreeable odor. The fruit succeeds the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which resemble those of the cherry-tree. It is of the size of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and of the color of an apricot. The outer rind is very thick, and resembles that of our nuts as they hang upon the tree, opening in the same manner when ripe, and discovering the nutmeg covered with its mace. It is then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to gather it, to prevent the mace or flower of the nutmeg from growing dry, and the nutmeg from losing that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> which preserves it, and in which its excellence consists. Those that are gathered before they are perfectly ripe, are preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and admired only in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. This fruit requires <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months to bring it to perfection. After it is gathered, the outer rind is stripped off, and the mace separated from it, and laid in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to dry. The nuts require more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>—they are spread upon hurdles, and dried for six weeks by a slow fire, in sheds erected for that purpose. They are then separated from the shell, and thrown into lime-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as a necessary preservative against <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. Nutmeg is greatly used in our foods, and is of excellent virtue as a medicine; it is a good stomache, promotes digestion, and strengthens the stomach. It also stops vomiting; is an excellent remedy in fistulas; and is happily joined with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, and other medicines, in diarrhoeas. It is observed to have a soporific virtue, and to exert it too strongly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> taken in moderate quantities. It has a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of astringency; and given, after toasting before the fire till thoroughly dry and crumbly, it has been sometimes known alone to cure diarrhoeas.

NUTRITION

Pages 753-753

in the animal-economy, is the repairing the continual loss which the different parts of the body undergo. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the parts of the body, the friction of these parts with each other, and especially the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, would destroy the body entirely, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the loss was not repaired by a proper diet, containing nutritive juices; which being digested in the stomach, and afterwards converted into chyle, mix with the blood, and are distributed through the whole body for its nutrition. In young persons, the nutritive juices not only serve to repair the parts that are damaged, but also to increase them, which is called growth. In grown persons, the cuticle is everywhere constantly desquamating, and again renewing: and in the same manner the parts rubbed off, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise separated from the fleshy parts of the body, are soon supplied with new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; a wound heals, and an emaciated person grows plump and fat. Buffon, in order to account for nutrition, supposes the body of an animal or vegetable to be a kind of mould, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> necessary to its nutrition is modelled and assimilated to the whole. But (continues he) of what <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is this matter which an animal or vegetable assimilates to its own substance? What power is it that communicates to this matter the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and motion necessary to penetrate this mould? and, if such a force exist, would it not be by a similar force that the internal mould itself might be reproduced? As to the first question, he supposes that there exists in nature an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of living organic parts, and that all organized bodies consist of such organic parts; that their production costs nature nothing, since their existence is constant and invariable; so that the matter which the animal or vegetable assimilates to its substance, is an organic matter, of the same nature with that of the animal or vegetable, which consequently may augment its volume without changing its form or altering the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the substance in the mould. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> question: There exist (says he) in nature certain powers, as that of gravity, that have no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> qualities of the body, but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon the most intimate parts, and penetrate them throughout, and which can never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under the observation of our senses. And, as to the third question, he answers, that the internal mould itself is reproduced, not only by a similar power, but it is plain that it is the very same power that causes the unfolding and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a> thereof: for it is sufficient (proceeds he), that in an organized body that unfolds itself, there be some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> similar to the whole, in order that this part may one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> become itself an organized body, altogether like that of which it is actually a part. NUX PISTACHIA. See Pistachia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">Nux Vomica</a>, a flat, compressed, round fruit, about the breadth of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>, brought from the East Indies. It is found to be a certain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> for dogs, cats, &c., and it is not to be doubted that it would also prove fatal to mankind. Its surface is not much corrugated; and its texture is firm like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> greyish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>.

NYCHTHEMERON

Pages 753-753
