the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> day and night, which together make 24 hours. NYCTALOPIA. See Medicine, n° 456.

NYCTANTHES

Pages 753-754

Arabian Jasmine; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the diandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which are, 1. The arbor triflora, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sorrowful tree. This tree, or shrub, the paristacum of the Bramins, grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> places in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Ceylon and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, where it is produced in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance, and attains the height of 18 or 20 feet. It rises with a four-cornered stem, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> leaves that are oval, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> to a point. They stand opposite, on short foot-stalks; are of a shining brownish-green on the upper-side, a more vivid green on the under, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> that is astringent and somewhat bitter. From the middle-rib, on the under-surface of the leaves, proceed on both sides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cotylae, or smaller ribs, which run nearly to the margin, and mark the surface with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of their arched furrows. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and highly odoriferous, having a sweet delectable smell emulating the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, consist of one petal deeply divided into eight parts, which are narrower towards the stalk, and dilated towards the summit. They stand upon foot-stalks, which emerge from the origin of the leaves; are rigid, obliquely raised. NYCTICORAX raised towards the top, grow opposite in pairs, and are divided into three short lesser branches, which each supports five flowers placed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, without partial foot-stalks. The fruit is dry, capsular, membranaceous, and compressed. It is generally asserted of this plant, that the flowers open in the evening, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Fabricius and Paludanus, however, restrict the assertion, by affirming, from actual observation, that this effect is found to take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> only in such flowers as are immediately under the influence of the solar rays. Grimmelius remarks in his Laboratorium Ceylonicum, that the flowers of this tree afford a fragrant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which is cordial, refreshing, and frequently employed with success in inflammations of the eyes. The tube of the flower, when dried, has the smell of saffron; and, being pounded and mixed with sanders-wood, is used by the natives of the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> for imparting a grateful fragrance to their bodies, which they rub or anoint with the mixture. 2. The sambac, noted, like the other species, for the fragrance of its flowers, is a native likewise of India; and is cultivated in our hovels, where it generally rises with a twining stem, to the height of 18 or 20 feet. The leaves are opposite, simple, and entire; but in different parts of the plant assume different forms: the lower leaves being heart-shaped and blunt; the upper, oval and sharp. The flowers are white, inexpressibly fragrant, and generally appear with us in the warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-months. Strong loam is its proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. There is a variety of this species with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> flower, which is much larger and more fragrant than the former.

NYLAND

Pages 754-754

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Finland, to the west of the province of Carelia.

NYMPH

Pages 754-754

among naturalists, that state of winged-insects between their living in the form of a worm, and Nymphæa, their appearing in the winged <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> most perfect state. The eggs of insects are first hatched into a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, or maggots; which afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the nymph-state, surrounded with shells or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of their own making: so that, in reality, these nymphs are only the embryo insects, wrapped up in this covering; from whence they at last get loose, though not without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty. During this nymph-state the creature loses its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Swammerdam calls it nympha aurelia, or simply aurelia; and others give it the name of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of the like import. See the article CHRYSALIS. NYMPHÆA, in anatomy, two membranaceous parts, situated on each side the rima. They are of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and cavernous structure, somewhat resembling the wattles under a cock's throat. They are sometimes smaller, sometimes larger; and are continuous to the prepuce of the clitoris, and joined to the interior side of the labia. NYMPHÆA, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">WATER</a>-LILY; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the polyandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. 2. The lutea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> water-lilies; both of which are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, growing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and ditches. Linnaeus tells us, that twins are fond of the leaves and roots of the former; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> drive away crickets and blatta, or cock-roaches, out of houses.—The root of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> has an astringent and bitter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, like those of most aquatic plants that run deep into the mud. The Highlanders make a dye with it of a dark chestnut colour. 3. In the East and West Indies grows a species of this plant, named melumba by the inhabitants of Ceylon. The leaves which rest upon the surface of the water, are smooth, undivided, perfectly round, thick, target-shaped, and about one foot and a half in diameter. The footstalk of the leaves is prickly; and inserted, not into their base, or margin, as in most plants, but in the centre of the lower disk or surface. From this centre, upon the upper surface, issue, like rays, a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ribs, or nerves, which towards the circumference are divided and subdivided into a small number of very minute parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are large, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-coloured, and consist of numerous petals, disposed, as in the other species of waterlily, in two or more rows. The seed-vessel is shaped like a top, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and circular above, narrow and almost pointed below. It is divided into several distinct cells, which form so many large round holes upon the surface of the fruit; each containing a single seed.—With the flower of this plant, which is sacred among the heathens, they adorn the altars of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>: they paint their gods sitting upon it; and make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such pictures to animate the minds of the pious on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and to raise their affections to heaven. The stalks, which are used as a pot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, are of a wonderful length. The root is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, extends itself transversely, is of the thickness of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s arm, jointed and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>, with long intervals betwixt the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>. The fibres surround the joints in verticilli, or whirls.

NYMPHEUM

Pages 754-754

in antiquity, a public <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> magnificently decorated, for entertainment, &c. and where those who wanted convenience at home held their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>-

NYSLOT

Pages 755-755

a strong town of Russia, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle; seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> marshes. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26°. 55'. N. Lat. 58°. 46'.

NYSSA

Pages 755-755

a genus of the order of dioecia, belonging to the polygamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. The aquatics, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-tupelo-tree. This has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, especially near the ground, and grows very tall. The leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and irregularly notched. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> come out from the sides of the branches, on footstalks of three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and are of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The grain of the wood is soft and spongy; but the roots much more so, approaching near to the consistence of cork; and are used for the purposes of cork in Carolina, where these trees are natives. They grow in wet places, and usually in the shallow parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. O O, The 14th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> and fourth vowel of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; pronounced as in the words nofe, rose, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of this letter is often so soft as to require it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and that chiefly in the middle of words; as goofs, reprofs, &c. And in some words this oo is pronounced like a short, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, blood, &c. As a numeral, O is sometimes used for 11; and with a dash over it thus, ō, for 11,000. In the notes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, O. CON. is read opus conduction; O. C. Q. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> confignitio; O. D. M. operae, denum, munus; and O. LO. opus locatum. In music, the O, or rather a circle, or double CO, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, called by us a semi-breve; and by the Italians, circolo. The O is also used as a mark of triple time, as being the most perfect of all figures. See Triple.

OAK

Pages 755-756

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See Quercus. Oak-Leaves. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of oak-bark in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>, is generally known. For the latter of these purposes, however, oak-leaves are now found to answer equally well, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather better. In the notes to Dr Hunter's edition to Evelyn's Treatise on Forest-trees, we find the following directions for their use by W. Speechly. The leaves are to be raked up as soon as possible after they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the trees. When raked into heaps, they should immediately be carried into some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> near the hot-houses, where they may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> to couch. Mr Speechly says it was his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> them round with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> hurdles, or any thing else, to keep them from being blown about the garden in windy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. In this place they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> them well, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> them in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> they happen to have been brought in dry. The heap is made six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet thick, and covered over with old mats, or any thing else, to prevent the upper leaves from being blown away. In a few days the heap <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> come to a strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. For the first year or two in which he used these leaves, our author did not continue them in the heap longer than ten days or a fortnight; but by this method of management they settled too much when brought to the hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, that a supply was very soon required; and he afterwards found, that it was proper to let them remain five or six weeks in the heaps before they are brought to the hot-house. In getting them into the pine-pits, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they appear dry, they are to be watered, and again trodden <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> exceedingly well, in layers, till the pits are quite full. The whole is then covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>-bark, to the thickness of two inches, and well trodden down, till the surface becomes smooth and even. On this the pine-pots are to be placed in the manner they are to stand, beginning with the middle row first, and filling up the spaces between the pots with tan. In this manner we are to proceed to the next row, till the whole be finished; and this operation is performed in the same manner as when tan only is used. The leaves require no further trouble through the whole season; as they will retain a constant and regular heat for 12 months without stirring or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>; and our author informs us, that if he may judge from their appearance when taken out, (being always entire and perfect), it is probable they would continue their heat through a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year; but, as an annual supply of leaves is easily obtained, the experiment is hardly worth making. After this, the pines will have no occasion to be moved, but at stated times of their management, viz. at the shifting them in their pots, &c. when at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> a little fresh tan should be added to make up the deficiency arising from the settling of the beds; but this will be inconsiderable, as the leaves do not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> much after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> couching. During the first two years of our author's practice he did not use any tan, but plunged the pine-pots into the leaves, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> covered the surface of the beds, when finished, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust, to give it a neatness. This method, however, was attended with one inconvenience; for by the caking of the leaves they shrunk from the sides of the pots, whereby they became exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and at the same time the heat of the beds was permitted to escape. "Many powerful reasons, says Mr Speechly, may be given why oak-leaves are preferable to tanner's bark. "I. They always heat regularly; for during the whole time that I have used them, which is near seven years, I never once knew of their heating with violence; and this is so frequently the case with tan, that I affirm, and indeed it is well known to every person conversant in the management of the hot-house, that pines suffer more from this one circumstance, than all the other accidents put together, insects excepted." When this accident happens near the time of their fruiting, the effect is soon seen in the fruit, which is exceedingly small and ill-shaped. Sometimes there will be little or no fruit at all; therefore gardeners who make use of tan only for their pines, should be most particularly careful to avoid an over-heat at that critical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>,—the time of flowering the fruit. 2. The heat of oak-leaves is constant; whereas tanner's bark generally turns <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in a very short time after its furious heat is gone off. This obliges the gardener to give it frequent turnings in order to promote its heating. These frequent turnings, not to mention the expense, are attended with the worst consequences; for by the continual moving of the pots backwards and forwards, the pines are exposed to the extremes of heat and cold, whereby their growth is considerably retarded; whereas, when leaves are used, the pines will have no occasion to be moved but at the times of potting, &c. The pines have one peculiar advantage in this undisturbed situation; their roots grow through the bottoms of the pots, and mat among the leaves in a surprising manner. From the vigour of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> when in this situation, it is highly probable that the leaves, even in this state, afford them an uncommon and agreeable nourishment. 3. There is a saving in point of expense; which is no inconsiderable object in places where tan cannot be had but from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. 4. The last ground of preference is, that decayed leaves make good manure; whereas rotten tan is experimentally found to be of no value. I have often tried it both on sand and clay, and on wet and dry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and never could discover, in any of my experiments, that it deserved the name of a manure; whereas decayed leaves are the richest, and of all others the most proper manure for a garden. Leaves mixed with dung make excellent hot-beds; and I find that beds <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> ed in this manner, preserve their heat much longer than when made entirely with dung; and in both <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the application of leaves will be a considerable saving of dung, which is a circumstance on many accounts agreeable. Oak Saw-dust is now found to answer the purposes of tanning as well, at least, as the bark. See TANNING. Oak of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. See Chenopodium.

OAK NYON

Pages 754-755

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bailiwick of the same name, with a castle. There are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many Roman <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> here; and it is a trading <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, seated in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, near the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5°. N. Lat. 46°. 24'.

OAKAM

Pages 756-756

old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> untwisted and pulled out into loose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, in order to be used in caulking the seams, tree-nails, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> of a ship, for stopping <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> preventing leaks.

OAKHAMPTON

Pages 756-756

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 47'. N. Lat. 45° 4'.

OAR

Pages 756-756

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, flat at one end, and round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the other, and which being applied to the side of a floating-veffel, serves to make it advance upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the oar which is out of the veffel, and which enters into the water, is called the blade, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, plat; and that which is within-board is termed the form, whose extremity being small enough to be grasped by the rowers, or persons managing the oars, is called the handle. To push the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or veffel forwards by means of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, the rowers turn their backs forward, and, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the blade of the oar in the water, pull the handle forward so that the blade at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> may move aft in the water: but since the blade cannot be so moved, without striking the water, this impulsion is the same, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the water were to strike the blade from the stern towards the head: the veffel is therefore necessarily moved according to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Hence it follows, that she <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> advance with the greater rapidity, by as much as the oar strikes the water more forcibly. Thus it is evident, that an oar acts upon the side of a boat or veffel like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> clas, whose fulcrum is the station upon which the oar rests on the boat's gunnel. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> veffels, this station is usually called the row-port; but in lights and boats it is always termed the row lock.

OBADIAH

Pages 756-756
or the Prophecy of Obadiah, a canonical book of the Old Testament, which is contained in one single chapter; and is partly an invective against the cruelty of the Ebonites, who mocked and derided the children of Israel, as they passed into captivity, and with other enemies, their confederates, invaded and oppressed those strangers, and divided the spoil amongst themselves; and partly a prediction of the deliverance of Israel, and of the victory and triumph of the whole church over her enemies.

OBELISK

Pages 756-756

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a truncated, quadrangular, and slender <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, raised as an ornament, and frequently <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> either with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">Obelisks</a> appear to be of very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and to be first raised to transmit to posterity precepts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which were cut in hieroglyphical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>: afterwards they were used to immortalize the great actions of heroes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of persons beloved. The first obelisk mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was that of Rameses <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which was 40 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Phius, another king of Egypt, raised one of 45 cubits: and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, another of 88 cubits, in memory of Arinoe. Augustus erected one at Rome in the Campus Martius, which served to mark the hours on an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, drawn on the pavement. They were called by the Egyptian priests the fingers of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, because they were made in Egypt also to serve as styles or gnomons to mark the hours on the ground. The Arabs still call them Pharao's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>; whence the Italians call them aquiglie, and the French aiguilles.

OBJECT

Pages 756-756

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, something apprehended <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> presented to the mind by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> or imagination. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. Object-Glass of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TELESCOPE">Telescope</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">Microscope</a>, the glass placed at the end of the tube which is next the object. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>.

OBJECTION

Pages 756-756

something urged to overthrow a position, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a difficulty raised against an allegation or proposition of a person we are disputing withal.

OBJECTIVE

Pages 756-759

is used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, in speaking of a thing which exists no otherwise than as an object known. known. The existence of such a thing is said to be objective. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBIT">OBIT</a>; (Lat.) signifies a funeral solemnity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> office for the dead, most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> performed when the corpse lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> uninterred: Also the anniversaries of any person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was called the obit; and to observe such <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> with prayers and alms, or other commemoration, was the keeping of the obit. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses they had a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, wherein they entered the obits or obitual days of their founders and benefactors; which was thence termed the obituary. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of obit or chantry lands is taken away and extinct by Edw. VI. c. 14. and 15 Car. II. c. 9.

OBLATI

Pages 759-759

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> persons, who devoted themselves and their estates to some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, into which they were admitted as a kind of lay-brothers. The form of their admission, was putting the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of the church round their necks, as a mark of servitude. They wore a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, but different from that of the monks.

OBLIGATION

Pages 759-759

in general, denotes any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a person becomes bound to another to do something; as to pay a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, be surety, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. Obligations are of three kinds, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, civil, and mixed. Natural obligations are entirely founded on natural <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>; civil obligation, on civil authority alone, without any foundation in natural equity; and mixed obligations are those which, being founded on natural equity, are farther enforced by a civil authority. In a legal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, obligation signifies a bond, wherein is contained a penalty, with a condition annexed for the payment of money, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between it and a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is, that the latter is generally without a penalty or condition, though it may be made obligatory; and obligations are sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of record, as statutes and recognizances. See the article Bond. Moral Obligation. See Morals, no 36—40.

OBLIQUE

Pages 759-759

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, something slant, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that deviates from the perpendicular. Thus an oblique <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, is either an acute or obtuse one, i.e. any angle except a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> one. OBLIQUE <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">Cases</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, are all the cases except the nominative. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">Case</a>. OBLIQUE Line, that which, falling on another line, makes oblique <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with it, viz. one acute, and the other obtuse. OBLIQUE Planes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALLING">dialling</a>, are those which decline from the zenith, or incline towards the horizon. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. OBLIQUE Sailing, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, is when a ship sails upon some rhumb between the four <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, making an oblique angle with the meridian; in which case, she continually changes both latitude and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. See Navigation, § 6.

OBLIQUUS

Pages 759-759

in anatomy, a name given to several muscles, particularly in the head, eyes, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

OBLONG

Pages 759-759

in general, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that is longer than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: such is a parallelogram, ellipse, &c.

OBOLUS

Pages 759-759

in medicine, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of ten grains, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> half a scruple.

OBRECHT

Pages 759-759

a learned German, born of a noble family at Strasburg in 1646, where he filled the chairs of civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distinction. He was of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; but when <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Strasburg, and went there with his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he was prevailed on to change; and accordingly abjured in 1684, and put his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Bossuet bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>. The next year the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> nominated him to preside in his name in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of prætor <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> Mr Obrecht applied himself entirely to public affairs. He was the editor, translator, and writer, of several learned works; and died in 1701.

OBREPTITIOUS

Pages 759-759

an appellation given to letters patent, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other instruments, obtained of a superior by surprize, or by concealing from him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

OBSCURE

Pages 759-759

something that is dark and reflects little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that is not clear and intelligible.

OBSECRATION

Pages 759-759

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby the orator implores the assistance of God <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

OBSEQUENS

Pages 759-759

a Latin writer, conjectured to have lived before the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Honorius's reign. He made a collection of the prodigies which Livy related in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There are several editions of those remains. Lycothenes endeavoured to supply what was wanting in the original.

OBSERVATION

Pages 759-759

among navigators, signifies the taking the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the stars meridian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>, in order thereby to find the latitude.

OBSERVATORY

Pages 759-762

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> destined for observing the heavenly bodies; being generally a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> erected on some eminence, covered with a terrace for making astronomical observations. The more celebrated observatories are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> observatory, built in 1676, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. at the solicitation of Sir Jonas Moore and Sir Christopher Wren; and furnished with the most accurate instruments, particularly a noble sextant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet radius, with telescopic sights. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> observatory, built by the order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the Faubourg, St Jacques. It is a very singular, but withal a very magnificent building, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Monsieur Perrault: it is eighty feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and at top is a terrace. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> between this and the Greenwich observatory is 2° 20' west. In it is a cave, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cellar, of 170 feet <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, for experiments that are to be made far from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, &c. particularly such as relate to congelations, refrigerations, indurations, conservations, &c. 3. Tycho Brahe's observatory, which was in the little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Ween, or Scarlet Island, between the coasts of Schonen and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, in the Baltic. It was erected and furnished with instruments at his own expense, Observatory pence, and called by him Uraniburg. Here he spent twenty years in observing the stars; the result is his catalogue. 4. Pekin observatory. Father Le Compte describes a very magnificent observatory, erected and furnished by the late <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, at the intercession of some Jesuit missionaries, principally Father Verbeest, whom he made his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> observer.—The instruments are exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> less accurate, and the contrivance in some respects less commodious, than that of the Europeans. The chief arc, an armillary zodiacal sphere of six feet diameter; an equinoctial sphere of six feet diameter; an azimuthal horizon of six feet diameter; a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> six feet radius; a sextant eight feet radius; and a celestial globe six feet diameter. 5. Bramins observatory at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>. Of this Sir Robert Barker gives the following account, Phil. Trans. Vol. LXVII. p. 598. "Benares in the East Indies, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seminaries of the Bramins or priests of the original Gentooos of Hindostan, continues still to be the place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of people; and there are many public charities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and pagodas, where some thousands of them now reside. Having frequently heard that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Bramins had a knowledge of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and being confirmed in this by their information of an approaching eclipse both of the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, I made inquiry, when at that place in the year 1772, among the principal Bramins, to endeavour to get some information relative to the manner in which they were acquainted of an approaching eclipse. The most intelligent that I could meet with, however, gave me but little satisfaction. I was told, that these matters were confined to a few, who were in possession of certain books and records; some containing the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and others the tables of astronomical observations, written in the Sanskrit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which few understood but themselves; that they would take me to a place which had been constructed for the purpose of making such observations as I was inquiring after, and from whence they supposed the learned Bramins made theirs. I was then conducted to an ancient building of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which, in its present situation, was converted into a stable for horses, and a receptacle for lumber; but, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yards and apartments, it appeared that it must once have been an edifice for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of some public body of people. We entered this building, and went up a stair-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> to the top of a part of it, near to the river Ganges, that led to a large terrace, where, to my surprise and satisfaction, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a number of instruments yet remaining, in the greatest preservation, stupendously large, immovable from the spot, and built of stone, some of them being upwards of 20 feet in height; and, although they are said to have been erected 200 years ago, the graduations and divisions on the several arcs appeared as well cut, and as accurately divided, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been the performance of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The execution in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of these instruments exhibited a mathematical exactness in the fixing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, fitting of the several parts, in the necessary and sufficient supports to the very large <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that composed them, and in the joining and fastening each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> marked A in the plate, whose radius is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet two inches, by their being at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with a gnomon at twenty-five degrees elevation, are thrown into such an oblique situation as to render them the most difficult, not only to construct of such a magnitude, but to secure in their position for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and affords a striking instance of the ability of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> in their construction: for, by the shadow of the gnomon thrown on the quadrants, they do not appear to have altered in the least from their original position; and so true is the line of the gnomon, that, by applying the eye to a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of an inch diameter at one end, the sight is carried through three others of the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a>, to the extremity at the other end, distant 38 feet 8 inches, without obstruction; such is the firmness and art with which this instrument has been executed. This performance is the more wonderful and extraordinary when compared with the works of the artificers of Hindostan at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, who are not under the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of an European mechanic; but arts appear to have declined equally with science in the east. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> Archibald Campbell, at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> chief engineer in the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> that could be brought within his eye at one view; but I lament he could not represent some very large quadrants, whose radii were about twenty feet, they being on the side from whence he took his drawing. Their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> however is, that they are exact <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of circles of different radii, the largest of which I judged to be 20 feet, constructed very exactly on the sides of stone-walls built perpendicular, and situated, I suppose, in the meridian of the place: a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a> is fixed at the centre or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the quadrant, from whence, the Bramin informed me, they stretched a wire to the circumference when an observation was to be made; from which it occurred to me, the observer must have moved his eye up or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the circumference, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> or some such contrivance, to raise and lower himself, until he had discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of any of the heavenly bodies in their passage over the meridian, so expressed on the arcs of these quadrants; these arcs were very exactly divided into nine large sections; each of which again into ten, making ninety lesser divisions or degrees; and those also into twenty, expressing three minutes each, of about two-tenths of an inch asunder; so that it is probable, they had some method of dividing even these into more minute divisions at the time of observation. My time would only permit me to take down the particular dimensions of the most capital instruments, or the greater equinoctial sun-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, represented by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> A, which appears to be an instrument to express solar time by the shadow of a gnomon upon two quadrants, one situated to the east, and the other to the west of it; and indeed the chief part of their instruments at this place appear to be constructed for the same purpose, except the quadrants, and a brass instrument that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be described hereafter. Figure B is another instrument for the purpose of determining the exact <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day by the shadow. Observatory dows of a gnomon, which stands perpendicular to and Obsidianus, in the centre of a flat circular stone, supported in an oblique situation by means of four upright stones and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-piece; so that the shadow of the gnomon, which is a perpendicular iron rod, is thrown upon the division of the circle described on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the flat circular stone. "Figure c is a brass circle, about two feet diameter, moving vertically upon two pivots between two stone pillars, having an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round horizontally on the centre of this circle, which is divided into 360 parts; but there are no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> divisions on the index to subdivide those on the circle. This instrument appears to be made for taking the angle of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> at setting or rising, or for taking the azimuth or amplitude of the sun at rising or setting. "The use of the instrument, figure b, was at a loss to account for. It consists of two circular walls; the outer of which is about forty feet diameter, and eight feet high; the wall within about half that height, and appears intended for a place to stand on to observe the divisions on the upper circle of the outer wall, rather than for any other purpose; and yet both circles are divided into 360 degrees, each <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> being subdivided into twenty lesser divisions, the same as the quadrants. There is a door-way to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the inner circle, and a pillar in the centre, of the same height with the lower circle, having a hole in it, being the centre of both circles, and seems to be a socket for an iron rod to be placed perpendicular into it. The divisions on these, as well as all the other instruments, will bear a nice <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. "Figure z is a smaller equinoctial sun-dial, constructed upon the same principle as the large one a. "I cannot quit this subject without observing, that the Bramins, without the assistance of optical glasses, had nevertheless an advantage unexperienced by the observers of the more northern climates. The serenity and clearness of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> in the night-time in the East Indies, except at the seasons of changing the monsoons or periodical winds, is difficult to express to those who have not seen it, because we have nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> to form our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> upon: it is clear to perfection, a total quietude subsists, scarcely a cloud to be seen, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the heavens, by the numerous appearance of the stars, affords a prospect both of wonder and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. "This observatory at Benares is said to have been built by the order of the emperor Akbar; for as this wise <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> endeavoured to improve the arts, so he wished also to recover the sciences of Hindostan, and therefore directed that three such places should be erected; one at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, another at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, and the third at Benares." <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Observatory. See Edinburgh. Obsidianus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the name of a stone which they have also described under the name of the Chian marble. It is a very smooth and hard marble, extremely difficult to cut, but capable of a fine polish; and was used among the ancient Greeks for the purpose of making reflecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>. The later writers have supposed the name Obsidianus to be derived from somebody Obsidianus, who was the inventor of this use of it; but it seems only a false <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPELLING">spelling</a> of the word Obsidianus, from seeing the images of things in it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBSIDIONALIS">Obsidionalis</a>, an epithet applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. See the article Crown. Obstetrics, or the Obstetric Art, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>. Obstruction, in medicine, such an obturation of the vessels as prevents the circulation of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, whether of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and vital, or of the morbid and peccant kind, through them. Obturator, in anatomy. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles. Obtuse, signifies blunt, dull, &c. in opposition to acute or sharp. Thus we say, obtuse angle; obtuse angled triangle, &c. Obi, or Os, a river of the Russian empire in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Isthmiaka, and running <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, joins the Irtis near Tobolsk; and, still keeping its name, continues its course north, and falls into a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> called Obiskaya, in about 63 degrees of latitude. The exact course of this river was unknown till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was surveyed by the Russians; who have given us good maps of it and of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The Obi forms the boundary between <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and Asia, and its course is upwards of 2000 miles in length. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCIDENT">Occident</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, the westward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the horizon; or that part of the horizon where the ecliptic, or the sun therein, descends into the lower hemisphere; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to Orient. Hence we use the word occidental for any thing belonging to the west; as occidental bezons, occidental <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCIPITAL">Occipital</a>, in anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the parts of the occiput, or back part of the skull. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCULT">Occult</a>, something hidden, secret, or invisible. The occult sciences are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECROMANCY">necromancy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">cabala</a>, &c. Occult, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, is used for a line that is scarce perceivable, drawn with the point of the compasses or a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are used in several operations, as the raising of plans, designs of building, pieces of perspective, &c. They are to be effaced when the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is finished. Occultation, in astronomy, the time a star or planet is hid from our sight, by the interposition of the body of the moon or some other planet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCCUPANCY">Occupancy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is the taking possession of those things which before belonged to nobody. This Blackstone calls the true ground and foundation of all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>, or Comment, of holding those things in sevency, which by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, unqualified by that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all mankind. But, when once it was agreed that every thing capable of ownership should have an owner, natural reason suggested, that he who could first declare his intention of appropriating any thing to his own use, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such his intention, actually took it into possession, should thereby <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> property of it; according to that rule of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS">law of nations</a>, recognized by the laws of Rome, quod nullius est, id ratione naturali occupanti conditur. This right of occupancy, so far as it concerns real property, hath been confined by the laws of England within a very narrow compass; and was extended only to a single instance; namely, where a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> was tenant pour autre vie, or had an estate granted to himself only (without mentioning his heirs) for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of another man, and died during the life of cestuy qui vic, or him by whose life it was held: in this case, he that could first enter on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, might lawfully retain the possession so long as cestuy qui vic lived, by right of occupancy. This seems to have been recurring to first principles, and calling in the law of nature to ascertain the property of the land, when left without a legal owner. For it did not revert to the grantor; who had parted with all his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, so long as cestuy qui vic lived: it did not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee; for all estates must be of the absolute entire fee, and not of any particular estate carved out of it; much less of so minute a remnant as this: it did not belong to the grantee; for he was dead: it did not descend to his heirs; for there were no words of inheritance in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>: nor could it vest in his executors; for no executors could succeed to a freehold. Belonging therefore to nobody, like the hereditas jacens of the Romans, the law left it open to be seised and appropriated by the first person that could enter upon it, during the life of cestuy qui vic, under the name of an occupant. But there was no right of occupancy allowed, where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the lands: for the reverionsman hath an equal right with any other man to enter upon the vacant possession; and where the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and a subject's interfere, the king's shall always be preferred. Against the king therefore there could be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> occupant, because nullum tempus occurrit regi. And, even in the case of a subject, had the estate pour autre vie been granted to a man and his heirs during the life of cestuy qui vic, there the heir might, and still may, enter and hold possession, and is called in law a special occupant; as having a special exclusive right, by the terms of the original grant, to enter upon and occupy this hereditas jacens, during the residue of the estate granted: though some have thought him so called with no very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety; and that such estate is rather a defeasible freehold. But the title of common occupancy is now reduced almost to nothing by two statutes; the one, 29 Car. II. c. 3., which enacts, that where there is no special occupant, in whom the estate may vest, the tenant pour autre vie may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> it by will, or it shall go to the executors and be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ASSETS">assets</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for payment of debts: the other that of 14 Geo. II. c. 20., which enacts, that it shall vest not only in the executors, but, in case the tenant dies intestate, in the administrators also; and go in course of a distribution like a chattel interest. By these two statutes the title of common occupancy is utterly extinct and abolished: tho' that of special occupancy, by the heir at law, continues to this day; such heir being held to succeed to the ancestor's estate, not by descent, for then he must take an estate of inheritance, but as an occupant, specially marked out and appointed by the original grant. The doctrine of common occupancy may, however, be usefully remembered on the following account, amongst others: That, as by the common law no occupancy could be of incorporeal hereditaments, as of rents, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, advowsons, commons, Occupancy, or the like, (because, with respect to them, there could be no actual entry made, or corporal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> had;) and therefore by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the grantee pour autre vie a grant of such hereditaments was entirely determined: to now, it is apprehended, notwithstanding those statutes, such grant would be determined likewise; and the hereditaments could not be devisable, nor vest in the executors, nor go in a course of distribution. For the statutes must not be construed so as to create any new estate, or to keep that alive which by the common law was determined, and thereby to defeat the grantor's reversion; but merely to dispose of an interest in being, to which by law there was no owner, and which therefore was left open to the first occupant. When there is a residue left, the statutes give it to the executors, &c. instead of the first occupant; but they will not create a residue, on purpose to give it to the executors. They only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to provide an appointed instead of a casual, a certain instead of an uncertain, owner, of lands which before were nobody's; and thereby to supply this casus omnium, and render the disposition of the law in all respects entirely uniform: this being the only instance wherein a title to a real estate could ever be acquired by occupancy. For there can be no other case devised, wherein there is not some owner of the land appointed by the law. In the case of a sole corporation, as a parson of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, when he dies or resigns, though there be no actual owner of the land till a successor be appointed, yet there is a legal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a> ownership, subsisting in contemplation of law; and when the successor is appointed, his appointment shall have a retrospect and relation backwards, so as to entitle him to all the profits from the instant that the vacancy commenced. And, in all other instances, when the tenant dies intestate, and no other owner of the lands is to be found in the common course of descents, there the law vests an ownership in the king, or in the subordinate lord of the fee, by escheat. So also, in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, where the laws of other nations give a right by occupancy, as in lands newly created, by the rising of an island in a river, or by the alluvion or dereliction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; in these instances, the law of England assigns them an immediate owner. For Bracton tells us, that if an island arise in the middle of a river, it belongs in common to those who have lands on each side thereof; but, if it be nearer to one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> than the other, it belongs only to him who is proprietor of the nearest shore: which is agreeable to, and probably copied from, the civil law. Yet this seems only to be reasonable, where the foil of the river is equally divided between the owners of the opposite shores: for if the whole foil is the freehold of any one man, as it must be whenever a several fishery is claimed, there it seems <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> (and so is the usual practice) that the islets, or little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, arising in any part of the river, shall be the property of him who owns the fishery and the foil. However, in case a new island rise in the sea, though the civil law gives it to the first occupant, yet ours gives it to the king. And as to lands gained from the sea; either by alluvion, by the washing up of sand and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, so as in time to make terra firma; or by dereliction, as when the sea shrinks back below the usual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-mark; in these...

OCEANUS

Pages 762-763

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the son of Cætus and Terra, the husband of Thetis, and the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a> and Fountains. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called him the Father of all things, imagining that he was produced by Humidity, which, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, was the first principle from which every thing was produced. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> represents Juno visiting him at the remotest limits of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and acknowledging him and Thetis as the parents of the gods. He was represented with a bull's head, as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the rage and bellowing of the ocean when agitated by a storm. OCELLUS the Lucanian, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of the school of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who lived before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> Ἀπολογίας, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> "the Universe," is the only piece of his which is come <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> entire to us; and was written originally in the Doric dialect, but was translated by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> into the Attic. William Christian, and after him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Nogarola, translated this work into Latin; and we have several editions of it, both in Greek and Latin.

OCHLOCRACY

Pages 763-763

that form of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> where-in the populace have the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> administration of affairs.

OCHRE

Pages 763-763

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a genus of earths, slightly coherent, and composed of fine, smooth, soft, argillaceous particles, rough to the touch, and readily diffusible in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Ochres are of various colours, as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, blue, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, green, &c.

OCKLEY

Pages 763-763

a learned orientalist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, in 1678, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he distinguished himself by his intense application to literature. At the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he took the degrees in arts, and that of bachelor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; but marrying very young, was precluded from a fellowship in his college, and this occasioned his being afterwards involved in many difficulties. In 1705, he was presented to the vicarage of Swavesey in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>; and in 1711, he was chosen Arabic professor of the university; but afterwards had the misfortune to be confined for some time in Cambridge-castle for debt. The above preferments, however, he enjoyed till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened on the 9th of August 1720. He wrote, 1. Introductio <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Lingua Orientalia. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the present Jews throughout the world; translated from the Italian of Leo <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, a Venetian rabbi. 3. The improvement of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason, exhibited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Hai Ebn Yokdhan, translated from the Arabic. 4. An account of South-west Barbary, containing what is most remarkable in the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>; written by a person who had been a slave there a considerable time, and translated from his manuscript. 5. The history of the Saracens, collected from the most authentic Arabic authors, in 2 vols. 8vo. He was not only well skilled in the learned languages; but also in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, as French, Spanish, Italian, &c.

OCTAETARIDES

Pages 763-763

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, denotes a cycle of eight years, at the end of which three entire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months were added. This cycle was used at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> till Meton discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

OCTAGON

Pages 763-763
or OCTOGON, in geometry, is a figure of eight sides and angles; and this, when all the sides and angles are equal, is called a regular octagon, or one that may be inscribed in a circle. Octagon, in fortification, denotes a place that has eight battions. See Fortification.

OCTAHEDRON

Pages 763-764
or Octaedron, in geometry, one OCTANDRIA (œœœ, "eight," and ἀνήρ, "man" or husband,) the eighth class in Linnaeus's sexual system; consisting of plants with hermaphrodite flowers, which are furnished with eight stamens, or male organs of generation. See BOTANY, p. 1292.

OCTANT

Pages 764-764
or OCTILE, in astronomy, that aspect of two planets, wherein they are distant an eighth part of a circle, or 45°, from each other.

OCTAPLA

Pages 764-764

in matters of sacred literature, denotes a polyglot <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>, consisting of eight columns, and as many different versions of the sacred text; viz. the original <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> both in Hebrew and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, Greek versions, &c.

OCTATEUCH

Pages 764-764

an appellation given to the eight first books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>.

OCTOBER

Pages 764-764

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Julian year, consisting of 31 days; it obtained the name of October, from its being the eighth month in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>.

OCTOSTYLE

Pages 764-764

in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of an edifice adorned with eight columns.

OCULUS

Pages 764-764

the eye, in anatomy. See there, n° 406. Oculus Belli, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the semi-pellucid gems, of a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> central nucleus: it is of a roundish form, and its variegations very beautifully represent the pupil and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">iris</a> of the eye; whence the name. Oculus Cati. See ASTERIA. Oculus Mundi, one of the semi-pellucid gems, of a whitish-grey colour, without any variegations.

OCYUMUM

Pages 764-764
basil; a genus of the gynospemia order, belonging to the didynamia class of plants. There are eight species, all of them natives of warm climates, rising from six inches to two feet in height, and having a strong aromatic smell, resembling that of cloves. One of the species is used in the kitchen, particularly by the French cooks, who make great use of it in their soups and sauces. This rises about ten inches high, sending out branches by pairs opposite, from the bottom; the stalks and branches are four-cornered; the leaves are oval, spear-shaped, ending in acute points, and are indented on their edges; the whole plant is hairy, and has a strong scent of cloves too powerful for most persons, but to some it is very agreeable. These plants are propagated by seeds, and will thrive in this country in the open air, and will even ripen their seeds if placed in a stove or airy glass-case. Oczakow, or Oczakow, a town of Turkey in Europe, and capital of a Sangiack of the same name, inhabited by Tartars. During a late war, here was a Turkish garrison of 20,000 men. However, it was taken by the Russians in 1737, and all those that resisted were put to the sword. The Russians themselves lost 18,000 men in the assault. The Turks returned the same year with 70,000 men to retake it; but were obliged to retire, after the loss of 20,000. In 1738, the Russians withdrew their garrison, and demolished the fortifications. It is seated on the river Bug, to the west of the Nieper, or rather where they both unite and fall into the "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black Sea. It is 42 miles south-west of Bialagrod, and 190 north by east of Constantinople. E. Long. 30. 0. N. Lat. 46. 30.

ODA

Pages 764-764

in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>, signifies a class, order, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> chamber. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> are divided into five classes or chambers. The first, which is the lowest in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, is called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> oda, from the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons that compose it; these are the juniors, who are taught to read, write, and speak the languages. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is called the little oda, where, from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14 or 15 years, till about 20, they are trained up to arms, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of all the polite learning the Turks are acquainted with. The third chamber, called kilar oda, consists of 200 pages, which, besides their other exercises, are under the command of the kilardgi-bachi, and serve in the pantry and fruitery. The fourth consists only of 24, who are under the command of the khazineda-bachi, and have <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> in the grand signior's apartment, which they never enter with cloaths that have pockets. The fifth is called kas-oda, or privy-chamber; and is composed of only 40 pages who attend in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s chamber.
