Every night eight of these pages keep <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> in the grand signior's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber, while he sleeps; they take care that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which is constantly kept in the room, does not glare in his eyes, lest it should awake him; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they find him disturbed with troublesome <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, they cause him to be awaked by one of their agas. Oda-Bachi, or Oddobachi, among the Turks, an officer <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> or corporal among us.

ODENSEE

Pages 764-764

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNEN">Funen</a>, with a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 27. N. Lat. 55. 28.

ODER

Pages 764-764

a river of Germany, which has its source near a town of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>. It runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> through that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and then into the Marche of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> and Pomerania, where it forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, afterwards falling into the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> by three mouths; between which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> Ufedom and Wolin. It passes by several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; as Ratibor, Oppeln, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, Glogau, and Crosten, in Silesia; Frankfort, Lebus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULM">Culm</a>, in Brandenburg; and Gartz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STETTIN">Stettin</a>, Cammin, Wallin, Ufedom, and Wolgast, in Pomerania.

ODEUM

Pages 764-764

in Grecian antiquity, a music-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, built by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>; the inside of which was filled with seats and ranges of pillars, and on the outside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> defended shelving downwards from a point in the centre, with many bendings, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>. Here the musical prizes were contested for; and here also, according to Ariosto, was a tribunal. De Odo et Atia. See False IMPRISONMENT. The writ de odio et atia was anciently used to be directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, commanding him to inquire whether a prisoner <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> was committed upon <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause of suspicion, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> merely propter odium et atiam, for hatred and ill-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> due cause of suspicion did not then appear, then there issued another writ for the sheriff to admit him to bail. This writ, according to Bracton, ought not to be denied to any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>; it being expressly ordered

OEDIPUS

Pages 764-765

the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is partly fabulous, flourished about 1266 B.C. It is said he was given by his father to a shepherd, who was ordered to put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in order to prevent the misfortunes with which he was threatened by an oracle. But the shepherd being unwilling to kill him with his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, tied him by the feet to a tree, that he might be devoured by wild beasts. The infant was, however, found in this situation by another shepherd named Phorbas, who carried him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLYBUS">Polybus</a> king of Corinth; where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, having no children, educated him with as much care as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been her son. When he was grown up, he was informed that he was not the son of Polybus: on which, by order of the oracle, he went to seek for his father in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>; but scarce was he arrived in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, when he met his father on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and killed him without knowing him. A short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, having delivered the country from the monster called the Sphinx, he married Jocasta, without knowing that she was his mother, and had four children by her; but afterwards being informed of his <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, he quitted the throne, and, thinking himself unworthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, put out his eyes. Eteocles and Polynices, who were celebrated amongst the Greeks, were born of this incestuous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>.

OELAND

Pages 765-765

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, seated on the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between the continent of Gothland and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Gothland, in between 56° and 57° of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 17° and 18° of east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is about 60 miles in length, and 15 in breadth; having a wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, with rising hills, and several castles. It has no town of any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>.

OENANTHE

Pages 765-765
WATER DROPWORT; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandra class of plants. There are five species; of which the most remarkable is the crocata, or hemlock dropwort, growing frequently on the banks of ditches, rivers, and lakes, in many parts of Britain. The roots and leaves of this plant are a terrible poison; several persons have perished by eating it through mistake, either for water-parsnips or for celery, which last it resembles pretty much in its leaves. So exceedingly deleterious is this plant, that Mr Lightfoot tells us, he has heard the late Mr Christopher d'Ehret, the celebrated botanic painter, say, that while he was drawing it, the smell or effluvia only rendered him so giddy, that he was several times obliged to quit the room, and walk out in the fresh air to recover himself; but recollecting at last what might be the probable cause of his repeated ills, he opened the door and windows of the room, and the free air then enabled him to finish his work without any more returns of the giddiness. Mr Lightfoot informs us, that he has given a spoonful of the juice of this plant to a dog, but without any other effect than that of making him very sick and stupid. In about an hour he recovered; and our author has seen a goat eat it with impunity. To such of the human species as have unfortunately eaten any part of this plant, a vomit is the most

OENOPTAE

Pages 765-766

in Grecian antiquity, a kind of censors at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who regulated entertainments, and took care that none drank too much, nor too little.

OENOTHERA

Pages 766-766

TREE-PRIMROSE; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the octandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which are, 1. The biennis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> biennial tree-primrose. It hath a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, thick, deeply-striking root; crowned with many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, oval, spear-shaped, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, spreading leaves; upright, thick, firm, rough, hairy stems, rising three or four feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with long, narrow, lanceolate, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting leaves, irregularly; and at all the axillas, from the middle upwards, large bright-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. 2. Octovalvis, or octovalved, smooth, biennial tree-primrose, hath upright, firm, somewhat hairy stems, rising a yard high; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, spear-shaped, pointed, plane, smooth leaves; and at the axillas large bright-yellow flowers. 3. The fruticosa, or shrubby, narrow-leaved, perennial tree-primrose, hath long thick roots; upright, under-shrubby like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> stems, two or three feet high; spear-shaped, lightly-indented leaves; and at the axillas pedunculated clusters of yellow flowers, succeeded by pedicellated, acute-angled capsules. 4. The pumila, or low perennial tree-primrose, hath <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots, crowned with many oval, spear-shaped, close-fitting leaves; slender herbaceous stems 10 or 12 inches long; garnished with spear-shaped, blunt, smooth leaves, having very short foot-stalks; and at the axillas smallish bright-yellow flowers, succeeded by acute-angled capsules. All these plants flower very profusely in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, coming out almost half the length of the stalks from the axillas; and as the stalk advances in stature, new flowers are produced, succeeding those below; in which order the plants continue flowering from about midsummer till October: each flower is moderately large and conspicuous, consisting of four plane petals, which with the calyx forms a very long tube below, and spreading above, generally expand most towards the evening; and are succeeded by plenty of seed in autumn for propagation. These plants are exotics from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; but are all very hardy, prosper in any common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation, and have been long in the English gardens, especially the three first sorts; but the oenothera biennis is the most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known. The first and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> species are biennial, and the third and fourth are perennial in root. They are proper to be employed as plants of ornament for embellishing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>-garden; they may be placed anywhere, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> effect a very agreeable variety three or four months with their plentiful blow of flowers. The biennial kinds must be raised annually from seed, for they totally perish after they have flowered. But the perennials, once raised, continue for years by the root. The propagation of all the sorts is by seed, and the perennials also by parting the roots.

OENOTRIA

Pages 766-766

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; so called from the Oenotrii (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); inhabiting between Poetum and Tarentum, (Ovid). Originally Arcadians, (Dionysius <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>), who came under the conduct of Oenotrus son of Lycaon, 17 generations before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 459 years, at 27 years each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, and gave name to the people. Cato derives the name from Oenotrus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a>; but Varro from Oenotrus, king of the Latins; and Servius from the Greek name for wine, for which Italy was famous; of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is Strabo.

OENOTRIDES

Pages 766-766

two small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, over-against Velia, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, called Pontia and Icilia; now Pensa and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISCHIA">Ischia</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Principato Citra, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. So called from the Oenotrii, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.

OESOPHAGUS

Pages 766-766

in anatomy, the GULA, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Gullet, is a membranaceous canal, reaching from the fauces to the stomach, and conveying into it the food taken in at the mouth. See Anatomy, no 353.

OETA

Pages 767-767

a mountain of Thessaly, extending from Thermopylae westward to the Sinus Ambracius, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> the mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> stretching out between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> to the south, and Pindus to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. At Thermopylae it is very rough and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, rising and ending in sharp and steep rocks, affording a narrow passage between it and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from Thessaly to Locris (Strabo): with two paths over it; the one above Trachis, very steep and high; the other through the country of the Aenianes, much easier and readier for travellers; by this it was that Leonidas was attacked in rear by the Persians (Pausanias). Here <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> laid himself on the funeral pile, (Silius Italicus, Ovid); the spot thence called Pyra, (Livy): who says, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to the east are called Oeta; and hence the poets allege, that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, night, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and stars, arose from Oeta (Seneca, Statius, Silius Italicus, Catullus, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Culex.) Circumstances which show the height of this mountain.

OETING

Pages 767-767

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and east by Franconia; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Neuburg; and on the west by that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>. It is about 40 miles from east to west, and 20 from north to south.

OFF-SETS

Pages 768-768

in surveying, are perpendiculars let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and measuring from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> to the hedge, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> extremity of an inclosure.

OFFA'S-DYKE

Pages 767-767

an entrenchment <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up by Offa, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, to defend England against the incursions of the Welsh. It runs through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, Denbighshire, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>.

OFFANTO

Pages 767-767

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. It rises in the Appenine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in the Farther Principato; and passing by Conza, and Monte Verde, it afterwards separates the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a> and the Terra-di-Barri, and then it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, near Salpe.

OFFENCE

Pages 767-767

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> committed against the law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> omitted where the law requires it.

OFFICE

Pages 767-767

a particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> trust, or a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> attended with a public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>.—The word is primarily used in speaking of the offices of judicature and policy; as the office of secretary of state, the office of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace, &c.

OFFICE ALSO

Pages 767-767

e also signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment appointed for officers to attend in, in order to discharge their respective duties and employments; as the secretary's office, ordnance-office, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>-office, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>-office, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-office, pipe-office, six-clerks office, &c. Office, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, denotes all the apartments appointed for the necessary occasions of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, pantries, confectionaries, &c. Office, in the canon-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is used for a benefice that has no jurisdiction annexed to it. Duty upon Offices and Pensions, a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s extraordinary perpetual revenue, consisting in a payment of 1s. in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> (over and above all other duties) out of all salaries, fees, and perquisites, of offices and pensions payable by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This highly-popular <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> was imposed by stat. 31 Geo. II. c. 22, and is under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax.

OFFICER

Pages 767-767

a person possessed of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> office. See the preceding article. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, or state, are, The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, the lord high-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the lord high-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, the lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the lord privy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, the lord-chamberlain, the lord high-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a>-marshal; each of which see under its proper article. Non-commissioned Officers, are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a>-majors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> sergeants, sergeants, corporals, drum and fife majors; who are nominated by their respective captains, and appointed by the commanding officers of regiments, and by them reduced without a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>-martial. Orderly non-commissioned Officers, are those who are orderly, or on duty for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; who, on hearing the drum <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> for orders, are to repair to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appointed to receive them, and to take <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in the orderly book, what is dictated by the adjutant, or sergeant-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>: they are then immediately to shew these orders to the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and afterwards warn the men for duty. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAG">Flag</a> Officers. See Flag Officers, and Admirals. General Officers, are those whose command is not limited to a single company, troop, or regiment; but extends to a body of forces composed of several regiments: such are the general, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general, major-general, and brigadier. Officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">Household</a>. See the article Household. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">Staff</a> Officers, are such as, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s presence, bear a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> staff, or wand; and at other times, on their going abroad, have it carried before them by a footman bare-headed: such are the lord-steward, lord-chamberlain, lord-treasurer, &c. The white staff is taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>; and, at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, each of these officers breaks his staff over the heart made for the king's body, and by this means lays down his commission, and discharges all his inferior officers. Subaltern Officers are all who administer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in the name of subjects; as those who <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> under the earl-marshal, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the subaltern officers are the lieutenants, cornets, ensigns, sergeants, and corporals.

OFFICIAL

Pages 767-767

in the canon-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> judge, appointed by a bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, &c. with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the spiritual jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. Official is also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> appointed by an archdeacon as his assistant, who sits as judge in the archdeacon's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

OFFICINAL

Pages 767-768

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, an appellation given to such medicines, whether simple <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, as are required to be constantly kept in the apothecaries shops. The officinal simples are appointed, among us, by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians; and the manner of making the compositions directed in their dispensatory. See PHARMACY.

OFFING

Pages 768-768
or OFFIN, in the sea-language, that part of the sea a good distance from shore, where there is deep water, and no need of a pilot to conduct the ship: thus, if a ship from shore be seen sailing out to seaward, they say, she stands for the offing; and if a ship, having the shore near her, have another a good way without her, or towards the sea, they say, that ship is in the offing.

OGILBY

Pages 768-768

an eminent writer, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, about the 17th of November 1600. His father having spent his estate, and being prisoner in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a> for debt, could contribute but little to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; however, he obtained some knowledge in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and afterwards so much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> as to procure his father's discharge from prison, and to bind himself an apprentice to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; when, by his dexterity in his profession, and his complaisant behaviour to his master's scholars, he obtained money to buy out the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and to set up for himself. But being afterwards appointed to dance in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASQUE">masque</a>, he by a false step strained a vein in the inside of his leg, which occasioned his being ever after somewhat lame. When Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Strafford was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, he was entertained as a dancing-master in his family, and made one of the earl's troop of guards; at which time he composed a humorous piece called the Character of a Trooper. He was soon after appointed master of the revels in Ireland, and built a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. About the time of the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in England, he left Ireland, and, being shipwrecked, came to London in a necessitous condition; but soon after walked to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where, being assisted by several scholars, he became so complete a master of the Latin tongue, that in 1649 he published a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. He soon after learned Greek; and in 1660 published in folio, a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliad, with Annotations. About two years after, he went into Ireland, where he was made master of the revels by patent. He then built another theatre in Dublin, which cost him about £1000. He published at London in folio, a translation of Homer's Odyssey, with Annotations; and afterwards wrote two heroic poems, intitled the Ephesian Matron, and the Roman Slave. He next composed the Carolics, an epic poem, in 12 books, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. but this was entirely lost in the fire of London; when Mr Ogilby's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Fryars was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and his whole fortune, except to the value of five pounds, destroyed. He, however, soon procured his house to be re-built, set up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-office within it, was appointed his majesty's coignographer and geographic printer, and printed several great works, translated or collected by himself and his assistants, particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. He died in 1676.

OGIVE

Pages 768-768

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of a Gothic vault; which, instead of being circular, passes diagonally from one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> to another, and forms a crois with the other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. The middle, where the ogives <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> each other, is called the keys being cut in form of a rose, or a cul de lampe. The members or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> of the ogives are called nerves, branches, or reins; and the arches which separate the ogives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> arches.

OGYES

Pages 768-768
king of the Thebans, or, as others, of Oggygia and Aetos, afterwards called Beotia and Attica. He is recorded to have been the first founder of Thebes and Eleusin. The famous deluge happened in his time, in which some say he perished with all his subjects, 1796 B.C.

OGYGI

Pages 768-768

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; so called from Ogyges, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, under whom happened a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deluge, 1020 years before the first olympiad.

OHIO

Pages 768-768

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, called by the French the Beautiful River, has its source between the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and the lake Erie; and running south-west through a most delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as also receiving many smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in its passage, at length falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, in about 37 degrees of latitude. The French had several forts on and near it; but the whole country through which it flows was ceded by the peace of 1763 to the British. O HETEROA, one of the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> lately discovered, is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 150° 47'. S. Lat. 22° 27'. It is neither fertile nor populous; nor has it an harbour <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> anchorage fit for shipping, and the disposition of the people is hostile to such as visit them.

OIL

Pages 768-770

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an unctuous inflammable substance, drawn from several natural bodies, as animal and vegetable substances. Animal oils are their fats, which are originally vegetable oils: all animal substances yield them, together with their volatile salts, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. Vegetable oils are obtained by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, infusion, and distillation. The oils by expression are obtained from the seed, leaves, fruit, and bark of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; thus, the seed of mustard, and of the sunflower, almonds, nuts, bennett, &c. afford a copious oil by expression; and the leaves of rosemary, mint, rue, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a>, thyme, sage, &c. the berries of juniper, olives, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> cloves, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>, mace, &c. the barks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, saffron, and clove, yield a considerable proportion of essential oil by distillation. The method of procuring oils by expression is very simple: thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> either sweet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bitter almonds, that are fresh, be pounded in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, the oil may be forced out with a press, not heated; and in the same manner should the oil be pressed from linseed and mustard. The avoiding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in preparing these oils, intended for internal medicinal use, is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance, as heat gives them a very prejudicial rancidity. This method holds of all those vegetable matters that contain a copious oil, in a loose manner, or in certain cavities or receptacles; the sides whereof being broke, or squeezed, makes them let go the oil they contain; and thus the zest or oil of lemon-peel, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-peel, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>-peel, &c., may be readily obtained by pressure, without the use of fire. But how far this method of obtaining oils may be applied to advantage, seems not hitherto considered. It has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to olives, almonds, linseed, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>-seed, beechnuts, ben-nuts, walnuts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>-berrries, mace, nutmeg, &c., but not, that we know of, to juniper-berries, cardamom-nuts, Indian cloves, pine apples, and many other substances that might be enumerated, both of foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> growth. It has, however, been of late successfully applied to mustard-seed, so as to extract a curious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-coloured oil, leaving a cake behind, fit for making the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-mustard. Certain dry matters, as well as moist ones, may be made to afford oils by expression, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, which being suspended to receive the vapour of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> thus be moistened so as to afford an oil in the same manner as almonds; and thus an oil may be procured from linseed, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>-seed, lettuce-seed, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-poppy seed, &c. As to the treatment of oils obtained by expression, they should be furthered to depurate themselves by standing in a moderately cool <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to separate from their water, and deposit their feces; from both which they ought to be carefully freed. And if they are not thus rendered sufficiently pure, they may be washed well with fresh water, then thoroughly separated from it again by the separating-glares, whereby they will be rendered bright and clear. The next class of oils are those made by infusion, or decoction, wherein the virtues of some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> or flower is drawn out in the oil; as the oils of roses, chamomile, hypericum, alder, &c. However, these require to be differently treated: thus, for the scented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, particularly roses, inflorescence does best; because much boiling would exhaust their more fragrant parts; but oils impregnated with green herbs, as those of chamomile and alder, require <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> boiling, before they receive the green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> desired. And, in general, no oils will bear to be boiled any longer than there remains some aqueous humidity, without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> oils prepared in the same manner, viz., by boiling and inflorescence, and then straining off the oil for use. The same contrivance has likewise its use in making essences for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the perfumer; not only where essential oils cannot be well obtained in sufficient quantities, but also where they are too dear. The essential oil of jasmine-flowers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-suckles, sweet-briar, damask-roses, lilies of the valley, &c., are either extremely dear, or scarcely obtainable by distillation; and, in some of them, the odorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is so subtile, as almost to be lost in the operation. But if these flowers be barely infused in fine oil of nuts, or oil of ben, drawn without heat, and kept in a cool place, their subtile odorous matter will thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the oil, and richly impregnate it with their flavour. And these essences may be rendered still more perfect by straining off the oil at first put on, and letting it stand again; without heat, upon fresh flowers; repeating the operation twice or thrice. Oils or fats may likewise be obtained, by boiling and expression, from certain animal-substances; for the membranes which contain the fat, being chopped small, and set in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">pan</a> over the fire, become fit for the canvas bag, and, by pressure, afford a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fat; as we see in the art of chandlery, which thus extracting the oily matter, leaves a cake behind, commonly called grease. As to the essential oils of vegetables, they are obtained by distillation with an alembic and a large refrigeratory. Water must be added to the materials, in sufficient quantity to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; and they should be macerated or digested in that water, a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before distillation. The oil comes over with the water; and either swims on the top, or sinks to the bottom, according as it is specifically heavier or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than water. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is applicable to the distilling of the essential oils from flowers, leaves, barks, roots, woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and balsams, with a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of circumstances, as by longer digestion, brisker distillation, &c., according to the tenacity and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the subject, the ponderosity of the oil, &c. Essential oils may be divided into two classes, according to their different specific gravities; some floating upon water, and others readily sinking to the bottom. Thus, the essential oils of cloves, cinnamon, and sassafras, readily sink; whereas those of lavender, marjoram, mint, &c., swim in water: the lightest of these essential oils is, perhaps, that of citron-peel, which even floats in spirit of wine; and the heaviest seems to be oil of sassafras. For obtaining the full quantity of the more ponderous oils from cinnamon, cloves, sassafras, &c., it is proper to reduce the subjects to powder; to digest this powder for some days in a warm place, with thrice its quantity of soft river-water, made very saline by the addition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, or sharp with oil of vitriol; to use the strained decoction, or liquor left behind in the still, instead of common water, for fresh digestion; to use for the same purpose the water of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> running, after being cleared of its oil; not to distil too large a quantity of these subjects at once; to leave a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the still, or about one fourth, empty; to use a brisk fire, or a strong boiling heat, at the first, but to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> it afterwards; to have a low still-head, with a proper internal ledge and current leading to the nose of the worm; and, finally, to cohabitate the water, or pour back the liquor of the second running upon the matter in the still, repeating this once or twice. The directions here laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for obtaining the ponderous oils to advantage, are easily transferred to the obtaining of the lighter; so that we need not dwell particularly upon them. Many of the essential oils being dear, it is a very common practice to adulterate or debase them several ways, so as to render them cheaper both to the seller and the buyer. These several ways seem reducible to three general kinds, each of which has its proper method of detection, viz. 1. With expressed oils. 2. With <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>. And, 3. With cheaper essential oils. If an essential oil be adulterated with an expressed oil, it is easy to discover the fraud; by adding a little spirit of wine to a few drops of the suspected essential oil, and shaking them together; for the spirit will dissolve all the oil that is essential, or procured by distillation, and leave all the expressed oil that was mixed with it, untouched. If an essential oil be adulterated with alcohol, or rectified spirit of wine, it may be done in any proportion, up to that of an equal quantity, without being easily discoverable either by the smell or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>: the way to discover this fraud, is to drop a few drops of the oil into a glass of fair water; and if the oil be adulterated with spirit, the water will immediately turn milky, and, by continuing to shake the glass, the whole quantity of spirit will be absorbed by the water, and leave the oil pure at top. Finally, if an essential oil be adulterated by a cheaper essential oil, this is commonly done very artfully: the method is to put fir-wood, turpentine, or oil of turpentine, into the still, along with the herbs to be distilled for their oil, such as rosemary, lavender, origanum, &c. and by this means, the oil of turpentine distilled from these ingredients, comes over in great quantity, and intimately blended with the oil of the genuine ingredient. The oils thus adulterated always discover themselves in time, by their own flavour being overpowered by the turpentine-smell: but the ready way to detect the fraud, is to drench a piece of rag, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in the oil, and hold it before the fire; for thus the grateful flavour of the plant will fly off, and leave the naked turpentine-scent behind. The virtues of oils being the same with those of the substances from whence they are obtained, may be learned under their several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Method of Purifying Rancid Oils. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, n° 497.

OKEHAM

Pages 770-770

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Rutlandshire, in England, seated in a rich and pleasant valley, called the vale of Catmose. It is pretty well built, has a good <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a free-school, and an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 45. N. Lat. 52. 40.

OKINGHAM

Pages 770-770

OCKINGHAM, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Waxingham, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, in England, noted for the manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 50. N. Lat. 51. 26.

OLAUS MAGNUS

Pages 770-770

archbishop of Upsal in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, succeeded his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> John Magnus in 1544. He appeared with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> in 1546, and suffered much afterward for the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. We have of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Manners, Customs, and Wars of the Northern Nations of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. OLD <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">AGE</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONGEVITY">Longevity</a>. Old-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">Man</a> of the Mountain. See Assassins.

OLD-WIFE FISH

Pages 771-771

See BALISTES.

OLDCASTLE

Pages 770-770

called the Good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cobham, was born in the reign of Edward III. and Oldenburg, was the first author as well as the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> among the English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>: he obtained his preceage by marrying the heiress of that Lord Cobham who with so much virtue and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> opposed the tyranny of Richard II. By his means the famous statute against profisors was revived, and guarded against by severer penalties; he was one of the leaders of the reforming party; was at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense in procuring and dispersing copies of Wickliffe's writings among the people, as well as by maintaining a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his disciples as itinerant preachers. In the reign of Henry V. he was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; the growth of which was attributed to his influence. Being a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the king delayed his prosecution that he might reason with him himself; but not being able to reclaim him to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, he in great displeasure resigned him to its censure. He was apprehended and condemned for heresy; but escaping from the tower, lay concealed for four years in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, until the rumour of a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was raised against him, and a price set upon his head: he was at last seized, and executed in St Giles's Fields; being hung alive in chains upon a gallows, and burned by a fire placed underneath. He wrote "Twelve Conclusions, addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> of England."

OLDENBURG

Pages 770-771

a learned German <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the 17th century, was descended from the noble family of his name, who were earls of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Oldenburg, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Westphalia for many generations. He was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bremen in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> English <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> for his countrymen, at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, after the usurpation of Cromwell: but being discharged of that employ, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Henry O'Bryan, an Irish nobleman, whom he attended to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he was admitted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in the Bodleian library in the beginning of the year 1656, when Cromwell was vice-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. He was afterwards tutor to William lord Cavendish, and was acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> the poet. During his residence at Oxford, he became also acquainted with the members of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> there, which gave birth to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> society; and upon the foundation of this latter, he was elected fellow; and when the society found it necessary to have two secretaries, he was chosen assistant-secretary to Dr Wilkins. He applied himself with extraordinary diligence to the business of his office, and began the publication of the Philosophical Transactions with No. 1. in 1664. In order to discharge this task with greater <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to himself and the society, he held a correspondence with more than seventy learned persons, and others, upon a vast variety of subjects, in different parts of the world. This fatigue would have been insupportable, had not he, as he told Dr Lister, managed it so as to make one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> answer another, and that, to be always fresh, he never read a letter before he had <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INK">ink</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, ready to answer it forthwith; so that the multitude of his letters cloyed him not, nor ever lay upon his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Among others, he was a constant correspondent of Mr Robert Boyle, with whom he had a very intimate friendship; and he translated several of that ingenious gentleman's works into Latin. Mr Oldenburg <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to publish the Transactions, as before, to No. xxxvi. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 25, 1677. After which the publication was discontinued till the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> following, when it was again resumed by his successor in the secretary's office, Mr Nehemiah Grew, who carried it on till the end of February 1678. Our author dying at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Charlton, near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August that year, was interred there.

OLDHAM

Pages 771-771

an eminent English poet in the 17th century, son of a non-conformist minister, was educated under his father, and then sent to Edmund-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He became usher to the free-school at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>; where he received a visit from the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> and Dorset, Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Sedley, and other persons of distinction, merely upon the reputation of some verses which they had seen in manuscript. He was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to several gentlemen's sons successively; and having saved a small sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, came to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and became a perfect votary to the bottle, being an agreeable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. He was quickly found out here by the noblemen who had visited him at Croydon, who brought him acquainted with Mr Dryden. He lived mostly with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> at Holme-Pierpoint in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, where he died of the small-pox in 1683, in the 30th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His acquaintance with learned authors appears by his satires against the Jesuits, in which there is as much learning as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> discovered. Mr Dryden esteemed him highly. His works are printed in 2 vols 12mo. They chiefly consist of satires, odes, translations, paraphrases of Horace and other authors, elegiac verses, imitations, parodies, familiar epistles, &c. OLDMIXON (John) was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>: he was a violent party-writer and malevolent critic, who would scarcely have been remembered, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Pope, in resentment of his abuse, had not condemned him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> in his Dunciad. His party-writings procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the revenue at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, where he died at an advanced age in the year 1745. Besides his fugitive temporary pieces, he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Stuarts in folio; a critical history of England, 2 vols 8vo; a volume of poems, some dramatic pieces, &c.; none of them worthy of notice, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> being that of falsifying history.

OLEA

Pages 771-772

the Olive-tree; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the diandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, 1. The Europea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> olive-tree, rises with upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> stems, branching numerously on every side, 20 or 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; spear-shaped, stiff, opposite leaves, two or three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and half an inch or more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and at the axils small clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, succeeded by oval fruit. This species is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sort cultivated for its fruit; the varieties of which are numerous, varying in size, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. It is a native of the southern warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and is cultivated in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities in the south of France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, for the fruit to make the olive-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is in so great repute, and is transported to all parts, to the great advantage of those countries where the trees grow in the open ground; the green fruit is also in much esteem for pickling, of which we may see plenty in the shops. 2. The capensis, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> box-leaved olive, rises with shrubby stems, branching numerously from the bottom, six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet high; small, oval, thick, stiff, shining leaves; and at the axils small clusters of whitish flowers; succeeded by small fruit of inferior value. These plants in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> must be kept principally in pots for moving to shelter of a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in winter; for they are too tender to prosper well in the open ground here: though sometimes they are planted against a warm south wall, and sheltered occasionally from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> in winter, by mulching the roots, and matting their tops; whereby they may be preserved, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes produce fruit for pickling: a very severe winter, however, often kills or greatly injures their young branches; therefore let the principal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> be potted in rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and placed among the green-house <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and managed as others of that kind. These trees are often sent over from Italy to the Italian warehouses in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, along with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-trees, &c. where pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plants may be purchased reasonably, which should be managed as directed for orange-trees that are imported from the same country. See CITRUS. Their propagation here is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> by layers. The laying is performed on the young branches in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Give plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and they will sometimes be rooted fit for potting-off by autumn; but sometimes they require two summers to be rooted effectually: when, however, they are properly rooted take them off early in autumn, and pot them separately, give water, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> till they have taken fresh root; and in October remove them into the green-house, &c. Those you intend to plant in the open ground, as before suggested, should be kept in pots; in order to have occasional shelter of a garden-frame two or three years, till they have acquired some size, and are hardened to the full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; then transplant them into a warm border against a wall; mulch their roots in winter, and mat their tops in frothy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Olives have an acid, bitter, extremely disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; pickled (as we receive them from abroad) they prove less disagreeable. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> olives, which are smaller than the others, have the weakest taste; the Spanish, or larger, the strongest; the Provence, which are of a middling size, are generally the most esteemed. The oil obtained from this fruit has no particular taste or smell, and does not greatly differ in quality from oil of almonds. Authors make mention of two sorts of this oil, one expressed from the olives when fully ripe, which is our common oil olive; the other, before it has grown ripe; this is called oleum immaturum, and emphaticum. Nothing is met with in the shops under this name; and Lemery affirms, that there is no such oil, unripe olives yielding only a viscid juice to the press. From the ripe fruit, two or three sorts are obtained, differing in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity: the purest runs by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pressure; the remaining magma, heated and pre- Oleaginous sed more strongly, yields an inferior sort, with some dregs at the bottom, called amara. All these oils contain a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of aqueous moisture, and a mucilaginous substance, which subject them to run into a putrid state; to prevent this, the preparers add some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which, imbibing the aqueous and mucilaginous parts, sinks with them to the bottom; by this means the oil becomes more homogeneous, and consequently less susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. In its passage to us, some of the salt, thrown up from the bottom by the shaking of the vessel, is sometimes mixed with and detained in the oil, which, in our colder <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, becomes too thick to suffer it freely to subside; and hence the oil is sometimes met with of a manifestly saline taste. Oil-olive is used in the simple balsam of sulphur, Locatelli's balsam, and several ointments. It is oftener employed in this last intention than the other expressed oils, but more rarely for internal medicinal purposes.

OLEAGINOUS

Pages 772-772

something that partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> out of which oil may be expressed.

OLEARIUS

Pages 772-772

son of Godfrey Olearius, D.D., superintendent of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, was born there in 1639. He became professor of Greek at Leipzig; and shewed his abilities in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by 52 exercitationes on the dominical epistles, and upon those parts of the epistles in the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> which are read in the public exercises, and which among the Lutherans are the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their sermons. He discharged the most important posts in the university, and among other dignities was ten times rector of it. His learning and industry were displayed in 166 theological disputations, 61 in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, some programmas upon difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, several speeches and theological counsels; which make two thick volumes; beside his Moral <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, his Introduction to Theology, which treats of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, and his Hermeneutica Sacra. He lived to a good old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, dying in 1713. His eldest son of his own name, was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius and learning, a professor in the same university, who published several works, but died young of a consumption before his father.

OLECRANUM

Pages 772-772
or OLECRANON, in anatomy, the protuberance of the ulna, which prevents the joint of the elbow from being bent back beyond a certain length. See Anatomy, no. 50.

OLERON

Pages 772-772

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Aunis and Saintonge, about five miles from the continent. It is 12 miles in length, and five in breadth; and is very fertile, containing about 12,000 inhabitants, who are excellent seamen. It is defended by a castle, which is well fortified; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> placed here for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of ships. It is 14 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Olfactory Lat. 46. 10. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Laws of Oléron, certain laws relative to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Richard I. when he was at the island of Oléron. These laws, being accounted the most excellent sea-laws in the world, are recorded in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> book of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. See Selde's Mare Clausum. OLFACTORY-NERVES. See Anatomy, no. 400.

OLIBANUM

Pages 772-772

(Frankincense), in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, a dry resinous substance, brought to us in detached pieces, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> drops, as it were, like those of mastic; but larger, and of a less pure and pellucid texture. This drug has received many different appellations, according to its different appearances: the single tears are called simply olibanum, or thus; when two are joined together, they have been called thus maculum, and when very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, thus fimbriatum; sometimes four or five, about the bigness of filberts, are found adhering to a piece of the bark of the tree which they exuded from; these have been named thus corticatum: the finer powder which rubs off from the tears in the carriage, nissa thuris; and the coarser powder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> thuris. This drug is not however in any of its states which is now called thus or frankincense in the shops. See the article Thus. Thus, Olibanum consists of about equal parts of a gummy and resinous substance; the first soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the other in rectified spirit. With regard to its virtues, abundance have been attributed to it, particularly in disorders of the head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, in haemoptoies, and in alvine and uterine fluxes: but its real effects in these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are far from answering the promises of the recommenders. Rerius is said to have had large <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of the good effects of this drug in pleuritis, especially epidemic ones: he directs a scopped apple to be filled with a dram of olibanum, then covered and roasted under the ashes; this is to be taken for a dose, three ounces of carduus water after it, and the patient covered up warm in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>; in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he says, either a plentiful sweat, or a gentle diarrhoea, ensues, which carry off the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Geoffroy informs us, that he has frequently made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this medicine after venefication, with good success; but acknowledges that it has sometimes failed. OLIGÆDRA, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of crystals composed of very few planes, as the name expresses. The bodies of this class are crystals of the imperfect kind; being composed of columns affixed irregularly to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body at one end, and the other terminated by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>: but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> and pyramid being both pentangular, the whole consists only of ten planes, and not, as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> kind, of 12.

OLIGARCHY

Pages 772-772

a form of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, wherein the administration of affairs is confined to a few <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.

OLISIPO

Pages 772-772

(Pliny, Antonine, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>); a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, situate on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the frith of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>; of such antiquity, that Solinus thought it was built by Ulysses: and Mela, probably to favour this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, writes, according the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> copies, Ulysses; both of them perhaps deceived by the similarity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. It was a municipium, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Felicitas Julia, a privilege granted by the munificence

OLIVE

Pages 773-773

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See OLEA. Olive-Press. In order to obtain the olive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the olives are first bruised in a rough trough, under a millstone, rolling perpendicularly over them; and when sufficiently mashed, put into the maye, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> trough, m, of an olive-pres, where a are the upright beams, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>; b, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, and c, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw; f, the board on which the screw presses; g, a cubical piece of wood, called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>; h, the peel, a circular board, to be put under the block. By <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the screw, all the liquor is pressed out of the mashed olives, and is called virgin-oil; after which, hot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> being poured upon the remainder in the pres, a coarser oil is obtained. Olive-oil keeps only about a year, after which it degenerates. Olive-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

OLIVER

Pages 773-773

the son and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Oliver, was born in 1601. He arrived at a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> portraits confessedly superior to his father, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any of his contemporaries; as he did not confine his subjects to a head only. In the collections of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and James II. there were 13 historical subjects painted by this Oliver; of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> are still preserved in the closet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Caroline at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of his wife is in the possession of the duchess of Portland. He died in 1660.

OLIVET

Pages 773-773
or Mount of Olives, (anc. geog.), a mount which lay a little without Jerusalem, on the east side (Zechar. xiv.); separated from it by a deep valley called Kedron (Josephus), or the valley of Jehoshaphat; distant about eight furlongs or a mile from Jerusalem, (Lake); five furlongs, (Josephus); which may be understood of the nearer part of the mount.

OLMUTZ

Pages 773-773

a town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, with a bishop's see, and a famous university. The public buildings are very handsome, particularly the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. It is a populous, trading, and very strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and yet it was taken, with the whole garrison, by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1741. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1758, he besieged it again; and when he had almost taken the place, he was obliged to raise the siege, to go and meet the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is seated on the river Morava. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 35. N. Lat. 49. 30.

OLYMPIA

Pages 773-773

(anc. geog.), with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Pista, (Strabo); so called from the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; described by Strabo, "as the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympius, before which stands a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of wild olive-trees, in which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> foot-course, so call- ed, because the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; and by which the Alpheus, coming <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, runs." A temple and shrine highly ennobled by gymnastic exercises; and distinguished by a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of veneration, and still more so by the statue of Jupiter, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Phidias, (Mela); situated between Olla and Olympus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> cognominal with those of Thessaly, distant 12 miles from Pylos; famous for games called the Olympian, celebrated the beginning of each fifth year, by which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> computed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, (Pliny); a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of four years complete being called an Olympiad.
